3.9/10 - A Difficult Math Based Puzzler for Nerds
This isn't a bad game and I do enjoy some difficult puzzlers but this is a wee bit too much for me to enjoy! I like to be challenged but this Math based game proves to be too much! On a positive note there are over 500 of these puzzles, cards and achievements.
You are provided with 10 numbers ranging from 1-999; the range increases as the puzzles get more difficult. You have to highlight these numbers either red or green in order to make these 2 groups "sum" equal each other.
If this information doesn't get your blood pumping, don't worry that's normal. There is no tutorial so come into this one with the mindset that these puzzles won't be breezed though. There is a problem solver website that can help you once you have been mentally defeated.
It’s worth $1-3 based on the length. Only buy this if you like hard math based puzzles!

Like Two Digits is Three Digits an insanely big pack of puzzles (300) and levelsets (14). The maps now look rhombic, but it's still the same principle: two colored piles of numbers in which you search the equal sums. Three digits means in this case numbers 1-999 and it can be really mixedup (supereasy puzzles in the middle of the game included). I wonder if the puzzle generator is somehow bugged. The fun fades fast out and the soundtrack becomes nervy even if you liked it in the first moment. Hopefully there comes no Four Digits anymore.
It's like throwing♥♥♥♥♥♥at a wall and hoping a piece sticks.

If you loved two digits, than this is one digit better, and that much harder. This is too difficult for me though. It never clicked for me how this was a puzzle and always was a very difficult search over possible combinations of set objects. In this sense I feel dumb.
I'm not personally into it, but maybe you find fun in adding two disjoint sets of numbers so that they add to the same number.

A part of what I wrote in my Two Digits review:
"250 levels with an unnoticeable increase in difficulty (at least not progressive) and too little variation, although the number sets are different and you come to know about different sorts of numbers, like prime numbers."
Unfortunately the same goes up for Three Digits! Yeah, of course it's difficultier, because we play with bigger numbers, but other than that, nothing new. I've totally completed Two Digits, so this is just plain boring for me. The only motivation I have is, that I always like to stay sharp and train my brain, but I probably won't finish this one. Not worth €1,-...
Btw:
- Achievement unlock after a restart > quit again > (still a) bug
- The level scroll bar can only be used with a mouse click + hold, 'Page Down' or 'Down Arrow' doesn't trigger movement. Extra annoying, because the scroll bar always goes back to the beginning of the level selection menu.
I don't get it.

Automation is a must own for petrolheads over there. It is still in early development and lacks many features but you can still have hours and hours of fun playing it. In its current state you are only able to create cars and engines, so if you are looking for the tycoon part of the game might be better to wait. Still there is plenty of good things to point right now.
- The game offers amazing tutorials, you will definitely learn something about cars and engines in the end of the day. The tutorials will help you a lot in the process of making your car, absolutely no need to be an expert. There is plenty of them but they are all worth watching, they are explained in a very didactic way.
- Lots and lots of parts. There is no other game that lets you build a car like automation, while the visual parts of the car lacks features compared to games like NFSU (however you can download more parts through the workshop), the mechanical part is unmatched, from engine blocks to suspensions. You will be able to create a good all around car, or a car for just a specific use. You are able to create cars from 1940 to 2015
- Mod support, the workshop offers many more customizations. Car bodies, headlights, hoods, spoilers, handles, rims, etc. This helps the game to grow more and more.
- Competent developers. You are able to reach them and ask questions about the upcoming features very easily. Game updates are not being rushed and they are taking their time to polish before the release.
- Complete UI. The graphs, numbers and stats of your car are all shown, so you can easily adjust something to reach the desired end of your car.

The Binding of Isaac is very unique because it takes the elements from the old-school Legend of Zelda, and polishes it. It wants you to succeed but it also tries to kill you. Unlike Dark Souls which is a hard game and has patterns spread throughout the game with items, enemies and bosses. The Binding of Isaac doesn't have a pattern. It can give you one of the best items in the first room or it can give you one of the worst items in the first room (no items are restrictly bad but some items are better than others). Not only does it randomly generate items randomly, but it also randomly generates rooms, bosses and various types of enemies randomly. If you are a very unlucky person and doesn't get good items in your rooms. That generally doesn't matter because you can still finish a run victorious. Look at a challenge called The Purist. The challenge starts you of with no item rooms and you are supposed to defeat Isaac (very difficult). It took me a couple of tries but eventually I got it (I think I was just being very lucky). The game doesn't get repetative and there are alot of synergies between items you will probably never see them all. Have fun exploring.

Paladins is my first multiplayer game and to be honest I'm in love with it. I haven't played Overwatch or TF2 to make any comparisons, so I'm going to give a completely unbiased view.
The gameplay is pretty fun and easy to pick. There are four main classes-Damage,Frontline,Flank and Support each with a variety of (ever increasing) Champions(as characters are called). The loadout and card system adds a level of strategy to the game, often becoming the difference between killing and getting killed. Every Champion handles in a different way and getting used to a particular champion is one of the most rewarding aspects of the game. Matchmaking is top notch and is mostly accurate, as in 80% of the time.
The graphics are colorful and cartoonish and the character models look cool, each standing out from the others. The mic system is slightly broken as in my mic accidentally got activated once and everyone could hear me cursing in my native language without me knowing(pretty embarassing). The sound design is improving with regular updates- Viktor a typical CoD Soldier whose gun used to sound like damp firecrackers now has a satisfying thud to it.
Now coming to some of the cons. While the community is generally friendly and welcoming, some players are downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s(though to be honest that's not Hi-Rez's fault). I've been in so many matches where when we played poorly in the first two rounds, a teammate kept cursing everyone and stayed AFK. If you are a new player, and are reading this, please never give up on a match even if you are losing, you can turn it around with just one good round. Another con is that the game has quite a lot of down times, though they don't last very long, its pretty frustrating to come home after a long hard day and opening the game only to find that their servers are down. Since the game is in Beta, there are some bugs, most common being the party bug wherein you can't create a party or get party bonuses even if you are in one.
Hi-Rez as a developer is really great. This game is not at all P2W as of now. Every champion can be bought with easily earnable in-game currency(though the prices have hiked, maybe it is a reflection of our own economy) and the items that you can only get for real money are just cosmetic ones, nothing that affects gameplay.
All in all, if you are a fan of hero based shooters or shooters, this is the game for you, and its free as well, so nothing to lose.

It is physically impossible to complete the achievements for this game, because you will die millions of years earlier than it takes to complete. Your time will be better spent jerking off into a watermelon.
That's not an exaggeration, by the way - it will actually take millions of years to 100% this game in its current state, and melon masturbation is a much better use of your time. In fact, some of the achievements don't even work - better enlist someone to help with that wanking.
Here's how the game works: you click on a lemonade stand to earn money from it, and you keep doing that until you have enough money to buy another lemonade stand. Then you keep doing it some more until you can afford the next investment, and you can buy managers to click on the investments for you so you don't have to keep the game open at all times. And that's good, because it means the game will continue earning money for you when it's not open. So basically, the game is an exercise in economical masturbation.
When you have enough money, you can reset to gain angel investors. Each one adds (at the start) 2% to your income, so if you have 50 your income is doubled, at 100 it's tripled, and so on. The standard strategy is to do your first reset at about 150 angels, and then to reset again every time you double them. Because of how they're generated, the more of them you have, the more money it takes to get the next one.
And therein lies the problem: you see, once you have enough angels, it takes
to double them, and then it will take
to double them the next time. And you won't be anywhere
to earning the last achievement when that happens. Look through the game's discussion pages, someone ran the game with a robot for 7 million years and didn't get anywhere
the 20th achievement.
The developers are wilfully blind to this situation, and instead of fixing the game so that it's possible to get the achievements, they're adding more stuff that the game's not yet ready for. Like the moon, where you hit the same 5-years-to-double problem at a tiny fraction of the angels it takes on Earth, but the final investments you need cost orders of magnitude more than on Earth.
Of course, you can also spend real money to get perks within the game, as is the model for free to play games, but you're only delaying the inevitable - you will eventually hit the impossible to progress stage, and your money will literally have been thrown away for nothing.

If you have played a medieval themed overhead action RPG on your phone then you have played this game before.  The gameplay is pretty decent  It feels like something I would have played on the original PlayStation.  The "vampire" part of the equation isn't very prominent beyond the bit of story you are fed.  Essentially the only way the vampiric "skin" of this game shows up is that when enemies die they occasionally drop healing orbs, but here they are simply red instead of one of the more common colors games use such as green, blue or white and are supposed to be blood.  From a game design aspect this is a small issue since this does not contrast well with the dark and sometimes reddish environment.  The other vampiric aspect is with the healing alters that are scattered throughout the maps.  The only difference from what you are used to seeing is that these alters are people on pikes, and instead of the usual healing particle effects (again green, blue or white) they show a sort of red blood splatter effect.  Otherwise, this is a business as usual medieval themed action RPG with swords and crossbows.  I wouldn't call this a bad game, but it just doesn't stand out on its own merit to me and, in my opinion, hurts itself by adding this vampiric element because it isn't implemented in any way that adds to the gameplay or story.  I also was not personally thrilled with the controller implementation (using an Xbox controller).  Some of the button choices were a bit odd.  An example would be that to shoot your crossbow you press the right shoulder button and to throw a grenade you press the right trigger which feels backwards.  The difference in attack buttons between your characters doesn't make for the smoothest transitions between them, which is supposed to be a core mechanic.  This is not something that you can't get used to, but you have to ask yourself if it’s necessary and/or does it add to the gameplay.  I don't believe it does.  My last issue was with the platforming.  Since the camera generally just floats from fixed point to fixed point you rarely get a good angle to judge your jumps and they are often times spaced exactly at the maximum distance you can jump edge to edge so you can’t adjust mid-jump to correct a misjudged angle.
The most jarring part of this game to me was the framerate.  Per my recording software the DX9 based engine is pumping out 60 fps, but the motion only appears to be about 15 or 20 fps.  It feels very jittery and caused a bit of eyestrain.  I believe migraine and tension headache sufferers should avoid this game.

**A bit of a bias opinion here, because I've only played this game local co-op, with my girlfriend (meaning it's more fun than if I were playing it alone)
Despite various very minor bugs, and one major one... We're enjoying the game.
The gameplay itself is a bit generic and unique. This is an action game with some RPG elements. There are 2 playable characters.
Player 1 is a warrior with dual wields swords. His special attacks include smashing the ground with a heavy attack and spinning around like a tornado.
Player 2 is an archer with dual wield crossbows. Her specials are fire arrows and throwing grenades (of various types)
Working together is important in the beginning, but as you become more powerful, you can both hold your own fairly well.
The unique mechanic is the ability to share life with each other (giving your own health to the other player) and the ability to use psychokinesis on enemies and your ally. The warrior has the ability to pull closer, while the archer pushes away.
This is used to solve some simple puzzles, progess through the levels, and generally beat enemies.
While an enemy is lifted, you drain them of blood, restoring some of your own health, while also causing time itself to slow down, allowing your partner to either pick up another enemy to heal themselves or to unload a flurry of attacks on enemies.
The RPG elements are more of an afterthought. The items you pick up are not randomly generated, instead following a nice, better equipment the further you go, path. Leveling up gives you a point to distribute into your skills. This is fairly easy to distribute, as most of the skills just relate to hitting harder, so whatever you use most, put your points into.
Stats can be gained by collecting hidden coins through the game. This is a nice exploration element, but a terrible attribute distribution method.
You are given 3 attributes to increase: health, strength (directly translates to damage), and luck (how much gold the enemies drop)
Because you can drain life out of enemies whenever you want, the only choice here is strength.
Gold itself is abundant and with only 2 shops (that don't change their wares, and I don't recommend buying them) you will quickly have a surplus of gold.
The story is... odd, and a bit inconsistent.
You are a human warrior trying to destroy vampires, and your partner is a vampire that, through holy arts, has been bound to you. After the first mission, you yourself are turned into a vampire. You then follow your original plan of stopping the vampires, but now all the humans hate you.
Throughout the game, you are given dialog choices, and can choose to be more on the vampire side or the human side. This is reflected very well in the NPC, but unfortunately very poorly in the player characters. While I have chosen the vampire route, it took a long time for the warrior to come to grasp with this, stating things such as, "I don't know why I did that." In the same context... The archer is often very cruel and uncaring about humans, but as you go further, she starts to show mercy.
On the otherhand, the scripts are very well written, with many welly played quips, especially between the 2 player characters.
Bugs and glitches:
I'm not going to say that the game is broken... But it does have an assortment of glitches.
Graphics that sometimes don't load correctly, poor level design which causes getting stuck on nothing, and the major one that broke the game for me....
In chapter 9 (last chapter?) There is a part where you enter a type of vehicle... We had missed a spot to explore, so decided to reload from the last checkpoint.
Upon doing this, I was locked into single player (player 2 could not join) the vehicle was gone (required to progress) and exiting the level from the entrance wasn't an option, because you jump down from a ledge early on.
There is no way to exit a stage early, nor is there a restart level option. So, I'm 100% stuck, and we have to start the game over.
Despite all of this, the game is really fun (with a friend)
It's your basic hack and slash, kill everything in sight game. But different enough to stand out.

This is a minimalistic endless runner with 1980s style futuristic visuals envisaging a dystopian 1990s, made in the 21st century. Seems a good idea, eh?
All you do is push the left and right buttons to turn, and stay on the road. Sounds easier than it actually is.
Its levels that are just a bit too long, so I really hate it when I lose near the end of a level, because that means I have to do the exact same thing yet again and hopefully not screw up and the end.
Also, the runner doesn't run in exact straight lines parallel to the roads you run on, so if you land too near to the edge of a long stretch, your runner may fall off near the end. You can't really correct your errors - your runner can only turn every so often so for example, you can't turn then turn back again fast enough to move "slightly to the left" to correct your errors.
The game is irritating like that.
Thankfully, as you run, some charming electronic music plays and an electronic voice speaks, and it gives you something to ponder about the world of the game, whoever the voice is, and whoever your character is.
...actually, I switched the music off after a while, because it get a bit irritating after the first few hundred times because it becomes repetitive and was too chilled out and I wasn't. It's not a fault of the music, but a reaction to it. I put on some faster-paced music and found that I was playing better. Is this cheating?
Overall, I recommend this game. It's simple, and it's annoying, but it makes my brain wake up, and despite its flaws, I seem to keep coming back to it.

Paladins is my first multiplayer game and to be honest I'm in love with it. I haven't played Overwatch or TF2 to make any comparisons, so I'm going to give a completely unbiased view.
The gameplay is pretty fun and easy to pick. There are four main classes-Damage,Frontline,Flank and Support each with a variety of (ever increasing) Champions(as characters are called). The loadout and card system adds a level of strategy to the game, often becoming the difference between killing and getting killed. Every Champion handles in a different way and getting used to a particular champion is one of the most rewarding aspects of the game. Matchmaking is top notch and is mostly accurate, as in 80% of the time.
The graphics are colorful and cartoonish and the character models look cool, each standing out from the others. The mic system is slightly broken as in my mic accidentally got activated once and everyone could hear me cursing in my native language without me knowing(pretty embarassing). The sound design is improving with regular updates- Viktor a typical CoD Soldier whose gun used to sound like damp firecrackers now has a satisfying thud to it.
Now coming to some of the cons. While the community is generally friendly and welcoming, some players are downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s(though to be honest that's not Hi-Rez's fault). I've been in so many matches where when we played poorly in the first two rounds, a teammate kept cursing everyone and stayed AFK. If you are a new player, and are reading this, please never give up on a match even if you are losing, you can turn it around with just one good round. Another con is that the game has quite a lot of down times, though they don't last very long, its pretty frustrating to come home after a long hard day and opening the game only to find that their servers are down. Since the game is in Beta, there are some bugs, most common being the party bug wherein you can't create a party or get party bonuses even if you are in one.
Hi-Rez as a developer is really great. This game is not at all P2W as of now. Every champion can be bought with easily earnable in-game currency(though the prices have hiked, maybe it is a reflection of our own economy) and the items that you can only get for real money are just cosmetic ones, nothing that affects gameplay.
All in all, if you are a fan of hero based shooters or shooters, this is the game for you, and its free as well, so nothing to lose.

I bought the Galaxy edition when it was on sale for half off because I heard a lot of good things about it from friends but never really was too in to the whole grand strategy thing, but I've been in a really big space mood lately and wanted to try something new. I figured "Hey, I'll buy it, play it for an hour and a half and if I don't like it or it's not really keeping my attention, I'll just refund it." That was at 12:30am. The next time I looked up at the clock, it was 6:30am and I almost woke up the rest of the house when I screamed "♥♥♥♥".
Needless to say, I had and am still having a lot of fun with Stellaris. It's complex enough that there's a bit of a learning curve and requires some actual thought in to what you're doing, but it's intuitive enough that anybody can get in to it. It's relaxing 90% of the time, and intense the other 10%. The art and graphics for the game are absolutely gorgeous and the soundtrack is amazing. All the little random events that play out stories are fun to read and learn about. And the overall dynamic nature of each game makes sure that every single time you play is different.
My only major complaints about the way the game works is the technology research and the speed at which your leaders gain skill levels. Technology research is essentially a top-stacked deck of cars. You get three categories and the first slots are more or less the same each time you play, but after that it's almost entirely random, which means that there's an RNG aspect to what your empire can end up doing. One play through you might unlock Psionics research for soldiers, the next you might end up with the ability to make a giant amusement park on your planets. There's no planning in what technologies you go for, just the ones you hope you get, and that gets annoying pretty quick, especially when there are two or more techs you want to get for the same category at the same time but can only pick one (which frequently leads in to a "do I want to get this super rare technology that will completely make this playthough different from all the others? Or do I want to be able to upgrade my stations yet again so I can produce the larger ships I need to keep everything safe?" situation). My problem with Leaders gaining skill levels is that unless you waste a racial trait to give your species longer lifespans, your scientists will always end up at max rank of 5 right at the end of their lives. I've had several instances where I finally get my first wave of scientists to max rank and then send them to do research projects that require a rank 5 scientist, and then they die of old age on the way over there which forces me to hire on new rank 1 scientists and then wait 50 in-game years for them to be high enough rank again and hope i'm not in the middle of something when their window of not being dead while max rank is open.
Also there's a really obnoxious stall that lasts about 2 seconds every time the game autosaves, which when i have time sped up to fastest on ironman mode which causes the game to save every in-game month, gets VERY obnoxious, VERY quickly.
Those complaints aside, Stellaris is a game I'm going to enjoy for a long time to come simply because of how relaxing and engaging it is, and I encourage anybody looking for a similar experience to give it a try.

First and foremost, realize this is alpha, you're paying for early access, there are bugs.
That being said even now the game is a ton of fun to play. Getting into a small match and enjoying duels between two players is fun enough on its own. But then you get massive matches where everything is pure chaos yet still manages to suck you right in.

As if the melee combat wasn't great enough they go and throw in spells - and not a single one of them is lacking - every single spell is useful in a variety of ways and really opens up gameplay. Whether you enjoy sneaking around like a ninja, teleporting around like some multi-dimensional stalker, or blasting your enemy to pieces with a well placed fireball - there's a spell for you.
Probably the most fun though is finding new tactics and new ways to counter your opponents. You'll notice pretty quickly a few loadouts that are common amongst players and I take great pleasure in being able to adapt my combat style to most effectively fight them.
This game has huge potential and I can't wait to see where it goes.

NO THING is a minimalistic surreal action game set in a future ruled in a totalitarian regime.  You play as an office clerk who is sent on a mission to deliver an important message to the Ice Queen.  The game progresses through a third-person omniscient narration which dictates the story as you make your way through the labyrinth.
Taking the form of classic runner games, NO THING is played with only the left and right arrow keys to dictate the direction your character will move.  As you make more turns, the speed at which your character moves also increases.  It is import to note that on every level, you must turn a certain amount of times in order to progress the narrative to 100%.  However you must also run through the map at least once to progress to the next level.  There are certain orbs you can pick-up that will decrease your speed but on each level they can only be collected once.
With such a simple game design, the driving point of the game is the story.  As you progress throughout the game, you can easily see where the developers pulled inspiration from;
,
just to name a few.  The third-person narration plays the role of ‘big brother’ extremely well by utilizing the structure of the leveling system to reveal information about the player and what they should be doing.  Players familiar with the thought process of Winston in
will quickly realize the similarities in the perception and sentence structure of the narration in NO THING as the game progresses.
After about 2-3 hours, you will realize the brilliance in combining a runner game and a heavy plot, specifically one related to totalitarianism.  The simple and addictive gameplay hooks you in as a player and enslaves you into “delivering the message to the Ice Queen”.  The narrative voice is quite hypnotic, and will pull the player deeper into the game while the soundtrack will keep you wired, numb and autonomous, functioning similarly to slave songs.  You will effectively be fully immersed into roleplaying as the office clerk.
The game is rage-inducing if you have poor reaction times.  In order to progress the story, you must be able to clear a level completely, or else you’ll be stuck in a loop; listening to the same lines again and again.  Repetition is good for keeping player attention, but too long and you will eventually break out the trance and just become frustrated with the game.  Often times, you may feel that the game is just ridiculously unfair and just quit because there is no other way to get around a level.
I personally rate this game 7/10 for the thought-provoking storyline and great music.  Had the core gameplay included checkpoints and had been less difficult at the higher levels, the game would have been a solid 9/10.

An overall nice game with some flaws but worth your time if you enjoy this style of game (top down shooters) and/or zombie games!
The gameplay and graphics are very fun and interesting, very rewarding challenge and several different modes to play (although I was mostly interested in the story mode, myself), with secrets and collectibles to find and a good (albiet sometimes silly) variety of enemies to fight. The boss fights were a weaker part of the gameplay for me, they didn't feel difficult because they posed any kind of challenge, it was more they were difficult because they take a lot of time to beat, and so were more of an endurance test (although I found the final stage and boss to be a lot more fun). The graphics, as stated, are good; although they seem a bit unoptimized as I have a fairly high-end computer that runs much more graphically-intensive games with no slowdown, yet this game slowed down for me a lot (though it was never unplayable) even on lower settings. (EDIT: Turns out I was just playing with the wrong graphics card, oops! So the performance issue is actually non-existent for me, so thats one less negative for the game!)
The story and especially the dialogue itself really fell flat for me though, it felt very cheesy and try-hard, and the voice actors were clearly not professionals. The artwork in cutscenes was so-so as well, although I give the game a bit of a pass in this regard as the game was fun enough to play regardless, although I admit I'd have liked it even better with some more polish in those areas! The storymode is also fairly short (around 5 hours or so) but it felt like enough to me, I enjoyed playing it for about an hour a day over the course of a week. Plus, there are other modes to try out after that!
All in all I recommend this game to those who enjoy top down shooters with a bit of exploration, zombies, and going for high scores! Worth the time you'll get out of it for the price.

I beat the main game on normal difficulty, singleplayer.
I purchased Party Hard before it showed up in bundles and before its Streaming integration features. I went in with no expectations. Party Hard has a simple premise that seems like it could be super enjoyable. Go to a party and attempt to kill everyone there. Looking at the screenshots and trailers makes it seem even better with the wide variety of locations and insanity shown. Thats what I'm sure many people fell for, the seeming variety presented on the store page.
The game consists of walking around a single screen populated with npcs who aimlessly wander around the stage. The default character has a one hit kill melee attack that works in a very limited area. There are also a variety of interactables in each stage that can also kill party-goers or otherwise make the task easier like items and secret passages. The challenge comes from the fact that the npcs will discover dead bodies and promptly call the authorities. A single cop will then enter the stage bagging up any bodies that have been reported and any others he may find. If the npc who discovers the crime sees you in close proximity to the body then the cop will target you and chase down your character for a limited time, if he catches you the game ends. As the game progresses other npcs will be introduced who can also take you down for various reasons.
On paper this sounds great, a stealth game with all sorts of ways to kill the targets. The issue comes from, at least in my playthrough, every level ends up playing exactly the same with little variation regardless of design. There are four types of traps you can find in a level:
1. Single kill traps that activate if you are standing right next to the trap and an npc
2. Instant activation traps that kill whoever is in the traps hitzone when activated
3. Explosives that go off after a certain amount of time, usually waiting for someone to touch them first.
4. Poisoned refreshments which kill any npc that interacts with them until its kill limit has been reached.
This sounds like you have tons of options, especially when you watch the trailer and see all the quirky fun traps there are. In reality though, after one or two runs on a level you figure out what each trap does and start each stage just running to each one and activating them. There isn't really any planning involved. The npcs are truly random as far as I can tell meaning there is no way to predict them or encourage them to go to a specific area. Even killing someone to make them call the police can send them to one of two phones, sometimes the closest one, sometimes not, meaning you cant even account for that. So when you cant plan where npc are going to go you cant time traps appropriately, plus the default character is incredibly slow so most of the time if people are in range of an instant trap you wont be close enough to activate it in time to take advantage. So instead you just activate all the proximity traps+poison right away and activate the others whenever the chance arises. There are occaisonally some 'support' units you can call in to take out some people but they have a limited amount of kills before they leave similar to the poison, essentially each level has a certain amount of party goers that is guaranteed to be taken out by certain traps. The explosives are the most frustrating because an npc has to be very close to activate it, not in the blast zone but right next to the damn bomb. so even if you could kill a third of the targets with one bomb, you likely wont because no npc will actually approach the damn thing until the majority of them have dispersed.
So after activating all possible traps the game gets even more boring. Because the npcs are random you can't predict their movements, not even a little. This means you have to wait for them to be isolated which can take forever depending on the amount of npcs in an area. You can try and kill bunches of people in rapid sucession but more often than not this will lead to some npc randomly coming by to report you. None of the levels are hard. 90% of time I lost because I tried to do something other than slowly pick off targets. I lost for trying to have fun.
Perhaps the greatest sign that the gameplay is flawed is that in a few levels I figured out how to exploit the cops. They seem to be autopathed to take the shortest route to your character. So with some dumb luck I actually found some spots that ,if you walk in and out of, will change the shortest route making the cop run in circles till his timer runs out. Strangely though these were the levels I could have the most fun. I could string together wacky combos and attempt things that I simply couldn't during normal gameplay. I could actually make plans that, while they didnt always work, at least let me have some creativity with the game. Thats what I think is the biggest problem with this game, freedom. In games like Hotline Miami, Deadbolt and Gunpoint you can count on your enemies reacting in certain ways (even with some variation) This allows you to plan ahead and approach the game in your own way. Party Hard's lack of any reliable elements, save for the cops, make it so there is only one way to really play it and that way isnt very fun.
Its worth pointing out that I only played a couple of the DLC missions and only fiddled around with one or two of the alternate characters. I was already burnt out by the time I unlocked all that stuff to really see if anything would change. The short time I spent with the extra content was slightly more enjoyable but not enough to redeem the hours I spent on the main campaign.
While it certainly isnt central, the story is garbage, I'll bet its 'big twist' was guessed by at least half the players before it happened. The story's attempt at a serious tone also doesnt match the goofiness of the game itself. The music is decent but after playing a level for the fourth or fifth time it gets really tiring (Just like real club music)
Summary:
+Interesting idea and premise
+Quirky stages and interactions
+A lot of content past the main campaign
~Music
~Art
-Poorly Executed
-Random
-Bad/Pointless level design
-Charm wears off fast

This game was a lot of fun.
I really enjoyed the fluid combat, the vampiric powers, and some of the character designs. There's a very basic save the world plot which drives you forward, but it's not all that interesting. It does what it needs to do (serve as a reason to go from area to area) and no more.
There's a nice array of enemies which require different tactics to defeat, and some fun bosses.
In all honesty, the only thing I didn't enjoy were the short platforming sections - simply because it was so easy to miss and fall to your death. Luckily, checkpoints can be found frequently, and you can revist them to update your save; as well as visit the trader.
I played this with an Xbox 360 controller and it worked fine. No idea what it's like with a mouse and keyboard. Don't want to think about it.
One strange thing which kept happening to me, was things looked like they were stuttering or lagging, but weren't. It's really weird and difficult to explain. It didn't affect gameplay in any way, it just looked like character animations were a bit stuttery - it could mainly be seen during cutscenes. However, like I said, it never influenced gameplay in the slightest; button input and commands were fluid and everything was responsive.
A shame the game wasn't more fleshed out.
I recommend it to people who enjoy loot driven rpgs, similar to Diablo, but who want to play as a blood drinking vampire.

If this was set in Nosgoth I could see this as a cheaply made cashgrab tie-in to the original Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain - as it is this is just a cheap hack and slash action/arcade game with vampires in it.
Nothing is really that hard, and the programming is basic, so there is a lot of exploits to use, if it gets too hard at times - and when you die, reloading is fast.
The camera is not the best in the world, the voices sound bored, and it is easiest to play as a shooter, but while some thinks that the action is repetitive, I found that it worked fine, considering the short game length
Honestly if you are looking for a RPG, look somewhere else - if you are looking for gameplay worth 5+ bucks - again look somewhere else; but if it is a rainy sunday, this game is on sale (I bought it for 2.50 euro) and you just want something easy and shallow to help you lose part of a day, then this game is alright.

NO THING has taught me several life lessons to simplify my ways of living.
Some of the most memorable would be that the neighbors are eating dinner, also they happen to be watching TV, and I could not possibly forget the fact that I have also been taught about their relative location, specifically, that they are located behind the walls and doors.
Jokes aside, this game is a runner genre game, if that is a genre, never heard about it before I laid eyes on this game, it had me interested in it ever since I saw the cover picture in the store. At first I thought that somebody made a vaporwave meme come to life in the form of a game. I was baffled by the fact that the only gameplay is just switching directions by 90 degrees to the right or left and as I would soon learn, having to go a full 360 degrees to save yourself from the endless void underneath the pathways you navigate that make up the levels. The trailer had me hooked, the game is one of a kind if there aren't any other like it, which had me thinking about spending money on it.
So I did.
And I got what I wanted.
This is as simple as an indie about a simple office clerk gets, don't buy the game if you're not looking for uniqueness, it isn't even expensive, so I wouldn't say it's a waste of money if you don't like the game.
Not much to say about the plot as there's not much of a lead to catch onto, but you can make up your own ideas about what's happening in the game. The game has a pretty addicting soundtrack and it blends with the gameplay very well, the increasing speed as you turn makes it even better, in my opinion, all of that makes this game have a good replay value and a drawback effect, I just can't get enough of it. I've also found some exploits (level 3, turn slightly before the turned pathway and get stuck in the corner, press left/right repeatedly for a speed increase and point farming, if you want to place high in the leaderboards) and minor bugs (level 7 had me do some experimenting at the spawn point and I somehow had the character go diagonally, not straight, but this doesn't happen until you die repeatedly and respawn extremely quick, also can make you turn with little delay)
The soundtrack is stunningly amazing, can't wait for the DLC, will gladly pay for it, and would be even more glad to do so if the songs weren't simple loops ripped from the game, but I'll be happy with either.
I wonder what message the clerk was supposed to deliver though, probably a safety railing suggestion for every pathway.

Wow... Literally, wow. Evil Indie Games debut on Steam,
, seems to come out of nowhere but man, it does a great job in screwing with our minds! Set in a futuristic dystopia in 1994, you are (and repeatedly referred to as) the simplest office clerk tasked with delivering a message to the Queen of Ice. The game, as I would like to call it, is a precision runner where you play in a first person view and there is an ending to each level after achieving the required number of turns, as in directional turns. It sounds easier in words but trust me, it gets hard, like REALLY HARD, as the pace would continuously increase throughout the level and made even worse with tight turns, bumps and jumps in between. Missed a turn or overshoot a jump and BAM, back to the starting line for you! It literally took me 30 minutes just to get pass the first stage!
NO THING consists of 10 levels in total and each of them are told as a story by the narrator. This is one of the best points of the game, the backstory is intriguing and fascinating that will leave you wondering why and what is going on. The monotone narrative accompanied by seriously catchy tunes will get you humming the thing even when you've stopped playing, especially if you're stuck at a level for a while. There are a score system implemented in the game but to be honest, I haven't quite got the whole thing figured out yet.
Despite all the positive points, I guess the biggest flaw that NO THING currently have is the lack of contents. As I've mentioned previously, there's only 10 levels and depending on how good you are playing this type of games, it can be a pretty short experience. Luckily, they're planning to release a free DLC in the near future, titled EVERYTHING, which may be a new mode or a new story arc as a whole (if anyone have more information regarding this, I'd appreciate it if you can share it in the comments section below). Oh, and they're also planning to release the soundtrack DLC. Yay!
For those who enjoyed runner games, or futuristic dystopia setting, in general and wouldn't mind a little challenge, I have no problem recommending this title to you guys! At the price tag of $4, this is a steal for this kind of gem.

This game is a surprising amount of fun..... at the start anyway.
NO THING is a game in the same vein as Temple Run and Boson X. Your character runs forward non stop and you move them left or right to avoid obstacles and death. I've always had a guilty pleasure for these games as they kill some time and can feel very rewarding when you finish a level after failing at it so many times.
This is what NO THING is but has a interesting concept behind it. You play as a office clerk who is delivering messages to people. As you run about the place, a robotic voice talks to you about a lot of different things such as Totalitarianism and Mundanity of everyday life. This is annoying in its own way though as you have to restart the level from the beginning    if you die, meaning you have to listen to the same piece of dialogue over and over again.
After a couple of levels, this game does start to become a little bit boring. You end up finishing a level out of determination rather than enjoyment. The graphic glitches and colours that they throw at you can make it hard to concentrate which adds extra challenge but could also cause quite a headache.
I would still recommend this game. If it goes on sale for a couple quid, I would pick it up. Its only about 2 - 3 hours of gameplay, depending on how good you are at these type of games, and does try to do something interesting with a simple gameplay mechanic. 7/10.
(Note: Great game to play whilst listening to "OK Computer")

When I first saw the screenshots and read the about the ambition behind Deus Ex, it seemed like one of those games with its head in the clouds and no way to deliver on all the promises it made. The gist of it was that it set out to be a hard science fiction "shooter RPG" taking place in a dystopian near-future setting where terrorism was commonplace, the underclass were being wiped out by a plague many suspected was government-engineered, and a half-dozen shadowy organizations, from the Illuminati on down, were all vying for Control of the World. In the middle of all this was you, and you got to play what amounts to a cop.
That was the set-up, and all I needed at the time. I picked up the game based totally on the strength of its spiritual predecessor, System Shock 2, which I'd absolutely loved, and figured it was going to be more of the same: Encounter baddies in a large, involved environment and solve a number of combat and situational puzzles in your method of choice, while developing your character down one of a handful of skill paths. Play the psychic, the combat guy, or the hacker. Expect spooky AIs whispering in your ear throughout and expect to get some kind of amazingly overpowered lightsaber-y weapon near the end, the option to be good or evil for added replay value, and a healthy sprinkling of journals to pick up so you could follow the backstory if you felt like it.
I was right about the AI and the lightsaber.
This game is basically System Shock 3, but seven years before BioShock and with a much more open-ended slant on the 'Shock style of game. It's really the ultimate expression of DIY character development within a game world, but without the ridiculous handholding so many other games resort to in order to move the plot forward. The focused linearity of 'Shocks 1, 2 and Bio isn't here; you're free to roam, and the plot is there in abundance but doesn't leap into your arms for you. There's reams of dialogue, there's often a peaceful (or at least sneaky) solution to puzzles, and many levels exist solely to further the plot. You're left entirely to your own devices for much of the game, only given a broad idea of what has to happen or which point you need to reach. How you go about that is entirely up to you.
That's not to say the whole game is entirely freeform — it isn't. But it manages a linear design in such a way that you neither notice, nor care even if you do.
Nearly every scenario has five-plus ways to complete it, and half-finished concepts abound. The designers would toss in three or four obvious ways to go about something, then maybe stack some crates to a back window or give you a robot control widget and just let you figure s**t out from there, were you so inclined. The game had enough "open" systems in place to basically compensate for anything you could possibly do.
The Brute Force and Stealth n' Assassination approaches are always viable options as well, so if your tricky Bond-like play of brazenly bulls**tting your way into a huge corporation's main building doesn't work and you get turned away at the door, you can always opt for the unofficial Plan B and just blow the everliving crap out everything in your path. Or, just skip all foreplay before you even get to the prom: Knock everyone's head in from half a mile away with your customized, ridiculously overpowered rifle, then stroll into an empty level and do as you please. No quicksave/reload shenanigans necessary.
On top of that, because of the way the game was designed, smart players are given access to what amounts to the entire plot well before it's supposed to happen, but only if you're clever (and only if you care). You spend a good one-third of the game on the side of Law and Order, so it's a bit disconcerting to discover a huge underground base underneath a manhole cover in the central part of New York City, or maybe a prototype weapon designed by a shadow government in a hidden room behind your dead brother's ex-girlfriend's apartment; but, as you might expect, these places tend to be secretive and require quite a bit of effort on your part to find. None of these hidden areas have big neon signs over them.
Should you not find any of these, the game continues as normal. If you do, though, you get a lovely sense of chucking a giant monkey wrench in the works, when in reality the game is perfectly prepared for the player to find this stuff on the off chance and reacts accordingly. Crack open the developer cheat and take a look at the quest flags: There are hundreds of them, flagging virtually everything you could possibly do, from walking into the women's bathroom by accident to killing off major characters hours before they're supposed to even play their part. Nothing goes unrecorded. This was a herculean bit of coding on the part of the developers, and it's rare you see s**t like this anymore these days; usually, design of even forward-thinking games leans much more in favor of heavily controlled player herding for major plot events, not a "maybe the player will do this" approach.
While the moral lines are not actually color-coded (i.e. there's no "Good Points" and "Bad Points" to accumulate), human nature means that most people will guide their nanoaugmented private-military-science-project-c*m-UN-peacekeeper JC Denton through the game as either a good-guy cop, or a total a**hole. People tend to go for extremes in these kinds of games. Cleverly, the rationale for both makes sense in the game world, so the morality of the choice is totally up to you. No matter what you do, it's never wrong.
As your brother Paul points out early on, you don't
to use lethal force in this game. JC is completely decked out in state-of-the-art nanoaugs and can easily subdue any criminal that regular police would have to resort to lethal force for. JC doesn't need lethal force. He's way too powerful for that. The few times when you do have to kill, it's against some giant killer robot or super nanoaugmented badass who borderlines on the immortal anyway. Lethal force against those far weaker than you should, you'd think, only be used as a last resort and only when absolutely necessary, and the game allows you to pursue this path of your own accord.
On the other hand, you're a multi-billion dollar killing machine. Not only should you not feel guilty about slaughtering an entire island's worth full of terrorists, that's what you were literally made to do. It makes perfect sense in the context of the game world, and it's something the game reinforces positively as you go. The terrorists are certainly using lethal force against your co-workers, the vast majority of whom are just doing their jobs. The United Nations police force you belong to is never painted as any kind of obvious aggressor. Your team aren't a bunch of jackbooted puppy-kicking Gestapo or anything. They're cops, doing their job fighting off a heavily-armed terrorist force. Most of the time they're even outgunned, which is where you're supposed to come in.
So really, where do you draw the line? You're blatantly more powerful than most of the enemies you fight. Those guys you mow down so easily are weak for a reason; they're nothing compared to the kind of kill power you have wired into your very body, and it is literally your job to be a military powerhouse when other measures of crowd control have failed.

What to say about Deus Ex...... It's Awesome with a few stipulations.
GAMEPLAY
I'll be honest, you are fragile. Stealth is a huge part of what makes this game fun, and while it is possible to run in guns blazing, its nowhere near as satisfying as taking out entire squads of enemy soldiers stealthily, or even just sneaking by them. The game rarely forces the player to deal with the enemy, leaving a lot up to choice. Enemies hear movement, and roam in patterns that can make stealth difficult for first-timers, but there's always more than one way to the objective. Areas can be accessed with lockpicks, multitools, and explosives, which provides a great teal of freedom. Some keyboard and mouse configuration may be required for a more modern gaming experience.
STORY
It was interesting. I don't want to spoil anything :D
VISUALS AND SOUND
It is a game from the late 90s/ early 2000s (I don't remember which), so the graphics are dated. There's no argument about that. The music is very well composed and lends a lot to the tone of the game.
TL;DR
If you can see past the aged graphics and the learning curve, this is a real gem. While certain aspects have aged significantly, some can be fixed with the "New Vision" Mod. There also exists a steam-supported mod called "Revision", but this really changes things up and while it is a very good mod, you should play the base game first.

Why not?
It lacks substance.
The first few missions were kind of fun, but already the flaws couldn't be ignored.
You have the killer and move through a party of people you have to kill. You have to kill everyone, in fact.
You can set traps; but, the traps are pretty boring and don't do too much at all. No, you can't be very creative in killing and you can't kill everyone, when you think a lot, and set everything perfect.
No, most of your victims you have to kill with your hand/etc.
So, the first missions were fun, because not too hard. It was nice to kill some time, setting traps, killing people.
Then, in later missions, it gets pretty hard pretty fast. When someone spots you killing someone, the police comes. You were able to get away in the beginning, sometimes, sometimes not, but later it's nearly impossible, then there are bouncers that want to kill you etc. So you have to be patient and careful on a level that is just annoying. Set the nearly same boring traps all over again to kill a few and the rest: boring waiting til nobody can spot you.
I'm frustrated, because I haven't even played a third of the game and there are no real surprises that make playing more interesting. Just grinding. And nothing else.
After all: The game is a disappointment; the trailer gave me the impression of some kind of macabre chain reaction game, as if you could plan to kill the whole party with good planing and one final blow, instead you get a cheap stealth game with clumsy controls.

This Pre-Sequel is not the same quality as the previous Borderlands. It feels cheap and untested for the majority of its game play and has quite a few outstanding issues: Geometry problems (vehicles going off the map), mobs shooting/running/flying through structures and various terrain glitches just to name a few engine based issues. I personally on SteamOS have problems with some Guns' rate of fire suddenly changing in the middle of a fight for no apparent reasons. For the AI, enemies love flying and they also love getting stuck while flying or they just stop doing whatever they were doing to give you time to shoot them down. (pretty)
This release of Borderlands also adds a few mechanical gimmicks, the main one being the low gravity and the absence or presence of an atmosphere. Unfortunately it just doesn't work very well, Your character is supposed to benefit from the low gravity using an Oz kit. Using the Oz kit you can apparently fly, move quickly across terrain etc... This is probably true, if you are an enemy. You on the other hand don't fly or move quicker. It feels like you're stuck with Marry Poppins' Umbrela and all your enemies have Tribe based jet packs. The low gravity/lack of atmosphere thing ends up turning combat into Stay Puft Marshmallow Man vs An annoying bunch of prepubescent kids.
Combine the slow motion fights with the few vehicles in the game and you've got quite a contrast and it's not to say that vehicle combat is any better. In most fights with vehicle weapon systems, you can stop, aim, put the vehicle in reverse, step back a little, aim, kill and you're done. The combat is just massively disappointing in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. It is slow and not exciting at all.

I'd like to start this review by saying that I'm not a fan of the runner genre. I find this game to be immensely frustrating, as such, but I gave myself five before coming back to review it.
It's also frustrating as all hell. Due to my own failings, of course, so I can't really blame the game for that.
.Premise.
You're a messenger of sorts. The simplest office clerk. You're delivering a message to the Queen of Ice. You'll find out more about yourself through the robotic narrator as you run through and complete the stages.
.Gameplay.
Run. You move forward automatically and it's up to you to turn left or right to avoid death. That's all there is to it. The game tries its best to distract you with on-screen visual interferences (like colour changes and graphical glitching/blurring) and a nonsensical "story" that punctuates moments in your progress with a robotic voice reading a line of text that flashes across the screen.
As you progress, things get more difficult. The speed of your run increases, and so the precision of your turns will need fine-tuning.
Focus is the name of the game here and if you're easily distracted, you'll fall out of your groove and go plummeting to your death. Once you die, you start the level again from the beginning. Then, you try again and again until, finally, you either finish the stage or hit the escape key and go play something else while you cool off.
You can use either keyboard or gamepad. Either works just as well.
.Soundtrack.
So good. I've only managed to get to the second level in my hour of play, but the first track was synthetic... upbeat... electronic... awesome and the second track was a slower, more mellow synthetic upbeat electronic awesome. I assume each stage has its own individual song that plays throughout the entire run.
.Graphics/ Art Style.
Trippy to say the least. The face on the game's banner appears throughout the stages, which are always awash in bright, solid colours. If you have a history of epilepsy, please do NOT play this game.
.Longevity.
That depends on your skill level. I'm god-awful at this game and it took me about fifteen minutes to get through the first level. The remainder of my time was spent floundering over level two. If you're an expert runner, you probably won't get as much time out of this as the average Joe.
.Bottom line.
If you're a fan of the runner genre, this game will be a great addition to your library. If you're on the fence about the genre or are new, you may still get some enjoyment from the soundtrack and surreal atmosphere. Just be warned: patience is a virtue.

The idea of NO THING is very simple: you are a simple office clerk with a message you must deliver to the Ice Queen. The gameplay consists of you navigating levels with nothing more than your left and right keys. Though it sounds easy at first, NO THING is anything but.
You start on level one which is an easy introduction of what is to come. You must follow the path in front of you turning left and right when needed. There is a voice speaking to you as you play, telling you things, some which make sense and some which don't (not right away anyway) and a rather awesome soundtrack playing. You'll see images whilst you play that'll change depending on what's being said. You should spend your time playing NO THING listening and looking very carefully.
The levels progressively get harder, not just from level one to level two, but whilst you are actually playing them. Platforms will move, appear and disappear. Graphics will flicker, glitch (intentional) and change colour. Images will change, enlarge, shrink and move through platforms. Everything that happens is there to test your focus and concentration;
NO THING is all about your perception of things and requires you not only to evaluate your surroundings quickly but to also ignore all of the background distraction. Platforms come in different sizes, some being thin and some wider. There are others which are slanted, some which don't properly connect and some which are slightly off centre. You must be alert at all times whilst playing because even clicking half a second too late could be the difference between winning a level and starting all over again. As you run you gain speed continually though I've not yet worked out if this is linked to the amount of turns you take or how long you've been running for. Your speed can work for you or against you, often being helpful for flying from one platform to others that would have been out of reach at a lower speed, but it also makes things a lot harder as your reaction speed has to increase with it. You can find red blocks in certain places to reduce your speed if things start getting a little out of control.
Falling from a platform doesn't always mean death though. Many levels weave in and out of each other and are on different heights so if you can react quick enough you can find yourself at another part of the level and just continue running.
Your paths will grow as you progress in the stage and some of them require you to repeatedly run the same path multiple times before something new opens. Often you'll find this will happen quickly and throw you off guard. You can also take different paths, though they'll all eventually lead to the same place, after all, choice is just an illusion in a totalitarian world.
But the enjoyment of NO THING doesn't just come from the gameplay itself, what really grips you is the story and the way you experience it. Everything, from the dialogue to the music to the images, it just keeps you wanting to play, to find out more, to reach the end. You'll spend the game trying to work out what's going on in this world, with you, and the voice but slowly you'll piece things together bit by bit.
I found NO THING to be oddly relaxing. When the gameplay wasn't frustrating because i'd failed so many times, the pressing right and left at the right time combined with the soundtrack was oddly calming. At some points when you find your rhythm the game flows perfectly and the levels are long enough that when they aren't too hard and you know the route you need to take, it just works.
There are only two negative things I can really find about the game, the first is the lack of some kind of a free runner mode. Given the games intense difficulty it would be enjoyable to have endless (or large) levels to practice on so you don't have to continuously repeat a level you're stuck on until you beat it. This is directly link to my second issue which is the fact that the game can feel repetitive at times if you cannot complete a level. There was one particular part where I was reaching 99% and missing the last turn meaning I had to replay the entire level over and over hearing the same dialogue. Though the voice-over is what makes the game so good, hearing it for the 12th time after doing the same bit of a very long level 12 times is rage-inducing. I think a checkpoint system would help but in the same breath I think it'd take something away from the game. The grinding and repetitiveness is a good mirror of life in a totalitarian regime.

This is my time leaving a review, having finished the main game and most subquests at 38hours.
This is by far, the best game I have played in terms of storytelling and soundtrack. The combat is great too, but I can honestly say that no other game has had such an impact on me in term of the characters, the story, and soundtrack. Other RPGs series such as The Witcher, Fable or Mass effect might have a few touching moments, or solid tunes (a few moments in particular come to mind) but I can honestly say that NieR:Automata has more of that than those 9 games combined.
The dynamic soundtrack is a masterpiece, with most songs have multiple variations, shifting and changing in intensity as you progress throughout a zone, or as a battle intensifies in a seamless way that will impress and amaze. It may be cliche'd to mention how you'll get goosebumps or a chill down your spine as a result of a song, but I'll say it anyway, you will experience this phenomenon playing this game.
The combat is also very interesting, mixing hectic bullet-hell and hack'n'slash in a way I hadn't seen before (not having played previous games in the series or other platinum games). It's always fresh and engaging, with more than enough depth.
English: Subs or dubs? I played with dubbed english and didn't think the mismatch between mouth and sound was too distracting, or I was otherwise too engaged to care. 2 moments in particular in 35 hours wasn't too bad. I'm not convinced that the talking during combat, subtitles, hard mode and bullet-hell will mix well so I think I made the right choice with the high quality dubs. Some great english voice acting. But I haven't experienced the subs yet, I can let you know after my next full playthrough, which will be very soon: a testament to the very high quality of this game. Just as soon as I recover emotionally I'll get right back on it.
There is an original game called NieR or Nier:Gestalt, but I didn't feel that I lost too much not having played it (not having played it yet, it's been ordered I can assure you). Same as with the prequal series to Nier called drakengard or drag-on-dragoon, not too much was lost. They would have helped sure, and with a bit of research I can see might have made a few scenes more even more impactful, but I was never lost or confused as a result of not having played the original. Although a sequal, NieR automata stands on it's own competently, don't feel you have to hunt down the original game to enjoy this one.
You've not finished until you see endings A,B,C,D and E, don't be fooled by ending A or how it LOOKS like it's a repetitive play-through to see ending B (it diverges quite a bit and there is a lot you haven't seen, don't worry). Developer should have called it the end of the prologue or end of chapter 1, it's an utter shame if anybody misses out on the game thinking it's over, when it's only just started because of this wording mistake. If it's not 25 hours +, then you're not finished I promise.

I originally picked up Automation before it came to Greenlight, and even back then I was recommending it to car-nerd friends of mine.
As it stands at the moment, 23rd July 2015, what you get is a car design system. Giving you the ability to design vehicles in a period ranging from 1940 through to 2020, with a variety of different technologies and materials becoming available with time.
I'd talk though all the various parts of the designer screens, but there's enough videos on youtube by now for you to actually see it for yourself. However I will say that it's quite an intuitive system. The body designer is simple enough that just about anybody can make something they like. While the engine designer is willing to give you enough hand holding to talk you though why your design keeps exploding - and how to fix that. It's even able to show you how to develop a better engine for what you want to achieve. Want to build a high revving lightweight engine for use in a sports car? It gives you enough information to figure out how to do that. Want a heavy duty low-revving truck engine? Or an economy car engine? Same thing.
What it doesn't yet have is an actual career mode. And yes, that probably means that as it stands right now it's more of  a design tool rather than an actual game. But I'm confident that the guys behind this thing can get it done, given how much progress they have made already in the time I've been watching them.
Is it worth the money?
If you're a car nerd I'd say it is, but if you want to wait till they've got the career mode done I'd entirely understand your apprehension.

Devs seem to be very stubborn and do not realize the significance or timing of certain things in the automotive industry such as the year certain features were introduced or just how huge different types of engines are in certain markets/applications. Developers seem very reluctant to add new engine formats such as flathead, diesel, rotary, 2 stroke, Atkinson/Miller cycle, or different engine layouts such as single and twin cylinder engines or even something as simple as superchargers despite most of these having extensive use in the real world. I understand they want to get things such as a campaign and the UI running smooth and bug free before delving in and retooling their entire menu layout to accomodate new branching options... but as a player I value experimenting with engine design over any sort of campaign. However, despite this seemingly slow progress that is reluctant to ideas that would take this game to the next level this game has a TON of untapped potential.... and assuming the devs can actually finish the main chunk of the game before they all die of old age it is going to be as close as you can get to the engineering sim I've always wanted.

The game also allows the player to engage with the enemy or areas in a number of ways, it doesn't have to be as simple as point and murder if you don't want it to be.
That being said I feel that some of the contents within the story, like the characters, aren't quite up to the standards that I've come to expect with some of the games that I've played in the recent years. Maybe games like Spec Ops The Line, Kotor 2, Telltale's The Walking Dead season 1, and The Last of Us (just a few examples that spring to mind for me) shouldn't be compared to, and in turn hold back, my enjoyment of an older game but this is what happened continually in Deus Ex.

Call me biased, but I've owned and played this game since it was in beta. At the start I was brought back by quirky characters and a sence of humor that rivaled the old Ratchet and Clank games then all thrown into a hilarious adventure with other players. It all began with a deep nostalgia trip to when games were fun and light hearted. Secondly, the thing that sold this game was the soundtrack. The military marches of the Dominion, impending doom to those under their boots, and the light hearted hopeful tunes of the Exiles, looking for a new home after being chased through the galaxy by the imperial destroyers. Most importantly Wildstar's devs have been deticated and hard at work interacting and forming more and more lore for the players to imerse themselves in.
After playing a little longer the game fell to a single problem, it wasn't ready for release on launch. Bugs galore, many, many issues with servers going down and lag out the wazoo, PVP was unbalanced and had huge cue times, dungeons were even worse. Most of the comunity started to leave and the tide of players disapointed in the game for it's falls was nearly enough to kill it.
Still, I continued to play, absorbed in an awesome sub community of roleplayers who managed to keep my interest in the game strong. In all reality, the roleplaying community is probably what saved the game from losing everyone, (That and the overwhelming population of aurin.) Patch after patch and update after buggy update the game slowly became what it should have been on launch. But there was still 2 problems... The Exiles held a good 70% of the population, and the whole population wasn't enough to stave off some fairly long cues.
Steam... Today I'm glad to anounce that Wildstar is ready. After 2 years of twilight on the edge of death, the game is ready for you to come and play. Nearly all bugs have been fixed, the servers are stable and the game is as fun as it ever was in beta. Let us bring this game back to life, flood the servers until they bring back the dead servers. Make the devs cry under the playerlode. Because I know that I want to see Wildstar back in it's prime with optemistic players running through an unexplored world of posibility and hilarity.
If you're on the border of giving this game a chance, I chalenge you to get on the PVE server Evindra just for a few moments, Exile or Dominion, and meet up with some players, go into the capital city and find some older players if you make it that far. Learn what truly makes this game great. If anything, it's the community that's always willing to help, take in new players, show them the ropes and run a few dungeons.
Now enough standing around reading this.
You've got places to be cupcake.

NO THING is an atmospheric runner game where you turn left and right while a computer voice directs you and tells you about the bleak expressionist dreamscape you inhabit.
I enjoy this game a lot, but it's a matter of taste. (You have to tolerate repetition, enjoy vague sad stories, and be resistant to motion sickness.)
First off, it's very inexpensive.
If you like cryptic surreal media like OFF, Yume Nikki or Twin Peaks, you will feel at home here.
The narration is depressing, evocative and mysterious. The narrator talks about isolation and tedium and occasionally gives away bits and pieces about your role in the world.
The main sources of difficulty are long levels and the unintuitive camera perspective. Once you get used to it, it's still very fun. The gameplay is reflex-based and feels kind of like Super Hexagon.
The level design gets hostile, arguably downright cheap from level 4 on, with trial&error and leaps of faith.

I'll sum up this game in a single sentence: Turning left and right gets progressively harder.
There you go. Save yourself $3.99 and use the time you would have spent playing NO Thing doing ANYthing else.

This is a fun adventure game that references the old school roguelikes with many aspects of it's gameplay.

One important feature of this game is permadeath: when you die, you have to start over from the beginning. While this may seem frustrating (and it sometimes is) the game manages to keep itself from becoming boring by having randomly generated dungeons each time you go through. Dungeons come in many flavours, from the big and sprawling, to the small and simple; some dungeons might have cavernous rooms complete with waterfalls, or libraries that seem inviting and warm until a mage appears down a hallway and ends your game for you.
The weapons system, while somewhat basic, has multiple weapons all with their pros and cons. Hammers and maces have a slow speed, but they can knock enemies back; swords are slower than daggers, but they have a better reach. Bows are good for getting rid of the annoying flying eyes, and their more powerful counterpart, wands are just more fun. When you find a weapon in a dungeon it can be made of a variety of materials, including gold - which makes for a very cool looking hammer. They also come in qualities and some weapons may only be good for setting of traps.
The game also has a very good sense of atmosphere, the music goes very well with the style of the game, and the graphics (engine wise) are very good. The lighting is very smooth and the engine allows for some nice effects. The art is very well done and fits with the style of the game very well. This all combines to make the game a very immersive experience and even with the best armour hearing an enemy shout from behind you is enough to make you flinch.
Howevey, as this game is in early access there are some issues with balance, such as mages being extremely powerful, especially on the first level, when you don't have a lot of health. Hopefully all the issues will be fixed in the future and many new features will be added.
Also, some people may point out the lack of a tutorial - while there is a very rudimentary one on a piece of paper in the spawn area, I think this game is pretty well off without a detailed tutorial. Besides the bad use of randomization the entire combat system is "Hold down left mouse button, let go when neer enermy".

You also cant sell anything and there are poison monsters on the first level that will drop your HP down to 1 if one of your two random potions was not an anti-poison potion.
In short, the game is bad because whether you win or lose is entirely dependent on luck, and not player skill.

You are given many tools, props, and places to hide bodies to use to your advantage.  Poison, Fire, Bombs, Bear Traps, Bookshelves, or even an old knife will work. Not the best reviewer out there, but here is my take on the game as a casual strategy player.
Pros:
- Extensive government / ruling types.
- Large battles.
- Alliances, Federations, Vassals etc
- Events  (Think Medieval 2 Total War style)
- Forever changing galaxy with empires rising or falling & events spicing things up with a galaxy crisis.
- Sectors to avoid management hell.
- Workshop and decent mods.
- Game is not short, you won't win it in 5 minutes, let alone 5 hrs.
Cons:
- A few bugs, mostly visual - not game breaking.
- Limited range of default ship models (fixed by mods).
Feedback (Stories) for Developers:
1) As a user I would like to see an empire history log & family succession tree for monarchies.
2) As a user I would like more control in fleet battles (examples like Sins of a Solar Empire)
3) As a user I would like detailed planetary invasions / defences:
-- Think total war series - conquer the castle, bang the princess etc.....
-- Would like to build different defences (Ground to Air / Space / Ground).
-- Would like to strategically position & control troops in battle when invading / defending a planet.
Keep making this game awesome & take my money (buying DLC now as I finish this review).
