Wildstar is the type of MMO that tries to do something different, while still keeping things familiar. Everything toes the line between old school and new cool, and manages to keep stuff fresh.  Combat is fast paced action with an emphasis on movement and dodging out of telegraphed attacks. Everyone gets the ability to interrupt casts, which does more than just stop an attack, instead allowing you to deal extra damage.
The story is really interesting when you get deep into it, but admittedly can be a little difficult for a newcomer to get invested. You get little snippets here and there, the majority of them coming from the really well down solo instances that happen once every 5 levels or so. Beyond that, there's tons of little lorebooks and datacubes which build up the world and give you a reward for exploring every nook and cranny.
There is a lot of fetch and kill quests which can bog you down, but there's also a bonus in that most kill quests can be completed either by killing lots of little things, or just one really big boss. There's a bit of variety with your Path quests and more so with the challenges that pop up naturally while questing.
Beyond that, there's the dungeons and raids, which are by the far the best available out there. They're fun, challenging, and unique. You are going to need a lot of patience getting through them the first time, but battles never feel cheap. There's always something that could be done better, and with enough practice, any group can beat any boss.
While Wildstar is not really a "sandbox" MMO, it does offer one of the best Housing systems of all time. It lets you take nearly every single item in the game and stick it in your house and customize to your hearts content. You change the house (or build your own), change your ground, sky, music, and more. Even if you're not all that great at design, you can put in prebuilt plugs which give you a bunch of set decor and sometimes come with little challenges and quests of their own.
There's a lot in Wildstar to enjoy. It's biggest failing is probably never quite getting as popular as it needed to really drive all it's features home. But what's there right now is amazing, and there's tons of new stuff still coming.
Update: If there's one tip I can recommend to any new player, it's just enjoy at your own pace. Don't feel pressure to hit end game. Go and see the sights, play around with housing. Take time and have fun.

This is a seemingly very simple game, however I think it goes deeper than that. I actually managed to get past the first two levels and the dialogue was the most interesting thing I have yet to hear. It's like a book that you have to read over and over to really understand the meaning. It's like Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥(perhaps not AS complex) or As I Lay Dying by William Faulkner. At first it seems like it's all nonsense with seemingly poor sentence structure, awkward phrasing but then you realize it's like that for a reason, and since the arcade style game is actually challenging, it forces you to restart and really listen to what it is saying.
****-SPOILERS-**** sort of...
The game talks about you, a supposed "simplest office clerk" and the third level especially talks about people in your ear and it tells you to think two times implying (what I think would be) that you think twice before speaking and that you're supposed to listen to what "they" tell you. It does say after all that it is set in a totalitarian regime.
It gives off an almost "what's the point" sort of feel, as it also talks about you the "simplest office clerk" working 8 hours and sleeping 8 hours watching tv for 8 hours and things of those sorts, a routine that is mundane and what seems pointless. You having an office job that you work for 8 hours for, to bring bread to the table, only to be stuck in routine and do nothing in your spare time but something ordinary such as watching TV.
Life loses its meaning as it also talks about all those pointless interactions with people you have on a daily basis, one line in the game went along the lines of 'they hear you, but they don't really care about you or what you have to say' because to them you're just another "simplest office clerk". Emphasis on "simplest". They could have just said "office clerk" but no, the simplest was added, and I think that was just to put more emphasis on the whole concept that maybe this really all is pointless, working 8 hours a day, and sleeping 8 hours with people telling you what to do in your ear and you having to think twice about what to say because you're in a totaliatrian regime.
ANOTHER line that I really found interesting went along the lines of "hoping for happiness" after you do everything that they tell you to do. But I mean really, what happiness can you achieve when all you've done and will ever do is be a simple office clerk. It really (I think) focuses on the mundane aspects of life and puts a big emphasis on the whole "what's the point ordeal" and the repeating and following orders like a machine day after day.
Play level 3 and you'll get EXACTLY what I'm trying to convey. It's a really fantastic game. It doesn't need to be complex to get its point across, and I love these sorts of games where it really makes you think, yet it's so simple. Like Papers, Please. Maybe I read too much into this, but if you make it to the third level, and really listen to the dialogue, even in level two, you can hopefully see what I'm talking about.
Oh, another thing. What helps me pass levels is when you're turning, wait until half of the next platform horizontal to you is past your screen before you press to switch directions. I found it helped me with timing, and gave me a bit of reference as to when to turn.
ALL IN ALL, GREAT GAME.

Normally when i play an MMO i get to max level, play for a  month then quit because I'm bored. Wildstar really hooked me though. Having logged over 3000 hours in the last 2 years, here is my review:
Pros: Action Combat, Limited action bar, Dungeons, Raids, Style, Humor, Cash shop, Costume system, Lore, Housing, Classes, Addon support, Community
Cons: Open world content (post max level), optimization, population.
First and foremost, the combat in this game is absolutely amazing. The telegraph system is great at communicating what you should be dodging and most of the time you know exactly what killed you and how you messed up. Most of your abilities are skill shots so you have to aim your abilities. The telegraph system makes dungeons and raids a blast. They are absolutely my favorite part of the game. I never thought I would raid in an MMO, but damn these things are so fun.
The classes are really well balanced. I have at least one of each class at max level, and while I will never get bored playing my Spell Slinger, if I want to change up the play style i can hop on a stalker or a medic, dish out competitive DPS and have a different experience in combat.
I love the colorful cartoony style in the game and the humor is great. I definitely suggest reading the quest dialog the first time through. The lore and the humor is pretty great. Every time you level up and hear the announcer compliment you in different ways makes you want to hit the next level just to hear what he is gonna say this time.
The costume system is very similar to Guild Wars 2. An armor piece drops, you open your holo-wardrobe and unlock in there, now you can dye it and use it in a costume. I have spent so many hours in the costume system just tweaking things and seeing how different armor and color combinations work together trying to find that perfect costume.
The Cash shop is very fair. Almost everything in it can be bought for free with an in-game currency called Omnibits that you earn just from playing. Alternatively you can spend real money on Protobucks. Everything in the cash shop is cosmetic, or a convenience boost (flask of xp, flask of riches, costume slots, bank slots, etc). You never have to spend a dime to unlock anything except for the madame faye RNG boxes or recently the subscription bundles. The items on the cash shop are usually pretty cool, but none of it will make you a better player. Just a more stylish one.
Housing is by far the best I've ever seen in an MMO. I suck at it and that makes me sad. There is a big community in housing that loves to help out and make crazy housing plots. You can visit other people's housing plots and see some incredible builds. If, like me, you are bad at housing, some people are willing to make you a home, just give them the theme you want (and some platinum) and they will build something great.
The biggest problem this game has currently is the population. I suggest finding a guild that focuses on your desired end game and joining up. Most guilds will answer your questions, help you with gearing and runing and help with your action bar so you can be competitive. The community in this game is pretty great. If you like doing dungeons, finding a guild that enjoys them too makes it a lot easier and faster to get a group together and get into the fun stuff.
Optimization isn't great. While I can get 60 fps on the highest settings most of the time, 45-60 fps in raid, 40 fps in the main city and 100 fps in housing, most people don't have the computer specs I do and optimization is a gripe I hear a lot. The most significant issue i've run into with this is memory errors. They used to happen pretty frequently in raid due to the amount of stuff going on, it seems they have fixed that issue. Every now and then I get dropped frames, which are usually attributed to the amount of addons I use. I have found that purging addons I no longer use and deleting my addon save data helps a lot if the game starts feeling bogged down.
TL;DR: Wildstar is fantastic. Hit level 50 and do some dungeons, battle grounds, and get into a Genetic Archives (GA) raid to really give it a shot. I've played a lot fo MMOs and none of them compare to this IMO.

Delver is a roguelike- it's your basic dungeon crawler with permadeath in a somewhat generic fantasy setting that mostly impresses with a charming retro pixel look. That look, however, may be enough to get you interested.
As always, story is trivial and not even worth bothering about; there is a dungeon, there is a MacGuffin to retrieve from the dungeon, there are many enemies between you and said MacGuffin, and that's it.
Each game drops you in front of the dungeon, where a small camp has been set up; your equipment is chosen from a small random pool of low-quality weapon and armour, and then you delve in.
Navigating the labyrinth is easy and smooth, and the game instantly reminded me of Minecraft and Eldritch; it has the same blocky pixel look and oddly warped architecture. Older players will also think of Ultima Underworld (if UU had taken place in a more cartoonish world). Move with mouse and WASD, pick up and interact with E, attack with Space or Mouse, that's it; no jumping, crouching or extra casting buttons. It's simple yet effective.
Combat can be a bit botchy. Melee attacks can be "charged" to deal more damage, archery and spellcasting from wands or scrolls is straightforward, but there is no crosshair at all and it can take a while to adjust to that- I found myself constantly aiming too low to actually hit my targets. With a melee weapon that means a missed swing, but wasting a wand charge just because you didn't connect with the collision box hurts. The controls themselves, however, are precise and reliable so you'll get used to it eventually.
Killing enemies gives you money and loot and also experience; once you level up you can beef up your attributes as usual. Even a single extra point in speed or attack has noticeable impact on the game ,so it really matters, and that is a welcome touch. No need to put several points into an attribute before it pays off, you instantly benefit from your investment.
Difficulty is absolutely okay- a bit on the "hard" side but that's what one expects from a roguelike. The permadeath is slightly softened by the fact that you keep your money; after a while the coins allow you to buy some better starting gear in the camp, so you enter a new dungeon with better equipment and better chances to make it deeper.
So you have a roguelike that does nothing new. It absolutely delivers what you expect from the genre, dresses it in nice retro graphics and runs with it. It's more charming than breathtaking, more "familar fun" than the next brand new indie hit. It's worth checking out if you like a fun dungeon romp.
Delver's also still in development, so take into account that there's clearly MORE to come.

Delver is an addictive first-person Rogue-like, which implies randomization and permanent death -- you will lose your save data if you die. The graphics are fairly simple, being LWJGL (nerd talk), but have recently been updated into amazing pixel art that it beautiful to look at. Gameplay is pretty simple, based around a set of attributes, which from my memory, are Attack, Speed, Health, Magic, Agility, and Defense. You can change these around when you level up.
This game is not a role-playing game, or at least, it isn't by my view of the term. You won't be having thoughtful talk with the bandits encompassing the first two floors of the seven-floor dungeon -- you will instead smack them multiple times with your warhammer until they die. It has a story that's only implied, and is quite open to exploration: something about undead being raised with an orb.
I absolutely recommend this game to action RPG lovers everywhere, and it's only going to get better, because it's still Early Access; it'll get updated!

Quite possibly one of the best games I've played ever.  Definitely sitting comfortably at my GOTY spot until MAYBE something comes along that might dethrone it.  But after looking through the rest of the titles that come out this year, highly unlikely that's happening.
The only complaint I have is that instant-use items with no cooldowns kinda breaks most of the challenge that hard mode would have.  So long as you don't die in 1-hit, you can usually save yourself by spamming healing items.  Also the slow-down near bullets chip kinda breaks some sections.  Oh, and the resolution bug is kinda irritating, but is fixed by installing an easy-to-install mod named "FAR" (Fix Automata Resolution).  I also don't like that the game is locked to 60 FPS.  It still feels nice and all, but I have a 144hz monitor and I'm running a GTX 1070.  I wanna experience it ABOVE 60 FPS.  Oh well.  Still pretty solid port otherwise, good graphical options and the like.
The story was heart-wrenching and kept me in tears a lot of times, and the true ending was just...  More than I could handle.  I don't think I've ever had a moment in a game touch me quite like that did.
Please, do buy and play this game.  It is a masterpiece crafted with a self-evident love for games.  It's unlike anything I've played or experienced before, and you're really doing yourself a disservice by not playing it.  I will say that for some, it might not be worth the $60 price tag, even though it was well worth it for me, but if that is the case, I strongly recommend picking it up while it's on sale.  You will not be disappointed.

This game is a masterpiece, and you are REALLY missing out if you aren't playing it.  I expect this to shoot Yoko Taro onto the map of directors up there with Hideo Kojima.

You could be forgiven for playing through most of the first playthrough of Automata and perhaps thinking the overall experience is a little shallow. At the time of writing I am most of the way through the second playthrough, and the way the game has progressed in terms of gameplay, as well as mixing up the narrative, has been highly enjoyable throughout.
Platinum have a history of awesome action games, and this may well be their finest work. The way it blends various different shmup mechanics and side scrolling platformer elements with the more familiar Platinum beat 'em up gameplay is very satisfying, and the way in which the difficulty balances with your progress gives me the impression I’ll be playing this on and off for a very long time. The soundtrack also needs a mention for its exceptional beauty - it plays to the game's narrative and features a number of tunes which are just well written, fabulous pieces of music.
So in summary, the hype is real. I'm not really usually a big story guy in video games - if the gameplay is tight and it's fun to progress, I rarely find myself getting emotionally invested in a narrative. Here however the writing and overall tone of the story really gels with the rest of the game, creating an experience which I am really intrigued by. Peeling back the layers keeps surprising me, and I can't wait to jump back in.
The PC version sadly isn't without a couple of minor issues - the most major of which is easily fixable with a highly publicized fix (see the forums). None of these issues are game breakers however, and with the game's immense success and incoming additional DLC later this year, I’d like to think Square Enix are committed to this project, and we'll hopefully see a patch before too long. In a year where Japan has really shown the rest of the industry how you need to evolve video games in this day and age, NieR Automata is an absolute masterpiece of intelligent, thoughtful game design and a masterclass in how you write a good videogame story.

Ever since Splinter Cell Conviction I've been dying to see more stealthy action games. So, it is with great pleasure that I can inform everyone that Future Soldier delivers on this front. The tag-and-shoot element from SCC is back, now called Sync Shot. It works the same way; you tag up to 4 enemies and hold a button to shoot them down, all at the same time.
The graphics are detailed and sharp, and the voice overs are once again solid. It's a realistic looking game, and it looks great in motion with all the visors and gadgets.
Unfortunately the game becomes more of an action game during the last few missions - note that there's still some stealth involved, but it's more fast paced than the missions leading up to these last couple of levels. Nothing frustrating or annoying, but it's just someone people will notice I think.
With 10 hours of gameplay (single-player) the game was also surprisingly lengthy.
So - an incredibly fun game, and that's what games are all about.

In an era when classic 4x and other strategy titles can be picked up for £5, I was stubbornly wary of parting with my cash, caught between a mixed bag of reviews. But then I had a beer, and I made the leap. Being so cynical, yet having enjoyed my time with this game so much, I’ve taken the time to write my own review which will hopefully help someone somewhere to make up their mind, one day.  Maybe.
Who I am (where I'm coming from):
A nostalgic and tight fisted SMAC[1] head who pines after hard sci-fi, immersive storytelling and believable AI, living stubbornly in the illusion that programming these things ‘surely can’t be that hard, they’re just being lazy.’ I think low bandwidth Natural Selection[2] 1.0 three hour epics were the high water mark of western civilisation. Or at the very least were damn good fun.
-------------------------------------------
The Short, (the summary), buyers guide – Quick(ish) answer to the question “should I fork out £30ish for this game, right now, in this economic climate and these end times, where moments have never been so precious now there’s a tortilla bashing maniac with his finger on the button?”
In a word, Yes. Here’s why I think what I think.
This game is an excellent and immersive strategy title that tells a story. There is a strong role playing element and while an imagination is essential to making the most of your time playing it, you’ll still enjoy the game if you want to just switch off and burn every living thing in the galaxy, or turn it into a pretty spreadsheet. Stellaris throws a seemingly endless narrative of events, graphics and quirks your way, and while it doesn’t have the complexities of some of Paradox’s other titles, this is a deep and engaging strategy experience.
But… it isn’t just a pretty space challenge; it’s also a lot of fun. So much fun, I haven’t been tempted to hollow it out through min maxxing my way through it, which given my robotic tendencies, is possibly a first (It also made me question why I continued playing so many other, vaguely similar titles beyond the point at which they ceased being ‘fun’).
Be a race of xenophobic space mushrooms, purging the galaxy on an interstellar religious crusade. Be the fanatic scientists, unlocking the secrets of creation to hasten the evolution of their species only to doom an entire galaxy with their hubris. Be the shrewd peace loving diplomats, slowly manipulating their way into becoming an economic power house.
This is an immersive, fun and complex (enough) strategy game that is more than worth it right now (do get the leviathans expansion however– essential reading). Stellaris feels like a gem to me. A slightly polished gem too. It has plenty of issues and room for improvement (more on this in the long review), but far from making me feel short changed, I can see it has an exciting future. The team are dedicated and work hard, consistently producing beautiful things. They are involved with the community, responding to sensible feedback and requests, as well as not so sensible feedback.
To say this is a perfect game is absurd. And I’m definitely guilty of looking back on my gaming past with rose-tinted-to-the-point-of-being-deluded-kaleidoscope goggles.
But…
If you like 4x or anything sci-fi this is a no brainer. If you’re new to these concepts then this is a fantastic experience, and suitable for anyone who’s ever logged into a COD server with chat enabled and wished the sun would implode while there’s still time to eradicate us permanently. I've known Deus Ex since the age of ten but I never thought of writing my opinion.
Deus Ex is something big, something strong, something powerful, more than an adventure, it's a life lesson and a reflection about our humanity.
This is one of my favorite games for a simple reason: it's "perfect". Indeed, the graphics are old but is it necessary to be visually beautiful to achieve excellence? I don't think so.
A video game must be able to offer emotions and a good gameplay, Deus Ex can make it !

The narration is also excellent because it's about conspiracy but with intelligent and complex writing. The game avoids big clichés. We can think about the human race, our future, i's enriching. Moreover, there are many cultural references.
For all these reasons, i still play Deus Ex nowadays.
Finally, I thank a man I admire for his genius, I mean the creator of this game: Warren Spector.

Hexcells is, on the most basic level, a more sophisticated version of Minesweeper. You are given a layout of golden hex tiles, possibly with one or more of them already highlighted or flipped. Flipped tiles have numbers on them, and also labels indicating whether or not adjacent tiles which should be highlighted are continuous or non-continuous (or no designator at all). There are also row and column labels which allow you to see how many tiles need to be highlighted in any given row or column.
Each puzzle mixes these up in a unique way to push you to solve it.
Thinking about this game as a more sophisticated version of minesweeper is, I think, fairly ideal, because that is more or less what it is, and the function it serves. It is something to throw away a bit of time on, not sit down and play continuously.
But even then, you’re not looking at it taking all that long to complete; the whole game takes less than two and a half hours to solve, and that’s assuming you’re trying to get a perfect score on every stage.
It is about as fun as Minesweeper is, and I’d basically consider it filling that role in your game library.
My advice? Pass. It isn’t a bad puzzle game, but it isn’t anything remarkable either. If you did get it as part of a bundle or something, it isn’t a terrible thing to install and just screw around with when you’d mess around with solitaire or minesweeper or whatever, but I wouldn’t go out of my way to buy this.

First, let me be clear that this is NOT one of those rubbish Early Access/Greenlight games that Jim Sterling (thank God for him) makes infamous. Quite the opposite. This is a game with a small, but highly passionate and committed, team of developers who are continually making additions and improvements to the project (watch any of the Dev Updates on the Automation YouTube channel for evidence.) The game is definitely in an unfinished state but there's already quite a bit of quality content available.
Second, ask yourself this question: do you, or have you ever, wanted to build your own car? At this point in development, that's really all you're doing. But even in a simplified state such as this, it is still quite an involved and difficult task. There is a rather steep learning curve (especially if you have little experience in auto mechanics) but once you figure out the basics, building a car is a pretty smooth process. As I said, all you can do at this point is build cars and then run them (Note: not actually drive yourself though) around a virtual test track; there are three built-in but the forums have numerous other fanmade tracks. Eventually, the tycoon aspects of the game will give exponetially more things to do with your cars.
Overall, what you have here is a solid foundation with a lot of potential going forward. If you're a petrolhead, this is a must buy. $30 may be a bit steep at this stage of development (I very much enjoy the game and will concede that fact) but it is worth the investment, IMO.

This is a story about potential. If you like management games, business games and games where you design and create something, this will be definitely up your alley. Be aware that right now, the game is still somewhat early in its development stage.
You can already create a variety of engines, be it inline 4 or 6 cylinder ones or V6 and V8 engines. There are options to turbocharge your creations as well. However, all of this comes with the ability to customise almost every part of what you create in great detail and realism. To help with the mechanical engineering jargon and explaining what everything you touch does, the game comes equipped with a rather comprehensive set of tooltips and narrated videos, which will help you understand what parts of the engine do what. Especially this latter part is worthy of applause, since you will not only understand the game better and have more fun, you will also gain some actual knowledge of the workings of engines, suspensions and so on.
The game aims to be along the lines of Motor City, where you will create your own car company, build factories, design cars, engines and then sell them on the market through various good or turbulent times. The campaign is currently not yet implemented, but it is the one aspect I am truly thrilled about.
The creator part of the game is already pretty amazing in itself; designing engines and then testing them is a lot of fun, despite the fact that (right now) there's nothing else you can do with them, except put them in a chasis and have the car run a test track.
But, again, if you like these kinds of games, I strongly recommend you keep an eye on this one. It'll be a gem!

I am still very new to Automation, having played the stand-alone less than 30 hours and steam 24 hours as of this review, but considering every minute of that play-time was spent just tweaking and building engines, with some car building thrown in as well, I can safely say the full release of this game will easily be worth the current price.

Basically, if you like the idea of making your own engine from top to bottom and even getting to design the car it goes in with every detail thrown in from paint color to transmission and wheels, then you will like Autmoation in its current state.
However, if you like mechanical engineering but are more interested in the tycoon part, you might want to wait a little while unless you want to get your early practice of building engines in.
However, if you just want your run of the mill tycoon business game, Autmation may not actually be the best game for you.
From my current prespective of this game, it will be centered around the design and building of both engines and car designs, alongside the business aspect and market that would be associated with designing a car and trying to market it.
So if you just want to run a business, you will have quite the wait, and possibly should find a different game.

TL;DR
An overall excellent game that I would highly recommend to anyone.
Now, for the detail. First, I'd like to say that I have played this game for far longer than my steam hours. I played the gold edition disk for about 3 years before adding it to steam. I'd estimate I have something in the 600 realm of hours, 700 if you include steam time.
EDIT: 600/700 on gold edition CD. Add that to steam time.
On to the actual game. This game is a fantastic and educational experience about the middle ages. Even though some of it is innacurate 95% is correct, and you will most likely learn at least a few things you didn't know. To start with you have the option of 5 different factions, and by destroying other factions you unlock them as playayable. (orrrrrrr, you could just go into the files and change it so you can play as all of them straight away :)
The campaign map is a well designed and easy to look at part of the overall game, with a clear layout so that you can tell what is going on instantly. The controls and design for building and recruiting are made easy also, and the advisors are helpful to new players. (though annoying for more experienced ones) and you can get involved straight away.
Now for the best part. The battles are an overall incredible experience where you can lead an army into various types of battles; from raiding and capturing a castle to a field war of skill. As you play more, you can win fought out battles that you normally would not be able to or if the odds are stacked against you, and you become a true commander and build your empire.
The DLC (Kingdoms pack) is actually a very worthwhile DLC, bringing in 4 new campaigns packed with new factions, units and maps, however I would not recommend playing these until you have at least got the hang of the main campaign, as these are far more in depth and you will get more out of them after obtaining a basic level of experience.
To conclude, this masterpiece is my personal favourite in the series and I'd strongly recommend you play this over any other Total War title. If you are considering it, buy it. If it goes on sale, even better. Buy it as a gift. I'm sure someone will love it.

This review post, is not the comprehensive summary type, but something of a small (I wont go into detail regarding my conclusions, for brevity and as this is not the place for a propper spoiler filled discussion) summary of my assesment of Nier: Automata. Forgive me if the tone of this is somewhat pompous, again, it might be a summary for myself. I wish I could elaborate my points with explicit examples, but there seems to be some character limit which stops me from lengthening the review.
The OST is grand and in a tier of its own. It speaks for itself; go listen. This is not platinum's most exquisite combat, but bears their flair and is fluid. Story wise... while i dont hold it in as high a regard as many, I like it and recommend it greatly. Themes of identity, existentialism, suffering, hatred, conflict predicated on lack of understanding (etc etc the list goes on) are all present in various forms. While none of these are handled in a way yet unexplored in other media, it is still fairly novel, considering the title's general level of competence, among video games.
My praise is that the story and themes are well handled with personality, intent and ambition. The characters are well presented, becoming somewhat tangible and sympathetic even with only a small amount of material to them. Furthermore, the game is noteworthy for its use of the medium in presenting various perspectives to the player. Storytelling media can conjure many perspecives through many methods, games set themselves apart by adding the ability to form perspectives affected by player interaction. Or even just player presence. What Nier adds to this typical arsenal that is not oft seen in other games, is the exploration of the same or related scenarioes. EX, revisiting a previous scenario with new revelations such that a new perspecive is formed from contrasting with -and compounding on a previous perspective. Fans of the first Nier will know what I refer to. Though, I feel the first game was better in this regard, and part B does drag somewhat. I digress.
My chief critique for Nier:A, regarding artistic merit, is that, to me, it mostly just touches upon and mentiones its themes. At least, compared to a larger body of works, it could stand to probe deeper, and explore questions more fully. However, the work has seemingly touched people, and for the developers, as for any creator, that is likely more than enough. ^w^
My other critiques lie in how (aside from the current technical bugs, try the mod/fix FAR), while not short on material, it could hit harder still. And how sidequests, while core in how they add to the world and feel, severely hinder the much more intense pace of the main story. The lost intensity  could help the story build even better. Several story beats send mixed signals and information, this is mostly great, and also intentional. But, there are instances of world details and stakes being unclear and unexplained to the player in such a way that it undercuts the emotional impact of select scenes. Had the player been clear on the stakes for these scenes, they way the characters clearly are, their effect could have been greater.
This however, mostly apply to endings A and B, the holistic effect by the game's full end is quite good and even. And, for lasting impressions, I think that is what matters the most.
While I was not one of those who cried, nor did it come close, I did feel emotion. It did prod well at the right areas. For me I guess it just needed even more material and more of the precision, depth, cohesion, and nuance found in the best of other media.
I recommend this game on these grounds:
-It is different and project of ambition. It has a worthwile identity.
-It story and gameplay are both competently executed.
-It makes use of the medium. While not every game needs to be Automata. There is lots to be learned here, both in regards to detail and to approach.
-Its core philosophy resonates with me.
Note:
The game covers multiple playthroughs and endings. Keep playing. Notably, while playthrough 2 is a retread with new revelations, events thereafter are completely new. Thus, this first half up to endings A and B can be considered but the first act. Endings A, B, C, D and E should all be reached for the full experience.

No Thing is a weird blend of the traditional infinite runner genre, vaporwave aesthetic, the slight nausea of big airtime akin to a surfing mod in an FPS game, and visual disorientation. For a game with only two buttons it is surprisingly deep, both in execution potential and theorycrafting optimal routes; should I take this cube now? Next lap? Never? Players can tailor their choices to match their skill levels and try to complete this surprisingly difficult game.
What's also exciting about No Thing is the speedrunning possibilities. Given the technically optional nature of many of the blocks, the varying level completion requirements, and the opportunities to deviate from the intended course, you have a lot of unique ways for players to approach the challenges and try to finish the game as fast as possible. It's also a punishing game for a speedrunner; dying late on a level like 7 or 10 will set you back multiple minutes, meaning that there will be fairly big gaps between runs with 0 deaths and those with even a single death.
I would recommend this to most people who enjoy a unique challenge in their games. Level 7, for example, reminded me of the frustration I experienced in trying to complete Veni Vidi Vici in VVVVVV for the first time. The game lacks in depth of gameplay elements so if you're looking for something with a conceptually broad scope then you'd best look elsewhere. Additionally, while streaming the game I had a viewer experience some mild motion sickness. If you're prone to a motion sickness response from games, stay away.
Overall, this game is super satisfying and I definitely got more than my money's worth with the cheap price point. I plan to stream more of this game, and now that I've completed a run I'll be attempting speedruns of it as well. I encourage others to challenge themselves to do the same.

Party hard is a 2d pixil indie MURDER game,
developed by Pinokl Games and released Aug 25, 2015.
I should probably point out that my review and experience is only for the single player part of the game. I didn't hook up my twitch account and stream the game
.
I live by myself, and my birds don't know how to use controllers so I couldn't try out local co op.
I also didn't try out any DLC or workshop maps except for Dark Castle... which was Free (Also highly recommended if you buy party hard. that was a fun level.)
As far as the game is concerned this is simply a story about a man who just really wants some sleep, so he goes over to a neighborhood party and murders everyone.
There is a wee bit more that I could say about the story, but lets just say after you complete a level there's a short cut scene story going on, and at the end there's a bit of a twist.
The mechanics for Party Hard took me a while to get used too. Honestly it got to the point where I'd just stop playing and do something else, then come back to the game to try again.
The general idea is: Be patient, and the slower you complete the level, the easier it is to complete the level. The problem? I wanted to beat this game, and I didn't feel like being patient! So I died a lot to impatience.
Actually I don't know how much "fun" I had playing the game. It became more of a competition to see if I could get through the game, and grab the achievements. 12 hours and all of the achievements is a pretty good amount of time to spend playing an indie game... but I can't shake the feeling anyone not interested in achievements would probably play a few levels and just play something more enjoyable.
Not to bash the game... but... honestly the only thing driving me after beating the game
was the allure of getting the various achievements.
This is a tough game to say "you should get it!" or even saying "Don't get it!" It falls right between the lines yet again. I'll recomend it, because it works, it is entertaining for a while, and I didn't hate the time I spent playing the game...
But as far as a single player experience went, It's kind of "meh".
Thank you for reading my Review! Atratzu signing off.

Deus Ex is something big, something strong, something powerful, more than an adventure, it's a life lesson and a reflection about our humanity.

A video game must be able to offer emotions and a good gameplay, Deus Ex can make it !
To begin, I have to talk about gameplay. It's incredibly rich. Do you like to use force ? Then get the GEP gun. Do you like subtlety ? So hide in the shadows. Do you want to play as a hacker ? So hack the security systems. Do you like social contact ? Then discuss with the characters. Anyway, you just want to explore the places  ? You have this choice too.
You can also upgrade your skills and your body through nano-technologies.
About the universe, it's great cyberpunk, very realistic and immersive. The music is also great because it respects the spirit of places, situations, and there is a lively world. It's a pleasure to travel through cities such as New York, Hong Kong or Paris.
The narration is also excellent because it's about conspiracy but with intelligent and complex writing. The game avoids big clichés. We can think about the human race, our future, i's enriching. Moreover, there are many cultural references.
For all these reasons, i still play Deus Ex nowadays.
Finally, I thank a man I admire for his genius, I mean the creator of this game: Warren Spector.

Awesome game!  I thoroughly enjoy this game.
Each time you die, you start over.  But the experience is never the same.  It has a great replay value for several reasons.  First of all, the dungeons are randomized.  You will never see the same dungeon twice, which really keeps things interesting.  Second, you can play with friends.  Play through by yourself, and then get a different gaming experience by playing with some friends.  Third, you unlock a ton of cool stuff!  When you play though the game, if you get far enough, you will unlock new races, variations, hats, and companions.  All of this stuff keeps the game fresh, even after you have played through it a few times.
Another aspect of the game that I really enjoy is that this game is a challenge.  If you enjoy challenging games, then you will probably enjoy this.  If you are new to gaming, or just prefer casual games, this game might not be your cup of tea.
The biggest downside is that the game really needs an update, as it lacks balance in a few areas.  For example, I feel like the warrior falls off too hard.  He becomes really useless towwards the end.   Also some of the perks seem really useless.  Other than that though, this game is great and one of my favorite steam purchases so far.

I feel the videos and description of this game are very misleading.  The game is basically a hybrid between a platformer and a bullet heII game, with some random RPG filler content.  Gameplay consists of trying to make it as far as possible through randomly generated stages, and seeing how many "achievements" you can complete before you die.  There is no persistance and no saving your game when you haven't died.  Yes, I went into the game expecting "permanent death".  But not being able to save my progress when I haven't died was a serious bummer.  Same with there being a timer on every single level.  I went in expecting something akin to a hardcore terraria focused more on platforming and leveling instead of digging, and instead I got Contra with 1 life and no continues lol.
Putting my being mislead bias aside and just playing the game for what it's worth, there are other mechanics that didn't quite sit well with me.
The first being, the unlock system.  When you die, 0 to 4 chests will be displayed on the death screen.  I still haven't figured out what decides how many you get.  Anyway, you click each enabled chest, and it will give you any unlocks/challenges you've completed, or add a handful of points to your final score.  Here's the rub.  Unlike some games of this genre (FTL comes to mind), most of the unlocks have a very low chance of even unlocking.  For instance, one or two of the easier race unlocks require killing 15 monsters before dying, just to enable a 20% chance of unlocking it at the death screen.  20 percent!  For me, this turned into a 2 hour grind, repeatedly doing the same thing over and over, hoping to unlock something new to give me an easier start, only to have bad luck determine my 2 hours were wasted.  When I finally did unlock a couple new races and a "hat", their bonuses were pretty miniscule and ultimately left me feeling like they wouldn't help me much in further playthroughs.
Secondly, the constant feeling of being rushed.  When I first jumped into the game, I wasn't using a wiki and was playing blind.  Right off the bat, I was starving trying to figure out crafting combinations.  I start Googling looking for a wiki, start testing some crafting..  suddenly I'm being told I need to leave the level because the evil surface monsters are coming to get me.  About the 5th time it told me that (during another playthrough), I decide ok, I saw some awesome looking things in the trailer videos, lets see if we can fight the evil empire like we did in FTL!  ....nope.  Giant purple heads hit me for 9999something damage, despite me having like 10 hp lol.  I understand this is an intentional part of the gameplay, but as a new player (and even after playing a couple hours) I found this mechanic to be more annoying than fun.
Lastly, the crafting and inventory management.  The game has no level persistance and you have to keep moving to avoid hunger and the death timer, yet you have to stop and decide what items you want to keep or throw away/sell, manage durability, craft new tools just to progress each taking many clicks (make 2 piles of sticks, combine for first handle, combine with stick again for 2nd handle, combine stick with planks instead for sword handle, combine ores/bone/wood and such just to create a single useable material, only to require combining 2-4 of those materials for blades or 3-6 for armors...yeah.  It's just surprisingly time consuming for a game where you just lose everything soon as you die anyway.  With no in-game recipe list and no way to make crafting new weapons/tools faster, it feels like a massive speed bump slowing down otherwise fast paced gameplay.
If the game had some sort of persistant..  sandboxy...  whatever type mode, that could take advantage of the RPG/Rogue-like aspects and crafting, I would likely have 0 complaints.  Even if said persistant mode kept the permanent death (Don't Starve for example.  FTL also, to a lesser extent).  The graphics/music are both pleasant, and the fighting itself was responsive enough to be enjoyable.
I'm also annoyed at the comment that this game was influenced by a game like Monster Hunter, where 99% of the gameplay is 'permanently' upgrading your character with new equipment, crafted from rare items procured from complex and sometimes extremely difficult enemies.  I don't consider grinding for a chance to start a new run with slightly elevated stats, the same thing kek.  Just not for me I suppose.

WildStar is the platinum to the gold standard for Raiding, in the MMORPG genre.
(Ignore the steam time played for me. I hav 2345 hours on my main character, and 312 hours played on my 2nd main character)
If there is anything to play WildStar for, it is to experience the brilliance and sheer difficulty, and sense of accomplisment of the Raids in WildStar.
The raid content in WildStar is a refresh of classic large format raiding content, bringing back significant elements of teamwork and difficulty, along with whimiscal technology themed instances, kooky characters and legitimately difficult raid boss encounters.
WildStar is aa breath of fresh air in an industry stagnanted with casual, easy, and mindnumbing content designs that practically hands out gear just for being in game.
WildStar requires players to cordinate, and strategize, and then execute properly to find success, and that makes playing this game feel like playing MMORPGs for the first time again.
If you love to raid, it would be a shame to not expeirence WildStar's incredibly interesting, well designed, and difficult raid content.
WildStar as a Free To Play game, is very fair, and gives more of your money's worht in a purchase than most other MMOs currently on the market.
WildStar's cash shop system has lower prices relative to the items being sold, and most can be bought for account wide purposes.
For example
Weapon skins are roughly 5$ USD come in a 6 pack, one skin for each of the 6 classes, that can be claimed into your costume wardrobe. These are permanent claim, and can be swapped in and out unilimited amount of times and used on as many characters you have of that class. So for 5$ USD you get 6 Account Bound weapon skins, use them and unlimited amount of times.
As compared to 10~20$ in other MMOs that are single per character, non account bound.
Costumes, 10~15$ are account wide, no class restrictions, can be used on an unilimited amount of characters, repeatedly, with no restrictions. As compared to other games, which may have 15~25$ costumes, that are single character claim.
And ontop of that, there is a cash shop coin drop system, called Omnibits, that you collect up account wide, and then buy most of the cash shop items, without ever touching your wallet.
In short, in WildStar your money goes much farther. What you buy is worth the money, and if you can't buy, you can still work to get cash shop stuff.
WildStar's gameplay is incredibly dynamic, complex, and straight up fun. It combines Sprinting, Dashing, Strafing, Double Jumpping, and aiming all in the same package.
It is the most complex and involved combat and gameplay system in the MMORPG genre, and allows for a lot of fun ways of approaching PVE Encounters, and even just screwing around with things like Housing, and Exploration.
If you're tired of same old, half attempts with Tab targets, standing still, autoaim locking, and stutter stepping, WildStar throws all of that away, and allows you complete freedom of motion. Strafe away while DPSing like mad.
(I recomened geting a Razer Naga or Logitech G600).
In WildStar the game doesn't use Reticles, or Tab Targets, instead it uses geometric shapes called "Telegraphs" on the ground that indicate where you will hit, what is trying to hit you, and what is being casted to where.
No more mashing tab to cycle targets trying to find the right one. no more manual direct selecting a target. Aim, place your telegraphs at your target's location,and fire away.
TLDR;
WildStar is a very incredibly well done Raiding scene MMO that will challenge you and make you feel accomplished. It's extremely well worth your money when you buy something, but if not it drops a free in game cash shop currency regularly for you to buy cash shop stuff with. It has incredible combat that's a culimination of many other systems into one big and incredible system.

Medieval 2 Total War is the fourth game in  the Total War series. It is a combination of turn-based camping and real time battles.
Medieval 2 TW is a great game for every fan of the medieval time period and for every fan of a good strategy game.
The Grand camping is great fun as in every Total War game, but when it comes to real time battles, Medieval 2 stands out.
Player can set his own custom battles, where he can choose variety of factions to play. Custom battles can be ground battles or sieges of villages, towns, castles, forts etc. I find custom battles really epic and fun to watch. Watching artillery breaking down walls and killing loads of men is just great fun.
Another great thing in this game is multiplayer. You can play coop camping with your buddy or join/host a loby and play some epic battles/sieges with up to 8 players.
With M2TW Kingdons, you get 4 new DLCs and they come with their own campings, factions and units. Every DLC brings a new time period so you can experience the whole Middle Age from Crusades to finding America.
The MODS. Oh, yes... Good mods are what TW games are known for. There is a great modding community for this game. Mods like Westeros Total War, Elder Scrolls Total War, Third Age Total War etc. make a whole new game out of Medieval 2. My favourite mod is Third Age Total War which adds 2 new campings (Third Age Camping and The Fellowship Camping). This mod changes all the faction in the game with factions from Tolkien's Lord of the Rings books. There are Orcs of Misty Mountain, Mordor, Gundabad, Gondor, Rohan, Elves, Dwarves... Every faction has it's own units (yes, there are orcs, trolls, even Sauron, Balrog and  other iconic characters from the Middle Earth) and every unit looks like it came from the LotR movies.
A good number of these mods can be played online!
If you like medieval time period, if you like knights and epic battles, hell even if you just like Lord of the Rings, get this game (with Kingdoms DLC if you want to mod it!).

First, I'm going to preface this review with a couple notes.  If I could I would give this game neither a thumbs up or down.  So the best I can do is give it a thumbs up but I'll also give it a 4 out of 10.
To sum up what this game is, a poor man's Castlevania.  It feels like there is a rich world to explore but ultimately falls flat in showcasing it.
Character progression is done through leveling and assigning points to various passives and finding predetermined gear scattered throughout the linear levels.  Ultimately you will be using the same attacks and strategies the entire game.  Though I suppose the progession doesn't have to be too deep considering how short and easy the game is.
The voice acting is atrocious.  You will either become very annoyed any time someone opens their mouth or you will get a good laugh in between combat sequences.
There are worse games out there but Blood Knights isn't a whole lot better.  If you love vampires this game will quench your thirst (pun intended) for a few days.  15$ is way to much for this title though.  I picked it up in a bundle that is still available here:

I love the economics of the game. “How to gain the most gold and experience within limits” was a mini-game that I played continuously.
There’s nothing original about this game but for the life of me I couldn’t stop playing it. This is what it felt like playing Blood Knights. I enjoyed maximizing the gold boosts and experience boosts so that I could get those end tier weapons really quick from the shop trader. I think that alone was what kept me playing the game to the very end.
Some parts of the game are frustrating such as the platforming sequences due to undefined areas or camera shifting which lead to instant death. I’m forced to backtrack to checkpoints so that I don’t have to fight enemies over and over when I die due to bad jumps.
I like how my look changes when I change equipment. The graphics aren’t too amazing but they aren’t ugly either. Although I had fun playing on hard more the entire time, I wouldn’t play again even if there was a new game plus feature as there were a lot of aspects that were rough about the game such as the synching of cut scenes, odd voice acting, the hero becoming a sarcastic jester of sorts, enemy bosses that had potential to be great but were doomed to be uninspiring.
Blood Knights is a good bang for your buck as it a semi-solid action RPG that you can bite and suck on for a good few hours, granted that you are willing to ignore some of it’s flaws. It will suck a good chunk of your time and you won’t regret it as long as you buy this game during a sale.

What can I say, an action-RPG game set in a world with vampires and humans. Overall, it was a fun hack'n'slash... but short one. I recommend it though, as it was nice.
Pros:
-good graphics and sound
-some plot twists
-moral choices
-no bugs or crashes that I could find
-character upgrades (both gear and abilities).
-platformer (lots of jumping around, and it's nice when the camera works with you, not against you).
Cons:
-too short (normally you'd need 2 plays to get all content if you want to check both sides, but overall my almost 6 hours were one full play)
-the damned camera - the game is clearly aimed at consoles so the camera moves as you move, and it's annoying and creates problems in several parts of the game as your characters move further according to the camera. So, for example, you might click the left arrow to jump but as the camera shifts you also need to click the up arrow as your trajectory on the next jump, despite being the same, would now land you over the edge. Horrible camera, most annoying part.
-minor inconvenience: the SHIFT key is not an UP arrow for ages. This confused me and can turn away other players when they want to suck blood. You use SHIFT, not UP arrow.
Overall, as I said, it was a fun hack'n'slash with a terrible camera and a bit short. Still interesting while it lasted.

As a stand-alone game, not factoring the other Borderlands titles into this first part of the reivew, this game is lacking.  The slower movement due to the moon's environmental atmosphere is astonishingly disruptive for the gameplay goals laid out.  Quests are all across the maps and often cannot always be travelled to quickly aside from through this atmosphere.  Because of this atmosphere, enemies tend to move very slowly, allowing for near-perfect if not perfect aim far too easily, hardly making it a challenge.  It is a chore simply moving slowly.  The soundtrack lends to the snorefest as you are trecking mindlessly through each area with the ocassional floating enemy you can track until you feel like easily planting your cursor on his brain-pan.
Now, bringing the other titles into mind, comparatively, this game is, by far, worse than the previous Borderlands installments.  Aside from the slow movement and easily lined up enemy heads, the world is not exciting.  The quests are very bland with little sense of accomplishment upon completion.  Item drops are not exciting, and boss fights are fairly easy once patterns are recognized.  In some cases, quests are the same with a different skin.  For example, racing track quests/patterns are simply set in a different background.
The one thing that this game has going for it is the humor.  Worth the price at $5 on sale.  Otherwise, I would not suggest getting your hopes up on this game matching or beating the overall quality of its predecessors.  If you take away anything from this review, it is this:  Borderlands The Pre-Sequel is a DLC-quality game at a full game price.

My Review for The Adventures of Tree
Taking on the role of a formonger named “Tree”, you have to save the island from the evil Florps. There are a number of ways to win, such as to
Story 8/10
Good Different choices brought more game time and fun
Good Very fun and clever dialogue make this game enjoyable
Bad The florps are not in the game (Only 1 or 2) until you get to the final parts of the map which was annoying because I wanted to see more
Graphics 7/10
Good The cartoon like graphics showed happiness and joy but it also knows how to make the enemies look evil and dark
Bad Most of the items are poorly drawn and don’t have any straight lines or symmetry. Sometimes I enjoy that simple drawing but I believe it could have been done better
Gameplay 8/10
Good The combat was at first very difficult and I had to spend a bit of time trying to hit the enemy without being hit. But after you master this, the combat is very enjoyable and has a good level of difficulty
Good The weapons and armour had a good variety and each item had different effects to help the player
Bad The quests were basic but many didn’t point me in the right direction and I had to spend quite a lot of time looking around for just one item
Bad The consumable items had a good variety but many of these items (such as poison) had no reason to be in my inventory and there was no quest I could find that wanted that item
NPCs 7/10
Good The enemies attacked mostly in close-up and they run towards you when you are close enough but some do attack with range and some enemies just run away. This made sure I didn’t have to repeat the combat over and over again so I had something different all the time
Good The friendly NPCs sold items, gave quests or just random chatter. Each NPC looked different so everyone in the game was different
Bad Some NPCs were hard to find for quests and it would have been useful if they all had names so then the quests were easier, although I do enjoy the difficulty.
Music/Sound 9/10
Good The music in the whole game was so fluid and I loved it completely
Good The sound effects of fighting and actions in the game were on average because some sound effects didn’t make sense to me but I did not mind it that much
Good The NPC sound effects were very good and each enemy sounded different so when I couldn’t see the enemy in caves, for example, I could hear the sound of them so I would know what enemy it is
Settings/Configuration 8/10
Good Setting the audio was very easy and there were many options
Good Setting the graphics was basic and many of the options are already set perfectly for me to play
Bad There was no difficulty setting so I couldn’t make it a harder/better experience for me
Final Rating

Once upon a time, there was a handsome♥♥♥♥♥Canadian from Kamloops, BC that enjoyed the simple things in life - Cold beer, real maple syrup, bacon, poutine, and tax-funded healthcare. He didn't want after much, but one thing he did desire was a quality sci-fi grand strategy game that was highly customizable, with various 'endgame' challenges and an excellent random faction generator. He searched high and low, or at least he waited patiently and hoped, and one day his patience was rewarded by none other than Paradox. And from that day on, he Grand Strategied happily ever after.
Yes, friends, Stellaris is that fabled game. It is a wonderful introduction not only to sci-fi space strategy, but to the real-time grand strategy genre as a whole. Taking cues from past Paradox titles, as well as successful turn-based 4X titles such as the Galactic Civilizations series, Stellaris delivers an experience that frankly, has been sorely lacking. As a huge fan of other Paradox titles, as well as anything to do with SPEHSS, this game grabbed my eye easily and then pulled it out of the socket and proceed to make sweet hanky-panky with my skull.
Where to start... Stellaris is easily one of the most accessible, least intimidating grand strategies out there. It has enough complexity that you still need to pay attention to what you're doing and who's around you, but especially for people that have never played a GS game or have only lightly dabbled in the genre, you'll likely really enjoy this one. Veterans and hardcore fans of Grand Strategy might find Stellaris a little to simple and easy mind you, so keep in mind that YMMV.
-MODS-
One of the things that I love most about Stellaris though is how easily and extensively it can be modified however. Want to add a Star Destroyer, the Pillar of Autumn, or a Mars Class Battlecruiser as a ship model? Custom ship themes will allow you to do this. If it can be made into a 3D model, imported into a theme, and then packaged and put up on the workshop, then you can have it in your game! The same goes for everything from your empire's symbols, flag backgrounds, race portraits, names, etc...
-GENERAL GAMEPLAY-
Gameplay in Stellaris plays a lot like Victoria, Hearts of Iron, CK, EU, etc... in that you're given the world map (In this case, a galaxy populated by anywhere from dozens to hundreds or thousands of stars) and left to conquer it through a variety of means. This could be done by peaceful acquisition of occupied planets and settling of unoccupied ones, it could be through the flexing of military might, or through shrewd diplomacy, by getting other races to fight eachother so you can swoop in and "clean up" the leftover mess. Standard fare. But be cautious, because there are some crazy powerful "Fallen Empires" that you can include in your game, and frankly they're massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Never trust them. Ever.
Politically, you may have to deal with everything from elections to usurpers to racial, independence, or economic driven riots and rebellions. The political system, while not terribly deep, does make the game more interesting and the fact that some of the people of your worlds may develop new traits that put them at odds with the rest of your empire will keep you paying attention to where you draw future colonists from and where you station your fleets. Some of your more distant worlds may require a peaceful "persuasion force" of battleships in low orbit to keep the population from getting any smart ideas.
Star systems are handled in two ways: Cores and sectors. Core systems are few, and allow the player to have direct control. Typically, these solar systems will be either in the heart of your empire, or they'll be on a particularly dangerous border where you need to be able to control military defense infrastructure directly. Sectors are basically automatically governed, but you can set some rules and limits to how that's done. One of the good things with sectors is that a governor applied to a sector will apply their bonuses to every world in it. So if you have a sector with a ton of industry, and a governor with a bunch of industrial production bonuses, then you've got yourself a recipe for fleet spam!
-COMBAT-
Battles are handled in real time. There are some formation orders that you can issue to your fleets, but battles are pretty much hands-off affairs of "Point your fleet at their fleet, fly at eachother, and shoot ALL THE LASERS". Basically, the *FREEM*ing will start and won't stop until one side is dead or runs off. It leaves something to be desired, but with how big and crazy battles can get, I see why they did it.
-COLONIZATION-
Colonizing worlds is really similar to the Galactic Civ series - once your scientists scan a habitable planet, you have colony ships loaded with colonists who carry the traits and ideals present on their world (multiple different groups of ideals and/or species on one planet will give you a choice of which group to recruit from if applicable), and you tell said colony ship to colonize a world. It will do so, upon which you pick the tile to make landfall on, clear away any hazard tiles, and then have a finite number of tiles available to settle on in direct relation to the size of the planet or moon. Be aware that your race's homeworld ecosystem type will directly influence which planets you can settle on at first. If you play a race of anthropomorphic Polar Bears from an arctic world, then you can only settle on arctic, alpine, or tundra worlds to start. Anything warmer will be too inhospitable for you until you research the right tech to either settle them or, better yet, terraform them. The same goes for other climates.
-UPGRADES-
Upgrading and designing new ships was done with ease-of-play in mind. This is great for the player that wants to just come up with new configurations and play the game itself, but for players more partial to Galactic Civ's method of build the whole ship piece by tiny piece, it won't satisfy. However, for the former it is extremely satisfying. You pick your ship class, you pick the hull design or hull segments you want (IE Front A/B/C, Midsection A/B/C, Engines A/B/C) and then populate it with weapons and modules that correspond to the available size or type slots on the hull pieces (S/M/L/X/T/P/H). When  updated versions of the weapons or modules become available, you simply open that ship, replace them in the design, and overwrite it. All ships of that design will auto-update over time and for a fee. No deleting mountains of obsolete designs like in GalCiv, Paradox knows how to make things simple!
-RANDOM EVENTS-
In terms of random events, I don't want to spoil anything but rest assured - there are a ton of them and they're all over the place. From planet-based events, to entities and units in star systems, anomalies, multi-stage investigation missions, election promises, and more!
-THE GUD STUFF-
Honestly, and we all know Canadians can't lie worth a damn anyway, Stellaris is one of the best games to come out of 2016 in my opinion. It takes elements of what make Grand Strategies so great, combines them with elements of what makes Sci-fi 4X so great, and then gives a simplified version of both styles of game that still has enough challenge, depth, and complexity to keep the average person entertained. And while some criticize Paradox for their habit of supporting games for years after release with mountains of tiny, cheaply priced DLCs and a few big expansions, I for one love this model. It will keep the game fresh in exactly the way I want it to be, without having to pay for the stuff I don't want.
TL;DR, Stellaris is something of an underrated diamond in the rough. Paradox created a real gem here, and if you love strategy games (and moddable ones at that), then you absolutely don't want to miss out on Stellaris, which deserves a solid 8.5/10 in my books.

Originally, I was pretty hyped for this game. A long while ago, I posted a very positive, albeit theatrical review of this game. However, time has changed. I played this game for quite a while, progressing as I could and playing quite a bit. But, honestly, I eventually reversed my opinion almost entirely.
This game had so much potential. The weapon building system is probably the only good thing about it. Building weapons and testing them is hours of entertainment.
But, the problems begin here:
--Microtransaction hell.
This game suffers greatly from how the developers put in so much content, and then made so much of it based around microtransactions. Any valuable clothing, taunts, or extra weapon space is entirely dependent upon how frivolous you can be with your wallet.
--Getting cash and experience is a slow, strained crawl.
Eventually, after the first few levels, you'll find yourself going ten straight games, only putting a small notch on your experience meter. This limits what you can unlock, as quite a few of the slots for weapons (which aren't dependent on you spending money) depend on you leveling up. Slowly but surely, you'll finally reach the next level-up, but to be on-par with everyone else on your level, you need "Blutes" to unlock new weapons. However, it is such a slow drag to get the Blutes you need to change your weapons' configurations that it's hardly worth trying. Eventually, you have to be frugal with what you buy, which is odd in such a balls-to-the-wall game.
--Weapon level-ups take an eternity.
I believe I reached level 15 before finally being able to actually upgrade one weapon piece. And, even then, it provides a pathetic boost to the part. All of the upgrades for your weapons depend on points you earn (or, simply, kills you get) while using that weapon. Therefore, if you create one weapon you really like and use a lot, you could eventually level that up after an eternity of unlocking the parts for it, and then continuing on to upgrading those parts' stats. However, if this weapon isn't an all-around death machine, you're in trouble. For instance, if you have a one-shot launcher that performs incredibly well, you might find that it lacks in range, speed, or explosion size. So, to compensate, you create a powerful automatic weapon. However, that new weapon will not be on-par with your old one by far, and you have to focus on getting kills with this new automatic weapon to have a chance of leveling it up. You have to train yourself to stop using the weapon you adore so that you can level up this pathetic new gun so that it compensates for the hole in your defenses from before. And you'll find that you've become less proficient at killing than before because of the drastic change. It's not worth it, and if the leveling system was a bit more fluid and quick, maybe it would be fun to try new weapons with older ones.
--This game isn't really Play-To-Win like they say it is.
True, you don't have to pay anything to do well. However, if you do pay, you get Double (or more) XP and Blutes with just about any microtransaction pack, making you advance faster than someone who decides to not pay anything. Also, paying gets you extra weapon slots, and, in this game, having a large inventory of diverse weapons for every situation will benefit you more than having one specialized loadout for one specific purpose.
--Balls-to-the-wall goes over-the-shark.
This game's comedy seemed fresh and hilarious at first. But, soon, an obese woman twirking on the Victory/Defeat screen gets old. And so does dragging out death animations for humor. This game might have a style, and it works on some level, but its over-the-top nature will become grating and annoying to just about anyone who has to sit there and stare at it for hours.
Summarization: Good concept, one fun mechanic/system. HORRIBLE EXECUTION.

Deus Ex isnt a flawless game, no, but a pretty ♥♥♥♥ing good one. It was a great game back then and it still holds up.
Deus Ex is a Dystopian-Cyberpunk themed first person shooter/RPG with a heavy emphasis on the Main Story. You play as a Badass Agent called "JC Denton" working together with your Brother Paul Denton for a Organization called UNATCO. You travel all around the Globe starting at New York, a city in chaos that is only a former shadow of itself to Hong Kong and even Paris.
The Gameplay of Deus Ex is that of a basic first-person-shooter with a sandbox-like approach to the game. You can be a silent Assassin who uses only Melee Weapons or you can be a GunNut who goes in Guns' blazin and kills everyone in sight. Or you play as a Pacifist who's also a elite hacker that just passes by Enemies undetected and uses a security drone to see enemies from afar. You can approach the missions as you please.
Positives:
-Fantastic Soundtrack
-Excellent Story about Conspiracys and secret organizations like the Illuminati, MJ12
-Sandbox-like Gameplay, you can play as who you want be it a Assassin, a Soldier, Pacifist or a hybrid. The Choice is yours
-a awesome Main Character, JC is a more realistic RoboCop who's also a releatable character, hes just very Human-like after you discover who JC really is.....
-Nano Augmentation allows for even more Variation. Being able to deploy a Drone with an EMP Charge or being able to regenerate Health or being ressistant to Poison and Fire, Being as fast as a Olympic Athlete and jumping like a god, NanoVision, you name it! Be careful though, can only have a limited amount of Nano Aug's installed
-The Playtime being between 20 if you rush the Game and do only the Main Missions, 37 - 40 if you take your Time explore the whole Game
Contras:
-Outdated Visuals (its a old game i know but it wasnt even the best looking one when it released)
-Hit or Miss Voiceacting is very present in this Game. It has probably some of the best VO i have heard in my Life but also some of the absolute worst, in a Game that is "Dialogue Heavy".....
-Mentally Handicapped A.I so dont expect Metal Gear Solid or something...
-Odd and Weird Gunplay. The Gunplay in Deus Ex isnt really that great...Only because of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Aiming System that they implemented. If you dare to move a inch while shooting you while miss like a whole Assault Rifle Clip. To succesfully hit someone you have to crouch and wait till your Crosshair shrinks, if done correctly you will be much more precise.
-Some Skills and Nano Augmentations being completely useless and/or situational (cough swimming)
-A somewhat dissapointing last-level, dont get me wrong the build up to the Finale was fantastic and all but the Level itself was just boring and frustating. Because Plot there are respawning Enemies including the Grays (i wont spoil it for you who the Grays are) who are the last kind of enemies that you will encounter in the Game
Nooooow lets wrap this up, shall we?
Deus Ex gets a 9/10.

It looked great when I saw it on sale, so I picked Delver up. There are definitely a lot of good things going on with this game, and it has the potential to scale into something truly massive and amazing over time. I haven't tried the custom mod tools yet, though I'm hoping they provide options to greatly increase the depth of content available.
After finally playing through it in its current state, I feel like I missed something - or the game is missing something - because it took me all of 1.6 hours to learn the game and complete it (even the run back) and the lack of a meaningful ending left it feeling like a hollow victory.
I'd really love to talk with the developer and community together sometime to explore the current state of the game, and determine ways in which Delver could be made more amazing and worthwhile for everyone to buy and play. I was hoping for something that scales more like Diablo, 20+ floors and constantly rotating out gear for better stuff throughout the game, multiple classes with variations, well-defined boss enemies, or just to have truly everything randomized and have every experience be a new adventure. Right now the potions and dungeon layout are the only things which change, the variety of loot is rather static, and I come in exactly the same every time.

There are a lot of reviews on here already explaining the pros and cons of Wildstar, most of them with merit and should be taken to heart, be it negative or positive.
I'm going to take this opportunity, however, to talk about the community you are about to join.
I have been very fortunate to be a member of this community since beta, and am amazed that the majority of the player base is still as friendly as ever. Accepting, inviting, helpful. It almost seems like a limitless amount of guiding hands to usher people forward in the game.
There are, of course, some chat channels where you will need a thicker skin than in others. But even in those chats the people willing to help out new and old players alike greatly outweigh those that would dismiss you. The community of Wildstar makes the game feel like a home away from home while sitting at home.
The height of friendliness lays in the gem of Wildstar, housing. Be it advice on how to get started, player run contests for fun and prizes, or people giving away decor just because they're in a particularly good mood that day, there is never a lack of helpful, wonderful, people.
This has been, for me, a game that has built lasting friendships. I hope your experience with the players of Wildstar mirrors my own and many others.

Picture WOW, but in space, with space cowboys, bundled up with borderlands-like quirks. i have spent countless hours playing this as a F2P player, and might i say, the experience is truly rewarding. last i played (which was about 1-2 months ago;had to stop due to technical issues) there was, and probably still is, this currency known as omnibits, kind of a silver level currency (bronze being actual game currency to purchace most usable items, and gold being protobucks, wildstar's prenium currency) Omnibits can be used in place of protobucks (for a higher price of course) to purchace various items, consumables and services, and as an added bonus they also drop alongside regular loot. using omnibits, i have purchaced several cosmetic dyes, and expanded my character slot allotment from the F2P base of 2 to a total of 6 slots. i have a lvl 32 main, and a lvl 20 alt. housing is unlike anything i have ever seen in an MMORPG, complete and utter freedom to do what you want, create whatever plot that you want

I've really enjoyed what I've played of car mechanic simulator 15, but I was looking around for something a little more in depth. I came across this and gave it a go.
I set out to make an awesome muscle car with a powerful v8 engine. I'm not much of a car expert, but the tutorial videos explain every option in the design process very well. I enjoyed the explanation of RPM and torque, very australian.
I gave it a standard 70's muscle car shape, Standard double circular headlights and the like. I went on to make the engine, was a fairly nice looking v8 with 32 valves. After a bunch of tweaking, I eventually got the engine to stop knocking and in a reasonable working order. Building the rest of the car was just as detailed, such as suspension, brakes, internal parts such as seats, safety features and so on.
Finally I sent it to the test track. It basically did poorly in every category, except safety. It ultimately became the perfect overpriced car for a man to buy in a midlife crisis that knows nothing about cars, but is too safety conscious to buy a motorcycle.
