Medieval 2 Total War is the fourth game in  the Total War series. It is a combination of turn-based camping and real time battles.
Medieval 2 TW is a great game for every fan of the medieval time period and for every fan of a good strategy game.
The Grand camping is great fun as in every Total War game, but when it comes to real time battles, Medieval 2 stands out.
Player can set his own custom battles, where he can choose variety of factions to play. Custom battles can be ground battles or sieges of villages, towns, castles, forts etc. I find custom battles really epic and fun to watch. Watching artillery breaking down walls and killing loads of men is just great fun.
Another great thing in this game is multiplayer. You can play coop camping with your buddy or join/host a loby and play some epic battles/sieges with up to 8 players.
With M2TW Kingdons, you get 4 new DLCs and they come with their own campings, factions and units. Every DLC brings a new time period so you can experience the whole Middle Age from Crusades to finding America.
The MODS. Oh, yes... Good mods are what TW games are known for. There is a great modding community for this game. Mods like Westeros Total War, Elder Scrolls Total War, Third Age Total War etc. make a whole new game out of Medieval 2. My favourite mod is Third Age Total War which adds 2 new campings (Third Age Camping and The Fellowship Camping). This mod changes all the faction in the game with factions from Tolkien's Lord of the Rings books. There are Orcs of Misty Mountain, Mordor, Gundabad, Gondor, Rohan, Elves, Dwarves... Every faction has it's own units (yes, there are orcs, trolls, even Sauron, Balrog and  other iconic characters from the Middle Earth) and every unit looks like it came from the LotR movies.
A good number of these mods can be played online!
If you like medieval time period, if you like knights and epic battles, hell even if you just like Lord of the Rings, get this game (with Kingdoms DLC if you want to mod it!).
You can get this game for 1-5 dollars on sites like♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and it is definitely worth it's full price! (not like some other Total War games, sadly).

My honest opinion:
The AI is what really stands out. It's just as competent in battle as Attila's (the most recent TW title) is, and does well in the campaign, too.
The tactical (battle) part of the game has aged incredibly well, all things considered. The combat mechanics are robust, and abilities are important (though a bit 'busy' in terms of interface, and fire-at-will is not always enabled by default on units that are meant to only fight at range). The asymetry in rosters means that combat can really vary a good deal, yet the balance feels just right.
The strategic (campaign) part of the game aged less well. It's certainly playable, and it, too, feels balanced yet complex, but I'd be lying if I said the user-interface was all that good. As campaign UI goes, it's somewhat cluttered IMO, though I'd argue it's probably better than N:TW's was.
In technical stuff, it's really, really stable, something that inexplicably was not the case in Empire and N:TW... in those games, I seemed to get sound glitches on the campaign screen, crash during battles, and so forth pretty much every campaign, forcing constant saving to be ready. Here, though, the game never seems to glitch up or break down.
In artistic stuff, the game does quite well. For the era it was made in, the unit cards are good, and the unit models are surprisingly detailed when you zoom all the way in. The music is great, too. And the voice-over is, as always, the one mixed-bag (aside from the campaign UI, which was mentioned above). Voice-over work is terrible for units, but acceptable for in-game advisor and narration of pre-battle stuff (in historical battles, etc.).
Overall, is it worth it for $20.00? Well, without mods I could see arguements that $20.00 is too high... but bear in mind how long the game has existed and how many people made mods for it, and it becomes evident that there will be plenty of mods to wade through and try.
So, I marginally recommend it. A decade ago, I'd say to pick it up in a heart-beat... today, it's still just as good, but should really be a bit cheaper given that you will want to get the Kingdoms expansion as well and, hey, it's a pretty old title now (both it and the ex-pack).
On sale, though, it's a no-brainer: pick it up.

Blood Knights... Blood Knight?... well it should be called Blood Knight because there is only one knight and the Vampire Mistress Alysa... isn't exactly a knight but more a Huntress.
Okay now that the basic title misleadings are out of the way, lets write something about the game itself.
Well you might have guessed it, Blood Knight(s) is about Vampires, you play as either a Vampire Huntress which was bound by a contract or as a human knight.
The basic idea behind this is / was, to exploit the Vampires power against their own kind... but as such plans are always prone to fail, this case here makes no difference.
Very early in the game, the male human counterpart finally dies and turns into a full vampire... much to the displeasure of his following knights and the priest Bartholomäus.
The priest and the knights, now your enemies, catch your strange duo in no time but fail to properly execute them, again these type of mistakes are prone to lead to ones downfall.
You don't push a hero from a cliff and leave in the thought that the fall has killed him. You behead him, chop him into pieces, burn his remains and spread them in the ocean.
That is proper hero disposal procedure, to be read in the "The Top 100 Things I'd Do If I Ever Became An Evil Overlord" paragraph 13, which can be found here:
.
But to their defense, neither the priest nor the knights probably read that written piece of knowledge nor are they anywhere near of being an evil overlord.
Now without further spoiling the storyline, lets say something about the gampelay.
(To be fair, Blood Knight(s) is probably a game you would want to play together with a friend, a huge monitor / projector or tv and a box full of cooled beer, neither was to my avail during my run... which kinda reduced its possible fun factor.)
The principle is simple, it's a basic third person hack and slash game, with rpg elements, based upon a very very linear storyline and with only the smallest amount of free choice a player can get. This manifests itself with having the freedom to chose weapons and gear as well from a short list of abilities which can be upgraded as well.
Now each of those two playable characters (Alysa the Vampire Huntress and Jeremy the former Knight) feature a very different set of gamplay, focusing with Alysa only on ranged fighting while Jeremy is more fit for the rough close combat brawl.
And here is also the point with the most lost potential, combat just doesn't feel super awesome with neither characters, just okay-ish.
Alysa for example seems to be somehow overpowered which shows mostly during the endbosses where she can run before a boss for hours, pumping he/she/it full of arrows from safe distance, while Jeremy has serious problems with everything that can't be stunned or tossed or in anyway kept from harming him which is mostly the bosses or minibosses.
Another flaw or rather an uninteresting necessity (in single player), is the switching between chraracters, it does not work well with the rather fast paced combat and you always have the feeling that you made the wrong choice.
My biggest grudge is with the jumping sequences and the incoherent camera angles such sequences always seem to come with. An annoying amount of deaths was caused not by the game being ultra unfair or hard BUT by strange camera angles during those jumping sequences.
To its redemption, as sayed, combat is rather fast paced, it won't let you hang for hours searching for something to battle, puzzles (if those could be called that way) are easy and the game provides you with a steady stream of gear and gold as well as experience points for leveling up. Save points are also not very rare and in my opinion are not to badly placed.
So to say something about performance, first time starting, I was plaqued as many others with this strange stuttering where the framerate was down to 5 - 10 fps, a pc restart solved that problem. There was only one instance I could call a BUG where the game script broke and did not notice that I had liquidated all enemies in an area. Luckily there was a save point just before that and reloading an redoing that one segment brought me save over it.
All in all, this is not a bad game and could be a fun game with prerequisites like a second player, a cooled box of beer and a huge monitor.
Having written down all of this, I will give it a positive note.

Once upon a time, there was a handsome♥♥♥♥♥Canadian from Kamloops, BC that enjoyed the simple things in life - Cold beer, real maple syrup, bacon, poutine, and tax-funded healthcare. He didn't want after much, but one thing he did desire was a quality sci-fi grand strategy game that was highly customizable, with various 'endgame' challenges and an excellent random faction generator. He searched high and low, or at least he waited patiently and hoped, and one day his patience was rewarded by none other than Paradox. And from that day on, he Grand Strategied happily ever after.
Yes, friends, Stellaris is that fabled game. It is a wonderful introduction not only to sci-fi space strategy, but to the real-time grand strategy genre as a whole. Taking cues from past Paradox titles, as well as successful turn-based 4X titles such as the Galactic Civilizations series, Stellaris delivers an experience that frankly, has been sorely lacking. As a huge fan of other Paradox titles, as well as anything to do with SPEHSS, this game grabbed my eye easily and then pulled it out of the socket and proceed to make sweet hanky-panky with my skull.
Where to start... Stellaris is easily one of the most accessible, least intimidating grand strategies out there. It has enough complexity that you still need to pay attention to what you're doing and who's around you, but especially for people that have never played a GS game or have only lightly dabbled in the genre, you'll likely really enjoy this one. Veterans and hardcore fans of Grand Strategy might find Stellaris a little to simple and easy mind you, so keep in mind that YMMV.
-MODS-
One of the things that I love most about Stellaris though is how easily and extensively it can be modified however. Want to add a Star Destroyer, the Pillar of Autumn, or a Mars Class Battlecruiser as a ship model? Custom ship themes will allow you to do this. If it can be made into a 3D model, imported into a theme, and then packaged and put up on the workshop, then you can have it in your game! The same goes for everything from your empire's symbols, flag backgrounds, race portraits, names, etc...
-GENERAL GAMEPLAY-
Gameplay in Stellaris plays a lot like Victoria, Hearts of Iron, CK, EU, etc... in that you're given the world map (In this case, a galaxy populated by anywhere from dozens to hundreds or thousands of stars) and left to conquer it through a variety of means. This could be done by peaceful acquisition of occupied planets and settling of unoccupied ones, it could be through the flexing of military might, or through shrewd diplomacy, by getting other races to fight eachother so you can swoop in and "clean up" the leftover mess. Standard fare. But be cautious, because there are some crazy powerful "Fallen Empires" that you can include in your game, and frankly they're massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Never trust them. Ever.
Politically, you may have to deal with everything from elections to usurpers to racial, independence, or economic driven riots and rebellions. The political system, while not terribly deep, does make the game more interesting and the fact that some of the people of your worlds may develop new traits that put them at odds with the rest of your empire will keep you paying attention to where you draw future colonists from and where you station your fleets. Some of your more distant worlds may require a peaceful "persuasion force" of battleships in low orbit to keep the population from getting any smart ideas.
Star systems are handled in two ways: Cores and sectors. Core systems are few, and allow the player to have direct control. Typically, these solar systems will be either in the heart of your empire, or they'll be on a particularly dangerous border where you need to be able to control military defense infrastructure directly. Sectors are basically automatically governed, but you can set some rules and limits to how that's done. One of the good things with sectors is that a governor applied to a sector will apply their bonuses to every world in it. So if you have a sector with a ton of industry, and a governor with a bunch of industrial production bonuses, then you've got yourself a recipe for fleet spam!
-COMBAT-
Battles are handled in real time. There are some formation orders that you can issue to your fleets, but battles are pretty much hands-off affairs of "Point your fleet at their fleet, fly at eachother, and shoot ALL THE LASERS". Basically, the *FREEM*ing will start and won't stop until one side is dead or runs off. It leaves something to be desired, but with how big and crazy battles can get, I see why they did it.
-COLONIZATION-
Colonizing worlds is really similar to the Galactic Civ series - once your scientists scan a habitable planet, you have colony ships loaded with colonists who carry the traits and ideals present on their world (multiple different groups of ideals and/or species on one planet will give you a choice of which group to recruit from if applicable), and you tell said colony ship to colonize a world. It will do so, upon which you pick the tile to make landfall on, clear away any hazard tiles, and then have a finite number of tiles available to settle on in direct relation to the size of the planet or moon. Be aware that your race's homeworld ecosystem type will directly influence which planets you can settle on at first. If you play a race of anthropomorphic Polar Bears from an arctic world, then you can only settle on arctic, alpine, or tundra worlds to start. Anything warmer will be too inhospitable for you until you research the right tech to either settle them or, better yet, terraform them. The same goes for other climates.
-UPGRADES-
Upgrading and designing new ships was done with ease-of-play in mind. This is great for the player that wants to just come up with new configurations and play the game itself, but for players more partial to Galactic Civ's method of build the whole ship piece by tiny piece, it won't satisfy. However, for the former it is extremely satisfying. You pick your ship class, you pick the hull design or hull segments you want (IE Front A/B/C, Midsection A/B/C, Engines A/B/C) and then populate it with weapons and modules that correspond to the available size or type slots on the hull pieces (S/M/L/X/T/P/H). When  updated versions of the weapons or modules become available, you simply open that ship, replace them in the design, and overwrite it. All ships of that design will auto-update over time and for a fee. No deleting mountains of obsolete designs like in GalCiv, Paradox knows how to make things simple!
-RANDOM EVENTS-
In terms of random events, I don't want to spoil anything but rest assured - there are a ton of them and they're all over the place. From planet-based events, to entities and units in star systems, anomalies, multi-stage investigation missions, election promises, and more!
-THE GUD STUFF-
Honestly, and we all know Canadians can't lie worth a damn anyway, Stellaris is one of the best games to come out of 2016 in my opinion. It takes elements of what make Grand Strategies so great, combines them with elements of what makes Sci-fi 4X so great, and then gives a simplified version of both styles of game that still has enough challenge, depth, and complexity to keep the average person entertained. And while some criticize Paradox for their habit of supporting games for years after release with mountains of tiny, cheaply priced DLCs and a few big expansions, I for one love this model. It will keep the game fresh in exactly the way I want it to be, without having to pay for the stuff I don't want.
TL;DR, Stellaris is something of an underrated diamond in the rough. Paradox created a real gem here, and if you love strategy games (and moddable ones at that), then you absolutely don't want to miss out on Stellaris, which deserves a solid 8.5/10 in my books.

This review post, is not the comprehensive summary type, but something of a small (I wont go into detail regarding my conclusions, for brevity and as this is not the place for a propper spoiler filled discussion) summary of my assesment of Nier: Automata. Forgive me if the tone of this is somewhat pompous, again, it might be a summary for myself. I wish I could elaborate my points with explicit examples, but there seems to be some character limit which stops me from lengthening the review.
The OST is grand and in a tier of its own. It speaks for itself; go listen. This is not platinum's most exquisite combat, but bears their flair and is fluid. Story wise... while i dont hold it in as high a regard as many, I like it and recommend it greatly. Themes of identity, existentialism, suffering, hatred, conflict predicated on lack of understanding (etc etc the list goes on) are all present in various forms. While none of these are handled in a way yet unexplored in other media, it is still fairly novel, considering the title's general level of competence, among video games.
My praise is that the story and themes are well handled with personality, intent and ambition. The characters are well presented, becoming somewhat tangible and sympathetic even with only a small amount of material to them. Furthermore, the game is noteworthy for its use of the medium in presenting various perspectives to the player. Storytelling media can conjure many perspecives through many methods, games set themselves apart by adding the ability to form perspectives affected by player interaction. Or even just player presence. What Nier adds to this typical arsenal that is not oft seen in other games, is the exploration of the same or related scenarioes. EX, revisiting a previous scenario with new revelations such that a new perspecive is formed from contrasting with -and compounding on a previous perspective. Fans of the first Nier will know what I refer to. Though, I feel the first game was better in this regard, and part B does drag somewhat. I digress.
My chief critique for Nier:A, regarding artistic merit, is that, to me, it mostly just touches upon and mentiones its themes. At least, compared to a larger body of works, it could stand to probe deeper, and explore questions more fully. However, the work has seemingly touched people, and for the developers, as for any creator, that is likely more than enough. ^w^
My other critiques lie in how (aside from the current technical bugs, try the mod/fix FAR), while not short on material, it could hit harder still. And how sidequests, while core in how they add to the world and feel, severely hinder the much more intense pace of the main story. The lost intensity  could help the story build even better. Several story beats send mixed signals and information, this is mostly great, and also intentional. But, there are instances of world details and stakes being unclear and unexplained to the player in such a way that it undercuts the emotional impact of select scenes. Had the player been clear on the stakes for these scenes, they way the characters clearly are, their effect could have been greater.
This however, mostly apply to endings A and B, the holistic effect by the game's full end is quite good and even. And, for lasting impressions, I think that is what matters the most.
While I was not one of those who cried, nor did it come close, I did feel emotion. It did prod well at the right areas. For me I guess it just needed even more material and more of the precision, depth, cohesion, and nuance found in the best of other media.
I recommend this game on these grounds:
-It is different and project of ambition. It has a worthwile identity.
-It story and gameplay are both competently executed.
-It makes use of the medium. While not every game needs to be Automata. There is lots to be learned here, both in regards to detail and to approach.
-Its core philosophy resonates with me.
Note:
The game covers multiple playthroughs and endings. Keep playing. Notably, while playthrough 2 is a retread with new revelations, events thereafter are completely new. Thus, this first half up to endings A and B can be considered but the first act. Endings A, B, C, D and E should all be reached for the full experience.

Minesweeper on hexes with more variety in the numbers for rules. Starts simple ("2 neighboring hexes should be lit up") and gets more complicated ("20 columns of hexes, with a few lit to start, and a particular number of hexes to light in half of the columns, then along some of the diagonals, and some of those are continuous and others cannot be continuous and..."). You can work it all out from the information given.
Good puzzle design. Only about an hour of play to get a perfect score on every level, but it is a worthwhile hour.

Hexcells is the spiritual successor of the minesweep game that used to ship on windows.
It improves on the original concept by using a hexagonal board and some really clever extra hinting system.
With those extra hints it ends up feeling like a cross of minesweeps with sudoku.
In short, I L.O.V.E.D. it!
Its simple in it's presentation and yet brings a really complex intelectual challenge.
It is very clean and minimalistically designed but the result of this design is quite beaultiful and easy on the eyes.
There is no time pressure at all and you can do it wrong and retry each level at will.
The complexity of the puzzles scales gradually as you learn to read and to factor in each kind of hint but the last levels are a real challenge, large boards with all kinds of hints used together, forcing you to go back and forth through the board solving a little here and there until things start converging.
It is short but not too short for its price.
Worth every cent!

So, Automation. You ask: "What is Automation?" I answer: "It's a game that will change the perspective of the universe we live in."
...
No, wait, scratch that.
Well, in Automation you build cars. And that's what I wanted to do since I was a little kid. I LOVE this game. You can build your dirt-cheap hatchback or your two-million-dollar luxury car that handles like a boat. You can design the cars' exterior and engine just like the way you want.
Automation is a really solid game. It's actually pretty well polished regarding that it is an early access game. I've noticed some minor bugs here and there but there's actually not that many. The game still needs more content such as more car bodies, engine types and so on, but luckily there's going to be more.
Updates come rarely, but luckily they're always big. And they're not just like "Look, we got a new text box, how cool is that?", no, there's always new content. (Actually having big updates more rarely is better than small updates frequently. In PAYDAY 2 there's an update every GODDAMN week!)
The only bad side I can think of is that you can't actually drive your cars, but I understand it, as a driving model is hard to do with a 3 man dev team, and the game is about building cars, not driving them.
And if the lack of game modes annoys you, the forums are full of community challenges where you can test your mettle against other players.
To sum it up, the game maybe isn't worth the price of 27,99€ with this amount of content, but if you're even slightly into cars, I cannot do anything but recommend it.

A stealth game with clunky controls, broken line-of-sight, a useless main attack, ineffective and sparse traps, indistinct visuals, psychic guard AI, and make-or-break RNG.
A nice idea in theory but utterly dreadful execution. The only winning strategy is to hide in an empty room and wait for people to come by so you can pick them off one-by-one. You have no real influence over their decisions, so you can be standing there for whole minutes at a time with nothing to do. Even once a character enters, killing them isn't as easy as it sounds, since your main attack only extends horizontally, and has about a five-pixel range at best. It's like watching paint dry and eventually it's hard not to get bored and leave, even though leaving means certain death at the hands of the clunky controls, psychic cops, and one-use-only escape mechanisms.
Finally, to top it all off, the slow movement speed and slug-like pace makes restarting a level a tedious frustration.
Overhyped and utterly overpriced - it's a game that's more enjoyable when you're watching a streamer play it and get frustrated than when you're the one actually playing it.

Once upon a time, there was a handsome♥♥♥♥♥Canadian from Kamloops, BC that enjoyed the simple things in life - Cold beer, real maple syrup, bacon, poutine, and tax-funded healthcare. He didn't want after much, but one thing he did desire was a quality sci-fi grand strategy game that was highly customizable, with various 'endgame' challenges and an excellent random faction generator. He searched high and low, or at least he waited patiently and hoped, and one day his patience was rewarded by none other than Paradox. And from that day on, he Grand Strategied happily ever after.
Yes, friends, Stellaris is that fabled game. It is a wonderful introduction not only to sci-fi space strategy, but to the real-time grand strategy genre as a whole. Taking cues from past Paradox titles, as well as successful turn-based 4X titles such as the Galactic Civilizations series, Stellaris delivers an experience that frankly, has been sorely lacking. As a huge fan of other Paradox titles, as well as anything to do with SPEHSS, this game grabbed my eye easily and then pulled it out of the socket and proceed to make sweet hanky-panky with my skull.
Where to start... Stellaris is easily one of the most accessible, least intimidating grand strategies out there. It has enough complexity that you still need to pay attention to what you're doing and who's around you, but especially for people that have never played a GS game or have only lightly dabbled in the genre, you'll likely really enjoy this one. Veterans and hardcore fans of Grand Strategy might find Stellaris a little to simple and easy mind you, so keep in mind that YMMV.
-MODS-
One of the things that I love most about Stellaris though is how easily and extensively it can be modified however. Want to add a Star Destroyer, the Pillar of Autumn, or a Mars Class Battlecruiser as a ship model? Custom ship themes will allow you to do this. If it can be made into a 3D model, imported into a theme, and then packaged and put up on the workshop, then you can have it in your game! The same goes for everything from your empire's symbols, flag backgrounds, race portraits, names, etc...
-GENERAL GAMEPLAY-
Gameplay in Stellaris plays a lot like Victoria, Hearts of Iron, CK, EU, etc... in that you're given the world map (In this case, a galaxy populated by anywhere from dozens to hundreds or thousands of stars) and left to conquer it through a variety of means. This could be done by peaceful acquisition of occupied planets and settling of unoccupied ones, it could be through the flexing of military might, or through shrewd diplomacy, by getting other races to fight eachother so you can swoop in and "clean up" the leftover mess. Standard fare. But be cautious, because there are some crazy powerful "Fallen Empires" that you can include in your game, and frankly they're massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Never trust them. Ever.
Politically, you may have to deal with everything from elections to usurpers to racial, independence, or economic driven riots and rebellions. The political system, while not terribly deep, does make the game more interesting and the fact that some of the people of your worlds may develop new traits that put them at odds with the rest of your empire will keep you paying attention to where you draw future colonists from and where you station your fleets. Some of your more distant worlds may require a peaceful "persuasion force" of battleships in low orbit to keep the population from getting any smart ideas.
Star systems are handled in two ways: Cores and sectors. Core systems are few, and allow the player to have direct control. Typically, these solar systems will be either in the heart of your empire, or they'll be on a particularly dangerous border where you need to be able to control military defense infrastructure directly. Sectors are basically automatically governed, but you can set some rules and limits to how that's done. One of the good things with sectors is that a governor applied to a sector will apply their bonuses to every world in it. So if you have a sector with a ton of industry, and a governor with a bunch of industrial production bonuses, then you've got yourself a recipe for fleet spam!
-COMBAT-
Battles are handled in real time. There are some formation orders that you can issue to your fleets, but battles are pretty much hands-off affairs of "Point your fleet at their fleet, fly at eachother, and shoot ALL THE LASERS". Basically, the *FREEM*ing will start and won't stop until one side is dead or runs off. It leaves something to be desired, but with how big and crazy battles can get, I see why they did it.
-COLONIZATION-
Colonizing worlds is really similar to the Galactic Civ series - once your scientists scan a habitable planet, you have colony ships loaded with colonists who carry the traits and ideals present on their world (multiple different groups of ideals and/or species on one planet will give you a choice of which group to recruit from if applicable), and you tell said colony ship to colonize a world. It will do so, upon which you pick the tile to make landfall on, clear away any hazard tiles, and then have a finite number of tiles available to settle on in direct relation to the size of the planet or moon. Be aware that your race's homeworld ecosystem type will directly influence which planets you can settle on at first. If you play a race of anthropomorphic Polar Bears from an arctic world, then you can only settle on arctic, alpine, or tundra worlds to start. Anything warmer will be too inhospitable for you until you research the right tech to either settle them or, better yet, terraform them. The same goes for other climates.
-UPGRADES-
Upgrading and designing new ships was done with ease-of-play in mind. This is great for the player that wants to just come up with new configurations and play the game itself, but for players more partial to Galactic Civ's method of build the whole ship piece by tiny piece, it won't satisfy. However, for the former it is extremely satisfying. You pick your ship class, you pick the hull design or hull segments you want (IE Front A/B/C, Midsection A/B/C, Engines A/B/C) and then populate it with weapons and modules that correspond to the available size or type slots on the hull pieces (S/M/L/X/T/P/H). When  updated versions of the weapons or modules become available, you simply open that ship, replace them in the design, and overwrite it. All ships of that design will auto-update over time and for a fee. No deleting mountains of obsolete designs like in GalCiv, Paradox knows how to make things simple!
-RANDOM EVENTS-
In terms of random events, I don't want to spoil anything but rest assured - there are a ton of them and they're all over the place. From planet-based events, to entities and units in star systems, anomalies, multi-stage investigation missions, election promises, and more!
-THE GUD STUFF-
Honestly, and we all know Canadians can't lie worth a damn anyway, Stellaris is one of the best games to come out of 2016 in my opinion. It takes elements of what make Grand Strategies so great, combines them with elements of what makes Sci-fi 4X so great, and then gives a simplified version of both styles of game that still has enough challenge, depth, and complexity to keep the average person entertained. And while some criticize Paradox for their habit of supporting games for years after release with mountains of tiny, cheaply priced DLCs and a few big expansions, I for one love this model. It will keep the game fresh in exactly the way I want it to be, without having to pay for the stuff I don't want.
TL;DR, Stellaris is something of an underrated diamond in the rough. Paradox created a real gem here, and if you love strategy games (and moddable ones at that), then you absolutely don't want to miss out on Stellaris, which deserves a solid 8.5/10 in my books.

Hexcells is a minimalistic puzzle game in which one has to decide if orange hexes are either grey or blue ones with the help of several hints.
~ The puzzles slowly become more complicated with more clues to look at over the time. All three games (Hexcells, Hexcells Infinite and Hexcells Plus) have different mechanics added to the original in the beginning.
~ The game is extremely relaxing. There is no "Game Over" screen and no timer. You can solve the puzzles at your own pace with calm music in the background and fitting melodic sound effects.
~ Every single puzzle of the three Hexcells games is entirely solvable with logical thinking and without the need to guess during any of them.
~ Hexcells Infinite offers an additional mode in which you can generate puzzles with random seed codes.
Without doubt one of the most polished puzzle games I've seen, and even though I dislike Minesweeper, I love this game to bits.
Highly recommended.

It IS an abstract puzzle, like minesweeper or sudoku or something like that, and it has a nice atmospheric sound and visuals to go along with it, but that's all it really is, honestly. It feels really insubstantial. Simply adding more levels isn't what I want, either. Nor is adding more mechanics. I just think it's hard to make an abstract puzzle game feel as fun as some of the other games out there. It took me 2-3 hours to 100% and I didn't really end it feeling like I was glad I played it.
Plus, the music loop starts to get annoying after awhile. It's too short, plays too often, and isn't mixed in with other tracks.
And the core gameplay loop is pretty much just - reveal the obvious stuff, then hunt around for the next thing you can reveal. That's not that fun to me compared to what you do in other games. It's not the lack of action or anything - I'm fine with slow-paced, turn-based, or other puzzle games. It's just the lack of problem solving - this game is all deduction and very little intuition. I like working with and experimenting with a hard problem and going over it in my head and trying different avenues of solutions and trying to come up with observations and rules and constraints that I can use to simplify the problem. You can find that core gameplay loop in lots of excellent puzzle games, but you won't find it here.
If you like minesweeper or sudoku you should definitely give this a try. Otherwise, even if you're a huge fan of puzzle games like me, I'd probably avoid this. You're not going to find that problem-solving engagement and stimulation here, unlike what you'd find in lots of other puzzle games. There's no experimenting, discovery, or anything like that. It's just "oh here's the next spot for which I can prove its contents" and "hmm, where's the next one?".
As a counterexample, an abstract puzzle game I DID enjoy was Splice (you might argue that it's not TRULY abstract since it uses a sort of biological metaphor, but I think of it as one). That game has plenty of that "problem solving high" you get as you experiment and observe and work through a complex problem.
Buy the bundle with Plus and Infinite! Got it on sale for less than three dollars, and got about 20+ good puzzling hours out of all three. Totally worth it.

I couldn't get into it the first few times I played it and I disliked it from the first few hours of gameplay but after a few recent restarts I learned to appreciate it. There are loads of gameplay features but much of them are pretty broken if not outdated, which was initially one of the main reasons I disliked the game at first.
There are a multitude of skills you can upgrade that are given to you right from the beginning: Lockpicking, Electronics, Medicine, Computer, and Swimming. The Weapon Skills in the same window are Heavy, Pistol, Rifle, Low-Tech, and Demolition. If you don't know what weapon you just got benefits from what skill, you can check the info on its description.
I realized that the skills aren't actually mandatory for the game's progression and I'm pretty sure you don't even need to upgrade any to beat the game; they're there to make certain play-styles easier on the player so should you obtain enough points to upgrade. For example, Lockpicking just decreases the amount of lockpicks you use for a heavily-locked door, Computer allows you to hack computers if you don't feel like or just haven't found the login/password for a terminal, and all the Weapon Skills increase damage & accuracy. As a good role-playing game goes, you can't legitimately max out everything in one playthough, at least not as far as I know anyway.
Fancier upgrades can be found in the game via augmentation canisters that are located throughout the game with various functionalities that all eat up your energy meter when used. You're not a shake flashlight so you have to recharge your energy meter when appropriate via these recharging robots or a certain recharge item you can find throughout the game.
Augs consist of things like the ability to lift heavier objects, run faster, EMP shield, and more. Each canister gives you a choice of what two augs you want to install to its desired slot. Unfortunately you can't replace already installed augs so you need to choose wisely on what you want to have. You can  quicksave/quickload to see how one augmentation works if you must. There are also upgrade canisters you can find that upgrade said installed augs for improved functionality.
During my mostly-stealthy, mostly-non-lethal playthrough I found only a select few augs to be of any use and some I regret installing.
Taking damage is pretty unique in this game as each limb has their own HP.
If your legs' HP reach 0 you'll have to crawl instead of walk. If your arms', then your efficiency with weapons is decreased. If the head's or torso's reach 0, then you die. With medkits you can heal each limb individually. Miraculously you can practically regrow your limbs via food & drinks though you'd have to consume a hefty ton of those for that idea to come to fruition.
Much of the game has you doing things manually with one of these things being the inventory. There's no inventory-tetris in the game despite several items taking up more than one space which can be a real pain sometimes. You can't rotate items so if something takes up 2 squares of inventory space horizontally then you'll have to make 2 empty horizontal slots yourself since there's no auto-arrangement when it comes to inventory space. It's a bigger nuisance if you're trying to pick an item up but you don't know how much space it needs so your only choice is to ignore the item altogether or drop several items on the ground hoping you've made enough room to even pick it up.
One of the selling points of the game is how there really are multiple solutions to problems as advertised.
Door's locked? You can lockpick it. No lockpicks? You can shoot it, hit it with a melee weapon, or use explosives depending on whether or not the door's weak enough. Is the door immortal? Either find a key or find an alternate path. The game's designed for each level to have at least more than one way to get through something save for one part of the game. You're even rewarded with supplies and usually skill points for exploring nooks and crannies.
And of course you can go about the entire game using non-lethal measures.
The gunplay is a little unreliable until you upgrade the appropriate weapon skill and/or you upgrade the weapon of choice with upgrade mods that you can find throughout the game. It's even more unreliable to go guns blazing in the beginning as well. Your crosshair is spread wide open until you stand still for a bit but even then the bullet can look like it just went outside of the crosshair diameter. For some reason the crosshair thing applies even to melee weapons, even if it's not visibly shown. I'm not entirely sure how the gunplay is played out if I upgraded their appropriate weapon skills since stealth was so strongly encouraged and that's how I often like to play games like this.
The AI awareness when you're sneaking about is weird. They're certainly "functional" but how they work can easily shatter one's suspension of disbelief; they don't often hear gunshots when it looks like they should, sneaking up to them & colliding with their models doesn't alert them, and etc. etc.
For some reason, to do a 1-hit takedown, lethal or non-lethal, on most humanoid enemies you have to hit them on their lower back for it to work. Hitting the head steathily just treats it as regular damage. You also have to collide with their bodies as you swing your weapon an inch above the belt region, otherwise it's just relied on RNG on whether or not you hit the desired spot.
The tranquilizer darts are said to be "quiet" but it's hardly so when it doesn't instantly take them down and the enemy just runs in circles until they finally go down. Only if they're alone (as well as not being near an alarm button) will it be considered "quiet" as no one will be alerted while they run around until they drop. Even if an alarm is tripped in any manner it's easy to just hide and wait until the alarm silences and then everyone just goes about their usual stuff.
You can loot a body, whether unconscious or dead, and can only pick them up when their inventory is empty. But there's no point in picking bodies up aside for comedic purposes since no one cares if there's a new body on the floor; all anyone cares about is if they "witness" the attack itself.
The story is very interesting to say the least even if they are often portrayed through silly voice acting. Depending on what you do throughout the game, certain dialogue pieces change, characters die, characters appear at a different time, and so on. Sadly the story as a whole doesn't change no matter what you do aside from the endings.
I found several bugs & glitches throughout the game. One that can potentinally ruin someone's playthrough are possible CTD's during critical parts of the game, though I've only come across that once. Basically, each time I loaded up this particular save file the game would crash immediately after the helicopter I saw left the area so I had no choice but to load up the next recent save file.
Despite the FPS-looking nature of the game it's overall a role-playing game, though it looks like you can treat it like an action game if you so desire.
I played the game without mods and it's been overall fine if you can deal with the bugs & small text.
You'd also have to look past the outdated/broken graphics & certain functionalities of some gameplay mechanics and shoddy voice acting but if you can get by those then there's a better chance that you can see the game's probably not just something people put on nostalgia-glasses for to praise it.

The popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. The multiplicity of ethnic, cultural and musical conditions needed to spawn Jazz was thus unique to the United States, and specifically to New Orleans. The necessary philosophical impetus for Jazz, i.e. , democracy and freedom of individual expression supported by group interaction, are also American institutions.

Yoko Taro is simply a genius. The story complexity, the overarching themes of existentialism and humanism, the emotional lability that's produced, how we are goaded into thinking about situations from one perspective only to be ripped away and shown how little we know when faced with a new perspective, a perfect menagerie of gameplay styles with seamless switching, side-quests that mean something and have value, and so, so much more make this possibly my favorite game to this point. This has been said to be a perfect representation of a story that couldn't be told in any other medium, and I agree. One would find difficulty not learning more about themselves while playing through at least the first 5 endings. So many people like myself have written verbose reviews because words won't do this game justice. To anyone who is on the fence about this masterpiece... dive in. This perfectly encapsulates everything we need see more of from the gaming medium.

(THIS REVIEW IS SPOILER FREE AND IT'S LONG)
NieR: Automata,
the game where people usually stop by for the booty, but stay for the story.
I'm gonna get this off my chest: this game is a masterpiece, EVERYONE needs to play it. This is a game that will make you feel oh so many emotions throughout the story (NEVER stop after the first ending, you should at least play the first 5 endings, especially ending C and/or D, the most frustrating one but it's also the deepest and most depressing endings out of the main endings)
This game may be considered as a masterpiece by many many people, but that doesn't mean it doesn't have flaws(maybe not flaws but definitely things i did not enjoy) Here are the pros and cons:
Pros:
+ Unforgettable story, like no joke this is one of the best stories i've ever followed through. I'm not gonna say anything else as it's easy to spoil it, seriously go and experience it for yourself.
+ Unforgettable characters, 2B, 9S, A2, Pascal and then some, the bosses are all amazing, i don't think i have encountered a boss that i didn't like or thought was boring, all of the boss fights were entertaining and different(except for a few exceptions here and there) Some were frustrating and some were easy.
+ Let's continue on the unforgettable trend, the soundtrack, the ♥♥♥♥ing soundtrack, holy hell how do i describe it... I can't, you have to experience it on your own. It's perfect for this game, Keiichi Okabe is a genius. This and The Witcher 3's soundtracks are the best in my books so far, soundtrack is an 11/10 from me.
+ The fighting system in general, it's just so smooth and it feels so damn nice.
+ The setting, there aren't many areas in the game, some may think that it's too small but i think that what the developpers were actually trying to do was make the map not too big and not too small so you can familiarize with it and have jam packed things on every nook and cranny on the map and i think they did an amazing job at that.
+ The amount of endings there are, in general there are 26 endings but the first 5 ones are the real main endings and all 5 will make you leave your game with different emotions, mostly sadness but also awe and maybe even a bit of joy, depends on who you are.
+ After you finish the story, you get chapter selection which is honestly one of the most awesome and useful addition to this game for people who want to replay certain parts or want to get all endings
now on to the cons, i honestly couldn't find anything terrible in itself but there are a few things i was not a fan of:
Cons:
- The saving system, it's not bad but it's not the best neither, i'm not a big fan of the "you can't save anywhere, you have to be at specific locations in order to save" bit of it. A lot of times i had died and last time that i was ABLE to save(i'm paranoid so i save whenever i can) was about half an hour to an hour ago and that frustrated me quite a lot.
- The port, honestly it's not too terrible but i do wish the optimization was better but i didn't exactly have a problem with it, was able to play it at playable fps on the highest settings (absolutely turn off AA, it WILL kill your fps guaranteed!)
- Controls are okay but the evade system by double tapping the WASD keys screwed me up a lot because either i did it too fast or the game just wouldn't pick it up and also because there aren't any dedicated evade keys for the M/K, us users of the M/K can't use the debug system, not a big problem but it would be cool to see what it's like.
Conclusion:
Once again, this game is an absolute masterpiece, it's definitely worth the 80$ price tag (Thanks Canada, in USD it should be $60). NieR: Automata is now my favourite game for various reasons(not gonna state them here since it's somewhat personal i guess and maybe because i'm too lazy to write them all down) and this game is absolutely the GOTY for me atleast since i feel like it will be disregarded in general because of BOTW. This game get's a full 10/10 from me, if you are still reading this then i'm sure you get the message already,
buy the damn game already!

Fun little hack 'n slash.
+ Decent graphics, fun locations, okay story, short playtime. Game ran smoothly and without a single bug or crash. Some fun platforming puzzles. Music and ambiance is good, though nothing special. There are some branching narrative choices that seem to affect reactions and outcomes.
- Linear progression. Annoying camera control  - as in, there isn't any. All movement is done via WASD on the keyboard, and the camera auto-rotates. I got used to it, but it felt unnecessarily restrictive. Other users have complained about the voice-acting, and yes, it is pretty terrible. Lack of tutorials - had to look up a walkthrough several times to learn a key combo so I could progress (when in doubt, try Shift + LMB).
Not a must-buy, but if Blood Knights tempts you, get it when it is on sale for around $1-2. Otherwise you'll feel ripped off. There simply isn't enough content or replayability to justify the $15 retail price.

Let me tell you about the old days. When we skirmished them with gunfire and arrows to reduce their ranks, then we held them with our infantry and slammed them in with our cavalry.
Total War is a long running franchise made by CA (Creative Assembly.) This franchise is known for the tactical and wide scale gameplay. For those who are not familiar with total war it works like this. The campaign plays like a grand strategy, you have build, recruit, run politics, diplomacy, and warfare each and every turn until you win. When your army engages an enemy are it is brought to more of an RTS setting where you control your army to either annhiliate, defend, or route your enemy. Multiplayer is all about the RTS setting, however, there are ways to play multiplayer campaigns, sadly they are hard to setup.
Pros

-Realistic combat: There is friendly fire, moral levels (enemies, allys, and your army will route if moral is too low), and realistic counter units.
-In depth strategy both multiplayer and single player
-Many factions to choose from
-Looks great for being an older game
-Has historical battles that you can play
-Provides hours of entertainment
Cons
-Can be very difficult to understand
-Pathfinding bugs
-Lacks naval battles
-Units will sometimes ignore your orders, even if they don't have the bonus effect "Will charge without order"

Borderlands and Borderlands 2 were EPIC games.. I see alot of negative reviews trying to compare this installment with the other 2. This is a "good" game. The story line fills the void between the first and second game and connects Jack with the first and second vault, 3 bosses from BL2 and ties Athena along with the original vault hunters into the story and "connects the dots".  2K Australia KILLED the backstory with the thick "crocodile dundee" crap. We get it you're Australian.. get over it. Do you HAVE to lather the character content with "shrimp on the barby" crap jokes and NPC's that you need a speech translator to understand what they're saying?  Another thing I don't get is the "ambiguously" gay/ gay/straight thing that gearbox is trying to experiment with.  Personally.. I could give a rats a55, but when you're 1/3 into a story and you can obviously tell somebody in Human Resources said "Hey.. we need a gay character.. Write it in"  JUST to have alternative characters.... C'mon.....  The playing characters skill trees are O.K. Not as good as BL2, and a ton better than Borderlands. They stuck with the same crappy scaling from TVHM to UVHM. The short, redundant campaigns suck.. run all the way over here, do 1 mission, turn in, run alllllll the way back and do 1 or 2 more, rinse and repeat.
Whats good? Character building. The changes in adding points to the skill trees and adding class mods is a TON more noticeable in this game than BL2..... Especially the blue and purple class mods. They threw in O2 kits and the Grinder. I HATED the fact I had to keep up with oxygen when I started playing, but the buffs from the O2 kits are killer. I see they're playing around with something you have to manage besides "cool down" and ammo consumption.  The cryo-laser weapons are kick a55.
It"s a "good" game.. It doesn't have the "shine" like BL2 or the first game does, but it's a good halfway point to get caught up on the story, learn a few new skills and pray that Crocodile Dundee doesn't show up in the 3rd installment.

First off, I had a very strong dislike for NBA 2K after 2K15 and 2K16. There were a myriad of issues that made me, a die hard fan of everything they did previously legitamately hate them as a company. I was overjoyed at reading Ronnie 2k's Instagram and seeing him get flamed hard by bitter fans. Watching 2k degenerate over the years made me wish EA did anything relevant at all with the Live franchise that was really good way back. And I am not a huge fan of EA either. But this game is different. I mean really different. Their are minor gripes and things that seem wrong but I don't even want to mention it for fear that an update would mess it up somehow. This game is the best basketball game I have ever played with not even a close second running behind.
Remember 2K16 when a dominating rim abuser big like DeAndre Jordan or Anthony Davis would get the ball down low and for some odd reason throw a horrible lay up that missed? Yeah that's gone. Now punishing dunks as it should be and is in real life. Russell Westbrook is an incredible athlete and a pest defensively. Steph is dropping it in if he's open from almost anywhere. His layup animation isn't the same floating high ball everytime, either. It's crisp, it's fluid, I almost can't believe it's real. You can time steals. Let me say that again: YOU CAN TIME STEALS. It's not an instant foul like the previous versions. You can actually time it so that you can rip the ball during the opponents dribble. This shouldn't be a monumental achievement but somehow it feels like it is. Just from a basketball standpoint, it is the closest thing to NBA ball I have ever played on anything ever.
As far as graphics go, I was recently watching the US Olympic team in 4k through a Comcast sampler. The camera angles where nice and the action was great. This actually looks a lot like that. And that looked better than any basketball coverage I had seen before. It's beautiful, it's fluid, again, it's almost unbelievable. Combined with the great realism and fun to play action, there has never been a game even close to this in terms of quality.
I want to make it clear that I absolutely hated Visual Concepts before this game. I felt they had killed a great franchise. I felt that greed pushed them to forget about what made their game great. I was totally expecting this game to be a reskin of 2K16. I was disappointed when the game didn't release at midnight. I had set myself up for disappointment. This is one of the best games I have ever played. I'll be honest, there are areas which need to be improved, but on the whole, it is an excellent game. Here is a run down of the positives and negatives as I see them.
The Positives
*An excellent UI which has the best intentions. You start off controlling your empire from the system view. But soon, as your empire expands, you need to rely on the galaxy map.
* Simple combat. You can't control tactics in battle, but how you wage a large scale war, where you send vessels, fleets and what systems you attack can make the difference between victory and defeat.
* Starship creation is simply brilliant. While the look remains the same, the design of the weapons, shields, power, engines, etc. means your designs are limited only by your imagination.
* Planet system: this is simply great. There are numerous types of planets and at the beginning you are limited to what you can colonise. This is the best idea I've ever seen.
* Species created - unlimited choices and ways to design species with the AI ones created at the beginning of a game too mean no two play-throughs will be the same.
The Negatives
Sectors - I wish these were optional, but the way the game has been programmed means that they must be used.
Planet Management - Micromanagement of planets is not really a strong point of this game. If you like a lot of control over every planet, then you might be disappointed. Even when you are micromanaging planets, the information provided is limited and it is hard to make decisions.
Despite the negatives, this is a firm favourite game and I recommend it to anyone who likes science fiction, empire building or empire management.

When I got this, I was actually hoping for Jedi Knight 2-esque sword-centric gameplay mechanics. I was actually quite surprised in that the swordplay is coming from a completely different approach. My first couple matches were more akin to an old-school Unreal Tournament match than actual dueling or sword-play. It almost seems to me that perhaps if the characters' speed was somewhat less, and jumping wasn't so exaggerated (you also even see a lot of--again--old-school "bunny hopping"), then the players would have to be more methodical and deliberate in how they wield the swords. Also, especially after my first match, it struck me that while learning the wielding mechanics must surely give you an advantage, it seems that in most circumstances simply just button-mashing and swinging the sword in random directions does the job just fine. Point in fact, that's mostly what I witnessed, generally speaking. Of course, one could argue that the above is simply a matter of taste (and also consider my previous leanings toward JK2) and that many people enjoy the fast-paced combat. Thus, now that my main grievances have been mentioned, I feel that it must be said that for a dev-team of only two people the game as it stands is quite an impressive achievement. The graphics are actually quite pretty (although the bloom/HDR effect might be too glaring in some places), and while the maps are small, they're designed well enough to serve as makeshift funnels for the players in such a way that you--again like in UT--can't go but a few seconds without needing to charge in or defend yourself. Here again though, I do feel the need to point out that I found the 360 degree sword system description quite misleading, since that doesn't actually seem to be the case in practice. That would almost imply mouse-controlled sword movement. I personally found it, with all the button-mashing and jumping around, quite difficult to actually defend myself with my own weapon. It's more effective (and non-lethal for your character) to simply roll away and swing random blows at your opponent. So for future players and purchasers, I do believe that should be clarified more on the product page. But I digress, I should mention that there is partially complete character customization that defintely shows a lot of potential to be very attractive especially if the devs follow through with their planned content updates. I honestly believe that this game can turn into a true gem if some combat and gameplay balancing issues are addressed to actually make it worthwhile on how to learn how to use the sword (which seemed to me to be a major selling point/factor?) skillfully and if the devs follow through within a relatively timely manner on content. Even if it's just small, consistent patches. And for those who might be wondering, yes I did watch the training videos. Some of them several times. But I do have to also say that there seems to be a precedent for some Indie and/or Early Access games to die out, especially in MP, when the aforementioned updates do not occur or are very delayed. I really don't want to see this game kick the bucket before its prime, and it has loads of potential. And also, despite all my groaning, there are enough tense or exciting/fun moments to make the game worth picking up and playing occasionally for some gamers. So I'd say it's worth a buy for some, bearing what I've written in mind of course. To the devs: it's all just constructive criticism, keep up the good work. You've got a very solid foundation for an excellent indie title. It's few and far between that you get to see an indie title with such high graphical fidelity or unique gameplay. Maybe introduce a gameplay mode that enhances and encourages dueling and duelists? Hey, it worked for JK2! :D
*Edit:
As I'm looking at some of the other positive reviews, I noticed that quite a few people mentioned the game Chivalry in comparison to this game. Incidentally, I had actually written that into my first part of my review above, but took it out because I thought it was long enough already. Well now I'm going to make it longer, so if anyone is reading this, bear with me. And if not, well it never hurts to brush up my writing skills I guess lol. But I also own Chivalry also, essentially hoping for some meaningful, in-depth combat again. While some people might look at how many hours I've played of this game or that game, I don't really need to sink countless hours of my life into something to be able to speak with experience. I think most people that are reading these reviews are gamers and have been gamers and know what I'm talking about. Essentially I came away pretty disappointed. Sure, there is a comparatively sophisticated (speaking of Chivalry [hang in there, I'm going somewhere with this]) directionally-based combat system, and the classes do add some measure of tactical depth, but basically button-mashing can all too easily triumph over the attempted practiced, methodical approach. In effect, what I'm pointing out for KR is that although the sword system is touted as a major selling point of this game, and even showcased in the trailer, the gameplay mechanics nor the realities of the game as it is does not encourage, let alone reward, the player for learning how to wield the sword effectively. I didn't really get from the trailer or the product page that it was seeking to achieve the same flavor and, well, chaos that occurs in Chivalry. Last thing I wanted to mention is that from a practical/realistic/historical point of view, that kind of...flailing could only be useful in a very specific, and limited manner. When soldiers marched against each other, effective militaries of the day would obviously be in some kind of formation (rank and file, phalanx, testudo, etc.) and would therefore be pressed together on both sides. Once the opposing forces eventually charged each other's lines the men in the front would only have that claustrophobia increased. Again, historically speaking, the effect of that being the men in the very front couldn't move, use their weapon, or manuever. The men in the ranks behind them (mostly) couldn't hit the enemy at all. Thus, the prevailing tactic of the day was for the front ranks to plant their shields and intentionally be pushed by their companions behind them. Naturally that doesn't make for a fun game. But once the combatants began to have some "elbow room" so to speak, perhaps that flailing could possibly have been effective for that very narrow stretch of time. But once the combatants had spread out further, for various reasons, it's obvious and only logical that the men would bring whatever methods, training, and skill to bear if only because it was essentially a matter of survival. Chivalry (just like my comparison above) is very much alike to KR and UT in that despite the relative "thinness" or rather absence of any organization/structure/formation, method, practice, and skill do not guarantee a correspondingly effective kill ratio. In fact, I would go as far as to say that as the game is, speaking in a broad/general analyses, that it is more effective to utilize rolling, bunny hopping, and trying to circle around your opponent while simply striking with your weapon. As in, ignoring the blocking, parrying, and intentional sword swings entirely. Of course, for the sake of completeness I should mention that in Chivalry, the characters don't move quite as quickly which makes logical sense. However, what doesn't make sense is thse big, broad-shouldered, armor-laden, giant-sword-wielding--soldiers? Mercenaries? Erm...princes? Can bunny hop to a height as would occur only if fighting on, perhaps, the moon, roll in full armor, like a gymnast, and swing huge weapons like candy canes. Therefore, after all this long-winded analysis, I find that, unlike my first part of this review, I cannot recommend buying this game as it stands, if at all.

Kingdoms Rise is a game with a great deal of potential and the FlyLeapStudios is clearly working hard at that as stated by themselves and through their first patch which has alleviated a great deal of issues that were plaguing the game. The game is clearly Early Access so you have to understand the game will eventually be something worth your time and money but it needs a bit more polish. This review is written based on playing with a rather strong computer so just bear that in mind, your experience may vary.

The Good

The good in this game is that the groundwork is clearly there for a great highly tactical chaotic sword and magic game. The art work is of a high quality and the animations are certainly well done and seamless. The gameplay is fluid for the most part and the game is functional. The combat can be quite fun as you swing, dodge, roll and use magic with relative ease to defeat your enemies. The magic spells are varied and can mix up your gameplay quite a bit. Do you want to be a stealthy guy who can assassinate someone? Do you want to be a guy who can take a lot of hits and get into the heat of battle? You have many options when deciding on the type of warrior you wish to be. The various swords in the game also have unique stats that help make your warrior be more true to your desires. Swords have stats such as increased damaged, increased back attack damage, etc and it all works quite well. Especially with the new patch that balances magic and swords out more. It is easy to be swept up into the frantic combat and I never found myself bored of it.
The character creator has a decent selection of varying armor pieces for your character to wear and make him (and soon to be her) look unique to a certain extent. In the battlefield you may lose some of your identity but you can stand out depending on how creative you get. Also the team plans on adding more game modes into the game to spice up the rather lacking selection at the moment.

The Bad

This is an Early Access game so these problems I address could very well and probably will be gone within a month or two so take this with a grain of salt. Don’t dismiss the game because of what I say here, it is a game in progress and will evolve. The game has few modes to keep you interested right now. It’s your standard generic fps fair of Deathmatch and King of the Hill. The replay value isn’t much at the moment unless you really enjoy those.
Spawn camping has been somewhat of an issue in my time with the game in so far as team modes are concerned. In free for alls I was never once spawn killed. However in team matches if one side was overpowering another it would get to the point the other team would camp the spawn and keep you locked inside of it. Without a moving spawn point this can be an issue and while you can fight your way out eventually, the spawn system shouldn’t work like that. It has been proven in countless games that fixed spawn points typically lead to spawn killing.
Something about the combat doesn’t feel very meaty. It feels like I’m not really fighting so much as I am swinging a sword vaguely at the direction of pixels which pulled me out of the experience a bit. Also magic really needs some better animations, it is very easy to be blindsided by it with no warning. As I said in the last part the gameplay is still good but it needs more fine tuning to achieve all that it can.

The Conclusion
The game itself again is Early Access and the gripes I mentioned I know will be stamped out a couple months time. The game does have a lot of positives going for it. The combat is smooth and the mechanics are definitely there for an excellent experience. The game is fun as it currently stands but the replay value is little at the moment. When more modes get added in and other gameplay mechanics I feel the game will have a far more powerful draw on peoples wallets. For now however the game needs more fine tuning and you can find better games with more replay value for your money. Keep an eye on patch notes and wait for some big updates before jumping in.

Wildstar is a collection of many different mmorpgs brought together to form a unique and fun experience.
--
What I like
The game's action combat is one of the best in its genre. Moving from a tab-targeting system to Wildstar's free-form action combat can be daunting at first and can feel clunky. After playing for a little while, things begin to click and everything becomes fluid and effortless. The telegraph system allows for more complex attacks to be thrown at you with still feeling fair if you get hit.
PvE - Instanced content is divided into four separate categories: Raids, Dungeons, Adventures, and Expeditions. Each are designed well, forcing each role be it tank, dps, or healer to participate and stay mobile and alert to their surroundings. This game is less Tank'n'Spank and more calculated and thought out.
Battlegrounds - The game modes are a capture the flag, king of the hill, and a ... reverse capture the flag (I don't know how to explain it). Each one is fun and easy to understand. I've had many close matches with me at the edge of my seat, heart pounding and the clock ticks down to see which team wins. You also won't always be fighting the opposite faction on BGs, this speeds up queue times.
Balance - No class stands out as overpowered in PvP or PvE, rather each class excels at different tasks and will shine when met with that task.
F2P model - Without a doubt the best one you will find. The cash shop contains only cosmetics, and XP/reputation boosts. Most everything in the shop can also be bought with currency acquired in-game so most of the cash shop items are essentially free in themselves.
Housing - The possibilities are seemingly endless. Many players refer to it as the "true endgame".
Exploration - Nothing has killed a game for me more than an invisible wall, and I have yet to run into one in Wildstar. I have found myself way off the beaten track without being forced to turn around. Granted there are some areas that will kill you if try venturing into purposely walled off areas or out to sea, but it is forgivable.
Humor - My favorite games of all time have silly humor sprinkled throughout just to lighten the mood and Wildstar has it in spades. This game has a serious story, but knows not to get too full of itself.
Lore - There is so much to read and find, I don't think I will ever get to read all of it.
--
What I don't like
The time to kill players - In lower level PvP is ridiculously long due to the lack of dps yet to be unlocked through ability points and amps making objectives hard to complete resulting in long drawn-out stalemates. This however is not an issue at level cap.
Tradeskills (crafting) - More specifically the ones that create armor and weapons, while useful because you can craft raid quality gear,  have a random element that can completely ruin the gear you are trying to make and waste your materials in the process. In addition there are materials that can only be purchased which can be very expensive when trying to get crafting vouchers to learn high level gear (we are talking 20 platinum worth of materials just to learn how to make the gear you want).
Bug Fixes - Bugs happen and should be expected, I will never mark a mmo poorly for a few bugs. I will mark for how long it takes to fix those bugs however. Carbine is somewhat slow at fixing minor annoyances. If there is a game-breaking bug, they do their best to squash it fast and for the most part it is done in a reasonable time. With smaller things it takes quite a while for them to get fixed as I imagine are not a high priority.
The difficulty - I hate saying this, but Wildstar has a steep difficulty curve. I have seen many players get frustrated and leave the game because of the difficulty. The challenge the game provides is good, it is rewarding when you succeed. But the amount of expectations and information given to new players comes too fast for some and can completely turn a person away with they miss a single bit of information.
--

Major difference with other space 4x games:
- Ethics: Every race has  2 or 3 ethics that describe the wants and needs of that race. Depending on how different a conquered race ethics are from your empire, they will be easily or never assimilated. Ethics of any race can change (including your race) for a variety of reasons and brings all kinds of positive and negative with them. This makes the races unique and richly diversified.
- Warscore: When you go to war, you declare war to someone and then choose a bunch of objectives that you want to accomplish. As the war progress and if you win battles, your warscore gets higher until it reach 100 points. Then you win all your objectives (or the enemy wins all of them). Its peculiar to say the least. Different take on conquest very similar to Europa Universalis.
Pros:
- Strategy of building your empire is very deep and interesting. And don't fret young padawan, as your empire gets bigger, you will also unlock with new teknologies a myriad of buildings, influence, edicts and other tools to help you manage better that biiiiig empire of yours. The tek is very well balanced because you seem to get the right tek just when you start straining because of the size of your empire.
- You don't control battles, so all you can do is design your ships properly to be better against the enemy's ships. There is a kind of rock-paper-scissors-shotgun deal for the weapons and defences that makes it suprisingly deep compared to the  seemingly simple choices that you have.
- Graphics are superb except for battle and ground combat which are simple affairs (No sword of the stars kind of battle here)
- Sound is awesome. Music is so good that even after many hours, i still don't get tired of it.
- The AI is very very very good. Human-like would be a good term. It knows when you are nasty and bad and if you becomes too big of a threat, it will band togheter a couple of empires and come kick down your door. Trying to defend 3-4 systems at the same time from different fleets with your 1 big fleet sure is challenging. And the universe is big. Very very big. The logistics of defending your big empire becomes very hard. You WILL understand just how the romans felt at the end of their reign. Hehehehe
- No bugs that i've seen
- The game is still supported after more than 1 year. They are still refining it and god it has aged like fine wine. Many small things that were an irritant or were missing have been added/improved and the game is much shinier now because of it.
Cons:
- Space battle are simple affairs. Generally the one with the biggest fleet wins, but it depends also on the design of the fleets. This make them quickish and uninteresting.
- Ground combat is even simpler than fleet combat. More troops wins and no troops design.
- I hate the ship design screen. It's functional, but i somehow can't stand it.
