Stellaris is a phony.
There is a critique of writing where you quickly determine an author is self-indulgent (like my tldr reviews).
Paradox and the devs of this game are self-indulgent-- to the point of aggressive masturbation.
Stylistic preferences aside, the lack of good sense in this game speaks to individuals with absolutely no real world experiences. Imagine an author who wrote a story about firefighters, but who had zero experience with first responders. Quickly someone might reply, "How could anyone have experience running an interstellar empire?"
You couldn't, but for a game to have any resemblance of credibility or enjoyment in needs to meet players' basic, ubiquitous, experiences. In my opinion, it needs to make some rational sense.
For example, if a group of home invaders enter your house and beat you and your family within an inch of your lives, you don't get decide when when it ends or under what conditions. No one has to actually experience a science fiction universe to understand how violence works. Given Stellaris, these devs apparently don't understand how violence and force of arms work -- or they are ignorantly forwarding some idealized worldview of their own.
Instead, the folks at Paradox seem to have channeled their undergraduate poli-sci and psychology classes into how they guess or want the elements of national power work. How often have you had someone try to use complex language to hide their lack of competence and knowledge? That's Stellaris. Phony. Good gameplay isn't measured in average syllables per word.
Maybe it's like listening to someone try to talk about sports after they caught an hour of ESPN at their Barber Shop. If you know anything about sports, you immediately identify the person as a phony -- and smile graciously.
Normally Paradox makes games based on history. That has offered them a nice crutch, because their flaws and problems can be attributed to balancing gameplay with historical events. Not so with Stellaris, because there are no historical events to use as an excuse for bad design.
It's a typical complaint that no Paradox game is playable until after a year of players providing them free consulting. I held out about year in the hope things would be improved. I didn't wait long enough.
In fact, all their marketing hype about "social complexity" in Stellaris seems to result in SLOW, boring, unimaginative gamplay. A big open galaxy, but the player is locked on railroad tracks for the whole game.
I suppose fans might counter with...
"But it looks great!" -- says the person who has never dated someone super-hot that turns out to be nothing more.
"It's needed for PvP balance!" -- says the person who doesn't know that getting your butt kicked has been a fun part of 4X going back before VGA Planets. I'm sorry, but only the champions in my league got a trophy when I was growing up.
"Use patience and let each game develop!" -- says the person most interested in a Federation victory. I have to admit, if you're the kind of person who wants to watch an undergraduate social interaction simulator for hours this could be the game for you. That said, I would still point you towards the Democracy game series as generally better.
"It's insanely complicated and the balance is really complex!" -- says the person who didn't realize that influence and energy are the only two resources that really matter and are both used in a simple dynamic friction pattern. Stellaris' marketing illustrates a complex maze, but the player is only given access to the dominant strategy path. Attempting any individualized play will result in immediate frustration.
Don't take my review as gospel obviously, but as you read positive reviews for Stellaris you are going to encounter a lot of excuses for this game.
I feel like this game's devs kept all the fun for themselves and paid for it from our wallets. Stellaris is a phony.

There are only two problems I have with the game, and one of them isn't the game's fault.
The first is that the story gets pretty cliche Japanese at certain points, which may not be a negative for some people.  There is, for example, a male antagonist that has long white hair and is fairly feminine.  This doesn't really detract from the story at all, it's just an over-used cliche or stereotype.  It's possible this was done on purpose though. I wouldn't know.
The other problem is that the port isn't flawless.  I recommend either using Borderless Gaming if you want a true 1080p resolution, or using one of the fixes online that also has options to improve performance.
Other than that though, this game is a work of art, and I do not say that lightly.  This is also the only game I've played that somehow managed to get something in my eye.
As a final note, I'm someone who hasn't played any other games connected to this one.  The first Nier, and the Drakengard series.  I've never touched 'em.  But at no point did I ever feel like I was missing out on something, so if that's a concern for you, I wouldn't worry about it.  I'm sure there are nods to the other games, but nothing really struck me as 'off' like it didn't belong.
EDIT: So there still hasn't been an official patch (As of 23/11/17) to fix the resolution and optimization issues some people have been having.  I'm going to leave this as a positive review because I enjoyed the game so much despite its flaws, but I think this game is being heavily mismanaged.  They're just riding on the unexpected success.  They better not kill this game (Series, hopefully) by being greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and not putting the money upfront to properly port their games and support them post-launch, at least for a while. Splatter is a simple, twin stick style shooter based in the modern zombie apocolypse with some extra threats.
At first, I didn't think much about this game. The first level was a bit bland, but then as each level progressed, I managed to enjoy the somewhat cautionary events that occur. You don't just 'run n' gun' your way through bad guys. There are a lot of corridors and corners for you to look around carefully with your flashlight. Thankfully, the lighting is used really well, since peaking through dark doorways is half the fun in the early levels. Guns feel okay to shoot, but not great. Nonetheless, killing zombies is still fun, with the excessive gore we all want from a zombie game.
Not to mention, it's terrifying learning about a new monster enemy after walking into a dark room. Admittedly, the frog monsters scared me at first and made me panic due to their strength. That's great! Few games do that, and I enjoyed reacting like this in a zombie game. Heck, the creative variety in enemies is amazing and should be advertised better, since it really caught me offguard discovering the amount of dangerous, new, non traditional zombie enemies.
Gameplay is simple. Point at something and shoot it. That's it. Ammo is scarce, so should eb treated appropriately, which is what I expect from a zombie game. There is a variety in levels. SOme levels you get from point A to point B, shooting everything in your way, then you'll have a vehicular based survival mission and maybe a defense based mission afterwards with some boss battles and hidden stuff to find in hub areas and regular levels.
There isn't much to say about this game in terms of negativity. I bought this for 15p with very low expectations, but ended up enjoying this game a lot! However, I wanted to pay attention to the story, but it didn't grab me. There isn't much to complain about for a 15p purchase. If anything else, I'd say the art design is lacking, but it gets the job done. Some enemies seem to stand out too much from the overall art design which kind of bugged me.
If this is ever 15p again, certainly buy it for a few hours of fun and some replayability. I would ahve also paid £2 at most if I knew it was this good. So 15p is amazing really. If you enjoy shooting large amounts of zombies with some challenge along the way, then certainly give this a go.

It's like...Disney's "Treasure Planet" with a dash of Jak n' Daxter. (With humor that ranges from Ratchet n' Clank to Ren & Stimpy.) Upon a simple Google search, I learned that the art style, the model that everyone followed, though was originally created by Cory Loftis. The same guy who did Frozen and Wreck-it Ralph. Which is awesome in my book.

I'm a soundtrack snob. I'm not even gonna lie. This game's soundtrack is SPOT ON for its atmosphere. It's got the right amount of cartoony-ness, but can completely flip the mood and injects the right amount of seriousness and peril (when it's required). In a way that meshes pretty well with the game world, and doesn't seem out of place. It's really well done. I'd throw so much money at Carbine if they made the entire whole soundtrack available for purchase.

If you're tired of "
", like I am, then this is a darn good remedy for that. The combat is actually pretty smooth and responsive. The abilities (which can be altered via points and swapped out on the fly for free...a nice touch) are all pretty useful and give a lot of versatility. But not too much where you feel overwhelmed and lost.
Plus...actually having to sprint, double tap a direction to dodge, and double jump as a mechanic is great. The game feels like an action console game. Not enough where you'll get exhausted, but enough to remind you that it's still important. Especially in dungeons.

Pretty darn friendly and polite community here. Questions actually get answered (with no ridicule). They even have some player run events with actual prizes and whatnot. Like in-game money and actual good stuff. I've only witnessed one negative player so far, who was just actively (but passive-aggressively to the point of annoyance) trying to turn people away from the game, by ONLY talking about the game's problems (which it has a few) and then repeatedly (but "casually") suggesting that they play something else. Ricky Barnes or something like that.
("Ya", that's how positive an experience I've had with the overall community. Where I can only remember one negative person.)

Yeah...this is one of the game's high selling points. The housing system is both simple to use and pretty indepth. You can build almost anything you can imagine with the vast library of stuff you're given. Crafted stuff, stuff from the regular vendor, and stuff that you can find in the real world. You can even slapping down mini personal dungeons, mini-games, and farming plots for crafting materials on your lot. The amount of customization is ridiculous.
Oh and btw, important detail. There are no "inns" out in the world. Your house (that you can port to from literally anywhere) is your "inn". Where you gain exp based on "how well" you decorate your lot. Which is a great incentive to give housing a whirl.

Costuming/Transmog is another really good feature. You can "learn" a piece of armor/a weapon in the game and add it to your library. With armor, it doesn't even matter if your class can't equip it. Which extends across all your characters and even cross faction. You can even create sets, save them, and dye them on various parts of each item. Dyes are the same way, but it's character specific. Which isn't bad since they're pretty easy/cheap to come by.

It takes a while for queue's to pop. But that seems like a population issue. Which would be made a non-issue via more people playing. So I just joined a guild and had no problem with getting into dungeons. I've even heard that there's a circle (think a mini-guild that you can be in up to 5 of at a time), where people congregate just for that. Dunno about PvP though, as I don't like PvPing.
My comp is almost 6 years old, and my FPS is between 30 and 50 FPS. But I've noticed that the game seems to be CPU intensive and not GPU intensive. But that's not really a game breaker with me personally. As the game doesn't run like it's in "Perpetual Bullet Time". Which is good enough for me. Some not so much.
Other "issues" that I've heard are all pretty subjective. Like questing speed (which seems fine to me) and no fully spoken voice acting for all quest dialogue.
All-in-all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a really good F2P MMO. There's a lot IN this one.

I am finally writing a review about this game.  I did play this game for many hours(it reset after deleting the game due to mod problems) and don't believe adding another review will help an older and known game as such. The graphcis, battles and the settings were all to my likings.  However, they seem to lack so much compared to Medieval II.  The campaign in Medieval II are so much more dramatic and rich with random events that all together weave a great story.  The Crusade and the Pope, Jihad, and Americas made the campaign much more interesting than just alliance wars.  I can sit here and list all the features that I like better than the newer games.  The newers games do have impressive visuals and smoother combat, as Medieval units sometimes seem completely mindless of the battle.  As far as the advantage of the newer games go, that is it.  Overall, Medieval II has much more culture varieties, random happenings to keep the faction instable, and more events to drive the campaign and make it feel fresh even after several turns.  When the next historical Total War comes out, I believe it should model itself more like Medieval II than the newer games.

If you want a short run down of the classes, here you go
Healing or DPS
- Spellslinger : Uses a dual set of pistols to infuse attacks with arcane power as well as physical damage. Light long ranged DPS/Healing class, focuses on burst heals and prevention of damage when healing. Spellpower is the unique resource.
- Esper : Uses mental magic to soothe or damage where required. Light class that can hybrid in both long range DPS or close range DPS. Hard to master in terms of getting optimal damage, as well as healing using large AoE heals making them ideal for raid healing. Psi Points are the unique resource for this class.
- Medic : Hybrid ranged class that deals damage or heals through a pair of resonators (technological zappy thingies). High damage can be put out by using sets of grids and cascades of damage. Best tank healers because of their consistent healing. Actuators are the unique resource for this class. Medium class, competes with stalkers for gear.
Tank or DPS
- Warrior : Wields a big♥♥♥♥♥sword to chop big♥♥♥♥♥baddies to pieces, uses kinetic energy to smack bad guys in the face. Great at holding threat off the squishies in a raiding situation. Heavy armor class.
- Stalker : Uses a pair of claws to shank bad guys in the back, with the ability to stealth to gain extra damage from a critical hit followed by backstabs. As a tank stalkers rely on deflecting, glancing and steadfasting hard hits to survive. Highest skill cap to tank well as this class. Medium armor, shares its loot with the medic class.
- Engineer : Only ranged tank, uses a gun and his little bot buddies to lay havoc to thy enemy. Fantastic at absorbing craploads of damage, being the best class for the job.

I can only recommend this if you already played all of Borderlands Game of the Year and Borderlands 2 GOY and feel like you need more.... and you get it on sale like I did!   Even then, eh I'm not really sure I can recommend it totally.
I did finish the game with the Gunslinger character, and after beating the final boss and watching the ending cut scene I did something I never did with a Borderlands game, I deleted it from my hard drive!  Normally I would go back in and try another character, but finishing this game burned me out.
For me, the biggest thing I didn't like was the level design.  Somebody just went too crazy with the level design and made the levels too maze-like and platformy - they were just not fun to constantly be jumping around these crazy levels trying to figure out how to get somewhere on the map.  I think my personal taste is I need a level design somewhat based in "reality", not something completly illogical like these levels here.
So yah, the level design ruined it for me mostly.  That and the feeling of disconnect with the story (at least I think there was a story - hard to say what happened exactly or why).
The main thing that kept me going was I did like some of the different new weapon and shield effects.  Made the combat feel somewhat fresh.  It also seemed like I was getting purples and oranges at a higher rate than the previous games, and those for me are the most fun to play around with and probably what kept me going to the finish.
On the other hand I did not like the tech tree stuff.  None of it seemed very interesting and until the end game I almost never used my special powers because it was not needed or fun to use.  Maybe it was just the character I picked?
In summary - if you get it really cheap and want more borderlands then it's ok, otherwise skip it and wait for Borderlands 3.

Automation is not only a game capable of soaking up countless hours of your free time, but it is a useful tool to expand your knowledge of automobiles and how the different parts interact to affect the characteristics of the complete car.
Before I started messing around in automation, I knew all of the basics of how cars worked, but I did not know
. Automation has been an incredibly effective teaching tool for me. Now I know how Air-Fuel fuel ratios affect compression, how an oversquare engine revs higher while generating less torque then a comparable displacement undersquare engine, and many other tuning aspects.
I am looking forward very much to the completed tycoon game mode, as you should also be. It will complete this simulator making so you can waste even more of your time playing it, not that it's a complete waste of your time. You could be doing much worse things then blowing 4 hours in automation, you could be stabbing a homeless person. Or drowning your sorrows in booze. And while things like these and other activities like them are fine in moderation, you certainly do not want to spend all your time doing them.

I know this might surprise some of you, but I’m not what you’d call an “expert” when it comes to cars. I know they generally have four wheels and an engine to make them go. I’ve learnt the “controls” and I know that you have to feed them petrol or they’ll sulk and refuse to move, but when it comes to the actual mechanics of the vehicle it’s all magic and voodoo to me.
Then again, the same could be said about a lot of things, I don’t know much about rocketry either but that hasn’t stopped me from putting some cool spacecraft together in “Kerbal Space Program”.
It’s with this “can do” attitude that I approach Automation: The Car Company Tycoon game in development by Camshaft Software.
Armed with the knowledge that “Red cars go faster” I dive straight into the game with visions of gull wing doors, sleek styling and cherry red paintwork racing through my mind.
Casting an eye across the design options it seems that an engine might be an important component, my “cherry chariot” will probably need one of those so I confidently click on the icon, expecting a few engine options to choose from, you know, cheap and slow, standard and reliable or fast and expensive.
This was not the case, you have to design your own engines too, a thought which filled me with dread and anticipation in equal measure.
The engine is the magic box that makes the car work, I’m vaguely aware of plugs that spark and shafts that crank but putting one together.... do some shafts crank better than others? I don’t even know what that means!
It’s at this point that I realised just how complicated piecing a working vehicle together is actually going to be.
Luckily, Automation is eager to lend a hand in the form of tutorial videos which you can access from within the game. This is an excellent and for me vital option which explains the various components, what they do and why they do it.
Four stroke configurations, head types, forced induction, headers, mufflers, these were all just words to me before I played automation, they’re still just words to me now too, but at least I know what they are!
Any game that can teach you something whilst you’re having fun can only be a good thing.
Every component and every material you choose will have an impact on your engines performance.
You can tailor your design to your requirements, if you’re building an engine intended for an everyday city car then economy and reliability will likely be more important to you than raw power.
Vice versa if you’re planning on building a super car, then a big, powerful and inevitably expensive engine should power your wagon for the super rich.
There’s a wealth of information and graphs you can pull up as you tinker with your design, looking for the torque, RPM or horsepower of your engine, it’s all there for you to see in its statistical glory.
Another really nice touch are the dynamic engine sounds which will change to reflect your design choices, A beefy V8 should have its own distinctive growl and it does!
When you’re happy with your engine, it’s time move on to the car design itself, what chassis would be best, which suspension options  should you go with, what about engine placement, drivetrain setups, tyres, breaking systems, the list goes on and on, to say that the design options available are comprehensive is an understatement.
The level of detail available can be mind boggling, but again, Automation is there with its quick hit tutorial videos and text to guide you through.
Once you’ve finished tinkering with your mechanical design, it’s time to do the important things like adding the trims and spoilers, positioning the headlights and painting the whole thing red.
Even in its early access state this design process is a comprehensive, slick and enjoyable experience.
We’ve finally done it, the “Cherry Chariot”, a masterpiece in botched engineering, is ready to leave the design phase and go into production.
So what’s next? Should we start sifting through supply and demand figures? Decide which territories are ripe for picking? set up production lines and start advertising the hell out of our mechanical marvel?
When the money starts rolling in we could invest in some R&D, maybe start work on a new design, “The Crimson Carriage” and move our plans for global vehicular dominance another step forward.
The answer unfortunately is no, at least not yet.
Automation: The Car Company Tycoon is still in development and as an early access title many of the planned features haven’t made it into the game yet.
Camshaft Software are planning some very exciting features in future updates.
There will be a campaign mode running from the halcyon days of motoring through to the near future, in game scenarios and the obligatory sand box mode.
The game will feature dynamic world markets, distribution and demand, target groups etc. which should give a full business tycoon experience and more mechanical and chassis parts than even the most demanding designer could ever need.
What you get at the moment is a very competent car design tool and that warm fuzzy feeling from helping fund development of what promises to be a detailed car design and company manager tycoon title.
I’m not going to pin an arbitrary percentage on to Automation at this stage, it’s just too early and there isn’t really a “game” there yet to rate. I will say that the design element that is in place is excellently implemented (think the car equivalent to designing that spacecraft in Kerbal Space Program).
I’m genuinely excited to see how development progresses and I hope Automation receives the company tycoon mechanics it deserves.
If the same care and attention lavished on the design aspect is spent on the tycoon side of the game then this could be something special.

I bought this game on the strong recommendation of reviews and other steam users. I can see the potential in this game, particularly for fans of Yoko Taro or anime-style games in general.  However, I want to save other players the annoyance of trying to play this on PC. The controls, graphics, and performance are far below what I would expect for a full-price purchase. Additionally, the menus and map function represent the very worst aspects of a console port.
As for the lauded story and characters, sure, they are interesting. However, you will put in far too much time wandering around an empty landscape and engaging in samey battles for each crumb of storyline and characterization.  Simply put, there's far too much busywork and annoying artifacts of game design in proportion to the positives of the game. I highly recommend you go online and read a summary of the story and four or five "real" endings, rather than play through hours and hours of poorly-optimized spectacle fighting.  I am confident you will see that the "amazing" story praised by reviewers is pretty generic and certainly not worth the hundred hours of mediocre gameplay needed to reach it.
I'm someone who buys games based on professional review scores and this is the first time where I felt that a high Metacritic score really let me down.  This game simply is not worth the effort for the vast majority of players who are not diehard Yuko Taro fans.  I felt so strongly about this game that I bothered to write a review (my first) just to warn off other players.  I was truly disappointed by a game that has so much potential in terms of story and characterization and yet buries it under:
1) pointless wandering around an empty "MMO-style" world;
2) unintuitive and clunky menus & interface;
3) repetitive combat against highly similar enemies; and
4) meaningless fetch quests, fishing and other content-padding exercises.
Really sorry to say it because the game gives many glimpses of a fun, original title.  It's simply buried under too much nonsense and console port elements.

Ah, the original Deus Ex. I played this game without many preconceptions, many years ago, and I have started three different playthroughs since then. This is a diverse game, with many subsystems, ranging from inventory management and preparation (for instance, making space for a rebreather so you can survive underwater for long periods), stealth, first-person shooting and melee, ambushes, and other such things. The game challenges you in many regards, has some excellently-written dialogue, and provides a wide host of options for approaching nearly any situation. The story raises deep philosophical questions, and haunts the player with an interpretation of the future that we've seen several aspects of come to pass in real life since the game was released.
Unfortunately, it's also a game of deep flaws. Augmentations, one of the game's most unique features, are very inflexible and awkward by the default setup. The controls for activating them (the F keys) are inaccessible, and the necessity of activating/de-activating ALL of them individually exacerbate this issue. The game often puts augmentations in awkward, esoteric locations, which can mean a player who is not thorough (or is unlucky) can easily miss entire features of the game.
The shooting feels clunky, especially with the almost robotic upward motion of the recoil and the invisible hitboxes (you can frequently hit a character you weren't actually aiming at by shooting near them, while things like chain-link fences will intercept your shots), and melee has its own problems (there's a sweet spot to hitting an enemy in the back that can be difficult to locate or unresponsive, often because your weapon hit an invisible hitbox instead). These aren't game-breaking issues, but combined with the awkward augmentation controls, they create an action experience that can be stressful and clunky rather than exciting and smooth.
The necessity of heavily exploring every level also highlights some of the game's most severe flaws. Many of the environments are very drab and difficult to navigate, and the unique soundtrack can't help but become grating after a certain amount of time is spent in an area (and is also strangely absent in a few areas, such as the Hong Kong river area). The game revisits several areas, which provides interesting contrast, but can also end up feeling like filler, especially when the storyline seems to come to a general halt in an area that has been repopulated with many enemies.
Even the game's best features can fall flat at times. The excellent writing is sometimes undercut by extremely hammy or sleepy voice acting; excellent cinematography is ruined by primitive graphics; tense fights in well-designed levels are derailed by strange AI behavior, the list goes on.
While Deus Ex is certainly what I'd call a good game, it is a gravely flawed gem. If you wish to tackle this classic, get the Revision mod on Steam, and play using the Biomod game mode; it improves and simplifies the augmentation system significantly, improves the level layouts and graphics substantially, and renders a heap of bugfixes onto the old game in order to make it shine as much as it can barring a full remake. Played in its original form, Deus Ex was an enjoyable and memorable experience for me - but also a frustrating and at times boring one.

Do you like Minesweeper? How about Sudoku? Do you like logic and deduction puzzles involving numbers? Then let me introduce you to Hexcells. It’s a short and reasonably priced game that will give your brain some much needed exercise involving a bunch of “Aha!” moments.
It starts off like Minesweeper, but then gradually adds more and more layers of complexity. The gameplay involves deducing whether the hexes need to be saved or destroyed. Black hexes contain numbers that you can use to determine if there are blue hexes (the ones you mark/save). For example, if you have a 0 hex, then 0 hexes around it need to be saved while a 3 hex means 3 hexes must be saved. You do that for a while until the game starts throwing symbols and numbers on the outside at you. A 2 at the top of a column means there are two hexes to save in that column. A -2- in a hex means that there are two hexes to save that cannot be adjacent to each other. The trailer is good about showing the gameplay. Not a single puzzle relies on guesswork. It’s all about your brain processing the information so that you don’t make mistakes. My playtime reflects the time it took me to have 0 mistakes on all the puzzles.
If number logic puzzles are your thing, then Hexcells really is a good choice of game that’ll last you a couple days.

The enemy AI is as basic as it gets, so most enemies can be shot to death from a distance and most bosses (including the anticlimactic final boss) can be killed easily by kiting them or running back and forth while attacking. Game progression is linear, and peppered throughout are a small series of choices for the player to make, though they only make a difference to the story if you make particular combinations of choices. Sound is buggy, and frankly, so are many aspects of the game. It's full of gameplay ideas that probably sounded great when they were pitched, but by the time the game was done, everything just ended up as a severely underpolished and generic hack n' slash. For all of its many faults, I will say that Blood Knights provides brief glimmers of really satisfying gameplay, and I did have enough fun playing it to devote just under 5 hours to beating it. It's probably worth at least one playthrough for most people, but with all that went wrong, I'd have problems recommending it at its ridiculous price of $14.99.

The graphics, the colors, the combat, the humor, the art style, the sounds, I mean everything was just perfect. It was so refreshing, extremely polished and well done. The only thing that disappointed me was the fact that you couldn't find groups for low level dungeons.. and damn, what dungeons !? If they were unappealing, it probably wasn't that a big of a deal, but they were just brilliant ! The pig boss who scratches his belly and drops flees/ads.. lol, that was funny to see for the first time ! And all those mechanics !.. So, if there were enough players to play dungeons with while leveling, just to break the questing monotony, I would've reached max level without knowing. But doing only quests, I got kinda burned and needed a break before reaching max level... Got back into the game after a while, reached max level and experienced the endgame. Dungeons are hard and keeps you engaged, and that's the best part of this MMO ! I had enough of faceroll/speed dungeons from other games. There are end game maps where all players get organized in order to reach a common goal - by doing meta chain quests and killing bosses. I didn't experienced raids (I'm not a raider generally), but it's well known that are one of, if not the best in the industry. Jabbit EU (Exile/Dominion) : /chjoin global
Entity NA (Exile): /chjoin lfg
Entity NA (Dominion): /chjoin entitylfm
Final thoughts: this game deserve at least a try. You might love it, or not, it depends on personal tastes, but it's good enough just not to give it a try.

So far, so good. It's not the old school classical Ghost Recon, but evolution isn't always bad. There are some missions where alerting enemies means you instantly fail, so it still gives you a good mix of both worlds. The gun play is pretty good, but the mouse issues need some resolving if you have a mouse that is reported as "not working" with the  game. My PC plays it at 40+ FPS, with slight dips during heavy explosions or low visibility now and then, so just make sure your CPU and GPU are ready -- any quad core CPU and 256-bit GPU oughtta handle it pretty well. It also supports ambient occlusion, global illumination, DirectX 11, and tessellation.
Other than the bad, the good things seem to outweight them. The game supports 4 player co-op so you can team up with 3 friends of yours and go through the levels, and it has the usual multiplayer mode as well.
Overall, enjoyable so far. Check it out if you're a Clancy fan, or just like the slower, more methodic shooters like these.

40 hours played while having fun at the cost of 40 Euro. Recommended. As a standalone 4X in space, the game is inventive and enjoyable. However, Stellaris is not on par with other Paradox titles and I am quite disappointed. My main complaints are the UI and AI.
Paradox is a studio that knows how to create a good UI. How could they create this mess? It looks fine at first glance, but once you've sunk your teeth into the game mechanics, you'll notice how you have to hop in the menu between different screens to get info you need. Simple stuff like splitting off damaged ships from your fleet, that has been in Europa Universalis IV for years, is lacking. Instead, you have to manually split the fleet one ship at a time - and even that in a very poor design. Even the map gives inferior information - oftenly, anamolies will simply not show up on the galaxy map if you don't research them instantly (and you'll have to check system by system to find where you left it) and sometimes it doesn't even show where there are habitable worlds. I smell a big patch coming to fix all that.
The difficulty, in at least the first 15 or so hours, of the game is simply resource management. It is brilliant, you really need to strategize to increase your output while at the same time being able to colonize. There are also some scripted events and random encouters that'll force you to build a few warships. So while this is a nice phase of the game, the AI is rather passive. Some will declare you a rival or try to make deals, some will make demands, but they will NOT challenge you at all. Which is a pity. I suspect that there will be a DLC or two to cover the grey zone between rival status and war. That seems to be Paradox's way of fixing things.
A lot of people complain about the sectors. I think it's an okay solution to the management nightmare any 4X/grand strat becomes when you have a large empire. My complaint here is the AI, and that there is no way to send resources to your sector to allow it to grow (unless it's hidden somewhere in the backend of the UI). It just can't handle difficult situations with sparse resources. You really need to micromanage and grow your colony before you hand it over to the AI. Which is contraproductive to the whole point of having sectors. It's a shame to call for a patch for something that should have been working from the start.
I have also read a lot of complaints about wars ending automaticly. This is just a different feature from what you might be used to. Once you have set your wargoals, you will automaticly sign a peace when you can afford them all (and the AI is beaten). If you didn't set any wargoals, you'll get a white peace because you can't add them at the end of the war.
Diplomacy, and the AI for the different factions, is on Paradox level. It might at times fell a bit bare-boned, but it is infinitely better than most other games. You will actually be able to deduct how different factions will behave (Gandhi will not nuke the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you with 50 turns to go) and can adapt to face the potential threats to your empire. If someone hates your slavery policy so much it risks a war, you can change it (with a possible hit to your happiness). I'd personally prefer a bit more fluff around the diplomacy. If you have two hostile empires at your borders, you can count on them ganging up on you somehow.
The pacing of the game is very slow, even by grand strat and Paradox standards. Researching something takes years, and even at full speed that will take some time. Resources tick in on a monthly basis instead of trickling in all the time.
There are other good features (research tree, race designer, you can investigate enemy shipwrecks after battles) and bad features (poor variety of interaction with primitives, no variety to deal with tile blockers, you have to build lvl 1 building and then click upgrade to lvl 2 and then click upgrade to lvl 3) but overall it's a good, albeit slow, 4X. I expect the UI to be fixed eventually, and with more events/less downtime where your only challenge is resource management, this would be an awesome game.

I wanted to like this game, but I really can't recommend it.
Yeah, sure, it starts off strong. The first level / area is friggin' amazing and pretty much flawless. The graphic and sound design are incredible, and really convey a sense of grandeur and scale that few other games can match. The combat style is distinctively Platinum, and both fast-paced and stylish. The story concepts are pretty cool.
Unfortunately, the execution is botched at nearly every step. While the combat LOOKS cool, you'll quickly figure out that it's about as deep as the kiddy pool - you've got light attacks and heavy attacks. One of them tends to inflict small numbers but much faster, and the other inflicts larger numbers, but slower. The different weapons don't really seem to have any particular strengths or weaknesses, and there's no particular moves that are particularly good in one situation or another - you just kinda flail at things until they go down, no matter how smoothly animated and stylish your character may look while doing it. There's always ranged attcks to spice things up a bit, but.... well... they don't. Pod attacks are very safe as they let you do very reliable damage from a safe distance and almost nothing in the game can retaliate effectively to gunfire, but the numbers they put out are pathetic and thus killing things with guns is an exercise in tedium.
On that note, seeing what exactly your character is doing is a chore sometimes - the camera tends to be awful. It frequently follows way too close to the action and lacks an auto lock-on by default, forcing the player to awkwardly mess with the right analog while fighting just to keep the enemy in sight, which is a minor but aggravating chore that never really goes away. Sometimes it just goes all screwy, either due to getting stuck or the angle you are at relative to the enemy, or getting stuck behind the enemy themselves.
Moving on to the enemies, they are boring, boring, BORING. Now, the bosses tend to get a pass - they are one of the things the game does right. But the small fry are some of the most lazily designed enemies I have seen in years. They aren't the least bit threatening or memorable, the vast majority just being some variation or another of rusty metal humanoids... and not very detailed ones at that. They are at best a chore to fight, and make up the overwhelming majority of your foes.
The game is long and has a lot of content, but much of that content is dull as dirt and feels more like a single player MMO than a fully featured game - it's particularly fond of fetch quests and escort quests, neither of which have become any less aggravating in all the years they've been around. This type of quest can be carried by good enough AI or memorable enough characters, but in this game, they're.... well, they're not.
The main cast is well fleshed out, but most of the side characters are either dull as dirt, outright annoying, or some combination thereof, which makes it very hard to care about any of them. When it comes to dealing with them, you're pretty well on rails, too - amusingly enough the game DOES acknowledge it in several places if the player does something unconventional, needlessly jerk-ish, or counter-intuitive... but usually just means of a joke ending that immediately makes you then go back and repeat your action the intended way.
The plot is also pretty heavy-handed too, and occasionally had me rolling my eyes. The topics it tackles are weighty and deserve to be treated seriously, but so many aspects of characterization and underlying themes were treated with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer. It got old pretty quick in several events. It doesn't help that the comic relief is mostly a swing and a miss, and rarely helps lighten the mood.
In conclusion, yeah, I would still stress that this game has some legitimate brilliance hidden away in it. The art, the music, the animations, the boss battles, and the story concepts are all absolute top-notch. But you have to suffer through so much to enjoy them, and for me personally, it was just too much work for too little reward.

ALMOST there, but a major lack of polish, poorly mapped keys and an inability to remap, combined with insta-death platforming ruin what is an otherwise enjoyable game.
PROS:
-Good gameplay
-Simple but good RPG elements for a hack n slash
-Cutscenes can be skipped easily
NEUTRALS:
-Graphics weren't bad, but they certainly aren't good.
-Voice acting was hit and miss. Overall not bad.
CONS:
-Controls can't be remapped.
-Default control mapping is TERRIBLE (WASD to move, F to dodge; very unnatural key especially when trying to move in the D direction)
-Camera can't be controlled. (Combine this with the poor default controls and instant death platforming...)
-Animations are clunky and awkward.
I skipped all the cutscenes (as I almost always do in games like this) and this was a breeze which is important as forced cutscenes (esp in areas where they are repeated due to deaths) is an incredibly infuriating experience, but thankfully here it is not.
However, the poorly mapped controls combined with an inability to remap keys is a major deal breaker. There are several platforming elements that result in an instant death and send you back to the last save point, which means you usually have to fight a number of mobs just to get a chance to make the jump again....and if you fall....fight those mobs again...tedious and frustrating since the only reason you will fall is due to the bad controls (the platforming elements themselves are VERY simple and straightforward).
With some polish this game can be quite fun, but it needs to fix the controls first and foremost.

Bean Bag Buccaneers is a two player children's game, the object of which is to pick up your treasure chest on the central island and sail back safely.Each player has a giant sailing ship as their main game piece. Each ship has a removable sail, two trigger-action side panels, and a huge spring-driven cannon. Players take turns moving forward along a prescribed track and shooting bean bags at their opponent's ship. A hit on one of the side panels will force it to pop off and give the player a free shot at the other side; a hit forcing the sail off becalms the ship for a turn.To add to the pirate flavor, each player also has an eye patch. Wearing these will slightly affect depth perception and add a marginal bit of sport to the shooting.This game retailed for the somewhat impressive sum of $16 back in 1962. With its huge plastic ships (close to a foot long), giant vinyl play mat, and the eye patches, it may well stand as one of the more overproduced games of the early 1960s.

I'm going to preface this review with a disclaimer: This game is very unfinished and while I will recommend it, you should be willing to buy a game that may not get all of the features it promises. I bought the game on sale and I do not regret my purchase. No onto the review.
This game, while being described as an action roguelike, is not a roguelike, but a rogue-like-like. It has some roguelike elements but it's missing some of the soul and core mechanics that roguelikes are supposed to have. That doesn't mean it's a bad game, but you should consider this before buying.
The basic concept of the game is simple: Delve into the dungeon, make it to the bottom, grab the treasure and escape alive. There are enemies and traps along the way to stop you of course, and the twist of needing to escape with your life adds more difficulty and stress to an otherwise easy game. If you've played a lot of rogue-like-likes before you shouldn't find it too hard to make it to the bottom and beat the boss, but making it back should prove a lot harder.
Besides the dungeon, there is also a camp area. The camp area lets you spend your collected gold after you die to start off a run with an item, or items. These items should not be ignored and can give you a very helpful early game advantage. This is a good touch, although I wish more was done with it and the NPCs there. But remeber: The game is still in dev.
Overall I'd say Delver is a potentially deep and interesting rogue-like-like with cool ideas, and is worth sticking with for the features planned in the future. The developer has plans to add a lot more depth in items, magic, enemies, character classes and even an overworld with NPCs.

Ah, the original Deus Ex. I played this game without many preconceptions, many years ago, and I have started three different playthroughs since then. This is a diverse game, with many subsystems, ranging from inventory management and preparation (for instance, making space for a rebreather so you can survive underwater for long periods), stealth, first-person shooting and melee, ambushes, and other such things. The game challenges you in many regards, has some excellently-written dialogue, and provides a wide host of options for approaching nearly any situation. The story raises deep philosophical questions, and haunts the player with an interpretation of the future that we've seen several aspects of come to pass in real life since the game was released.
Unfortunately, it's also a game of deep flaws. Augmentations, one of the game's most unique features, are very inflexible and awkward by the default setup. The controls for activating them (the F keys) are inaccessible, and the necessity of activating/de-activating ALL of them individually exacerbate this issue. The game often puts augmentations in awkward, esoteric locations, which can mean a player who is not thorough (or is unlucky) can easily miss entire features of the game.
The shooting feels clunky, especially with the almost robotic upward motion of the recoil and the invisible hitboxes (you can frequently hit a character you weren't actually aiming at by shooting near them, while things like chain-link fences will intercept your shots), and melee has its own problems (there's a sweet spot to hitting an enemy in the back that can be difficult to locate or unresponsive, often because your weapon hit an invisible hitbox instead). These aren't game-breaking issues, but combined with the awkward augmentation controls, they create an action experience that can be stressful and clunky rather than exciting and smooth.
The necessity of heavily exploring every level also highlights some of the game's most severe flaws. Many of the environments are very drab and difficult to navigate, and the unique soundtrack can't help but become grating after a certain amount of time is spent in an area (and is also strangely absent in a few areas, such as the Hong Kong river area). The game revisits several areas, which provides interesting contrast, but can also end up feeling like filler, especially when the storyline seems to come to a general halt in an area that has been repopulated with many enemies.
Even the game's best features can fall flat at times. The excellent writing is sometimes undercut by extremely hammy or sleepy voice acting; excellent cinematography is ruined by primitive graphics; tense fights in well-designed levels are derailed by strange AI behavior, the list goes on.
While Deus Ex is certainly what I'd call a good game, it is a gravely flawed gem. If you wish to tackle this classic, get the Revision mod on Steam, and play using the Biomod game mode; it improves and simplifies the augmentation system significantly, improves the level layouts and graphics substantially, and renders a heap of bugfixes onto the old game in order to make it shine as much as it can barring a full remake. Played in its original form, Deus Ex was an enjoyable and memorable experience for me - but also a frustrating and at times boring one.

One main reason I never got pulled into the story was the absolutely horrible voice acting. They had 1 real person doing voices for like 15 different characters. With the lack of facial variation in the game, I was often confused if it was a new or old character I'd just met up with. The reason the individual voice acting was so bad is there was a complete lack of emotion in the voices. Impressively lacking I'd say. Like they grabbed people off the street. But I think that there are a LOT of people who view it through star-struck eyes because they played it when it came out or it was the first game of this type that they played. Just as the original Halo has a special place in my heart, I realize I probably wouldn't think so highly of it if I started with the latest FPS games and THEN played Halo for the first time. But aside from Golden Eye, that was the first game of that sort I ever played--and right when it came out--so it left a huge impression on me.

Keep in mind that not having played this game since I was a little kid, my experience today is very brief. Why?
Well Deus Ex is a fantastic game, no doubt about it. I remember playing it several times as a kid and having a blast with what seemed like unbelievable game mechanics, excellent story and a very memorable time exploring the various surprisingly expansive environments of this cyber punk alternate future. I can say that much and know it to be true. However, I haven't played this game in a very long time and gave it a couple shots not long ago and honestly, the control scheme for this game is far more rigid and complicated than I remember. Maybe it's because I've grown to used to what many modern games offer in terms of up to date user interfaces, smoother gameplay and overall better weapon and physics mechanics. In respect toward Deus Ex, it hasn't exactly aged well on that front.
Now of course, there are TONS of mods available for this game, a revision mod available right here on Steam for free if you own Deus Ex: GotYE, plus other mods which do improve the game on numerous levels. But I'm one of those people who tends to prefer to vanilla version of a game in the face of modern innovations in gaming. But as for the story and available environments, Deus Ex does shine and if your one of those people who has no troble adapting back to older game mechanics without getting frustrated, this is truly a title for you and even more so, if your a fan of the current Deus Ex games, you'll see that "classic Deus Ex" experience you may have heard about.
As for performance, not much to say. It's solid as a rock as far as I can tell, runs just fine on Windows 7 and 10 OS'. I even see the occasional though rare update, not that I check the change logs or anything, but it's worth noting somebody somewhere is keeping the game up to date.
Overall, I did have fun at one point, but I just can't back into that mindset with having three quarters of my keyboard hotkeyed and the janky gun and stealth mechanics. But the point is, I had an immense amount of fun with this game once and I'm sure you may find that this is a gem of a game for you.

Do you like Minesweeper? How about Sudoku? Do you like logic and deduction puzzles involving numbers? Then let me introduce you to Hexcells. It’s a short and reasonably priced game that will give your brain some much needed exercise involving a bunch of “Aha!” moments.
It starts off like Minesweeper, but then gradually adds more and more layers of complexity. The gameplay involves deducing whether the hexes need to be saved or destroyed. Black hexes contain numbers that you can use to determine if there are blue hexes (the ones you mark/save). For example, if you have a 0 hex, then 0 hexes around it need to be saved while a 3 hex means 3 hexes must be saved. You do that for a while until the game starts throwing symbols and numbers on the outside at you. A 2 at the top of a column means there are two hexes to save in that column. A -2- in a hex means that there are two hexes to save that cannot be adjacent to each other. The trailer is good about showing the gameplay. Not a single puzzle relies on guesswork. It’s all about your brain processing the information so that you don’t make mistakes. My playtime reflects the time it took me to have 0 mistakes on all the puzzles.
If number logic puzzles are your thing, then Hexcells really is a good choice of game that’ll last you a couple days.

Do you like magic? Do you like killing monsters? Then this is a game for you to play. I'll try my best not to spoil any of the story, since the game's highlight is the story. You have a choice of 8 different elements you can combine into a spell, including Magick, which I will get to. Many of these spells have different effects and can be used differently. If you become experienced, you can perform these spells without an issue. The 8 different elements are water, life, shield, fire, lightning, death, earth, and snow. Already you can imagine some of these elements have opposites and combine into different elements. You are exactly correct. For instance, water + snow = ice. Also an example of opposites are earth and lightning. Earth and lightning cancel each other out. You can use these different spells you come up with in many different ways. You can use it by just using left click, you can press shift + left click to apply it to your melee weapon (which I will explain later), and you can apply it to yourselves by middle clicking with the scroll on the mouse. You think that's it in combat? NOPE. You start off with a staff and another weapon which you use by clicking shift + left click, that's also how you use the spell you apply to it. You can find different kinds of staffs and other weapons (which most are melee) that have different effects. Then, there's the Magicks. These books can be found in the different levels. There's a certain amount in every level that does things that you cannot do with normal spells. I'll leave it at that. The combat capabilities alone shows that this was well thought out.
Now, let me explain other things. Not only are there so many references to different titles, the comedy is rather classic, and can be appreciated. Hehe, I like the style of it. Even when you beat the story, that's not all you can do. You can fight monsters in an arena until you die, and there's even a PvP setup for this. Although, I do think some of these spells do need to be nerfed, due to some of them 1 shot or does a ton of damage. Even then, you can do different DLCs (which by the way costs money) that you can do, recommended you do this with friends. I do enjoy this game, even alone, and I come back to it from time to time. This is definitely a game to play with friends. Just remember kids: Vlad is NOT a vampire ;)

The whole Hexcells series are really great puzzle games. The blame is totally on you for any mistakes you may make. They give you all the tools to figure out each puzzle if you can figure out the logic. The learning curve for figuring out that logic is spot on. Ideally play through the series straight, as the second and third game do start with more complicated puzzles and slightly new variations sooner. The feel as you go through a puzzle is likewise great. Occasionally you may get stuck for a solid length of time. The payoff is well worth it though. When you figure out a new bit, you get a solid rush as you suddenly can tick through another dozen cells with the new information provided.
Only two small complaints for the whole series. There is no separate toggle for the music and sound effects. Fortunately the music track is quiet enough that you can play something else over it and mostly not notice it. The music is nice and mellow if you want that, but not really the most engaging when you are stuck at the same spot for a long while. I went with the Classical Complete Works station from Pandora and it suited the mood quite well.
Second, the puzzles towards the end get quite long and there is no means to save mid puzzle that I could find. I assume this was so that you couldn't cheese your way to perfection. I would prefer the game at least give you the option to save in the middle if you were quitting and have the save auto-delete when you continue to prevent that. They did implement this in Infinite though. 5/5

Heres a great recipie for a 5 star besiege meal
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1 teaspoon salt
1 tablespoon white sugar
1 1/4 cups milk
1 egg
3 tablespoons butter, melted
1. In a large bowl, sift together the flour, baking powder, salt and sugar. Make a well in the center and pour in the milk, egg and melted butter; mix until smooth.
2. Heat a lightly oiled griddle or frying pan over medium high heat. Pour or scoop the batter onto the griddle, using approximately 1/4 cup for each Besiege. Brown on both sides and serve hot.
Very hard, but satisfying.

I don't have all the endings yet, but I have the 5 that count.  Every playthrough is worth it.  Playthrough C can be a little rough, the feels are real, but the end is worth it.  This isn't the kind of game I usually buy, but damn it, I'd buy it again.  I've bought the OST.  I'll buy the DLC, and I'll buy a sequel if they make one, no questions asked.
I recommend this game to anyone.  Even those that aren't into this kind of game.  Easy mode gives you options to make the game extremely easy, so even if you're not a fan of combat, easy mode pretty much does your combat for you.
There are only two problems I have with the game, and one of them isn't the game's fault.
The first is that the story gets pretty cliche Japanese at certain points, which may not be a negative for some people.  There is, for example, a male antagonist that has long white hair and is fairly feminine.  This doesn't really detract from the story at all, it's just an over-used cliche or stereotype.  It's possible this was done on purpose though. I wouldn't know.
The other problem is that the port isn't flawless.  I recommend either using Borderless Gaming if you want a true 1080p resolution, or using one of the fixes online that also has options to improve performance.
Other than that though, this game is a work of art, and I do not say that lightly.  This is also the only game I've played that somehow managed to get something in my eye.
As a final note, I'm someone who hasn't played any other games connected to this one.  The first Nier, and the Drakengard series.  I've never touched 'em.  But at no point did I ever feel like I was missing out on something, so if that's a concern for you, I wouldn't worry about it.  I'm sure there are nods to the other games, but nothing really struck me as 'off' like it didn't belong.
EDIT: So there still hasn't been an official patch (As of 23/11/17) to fix the resolution and optimization issues some people have been having.  I'm going to leave this as a positive review because I enjoyed the game so much despite its flaws, but I think this game is being heavily mismanaged.  They're just riding on the unexpected success. I bought this game on the strong recommendation of reviews and other steam users. I can see the potential in this game, particularly for fans of Yoko Taro or anime-style games in general.  However, I want to save other players the annoyance of trying to play this on PC. The controls, graphics, and performance are far below what I would expect for a full-price purchase. Additionally, the menus and map function represent the very worst aspects of a console port.
As for the lauded story and characters, sure, they are interesting. However, you will put in far too much time wandering around an empty landscape and engaging in samey battles for each crumb of storyline and characterization.  Simply put, there's far too much busywork and annoying artifacts of game design in proportion to the positives of the game. I highly recommend you go online and read a summary of the story and four or five "real" endings, rather than play through hours and hours of poorly-optimized spectacle fighting.  I am confident you will see that the "amazing" story praised by reviewers is pretty generic and certainly not worth the hundred hours of mediocre gameplay needed to reach it.
I'm someone who buys games based on professional review scores and this is the first time where I felt that a high Metacritic score really let me down.  This game simply is not worth the effort for the vast majority of players who are not diehard Yuko Taro fans.  I felt so strongly about this game that I bothered to write a review (my first) just to warn off other players.  I was truly disappointed by a game that has so much potential in terms of story and characterization and yet buries it under:
1) pointless wandering around an empty "MMO-style" world;
2) unintuitive and clunky menus & interface;
3) repetitive combat against highly similar enemies; and
4) meaningless fetch quests, fishing and other content-padding exercises.
Really sorry to say it because the game gives many glimpses of a fun, original title.  It's simply buried under too much nonsense and console port elements.

It's "roguelike" which, if you're not aware, essentially means that you learn a few basics and then the rest of the game is randomly generated each time you play it from the layout of the rooms to the items that you get. In my opinion Isaac takes this way too far to the point that it's outright frustrating at times and feels like whether you win or not is mostly up to the rolls. At the same time, it's also not a very pricey game and for a couple bucks it's fun to play through a few times and keep on hand for when you want a break from meatier games that also require more time investment.
All in all if you can tolerate the annoyance of the random generation, as well as a healthy number of sometimes game-crashing bugs if you add the Wrath DLC, it's a fun title to keep on hand.

Hi everyone this game has made me want to write a review it is my first review and as I have only played for 2 hours this will be to the best of my abilities (as the time is now 3:33am and I have been up for around 26 hours now) and please I accept criticism.
Network Issues
I have had no troubles connecting to servers. I have not tried quick joining, I have selected the servers I have wanted to join.
Character Customization
So far in this game the Character Customization is pretty nice as far as armor and colors can go. You can change the armor on your left and right shoulders and arms independently, to mix and match some pretty menacing looking outfits. There isn’t much to choose from as of yet about 7-10 choices for each part you can customize, those parts being Head, Left shoulder, Right shoulder, Left arm, Right arm, Chest piece, Scarf (Shinobi style is my favorite), Groin, Belt, Legs, and Boots. You can even have different voices. So far as of playing I have yet to see the same two people be exactly the same (unless they were trying for it). The parts that you cannot change about your person yet are if I remember correctly Gender and Hairstyle.
Weapons
The combat in this game reminds me of Chivalry more than War of the roses, in the fact that you do not have to block in left right up down format, you just have to hold the right mouse button at the time the opponents swing would hit you and you will parry them completely. There are 5 swords to choose from so far, Stealth Sword (grants x5 backstab/flank damage) My personal favorite!!, Fire Sword (added ongoing fire damage/ may pierce block) Tank Sword( grants extra blocking time/reduces incoming damage a hair) Bowman’s Sword (extra ranged damage) and Mobility Sword (Gives you sprint speed without having to but away your sword/faster dodge rolls) Second personal favorite. Your choices for secondary weapons are as follows, An Explosive Throwing Axe (one time use 75-100 damage depending on how close the target is to it after it lands charges and explodes) Personal Favorite, A sturdy Bow (depending on the range and where you hit your target 25-100 damage multiple arrows 10 or more), a Mine ( 75-100 damage EXTREME KNOCKBACK, I have been sent flying off of capture points and into the void because of these nasty buggers), and a Trap ( a Gigantic bear trap that does either 25-50 damage and locks you in place for a few seconds, if the hunter is vigilant you are dead as soon as you trigger it)
Spells
The spells are as follows, Fireball (it’s a damage over time spell), Freeze ( Its pretty much a Trap you can use over again), Flame Drop (Execute your Target and everyone around him with this, But be warned cool down time is pretty major and you will hurt/kill friendlies), Teleport ( It’s a Teleport Spell)Choice 1 from me, Heal ( It heals you fully over time) Choice 2 from me, Phase Shift( turns you into a glowing ball that is immune to damage as long as you can hold it, really good for dodging heavy hitting swings from the fire and tank swords), Stealth ( turns you completely invisible, Be careful though your team members will not be able to tell if you are a friendly while invisible). Magic Invulnerability (Immune to all magic damage) For spells you get two choices, Teleport is a must if you want to have any kind of advantage in movement against a mobility sword!! Heal is just awesome, pop it in the middle of a fight and if you can block your opponents attacks you will be at full health in a matter of seconds.
Combat
Here are a few tips, if you plan on being ranged support with the bow, use the Bowman’s sword with a mine at your feet so you don’t get stealth killed. Spell choices for ranged in my opinion the best two spells are Teleport (to get to higher ground and have a height advantage against everyone on the field) and Freeze (just in case someone starts charging at you with a partner)
For you stealthy people, who just love to dash in and out with maximum damage, use the Stealth sword with teleport (required) and freeze/stealth/heal.
Anyone who wants to try taking on multiple melee combatants at once I suggest the Tank (hp damage reduction) or Fire sword (Pure raw damage). HEAL IS A MUST, and take fire drop just to run into a group cast it and get a good 4 or 5 kills.
Learning Curve
In the beginning, you will die. It will happen. Just learn from your mistakes and have fun.
Additional notes
The only three glitches I keep encountering are as follows, the in game scoreboard is glitchy at times with different resolution sizes, my name shows up as the only one typing in chat, and the other is that sometimes when I make a kill it says Player alive killed Dead Player.
Much respect to the two man crew that has brought this game to life. A few things I would like to see in the future if at all possible, an Assassinate button for when you are chasing down a target that is Sprinting (sword is on their back) away from you and you have either the Stealth sword OR the Mobility sword, or just an Assassinate button in general. A capture the flag type game mode would be awesome for this game, as would dueling servers. I would like the Spell Freeze to lock people in place so they cannot turn to face me if I hit them in the back with the freeze spell. I would like the Bow and throwing axe to have better crosshairs on the screen rather than having the translucent circle that is the size of my water bottle. The last thing I have an issue with is the teleport spell I would like it to negate fall damage if timed properly, as in someone is running under a tower entrance I want to be able to jump from said tower and a few seconds before hit teleport and land safely on the ground and give chase to them, instead of just going splat on the ground. Those are my wishes :D

Good game. Buy it.
Major difference with other space 4x games:
- Ethics: Every race has  2 or 3 ethics that describe the wants and needs of that race. Depending on how different a conquered race ethics are from your empire, they will be easily or never assimilated. Ethics of any race can change (including your race) for a variety of reasons and brings all kinds of positive and negative with them. This makes the races unique and richly diversified.
- Warscore: When you go to war, you declare war to someone and then choose a bunch of objectives that you want to accomplish. As the war progress and if you win battles, your warscore gets higher until it reach 100 points. Then you win all your objectives (or the enemy wins all of them). Its peculiar to say the least. Different take on conquest very similar to Europa Universalis.
Pros:
- Strategy of building your empire is very deep and interesting. And don't fret young padawan, as your empire gets bigger, you will also unlock with new teknologies a myriad of buildings, influence, edicts and other tools to help you manage better that biiiiig empire of yours. The tek is very well balanced because you seem to get the right tek just when you start straining because of the size of your empire.
- You don't control battles, so all you can do is design your ships properly to be better against the enemy's ships. There is a kind of rock-paper-scissors-shotgun deal for the weapons and defences that makes it suprisingly deep compared to the  seemingly simple choices that you have.
- Graphics are superb except for battle and ground combat which are simple affairs (No sword of the stars kind of battle here)
- Sound is awesome. Music is so good that even after many hours, i still don't get tired of it.
- The AI is very very very good. Human-like would be a good term. It knows when you are nasty and bad and if you becomes too big of a threat, it will band togheter a couple of empires and come kick down your door. Trying to defend 3-4 systems at the same time from different fleets with your 1 big fleet sure is challenging. And the universe is big. Very very big. The logistics of defending your big empire becomes very hard. You WILL understand just how the romans felt at the end of their reign. Hehehehe
- No bugs that i've seen
- The game is still supported after more than 1 year. They are still refining it and god it has aged like fine wine. Many small things that were an irritant or were missing have been added/improved and the game is much shinier now because of it.
Cons:
- Space battle are simple affairs. Generally the one with the biggest fleet wins, but it depends also on the design of the fleets. This make them quickish and uninteresting.
- Ground combat is even simpler than fleet combat. More troops wins and no troops design.
- I hate the ship design screen. It's functional, but i somehow can't stand it.

Stellaris is a phony.
There is a critique of writing where you quickly determine an author is self-indulgent (like my tldr reviews).
Paradox and the devs of this game are self-indulgent-- to the point of aggressive masturbation.
Stylistic preferences aside, the lack of good sense in this game speaks to individuals with absolutely no real world experiences. Imagine an author who wrote a story about firefighters, but who had zero experience with first responders. Quickly someone might reply, "How could anyone have experience running an interstellar empire?"
You couldn't, but for a game to have any resemblance of credibility or enjoyment in needs to meet players' basic, ubiquitous, experiences. In my opinion, it needs to make some rational sense.
For example, if a group of home invaders enter your house and beat you and your family within an inch of your lives, you don't get decide when when it ends or under what conditions. No one has to actually experience a science fiction universe to understand how violence works. Given Stellaris, these devs apparently don't understand how violence and force of arms work -- or they are ignorantly forwarding some idealized worldview of their own.
Instead, the folks at Paradox seem to have channeled their undergraduate poli-sci and psychology classes into how they guess or want the elements of national power work. How often have you had someone try to use complex language to hide their lack of competence and knowledge? That's Stellaris. Phony. Good gameplay isn't measured in average syllables per word.
Maybe it's like listening to someone try to talk about sports after they caught an hour of ESPN at their Barber Shop. If you know anything about sports, you immediately identify the person as a phony -- and smile graciously.
Normally Paradox makes games based on history. That has offered them a nice crutch, because their flaws and problems can be attributed to balancing gameplay with historical events. Not so with Stellaris, because there are no historical events to use as an excuse for bad design.
It's a typical complaint that no Paradox game is playable until after a year of players providing them free consulting. I held out about year in the hope things would be improved. I didn't wait long enough.
In fact, all their marketing hype about "social complexity" in Stellaris seems to result in SLOW, boring, unimaginative gamplay. A big open galaxy, but the player is locked on railroad tracks for the whole game.
I suppose fans might counter with...
"But it looks great!" -- says the person who has never dated someone super-hot that turns out to be nothing more.
"It's needed for PvP balance!" -- says the person who doesn't know that getting your butt kicked has been a fun part of 4X going back before VGA Planets. I'm sorry, but only the champions in my league got a trophy when I was growing up.
"Use patience and let each game develop!" -- says the person most interested in a Federation victory. I have to admit, if you're the kind of person who wants to watch an undergraduate social interaction simulator for hours this could be the game for you. That said, I would still point you towards the Democracy game series as generally better.
"It's insanely complicated and the balance is really complex!" -- says the person who didn't realize that influence and energy are the only two resources that really matter and are both used in a simple dynamic friction pattern. Stellaris' marketing illustrates a complex maze, but the player is only given access to the dominant strategy path. Attempting any individualized play will result in immediate frustration.
Don't take my review as gospel obviously, but as you read positive reviews for Stellaris you are going to encounter a lot of excuses for this game.
I feel like this game's devs kept all the fun for themselves and paid for it from our wallets. Stellaris is a phony.

So Deus Ex.
The definitive PC experience. One of few games which wouldn't work on consoles at all.
It's a cyber-punk First Person Role Playing Game in which you play as a cybernetically augmented special agent JC Denton on a mission to defeat a terrorist organization, all while a elaborate conspiracy uncovers itself through the course of the game.
The game starts with our hero arriving onto the Liberty Island, NYC. There, he has to free a captured agent and take the terrorist leader into custody. It is a simple and fairly easy mission, which really feels like a sandbox, where you can test different equipment, see which elimination method you prefer etc. All the levels are open and free to explore, and the game rewards you with useful items and extra skill points you can use to improve JC if you do so. There are always at least 2 ways to get somewhere, even when NPC's tell you there is only one way. You need to be resourceful, and outsmart your oponents. The game shows a staggering amount of detail, as every little thing you do affects dialog and NPC reactions.
Walk into the lady's restroom? Get scolded by your boss for doing so.
Don't give a hotel owner in distress a pistol? Well, you better come to him when JoJo shows up or he will die.
You can talk to many different NPC's to get intel, which will help you in your mission. What seems like a simple bum, can give you info about a secret passage, giving you a chance to avoid sniper fire.
Deus Ex's soundtrack is incredible; It's a perfect exaple of old video game OST's: Powerful, catchy and memorable, the kind you'll want to stand in place and just listen to. A fantastic thing the game did, was remix the game's main theme using church organs in the cathedral level.
The game itself tackles serious problems, such as which is better: globalisation or isolation, martial law or complete anarchy.
Now, let's get into gameplay. The gunplay is very outdated, it feels fairly sluggish and not rewarding. The stealth system, while not perfect, is enjoyable. The augmentation system enchances the gameplay a lot, by giving you lots of new fun abilities, such as higher jumps, stronger hits, or even a remotely controlled spybot with a EMP attack.
Overall, the game is great. The story gets deep, and while outdated, the mechanics are lots of fun. Subjectively, I'd say You should really check it out if you haven't.
