In a nutshell:
A charming little 2D side-scrolling platformer with a solid foundation in gameplay for anyone who enjoys the genre. Although you begin your journey with just a generic playable character armed with an axe and a few random items, after harvesting enough wood, stone and precious metal to craft more advanced tools and weaponry to better slay a variety of enemies, you will quickly unlock more playable characters, pets and hats with different traits, and you will be inclined to try the whole journey again. The game is fun and plays well as it is, and the new contents/improvements constantly being added definitely makes it a value-buy in the long run.
Gameplay:
You will move, dash, jump and double-jump to get you across from the entrance on the left to an exit located to the  right, stopping briefly to chop down trees for wood, mine some stones/ores and to harvest herbs and mushrooms. You will encounter slimes, boars, skeletons, spiders and many other type of enemies, and you may choose to engage them with well-timed slashes of your item in hand (i.e not necessarily a proper weapon), snipe with your bow and arrow or simply introduce them to one or all three types of elemental magic attacks should you desire. Gain experience to level up for better stats and special skills to aid you in slaying the final boss at the end, but with permanent death, it is likely that it will take you more than a couple of tries with one of many unlockable characters before you succeed. Get friends to play together and it will be even more enjoyable, depending on who survives better.

You know when you're hours deep into the late game of a 4X/civ-like game, and you suddenly feel horribly depressed about how you've spent your time? Where you think "what am I doing with my life? My friends are all leading successful and productive lives while I stare at tiny ships on my computer"? Stellaris is a game that will bring you those moments in spades. It is a game that despite its ultimately (I believe) sound design, boy oh boy does it turn into a slog.
The first few hours are of course great. The excitment of starting a star empire and exploring the depths of space filled with fallen empires and sci-fi mysteries, and the reassuring feeling that comes with knowing your territory is safe and your prospects are good are wonderful to have, but the problem with this game, beyond its UI system and your inability to control your fleets productively, is that it doesn't tie itself up nicely. It doesn't have a tech victory like in CIV; the only way to win is to destroy everyone else, grab 40% of the planets in the galaxy, or convince a majority of the AIs to join you. The former two will take hours and hours, assuming you're already well ahead of everyone else, and the latter is basically impossible because of some infuriating immutable societal characteristics other AIs have that will prevent them from liking you.
You will reach a point in the mid to late game where your terrorial expansion will slow down, and suddenly you'll realize that the last three hours you spent staring at your galaxy map only netted you two new planets and some mundane tech upgrades. Going to war with someone will begin to feel boring, because you're not so much asserting your will over someone to ensure your future survival so much as you're just running around from planet to planet, occuping as many as possible until the AI finally gives you what you want. Actually carrying out one of the game's victory conditions to fruition, even on the smallest map, is exhausting. You'll reach a point where you'd much rather start again and capture that initial feeling of excitement again, but then you think, what was the point of the last 7 hours then? Why did I stick with it just to give up?

A refreshing new title to the genre of 4X, Stellaris introduces new concepts and is fun for a while. However, because of its very slow pacing & progression it doesn't have the fun factor and staying power of better titles in the genre.
It's a good game at its core. But some design decisions ruin it for me. It will be frustrating if you are a gamer who cares about fun/time ratio, or just want to feel like you made progress in a play session. You will feel like it's a game you'd love to love, but you never manage to truly get into it because of its slowness and that feeling of "playing chained" it gives you.
- A real attempt at innovation. Mechanics like immigration (population can move freely between planets and empires if enabled), robotic & synth "build-able" population, randomly generated races (including how they look), anomalies you discover in exploration, enlightenment (think of it as making city-states out of barbarians in civ), uplifting (genetically engineering pre-sentient species to make custom population types with traits you want), etc are new and a truly fresh and welcome additions to the genre. On this aspect alone the game should be applauded.
- Great graphics & aesthetics. Love how planets, stars, and black holes look.
- A huge time sink. Which is good for a lot of people but not for everyone since it mostly comes from a diluted experience. But if you are the kind of player who likes to stick with a single game for a long time then this is a good investment for you.
- Big on exploration. It puts EXPLORATION back into 4X. Finding anomalies, new alien races, derelict ships, ancient artifacts and stories of ancient races, etc. Many varied events spice up the discovery of the universe.
- EXTREMELY slow. I am 75 hours in my first game and I haven't won yet. I will probably need twice that to win a single game. Everything takes forever and is not necessarily fun because too often you feel like the game is doing its best to slow your progress, thus a very strong feeling of "playing chained". Keep in mind, I AM PLAYING ON MAX SPEED! And only pause to issue orders when necessary.
- Too micromanagement intensive. It is strange to see so much micro in a game that has the universe as a playground. It feels like a missed opportunity to focus on macro mechanics.
- Tedious and repetitive on some tasks, like controlling survey ships system by system and no "automate workers" option like in similar titles. Note: Yes you can shift click to chain commands, but you lose the queue each time you find something like an anomaly so that's not practical. You will also eventually find a technology to automate survey ships, but that's gonna be way down the road and an expensive tech at that when you have better options.
- Some extremely unfortunate design decisions. One example is that building takes always the same amount of time, with no option to accelerate or speed up the process no matter your level of power of technology. A planet that has 20 population and every upgrade will build a new power plant in the same exact speed as that other new colony you just built and that has 1 single population. If that wasn't bad enough, if you have Mining network level 3, you can't just build that right off... you have to build the 1, then upgrade to 2, then upgrade to 3... each of them taking months of fixed time that can never be made faster, not even through buying the damn building with credits like similar games. This means that the game starts slow and stays slow, no matter how powerful you get. This is quite bad because--in most games in this genre--we accept the slowness of careful building at the start with pleasure and anticipation knowing that playing it carefully well will lead to a spike in power later as things build up into a snowball effect. In Stellaris, you never quite hit that "now watch me soar" phase. It's just a full game seemingly stuck in "slow settling" phase.
-
victory conditions and only 3 of them: (1) Own 40% of HABITABLE planets. Not just habited, but all habitable planets! ... and the universe is quite huge (2) Subjugate all other empires (that's a lot too because war is extremely slow, I'll explain why in the next point) (3) Have your federation (allies) control 60% of HABITABLE PLANETS, meaning even if you ally and conquer absolutely everyone, there's dozens or hundreds of planets for you to colonize still. Colonization being capped by Influence, which generates very slowly and is capped at 1000 storage, meaning you can't even stockpile it for the right time. Tedious! And there are no creative victory conditions like the science or cultural victories in civilization, just tedious conquest of the whole space one planet at a time. Even players who absolutely love this game will confess they rarely finish a game because it's so tedious to clean up for a victory.
- Warfare is usually where you get to blow off some steam and get some blood flowing in this type of games. But nope, not here. Warfare is as tedious and as plagued by slowness as everything else. First, travel is very slow and traveling back and forth takes FOREVER because your warp engines heat up and need to cool down at every jump, and they need also to build energy for a jump. Second, you can't outright capture planets... even if you invade them the enemy will take them back automatically at the end of the war. The only way to capture planets is to say you want them UPON WAR DECLARATION, and there is a point system that limits how many you can demand. You can't demand more than 4 or 5 planets each war (costs 17-25 points per planet and your maximum points are 100), which makes it problematic and a chore to take down the bigger empires. And you can't outright vassalize bigger empires because the score to vassalize is too big (over 100), you have to make them smaller first and that goes through slow conquest a handful of planets at a time. So you wage war, take a few planets, have to wait 10 years to be able to declare war again, rinse and repeat, and this for EVERY empire in the game. Tedious! Not to forget that even after you do this, you still have to colonize habitable planets that nobody took. Shoot me in the head please.
- Little sense of accomplishment at every play session. This is what absolutely kills it for me. Ok so you took a day off, you played Stellaris all day... and then you go to bed... feeling you did absolutely nothing. You wake up in the weekend, and do another full day of play thinking "ok yesterday was slow but today I WILL make progress"... nope. Not happening. None of the 4X titles--or strategy games in general--make me feel like this and it's not a good feeling.
Stellaris is a gem. But a very flawed gem at the moment. Most of its issues come from a single source: The feeling that the designers were singing
(in my mind in the rhythm of "let it go" from frozen) while making it.
The good news is that this is a Paradox game and it is still being worked on. Will they fix it? Do they even consider this slowness a problem? I have no idea. But in the meantime, the slowness is the biggest factor deciding if you will enjoy the game or not.
If sinking hundreds of hours in a single campaign is not a problem for you, you will probably like this game. It has enough innovation and eye candy to be likable. But if you actually want a game that has a pulse and decent pacing and energy, this game will frustrate you and you will move on to other titles relatively quickly.
I would still get it on a big sale just to see the innovations it brings. But I definitely don't see this game as having the staying power of better titles like civilizations and endless space in its current state. It is mostly something you would buy if you already played and are tired of better games like civ and endless space.

I had a hard time deciding whether it should be a positive or a negative review. I love this game. I can't go back to most of the MMORPGs I played before because they just aren't good enough after Wildstar. It has one of the most generous f2p models on the market and if you consider whether you should try it or not - try it.
The problem is, the things that make this game enjoyable were mostly made months or even years ago, and the recent developments have mostly been a streak of failures, bad decisions and poor management.
This game has a great setting. It's grimdark in a candy wrapper with a decent storyline, great characters and lots of little details scattered around. But one of the factions (the Dominion) is just not properly represented outside of its own questlines, giving you an impression of shallow cartoonish villains. The other (the Exiles), after a deeper look inside, shows a profound lack of integrity beyond common goals mostly revolving around fighting for survival.
This game has great PvP - but there is a lot of issues that snowballed into making the PvP community almost non-existent. Poor rewards, poor resource sinks, stale meta, a slew of small but annoying class balance issues - all there, all unattended. It still, however, knocks out any other PvP action I had in any other MMORPG. A competent PvP designer could make it flourish.
This game, in my opinion, needs better management and possibly game designers. There was a lot of bad decisions scaring off all kinds of audiences, be it poor marketing, counterproductive system reworks, effectively scrapping older content with reward creep and outright ignorance - and though there are some good decisions coming along the balance is far, far from perfect.
While all I said probably sounds scary, you shouldn't be all that discouraged. It's a great game. It is, by all means, free to play. You can have weeks or even months of fun here, and you probably will. But as things stand right now, do not get any false hope after you jump in, because the bar of quality was not, is not and quite likely will not be held.
This is what happens when WoW, Borderlands, and Ratchet and Clank have a threesome.

Welcome to one of the most amazing, underrated MMOs out there. Wildstar is here for any of you who love action combat, who love humor, sci fi settings, wild characters, creativity, challenge, and everything inbetween.
PvE content is intense. Players have tons of options and different builds to face the myriad number of challenges and mechanics that will confront them, whether alone or in groups up to twenty for raids. Challenges and achievements will keep you hunting, and paths will keep you working on everything you can.
PvP content is constantly getting adjusted and refined. It's been a weak point before, but Carbine refuses to give up on making the PvP experience better and more fluid for everyone. Every class has amazing specialities in the different styles that make for a difficult and wild fight.
There's also great customization, between the costumes that characters can wear, with different dyes and builds, and the Housing element. There's an ingame joke that level 14, when one gains the ability to get their own house, is the first endgame -- it's so easy to get wrapped up in creating the perfect home for your character that you could forget how much more there is to do outside! And yet when you do, you'll unlock more and more items to help customize your living space, from a place to relax with friends, to a hub for everything endgame, and everything inbetween!
The social scene is budding and constantly active, whether it is in seeking help for endgame content, learning about lore and plotlines, or simply roleplaying with friends - and for those in that crowd, there is a HUGE RP following willing to welcome in any and everyone interested in checking it out!
Overall, this is a fantastic game that needs every bit of recognition it can get. And if anyone needs help in furthering their adventures, I, for one, am always going to be out there on Nexus, looking for more recruits!

Negative:

I wanted to like this game, but I really can't recommend it.
Yeah, sure, it starts off strong. The first level / area is friggin' amazing and pretty much flawless. The graphic and sound design are incredible, and really convey a sense of grandeur and scale that few other games can match. The combat style is distinctively Platinum, and both fast-paced and stylish. The story concepts are pretty cool.
Unfortunately, the execution is botched at nearly every step. While the combat LOOKS cool, you'll quickly figure out that it's about as deep as the kiddy pool - you've got light attacks and heavy attacks. One of them tends to inflict small numbers but much faster, and the other inflicts larger numbers, but slower. The different weapons don't really seem to have any particular strengths or weaknesses, and there's no particular moves that are particularly good in one situation or another - you just kinda flail at things until they go down, no matter how smoothly animated and stylish your character may look while doing it. There's always ranged attcks to spice things up a bit, but.... well... they don't. Pod attacks are very safe as they let you do very reliable damage from a safe distance and almost nothing in the game can retaliate effectively to gunfire, but the numbers they put out are pathetic and thus killing things with guns is an exercise in tedium.
On that note, seeing what exactly your character is doing is a chore sometimes - the camera tends to be awful. It frequently follows way too close to the action and lacks an auto lock-on by default, forcing the player to awkwardly mess with the right analog while fighting just to keep the enemy in sight, which is a minor but aggravating chore that never really goes away. Sometimes it just goes all screwy, either due to getting stuck or the angle you are at relative to the enemy, or getting stuck behind the enemy themselves.
Moving on to the enemies, they are boring, boring, BORING. Now, the bosses tend to get a pass - they are one of the things the game does right. But the small fry are some of the most lazily designed enemies I have seen in years. They aren't the least bit threatening or memorable, the vast majority just being some variation or another of rusty metal humanoids... and not very detailed ones at that. They are at best a chore to fight, and make up the overwhelming majority of your foes.
The game is long and has a lot of content, but much of that content is dull as dirt and feels more like a single player MMO than a fully featured game - it's particularly fond of fetch quests and escort quests, neither of which have become any less aggravating in all the years they've been around. This type of quest can be carried by good enough AI or memorable enough characters, but in this game, they're.... well, they're not.
The main cast is well fleshed out, but most of the side characters are either dull as dirt, outright annoying, or some combination thereof, which makes it very hard to care about any of them. When it comes to dealing with them, you're pretty well on rails, too - amusingly enough the game DOES acknowledge it in several places if the player does something unconventional, needlessly jerk-ish, or counter-intuitive... but usually just means of a joke ending that immediately makes you then go back and repeat your action the intended way.
The plot is also pretty heavy-handed too, and occasionally had me rolling my eyes. The topics it tackles are weighty and deserve to be treated seriously, but so many aspects of characterization and underlying themes were treated with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer. It got old pretty quick in several events. It doesn't help that the comic relief is mostly a swing and a miss, and rarely helps lighten the mood.
In conclusion, yeah, I would still stress that this game has some legitimate brilliance hidden away in it. The art, the music, the animations, the boss battles, and the story concepts are all absolute top-notch. But you have to suffer through so much to enjoy them, and for me personally, it was just too much work for too little reward.

A game that sounds interesting and unique in concept and starts off fairly enjoyable, but swiftly turns into a repetitive, tiresome experience.
The first couple of levels are quite fun. It's thrilling as you silently stalk around parties, picking off guests one by one, gradually thinning the crowd until the satisfactory final kill. However, the game doesn't really offer much in terms of variation. Each level drops you into a loud party, with the simple objective of killing every single person there without getting caught or killed. Each level is more difficult than the last, with a new map and music, but the traps and weapons that are provided mostly stay the same, and it's this which makes the game rather monotonous. You keep doing the same thing over and over again. Think of 'Papers, Please' and how varied the game became from its first couple of levels. The gameplay here never really varies from the gameplay in the early levels.
The story isn't bad, but it's almost never actually incorporated into the game's levels, and as a result, you don't really care that much about it. The narrative is told in cutscenes which usually have next to nothing to do with the levels. I haven't finished the game, but that's becuase I've gotten stuck on a level where the only solution would appear to be to waiting around for ages for partygoers to wander off into quiet spaces where they can be executed. Nothing that I've played in the agme so far makes me want to continue.
Overall, a montonous game that offers little to no variation and a weak story. Not worth a buy in my opinion.

I am going to compare Hexcells to Minesweeper in this review, I understand that it is not suppose to be the same game, but they are the only two games in this genre that I have experience with.
First, lets look at the parts I like.
The music is peaceful, and the sound effects fit in nicely.
The game looks clean and modern.
Unlike minesweeper, it is not stressful to click on tiles. (Though, this does have the effect of making it a little less satisfying when you complete the puzzle correctly.)
I like the extra tile options {3} for three connected tiles, -2- for two disconnected tiles, and the numbers on the outside of the grid for tiles in that row or column.
I like the fact that there is no timer, so I don’t feel rushed. (I hate puzzle games that make you rush)
I also like that the levels are not too hard to unlock.
Unfortunately that is as far as the pros go for me.
Unlike minesweeper, it counts a mistake if you flag a number tile! This is frustrating, especially when there is no “think about it” flag.  It may help if tiles that have their conditions met grey out, even if I have to do this manually, it would help I think.
There is not a “replay” button on screen.  This only became a problem when I started really trying to get perfect scores, which was pretty quickly.
I could not swap the mouse buttons.  I don’t know why, but I couldn’t get the mouse buttons to register as “keys.” By default the flag and destroy buttons are opposite Minesweeper, which really really messed up my clicking!  And, because flagging counted as a mistake I couldn’t even have one safe button!  In the end, I had to use keyboard keys and even though it’s not so bad, the entire thing was really frustrating.
And here is the game braking issue!
It is so easy that once you know it is there, you can’t help but use it to your advantage, even if only accidentally!
Please, if you enjoy this puzzle game, and don’t know about this yet, don’t read below.
If you like puzzles you will like this. Buy it. It's one of the most satisfying puzzle games I've played.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS:
An extremely fun game, even though it is still in development. The directional-based sword fighting feels both weighty and satisfying, and though it lacks a little in fluidity you soon forget this as your blade cuts through your enemies.
Combat consists of directional-based attacks and parries depending on the movement of your mouse, but also allows for advanced combat tactics such as rolling, jump-attacks, locking, feinting (cancelling) and counter-strikes. It also has a decent array of spells that can change the course of battle; including invisibility, fireballs, bear-traps, teleportation and mines, with more to come in the future.
Graphically, the game is quite impressive. It looks fabulous and the maps are not only varied, but each equally fun to play; there's no one map that gives me the reaction "ugh, I hate this one." It also has a large amount of content for character customization, including specific armour or clothing pieces for specific areas of the body allowing you to carve out your own, unique champion. Often, I've recognized players not by the name above their heads, but by what they look like.
Bear in mind it is still in development, so you will have to forgive the occasional graphical bug (such as swords not appearing in the hands of a swinger) that while annoying, didn't particularly subtract from the overall enjoyment I had. Though I only played for a few hours, I had a blast of a time and would highly recommend this game to anyone interested in fantasy sword combat.
This game has great potential that it has already begun to realize and I cannot wait to see how they expand upon it in the coming months. I'd love to see some sort of progression system, new weapons with varied statistics and the ability to create clans/guilds with fellow players and battle it out in epic guild wars. I also hope they add larger maps with the possibility of larger player counts; 20 on 20 battles would be extremely glorious!

First time I played this game, it was back in 2k02 on PS2, and I was clueless how to end this game (I didn't go further than Hell's Kitchen).
Gameplay :
This game was revolutionnary back in the days, because you could choose HOW to play the game (wants to play stealth, guns blazed, both mixed). And because of that, you always find new things. Even after 100 hours, you'll still find new areas and new histories. The developers put a lot of love in this game.
Graphics :
The graphics and physics are good for 2k, and it was full of glitches. But still, the gameplay was so good that you passed over the glitches and enjoyed the game.
Sound/ambiance :
This game has one of the best soundtrack I have ever heard in a video game. The main menu theme is just biblical (fall in love first time I heard it), and other sounds played in different areas of the game are pretty awesome, even scary sometimes.
My advices if you want to play it :
First levels are kind of easy, and it introduce you to the game. I would recommend to make sure you understand game mechanics before entering Hong Kong. After leaving the Boeing 747, the game's difficulty increase drastically (new enemies, etc...). So, if you feel like you missed something, replay the game at the beginning, and be prepare to go further.
If it's your first playthrough, I would recommend this:
- At the start of the game, upgrade your skills Computer/Lockpicking/Electronics at Trained. It'll help you to deal easily with most doors/security spots without wasting dozens of Lockpicks/Multitools.
-  When Paul Denton give you the choice between 3 weapons at the start of the game, choose the GEP gun (a rocket-launcher very usefull against bots later in the game). You'll find on your way to the UNATCOHQ a mini-crossbow, and a NSF terrorist hold a Sniper Rifle near the main entrance of the Liberty Statue.
- Make sure to check every areas to find some stuff : there is a lot of hidden places.
- Through the game, I recommend to Master the Rifle skill, because you can OS every humans with an headshot and destroy turrets/cameras with one shoot. After that, upgrade Heavy skill to Advanced. It's necessary because holding the GEP gun make you extremely slow, and Advanced skill remove that slow. I would recommend then to upgrade Swimming/Medicine to Trained once it's done.
- For the augmentations, it'll fits your gameplay path. But I recommend to pick these ones : Speed Enhancment for legs, Cloack and Radar Transparency for Subdermal, Regeneration(OP thing)/Aqualung/Synthetic Heart for torso, Spydrone for cranial, and Vision Enhancement for eyes(because your vision is augmented).
I really recommend to purchase if you like challenging games.

I don't see what's so great about Deus Ex.
To get the game to run on modern PCs various mods are needed. Alt Tabing out of the game or using the steam overlay causes a spectacular crash either way. Without the relavant mods the game has absolutely attrocious framerate issues.
As a shooter the game is esoteric; aiming has nothing to do with actually trying to hit the target, it's determined by how long the player is willing to stand still doing nothing until the crosshairs decide to reach their smallest size allowing a projectile to land anywhere near the intended target; this, alongside the game's awkward default controls leads me to think that this game wasn't meant to be played using a mouse at all.
As a stealth game Deus Ex is laughably bad, enemies can't see the player even if he was standing directly in front of them as long as he was a sufficent distance from them. Don't bother with the tranquilizer darts as enemies will spas out shooting at the player and running to the nearest alarm; which would be the exact oposite of tranquil. The only purpose it serves is being able to knock out Men In Black to take their ammunition as a opposed to them exploding for no reason after death.
As an RPG the game holds very little options at all. What I do admire is that the game doesn't award skill points for killing enemies, which encourages going for the quiet approach. Skill points can be spent on the game's various skills, which include such wonderous options like Swimming. Honestly there's very little reason to spend points on any skill past rank 2 aside to fix the god-awful accuracy of all the guns in the game by leveling a weapon skill, since leveling lockpicking or engineering will see the player rarely ever run out of lockpicks or multitools. Yes, that's run out of, as in, it doesn't actually improve the player's ability; in the words of Spaceballs: "Even in the future nothing works!" since absolutely everything you use, lockpicks, multitools, armor, invisibility, will break and vanish after using it once and their relavant skills determine how long you can actually use it after activating it or determine the percentage a lockpick or multitool will knock off the lock.
The game has a focus on Augmentation, to get them the player must gather augmentation canisters and upgrades. Each canister has two options for the player to implant, and the choice is permanent. Really the only useful ones are Regeneration(medkits and the medicine skill became close to useless after that), Speed(the levels are way too large and way too empty to take things slowly), and Power Regulation, as everything else is too wildly situational and expensive in bioenergy to be useful, even when I did use other augmentations they seems to have absolutely no effect. Despite claiming that his vision was augmented the default light augmentation only makes the player glow like a Christmas tree instead of granting nightvision, which is soon made rather pointless anyways.
Comically, the game is hilariously easy for a simple reason, the weapons used by both the player and the enemy switch between useless and over-powered. About a quarter into the game the player is granted the Dragon Tooth, basically a lightsaber that kills absolutely everything that is human in one hit(even 'boss' enemies die to two or three hits with this thing, usually to only one if it hits the head); say goodbye to useless pistols and rifles that JC can't aim to save his life; yes, just sit there until your cataracts stop acting up JC, eventually you
to hit him! Really, there is absolutely no reason to use anything else except for it and the GEP gun. Speaking of the GEP gun, at the very start of the game the player is granted the options of getting a crossbow, a sniper rifle, or a GEP gun. Only mere meters away from the person who gives it to you is a free crossbow anyways. The GEP gun can kill anything is that is -or is not- human in one shot, it even comes with a lock-on feature to any target in the game! So there's the Dream Team: The Dragon Tooth and the GEP gun! Both available right at the start of the game! Incidentally the enemy also has access to such weapons, whom are virtually harmless as it takes them
to register that the player is a threat, that is if they actually see the player as their field of vision is about 5 meters far. Believe me I wanted to use the Plasma Rifle instead, but that thing is a peice of trash that deals no damage, takes too long to load, has an effective range about as big as its splash radious, the ammo is practically non-existent, and anything worth shooting at with it has an energy shield. All the other guns in this game suck for one reason or another actually, usually for their terrible damage and accuracy.
The game features a little economy which is close to pointless as there are very few shops that sell things the player actually needs, so if the player has been hacking ATMs since the start it would be best to buy absolutely everything they find that isn't food as they will have few chances to buy anything else unless they're fans of hoarding Soylent Green chocolate bars.
The story starts out rather predicably, the player plays as JC Dention, who they can actually give a 'real' name to which in true RPG fashion is mentioned only in text files on very few of the game's PCs. They work for the big bad gov'ment and have to stop the terrorists from stealing the useless vaccine for the plague, and I'm sure you already see where this is going. Mere hours(apparently a day, but I can't tell since there's no sun in this game) after joining the force JC betrays the gov'ment and fights for the terrorists and it turns out that the plague is man-made and the terrorists can make a cure! So with the help of some Artificial Intelligences and a bunch of useless jerks JC singlehandedly kills all the bad guys, launches some nukes, and destroys some bases before he reaches the final base that needs to explode and the game suddenly decides that it wouldn't be an RPG if there weren't final choices! Which feels rather token considering that game had no meaningful choices before that point, and it certainly didn't start there, since the only thing this choice does is grant a minute long cutscene and a quote from some moron from the 17th century before cuting to the credits.

I stumbled on Automation a long time ago, while looking for a modern version of Detroit (DOS). Automation is an all-encompassing car company simulator. I picked up the demo about two years ago, and have been following the game’s development ever since.
Rarely do I ever buy an Early Access game, but Automation as it stands today is WELL WORTH the $30.
It’s a little buggy following a complete UI overhaul. Although many features are still in development, you do have the ability to start designing all of your cars. You can make everything from classic steel body cruisers to modern day turbocharged super cars. The design features are powerful and addicting. It truly is unlike any other car designer I’ve ever played with, and it presents itself almost exactly as how you’d imagine a car designer should be.
I for one have designed a 1960's Licoln type car, a 1970's muscle car, an early 1990's era pony car, a number of economy hatchbacks, and a few mid engined hyper cars (like the Bugatti Veyron). The range of cars and the depth of the customization is unrivalled.
Automation could not be in better hands, as developers, Camshaft Software, work tirelessly. Unlike other developers, the guys at Camshaft have an open and positive relationship with their fans and the Automation online community, being active in all areas of the official forums.
As it stands today, it’s a great game. It has great potential. It has a great dev team. There’s very little downside. I highly recommend this title.

So.  Wildstar.  Worth the download or not?  I would say it's worth a shot.  The game's pretty, the races and classes are pretty unique, and it's a F2P game that isn't P2W.  Most of the items in store are cosmetics, and the rest are just things like xp potions that you can buy with Omnibits (an in game currency) anyway.
For starters, the combat system is the shining gem of this game.  Honestly can't play other MMOs now due to being spoiled.  Really though, while I don't play as much as I used to, I still raid with the guild I'm in to down Avatus, and I do RP.  I guess I can sum it up this way.
Like single player PvE?  It's pretty good.  The story in game is decent, but the best stuff is the lore.  If you want to see more lore stuff, pick up the Scientist path.
Like multiplayer PvE?  Yes.  YES.  Protogames is the best dungeon I've played.  Plenty of adventures, expeditions, etc.  The raids are fantastic.  Unfortunately there's only 3 raid instances at the moment, one being a boss in a box type deal, but Red Moon Terror is coming out soon.  The difficulty is definitely up there, though, and people that have played WoW stated that it's definitely more difficult.  But, this was my first MMO doing 20 man raiding so I can't confirm, and I've enjoyed it thus far.
Like PvP?  Ehhhhh.  Could definitely use more work.  Unfortunately it's in a strange place, but at least Carbine fixed Halls of the Bloodsworn so that you're not in a match for potentially 30 minutes screaming and tearing your hair out.
Like roleplaying?  Hello!  Welcome to a sizeable RP community on both sides.  Contact me in game if you need any help for RP stuff.  Like to build houses?  Wildstar has the best housing system I've seen.
Have played 2000+ hours over the span of two years.  It's worth a shot.

Definitely one of those few MMO gems. Wildstar's story is extremely well crafted and very humorous. The caretaker, albeit the Person in charge of reviving you upon death. is a primary example of Wildstar's humour saying things like:
"They say death is but a dream .. come back to bed dearest."
"Back again so soon? You barely had time to go towards the light"
I'm really digging the humour and some of the npc races are extremely adorable as well. Like the Lopp (Bunnys) in their search of shinies for their piles of treasure.
It's probably quicker to just make a list of things that I really like about the game and other stuff that could still be improved or is simply out of place. So here goes:
==============================================================================
The absolute pinnacle of mechanical raidboss design. You won't find anything quite like it in any other MMO. The telegraph based combat system coupled with the ruthless behaviour of raidbosses makes for a real challenge even more so in the second big scale raid - The Datascape. The first raid might be a lot easier, however especially for newly formed guilds it will pose a considerable threat. You will not be able to complete the instance unless your team is making a proper effort.
Let's take the first raid boss of the "Genetic Archives" for once (first raid). A big fatso on a platform trying to wipe your team from existence will serve as your first big hurdle. The Raid consists of 20 people and is split into the classic 3 roles - Tanks,Healers and Damagedealers. The Boss has 3 Major mechanics. In set time intervals the boss will start casting a vomit, which dishes out extremely high damage and is most probably going to kill you if it hits you. It will slowly rotate in a random direction which everyone has to roll out of as to avoid damage that goes for the tank as well. The second major mechanic is small bomb telegraphs which will be randomly placed onto people in the raid and will destroy a part of the platform your raid is standing on. So as to avoid people falling down into nothingness and dying you have to make sure to make those telegraphs blow up only once you're on the edges of the platform so the raid has enough to room to move around the boss as needed. The third major is big bombs place on one of the raid members. If you do not react in time and jump off the entire platform before the bomb blows up, your raid can kiss goodbye. If you jump off the platform with the bomb on top of your head, you will be blown back onto the platform on detonation - a knockup basically.
As you can see the bosses are pretty complex and require good communication between the members.This is still one of the less complex bosses in that regard. I just had to go a bit more indepth on raids since they are the absolute biggest feature wildstar has to offer but let's move on from here.
++Housing
Another amazing feature Wildstar has to offer and it's one of the best of its kind. I have seen people create custom spaceships, gigantic amusementparks, Hoverboard parcours and many more. The sheer amount of objects for decoration is ridiculous and what's more to it- most of the decor can be obtained by simple means even when you don't pay a penny for the game. That leads us to another point.
The way Carbine decided to monetize their game is almost way too fair. The shop prices are really low in contrast to other mmos and to top it all off you can even purchase every single item that is on the store by using the Omnibit currency which even free players can obtain by simply playing the game (time-based currency). So when you really want that sweet mount go and save up ! It won't take ages.
Basically the miniature version of raids. There is 6 Dungeons to choose from - 1 Tutorial one, 4 of the classic dungeons and Ultimate protogames. The classic dungeons are basically the introduction to what wildstar raiding feels like tuned down for 5 player groups. They are challenging, especially so if your group members are not overgeared.
Ultimate Protogames is basically a compilation of challenging Minigames clumped together into a dungeon and the result is a really refreshing experience completely different from other MMO's instance types.
These are the 3 activities you will be looking for once you hit level 50. Adventures are minigames such as a round of Moba or Tower Defense. Expeditions on the other hand are solo instances which add to the story and provide you with some nice goodies for housing or some dyes/pets upon completion. Worldbosses are Bosses which can be spawned in certain locations and whose mechanics when engaged will prove to be a fun and decent challenge. Mostly this is where zergs will happen.
====================================================================================
Leveling won't be everyone's cup of tea, the same held true for me. One of those problems is the lacking population at the moment which makes low lvl pvp hard. I love this game, Medieval 2 Total War in my opinion is the best Total War game to date, Rome Total War polished, and I enjoy the medieval era more than the Roman era. Objectively speaking there is an undeniable quantity of value in this game, before I downloaded mods I had about 200 hours. The vanilla version of this game is excellent. I could even play the campaign mode of the vanilla version after playing the campaign mode of these mods. Battles in this game are the best it will ever be and with multiple medieval eras from early to high to late where you have musket men and cannons. I could have an army of Mongolian cavalry fight an army of French pikemen and musket men. Possibilities in the battles are endless! Also, battles require tactical positioning, flanking, planning and using your brain in general. If you don’t like to use your brain, than don’t buy this game. If you do, however, you will find very interesting and creative ways to defeat your enemies. When to attack the enemy or hold position and send spearmen to the front, when you should retreat or hold fast. There is just so much fun to have in battles.
The Campaign mode has no story, like every other Total War game, based on the situation of your nation and other nations, plans and ambitions, you make your own story. Be the king of England and defeat the French once and for all, forge an empire of 2 land masses. Play as Byzantium and retake lost lands and lost lands of the Roman empire. When it comes to recruitment and construction it is balanced. Recruitment pools determine how many units you can recruit per turn and how long you must wait until you can recruit another one of the same unit. This prevents large and massive armies of heavy infantry running all over the place. Diplomacy feels real as in the medieval times there were no phones to call other leaders. Countries had to send a diplomat and wait for a response. Diplomacy is not as in depth as it could be, but this game is focused around war and military. Keep that in mind when you play the campaign mode. Trade, alliances, embargos, vassals, military access, the basics are all there. Events happen in the campaign mode throughout such as the Mongolian invasion, the discovery of gunpowder and the new world, and yes, this game includes the plague.
Overall, unless you are too stupid to use your brain in coordination and deep thought, you will enjoy this game and get your money’s worth without a doubt. Even at full retail price I would still find my money’s worth. Go buy it on sale if you are still sceptical, I did it, too.

Second best Total War title to date, second only to Rome 1. Only thing that makes it worse is the Castle/City feature, where each settlement is divided into two categories: Castles and Cities. Castles are obviously hard to attack, having up to 3 layers of walls, and recruit much better units. They are poor for getting money or raising population, you can't even set taxes to the castles. Cities recruit worse units (though depending on your faction sometimes the city parts are better than their castle counterparts, Italian Spear Milita and Venetian/Genoean Crossbowmen being examples of this) but are so much better for economy. Most of the time your armies will be composed of units that can only be recruited in castles, but if you take a city with it and lose a lot of troops there is no way to replenish them unless you send them to another castle.
That is literally my only gripe with this game. Graphics still kind of hold up, even 9 (holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this game is 9 years old?!?!) years later. Massive scale armies are often seen, the AI isn't entirely stupid and can be logical in their choices after you think hard enough. There is a stereotype (much like Civ V) that the AI will randomly attack you for no reason, but there are always logical reasons. Either they see you as weak and easy pickings, you are attacking (and beating) one of their allies, or you've taken lands that they wanted. If you really want to avoid war with a certain faction, just avoid those three things.
The game can be challenging at times, often times you will think you've won a war and then suddenly they have a full army besieging your capital, that carefully hid in the forests so you couldn't see them. The economy isn't as challenging as I'd like it to be, you can simply raise taxes as high as you can without having the happiness go below 100% (Yea for some reason the happiness can go well over 100%, it's weird) and don't garrison your cities with expensive units. As long as you're using your armies to conquer cities you'll never go into the red.
The game is challenging and interesting, no two campaigns will ever be the same. A lot of things are predictable, such as for me Milan always seems to be a huge power that gobbles up France and the Holy Roman Empire with ease, and Egypt always ends up winning in the east unless the Mongols decide to head that direction (they always beeline straight for Poland/Hungary/Russia in my games and get destroyed by knights). There are in game events such as the Mongol invasion, the Black Death, the Timurid invasion, Gunpowder being invented, and you can even travel to the New World late in the game. You will quickly learn to love and hate some factions, personally I hate fighting any italian faction just because their Italian Spear Militia are rediculous and their crossbowmen do waaay too much damage without taking much in return.
Overall the game is a 9,9/10 for me. It's my second favorite strategy game of all time, and there is a still active modding community that can spice up your games should you ever get bored of the same map/factions. Definetly worth the 20$, but you'll often find it on sale for much less. The DLC is definetly worth at least a try, it adds 4 new campaigns (different maps and factions, it doesn't add anything to the main game they're basically 4 smaller standalone games) which are pretty fun but a tad bit small and limited, which is to be expected given how small the regions are. If you liked any other Total War game or are interested in buying one to see if you do like it, definetly buy either this one or Rome 1 first.

It does currently suffer some from a somewhat wonky and inconsistent interface (things in the action bar are both selected and used when their corresponding number is pressed depending on the type of item) and it uses I and M binding for inventory and map, respectively, which doesn't really fit a quite fast-paced type of game. Delver is a dungeon crawler that is currently available in Early Access. Because of this, things I say about it may change as development continues.
Delver is a very simple first-person dungeon crawler: you start above ground with the task of Delving down several levels to retrieve an orb and return it to the surface. This is the gist of the story, and all you really need.
Along the way you'll collect loot, level up and customize your character, and fight hoards of orcs, spiders, bandits, and skeletons.
The game is great fun and simple enough to be picked up by anyone. Although initially challenging, I found that the game is exceptionally forgiving if you pump a lot of points into HP. The leveling system provides some flexibility to create what character you want to play, although this really only boils down to what weapons you will use the most.
The game is relatively short at this time, and I managed a successful run through very quickly. Even though character deaths mean starting over, I was able to finish the current game in about 4 hours. Levels are supposedly procedurally generated, but I noticed very similar set pieces several times on consecutive play throughs.
Nevertheless, I still recommend the game. I'm very excited to see where the game's development takes it, and the inclusion of a level editor promises some interesting modding can be done.
For the price of 8 dollars (I picked the game up on sale for 3), I do recommend the game wholeheartedly.

This is the story of how Handsome Jack became the man we know and love (or rather hate) in Borderlands 2. Gameplay is basically the same as the previous games with a few new quirks: The game introduces a depleting oxygen mechanic with a new item type called OZ kits for breathing in the new environment: Pandora's moon, Elphis. Elphis also has another feature: diffrent gravitational levels on different territories. This is where the other new features come in: butt slam, "double jumping" via your modifiers of your OZ kit. Oh and there are jump pads. And that's about all the new features you can expect.
The new classes are fun to play, they have a few funny lines (especially Claptrap), but they get repetative after a while. I was really missing some new original charecters, as none of the new ones stuck in my mind. Some of the quests did stick with a few pop culture references to Doctor Who, Star Wars or Pokemon.
It's still a fun game, though not as good as the previous one. You still get some new elements of the story of the already established characters. If you just want more Borderlands this won't disappoint you.

The best thing I can say about this game is that it's Borderlands. Apart from that, there really isn't much that makes this game stand out.
The story is... well, buying a Borderlands game (that isn't the Telltale game, I knew you were about to mention it SHUT UP) for its story is like reading Playboy for the articles, but it's always either bland or straight-up forced. Things just kinda happen out of nowhere and nobody has enough motivation to justify their acts.
The gameplay is different enough, with low-gravity and boosting and all that, which would be great if it didn't include the oxygen mechanic. Fortunately, playing Fragtrap spared me from it, but it seems really, REALLY annoying. The worst part is that it doesn't really add anything to the game. Being able to double jump and slam enemies and the like wouldn't be any different without having to manage your oxygen meter every once in a while.
Another thing that popped up was a serious levelling issue. Of course, this was probably just me not doing enough sidequests, and it has come up in previous games, but it is obnoxious as hell. I was pretty much always at least one level below what I should've been at for the main questline, which makes all the enemies and bosses significantly harder to kill. Fun.
Speaking of bosses, the bosses are awful. Most of the ones I was actually at level for were about as hard to fight as wet tissue paper, and the ones I weren't at level for had one-hit kill attacks. Again, might have just been my perpetual underlevelling, but holy crap if it isn't annoying getting OHKOed by lasers every five seconds.
Oh yeah, and the raid boss. Worst. Raid boss. Ever.
...
Okay, Pyro Pete might have been worse. But SERIOUSLY? The one raid boss in the base game is just the last boss with craptons more health and slightly more damage! I mean, it took three tries for me to beat it solo, and that's without using a fancy over-specced raid boss solo build. The ♥♥♥♥ing thing is supposed to take four people to kill! Why is it so easy?!
Now before I riff on something else, I just need to mention something: THE AMOUNT OF AUSTRALIAN ACCENTS IN THIS GAME IS TOO GODDAMN HIGH. I mean, the voice actors are American! Why are there so many bad Australian accents?! THEY'RE EVERYWHERE! And "Scav?" ♥♥♥♥ING "SCAV?!" REALLY?! AND DID YOU SERIOUSLY HAVE TO CALL THEM "OZ KITS" THAT IS THE DUMBEST, MOST FAKE-AUSTRALIAN-SOUNDING THING I'VE EVER HEARD.
Ahem. On that note, the humour. Oh god what happened to the humour. Granted, there are some jokes there that I can actually understand while not being Australian, but the dialog has a lot of Australia in it. Almost too much. Between the (probably fake) Australian slang and the odd insistence on not swearing (if anyone could inform me what a "son of a taint" is, that would be much appreciated), the dialog seems... forced.
Overall, it makes me wish Steam had a neutral rating option. If you liked the other Borderlands games, this might be worth a shot. If you're new to the series, go pick up Borderlands 2.
Oh, and the Season Pass is a ripoff compared to BL2, and it's not getting any better anytime soon because 2K AUSTRALIA SHUT DOWN AFTER RELEASING THIS GAME. Yeah. THAT bad.

A nice relaxing puzzle. Very reminiscent of minesweeper, and additional elements added later on also reminded me of Picross. I completed the game on a lazy Saturday and it gave me enough challenge that it didn't feel like a breeze. Additionally, it never vexed me by being too difficult or requiring me to know the intricacies of how everything worked (those hidden rules you find after doing a puzzle for a long time).
If there's one thing to note, it's that the "Perfectionist" achievement does NOT require you to get 0 mistakes on all levels, just to get all of those hexagonal "points". This is good, because there's several levels where I got 1 honest mistake and it didn't deduct anything.
The game also punishes random "spam n' solve" play by making it impossible to unlock later levels without X number of aforementioned hexagonal points. Why you would do that anyway is beyond me.
My only critique of the game is a lack of puzzles with all the elements added. Initially, the game starts off by showing you the base points, then shows you that lines and columns can have numbers too, and then shows you how to toggle everything; and suddenly, you're two-thirds of the way through the puzzles. Just a minor gripe, but getting Hexcells Plus & Infinite solves that problem nicely.

This is one of those "so bad it's good" games.
Or maybe it's a "so bad it sucks" game?
Perhaps you should give it a go and draw your own conclusion.
While I'm a non-smoker that wears glasses and is (probably) not your dad, I'm not an expert critic. My opinion is neither better nor worse than any other (IMO).
Unfortunately this isn't the end of the review.
Blood Knights follows the misadventures of Jeremy. He was a vampyre hunter but now he's Alysa's little ♥♥♥♥♥. This might be Jeremy's story, but Alysa seems to be the one with all of the advantages. The most obvious is that she has a sweet pair of.... auto-crossbows. If you don't mind the sound of "thwip thwip thwip" for nearly 4 hours straight, Alysa is your go-to gal for massacring all of those pathetic humans, stupid were-wolves, butt-ugly undead, and wimpy demons. Jeremy is more of a diplomat. He does most of the talking while Alysa looks at him with this constant "Is this geek for real?" face.
The plot (I nearly forgot!) involves finding and protecting something called a blood seal. It's like a bandage that protects the world from devastation. Somebody or something wants to cause the deluge, which could kill millions of humans. Somehow Vampyre veteran Alysa and vampire-newbie Jeremy have to work out their differences and straighten this mess out. While there is a village for purchasing supplies and a map-screen, this is a very linear game. You can't revisit previous areas to find stuff you missed or grind out some extra experience levels. Jumping all over the map would probably take focus away from the story. That was the part where you chuckle to yourself.
Anyway, each level involves lots of killing, platforming, switches, and traps. Attribute-boosting blood coins can also be found if you're willing to poke your nose in various places. Otherwise, expect the majority of your acquisitions to be equipment upgrades. Level-ups award skill-points, which can be used to unlock skills (fascinating!). Early on you might have a little trouble, because enemies do heavy amounts of damage. This game suffers from reverse difficulty. As you progress, the game gets easier and easier. After awhile, the enemies just seem really in-effective. Most of your deaths are going to come from the janky platforming sections, and a handful of traps.
The bosses of Blood Knights are the biggest losers on the planet. At one point you fight a succubus. Wait...Actually you impale a Succubus a hundred times while she floats in the air and does NOTHING. Before that, there's a fight with some big dude who was probably Jeremy's buddy. His attack pattern is spinning around with his axe, and doing some leaping move. In the very next stage there are enemies that have that exact same move-set! The final boss is also a bum. He runs like he's skipping through a garden of posies. He's referred to as "Rome's Greatest Warrior", which is just the biggest insult to Rome imaginable.
On its own, this game isn't good. It's still enjoyable though, thanks to how unpolished it is. The voice-acting is hilariously bad, the cut-scenes are silly, and there's this wonderful aura of ineptitude throughout the game. One of my favorite moments is
SPOILERS
when you defeat the Succubus. She's talking about where the bad guys took the Blood Seal, but then makes one last attempt at seducing Jeremy. For her trouble, she gets a bolt in the chest. Jeremy gets angry at Alysa for a hot second and then says "It's just... she might have known all their plans. Now we'll never know."  Alysa responds with "At least we know the last thing that went through her head."
That joke might have worked IF SHE WAS SHOT IN THE HEAD!
But, I think that's what makes it funny. If Alysa shot the succubus in the head and then made the joke, I'd probably just say something like "Seriously?" or "Oh...oh that was a joke...oh God." or *GROAN*. This screw-up completely justifies the scene.
Blood Knights is not a game I can recommend on normal terms. I'd compare it to a B-movie, but it's about twice as long, and requires you to hold a controller and press buttons. It's certainly not a good game, due to the complete lack of challenge and compelling game-design. This is something you can play high, or drunk, or on some experimental drugs not even fit for sponge consumption. Maybe that's appealing to somebody out there? I don't know.
All I know is that I actually don't regret the time I spent with this game. That's saying a lot, considering how short and precious a life is. I won't give it a thumbs up though

A halfway decent game, I'd recommend it more strongly except for a single really bad design choice, but I'll get to that in a moment.
Story was standard but enjoyable. Voice acting was fairly poor, but worked alright with the writing style I think so I didn't actually mind it that much. Environments were beautiful and varied considering the size of the development team. Gameplay was pretty good and the combat was responsive and seemed to be balanced really well. I played on normal and still died a fair few times, but always because I was stupid in combat rather than because of anything out of my control. Navigation was a bit of a pain at first, but I got used to it slowly. I did enjoy the different characters you could play and swapping between them during combat turned out to be useful. I thought it was just going to be a gimmick at first. It had some RPG elements, but nothing too great. Just inventoray management, limited skill and attribute leveling and a couple of story decisions that really didn't make a difference in the long run.
What I didn't get used to was the directed camera. I HATE directed cameras and it served no purpose in this game except to make some areas more hidden than they would otherwise be and to make combat more difficult. When an enemy is in front of me, I want to be able to see them, not have them hidden off my screen by a camera that randomly decided to zoom in on my character cause I entered a particular section of the map. I think directed camera's are one of the worst design decisions a developer can make, and it annoyed me throughout the game.
If you want a quick, fun dungeon crawler and don't mind a directed camera, then I would recommend this game. Otherwise, you may find it too frustrating with not enough good elements to make up for it.

One of the most important foundations for a purely pvp-focused game to have is a solid set of gameplay mechanics. And Kingdoms Rise more than delivers on this front. It has a well-executed, smooth and deep melee combat system where every single factor comes into play when fighting your foe, from basic things like movement and mouse control - sidestepping attacks, aiming your own swing well and knowing your sword's reach, dodging and rolling - to the advanced features of the combat system, including directional parrying, counterattacking ("locking"), and juking parries with feints.
The system truly allows for a master swordsman to outshine his opponents (up until the moment an adversary sneaks up on him unawares and cleaves him from behind, at least!), and the satisfaction of improving and seeing the results of your own improvement in-game is a huge part of what makes the game fun. And oh yes, don't forget the kills. Bloody, brutal and extremely satisfying. The game has an awesome, fluid set of animations even at such an early stage of development.
Then there are the ranged weapons and spells. I have a few minor gripes about them (I personally hate how stealth is spammable, even mid combat, and I also feel that plane shift is too strong) but overall, it's remarkable how well balanced abilities and secondary weapons are for a game so early in development. For the most part they bring even more depth (and fun!) to the game, without overriding the main flavour of the game, which is pure melee combat. I feel that teleport and heal  bring the most to the table in this regard, especially heal as it prevents "graveyard zerging" of a player who's already been engaged in heavy melee combat, but emerged victorious (albeit not unscathed).
Out of the box, this pre-alpha appears to be really buggy - lots of unimplemented things, settings not getting saved, missing menu items, and so on. Don't be put off - everything that *needs* to be working for you to jump straight into a game, is working. I'm actually happy that the menu looks like crap, the menu sounds are annoying and loud and everything looks like crap - because the real soul of the game is there. And gosh darnit, it's not even pre-alpha yet!

I wanted to like this game, but I really can't recommend it.
Yeah, sure, it starts off strong. The first level / area is friggin' amazing and pretty much flawless. The graphic and sound design are incredible, and really convey a sense of grandeur and scale that few other games can match. The combat style is distinctively Platinum, and both fast-paced and stylish. The story concepts are pretty cool.
Unfortunately, the execution is botched at nearly every step. While the combat LOOKS cool, you'll quickly figure out that it's about as deep as the kiddy pool - you've got light attacks and heavy attacks. One of them tends to inflict small numbers but much faster, and the other inflicts larger numbers, but slower. The different weapons don't really seem to have any particular strengths or weaknesses, and there's no particular moves that are particularly good in one situation or another - you just kinda flail at things until they go down, no matter how smoothly animated and stylish your character may look while doing it. There's always ranged attcks to spice things up a bit, but.... well... they don't. Pod attacks are very safe as they let you do very reliable damage from a safe distance and almost nothing in the game can retaliate effectively to gunfire, but the numbers they put out are pathetic and thus killing things with guns is an exercise in tedium.
On that note, seeing what exactly your character is doing is a chore sometimes - the camera tends to be awful. It frequently follows way too close to the action and lacks an auto lock-on by default, forcing the player to awkwardly mess with the right analog while fighting just to keep the enemy in sight, which is a minor but aggravating chore that never really goes away. Sometimes it just goes all screwy, either due to getting stuck or the angle you are at relative to the enemy, or getting stuck behind the enemy themselves.
Moving on to the enemies, they are boring, boring, BORING. Now, the bosses tend to get a pass - they are one of the things the game does right. But the small fry are some of the most lazily designed enemies I have seen in years. They aren't the least bit threatening or memorable, the vast majority just being some variation or another of rusty metal humanoids... and not very detailed ones at that. They are at best a chore to fight, and make up the overwhelming majority of your foes.
The game is long and has a lot of content, but much of that content is dull as dirt and feels more like a single player MMO than a fully featured game - it's particularly fond of fetch quests and escort quests, neither of which have become any less aggravating in all the years they've been around. This type of quest can be carried by good enough AI or memorable enough characters, but in this game, they're.... well, they're not.
The main cast is well fleshed out, but most of the side characters are either dull as dirt, outright annoying, or some combination thereof, which makes it very hard to care about any of them. When it comes to dealing with them, you're pretty well on rails, too - amusingly enough the game DOES acknowledge it in several places if the player does something unconventional, needlessly jerk-ish, or counter-intuitive... but usually just means of a joke ending that immediately makes you then go back and repeat your action the intended way.
The plot is also pretty heavy-handed too, and occasionally had me rolling my eyes. The topics it tackles are weighty and deserve to be treated seriously, but so many aspects of characterization and underlying themes were treated with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer. It got old pretty quick in several events. It doesn't help that the comic relief is mostly a swing and a miss, and rarely helps lighten the mood.
In conclusion, yeah, I would still stress that this game has some legitimate brilliance hidden away in it. The art, the music, the animations, the boss battles, and the story concepts are all absolute top-notch. But you have to suffer through so much to enjoy them, and for me personally, it was just too much work for too little reward.

On to other notes, there are tons of references to sci-fi, both modern and classic. These range from quotes, to easter eggs, to jokes. The designers of this game have to be fans, and they definitley have a sense of humor.

On the other hand, if you like a new experience, exploring, enjoy sci-fi and don't think it should be composed of noir grays with blood splatters but instead should be colorful and fun, give it a shot. Deus Ex to me is the greatest game ever made.

Bottom line is if you even have a slight interest in Action/Role Playing/Stealth or just terrific story telling in general then Deus Ex is a game that you must experience in your lifetime.

The first time I played 'Deus Ex' (also Game of the Year Edition), I was naive to the idea of a first-person shooter that can be played with stealth, let alone not killing anybody! The game was fun as an RPG action shooter back then, and even more fun now knowing that I can play it by sneaking around without killing anyone.
One thing about 'Deus Ex' that was so memorable to me back then was my in-game actions and decisions had consequence on how the story unfolded. Plus, discovering that there were multiple ways to traverse the environment and to defeat my enemies was a delight. Simply put, 'Deus Ex' was not just a video game to me, but a digital playground for me to experiment with different actions, weapons and general items at my disposal.
Almost 17 years after its initial release, the action, stealth and role-playing mechanics of 'Deus Ex' still hold up for the most part, naturally showing signs of age here and there. Undeniably, the game's graphic textures and character models are ugly by modern day standard; its gun action is not as buttery smooth as its contemporary; and its stealth componment can be glitchy and basic compared to what we have now. However, it is the non-linear and emergent gameplay in 'Deus Ex' that really help it stand the test of time.
Replaying 'Deus Ex' over a decade later made me appreciate its impact on modern video games. As dated as the game is now, it is still worth revisiting. Thankfully, the modding community has worked hard to keep 'Deus Ex' playable over the years. If three of the original creators of 'Deus Ex' -- Warren Spector, Sheldon Pacotti and Chris Norden -- could take a trip down memory lane by replaying the original game on its 15th anniversary, why couldn't we do the same?

The mechanics still hold up fairly well, and the levels, while boxy, are believable, and the models, while very dated, are still fine and don't really detract from the game, but I guess that depends on the graphic fidelity you're able to consider "good enough".  It's also quite obvious there are many many ways to complete each level depending on how you want to play.
There are 3 problems with the game.
1. It doesn't work properly on modern operating systems without the Deus Exe mod.  If a game is to be sold on steam, even if it's for the approx $1.20US I paid, it should work and be updated by the publisher to work, kinda like what GoG do.
2. Some of the mechanics are dated.  Things like stealth not always working properly and alarms getting tripped without any possible way another enemy could have known a guard was killed, and the hitbox, especially early game, is a dodgy for melee weapons.
3. Sometimes the level layout is confusing and it's easy to get lost especially early in a new location (HK market for example)
Things I really enjoyed that one doesn't see much in modern games.
1. A real do it your way feel to the missions.
2. You are given objectives rather than navigation arrows which makes exploring the level fun.
3. Mechanics that fit naturally into gameplay rather than having contexualised actions.  An example is cover based shooting.  Instead of pressing a button to take cover, then another to pop out and then another to shoot, and then another to get out of cover, simply look around the cover and shoot.
Didn't aged well, but still recommend.

Currently, as I write this review, I have logged 1.7 hours into Automation.
And I do not regret any single second of that time.
I have purchased a few early-access games over the last few months, and for the most part, I've been disappointed.  Lack of content, polish, or just a general lack of interest in playing them again.  I can already tell that Automation is not going to be one of those games, and I am extremely excited for what the future holds for this game.
As it stands at the time of this review, Automation is fleshed out pretty well.  The graphics are decent, and the engines look beautiful.  In terms of car aesthetics, there is some left to be desired.  There aren't exactly a lot of options, however, there's enough to work with to keep you coming back.  The engines are just outrageously beautiful.
Scenario mode is quite a lot of fun, if not somewhat challenging (that's not a bad thing).  But my real interest lies in Sandbox mode.  When I was younger, me and one of my best friends were obsessed with cars.  We created a fake brand name, drew up ideas for models and specifications.  I had forgotten about all of that up until now: and it's simply amazing to see some of the ideas we had become rendered in three-dimension.
I will admit that there is a ton of tutorials, some of which are kind of grueling to watch.  However, it's more or less a necessity, and you can learn quite a lot about automobiles from them, so if you're not mechanically inclined, it's an educational experience.
In terms of realism and simulation?  Well, this game pretty much gets it to a T.  It's extraordinarily accurate.  To test it out, I built a car based on an actual one: specifically, a 1998 Ford Crown Victoria.  Surprisingly, one of the models looked quite like the real car, so I chose it and made it look aesthetically similar to the real one.  Then, the real meat of the simulation: recreating the engine.  I won't go into all the heavy detail, so to save some time, I'll sum it up: I chose the V8 engine, selected the actual parts, crank, cam, the correct ratios, etc., all based on the real car.  When it all came out in the wash during the testing process, I was shocked at how dead-on accurate the engine audio sounded (I own the same car in real life).  My virtual Crown Victoria ended up rating at 202 HP and 268 ft. lbs. of torque (as opposed to 200 and 275, respectively, from actual factory specifications).  I couldn't believe it.
In short, if you have any interest in cars whatsoever, buy this game right now.  I haven't encountered any bugs, but the game has crashed once.  It can only get better from here, which is what excites me.
I'll probably come back and edit this after the next two modes are released, but I'm sure I'll have nothing more than positive words.

I've got sixteen hours in the game right now and so I'm ready to give some impressions. Understanding that this is an Early Alpha game and what that entails, here goes:
From the standpoint of gameplay, there's a lot to like here currently. Primarily there are the scenarios and the sandbox. The scenarios give the player various challenges that require tweaking an engine or a car to meet certain goals. It's a good way to understand not only how the game works, but also what is involved with enhancing a car or engine, not simply slapping parts together.
The sandbox is where the player can design a car and it's associated engine with technologies limited to the simulated year, starting in 1940 and continuting to the present day. To help the player "make interesting decisions" (to quote Sid Meiers) the game provides a critique of the final product in five catagories: Drivability, Sportiness, Comfort, Prestige and Safety. Additionally the player can also set his or her own goals, like keeping down costs or achieving a certain performance milestone, like a 0-62 time or top speed. There are a couple of test tracks where a sim driver (not you) drives the car and record a time which can be compared to other times. Additional test tracks are now available from fans via the forum.
In addition to the above two modes of play, there are also plentiful videos that explain pretty much every aspect of designing a car and engine. They are very well done and reasonably comprehensive. The videos play when you first try to use or tweak certain functions or features in the game, like the first time you add a turbocharger or adjust suspension. It's nice that way because you don't get the information till you need it.
The game is missing its campaign portion, but that's been well advertised here on the Store page. It's in Alpha after all. Also there are limitations to the depth of the sandbox, for instance right now you are limited to inline four and six cylinder engines plus V8 types. Also there are a good many but not comprehensive amount of starting bodies.
And there are bugs. I've come across a number of non-fatal LUA pop-ups, usually because I've been adding or deleted files outside of the game structure or been clicking the buttons to switch screens and menus too fast. Also there is a bit of a nasty bug that sometimes causes a car you create to not be saved when you exit the game. The bug has been reported and is actually pretty easy to avoid.
Graphically the game is far from cutting edge but it has all the graphic quality a player needs, there's nothing that limits what a player can do because of any limitation of the graphics.
The developers seem involved on the Steam and their own forum. And in something I can't recall seeing before, they have actually responded to pretty much all of the negative reviews, answering questions and requesting details on what troubles folks might be encountering. That's a nice thing to do, especially since as I understand there are only three of them.
So, do I recommend this game? With the qualifications that it is in Early Access, rough around the edges and not having all the planned final content, I can say that I do recommend this game.
