It'd be a bit useless to simply restate all the great pros of this game so many comments already pointed out before me.
I'm just going to state that I played over
on just my main character, and I have 22 characters in total, and I still haven't completed all content... Simply because I've lost myself in the gazillion of side activities offered by the game that you don't expect from MMOs.
I loved every bit of this game since the late beta, from the great diversity of class gameplays, the astonishing environments, the actually fun & fast leveling experience, and the endless customization of everything.
It's worth noting that I'm a
, and that this game is a roleplay paradise. Why? Once again, endless customization.
You can have hundreds of different costume pieces in your wardrobe, change at any moment, dye each piece differently (3 dye slots per item of clothing).
You are given a housing plot (in the sky!) per character, and each of them can hold up to 5000 different decors, 2.5k inside of your house and as many outside, decors that you can place completely freely in a 3D environment (X, Y, Z axis, 3 rotation, and scale), making the possibilities flabbergasting.
With instant teleportation between housing plots, you can be drinking a cup of the finest faerybloom tea in a canopy teahouse lost in a jungle one moment and dance in an underground city's club the next, not to mention the possibilities for Dungeon Master Roleplayers to manage the environment in real time, actually controlling traps, secret doors, ennemies...
And the best is, it's not even that expensive or hard to reach. You only need to be level 14 (Between 2 and 5 hours of gametime I'd say) to reach your free housing plot, and while other games have decors cost an arm and a leg even for a farming max level character, Wildstar offers a huge library of cheap items accessible directly from the housing UI.
I joined Wildstar over two years ago for the amazing content and gameplay. I stayed for the astounding housing and RP possibilities.
Now, I gotta scoot, my AI-controlled scientific base drilled into an asteroid (complete with multiple labs, spaceport, and view of Nexus from space) isn't going to build itself.

I have been playing WIldstar off and on since the first testing phase and I have to say, I think the only major flaw with the game as it stands today is the low population. That being said, Wildstar has had non stop trouble in one form or another since its launch, casual and hardcore fans alike have been driven away for a few reasons, including tedious end game,  broken mechanics, poor performance, slow content releases, but overall I think the biggest downfall was advertising that came too little to late.
The game has released on Steam now, and I just hope this does not end up being another false start in a pile of "o' sh*t we messed up, lets try something new to get people playing again".  I don't think the game will ever be as big as Carbine or NCsoft planned, but I can only hope it does not completely die. its not as bad as most people make it out to be, its just not innovative when it comes to gameplay, but you don't have to innovate to be successful.
Gameplay wise the game is set on the planet Nexus, an ancient world being fought over by two sides, the Dominion, a galaxy spanning empire who believes controlling the world is there birthright, and the Exiles, the outcasts, a group of "rebellious" peoples whose entire "everything" is build around NOT being part of the Dominion, retaining there freedom from an oppressive government etc.  There are eight races, four in each faction, classes are race locked but there are six of them so each race has a variety of classes to play.
The game, combat wise sits in between action and classic MMO combat, tab targeting is still in but mobility is very much important because you have to dodge, roll, sprint, teleport, jump and generally get "up out the way" of most enemy attacks. There are a variety of things to do in game PvE. PvP, the whole shebang. There are raids, dungeons, battlegrounds, and pretty much everything an MMO usually has. That being said given the population of the game I have to say you will be doing most of the content solo, and unless the Steam release picks up the player base you will probably have a hard time finding groups for group content.
All this being said, I have to wish that Wildstar finds its place, its been looking for it for years after all, population going up and down like a rollercoaster, but mostly just plummeting to its death, honestly just getting enough people interested that they don't have to close everything down should be goal enough at this point.

Bought this for sale 66% off at $2.50ish during a steam sale. I think this was money well spent for the hour or so of enjoyment I got out of the game. Even buying it at full price, it would have paid for itself.
The combat is pretty basic but it works well for the slow paced combat. The visuals are very reminiscent of Minecraft along with all the controls. The inventory system works well for allowing you to collect loot along your trip down the dungeon and the randomized potions give a little risk to using them each time you restart, which is frustrating but in a good way.
As for faults, the level/stat system is a little broken as you only need to put points into health for the first five levels and defense the rest to become relatively hard to kill. Ranged combat versus flying enemies, which is when it's needed, is a fools game unless you're using a lightning wand (almost hit scan), as projectiles have travel time and flying enemies juke around way too much to predict their movements. I just found myself running up under them and stabbing upward for a sure hit.
Finally, while I died the first time down the dungeon due to trying to figure out the system, I beat the game on the second try. I received a slash screen of text and then the game treated me like I had died. I'm pretty much not going down a third time until there are further updates, but as I said at the start, I got my money's worth already and I recommend a purchase, especially if it's on sale again.
TL;DR - It's an enjoyable game but has it's issues. Worth a buy, especially if it's on sale.

Blood Knights is an Action-RPG so cheesy that if it were a movie, it would be something that airs at 3 AM on the SyFy Network. Enjoying  Blood Knights requires a fondness for "So Bad It's Good" games. Those looking for a quality RPG should keep looking, but for people who like to laugh at - and with - their games, Blood Knights is silly, dumb fun.
Blood Knights' story is basic: two characters, one a balloon-boobed lady vampire and the other a former knight turned into a vampire, are on a mission to destroy or save a relic that will bring on a vampire holocaust or something like that. You won't pay much attention to the plot, although the bad script and worse voice-acting provide ample laughs.
Action is the primary focus of Blood Knights, either in single-player or local two player co-op (there's no online or LAN play). Kill monsters to gain experience and upgrade skills, loot treasure chests for better weapons and armor, and search for hidden items. Standard stuff. The combat in Blood Knights is simple, intuitive, and fast-paced, albeit very easy once you level up a few times; you won't die very much over the course of the five or six hours it takes to complete the game.
Blood Knights is silly, cheap, and charming. It's not a very good game, but it's hard to resist. Buy it during a sale and have a friend over for a laugh or two.

Blood Knights (Deck 13, 2013)
The whole time while playing I'm stuck thinking to myself, "I wish I had someone who could play with."
But before you call a friend and buy the game, take note:
This game has problems: it's graphically and aurally bland, it's unoptimised (runs unexpectedly slow for me considering the simple aesthetics), has an awful camera that is horribly unsuited to a game of this type, lacks features we've come to expect as standard from PC games (e.g. you cannot bind keys, you cannot change video settings beyond a single slider), and I suspect the game itself is a cut-down version of what was meant to be a much more ambitious project, hence the simple storytelling despite hints of a much bigger backstory, few locations despite what appears to be a much larger game world, very few sidequests, many useless items, etc. Then you also have a variety of bugs and glitches popping up randomly
Also, I havn't tried the game with a pad yet, but apparently you need TWO gamepads for the co-op to work.  Customer feedback is an indication that not all gamepads are equally supported (a Xbox 360 pad is recommended -- I don't own one).
Additionally, there hasn't been a single patch since release (as far as I know).
Having said all that, I am having fun. Not a lot, but the enjoyment is there. If only for the general cheesiness of the storytelling.
I have completed two single-player playthroughs, each time focusing on a different character (one is melee, the other ranged).  The melee character has proven to be a lot more satisfying (and challenging) to play as.  Note, you still need the ranged character for certain challenges.
I reckon the devs (Deck13) really need to start paying attention to this PC version (it's also on consoles). They're soiling their reputation in the process of ignoring the issues.
SCORES
Graphics:  61 %
Hints of greatness;  with other games we've seen these guys can do great art;  sadly lacking here.
Sound:  64 %
Cheesy voice acting;  some really nice atmospheric music though.
Execution:  50 %
Constantly moving, horrible camera that often causes you to lose your bearings;  also leads to many instant deaths as camera fails to reveal gaps and falls (game has some ill-considered platforming segments).  There are hints of a much larger background story that is never explored, sadly the developers have failed in their attempts to bring that story across in any way that is involving or interesting.
Addictiveness:  68 %
I've completed the game twice.  That's saying something for a product that clearly has its problems.
Overall:  60 %
Short but reasonably fun.  I havn't played co-op yet (remember:  game only has off-line co-op) but I can imagine it begin fun, provided the horrible camera doesn't follow one character, which could cause a puke inducing sensation for player two, who would be unprepared for the constantly shifting viewpoint.
To close off, the developers, Deck13, are so much better this.  They made the great Venetica, for crying out loud.  How and why they fell this low would undoubtedly make for an interesting post-mortem.

I honestly can not understand the high reviews of this game.
Sure, music is excellent and animations are fluid but almost anything else is either sub par or outright terrible.
Story manages to be overwrought and trite at the same time full of (nearly literally) deus-ex-machinae and convoluted but ultimately trivial twists. Characters are bland and rapid switches in tone and narrative pacing do nothing for their development.
Combat - which is supposed to be a strong point of the game is passable but not more than; 'trash mob' fights are repetative and easily solved with a few basic strategies even at highest difficulty. Boss fights are well coreographed but boil down to memorizing patterns and dodging appropriately. This works fine in shmup parts of the game but is awkward and almost boring in the action-rpg ones. Although boss fights 'feel' like they should be three-dimensional setpieces in the 'shadow of colosus' style they are for most part just dodge-jump-slash-repeat affairs in limited space
Aside from the few models - graphics is a massive dissapointment for a 2017 game - even a console port. Environments are washed out and bland. Most of the enemies are variations on a few  (admitedly neat) themes. Once player is bored of staring at B2s Zettai Ryoiki there is very little of visual interest in the game.
I persisted in a game for a while in hope of finding what is it that excites so many folks about it but overall found it it hollow and deeply unsatisfying on both gameplay, narrative and aesthetic.

This game's appeal is nostalgia for Caesar 3 and its ilk. Sadly, my nostalgia isn't strong enough to make this any fun.
EDIT: ... until you have a few nights of insomnia, enough to get through the slower parts of the "campaign" and then over the one or two unfair missions. After which, well, 50+ hours and 70% achievements, so I suppose I have to recommend it.
* Core gameplay is more convenient than the old games: you depend on walkers for haulage and distribution, but not for finding labor or maintenance.
* There's some nontrivial difference between the four factions, which makes your cities feel at least a little different.
But I'm a bit disappointed that nearly 20 years after Caesar 3:
* The informational displays in this game are *worse* than what we used to have, so it's harder to find the problems in your city.
* Large cities are still inherently unstable - some of this is a function of the fundamental rules behind the simulation, but with better diagnostics I suspect the problems would be easier to work around. To avoid instability you're pushed further and further into artificial layouts and cookie-cutter cities.
* The procedural maps have less character than the old games, which also makes one city feel much like another.
* Perhaps because there's not history or myth to extrapolate from, the campaign is an extended tutorial which is competent but unexciting.

I have been playing WIldstar off and on since the first testing phase and I have to say, I think the only major flaw with the game as it stands today is the low population. That being said, Wildstar has had non stop trouble in one form or another since its launch, casual and hardcore fans alike have been driven away for a few reasons, including tedious end game,  broken mechanics, poor performance, slow content releases, but overall I think the biggest downfall was advertising that came too little to late.
The game has released on Steam now, and I just hope this does not end up being another false start in a pile of "o' sh*t we messed up, lets try something new to get people playing again".  I don't think the game will ever be as big as Carbine or NCsoft planned, but I can only hope it does not completely die. its not as bad as most people make it out to be, its just not innovative when it comes to gameplay, but you don't have to innovate to be successful.
Gameplay wise the game is set on the planet Nexus, an ancient world being fought over by two sides, the Dominion, a galaxy spanning empire who believes controlling the world is there birthright, and the Exiles, the outcasts, a group of "rebellious" peoples whose entire "everything" is build around NOT being part of the Dominion, retaining there freedom from an oppressive government etc.  There are eight races, four in each faction, classes are race locked but there are six of them so each race has a variety of classes to play.
The game, combat wise sits in between action and classic MMO combat, tab targeting is still in but mobility is very much important because you have to dodge, roll, sprint, teleport, jump and generally get "up out the way" of most enemy attacks. There are a variety of things to do in game PvE. PvP, the whole shebang. There are raids, dungeons, battlegrounds, and pretty much everything an MMO usually has. That being said given the population of the game I have to say you will be doing most of the content solo, and unless the Steam release picks up the player base you will probably have a hard time finding groups for group content.
All this being said, I have to wish that Wildstar finds its place, its been looking for it for years after all, population going up and down like a rollercoaster, but mostly just plummeting to its death, honestly just getting enough people interested that they don't have to close everything down should be goal enough at this point.

If you are anything like me and are into strategy games and dark humor, then this game definitely delivers even harder than that pizza place that has a rule about getting the food to you in 30 minutes or giving you the pizza for free.
Serial Killer Simulator.. err, I mean, Party Hard is a game where you start out playing as a bloke trying to get some sleep, thus having to eliminate his partyloving neighbors. As the game progresses, you become quite the notorious killer, travelling the US to introduce avid partygoers to the blade of your knife. You also unlock additional characters to play as, each with a specific trait that defines their playstyle. In addition to using your trusty switchblade, you can also off people by setting up various traps at parties to make it look like an accident.
The different parties, traps and characters bring a nice variety to the table, although the core mechanic of the game remains the same - kill all the unsuspecting partygoers and don't get caught. The part of not being caught can be a dash tricky sometimes, which brings out the strategy part in this game. If you are looking to be knees deep in blood while flailing your matchete-equipped arms around like you're two windmills at all times, this is probably more of a Getting Arrested Simulator for you, meaning this game is probably not the best choice of entertainment for you in particular, unless you are into that sort of thing, of course. I don't judge.
If you, like me, are a sneaky dude getting a kick out of setting your party-enthusiast victims up to be trampled by a zebra or unleashing a zombie apocalypse at a beach party, step right in and grab a knife. A dark sense of humor is recommended, this game doesn't take itself seriously and doesn't encourage you to do so either. I mean, if it did, it would probably be not on Steam but in the ISIS training materials.
Party Hard does come with a handful of glitches, nothing major but be prepared for slight inconveniences or a few of "Why did that just happen right there????????" moments. If you're anything like me though, the latter will probably be because you did dumb stuff and are too proud or blind to own up to it.
Anyway, if you're anything like me and are hopelessly procrastinating doing your school project, work or household chores, this game might be relevant to your interests.

One heck of a learning curve, but once you understand what this is, you'll love it. It's not an rpg, a shooter, or a stealth game in the usual sense, but an odd mixture of the three that really can only be described as deus ex.
It's difficult for me to pinpoint what makes it so great, but from what ive gathered it has to do with the level design, and your choices of skills to upgrade.
For example: on one playthrough I built a "James Bond," type character who would sneak through levels with his silent pistol and use grenades and stealth drones to eliminate larger targets,
then on the another I made a hackerman type character who had very little in the means of combat, but could sneak past enemies to hack the security systems to turn off cameras and open doors.
On the next I built the deus ex equivalent of the terminator. Able to move so quickly and take so much damage that no army could withstand my reign of terror.
Once you understand the game, you can play it in just about any way you want... Except for master level swimming and poison resistance. Don't even try it.
Protips:
*The sides of the redicule do not indicate the exact margins of where your bullets may go. You are more accurate than you think.
*Robots are mean, avoid them.
*There is always a way to sneak into a compound, even if it appears to be a forced combat situation.
*running away is always an option
*The gep gun is the best option for a silent takedown.
*Remember to throw the Dragon Tooth sword off a cliff as soon as you get it. It's pretty useless.

Deus works a globalist anti-terrorist organization. This seems cool and all, but remember:
Your organization is being funded by George Soros, but it's the distant future where Hillary Clinton won and everyone hates George Soros by now, so he calls himself "Bob Page". This one of the greatest PC games of all time.
Story: ridiculously ahead of it's time with concepts and character-driven arcs
Gameplay: Hasn't aged well, but the open-ended scenarios in which you can tackle them with a wide array of approaches give you the idea that is not at all a standard old-school FPS
Graphics: Again, hasn't aged well.  Just look past those ugly faces and you'll be fine

This is one of those games where if you are able to overcome the flaws that naturally come from that era of games, you'll definitely get at least some joy out of it. It is similar to Half-Life in that regard. Deus Ex's real strong point is the freedom it gives players to play with whatever style suits them, and levels built around the varying methods of play. Deus Ex also leads the player through a dark world filled with conspiracies and huge scientific breakthroughs, all while the apocalypse is seen just over the horizon. The setting, music, characters, and sense of immersion are an acquired taste, but you will soon feel yourself in this world.

We all know the cliche's: cyberpunk, dystopian future, with a morally grey protagonist who ends up entangled in something far bigger than himself. Hell, what am I talking about? We LOVE these damn cliche's!
Deus Ex manages to deliver everything we love about the ol' William Gibson novels (which are turning out to be rather prophetic these days), while offering a pretty wide variety of CHOICE. What sorts of choices? From augments to multiple ways of handling situations. Wanna run-n-gun it? Do you. Wanna go Solid Snakin' it? Slither, homey. Wanna be diplomatic? Everyone needs friends. Just be sure to equip the augments that play nice with said play style.
Graphically, Deus Ex uses the ol' Unreal Engine. So don't expect face melting graphics. However, for retro gamers like myself, these "old" graphics lend to the atmosphere in Deus EX: a time when cyberpunk was more escapist and less like what we all now live.
In terms of difficulty, Deus Ex can be punishing. Particularly if you choose augments that don't work well with your tactics. At its time of release, this mechanic was still very experimental in gaming. Deus Ex definitely plays best on a second or third (or fourth or fifth) play-through.

AI bug, that's one phrase that I have forgotten for years until I played this game. Sometimes, when you go out of range of enemy, they retreat to their original position. But as they are retreating, you attack them(with range weapon), they will come back and attack you.   And you just adjust the distance between the enemies and you.  Once you get to the right distance(sweet spot), the AI don't know if they should retreat or attack, so they will keep turning back and forward, and now you can keep attacking them without worrying them attacking you.
One thing that I really didn't like about this game is the camera angles, it gets annoying when you accidentally jump off ledges because of bad camera angle.  As for other aspects of the game, like soundtrack, voice acting, and graphics, I have no complains, pretty mediocre stuff, but good enough for me.
One of the best thing in this game is the ability to switch between characters; being able to switch between range and melee characters make the gameplay much more fun and interesting. I mean, who doesn't like a game with vampire story lines, even if it is a cheesy one.
I know, it seems like I wrote bunch of bad things about this game but at the end recommend it(I should really stop doing that, maybe that's why my reviews get lots of not helpful votes, lol).  Well, when I think about it, I really want a sequel of this game(as long as it's not worse than this).  I want the same characters with cheesy dialogue and the mindless hack and slash(with exploitable AI bug). It was a fun game nonetheless despite all the flaws.

Pre-Sequel is much shorter than BL2 despite that it came with $60 tag on release . There are very few side-quest chains and 90% of stages are so similar that you won't feel like exploring them . You may already notice that more people are playing BL2 because there is just so little to do in this game outside of main story  .
It is not a bad game on sale but replay value compared to BL2 is very low . There is only 1 decent DLC for side story and we probably not getting another one . BL2 had 5 or 6 ? This game has like 1 raid boss ( no counting recycled story bosses in raid version ) There are few players in multiplayer because there is not one damn thing to do after you beat the game .
The biggest issue for me here is the lack of compelling story . New characters that acted as enemies were under developed and I felt rather bored playing it .There is just no feeling of urgency and excitement that I experienced with BL2 .
Elemental damage is not used strategically . For example robotic enemies are so far and between that you almost never need corrode damage. Lack of enemies and different enviroments makes it hard to proeprly use elemental guns for specific areas .Most enemies in Pre-Sequel are soldiers in armor and you often have to shoot the guy on harder mode to see what he is resistant to .
Combat is slightly better do to low gravity so there is a little bit more depth . You can move a bit faster around the map and there is more platforming.
All characters feel different from BL2 roster except maybe Wilhelm who has 2 similar skill trees to Axton . Skills are a bit more balanced in my opinion . In BL2 you had to build characters around few OP skills like Money Shoot on Salvador or you would not do enough damage  . I think Prequal handled that a little bit better by creating more synergy between skills which distributed power spike .
Score: 6/10. It is not a terrible game but I was highly disappointed by lack of content, poor stage variety and boring story .Prequal has nothing going for it aside from new characters and gravity mechanic which is a poor follow up to BL2 that was a near perfect game .

Plot:
I have to say I was a little worried when I first started playing this. I stumbled upon the Borderlands series accidently and started with Tales From the Borderlands. i actually been working backwards and have yet to play BL1, but am a huge fan of BL2. I saved up so I could play presequal, I was so excited for more background on some of the charectors I already loved.
At the beginning things didn't feel the same. I knew they weren't supposed to, but I was missing the old charectors, scenery, and familarity I felt with BL2. But as the game went on I fell in love with the story line. Handsome Jack, who was already an all time favorite charector of mine, was well done, and dynamic. His charector is constantly chaning and you really get to know the man behind the mask and what makes him who he is.
The final cut scenes had me on the edge of my seat. I flipped out, they were truly amazing! The only thing I wish was that we got to know Angel more, or even more about his back story as a programmer and after the amazing final cut scene there didn't feel like there was any closure.
To me it felt like the needed to add one more something to really connect presequal to BL2. Game was beautiful though and as an Artist I so appreciated the coloring, style, and overall look and feel of the enviorment.
Gameplay:
Has all the feel of the orginials. The only difference being these new lazar guns, the jumping, and oxygen. Guns aren't bad, the game didn't really need them though. the oxygen was way more fun then i thought it was going to be and the double jump really helps you feel like you are in a new enviorment.
The Moon curency is a little hard to see versus the stark purple Eridium. The final boss battle just wasn't like Warrior though, that was the only dissapointment. Depends on the person though, if you like the very alien side of Pandora, you'll love it, but if you like the less-explained more resonable (if you can even say that about an alien dragon) you might be a tiny bit dissapointed like me, it just won't have the same feel.
Also Concordia is no Sanctuary and I didn't appreciate the passive agressive political views. Violent, probably would recommend for a more mature aduience because of language; but humor is on point and well done.
Overall Presequal was amazing and I hope the next borderlands comes out soon, don't know if I can wait three more years!

There isn't full voice acting, and it kind of removed the immersion for me. For the voice acting that does exist, the English feels heavily forced and unnatural. I blamed the fact that they're androids for that.
On normal difficulty, the game also felt a little
easy. It ended up being more of a hack n' slash than it did being strategic and fulfilling. G's are given to you generously and as long as you're stocked on recovery packs, you're good to go for anything that comes your way, no matter how bad you are. Other than that, NieR: Automata seems to be a really well thought out and designed game. I had no issues with bugs other than the resolution problem at the very start of the game. I hope that your experience goes as well as mine did.

There is a lot I can say for this game. It has given me tons. I've played at least a dozen playthroughs on my own. I even started play-by-consensus version of it on Reddit, where the subscribers are citizens in the empire, form parties, run for election, and generate legislation. I use that to inform my playthrough (if interested PM me).
There is tons more improvement needed for the game. But that is what I like about Paradox. There games will get tons of free patches with major overhauls and great DLC. I never felt Crusader Kings was complete until the Old Gods came out.
That being said, Stellaris has some amazing potential. You can really feel the kind of diversity in playthroughs even at this early stage, just by choosing what FTL system you will use. I (like most) started with Warp, but Hyperdrive and Jumpgates are both fun...and most importantly. Play very differently.
With Warp, your ships are pretty much autonomous and free functioning, but their warp systems draw heavily on power and increase the cost for production.
Hyperdrive ships still require a good bit of power for their systems, I think the cost is reduced. What is most important is that they have some of the quickest cooldowns after arriving in a system. That being said you are dependent upon a pre-existing hyperspace network to get anywhere.
Wormhole requires the least amount of power and least cost to the ships. The ships have  a large spinup time (as the ships prepare to take off). However, you are very dependent on wormhole stations, and essentially create your own logistics/transport network. If you have 6 fleets moving through a system and only one wormhole station, you can expect a long wait for all of them. If you have 2 stations, you half that time, and so forth. Wormholes allow you to literally jump over enemy space into pockets of unclaimed terra nullius. However, for all these benefits there are major drawbacks. A smart enemy can target your logistics network and strand your fleets. Imagine sending a big fleet to confront an enemy medium sized fleet, while you are doing this, a smaller lightning raid takes out your wormhole stations and harrasses constructors at the closest system. All of a sudden your fleet is stuck.
This kind of variety is already ingrained into the gameplay, and I expect to see more of it. Just as Merchant Republics changed things for CKII, I imagine we will be seeing new ways the game can/will be played. There are some problems, but those will get handled in due time.

It's a fun little city builder in the vein of Caesar, Pharaoh, etc as has been talked about by many of the other reviews here. The only thing I would add is the upkeep on military units is perhaps a bit too high. Some mission objectives require you to have 4 military units built which, despite selling every available item in the trade menu, required upkeep that was easily 10x my income.
Some games encourage you to build massive economies with gold sinks like these, but you can only trade so much of any given item in a year, which caps your income regardless of how much production you have. This then pushes you towards building more housing and raising income by taxes, but when you're already producing as much as you can sell (and then some), there is no incentive to build more production buildings so now your new citizens are unemployed and taxes don't increase to the amount needed to maintain the army, etc, etc.
I can see why people play about 10 hours of this game and move on. So many of the builder elements are fun and engaging, but the military upkeep bit is like hitting a brick wall.

Hearthlands – A Blast from the Past
Sergio and Simon make a stunning debut on the PC with Hearthlands. You may be familiar with their work already under the company Artefact Games, a small indie mobile games development company, which they co-founded. Don’t let that fool you, as Hearthlands is perfectly suited for computer play. Hearthlands is a fresh take on the old city building genre of Impression Games’ titles such as Pharoah, Zeus, Empire, and Caesar. It doesn’t feel like a cheap copy pasta either. It builds on the genre in every way possible and has become my favorite in the entire genre.
The game’s graphics may give you some pause, but if you are able to embrace the style you will find yourself hours of enjoyment. This game plays similarly to the old city building tropes, particularly Pharoah, Zeus, and Casesar games. With that as a basis, I will explain what they do differently. The entire housing loop system was streamlined and simplified. Creating unique and interesting housing communities has never been easier and the beautification options allow you to create a lasting and unique design every time.
One of the biggest turn offs I had with the older games was how the industries required the same attention as the housing. This caused my cities to look haphazard and almost spastic as I plopped down random safety measures to protect these industries. True to form, Hearthlands has simplified the process completely removing this arbitrary need. Now industry stands alone and is much more flexible.
You might think that all this over simplification will make for a rather boring game, but you would be wrong. This game builds on the ideas of predecessors and becomes the true spiritual successor of the city building genre. The military system will seem quite unlike other titles of the genre. While you create forts to house your infantry similar to other titles and while they gain experience the same, it feels fresh. Individual units within each company gain experience and level up becoming more effective every moment they fight.
These aspects become increasingly important as you have more to worry about than your neighbors. Every map has a (toggleable) amount of baddies built into the area before you even arrive. These monster lairs become problematic as your city grows and will even start launching attacks against your city. Soon you will find yourself in a fight to cleanse the map and truly claim it.
As far as how combat is handled, don’t expect much innovation. You have very limited control over your forces. You can command them to travel to areas on your map and they will automatically engage baddies as they come within range of them. There are no special attacks or anything. Simply click and watch your guys fight their guys. The same goes for invading foreign cities. You dispatch your men, after a time dice are rolled and you win or lose with no say on how it goes.
That doesn’t mean they haven’t added anything in that area. Magic is a new feature to the genre that can greatly improve your ability to both command your city and fight your battles. Spells range from healing your troops and creating temporary phantom warriors to filling empty homes with people and creating raw resources to be exhausted by your city.
In addition to the magic interface, there is a research interface as well. This new tool allows you to collect research points from your ever expanding city and invest them into simple technologies. Some of these improve your tax collection. Others can improve your army’s capability. Some even grant ways to gain permanent sources of certain resources.
Graphics: 7
The style is unique and interesting. It seems to fit the feel of the game and is on par with other indie studios. Don’t expect A-list graphics here.

Music: 6
The music is just above average. There were no tunes that particularly grasped me, but they weren’t annoying either.
Story: N/A
Doesn’t really exist. There is a campaign mode, but it does very little to explain any sort of lore behind the game.
Content: 9
Almost a perfect 10. A lot of the content I could ever want is there, but I feel the game could use the steam workshop and a map editor. Even without these features the replay value is off the charts and there will be plenty of content and customization options to keep players coming back for as long as they choose.
Controls: 10
I didn’t have any complaints about the controls at all. Everything was fluid and functioned as expected.
Gameplay: 9
Glitches and bugs were extremely uncommon almost to the point of being nonexistent altogether. Gameplay was fluid and the mechanics work well. Almost a perfect 10, but there were some issues with the balance of goods production. Some goods seemed to require dozens more factories than others to output the same amount, but this is a minor complaint.
In conclusion, if you are a fan of the older city building games, buy Hearthlands. Anyone who is a fan of city builders will also almost certainly enjoy this game. Don’t expect much of an RTS though that is a different genre.
Pros
Good controls
Simplified interface and design
Simplified gameplay
Excellent replay value
Cons
Lack luster music
Lack of military control
No Steam Workshop functionality
Tl;dr: I rate this game an 8.2/10
Of note: The game is still being updated and some of the features and ratings of this review are subject to change.

I was tempted several times to vote this down and as i am writing this review i am still considering this.
This game is clearly made by people who love and know their cars and engines however it doesn't seem that they actually know how to make games. While the idea of building/repairing cars or running an automotive company is not new, they managed to go further and squeeze in so much micromanagement and "learning" into it that they made boring and somewhat stale simulator which also looks incredibly dated and cheap - from low res UI and videos, to stock music, this game feels like it was made at least 10 years ago or more.
However the main issue are the tutorials. Each section of the game, each part of the car, has its own video tutorial and the further you get into game - the lengthier they become. I get that the developers want to teach the player everything they can but i am 100% sure that i could've gone without such gems as "entertainment system keeps passengers entertained". Some videos go on for what it feels like 10 minutes and i honestly can tell that i did not learn or remembered anything they said, especially since some videos are not yet finished and only include agonizingly boring developer voice.
Again - i get the idea of trying to teach the player something valuable about cars but its one thing to include some trivia along as you play, and its another when you are force-feeding information which is actually required to play this "game". And you do actually need to learn things they mention in their videos unless you just want to mash sliders at random and hope for the best.
Overall i was impressed with the amount of fine-tuning and options they included but i also was thoroughly annoyed with their videos and stopped paying attention as soon as i got to the "trim" part which had the longest and most boring videos. Figuring out things for myself using tooltips, wikipedia and random clicking wasn't that much fun either.
I do hope that they are planning to change their UI (at least make it high res and look bit less like Windows 95) and completely revamp tutorials while making them interactive, this would make the game so much more interesting and engaging because as it stands right now its more of an excel-car-slider-clicker-video-learning-course than anything else.
Also the "tycoon" part of the game is not actually in the game yet - you can only build and fine-tune engines and cars just for the "fun" of it. I suppose its good enough for car enthusiasts but for a person who's more interested in the actual strategy/management aspect of the game - its going to be rather dull.
Oh what the hell - im voting it down. Someone has to be the bad guy.

A pretty casual roguelike experience. As of this post, I played it a few times and quickly made it far; only dying to either burst (Didn't get enough health or armor), or my own stupidity. It's very short, which I suppose is a good thing for a game like this. It's easy, but you still can't face-check anything until you get lucky enough with weapons, armor, and stock piles of food / potions. It does get easier as the game goes on, which is a bad and good thing.
The stronger you get, the less trouble you have and are capable of dealing with most creatures. But at the same time, before you get to that stage you struggle and have to back-peddle swing many monsters to survive. You do get a lot of wands I have noticed, which trivializes a lot of encounters; which should be their purpose. But the purpose is way too strong when you get a wand drop every other kill. And the mages almost always drop them, even if they are absolute crap -- it's a ranged weapon and you take 0 damage from back-peddling and killing the enemy.
Stats are not very clear on what they do besides Attack, Speed, and Health. It's obvious you deal more damage with Attack, move faster when you up speed, and gain more health everytime you level it up. Agility was very vague on what it did, and I still don't feel the effects. The same goes for defense and magic. They feel either too weak to actually present themselves as useful, or are just not straight forward enough.
I would recommend this game on sale. It's a decent time waster for a few hours, but it has very little to give after you play through it just a few times.

This is one of those games where if you are able to overcome the flaws that naturally come from that era of games, you'll definitely get at least some joy out of it. It is similar to Half-Life in that regard. Deus Ex's real strong point is the freedom it gives players to play with whatever style suits them, and levels built around the varying methods of play. Deus Ex also leads the player through a dark world filled with conspiracies and huge scientific breakthroughs, all while the apocalypse is seen just over the horizon. The setting, music, characters, and sense of immersion are an acquired taste, but you will soon feel yourself in this world.

We all know the cliche's: cyberpunk, dystopian future, with a morally grey protagonist who ends up entangled in something far bigger than himself. Hell, what am I talking about? We LOVE these damn cliche's!
Deus Ex manages to deliver everything we love about the ol' William Gibson novels (which are turning out to be rather prophetic these days), while offering a pretty wide variety of CHOICE. What sorts of choices? From augments to multiple ways of handling situations. Wanna run-n-gun it? Do you. Wanna go Solid Snakin' it? Slither, homey. Wanna be diplomatic? Everyone needs friends. Just be sure to equip the augments that play nice with said play style.
Graphically, Deus Ex uses the ol' Unreal Engine. So don't expect face melting graphics. However, for retro gamers like myself, these "old" graphics lend to the atmosphere in Deus EX: a time when cyberpunk was more escapist and less like what we all now live.
In terms of difficulty, Deus Ex can be punishing. Particularly if you choose augments that don't work well with your tactics. At its time of release, this mechanic was still very experimental in gaming. Deus Ex definitely plays best on a second or third (or fourth or fifth) play-through.

Hexcells proves that puzzle games don't need to be extremely complex to thoroughly enjoy.
Now if you've ever played Minesweeper then right away you'll realise the basic premise is the same in both games. You click on a hexagon and it'll reveal a number and that number is how many 'mines' are around that specific hexagon, sound familiar? What Hexcells adds onto the original Minesweeper experience is a more puzzle oriented design to its levels, with each progressively testing your knowledge of new mechanics that get introduced throughout the worlds. That beind said each level in a world has a set amount of 'mines' in predefined locations, some puzzles might take you multiple tries to first realise the pattern but once you do it's abundantly satisfying when you finally solve it.
This game has a very minimalistic approach to both its audio and graphics; there isn't much to complain about because it gets the job done. Simple hexagon shapes with an electronic ambience in the style of Solar Fields, with the added bonus of the game's audio playing in rhythm to your actions.
Honestly my biggest complaint with this game is that there aren't enough puzzles, if you're like me than it'll leave you with that feeling of "I want more!". Thankfully though this game is really cheap, I'd highly recommend a purchase to anyone interested in either puzzles or games like Minesweeper/Sudoku/Picross.

While this has numerous plotholes already, 2k Australia decided that this couldn't JUST be on the exact same borderlands 2 engine - They needed to add the most aggrivating low gravity jump platforming and useless o2 meters. The Engine is already deliberately slow - for loot hunting and team gameplay. When paired with low gravity it just makes the game so difficult to navigate. All the enemies also jump around to avoid fire within low gravity, massive parts of the game are made up purely by platforming and they even added jumppads for extra jumping - You can tell, they were proud of this mechanic. This is something they looked at during development and thought "Hey, that is great!". The o2 meter is useless. I don't really need to say more as it doesn't impact the game whatsoever. The game makes it out as if it is something you should always worry about, however, I can't ever remember running out of oxygen whatsoever.
The plot is very bare and riddled with holes, as borderlands 2 provides a pretty concise story of events, via echo-logs, character interaction and inferred dialouge, the pre-sequel decides to throw that out of the window and rushes to make an already standard, unseen plot into a cartoony farce. In an attempt to make a fan favourite villain into some sort of hero fallen from grace.
The story is also very, VERY insistant on parroting every outdated and cringey internet meme it can muster and goes to great lengths to make almost every character gay. Well over 50% of the women you find will do nothing but loudly declare their disinterest in men, while noteable male characters in the franchise are suddenly very open about their homosexuality and press it on the player.
It really does ruin the immersion of the game, as other games in the series didn't do this and it feels very forced. It also goes to extremes to insult, berate and laugh at certain gender groups. It is very apparent that the writing team is able to run rampant and include their personal internet agendas into this. I don't want your social issues. I just want to do quests and find loot with friends.
The playable characters are boring, one dimensional smartasses with nothing noteworthy about them. They try to tie them into the game by making some of them the sub-bosses of borderlands 2, however this just feels stupid as you mostly dispose of them with ease in borderlands 2 without a passing thought.
Somehow uglier than it's 3 year old predeccesor, with bland, boring enviroments to slowly run around in. Sometimes I got confused as to where I was just because every area looked the same. The moon's surface is exacly that, with reskinned enemies from borderlands 2 roaming the surface. Insides of buildings and areas are grotty, low res technology factories. Even the main city in the game is amazingly similar. The human enemies are all the same reskinned borderlands 2 enemies but with different names and australian accents. The weapons remain virtually unchanged, however they add in laser-weapons. I can count the number of genuinely unique enemies I encountered on one hand.
In short, it feels lifeless. It honestly feels so devoid of content that you could show this to anybody and they would claim it is actually very bad DLC for borderlands 2. Even as a fan of the series, I would recomend to save your money. I Bought this for £3.75, and I still feel ripped off. How depressing.

Pros:
It combines elements from Ceasar, Banished and Anno to create a very interesting city builder game.  The best way to put it is Ceasar's buildings and UI style with Banished's survival and inventory management and Anno's city evolution (Anno 1404 to narrow it down)
Gameplay is enough to keep you playing, and this game provides a fair amount of content compared to city builders of the same calibre.
I've not experienced any bugs while playing the game, the only thing that's happened was the game not tabbing back in when I tabbed out.  Forcing me to restart the game.
Tutorial is helpful for learning the basics of the game.
Cons:
There aren't any set maps to play off in free build.  You will have to use a randomly generated map and chance having your resources spread across the entire map, making it difficult and expensive to get resources.
The game offers little in the way if events, out of 90 minutes I saw 3 events: plague, robbers and AI rivals demanding money for 'projects'  There are no events which are good or neutral, only bad.
The economy system in this game is stressful and honestly, the worst part of the game.  There is no real way to achieve a stable economy, from the start of the game you just spend money, and earn a smidgen of it back through laughable tax rates or through trade with AI rivals, which we will talk about in a second.  The way the tax system works is the less people you have working, the more you tax, the more people you have working, the less you tax.  Simple.  This game requires you to keep building and building to keep your city evolving and preparing for invasions from on map enemy camps and off map AI rivals.  Because of this you'll never have unemployed citizens, meaning the tax rate is always low.  With about 1000 citizens I tax about 250 gold from them every tax rotation, thats about 1/8th of what I spent keeping them happy that rotation.
So, tax is useless, what about trade?
If you choose to play and trade with AI rivals, from the very start they will constantly demand money from you, sometimes it's 1600 gold, others it's 3200 gold.  If you accept, they like you more and are more willing to trade and less likely to invade.  If you decline, they invade you, this is just another way of adding challenge to the game, another way to burn your gold reserves.  I refused to pay a rival and before I could even build a troop of soldiers I had enemy war pigs riding in and destroying my city.  If you do pay them and trade you need to be a fast builder, they won't start off with requesting and selling simple resources like planks, or turnips, they will demand and sell luxury resources which you can't make yet or have no place in your city currently.  Making trade in the early game, near impossible.
I would like to mention that the three AI rivals I played with promised to pay me back, I didn't see a single piece of gold come back from them.
Not cool.
Summary:
Despite the not recommended I did enjoy the game.  But ultimately the economy aspects were just too much to recommend.  It just felt like it was all there to play against you and make the game harder but with no true challenge, because there was little you could do to beat the challenge.  in other words the game's economy mechanics are imbalanced and to really have a stable economy you cannot play with AI rivals and you'll have to play on a low difficulty.
A good modern option to those who enjoyed playing games such as Caesar III, Pharaoh and Zeus.

Delver, the Early Access Rogue-Like RPG.
I saw this game and it sparked my interest because it reminded me a little of Might and Magic World of Xeen. Then upon realizing it was a first person rogue-like game and not the typical side scrolling one, I had to get it.
The game looks and play beautifully, I changed the key bindings a little more to my tastes but it probably won't bother most on its default settings. On the games website you can buy a HD Sphax PureBD pack (You might recognize the name from the popular Minecraft Texture pack) for $4.90 (2.90€).  The game should be able to run on any computer than can use Steam, due to the simplistic graphics and the slider in the menu.
As far as the Rogue aspect of the game, it does it a little differently than say, Rogue Leacy. In that game, you only get the gold from each run to spend as you have to spend it all to enter the castle. But in Delver, you keep all of your gold from each run, but lose any equipment that you got. But once you buy something, you always have it, which is nice. You level up in the dungeon and have a series of classic RPG stats that you can increase, but Health should always be your number 1 priority when leveling as it was the only one that had a major difference to difficulty/gameplay. I got lucky on my longest run and found a warhammer with long reach and high damage. The wands you find will be very useful and they are the only way to get passed something that can happen in the game. Speed is probably the least useful stat in the game especially when matched against Health. I'd like to see a little more depth in the stats.
I really didn't notice any bugs that stopped my progress in the game and I could honestly see this game, in its current phase of development, packaged as a full game, I would certainly buy it again. 10/10 and good on the Devs.

I have taken part of this game since 2012 and i am still very excited about where this game is going. Think of this game as a blend of old car-building games like "Street Legal" where you design engines and bodies and mix it with business-simulations where you massproduce said cars in the millions in huge plants for the masses, or have a handful of extremely skilled craftsmen carefully sculpting 10 supercars a year.
For now, we have the engine designer and body designer with the business part of the game in the making.
Still even in this phase this is one of the best simulations out there on this subject. When i say simulator i mean it in a positive way, but it can also be considered a game depending on how serious you are approaching it and what you do with it. The developers are active on their forum and on their facebook page and communicate with the players on a regular basis and seems like really great guys.
You can make your own engines in almost every way concievable from small, cheap, weak and smoking cast iron engines straight out from a peoples car of the 60's eastern bloc to huge, high-tech roaring V8's in titanium with horsepowers in 4 digits from a modern supercar, all with a fantastic attention to detail for those who want to get knee-deep in technical specs. Heck, i've even taken specs from my real cars engines and used them in the game to get quite accurate results!
Design car bodies to make hideous and comical cars that should be killed with fire to spare mankind the horror or design beautiful cars fit for the nice salons and red carpet. Go for round, sleek aerodynamic shapes or why not a classic 70's box with wedges and angles everywhere? Make your own take on the huge barges with rocket-fins of the 50's or try to make a copy of the car on your own driveway!
I really look forward to seeing this game take off and grow. This is what a car tycoon game is all about. This is what other "simulators" and "tycoon" games should be if they had any decency and self respect. If you are a car nut like me you will not be disappointed.

Deu Sex is an action role-playing game.
You play as Jesus Christ Denton, a nano-augmented anti-terrorist agent.
Its a story with twists and turns and choices.
You will be taken to various loactions in New York, Paris and Hong Kong.
You are able to complete objectives in a multitude of ways including stealth, shooting, hacking, swimming, lock picking, etc. So you will have to use your skill points according to the way you intend to play.
Inventory space is limited so there are certain items you will have to abandon. You cant sell in this game.
Dropping items on the floor for later wont help either. Because some areas become inaccesible. And some areas seem to reset so your items disapear.
You are able to use augmentations which are special abilities. You find augmentation canisters and have a choice of 1 of 2 augmentations. No going back. The augmentations can be upgraded.
The game isnt too complex or hard to figure out. Its pretty straight forward. Its about whether you go in stealthily or guns blazing or a mixture of both. You may even go in sword blazing since you can actually get a blazing sword in this game.
You are able to get the most powerful weapon in the game litteraly right at the start.
Hacking doesnt require a minigame. The game pauses when you open your inventory. Weapons dont degrade, jam or break. Its a forgiving game.
I'd say the complexity comes from the story. And figuring out who are the "good guys" and who are the "bad guys".
Choose either to lead, to follow, to illuminate the world or to keep it in darkness.

I'd imagine if this was what happened to Abraham and Isaac back in pre-biblical times, religion might actually have changed quite a bit from what it is today.
The opening story to the game is simply heart-wrenching, as you feel the pain and fear within Isaac. As you play the game, you pray that Isaac stays alive and manages to escape his mom trying to rid him for the sake of God.
This is the first rogue-like I've encountered that actually drives people to stay alive using it's story. Most rogue-likes just throw you in a world where you have to save something/someone you love, or prevent some kind of world catastrophe. The Binding of Isaac, however, creates a mental repercussion on the player should Isaac die while being in the basement, his mother would sacrifice him. The drive to save this poor innocent boy from the hands of death guides the player to be as careful as possible and to strive on.
The use of religious artifacts and symbolism in this game is simply brilliant. The references it makes to the Devil and God is very interesting, and it is in no way offensive, albeit leaning more towards the dark side. The vast myriad of items, tarot cards, and trinkets all contribute to the high replayability of this game. It also gives the player a chance at creating multiple strategies to overcome the game. Needless to say, there will be many many moments where you will have to weigh in on the value of your items and reluctantly choose what you'd like to hold on to as you proceed through the levels. On top of that, the trading and economy system of the game is well-balanced, and makes for a good headache when deciding how much of your life to sacrifice in exchange for power.
The soundtrack is really nice, not exceptionally awesome, but there's a nice kick to it. Graphics wise, nothing too fancy.
Highly recommended, 9/10.

"A Sleeper hit from 2k Australia!"
One of the most boring, contrived, lazy and agenda-ridden games I've ever played.
I feel like I came away from playing this garbage with more questions than answers but I'll try to explain my reasoning to the best of my knowledge.
This game is designed to fit in around after the ending of borderlands 1. While this has numerous plotholes already, 2k Australia decided that this couldn't JUST be on the exact same borderlands 2 engine - They needed to add the most aggrivating low gravity jump platforming and useless o2 meters. The Engine is already deliberately slow - for loot hunting and team gameplay. When paired with low gravity it just makes the game so difficult to navigate. All the enemies also jump around to avoid fire within low gravity, massive parts of the game are made up purely by platforming and they even added jumppads for extra jumping - You can tell, they were proud of this mechanic. This is something they looked at during development and thought "Hey, that is great!". The o2 meter is useless. I don't really need to say more as it doesn't impact the game whatsoever. The game makes it out as if it is something you should always worry about, however, I can't ever remember running out of oxygen whatsoever.
The plot is very bare and riddled with holes, as borderlands 2 provides a pretty concise story of events, via echo-logs, character interaction and inferred dialouge, the pre-sequel decides to throw that out of the window and rushes to make an already standard, unseen plot into a cartoony farce. In an attempt to make a fan favourite villain into some sort of hero fallen from grace.
The story is also very, VERY insistant on parroting every outdated and cringey internet meme it can muster and goes to great lengths to make almost every character gay. Well over 50% of the women you find will do nothing but loudly declare their disinterest in men, while noteable male characters in the franchise are suddenly very open about their homosexuality and press it on the player.
It really does ruin the immersion of the game, as other games in the series didn't do this and it feels very forced. It also goes to extremes to insult, berate and laugh at certain gender groups. It is very apparent that the writing team is able to run rampant and include their personal internet agendas into this. I don't want your social issues. I just want to do quests and find loot with friends.
The playable characters are boring, one dimensional smartasses with nothing noteworthy about them. They try to tie them into the game by making some of them the sub-bosses of borderlands 2, however this just feels stupid as you mostly dispose of them with ease in borderlands 2 without a passing thought.
Somehow uglier than it's 3 year old predeccesor, with bland, boring enviroments to slowly run around in. Sometimes I got confused as to where I was just because every area looked the same. The moon's surface is exacly that, with reskinned enemies from borderlands 2 roaming the surface. Insides of buildings and areas are grotty, low res technology factories. Even the main city in the game is amazingly similar. The human enemies are all the same reskinned borderlands 2 enemies but with different names and australian accents. The weapons remain virtually unchanged, however they add in laser-weapons. I can count the number of genuinely unique enemies I encountered on one hand.
In short, it feels lifeless. It honestly feels so devoid of content that you could show this to anybody and they would claim it is actually very bad DLC for borderlands 2. Even as a fan of the series, I would recomend to save your money. I Bought this for £3.75, and I still feel ripped off. How depressing.

At its core, Hearthlands is a city-building game. However, with the addition of research, diplomatic relationship building and spell casting, it becomes much more. Just when you think everything is under control, the game throws a new problem in the mix, keeping the game interesting yet frustration-free. If you are looking for a deep and engrossing game that adds new complexity and fun to the city builder genre, you should take a look at Hearthlands.

This is a charming game evoking feelings of nostalgia for city-building games like Zeus and Poseidon. The mechanics are straightforward, but the new Campaign Mode is a good way of getting to grips with the game.
Its retro simplicity is both part of its charm and its main letdown: it gets boring and repetitive quickly, and although it's not a problem in-game when navigating the map the 3D graphics on the title screen are kind of cheesy. Although it didn't bother me personally, those seeking a more unique, cutting-edge building sim may find this too derivative of other titles.
It's worth noting that I am not reviewing the finished product and the developer has been very engaged with the community responding and taking on board any feedback, and on that basis it's well worth supporting this decent contribution to the genre.

Hearthlands is an awesome realtime strategy game where you can loose hours trying to develop your own kingdom and its economy, keeping all your citizens happy, trading with other kingdoms and defending against enemies.
As a 2D city builder in the Caesar / Pharoh mold this game isn't super complex (at least compared to something like Banished) but what it does it does quite well.  I had great fun with it!

Hearthlands seems fun, has all the potential to be fun, engages you for a while.. And then you realize that you are not having fun, you're just optimizing a pretty spreadsheet.
You can't skip missions, so you're kind of stuck without a challenge for quite some time. I stopped playing after mission 4.
Note that the performance is great, the atmosphere very well done, the animations are cute. It's just that the actual fun part of the game isn't there (yet?).
This game looks, feels and plays like a browser / mobile game. Asking 20 bucks is ridiculous.

The trading system is difficult to use yet it is possibly a must if your location doesn't spawn a certain needed resource.  The AI constantly ask you for increasing amounts of materials (sometimes that you don't even have access to) you deny them too many times the go to war with you.  The combat system is clunky and difficult to use.  Controls that you think intuitively should be there are not, it took me a while to get used to left clicking to get my units to move.  The peddlers reguarly don't get the required resource to the houses that need it, but there is no reason why they have everything needed.  When your houses don't have the luxury or food they downgrade then you don't have workers.

Really nice game, I used to love old Impressions Games (Caesar III, Pharaoh, etc) and Hearthland is taking the old recipe while successfully adding few extra layers of gameplay. Very well done and already a new classic!

Positive: A good addition to your library if you were a fan of the Caesar/Pharaoh/Zeus/Emperor games. There's a good tutorial that will teach you the basics, and a campaign mode that slowly introduces more advanced gameplay mechanics.
Negative: The graphics aren't good, but I quickly got used to it. The quality of the voice acting and the repetitive sound effects of some buildings and units are terrible and annoying though. I hope the dev updates the voices with better VAs and more speech variations.
Conclusion: Despite the mediocre graphics and bad sfx, I liked the core gameplay loop enough to give this a thumbs up.

First, the jumping is absolutely horrible. If you don't bother changing the standard FOV which is bad enough as it is, your character will seem stiff and difficult to manuever making for a frustrating experience at times.
Second, weapon balancing is beyond broken. Everyone uses beam or launcher weapons that need no real upgrades to because stupidly over powered. All the upgrades are completely pointless because all they seem to do is reduce damage or stability without giving any real reason as to why I should "upgrade" to a particular item.
Third, the microtransactions. These don't effect the game much at all but they are incredibly gimmicky. You have the typical two currency types, one that unlocks stuff for your guns and such and the other does basically everything else. As far as I know, there is no way to earn Spacebux from playing through the game.
Fourth, fiddly controls. C to throw a grenade? No crouch button (As far as I know)? Sprinting like Usain Bolt? Seriously, this is stupid and awkward and thankfully, they can be altered, but you need to make sure more than anything else that you don't lose some vital function by remapping.
Finally, graphics settings. Even if some might say the game looks fine, good for them, but this is a PC game. I want to be able to make the game look as outstanding or as horrible as I want. Even TF2 (Which this game very clearly draws inspiration from) has proper graphics options and that too is a free-to-play shooter.
Seriously, I really don't mind having to spend money to play a game. Even if it means that I don't have stupid gimmicky functions crammed down my throat to the point of choking me. The game would work perfectly if they just asked us to pay a single fee for everything in the game to at least work decently. Is that really much to ask for? I am not saying that every F2P game ever is♥♥♥♥♥♥ but at least take a page out of Warframe's book and don't add in stupid microtransactions and give it real functionality. Give it regular updates, fix the balancing and control issues and alter the microtransactions in such a way that stop it from being irritating and then this would be a great game.

You head inside and explore the dungeon killing enemies and collecting progressively better loot until eventually, you die. When you respawn, thinking that all hope is lost, you realize that your gold from your previous life is still with you. You also realize, going into the dungeon, that it's different each time. The Camp where the npcs live in the beginning has many shops and the dungeon is endless and randomly generated. You can collect and save your gold to buy better loot in the town or just find as much as you can before you're killed in the dungeon. No matter how you play, delver is a great, addictive, cheap and fun retro dungeon-adventure game that everyone should play

This video features a non-biased quick look @ the game only:
A sci-fi World of Warcraft.
Game Details:
Critically acclaimed and now Free to Play, WildStar is a fantastical sci-fi MMO where you can join your friends or undertake your own epic adventures on the fabled planet Nexus! Explore the huge and amazingly vibrant world packed with unique characters, exotic locations, thrilling challenges and dark mysteries. Recruit fellow citizens of Nexus to solve the primordial puzzles of the universe itself as you experience exhilarating action combat, deep character customization, and one of the most powerful housing systems ever seen in a MMORPG.

I will start off by saying this: This game, like every other MMO out there, has it's issues and bugs. But that doesn't mean it's not a good game.
I have been playing this game since before launch and have seen it come a long way and all the changes it's been through. But a constant has always been the community. I have never played a game where the community is so helpful to new and returning players. Whether it be answering questions, helping with quests, or giving them a few free items to start them on housing.
The combat is very fluid and busy. You really do have to keep your eyes out for telegraphs and move out of them. I really enjoy the combat and some of the challenges it presents. Not too much to say about this. You really have to try the game out to see for yourself.
Housing is huge in this game. The plots are pretty big and can be built up any way you want. People are immensely talented and creative with their building. I highly suggest, once you get the ability to have a house (level 14 from your factions main city quest), that you go explore any public houses you can. You never know what you will find! LOL
Crafting can be a little frustrating. Ok, a lot, depending on what one your doing. I have a maxed Architect, so I find that one pretty easy, along with the cooking skill.  I don't do any other crafting, but have heard some stories about the difficulty of the others. My suggestion: try out whatever your interested in to see how you like it. If you don't, go back to the trainer to change it to another. You can change your professions once every 7 days, I think it's 7 days. However, there is a timer on it and some minimal money associated with it. You can have 2 professions (1 gathering + 1 crafting, or 2 gathering, or 2 crafting, etc.) plus the cooking skill.
The artwork and design of the game is very pretty, in most areas. The colors are bold and bright. The humor is top notch. If you play with your sounds off, turn them on. Listen to the taxi drivers banter and the rez guy's insults to you when you die.
The music is fantastic!! Jeff outdid himself on it. Each zone has it own unique music theme, which you can get all in housing.
This game might not be for everyone. And, yes, there are some out there that just don't like it. Please be your own person and give it a try, if you want to. Don't let the naysayers/doomsayers make up your mind for you. This is a great game and I know you will have loads of fun.
All of these things combined make it a great game to play. But what keeps me playing is the community and, especially, the wonderful people in my guild.

Do you like MMORPGs?
- Wildstar is a great next-gen MMO, with fast action-based combat and cartoony graphics. It has the Guild Wars 2 Combat further developed and runs on the traditional PvE and PvP model such as World of Warcrat.
PvE content in Wildstar is very challenging and requires both good movement and good character knowledge to progress, same as PvP.
This game really changed my taste for MMORPGs and can't switch to other MMOs anymore. I suggest you to try it out, don't read reviews, don't believe anyone, try it out yourself and decide it!

Probably the best MMO if you like (difficult) dungeons and raids. Some of the most challenging content with unique classes and combat mechanics. The graphics are awesome and world/zones/dungeons are really cool. The character customization blows away most other games; it makes WoW's transmog system look like something the developers did overnight. I've never been one for collectibles but it's addicting in Wildstar.
It has the best F2P model I've seen in any game, you can essentailly earn anything from the store just by playing and you can't buy power or progression. It's basically restricted to convenience and aesthetics.
If you're used to having your hand-held and casually walking through content, you're gonna have a bad time. If you like twitchy, reactive combat with dark souls-esque boss encounters of grandeur then I really don't think there exists a better game.
It's definitely not perfect, not even close. It has plenty of downsides, specifically the leveling experience and pvp. I don't think there has ever been a time the pvp was balanced.
The leveling experience is a mess; there's an insane amount of quests and only ~10% are worth doing if you're trying to optimize the journey to lvl 50. Personally,  I actually kind of enjoyed it because of the einvirnonments/atmospehere of the different zones and constant threat of dying.
A lot of people don't like it for the theme or humour or graphics and I can definitely see why but it's something I enjoy. It's kind of a borderlands-like humor with a space twist but I don't feel they've overdone it. It adds some fun and makes it more immersive and unique; I really like the intros you get from the narrator when you go to a new zone for the first time and there's tons of lore (re: science path) if you're into that but none of it is forced.
The path system is pretty cool and gives you something to do other than grind and progress through the typical MMO loot ladder.
Explorer is fun if you really just enjoy running around and seeing how far you can go. Chances are if you can see it, you can climb it. The Science path is great for lore-boars out there and feels pretty endless. Soldier lacks a bit of content but has its  moments. Settler is kind of niche but is definitely beneficial for people who like to min/max, particularly while leveling and doing open-world content.
Oh also, you can do double jump, even on mounts! It sounds stupid and minor but it's something you'll really start to miss when you play other games.
If you like end-game pve, character customization. fun humor, collectibles, difficult combat, unique gameplay, massive boss fights, story/lore, exploring, and most importantly double-jumping then WildStar is what you're looking for. Like every game it has its flaws but the only true downside is that the population is too small.
The game gets a lot of hate. I don't get why there are already people here giving negative reviews. I don't think theres much merit to the "if you have nothing nice to say then don't say anything" mentality; it's important to be critical at the right time but people who don't even play the game and never really did are logging into steam just to tell other people not to play it.
It's definitely not for everyone but that's just the nature of, well, anything. Not everything was meant to be enjoyed by everyone. If you don't enjoy a game then that doesn't necessarily make it a bad game, it more than likely means it just wasn't for you. Go on any MMO forum you'll find the majority of complaints about a game are along the lines of "it doesn't have X feature like WoW" or "it's too pvp-focused and there's no pve!".
If you find yourself saying those things then you're simply just playing the wrong game. It's pvp focused because it's meant to be for people that like pvp; it's not a bad game because you only enjoy pve. It doesn't have raid finder/free loot/weekly raids you can stroll through casually because it's not meant to be simple and casual; that doesn't make it a bad game it just means you're playing the wrong game.
People complain it's too hard and needs to be easier so its more accessible but that's hog-wash, go play WoW if you want a casual themepark adventureland. There's a reason it's the most popular MMO around (hint: it's the easiest and most accessible). I truly believe most of my WoW friends couldn't do the end-game PvE in WildStar even if they tried and it's really not that difficult. It's just that most people don't want a challenge, even if they say they do.
If you put an obstacle in someone's way they tend to spend more time complaining than trying to work around it or overcome it.
