Summary:
Take a basic but twisted concept with a lot (I mean a LOT) of shallow Christian references, mix it with straightforward top-down RPG/shooter gameplay, an crazy amount of potential upgrade combinations and increasingly more difficult (and unlockable) bosses, and you have an addictive game with the apparently infinite replayability that is the Binding of Isaac. I was recommended this a long time ago, got it and intially wasn't impressed. But I kept playing it at said recommender's insistence, and now it's one of my favourite games of all time.
The good:
Easy to get started.
So much content for a game that is simple in its setup. There's a reason why there's a Binding of Isaac wiki.
The music is good.
The game doesn't give a crap about being superbly balanced. Be prepared for some really hard runs where you do awfully, and then some really awesome runs where you're overpowered as ♥♥♥♥.
It's a game I can play in short-ish bursts (45 min to over an hour). As much as I also love more intense games that hook you for days at a time, I have a special place in my heart for good games that I can also play a full round of in my lunchbreak, then forget about for the rest of the day while I get work done.
It's just.. fun. That's why I play games!
The bad:
It doesn't get quite as good until after you unlock the first dozen or so upgrades in the game, although this is quick to do. This was why I wasn't initially impressed.
So badly optimised, especially on a Mac. I guess this is why Flash is being slowly phased out.
No save option, other than achievements and overall game completion - you do one run at a time. If you need to leave in the middle, prepare to leave the game running in the background, or abandon it.
And of course, Rebirth is now out and apparently makes this gem of a game pale in comparison.
Still, until Rebirth drops to 75% off (I'm a cheapskate), I'll be playing this for a long time yet.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is and extremely enjoyable experience. Unfortunately for The Pre-Sequel, it had the bad luck to be the follow up to Borderlands 2, which is without a doubt the strongest title in the series. As a result, many Borderlands 2 fans who were excitedly awaiting TPS were left with a bit of a bad taste in their mouths, which I feel is a bit of an overreaction. This review is both an endorsement for TPS, as well as a bit of a comparison with Borderlands 2.
First and foremost, just as much has changed gameplay-wise between TPS and Borderlands 2 as had changed between the first Borderlands and Borderlands 2. For one, this game has classes that are not echos of the classes from the prior game, whereas in Borderlands 2, the classes are essentially the same as their counterparts in the first game. With all four/six Vault Hunters having class skills that feel different from what we've all gotten used to, it's a breath of fresh air. Where B2 did away with the first game's fall damage, TPS adds a double-jump mechanic that allows much more verticality to the levels, as well as allowing snipers a plethora of new perches. Borderlands 2 took its predecessor's "scrapyards and wastelands" setting and added some snow to the terrain, and even included a few areas with grass, seemingly doubling the color palate of the series. TPS takes said color palate and further adds to it, with a plethora of neon colors appearing throughout the game, particularly towards the final few levels. Where B2 added Eridium, TPS added Moonstones, and more ways to rid yourself of them. In B2, once you had maxed out all of your ammo capacities, Eridium really takes a steep decline in value, really only being used at that point for Tiny Tina's Slot Machines or to summon the Invincibles. In TPS, once you've maxed out all your ammo capacities, Moonstones can be used to buy static buffs for you and your party through Moxxi's "Moxxtails", be used to turn 3 pieces of loot into 1 piece of loot of a higher rarity at the Grinder, or be spent to open Moonstone Chests throughout the game for chances at better loot than average chests.
Also, the dialogue needs to be mentioned. Playing through the prior games in the series, you get a bit of a 'silent protagonist' vibe from the games. Well, TPS has given your character the gift of gab, and while you may not have dialogue options (say, ala Fallout), the fact that your character will respond to things going on in the world around you is refreshing and helps characterize each of their unique personalities. If you have multiple players in your party, they can even discuss things between each other, which I thought was a very nice touch. Just as each Vault Hunter has their own lines of dialogue, certain NPCs (Moxxi is a great example of this) also have different lines depending on which Vault Hunter interacted with them. Games in this series generally boast replayability as being one of thier strong suits, and this really helps to keep things feeling new when you're playing the story for the umpteenth time.
This review is only for the base game, so I'll only touch upon the DLC. The DLC here is nowhere near as strong as the amount of content available for B2, and only one part of the Season Pass is an actual story DLC. That being said, the Claptastic Voyage does have a great story, and essentially acts as an origin story for Claptrap in B2. There's two DLC classes, both of which are very enjoyable, same as in B2. The other pieces of the Season Pass aren't as good, and it feels almost insulting that the only way to add arena battles to TPS is through DLC. With 2K Australia having closed its doors, we're not likely to see any further DLC get developed.
So, for those of you who are still with me after all that text, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is most definitely worth playing, and will be enjoyable throughout. Unfortuantely, without anywhere near as much end game content and with only a fraction of the DLC options, the game does feel lacking once you make it close to the level cap. I wholly enjoyed TPS, as much if not more than Borderlands 2, simply for all of the little improvements it made upon the series mentioned above. Get this game on sale if you're expecting as much content as Borderlands 2 had, but definitely get this game.

Holy christ, I just saw this game on sale for one dollar and seventy-four cents. $1.74. Get it. This game is an absolute gem and a legend within the cyberpunk genre. An early rpg/fps entry that oozes nostalgia and exudes genius. I'm not the best at reviewing games, but there are those hidden amongst Steam that I feel are too amazing not to promote... this is one of them.
You play as agent JC Denton, a shiny new nano-augmented agent (successor to mechanically-augmented agents) in a counter-terrorist organization dubbed UNATCO. The secretive politicking and social banter you'll be exposed to can be overheard from enemies mid-conversation, read through security terminals throughout the gameworld, deluged via e-mails sent to your character (as well as other non-player characters, provided you can gain access to their accounts...) will influence how you want to play your character. Do you blindly obey the higher-ups in your organization, or lean toward the ideals of UNATCO's enemy--a 'terrorist' organization calling themselves the NSF.
Between the conspiracy theories, feeding homeless kids for intel, jumping on rats, getting turnt on zyme, breaking into storage rooms for bags of soy nuts... there's intelligent humor and timeless music to help you immerse yourself in Ion Storm's take on a futuristic dystopian United States of America.
OH AND NOT TO MENTION: REVISION. It's a breathtaking graphical overhaul of the game, provided as a free DLC through Steam. Deus Ex is given a facelift for the 21st century (which goes deeper than mere graphics, mind you) and you're also given the option to play the game with two of it's most famous mods-Biomod and Shifter.
Again, I'm no good at reviewing but by all that is holy, you need to pick up this classic masterpiece in PC gaming. $1.74, I still can't believe it!!!

This is it. This is the one game that every person who is deeply involved in this medium needs to play at least once, and realistically speaking, playing it more than once is not only recommended, but it adds even more fun to a title that is already above all others. You can invert your controls but there is no option to adjust mouse sensitivity. NOT a big deal - just creates a learning curve that I'm already getting used to. I'm having too much fun to care about this minor drawback.
It's been a while since I've had a new, easy-to-use, good-looking and smoothly-working space sim to get lost in and relax.
I HIGHLY recommend this game!

This game is the definitive 4x title of this year.  It isn't the greatest 4x I've played, but it is far from the worst.
It feels like and plays like an RTS while having the same depth and variety expected for a 4x title.  The true enjoyment the game offers is in the sandbox and in the arms race and interactions you have with the generated galaxy.  At it's core it is a very simple game with a lot of variety.  Despite that, it is a very enjoyable experiance and can consume hours of your time.
I recommend this over every other 4x release of 2016.  If you like grand space strategy games.
Possitives:
- Real Time Space Battles with ships.
- Exploring feels like exploring.
- No hand holding outside of the tutorial tips
- Tutorial tips are helpful instead of patronising.
- AI is constrained by the same rules as the player and smart, instead of being mindlessly brutal and cheating like in most 4x or grand strategy games these days.
- Amasing music and atmosphere
Negatives:
- The game limits how many systems you can directly control.
- When an AI enemy declares war on you, you have little control over when peace is decided or if the enemy decides to accept your terms of their surrender.
Most negative reviews stem from people who seem to be apparently upset mostly about these two negatives or the fact that this game limits the ability for someone to declare a total war.  However, I can look past these glaring issues to see an otherwise mostly enjoyable experiance.
If you're looking for a 4x title which is a little more in depth but still simple in presentation and is a space empire building game, this is the best one on offer from 2016.  I am sure there are better games which preceded it and better games which will come out in the future though.  I don't consider it a must purchase despite myself enjoying it far more than other 4x titles from last year.

TLDR: After the nice and relaxing Zenge, Michal Pawlowski rises to excellence with Art of Gravity.
As the game summary says, Art of Gravity is a voxel / physics puzzle game - and good physics puzzles are surprisingly hard to come by. Either the physics are clunky, or the level design is weak, or, most frequently, both. Michal elegantly solved both problems in one go - he built a sandbox game where the physics are taken very seriously, and chose a visual implementation that makes watching the mechanics in action a real pleasure.
Your task is to launch balls at cubes. Balls cause cubes to disintegrate into small cubes, which fly all over the place, damaging or destroying other cubes as they go. This is already fun - the kinetic energy of the action is really visceral. Then, the demolition becomes more and more difficult as new blocks with different properties are introduced (read: they become tougher and tougher), and you'll have more elaborate balls to wreak your havok as well.
With all the enjoyment of wanton destruction going on, I have to touch on one the game's only weakness - it's rather easy. Experimenting with new materials is superb, but then the solution just presents itself. 60-65 of the 75 levels flow by pretty self-evidently - only the last 10-15 were decent headscratchers.
Ah, I wanted to write a short review, but obviously couldn't :) I loved Art of Gravity, and while these games are short, they're excellent value for money at the low asking price. If you like puzzle games, make sure to give it a shot!

Hexcells is a really nice spin on the classic minesweeper we all know (and love).. Instead of clearing out squares, you now have to clear hexagons, which surprisingly creates new challenges to overcome. Things get even more interesting once new mechanics are thrown into the mix like a certain amount of marked hexagons being next to each other or having at least one gap in between marked hexagons. If you're hungry for a new kind of minesweeper, complete with an ambient soundtrack, a smooth difficulty curve, and a whole lotta hexagons, you can't go wrong with Hexcells.

I really don't have any cons to say about Wildstar. It's really easy to get into, but has quite a lot to learn and customize. The business model is extremely fair. If they had launched with a more Guild Wars style business model they might not have been so population hobbled, but this was originally a subscription only game.
I've played a lot of these action combat MMORPGs. I've got several hundred hours on TERA and Neverwinter, several thousand hours on Guild Wars 2. The thing Wildstar has going for it above all of it's competitors is performance. Performance isn't perfect, but compared to the other 3 I mentioned it's FPS is rock solid. TERA and GW2 have a problem with poor performance in heavy action and Neverwinter has poor FPS no matter what you're doing. If you have an i3/FX and a mid range GPU this is the action combat MMO for you. It manages to look good while running consistently even with heavy action on entry level to mid tier gaming hardware.

Toobie has one of the greatest legs and butt in all of videogames, if not THE best. Outside of the obvious sex appeal of all the character art, the characters are all incredibly well written and feel real in the world that they exist in. All of the characters in the game are all expertly written and the voice acting, whether you are listening to the game in English or Japanese, are absolutely superb.
One of the few instances of story telling and characters that could only ever work in the medium of videogames. If you have any interest in videogames as a form of art, or something more than just writing to get a character from one room of killing to another, you would be doing yourself a disservice by not playing this game. Outside of the writing, that gives each character their own unique personality and traits, the story itself is all very well paced and will have you guessing and questioning the game, yourself, and the world that this videogame exists in, long after the game itself has ended.
Thanks to Platinum Games, this is one of the most entertaining games to play, even if you are just in the game for the music/ story. There are loads of customization options to help make the character you are playing as excel at how YOU play. The various weapons in the game all feel great, have just the right amount of weight and oomph to them, and best of all they FEEL ecstatic and satisfying to hit enemies with. The movement options in the game also feel very good and your character feels very responsive and tactile to control, at all times.
I am running the game on an i5 4570 with an r9 290 and although the port itself was not the greatest, thanks to the modding community, this game ran very well on my machine. Your mileage may vary, admittedly, but with the mods made by steam user Kaldaien I was able to play this game at a very comfortable framerate and visual fidelity.
This is one of the most truly beautiful games I have ever had the opportunity of playing and long after 100%ing this game, I still regularly think about this game and what an experience it was to have played it. If you are a fan of good writing, great music, interesting and well "endowed" characters, great gameplay, and don't mind a little bit of crazy sprinkled around, this might also end up being of your favorite games, as it was for me.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is and extremely enjoyable experience. Unfortunately for The Pre-Sequel, it had the bad luck to be the follow up to Borderlands 2, which is without a doubt the strongest title in the series. As a result, many Borderlands 2 fans who were excitedly awaiting TPS were left with a bit of a bad taste in their mouths, which I feel is a bit of an overreaction. This review is both an endorsement for TPS, as well as a bit of a comparison with Borderlands 2.
First and foremost, just as much has changed gameplay-wise between TPS and Borderlands 2 as had changed between the first Borderlands and Borderlands 2. For one, this game has classes that are not echos of the classes from the prior game, whereas in Borderlands 2, the classes are essentially the same as their counterparts in the first game. With all four/six Vault Hunters having class skills that feel different from what we've all gotten used to, it's a breath of fresh air. Where B2 did away with the first game's fall damage, TPS adds a double-jump mechanic that allows much more verticality to the levels, as well as allowing snipers a plethora of new perches. Borderlands 2 took its predecessor's "scrapyards and wastelands" setting and added some snow to the terrain, and even included a few areas with grass, seemingly doubling the color palate of the series. TPS takes said color palate and further adds to it, with a plethora of neon colors appearing throughout the game, particularly towards the final few levels. Where B2 added Eridium, TPS added Moonstones, and more ways to rid yourself of them. In B2, once you had maxed out all of your ammo capacities, Eridium really takes a steep decline in value, really only being used at that point for Tiny Tina's Slot Machines or to summon the Invincibles. In TPS, once you've maxed out all your ammo capacities, Moonstones can be used to buy static buffs for you and your party through Moxxi's "Moxxtails", be used to turn 3 pieces of loot into 1 piece of loot of a higher rarity at the Grinder, or be spent to open Moonstone Chests throughout the game for chances at better loot than average chests.
Also, the dialogue needs to be mentioned. Playing through the prior games in the series, you get a bit of a 'silent protagonist' vibe from the games. Well, TPS has given your character the gift of gab, and while you may not have dialogue options (say, ala Fallout), the fact that your character will respond to things going on in the world around you is refreshing and helps characterize each of their unique personalities. If you have multiple players in your party, they can even discuss things between each other, which I thought was a very nice touch. Just as each Vault Hunter has their own lines of dialogue, certain NPCs (Moxxi is a great example of this) also have different lines depending on which Vault Hunter interacted with them. Games in this series generally boast replayability as being one of thier strong suits, and this really helps to keep things feeling new when you're playing the story for the umpteenth time.
This review is only for the base game, so I'll only touch upon the DLC. The DLC here is nowhere near as strong as the amount of content available for B2, and only one part of the Season Pass is an actual story DLC. That being said, the Claptastic Voyage does have a great story, and essentially acts as an origin story for Claptrap in B2. There's two DLC classes, both of which are very enjoyable, same as in B2. The other pieces of the Season Pass aren't as good, and it feels almost insulting that the only way to add arena battles to TPS is through DLC. With 2K Australia having closed its doors, we're not likely to see any further DLC get developed.
So, for those of you who are still with me after all that text, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is most definitely worth playing, and will be enjoyable throughout. Unfortuantely, without anywhere near as much end game content and with only a fraction of the DLC options, the game does feel lacking once you make it close to the level cap. I wholly enjoyed TPS, as much if not more than Borderlands 2, simply for all of the little improvements it made upon the series mentioned above. Get this game on sale if you're expecting as much content as Borderlands 2 had, but definitely get this game.

The original Deus Ex, despite being published by EIDOS sixteen years ago, despite the aged graphics and inputs, yet feels incredibly modern.
The game is set in a quite close time in the future, the year being 2052. The world people used to know is changing dramatically to the worse: a plague called the Grey Death is decimating thousands around the globe, terroristic organizations are killing innocents in the streets and security forces strictly rule the everyday life of the populations.
The player will find itself in the clothes of JC Denton, a global counter-terrorism agent working for UNATCO, organization known for their massive training which goal is getting the best outcome of every possible hostile situation.
With the game progressing however, certain events will have the player question about the real intentions behind the agency, eventually leading to a world-sized conspiration brought forth by obscure individuals that act behind the scenes of politics.
The gameplay, which might feel 'surpassed' by younger players revolves around several missions which the player will have to complete in the most desired fashion: whether it is rushing with heavy weaponry through security and electronic circuits or resolving the situation in a more calculated way, using the tools the game provides to safely reach the goal of your mission without alerting anyone, it is up to the player to select its approach, meaning there is no linear path the player is forced to follow.
The ambientation and the soundtrack are highly immersive: the semi-apocalyptic aspect of this world is well complemented by the haunting music and overall dark areas of the game.
Since I had the pleasure to replay a gem of the past like this one, I can't but recommend Deus Ex. Do not be fooled by the old visuals and controls, as this game can certainly hold its own if compared to today's most games plot and gameplay depth.

Im kind of torn apart by this game. I would like to recommend it, but only because of it being a game in a genre with not many choices and not because its a really good game.
I also realized, that there arent many negative reviews rating this game in its finished state, so i will have a go for it. Im sorry that its so long, i will start with positive, follow with negative and end with a resumée.
At first the positive things:
1.) Its a city builder with mechanics similar to games i loved playing. Such as Emperor Rise of the Middle Kingdom, Caesar and Pharao. It uses the *Walker-Mechanic with doing so, i kind of hated this mechanic and rather prefer a hybrid of area of effect and walker. (*Explanation for what Walker are scroll to the end.)
I have to say though, that while having the walker mechanic in this game, it at least is done well and limited to an acceptable amount. Also some buildings have an area of effect type mechanic behind, such as gatherers or hunters, watchtowers or miners.
2.) Its deep. Not only the economic aspect of it is deep enough with many different goods, it also offers a diplomatic aspect similar to the ones in the old City Builder games (traderoutes, attacking/invading, being attacked, giving gifts or handing out goods to increase popularity with factions). On top of it you have to deal with several neutral factions, such as undead, goblins, wild animals and other creatures.
I have to say though, that it is a bit unbalanced in that aspect.
You can build your city and get no problems for at least an hour playing, suddenly the game decides to spawn a pack of wolves near your city.
A pack means about 12 wolves, which are so strong that killing even one needs a strong military force and several towers. And sometimes the game decides to spawn 3,4 or even 8 of these packs in a timeframe of 5 minutes. They are then simply ripping your town apart. More about that later.
3.) Several factions with different strengths and weaknesses to play, many customization options for your session, such as how many opponents you have, how you look or how the gameworld is made.
Also starting conditions. All of that easily gives dozens of hours to play and each attempt will be different if you wish.
Now the negative things that even might drive me away:
1.) It looks HORRIBLE:
I mean really bad. It starts with you getting into a main menu screen having a picture that would even look bad for a game from 1990.
I would even say that games like Knights and Merchants had a better looking and higher resoluted menu screen.
Point is, you could overlook that if it was only this, but the whole game looks just like from at least 15 years ago.
And not in a nostalgic way.
I can be bothered to play a Pharao with a 800x640 resolution and no widescreen or zoom options, but at least the sprites in these old City-Builders look good and the overall presentation is well done.
Hearthlands sadly has a horrible presentation. Animation quality of each character is abysmal, the colour palette...i question the choice and cant believe a sane person would call the whole package to look good. In no way. This problem goes on with all presentation aspects you can think of.
The sounddesign is mediocre at best, music isnt noticeable and far from good, the menu layout and UI is...not well designed. In the end you have a complete package where every aspect of the game is literally just ugly for eyes, ears and your brain. I think the only nice thing to look at is the world map, but you maybe spend 10 seconds at most in that window every 10 minutes.
If at all...
2.) No multiplayer: Emperor already had multiplayer, it can be done and quite easily even. And the City-Builder Genre screams for a game like that with multiplayer. Its still a good game without, but it could have delivered a unique experience here. I know such a feature costs alot, time, money and workforce. So i hope it will be something to be considered for a follow up title, see more in the Resumée.
3.) Diplomacy seems shallow at places:
You can get a good stance with each faction in this game, hand them out resources when they ask you a favor, gift them stuff and have trade agreements.
But dont give them what they ask for only one time and you will instantly get a notification telling you that they invade you in no time. I had a game where i built up my city, traded with people, gifted them resources and helped them out several times.
My popularity was up and running.
Suddenly the game decided to throw about 30 wolves at my city.
I wasnt prepared and had to build wooden towers, train soldiers and build watchtowers.
During a quite long fight that didnt want to end because the game threw more and more wolves at me, a factionleader asked for 16 logs.
Logs normally are easy to produce and i could hand them out, but not while having to build wooden towers to defend my people from extinction. I rejected.
When i was nearly done defending, killing the last 4 wolves, the notification came. You are going to be invaded. Great, so i can forget that session. Btw, here a multiplayer mode could help alot. Not only would i deal with real people that arent totally irrational, but also could a friend you play with aid you with ressources or soldiers.
As could you do that for him/her.
Resumée:
Its a solid game in and of itself. It has enough to keep you busy, is deep enough to stay interesting and has content to fill many hours.
The genre is lacking anyway these times, and leaving people who like strategy and build-up games with not many choices. So its not that hard to fill this gap with the only competition being the Anno-Series, Lethis or the old games of this genre. But thats where it starts to fall off, even in such a "dying" genre, its quality is questionable.
Mostly its look and presentation is driving me away.
If it was looking as good as Lethis Path of Progress i would call it a great game you have to buy.
The lack of other features, such as a campaign, missions and quests and most important a multiplayer feature, just push me over the line of calling it a very flawed game that fills a gap in an under-represented genre.
I have one hope and request to the developers:
Do a follow up. Hire an artist and do the same game with the same ideas, but then do it with someone slightly talented drawing some better characters, buildings and so on, so it looks better.
Get better animation quality, maybe also get a unique setting.
Then implement multiplayer on top of it with all that is needed to play with at least one other person and i wouldnt hesitate to buy this game for full price and call it game of the year.
I think you are talented in some aspects and the overall idea and the mechanics, the content and depth are really good. Get presentation to an acceptable level and you are up and running to maybe help this genre to new glory.
*For those not knowing it: Walker are "NPCs"/People/Worker in the game sent out to distribute services. So people in the game dont get food with visiting a store and buying it or getting it from a storage, you have to build a deliverer, which walks around in the city to bring food to people.
This applies to all services.
Problem with it is, that you have to look whether all houses get their stuff, which can turn out to be fiddling with the city layout and sometimes be bothersome.
In older games of this genre you for example built a temple, which spawned a priest walking through your city.
Whenever he passed a house/building he decreased the demand of the service he offers, in this case belief. The whole point of city builders was to place each building in a way, that the spawned walker reached every building in time before negative things happen.
Buildings could collapse, catch fire, people catch the plague or their houses downgrade because they didnt get the goods they needed.
This turned City Builder into puzzles, where you could build after a maximum effective layout.

I have a feeling this review will be removed once the game is removed from Steam, but I feel the need to say my piece.
Upon reading the developer's recent update about the removal of TLK from Steam, I knew I had to buy it and play it.  With mostly negative reviews I was going into it expecting poor content, but (not entirely) to my surprise I found that I enjoyed this VN.  Sure, it had a few flaws, but it was overall quite charming.  My only criticism would be about the pricing.  I bought it on sale for a little over $2, which I think is a much more reasonable price than the original simply because of the game's length.  My favorite part?  The artwork--the character artwork is beautiful.

Overall, True Lover's Knot is a disappointment.  While the concept is interesting, the game does not live up to the potential in it.  While I could forgive the fact that the background art and the character art don't always mesh well, the shallowness of the characters and the lack of gameplay options do the game in.  With such a small cast of characters, I expected much more depth and personality.  Two of the characters could be removed completely and not affect anything.  I also found Santi both extremely distasteful and rather creepy which leads into my other major problem with the game.  The lack of gameplay choices.  For example, I can't choose to avoid Santi all together and go on the tour with Lucas instead.  There's even a part where the choice to return to the cruise ship just cycles me through the same dialogue until I agree to spend the night with Santi.  I did appreciate the fact that I could choose not to end up with either of the love interests, but it wasn't enough to save the game for me, and because there are only three ending options, the replay value of the game is extremely limited.  The puzzles within the game also don't add much to the experience and are extremely repetitive   If you're looking for a a good visual novel style game, this isn't it.

This game is the definitive 4x title of this year.  It isn't the greatest 4x I've played, but it is far from the worst.
It feels like and plays like an RTS while having the same depth and variety expected for a 4x title.  The true enjoyment the game offers is in the sandbox and in the arms race and interactions you have with the generated galaxy.  At it's core it is a very simple game with a lot of variety.  Despite that, it is a very enjoyable experiance and can consume hours of your time.
I recommend this over every other 4x release of 2016.  If you like grand space strategy games.
Possitives:
- Real Time Space Battles with ships.
- Exploring feels like exploring.
- No hand holding outside of the tutorial tips
- Tutorial tips are helpful instead of patronising.
- AI is constrained by the same rules as the player and smart, instead of being mindlessly brutal and cheating like in most 4x or grand strategy games these days.
- Amasing music and atmosphere
Negatives:
- The game limits how many systems you can directly control.
- When an AI enemy declares war on you, you have little control over when peace is decided or if the enemy decides to accept your terms of their surrender.
Most negative reviews stem from people who seem to be apparently upset mostly about these two negatives or the fact that this game limits the ability for someone to declare a total war.  However, I can look past these glaring issues to see an otherwise mostly enjoyable experiance.
If you're looking for a 4x title which is a little more in depth but still simple in presentation and is a space empire building game, this is the best one on offer from 2016.  I am sure there are better games which preceded it and better games which will come out in the future though.  I don't consider it a must purchase despite myself enjoying it far more than other 4x titles from last year.
8/10

Binding of Isaac has provided me with one of the most frustrating, yet funnest and most addicting game experiences ever. This is the only game where you can defeat devil himself and die to a fly in the next room. Then swear to uninstall the game or swing at your computer but after 5 seconds proceed to play 10 more games.
Game has a lot of replay value because of its randomized features and several unlockable characters, multiple endings, tons of enemy types and items and big learning curve.
The music is superb, and the art style is charmingly disturbing as is the story.
Overall I recomend this game 100% to everyone who can get past the bizarre aesthetic and sometimes irritating rogue like elements.

Summary:
Take a basic but twisted concept with a lot (I mean a LOT) of shallow Christian references, mix it with straightforward top-down RPG/shooter gameplay, an crazy amount of potential upgrade combinations and increasingly more difficult (and unlockable) bosses, and you have an addictive game with the apparently infinite replayability that is the Binding of Isaac. I was recommended this a long time ago, got it and intially wasn't impressed. But I kept playing it at said recommender's insistence, and now it's one of my favourite games of all time.
The good:
Easy to get started.
So much content for a game that is simple in its setup. There's a reason why there's a Binding of Isaac wiki.
The music is good.
The game doesn't give a crap about being superbly balanced. Be prepared for some really hard runs where you do awfully, and then some really awesome runs where you're overpowered as ♥♥♥♥.
It's a game I can play in short-ish bursts (45 min to over an hour). As much as I also love more intense games that hook you for days at a time, I have a special place in my heart for good games that I can also play a full round of in my lunchbreak, then forget about for the rest of the day while I get work done.
It's just.. fun. That's why I play games!
The bad:
It doesn't get quite as good until after you unlock the first dozen or so upgrades in the game, although this is quick to do. This was why I wasn't initially impressed.
So badly optimised, especially on a Mac. I guess this is why Flash is being slowly phased out.
No save option, other than achievements and overall game completion - you do one run at a time. If you need to leave in the middle, prepare to leave the game running in the background, or abandon it.
And of course, Rebirth is now out and apparently makes this gem of a game pale in comparison.
Still, until Rebirth drops to 75% off (I'm a cheapskate), I'll be playing this for a long time yet.

One of the most disappointing VNs, and I have played a lot of them.
For the most part this is a kinetic novel (ie, only couple choices) and is of the otome variety (ie, you are a girl mainly choosing guys). I found the artwork very nice, but the backgrounds, which are photographs, are a bit lackluster. The story, or lack thereof, was bad. Some parts of the dialogue seem very rushed, especially the endings. I felt for a kinetic novel, it should have carried stronger themes and/or tried to invoke more feelings since there really are no decisions to make. The game takes about an hour to beat, maybe 90 minutes if you read slow.
On a technical level, there are some issues as noted by the other reviews as well. If you choose the "wrong" option in a dialogue choice the entire segment repeats, over and over again, until you choose the "right" option even though you didn't want to choose it. Pure laziness that they didn't want to write the text for an alternative path. The other major gripe is the "mini-game" that takes up probably half of your playing time. A very boring match-3 game with no redeeming qualities. As a tip, you can make moves that do not result in a match, so it is actually much easier once you realize that. Just keep on moving stuff around to get big chains along the edges.
In summary, short match-3 laden game with a cliched non-story story. Only positive is that the artwork is decent, otherwise run away from this title. Bad game that even if free I would recommend you pass on.

I didn't play WildStar when it came out in 2014, but I wanted to get into it when I recently heard it was gonna come on Steam. I've tried other MMOS, but they all felt empty and have bored me. However, I'm amazed on how this one, is the exception.

+The combat system is pretty good. Fast-placed and exciting.

+You can have your own house.

+The community is helpful, kind and friendly to new players.
+CUPCAKE!
Those are just a few pros of the game. I guarantee you there are even more.
As hard as I try to find a con, I can't really see one, but you don't loose anything with trying WildStar if you're into the MMORPG thing. You will have a good time.

Splatter - Blood Red Edition is a film-noir-influenced top-down zombie shooter with a crazy sense of humour.
You play Max, a hard-bitten guy interrupted in his house one night by his ringing doorbell. He answers the door, only to see a crazed zombie being gunned down by a soldier in the hallway. At the soldier's insistence, Max leaves the house and follows the soldier out onto the street, where he sees chaos has taken over the city. Picking up a pistol from a nearby dead body, Max proceeds to shoot his way through hordes of zombies in his escape from the city and onwards.
Splatter has great graphics. Everything is played from an overhead view and characters and enemies look quite small, but everything is nicely detailed and reasonably animated. The graphics remind me of a cross between early Grand Theft Autos (GTA 1 or 2) and the fantastic 90s adventure game from Empire, Dream Web.
Interspersed between the game levels are atmospheric graphic-novel-style cut scenes with completely over-the-top voice acting reading a typical film noir script. It's like an indie version of the first Max Payne, and it's alternately appalling and hilarious, or sometimes both at once.
Graphics options are fairly numerous and on my aging gaming laptop (first-gen i7 with 485m graphics) the game mostly runs well at full HD with everything at Max (except for shadows, which are 'nice' -- the highest setting caused weird flashing on my laptop), with only an occasional pause or slowdown in sections. In typical film noir style, it's almost always dark and raining, and it looks good.
Sound is mostly pretty good, although the standard pistol sounds decidedly unimpressive. There are appropriate groans and growls from the zombies and other creatures, and suitably squishy sounds when you shoot them.
The game has full voice acting that is very appropriate to the style. Some of it is awful and some of it is good, but it's all over the top and is mostly great fun. I laughed out loud in a few places at the absurdity of the script and the actors hamming it up. Assuming that it's what they were going for, it's very well done.
Splatter plays like most other top-down shooters: WASD moves your character, while mouse aims his weapon around him, and LMB fires your chosen weapon. RMB is used for tossing magnesium flares, which scare the zombies away, allowing you to break their charges and more easily pick them off. Weapons are easily changed to once collected just by scrolling the mouse wheel.
Enemies are very numerous and range from normal zombies, to overgrown super-zombies, weird crawly maggot things, annoying leaping creatures that like the shadows, and various other evil flesh eaters. A nice addition over other zombie shooters is that the zombie hordes charge at you when they notice you, reminding me of the infected from 28 Days Later; these are no shambling corpses!
The environment is mostly destructible, allowing you to use cars and other explodey things as booby traps for the unsuspecting hordes. Your pistol must be super powered, though, as one shot is usually enough to detonate even the strongest-looking vehicle parked on the side of the road.
The game keeps you playing with upgrades, which you can purchase at set points through the story by using cash collected from killing zombies. It doesn't make a whole lot of sense, but it works well at keeping the player interested, even if it does feel a little grindy. Weapon upgrades are definitely worthwhile, though, with the top-of-the-line pistol upgrade giving you bursts of magnesium-infused bullets that have a chance of causing your targets to flee for a short time.
Pros:
+ Great graphics
+ Silly script and humorously overdone voice acting
+ Good range of weapons and upgrades
+ Trading cards
+ Achievements, most of which are actually pretty satisfying to get
+ Great sense of humour ("It must be Art" Wtf!? This one made me laugh!)
+ Shooting up the scenery is fun, if a little unrealistic at times
Cons:
- Some grammar errors in the writing
- Some mispronunciations and not-so-great voice acting as well
- Some of the enemies really annoy me (but I suspect they're meant to, so it's not really a con)
Splatter - Blood Red Edition is a fun top-down zombie-and-weird-creature shooter with film-noir influences. It has a great sense of humour and doesn't take itself too seriously. Recommended for good fun and (mostly) mindless violence.

is a simplistic and entertaining top-down shooter with a graphic-noir theme. There isn’t much depth to the gameplay or storyline, but it is pleasantly addictive and has an engaging pace of progress that will suck you in. If you happen to have any real life friends, you can maybe have a bit of fun with those for a few hours. If you don't have friends, you also can play the horde mode solo and compete on leaderboards.

Despite being a little janky and very simple graphically, Art of Gravity does a nice job of wordlessly teaching and engaging you in 3D demolition puzzles that have little to do with gravity.

That being said, there are only maybe 5-10 puzzles that will take you more than a couple minutes to plan out. I had high hopes for a few of the achievements that sounded like they’d bring a second life into a few puzzles. However, the puzzles that do leave you with the option to use less orbs on them are usually really forgiving. You’ll bumped into each one without breaking a sweat.
Also, that damn jingle sound effect is back from Zenge and it still clips itself and is as cheesy as ever. Thankfully, you can disable the sfx and bgm if you’d rather listen to music or a podcast.
Can barely recommend it on its own, although it’s a killer deal as a part of the steam ‘Relaxing Puzzle Box’ Bundle which also includes several other games by Michal Pawlowski.
The game does hold a lot of potential however. A few more types of orbs or bricks or portals could create some more engaging puzzles. Sadly, like all the other Puzzle Box games, it ends rather quickly, has no steam workshop and is more of a tech demo/mini project that displays an interesting puzzle idea that the devs had.
Still, Art of Gravity is a good way to loosen up while mulling over some straightforward puzzles.

I love city-building, resource production games and this game fits nicely into that genre.  While it brings many interesting systems that are frequently overlooked in other games (including combat, magic, RPG elements, and world diplomacy), Hearthlands still feels too unbalanced at this point.  Neighboring nations ask for too much (even on Very Easy) and will invade and destroy your city on a whim.  Production chains are unclear and while there is plenty of information at your disposal, I never felt like goods were flowing like they should.  Recommended if on sale and you like this genre.  Not yet recommended otherwise.  I will keep playing and update review if I overlooked anything.
PROS
+ Adds interesting concepts to the city-builder genre including diplomacy, trade, and military
+ Many options for creating new games to your liking
+ Lots of spells and technologies to research and unlock
+ Rival countries and local monsters add much needed depth
CONS
- Graphics are plain and uninteresting
- Resource production is confusing and unclear
- Production chains are unbalanced; either never enough or always too much
- One wrong move and your entire city can be completely destroyed (frequent Rage Quits)
- I frequently experienced more frustration than fun
- Other games achieve this formula much better (Banished, Anno 1404, etc)

TL;DR: Texas Secession leads to Universal Domination.
The Interstellar Android Confederacy rose from the United Texas Protocol, with one thing in mind.
Power.
They built up their military, ships emerging from the humble spaceports like magic, having no need for petty diplomacy. Many empires attempted to overthrow the Confederacy, but we had the federation. Together, the Tuxkan Empire and a young upstart empire, formerly a vassal of the Gox-Gox Sovreignty, expanded and grew. The Sol de Tejas entente was expanding. However, our expansionist view resulted in secession. We refused to contribute to the Entente's navy any further, so the Texas Protocol decided to secede.
Under the rule of Consul Houston, we reformed ourselves as the Interstellar Android Confederacy. And we grew, we expanded, and we conquered. With General Thalos heading the Houston Engagement Fleet, we conquered, we grew, we survived, we prospered.
And we were immortal.
We  survived an onslaught of wars as the galaxy desperately fought the tides of change, humiliating those who dared to attack us, absorbing those who were weaker. Those who could saw no reason to try and stop us. After several years of conflicts, we had the most powerful navy of the galaxy. We maintained peace through force.
Then, there came the day that the universe stopped. Even Consul Houston, with 50 years of leadership under his belt, held his breath with apprehension. The formerly reserved empire whom we dubbed the Observers, had not stirred in several decades. They repaired a shipyard. Then two. Then ships, ancient in design, were being produced.
The sleeping giant had awoken. They were taking aim. Nobody could hide.
The Observers demanded that the Confederacy become servants, that we would deny ourselves freedom in exchange for safety.
The Confederacy thought differently, and a lone Observer ship, older than the our empire, came bearing tidings of war.
We took the initiative, we would not rest until the Observers were obliterated, and we sent in our Primary engagement fleet. Everything was going swimmingly, we had taken out a shipyard and conquered one of their three planets before the month was out, and then Admiral Thalos sent a transmission. He was under attack by a powerful fleet the likes of which had never been seen before, desperately trying to hold them off, to deny the inevetable. His once proud fleet was now a mere five ships, but he refused to retreat. We sent in our remaining Armada just as Thalos reported the Observer fleet had reached the system he was in. It was only a matter of time, he had lost two more ships in his most recent engagement, and the remaining three were extraordinarily damaged. He was making his final transmission, letting his crew say their goodbyes in the days before the fleet finally closed the distance, when a second group of ships warped in.
The Jacinto Armada had arrived, commanded by Unit 4/3, they were able to exterminate the Observer fleet with ruthles efficiency, leaving nothing but debris in their wake.
The Observers sent in another transmission, and surrendered. It was over, we had won.
For the next century, we had peace. We had expanded throughout the entire galaxy, our banner proudly flying over almost every system.
Then we heard subspace transmissions. Whole systems had been consumed by extradimensional invaders to the east, while a smaller empire had been entirely consumed by a swarm of spacefaring parasites. The future is certain, we shall prevail. The only question is when.

Alright, I just downloaded the Steam App, and I switched from the Standalone Client to the Steam app. On the Standalone Client I have done about 30 Days Non Stop. Done three different raids, played all the dungeons, multiple playstyles. tried various in game careers (Yes thats a thing, you can make a living in game by cooking, crafting and even playing the market)
and I am still doing scientist work constantly looking for bits and pieces of lore and what more things to explore and more.
This game, has made make take MMO's very seriously and had made me want to devote my time to it fully, and thats not something most games have achieved. The last game to do that was Dota 2, so this is a pretty big deal.
It has a very open playstyle and character path, you dont have to fight and fight for the entire end game. One thing I enjoy is what I call "Your own story" You can play how you like, become a chef, an armourer, a weaponsmith, an economist, a raider, a builder, and you can profit from that, or just make it a hobby. Whats controversial here is the amount of effort required. Some people want these things to be handed to them on a platter, I'm not sure myself, I worked hard for my cooking skills, I'm still working on them.
Moving on to combat. Pros
-Incredible Player Housing (This could be an entire game by itself). You can make almost anything; massive mansions, desert islands, floating treehouses... It's the best housing system in any game I've ever played.
-Fast Paced Action Combat (that's easy to understand). The game eases you into dodging and interrupting, so that by level 50 you're prepared for the bullet-hell like attacks of some of the later bosses.
-Each of the classes is unique and amazingly fun to play; even the old standbys like Warrior have a few unique twists to make them feel fresh. I recommend trying out the Medic; it's super easy to pick up, incredibly effective at both DPS and healing, and unlike any other MMO class I've played. The Spellslinger is also super iconic and fun.
-Epic Instanced Content (that's not impossible to get into). The game's dungeons and raids are challening, but not impossible, and feature massive set pieces, memorable bosses, and crazy mechanics.
-A Beautiful World: No gray and ugly plains here. No matter where you go on Nexus, you're bound to find something beautiful and bizarre.
-One of the best Transmog systems in the genre. Costumes are saved account wide, and you can create custom looks without regard to level or class.
-Fun Science-Fantasy Setting (Think if Borderlands and Star Wars had a baby with Firefly as a Wino Aunt)
-One of the best soundtracks I've ever heard.
-Mentoring system allows you to play with your lower leveled friends.
Cons
-Leveling can get repetitive. The early game is pretty varied, but after about level 20 characters are steadily funneled into a standard storyline, and there are very few alternative leveling paths.
-A lot of the solo level 50 content revolves around daily quests.
-Game relies on the traditional Two Faction model. At the time of this writing, the factions cannot communicate without a special addon, nor can they directly trade or team up. There are plans in place to change this, but it can be frustrating; especially if you feel seperated from friends, or forced to start over.
-At the time of this writing, faction population skews heavily toward Exile side, due to the immense popularity of the Aurin race and a lack of marketing toward the Dominion faction. Both sides are still very active, but Exiles are much more so.
-Early Exile Zones tend to be more exotic and detailed than their Dominion counterparts.
- While each zone is unique, beautiful, and memorable, the Eldan Exo Labs you frequently visit tend to look nearly identical.
-The game is poorly optimized, and may struggle on weaker hardware. If you have an AMD CPU, you will almost certainly face trouble as the game is not designed to run on multiple cores at once. Both NVidia and Radeon GPUs will work fine, though, provided they have enough power.
-Players with slow computers or internet connections will have difficulty engaging in the upper-tier content, as much of it is dependent on reaction time and visibility.
-Rewards for Expeditions, Adventures, and Dungeons are subpar compared to rewards from the much easier Arcterra content, though Expeditions are a good way to get gold and renown.
-The Rune Crafting System (which is used almost exclusively during the End Game) is weighed in such a way that it's more efficent to use microtransactions instead of gold to modify your equipment. This is alleviated somewhat by the fact that you can earn micro-transaction currency by playing the game (even if you don't subscribe) but it can get expensive, especially if you plan to raid. This is the only real Pay-To-Win element the game has.
Despire all of that, I still think Wildstar is worth a shot. The game is gorgeous, and the new cutscenes make it feel like you're playing a Science Fantasy Cartoon. The instanced content is super fun, even for someone like me (whose only prior raiding experience comes from City of Heroes! Not a game known for challenging group content). Expeditions (including the new Vault of the Archon) feel like you're staring in your own science fiction movie, and often feature unique mechanics that make the whole deal a touch more exciting than just killing enemies. Adventures are similarly game changing; often emulating games of other genres. Siege of Tempest Refuge is a Tower Defense, War of the Wilds is a MoBA or PVP Match, Crimelords of Whitevale is a crime drama, Malgrave Trail emulates a certain pioneering simulator, and Bay of Betrayal has you using Technopathy to infiltrate a transhumanist cult. Dungeons and Raids are more old school, but often feature complex mechanics that'll make you rethink how MMOs are supposed to work.
The thing that grabbed me the most, however, is housing. It is insanely detailed and easy to pick up, and you can create practically anything. Builders like Jabbit Tooth (D-Entity), Proxima Dust (D-Entity) and Katia Managan (E-Entity) consistently blow my mind with their creations. This focus on customization and creativity has also attracted a friendly roleplay community that have crafted some amazing storylines. Even if you're not that big of a raid person, the game provides you with the perfect framework for building your own story on Nexus.
If you've ever played an MMO, or are just curious about trying one out, I strongly recommend giving Wildstar a shot. Play it long enough to get through the early zones. Hop into an expedition, adventure, or dungeon. Take a tour of the housing plots. Even if you don't end up staying, you'll be glad you gave Nexus a visit.

Hexcells is a minimalist puzzle game that I like to think of as a combination of Minesweeper and Sudoku. A comparison that has probably been made elsewhere. Every level is basically the same. You’re presented with a variable number of cells with a number in the top right corner telling you how many blue cells there are in the puzzle. The challenge is figuring out which cells are blue and which are numbers. If you guess incorrectly, it’s counted as a mistake that will affect how many points you get at the end of a level. The numbers on or adjacent to cells are telling you how many blue cells are connected to them. It’s up to the player to figure out the pattern by examining the numbers. In general terms, if there are two unknown cells connected to a cell that has the number “2” on it, they’re both blue cells. There are several different mechanics used to confuse the player and make them logic out the solution. Upon completing a level, you’ll be rewarded with points that are used to unlock additional groups of levels. As such, this does requires you to complete most of the puzzles with a minimal amount of mistakes in order to progress forward.
The original Hexcells contains 30 puzzles and is the easiest of the three games. I would recommend playing this first just to get a feel of what each title will expect of you. However, it’s not required as each entry does a good job of explaining itself and gradually introduces you to the various mechanics.
Here’s the problem I have with the entire Hexcells series. It’s a pretty good puzzle experience, if you play it how it’s intended to be played. However, I feel that they have a problematic design flaw: all of the puzzles can be cheesily completed. If you’re stuck at a certain sequence, you can just click through the rest of the puzzle making as many mistakes as you like. (I had some puzzles at 50-60 mistakes). What about the points you would get from a near perfect completion? Well, once you nearly finish the puzzle, take a screenshot and then instantly replay the level with your own personal guide. It’s possible to win all three games this way without much effort on your part.
It’s a minimalist game so there really aren’t many settings to change. Since its running on the Unity engine, the Unity launcher menu pops up when you start the game every time. It allows you to change resolutions and turn fullscreen on/off. The graphics quality is set to beautiful and can’t be changed. However, I was able to play this on a basic, five year old laptop running Linux Mint and there was absolutely no trouble running it. Alternative keys can be changed here as well. Hexcells Infinite was the only game of the three that allows you to swap the left and right mouse button functions.
Overall, I think the Hexcells series is a decently executed puzzle idea with plenty of content. I take issue with the lack of anti-cheat but it's not enough to make it an anti-recommendation. (Thanks to a friend for making a case to change my mind on this). It’s a fun logic number puzzle series. And I did play the three games how it was intended too, with a few exceptions. I had quite a bit of fun deducing the my way through the levels and had several “aha!” moments despite it’s more casual nature. Additionally, it maintains a mellow and atmospheric experience that I can appreciate. While there is the less honorable part of myself thinking “you can just easily ‘cheat’ this game and not spend hours on it”, that doesn't disqualify it from being a decent puzzle game. So, if you can avoid cheating yourself, get the Hexcells series. But if you can’t restrain yourself from looking up help on even the slightest bit of challenge, I probably wouldn't get it. Otherwise, that's my thoughts on this series.

I was expecting a puzzle game of casual difficulty--something to pass the time while I chatted with friends--and that is what I found, but I failed to predict how complex and interesting could be without an intimidating difficulty curve.
What I certainly did not expect was the beautiful soundtrack.  Words alone are not enough to describe this.  Every tile you touch adds a pleasant echo of a note to the tranquil melodies singing you to sleep as you progress.  It's the most soothing and relaxing puzzle game I have ever played, each step as rewarding as suspenseful in mild strokes.  Not only that, but the level design is brilliant.  Start from multiple points and work your way through your own way, depending on which clues you find first.
You will especially love it if you have ever played a Picross game.  I highly recommend Hexcells and I shame myself for having taken so long to try it.  I have not been so tickled by puzzles like these since my old subscription to Games Magazine in the 90s.
Edit:  One small issue I should mention.  I could find no volume option other than to mute and the game was initially too loud for me.  If you're playing on Windows, right-click your volume on the taskbar and use the Volume Mixer, and this is easily remedied.
I swear, after 2 hours of play I was seeing blocks everywhere. Beats Oculus Rift any day of the week.

You guys, this game is adorable.
Splatter is a twin-stick zombie shooter in the vein of... hell, pick something. Your character embarks on an epic, rain-soaked journey from his living room to a mysterious government lab in search of the source of the mutant undead plague that has torn your city apart. On your quest you find a wide assortment of weapons, along with cash to upgrade them. The upgrade system is a particularly good one, allowing you multiple upgrades on a single weapon to turn it into an absurd all-in-one death-dealer.
There's a surprising amount of content in each of the game's lengthy levels. Several have NPCs you can interact with, as well as optional sidequests for additional weapons and ammo. Some are centered around clever setpieces like a subway ride or a thresher driving sequence. Then there are additional secrets to find like armor upgrades and golden gun parts that I'm not clear on the purpose of, but by now it should be clear that there's plenty to do in the game's dozen or so open levels. Worth mentioning also that, aside from the gory action, there are some genuinely tense sections thanks to the lighting and encounter design in some of the darkened buildings and narrow corridors.
What makes this game adorable is the presentation. Your "hero" is a fedora-wearing trenchcoat-clad iconoclast who can't help but be a condescending♥♥♥♥♥♥to everyone he meets. I can't overstate this... in the cutscene where you arrive at the shopping mall, he monologues about how the place once attracted a different mindless herd of consumers. You're essentially playing the EUPHORIC guy unironically and it makes the game like ten times funnier than it should be. I honestly can't tell if it's a giant parody or if you're supposed to be taking his gravelly fussing seriously, but either way it elevates the game from bargain-basement shooter to something special. Coupled with the solid gameplay, graphics, and level design, Splatter proved to be an unexpected gem.

In Hearthlands, you build a town. You place buildings, build paths and after a short while, settelers arrive. I reviewed this game when it was in Early Access with a negative review (getting 31 upvotes and 13 downvotes), and now, after thorough testing after its release, I'm giving it a (slightly less) negative review.
WHAT'S STILL BROKEN :
* Combat -- Can't control units directly, can't retreat, can't pinpoint attacks, your soldiers will attack completely uninvolved enemies during a battle (even if they're on the other side of the map), enemies sometimes spawn "underneath" your units and you can't do attack while being attacked.
* Economy -- Immigration is broken for the "Western" culture at sufficiently high levels of population, path-finding and storage with its limits are just too dumb that you may need half of all land for "haulers".
* International Relations -- Enemies can burn down your cities, but you only get the option of sending a punitive expedition without actually engaging in combat.
WHAT I LIKE :
* GOOD ECONOMICS/WAR/MAGIC: In any economy-management-with-warfare game, I want to be able to focus on the economy, then get bored, and go into war, reaclimate the economy of the new territory, and repeat.  This works brilliantly with this game, with an extra alternate focus: focus on your magic, then run out of magic points.  The Settlers series is similarly enjoyable in this fashion.
* GOOD ECONOMIC PLANNING: In the chain of any economic needs (i.e., turnips to pigs to leather to boots), you can find out what producers/manufacturers were glutted and have an exact reason for it (i.e., shortage of goods, shortage of land, *sometimes* no storage).
* GOOD PATHFINDING: In indirect economic management systems, there's always the trouble of storehouses cluttered with goods.  If this happens, the transit system merely takes resources from producers (like lumber) to manufacturers (like the sawmill) without the intermediate storehouse.
WHAT I DIDN'T LIKE :
* RIGID COMBAT: This is still sort'a true.  If my villagers are being mobbed to death by goblins, and I have my army attack, if they see a gigantic spider nest on the way, they'll throw in a molotov cocktail into it just for fun.  (Sigh, retreat still doesn't work, and sometimes spawned enemies spawn underneath buildings or units, where they attack without risk, and archers attack at the most distant range only, causing a backup of huge amounts of archers that can't advance because they're blocked by other archers, etc..)
* TRADE WAS ODD: It required multiple configs at "nation" level and at the "building" level of markets.  This has totally been simplified.
WHAT I DON'T LIKE NOW :
* Conquering enemies doesn't actually create a combat scenario.  You pick units, send them to attack, and then hear back "Success!" or "Failure!", which is very different from the actual combat in your first city map where you battle graveyards and ghosts.  My achievement for "Defeat the Dragon" was accomplished without anything so much as a "Success!" message after assigning units to attack.
* In line with the above, it seems like the dev team saw the biggest problems in the Early Access, tackled them in the simplest and most direct way (technically correct), and then left the bigger, empire-management-within-a-city-management-game issues aside.
With all that considered -- I say, good game.

Fun game reminiscent of the old Impressions Games city-building series, adding a few extra things like Research, Spells and different nations/factions/tribes? to pick from, each with their own pros, cons and economy.
The tutorial is a lengthy but rather narrow overview of the gameplay/objectives, I feel it could be worked on a little bit as newer players and those unfamiliar with the likes of Pharaoh, Caesar et al, will finish it only to get steamrolled in the actual match by hostile neighbours or a failed attack on a mob spawn. Yes, there is a learning curve and the game will remind you of that during your first matches, but if you persevere there is a great sense of accomplishment from getting your little hamlet to a bustling empire.
Each nation has a playstyle (due to economic differences and buffs/penalties) and I suggest you try each of them before you decide on which one you feel most comfortable with to strengthen your strategy with it before trying more "challenging" ones.
Matches will often start with players scattered in a continent. Each player is confined to a set area littered with hostile mobs and resources. You must develop your economy and military, and protect your town from goblins, invaders and the occasional undead. There's no direct control over population or units. Players only interact with each other through trade, requests for goods and invasions. By players I mean AI, as there is no Multiplayer mode.
Sound is ok, the songs are MIDI-esque but certainly fitting.
The graphics are ok and they do a good job of supporting the fantasy setting along with the music.
The game is frequently updated and I look forward to update this review as development goes on.
If you know IG's series and have an itch for something similar, you might want to take a look at this game, otherwise I think it might take you a while to get into the game to really enjoy it.
I can't say it is bad, but it is certainly not for everyone. I liked it, tho and hope to see it grow into something of an indie spiritual successor to Pharaoh.

Post launch review (addendum to previous comments):
Hearthlands has finally left Early Access and it gained a few extra things:
- 12 mission campaign, which will guide you through the different aspects of getting started, providing for your population, setting up industry and military, and meeting the different nations and their specific production chains and units.
- One extra song that fits into the soundtrack and is good.
- Some quality of life improvements here and there (mostly UI stuff).
I'll say the only thing I still struggle to do is to effectively measure my own military strength as I've had squads (with a max total of 8 units each) wiped out by wolves' dens in the wilderness. With +1/+1 upgrades.
Other than that the gameplay feels on par with IG's flagship titles (no Religion, Fires or Collapsing Buildings tho - I can do without the last one tbh), it's relatively easy to get going once you get used to the nation you are playing as, but you can still screw up enough to warrant a restart (haven't even been close to running out of gold, it's more of a failure to judge when my units are enough to clear the map of hostiles). Also, combat is tricky sometimes in terms of positioning and aggroing, since you have no control over either.
While these things may take something away from the game, they're not enough to not have fun with Hearthlands. The dev team is only 2 guys (I think?), but they're passionate about their project and actively update and improve things here and there.
It's a fine game and if you played Pharaoh, Zeus or Caesar, take it for a spin.

On one hand, the idea of researching multiple techs in dissparate area is a great idea, not only forcing the player to build infestructure in all three areas, it also adds depth in how the player must choose his priorities in three lists, instead of just one. The player can choose to focus on one of them, or try to balence all three, each with their own array of benifits, so some empires will need some trees more than others. However, while games like have a complete skill tree for all three areas, stellaris instead decides to just give you a set of three or four technologies picked from your pile of possible techs to research. There is no way to plan ahead or even to check what postrequisets there are. Just what you are delt each time.

It's a strange, yet frustrating Galexy

Much like on other games of this type, there is a variety of hospitable and inhospitable planets, with the former commong a number of different biomes. While you can only settle some of them at the begging, more become availible with technology(Which, again, is delt randomly). However, there are waaaaay to few habitable planets, and even fewer that you can actually settle in the early game. Other than settling planets, you can also claim territory by building fronteir outposts, which are very expensive. And remember: you can only build in terrirtory you have actually claimed with one of these two structures. This is combined with how the inhopitable planets that produce resources are not as common as they should be, and when they do come up, they are not very productive.This, combined with the AI(which I will get to in a bit), making expansion and resource collection way to difficult.

Bits of S@@t

The resourse system is far too simplisic. You really only have three: influence, minerals, and energy(credits). You minerals and energy with buildings, energy keeps things running, minerals build new crap. The influence system is kind of nice, since it can be used for a number of things, and actaully feels inherently valuable. Yes, I now there are strategic resourses, but in my time with the game, I found barely any.

The AI is swift and brutal

All the other stuff is not that bad, and even if they were the only issues, I would probably get a lot more fun out of it.. But, they have their effets compounded here. Even on low difficulty, the AI is way to fast. By the time you build your third outpost, they will already have a military you could not possibly compete with. In less you are lucky they will claim far more territory(and therefore power) from the player. They will quickly encircle you. You say"don't you just need to play smart and competitive to survive." to which I say,

  • Research new ship components, while also researching better buildings, researching policies and other administrative technologies, while at the time researching all the anomolies and other s$$t you encounter. Unless you are insanly luck, you will never get the tech you need at the right time.
  • You need to collet all the resourses all at once. There is no "first priority." They are ALL first priority. You need a ton of preatty much everything right at the start, and it needs to constantly grow as well.
  • Due to the two above, your competitors will not only grab far more territor, they will basicly encircle you, realize you are militarily week, and then conquer you.
    • Conclusion

    Look, I don't hate paradox. I love their games (yes, even Victoria). But I feel their expulsion into the 4X gener just did not pan out. That being said, if this still looks interesting, and are willing to fight the abusively high difficulty curve, there is probably a preatty great game underneath.
Tricky and fun building/management game with surprising complexity to the resource and production chains. Could really do with a bigger map and world though, the lack of scope is a letdown.

Stellaris is the most exciting 4x space game in years.
By "exciting" I'm not talking about gameplay (although  your heart starts pumping out of your chest when a big, nasty federation declares war on you...);  what I mean is that Stellaris has elements  of space 4x like no other games in this genre, and it includes genre twists and seeds for future development that are even more exciting.
First, let's talk about what Stellaris is
.  This is not a Galactic Civ or Masters of Orion quick "civ building" game.  Yes, you do explore space, build your empire, and develop new technologies--but you don't blast off and land, become a colonizing machine, and spread out as fast as possible, fighting anyone in your way.  This is more of a marathon game, and a bit more of a brain-burner.  In Stellaris you also do not control battles (like a RTS games) or even have influence over battle progress (like Endless Space);  Stellaris combat is more like Paradox's Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis:  you design your ships, build as many as you can, then send them into the fray--and pray.  (Yes, deathstacking is a valid strategy if you can afford it!)
So what
Stellaris?  A "grand strategy" game--meaning you take the long view from 10,000 feet, fiddling with numbers and ideas over a long haul, instead of rolling up your sleeves and getting your hands dirty with each little unit and detail.   You start with one planet and system, then explore the galaxy, expanding--sometimes verrry slowly--struggling with your neighbors' opinions and sometimes their ships--but more often, struggling with your economy, with your research output, with the happiness of your people, etc.
So far, this probably sounds like the perfect 4x game for accountants, right?  But Stallaris makes this interior struggle of improving your economy and fleet and population growth and happiness (etc.) challenging and interesting.  Especially because you play a distinct alien race with distinct cultural beliefs. And you are surrounded by dozens of other alien races, each with their own agendas (unlike Galactic Civ, for example, which has--what?--six races?  Eight?)  And you can create your own race and culture, too.  The game also breaks up a bit of the "numbers game" by including quests you complete from survey ship missions, too.
So it's a nice game--but there's more.  It includes new ideas other space 4x games do not.  Edicts and policies is a great example:  these policies help either a planet or your entire empire, enforcing your ideas to further your goals.  Would slavery of minority races in your empire help your mineral output?  Okay, then do it--but face the stiff opinion of other civs and the possibility of revolt.  Want to encourage free thought so your research moves faster?  Okay, do it--but all those "free thinker" types might not love your society and just might ignore your civ's core beliefs.  There are many of these edicts and policies, and your research can even unlock more.
Also, you cannot micromanage.  It is not allowed.  This is a grand strategy game and you are the emperor--and the emperor never controls every little thing.  So you only get to fiddle with a handful of planets directly, then have to appoint governors to oversee your holdings ("sectors").  This feudal system works well, both because it helps with your task load and because the frustration it sometimes brings mimics what true leadership is like ("Are you SERIOUS?  What are they DOING in Gamma Sector? Aargh!")
Stellaris innovates in other areas, too.  For example...
To sum up, and as you can see, I think Stellaris is a truly interesting game.  Gameplay is fascinating and satisfying, and as of December 2016 I easily recommend it.
That being said, I am even more excited about its future development.  There are a few weaker spots in the game...
I hopped on the Stellaris "developer's diary," just to check it out, and was immediately thrilled by what they were saying (as of this writing, they were including a culture tree for "tall" civs, much like the traditions paths in Civ V)   And as of now, they are offering it through free patches, not $$$ DLCs, which is refreshing!
I am very hopeful that this "good" game will become absolutely "great" as the months and years roll by.

Fun game but it becomes a grind at the end, esp when its two big alliances.
