It's an odd way to start a video game review, but I'm convinced NieR: Automata ought to be viewed as an artistic achievement and perhaps even a manifesto. Unquestionably, it is a love letter to practically every genre of video game--and this particular game demonstrates an unshakable confidence in a certain idea: that video games may exist as an art form without sacrificing any of the sheer joy that comes with playing a great game.
The problem with many "artistic" video games is that the people creating those games don't understand how to properly tell a story in this kind of medium. Developers who want their games to be viewed as an artistic accomplishment try making games the same way as somebody would make a novel, a film, a comic book or a TV series. Video games, of course, are none of these, nor do they follow the same rules. The medium that video games could maybe be best connected to is a choose-your-own-adventure novel, and the two forms are still distant cousins at best--ones who haven't really spoken to each other since the early '90s, at that.
Once video games began to attract big budgets, game companies tried to make games follow the same conventions as big-budget movies and TV shows. Worse yet, game companies tried to make games that could serve as good art, but in doing so imposed the rules of movies and television; they imposed rules in a medium which so defied them that an Italian plumber could quite easily serve as a superhero without any supernatural accident (like Spiderman), unique birthright (Superman) or any fortunate series of prior events whatsoever--and this simple plumber mascot's image would go on to sell hundreds of millions of games over recent decades because the company who created it understood the unique freedom of the medium.
What Yoko Taro and Platinum Games apparently never lost sight of while making NieR: Automata is that the best way to tell a story through a video game is by no longer imitating television and film. The video game is its own art form and this art form has found its own voice. Unlike most major forms of media--though television is a debatable point here--video games have only ever existed in the postmodern era, and are perhaps the best vehicle to express postmodern ideas and running themes, such as:
-fragmentation, especially of the self.
-subverting the search for meaning.
-black humor and irony.
-magical realism.
-temporal distortion.
-poioumena (the process of creation).
-asking huge questions without an expectation of big--or even coherent--answers in return.
-transhumanism.
Playing the game, you might notice that NieR hits every single one of these ideas over and over again. Even as it piles cliche after cliche on its surface--zombies? robots? adam and eve? aliens? post-apocalyptic future? sure, why not all of them!--there runs a game as deep as a sword plunged through an android's heart. And this, perhaps, is where the strongest case can be made for this particular game being not only one of the great games of 2017, but being one of 2017's great works of art. NieR: Automata starts with ideas that we all thought had been explored as much as they ever could, yet still manages to discover a way to breathe new life into them.
Even more remarkably, it does this in a way that could only have worked as a video game.
So, go on. Go have some fun with the 26 different endings.

I can't recommend this game enough. The PC port is a bit wonky, with some driver issues for AMD gpus and resolution issues on all systems, but this game is worth it if you have the patience to deal with looking for fixes and workarounds. The combat is smooth and satisfying, with skills that can be modified to suit your preferred play style and weapons that can be swapped around to alter your combos and movesets. The open world is a little small, but that works to the game's benefit as it becomes much easier to memorize the layout of the areas. The game also switches seamlessly between standard open-world action-rpg segments, 2d side-scrolling segments, and top down twin-stick shooter segments. Last but certaintly not least is the story. In fact, the story is damn near the most compelling part of this game in my opinion. I won't spoil anything here, but the full story requires multiple playthroughs, each of which adds new layers of information and context to the story and the characters in the game. I highly encourage you to experience the emotional roller coaster of Nier: Automata's story.

I enjoy the combat, but that is about as far as it goes for me. The UI, inventory system, quest structure, and short playtime are my biggest quips. The game is painfully short, which is a shame considering how fun it can be. This is justified in the idea that you can play the game over and over again and each time its slightly different, and you achieve a different ending. Personally, I have no interest in playing a game Ive already finished numerous times to see a few new things. I just dont get how that would be something anyone would WANT to do. The different ending and a few new side quests arent enough to renew my interest. Mainly because the side quests Ive encountered are terribly mediocre. The majority seem to be time trials/minigames where you do some simple activity like running toward a finish line or killing X amount of robots in X amount of time. All of which are unimaginative and shallow, and they only get more difficult, that is the only difference for each stage of those quests. Some of the story quests are crap too. Go ask the resistence leader about this. Go ask the robot mayor about that. Go back and ask the leader about this other thing. Fetch quests, and go here and collect this quests. I was not a fan of backtracking to a previous zone simply to ask someone about a plot point. I mean what they dont have phones in the future? Cant they just contact those people over radio like you do with Yorha operators? It seems like they stuff those boring parts in just to buffer and fill the game to make the playtime longer. Considering how short it is, and the amount of filler quests, the game ends up seeming rushed and feeling a little light. But I can say that I am glad they didnt make everything a crap fest like Andromeda, where 90% of all the quests are mind numbingly boring and mundane tasks. A lot of the quests in this game ARE great and fast paced. There are some great bosses and moments. There are also some very interesting plot points, and ideas like can androids like 2b and 9s have feelings and how would they react to various scenarios. Its also awesome how 2b and 9s interact. But since they are mostly emotionless androids, it also means that they are sadly boring and shallow characters. They have no depth, fittingly. Yes I know they are basically robots but that doesnt change the fact that they are one dimensional black and white characters that are extremely unoriginal. As fascinating as the idea of a robot pondering emotion is, its been done SO MANY times, and its somewhat of a cliche now. It is still an interesting concept despite the unoriginality.
Overall the game is a lot of fun, and has great moments. But for $60 it was definately not worth it for me. I am no fan of hack and slash beat em up games though. I heard that this was an RPG of sorts so I got it, but sadly there isnt much RPG stuff in the game at all. The game is not crap, its a solid 7/10, but for myself personally, the $60 would have been better spent on a game that would hold my attention and interest longer than a mere 20 hours.

So you go through the game making new sectors that you can not maximize. Next is other races. The programmers have gone out of their way to every other race a pain in the rump to deal with. Even the cavemen you meet on a far off moon will be problematic. If you make them slaves, it makes someone upset, if you make them citizens, they want indipendence and will revolt.  It is virtually impossible to just kill them off. Actual  opponents are far worse. At the begining of each war you must declare the war objectives to give the opponent a chance to respond to your demands and prepare for them. You then score points as you succeed. Should you kill off every soul on a planet and land 6 armies there, it still isnt yours untill the opponent is forced to conceed it is yours through treaties based on your warscore. There is a limit to what you can win through war, so a large territory might take you 5 wars to win it all even though you killed every ship and station in their empire 4 times over. 50 hours in and I just cant bring myself to put up with all the headaches and stupidity in this game.

Not often is it that a new innovative game using a simple concept lands on my lap.  Much to the nature that was
, you'll be introduced to new concepts through simple puzzles before being thrust into some of the more advanced puzzles.  That said, I originally thought that
was going to be a pretentious art game.  However, I was pleasantly surprised when I saw what
had to offer.
In your arsenal are white balls (the weakest), red balls (which are more durable and stronger), and blue balls (which phase through all blocks in its bath and can destroy glass).  Against you are white blocks (weak), red blocks (strong), path balls (which spit out balls in directional paths after being struck), and teleportation balls (which are green), which must ALL be destroyed..and are occassionally surrounded by glass.
There are 75 levels and most of the puzzles.  Again, they are mostly simple, though there are a few that will have you scratching your head as you ponder about the solution.  You'll be able to figure out the solution, though...if you give each puzzle enough time.  A single playthrough ended up taking me 2 hours, though each playthrough now may take much less time.
If I have any complaints about
, it's that the replayability is low.  For only $1, you'll find approximately 2 hours worth of gameplay...about the length of Portal.  It's nice to see cubes explode, but like with most puzzle games, you'll figure out the solutions and have less reason to come back to it...unless you want to relive a relaxing puzzle game, that is.
Do I recommend
?  To be honest, I'd say that for asking price, it's worth it.  Though if you want to wait for a sale when this game is discounted, I wouldn't blame you for it, especially since it's essentially 50 cents per hour.  If you're looking for a casual puzzle game with a new, but simple concept involving balls, trajectory, and gravity, I'd say to consider giving this game a try.

Puzzle games on Steam whether they’re in 2D or full 3D, shall always represent the much needed break from narrative-based titles. Those games that like to focus on more things at once, tend to stress gamers to a certain degree. And if you test them out + write about them on a regular basis like I do, well, you definitely need gaming’s equivalent of a pause. Without racing towards the other extreme: casual, mobile “games”. Irony has it, that Art of Gravity is also on mobile platforms, yet it cannot share the shame of any pathetic cash grabs as it sadly has to share space with them on smartphones or tablets. Unless you buy the PC version, of course.
Lucky for us Steam gamers, we have literally hundreds of options to choose from. The one I’m reviewing today, is among the better ones on the Store and its small price tag, really doesn’t do this game justice. On both PC and iOS, Art of Gravity’s asking price is still one single buck. Its developer/publisher is by no means, a newcomer. Hamster On Coke Games (creative title, I know) have already graced gamers with other affordable brain teasers such as, Hook, Zenge or klocki.
The story in Art Of Gravity features the complex system adopted primarily by puzzle games. No story here, buddy! What, you really expected a plotline to these abstract & physics-based gameplay mechanics? It plays perfectly well without needing so much as a flimsy explanation or context. Not even a tutorial and this slightly annoyed me. Nonetheless, I don’t blame the devs for wanting players to dive right into the action though. Art Of Gravity has so many levels of various length in terms of completion time, that you won’t feel left out or bored. As with any similar titles from this genre, playing in short gaming sessions is the rule of thumb.
If you played enough Steam indie titles so far, you’ll recognise Art of Gravity as being Unity-powered, right from its launch menu. What’s a certainty to me in such fortunate cases, is the stability which Unity Engine provides to all titles which feature its assets. While it isn’t by any means a pretentious game, Art of Gravity does looks great and I really enjoyed its minimal looks mixed with the voxel-style. You won’t have any trouble running this title, even on an older PC or low-end laptop.
The soundtrack is severely limited but the sound effects are balancing that issue out, at least partially. I’d still recommend you listen to any tracks you might prefer and simply mute the repetitive tunes from in-game. Your choice, as always.
Art Of Gravity might lack a story or sound diversity, yet its gameplay is the perfect combination of eye candy and seemingly-simple puzzle design. I assure you that this is not the case. Sporting 75 levels of increasing complexity, you’ll definitely learn to play efficiently as you spend more time with it. The dev team prides itself on the fact that players are left to discover the gameplay mechanics by themselves. I guess, it’s part of the charm. Even the title screen appears after you’ve complete the first level quite out of the blue. Or purple to be more exact.
Colors play an important role and are used to distinguish between the several types of “materials” you’ll need to break apart with the balls you control. The spheres in question can be set on predetermined trajectories (collision courses, more likely) and Art of Gravity’s ultimate goal is to smash through the colored blocks, until they crumble to small pieces which fall from suspension. I might have phrased this more complicated than it truly is. In any case, it won’t be straightforward since various “walls” or block types can take multiple ball collisions until they are finally crumbling.
The bonus objective on some levels (and prerequisite for unlocking some of the game’s Achievements) is to crush all the blocks with as few balls as possible. You’ll be saving only one, in most cases. And even then it shall take some creative thinking, not to mention patience. You probably knew already, that puzzle games shouldn’t be treated with haste. Half of the fun is just the part where you figure them out. The rest is reserved, just for watching it play out. Seeing those small, colored pixels crumble and fall from considerable height, it reminded me of the late Lionhead Studios’ Black & White 2 logo.
Sad pandas right now, eh? Much like the (proper) god game genre itself, interactive logos are also a thing of the past.
Art Of Gravity wasn’t discounted so far, mainly because it is more than decently priced. If you’re still uncertain, wait  for a bundle offer perhaps. I do hope they shall surface for this title eventually. For now, collectors shall have to contend with Steam Achievements.

Ok now for stuff I don't like this game.
It's simply horrid. you turn if off immediately. There is this chicken noise also that chimes every 5 seconds, making you pull your hair out, especially if you're wearing headphones.
First, there is a goblin that takes a beeline path from his base to yours. The same exact path every time. At first you have to chase him with the couple troops you can muster, but then you just end up placing a tower in his path to destroy him. Next, a sewer opens up in some random spot near your town, and 3 jelly monsters pop out of it. You just park your troops on top of this to stop them. But since everything is on 5 minute timers, you just leave some troops on top of this forever and let them level up. Then unless you pay out the nose to the other factions demanding constant crap from you, they will eventually attack. This isn't much of an issue though, because they just show up on the edge of the map and stand there until you can get around to killing them. Or you can just leave them out there and completely ignore.
After you raise an army, you think "Hey I should go attack my enemies". So you pull up the combat screen, say which enemy you want to atatck, how many troops you want to send, and then receive a message you lost. You don't actually get to see the battle or know how you lost, you just lose. It does say the power level of the enemy to be "35" and mine to be "65", but how many troops you need to send after a level 35 enemy or why you even lost is a mystery.  I can conceed that perhaps if I played long enough to get to power level 300, it may be possible to beat a level 35 enemy, but not seeing battle or anything other than "you lost" is kinda a turn off and not much fun. Plus you can only have 10 (I think) total squads, and I was at the max. But perhaps you can send in only expensive horseman to win and not a a mix or archers, axeman, and pikeys like I did. But honestly it was so infuriating sending my entire army in to squash an enemy and just getting a message "you lose", I never actually attempted it a 2nd time. I just never saw the point.
Then a troll spawns on the map and starts killing your new arrivals as they walk right by his hole and you think "Okay, now it's on!". Did I mention there is only 4 troop types? You send the troops in and attack the troll. you notice one guy getting pummeled is an archer and maybe he should retreat. Nope can't move him. Hey I should have my swordman form a defensive line in front of the archers. Nope, everyone just stays in some ramdom cluster jumble, zero control. You basically just watch it unfold and do nothing.
Now this is where you would expect the game to shine but sadly it doesn't. You quickly learn that you need to be around metal, and you need to get rank 3 mining (underground) before you exhaust the metal or you will never get any more, ever. Then you basically err on the side of caution and stash as much food and wood away as you can while slowly building up commodities like boots and pillows. There was a couple others, but I cant recal. oh yeah chairs! There aren't a lot of options. If you do get a surplus of anything, you just sell it off, but the interface is so clunky and tedious, it's usually easier to just toss up more storage as you will eventually need the goods. Magicite stared at me from the steam page for months before I grudgingly tried it on a hunch. I found a game that was pretty, fluid, simple, and fun.
The permadeath works - it's not lame. Every death or two gives you more hats, classes, or ideas on how to progress. Instead of being a burden, the permadeath acts as a way for you to clean the slate and do better. It's healthy.
The game lasted me around 15 hours. I beat the boss multiple times, each taking me around 20 minutes (i think). Eventually you get used to how the enemies work, and the game becomes an exercise in muscle memory. Unlike similar games (like rogue legacy), this muscle memory doesn't get challenged very much. It won't put you into situations where 3-4 enemies with different powers are spewing them all at once, and you have to navigate the world to defeat them. Instead, magicite tests your patience. You have to identify each enemy and be careful with them - because regaining health is difficult. By the end of the game you'll be taking enemies out at range more often than not, because you won't be finding enough potion materials to heal yourself. Only one or two equipment/hat/trait/skill combinations can keep you healed, and even then it's tiresome and slow to heal to full (notably, the ice queen hat, clairvoyance skill, and high MAG).
After all this invested time, my big gripe is that melee is just too important. The three different general paths (melee, archer, magic) are fun and play differently, but it always boils down to using your sword. No matter how you build, the sword is the only ifinite source of damage; your magic will run out fast and regen slow, and your arrows compete with armor for crafting materials. So it feels a bit like the magic/archer classes are more work than they're worth. Even with the right skills and playstyle, it doesn't usually feel like they're really worth it.
After unlocking most of the items, hats, and races, I think i'm done with it. But at this price, 15 hours of gameplay for $10 was pretty reasonable.

Oh my god, this game is SO SLOW. Your ship moves at an absolute crawl. I know there are boosters to get later, but two hours of primarily waiting while autopilot drifts forward for minutes is absolutely mind-numbing.
Also, the menu controls are terrible. You can't navigate the menu with a controller, so you HAVE to use a mouse, but (at the very least) the mining mini-game is impossible with the mouse, and you're much better off with a controller. There's no one or the other, you're forced to switch between the two constantly, and there's no in-game tutorial for the controller, only a reference map.
On top of that, the combat is little more than a game of chicken or chase - you don't move fast enough to evade shots, and your hitbox is gigantic, filling half the screen. Your only option is to try to get behind whoever is shooting at you, ensuring that you will be taking constant damage in battles with more than one other enemy.
In short, this game is painfully slow, has a messy interface and the plot is paper-thin. Do yourself a favour and go buy Freelancer instead.

While I recommend this game overall, unfortunately it is a huge step back from The Lost Crown and the previous two Dark Fall titles in a number of ways. While it is most similar to the first Dark Fall: The Journal in both tone and setting, with of course being a graphical leap over the original, it lacks the series and its spin off's(The Lost Crown) rich lore, notably in its lack of virtually any supporting flavor text which added so much to the series aside from scattered newspaper clippings. The other titles all had a novel's worth of extra materials that added to the stories. What's left is a point and click stumble through a rehash of the Dowerton Train Station and Hotel that we already explored long ago. And with the cumbersome method of panning and up and down, a very tedious stumble at that. Several times now I've had to check a guide on where I went wrong only to find I didn't pan up at one overly specific spot. In addition the Penumbra/Amnesia style mouse interaction with some puzzles is clunky to say the least, and not even casually hinted at. It can be quite difficult to intuit where exactly you are supposed to move the stupid mouse to get a reaction, or you find yourself clicking things to no avail only to find you were supposed to drag them to the side(spark plugs...) despite it not really making sense to do so.
Putting aside these design and technical issues, the game still stands as a great little horror adventure title to play through. It is atmospheric and has a few nice jump scare scenes and a continuation of the Dark Fall storyline is always a good thing.

This is a fun game for those who like the grand strategy genre of games. For those who dont care for them, or want to ease into them to see if they like them, this probably isnt the game for you.
The game shows its age in 2016, but having just got it on sale with Victoria 2, for only a dollar in a bundle, I thought Id give it a try. Now I wish I had found this game when it released, well over a decade ago judging by its win XP requirement.
The interface is clunky, to put it lightly. There is no manual (except online), so be prepared to do a lot of trial and error, and wondering about what stuff actually does.
The graphics are dated and sprited based, but manageable.
The AI is actually pretty good, and will present a very strong challenge to any new player on below normal settings.
A single campaign can take more than 40 hours to complete, to get through just 100 years, day by day. This is one of those games where you NEED to be into the genre to find it pleasurable or youll end up quiting very, very fast.
Be prepared to micro manage.
Some tips:
First, if you have windows 10, go to the executable and set compatibility mode to Win XP SP2. Not 3. SP 2. Otherwise the game crash. If you are asked to install direct 3D, just say yes, otherwise the game wont run. Second, if running win10, the game may crash on shutdown, or reloading a save after you have already been in a game, exited to main menu, and then tried to load the game again. Due to this youll lose all recorded hours you played the game (as recorded by steam) if it crashes on shutdown. I have about 60 hours, but crashed twice on shutdown after 2 very long sessions.
Do not let the computer run your trading, ever. Set it up manually.
The windows that pop up, you can right click them, and select when and how they pop up. Turn off spam like third party diplomatic deals, railroad completions, etc, or it gets very frustrating, very fast.
If you lack manpower and wonder why, it means you need to convert some farmers into soldiers. Your soldier pop is low.
Starting off in Europe is going to be tough. There are a billion tiny provinces everywhere and the user interface is not very good at sorting out useful information for you at a glance. The internet Ive seen recommends Brazil as a good newbie nation. I had decided to go with Prussia, and it was a tough learning curve, but can be exciting if you like a challenge right off the bat.
This website:
will explain everything about the games mechanics, so have it handy when you have a question.

+ Balance; I harp a lot on balance in many of my reviews because it is important to me. This game has great balance. You can pick up any Champion and do well as long as you know how to play them, and no one Champion has a straightforward advantage.
+Visuals; Whileit may not be as appealing as Overwatch, it's a good looking game nonetheless.
+ Optimization; even on max settings, this game can stick a solid 30 FPS on my absolute potato of a computer. Any half decent rig will have no trouble running this thing.
+ Gameplay; Gameplay is fluid and teamwork oriented. If you don't work as a team or play your role properly, your team won't do well.
Mixed Feelings:
+/- In-game Shop: Now, I'm not talking about the cosmetics shop or the the loot chest shop (which frankly, I don't know how I feel about either), I'm talking about the shop while you're actually playing the game. For new players, it will seem confusing as all hell. For people who have played MOBA's like SMITE or League of Legends, you will understand the gist of it. The shop seems too limiting, however. Only a maximum of 4 items can be bought, and you can only buy one item form each "tree." It isn't by any means a deal breaker, but is still rather annoying.
Cons:

You'll find the occasional toxic person, but I also found a lot of people to be generally annoying. I'm well aware that I'm most likely a jerk to some degree, but the amount of Russian kids, mic spammers, and people who generally don't know what Push to Talk is is frustrating and annoying to me.

Although this game has so much potential, it has too many problems to justify continued play. For people who love 4X games, this is not for you. The expansion part of Stellaris is heartbreaking. You may control around 5 planets based on your government type and tech. Any extra planets quickly drain your resources and finances. You can put them into a sector controled by an AI as part of your empire but you no longer have direct control of what is built there. So you go through the game making new sectors that you can not maximize. Next is other races. The programmers have gone out of their way to every other race a pain in the rump to deal with. Even the cavemen you meet on a far off moon will be problematic. If you make them slaves, it makes someone upset, if you make them citizens, they want indipendence and will revolt.  It is virtually impossible to just kill them off. Actual  opponents are far worse. At the begining of each war you must declare the war objectives to give the opponent a chance to respond to your demands and prepare for them. You then score points as you succeed. Should you kill off every soul on a planet and land 6 armies there, it still isnt yours untill the opponent is forced to conceed it is yours through treaties based on your warscore. There is a limit to what you can win through war, so a large territory might take you 5 wars to win it all even though you killed every ship and station in their empire 4 times over. 50 hours in and I just cant bring myself to put up with all the headaches and stupidity in this game.

I've been playing Wildstar for over 2 years now. I was in the Close Beta back in April 2014. I've never loved playing an MMO as much as I have loved playing Wildstar.
The setting and story of the game is amazing. There's soo much lore to this universe. Of all the games I want to see a cartoon series to come from, Wildstar is on the top of that list. A group of exiles rebelling against the empircal dominon, an advance alien race that plays god, a mysterious planet that holds the god like race's experiments.
Over the 2 years this game has had its ups and downs. But it was still able to hold a small hardcore playerbase of dedicated fans.
PVE:
This game has some of the best dungeons I have ever seen. They are a challenge, they take teamwork, they take communication (and honestly they should have in game voice chat for that).  Beating the Skullcano boss for the first time was sooo rewarding. My friends and I had to refight that boss 5 times, but when we finally learned how his mechanics worked and were able to take him down was soo exicting and rewarding.
Even though some of the people did not enjoy the adventures, I found them really fun. They're not as difficult as the dungeons they're still interesting. You go through them voting with the party on what paths you want to take.
Shiphands are the easist mini-dungeons, but they are still fun to run with friends. They don't require as much teamwork and you can run through them by yourself. Simple and fun.
PVP:
So all PvP in general is fun, but at the current time, there's not a lot of people PvPing. Hopefully with the Steam launch PvP can pick back up again because I loved the PvP in this game.
Battlegrounds are probably my favorite, the focus of the game is to do the objectives while preventing the enemy team from doing the objective.
Arena are enjoyable if you have a team together. Just go in and kill your opponents.
Warplots I've only done once, but it was really fun. A little laggy but fun. Their biggest problem is that they need to be coordinated, probably by a guild.
Overall this is a fun MMO and once it's been f2p for almost a year, you don't lose anything if you try it out. So hit that download button and join us on Nexus, worst case scenario you didn't enjoy it and you just uninstall it, won't lose any money.

First of all, I have over 2500 hours on this game, and played since release and stopped a couple months ago.
Pros:
- Best combat system of any MMO in the market. The double-jump, sprint, telegraph system makes for a very mobile and active combat and the interupt system makes many mechanics engaging and punishing in a good way.
- Raids and dungeons are really amazing. The first are fun and progression is amazing.
- Housing is on point and probably the best housing system in any MMO. Housing is basicly a game of its own for some players.
- Character customisation (costumes and dyes) is really great. You can have 6+ costume slots that you can change on the fly with the pieces you want with multiple dye slot per gear. Costume will hide your real armor.
- Mounts and hoverboard are pretty and fast and can be obtained as soon as you create your character.
- Game improved massively since launch in 2014.
- No P2W elements. Everything from the cash shop can be obtained for free with Omnibits or with Platinum through the Auction House.
Cons:
- Small population, resulting in very long queues for content, and some content just can't be played. Leveling dungeons/adventures/pvp are not possible unless there is a giant influx of new players (like steam release for exemple).
- Adventures never played with LFG. Because of poor rewards, long instances with a lot of RNG.
- The low revenue reduced the size of the team and therefor the speed of new content release. Basicly no new raids since launch and 1 dungeon.
- Gear creep completly negates old content. A veteran dungeon with full last tier raid gear will take 5 min to complete in Gold. While a bunch of fresh 50 might take 45 min to get Bronze. Once you start obtaining raid gear, the rest of the entire game is trivialised, leaving only raid to do.
- Because of no new content, veterans have nothing to do once they have full BiS gear.
I will avoid talking about PvP as I am a PvE veteran and, out of those 2500+ hours, have only spent maybe 100 on PvP, quite possibly much less.
All in all, the game at its core is amazing, with insane combat system and amazing dungeons/raids. But because Carbine suffered ALOT from low revenue and bad launches, there is nothing left to do for veterans.
If you are a new player, I definitly recommend this game, as you will have a lot of things to do for quite a long time. Genetic Archives and Datascape progression will take months/years with a fresh guild without people to carry you.
If you are into housing, than this game is also for you as you can litterally create anything you want. LITTERALLY ANYTHING.

I own every game in the Borderlands series, and I am eagerly anticipating Battleborn, another GEARBOX game, however, I CANNOT fully endorse this game.

Cons:
The best vault hunters are the 2 DLC's. Athena is 3rd best I guess?

Oh, and a lot of the new unique guns for this game are MORE TALKING GUNS.
The humor, if you can call it that, is the weakest entry in the series.
This game is so irritating, and it does it on purpose.
To reiterate, this game actually hates you, the player.
You see, this is what happens when you hand off a project to the B-team. 2K Aus tried, but they ultimately failed to make a worthy chapter in the Borderlands canon. If 2K were From Software, then Borderlands would be Dark Souls, Borderlands 2 would be Bloodbourne, and I guess Borderlands TPS was trying to be Dark Souls 2. Dark souls 2 is at least a good game. It's not great, it's just good. They took the original and updated the combat mechanics a lot, made a ton of new weapons, while keeping some staples of the series, and gave us the next chapter of the story. While the bosses weren't all great, (Dude in armor for a majority of the 21 bosses there) at least they weren't some of the annoying bosses like Deadlift found here.
This game actively tries to make you want to not play it. At all times, there is some NPC talking away, interrupting anything you wanted to do, like listen to Echo recordings that you have found, because they are so ♥♥♥♥ing ADHD that they prompt you do do♥♥♥♥♥♥every ♥♥♥♥ing 4 seconds. Grinders, Claptraps, Jack, all of them constantly talking, even if the prompt were programmed to go off after 20 seconds that would be a relief but this game doesn't have the goddamn patience to let you explore, which was an attractive feature in BL 1-2. Even the Claptastic Voyage DLC actively tries to annoy you with.... Just... you have to see it... I can't.... POP-UPS. YES. You read that correctly. Someone decided to add popups, glitches, and viruses..... AS A GAME MECHANIC?!@?!?!??!?!?@?@?!??@
On top of that there's the stupidest map designs, which was also a weakness in Dark Souls 2. Instead of looping around and finding a shortcut back to a travel station like BL2 and Dark Souls, it instead copies Dark Souls 2 in having levels that are just long stretches that you run through, often stymied by lava (of the instant-death variety) and badasses. OK maybe the badasses in BL2 weren't actually hard enough, they just absorbed more bullets, but in TPS, every ♥♥♥♥ing badass has a rocket launcher or a laser, and you're pretty much guaranteed to go into FFYL mode without your action skill, even sometimes with. Grinding seems to be the only way to beat them because if you are both the same level, the game is not working in your favor.
Final Verdict: Seems like 2K just want your money at this point, which is a shame because Gearbox was doing some very interesting things. Also this game is like an annoying kid that you hang out with only because he lives on your street, but he's so ADHD that you just want to grab them and shake him violently while screaming at him to just shut the hell up for a minute.
4.5/10 - If this game didn't actively try to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off at every turn, it might be worth returning to. As it stands, just watch a "Borderlands TPS the Movie" video on youtube to get the story, if you need to.

For some reason, I had no Internet when I was playing this game, so Steam didn't record it, but anyway, I'll do my first review of a game ever.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes City Building games and Strategy. Well, at least, I will recommend it in the future.
Here's a few problems:
- Since this is still an unfinished game, there isn't any good tutorial
- The game's civilizations are not balanced. I have found that playing with Eastern is by far the easiest way to play.
- Some limitations of the game are a bit annoying. For example, everybody should be able to fish. There is no geographical exceptions to fishing usually. Everybody used to fish because it was available as a source of food.
- The game is EXTREMELY HARD or COMPLETELY EASY. The difficulty meter is broken I'm telling you. Unless nothing costs a thing, it can get really hard. Everybody starts being mad with you all at the same time, even if you trade a lot.
- I often feel like the guys that deliver the stuff just deliver food or something. Everybody needs beer or something and since there's only 0.1 of food left, he decides to deliver food instead, which ends up causing the houses to devolve.
- I have seen a few bugs in the flag colour selections. I try to switch colours, but then it switches the logo, and when I want to select white and I'm at black, I need to pass by yellow, which switches the other colour, so I have to go all the way back to black, select the other colour, etc.
- Getting a steady income is actually really hard. When you start making soldiers, making enough money to pay for them all is really hard. Apart from taxes and trade, there's no income, if you're an Easterner.
- Sometimes, I get overloaded with a bunch of resources. In my last gameplay, I had over 500 wurst. I was selling all the meat I could, but I had to make wurst to make my people eat it, but then there was too much food and all. The problem here is that, we can't throw away resources or sell them at a reduced price to "nobody".
- Other countries start with soldiers and get a lot of them really fast, whilst it takes ages for us and we have none in the beginning.

Genre: city builder Settlers-style
review: version 0.7.3
-------important note----------
Hearthlands is not too difficult! Those complaints come from people who play on "normal" setting and can't deal with it. Hint: You can set it to "very easy" and adjust every other aspect in the settings!
------------------------------------------------
Hearthlands must have come a long way in the past couple of months because I can't see any of the mentioned negative points. This game is pretty fantastic by now. People complain about the difficulty. Well, that's more of a misunderstanding. Your neighbours will bully you and eventually invade you if you don't build up defences. That's how it should be btw.
So don't just build a farming community and expect to be left in peace. Build some troops.
If you don't feel like fighting, then you can comfortably set the a.i. to passive mode. You can also improve relations by trade and other means.
You can also select a sandbox mode. You can set up the game any way you like. Difficulty, number of opponents, kind of dwellings...
You can select 1 of 4 cultures to play as. The options are huge.
Hearthlands even feels polished by now. You finally have a zoom function which I imagine must have sucked without. The game runs absolutely stable. There's so much to do and it's just so much fun. Can't believe this has been under the radar for such a long time.
The devs are providing frequent updates, so it's gonna get even better!

There are no game overs (so you can continue on despite guessing or making mistakes) but I think you can do the puzzles without guesswork.
The controls are pretty simple (left click to mark as a mine, right click to reveal) but it took me a little while to figure out that you could restart the stage by clicking on the word MENU on the top left corner (I tried pressing random keys on the keyboard to no effect).

It's an odd way to start a video game review, but I'm convinced NieR: Automata ought to be viewed as an artistic achievement and perhaps even a manifesto. Unquestionably, it is a love letter to practically every genre of video game--and this particular game demonstrates an unshakable confidence in a certain idea: that video games may exist as an art form without sacrificing any of the sheer joy that comes with playing a great game.
The problem with many "artistic" video games is that the people creating those games don't understand how to properly tell a story in this kind of medium. Developers who want their games to be viewed as an artistic accomplishment try making games the same way as somebody would make a novel, a film, a comic book or a TV series. Video games, of course, are none of these, nor do they follow the same rules. The medium that video games could maybe be best connected to is a choose-your-own-adventure novel, and the two forms are still distant cousins at best--ones who haven't really spoken to each other since the early '90s, at that.
Once video games began to attract big budgets, game companies tried to make games follow the same conventions as big-budget movies and TV shows. Worse yet, game companies tried to make games that could serve as good art, but in doing so imposed the rules of movies and television; they imposed rules in a medium which so defied them that an Italian plumber could quite easily serve as a superhero without any supernatural accident (like Spiderman), unique birthright (Superman) or any fortunate series of prior events whatsoever--and this simple plumber mascot's image would go on to sell hundreds of millions of games over recent decades because the company who created it understood the unique freedom of the medium.
What Yoko Taro and Platinum Games apparently never lost sight of while making NieR: Automata is that the best way to tell a story through a video game is by no longer imitating television and film. The video game is its own art form and this art form has found its own voice. Unlike most major forms of media--though television is a debatable point here--video games have only ever existed in the postmodern era, and are perhaps the best vehicle to express postmodern ideas and running themes, such as:
-fragmentation, especially of the self.
-subverting the search for meaning.
-black humor and irony.
-magical realism.
-temporal distortion.
-poioumena (the process of creation).
-asking huge questions without an expectation of big--or even coherent--answers in return.
-transhumanism.
Playing the game, you might notice that NieR hits every single one of these ideas over and over again. Even as it piles cliche after cliche on its surface--zombies? robots? adam and eve? aliens? post-apocalyptic future? sure, why not all of them!--there runs a game as deep as a sword plunged through an android's heart. And this, perhaps, is where the strongest case can be made for this particular game being not only one of the great games of 2017, but being one of 2017's great works of art. NieR: Automata starts with ideas that we all thought had been explored as much as they ever could, yet still manages to discover a way to breathe new life into them.
Even more remarkably, it does this in a way that could only have worked as a video game.
So, go on. Go have some fun with the 26 different endings.

The Binding of Isaac is an indie flash game.
But it's really flippin' awesome.
The story is about a boy named Isaac, who lives happily with his Christian mom until the voice of God tells her to kill him. Isaac slips away into a trapdoor in the nick of time, and goes to the basement, caves, and depths and fights monsters there.
The core gameplay is similar to the first Legend of Zelda, as it's about shooting tears to damage enemies to open doors to get to bosses. You can also get pennies, keys, bombs, pills, cards, and stat upgrading items or spacebar triggered items from special item rooms. You get one item in each item room and after almost every boss (minus final bosses), however, you can gain other items from cursed rooms that have spike doors, challenge rooms that require you to fight waves of enemies, and sometimes golden chests that require a key to open. By the end of the 5 randomly generated floors before mom, your baby should be signifigantly stronger. You can also preform well on floors to get deals with the devil, which can give you damage, flying, let you turn into a cat, and more at the cost of some of your total health. However, you can also deny the devil and get chances at angel rooms that give you other stuff like halos and guardian angels. Let me tell you, it's really fun, especially when you are very strong.
Graphics are probably the turn-off for most people, that and the religion stuff. They are hand drawnish like Super Meat Boy, but they are all "edgy" and or disgusting on purpose, like most of this game. I honestly was not very disgusted by it at all, but it's not something I'd show to young kids.
The challenge level with this game can get pretty intense with this game, but I picked it up rather quickly.
Music is good. That's all I can say.
The DLC doubles the items in the game, and from what I hear, it's way better with than without.
Value with this game is great, as it has infinite replayability. (hint: buy it when it goes on sale with dlc for ~70 cents USD)
Negatives: graphics for some, religion for some, hard for some, it's a flash game, it can get kinda buggy.
This game deserves a better review.

Pros:
+ Balance; I harp a lot on balance in many of my reviews because it is important to me. This game has great balance. You can pick up any Champion and do well as long as you know how to play them, and no one Champion has a straightforward advantage.
+Visuals; Whileit may not be as appealing as Overwatch, it's a good looking game nonetheless.
+ Optimization; even on max settings, this game can stick a solid 30 FPS on my absolute potato of a computer. Any half decent rig will have no trouble running this thing.
+ Gameplay; Gameplay is fluid and teamwork oriented. If you don't work as a team or play your role properly, your team won't do well.
Mixed Feelings:
+/- In-game Shop: Now, I'm not talking about the cosmetics shop or the the loot chest shop (which frankly, I don't know how I feel about either), I'm talking about the shop while you're actually playing the game. For new players, it will seem confusing as all hell. For people who have played MOBA's like SMITE or League of Legends, you will understand the gist of it. The shop seems too limiting, however. Only a maximum of 4 items can be bought, and you can only buy one item form each "tree." It isn't by any means a deal breaker, but is still rather annoying.
Cons:
- Community; From what I've heard, Overwatch has a pretty toxic community at the moment. Paladins is similar. You'll find the occasional toxic person, but I also found a lot of people to be generally annoying. I'm well aware that I'm most likely a jerk to some degree, but the amount of Russian kids, mic spammers, and people who generally don't know what Push to Talk is is frustrating and annoying to me.

Time for another update!
I'm still playing the hell out of this game and the devs are still updating content and tweeking, including adding more buildings to the game and messing with the AI.
One major change I'm not so sure I enjoy is that invasions are now handled off screen and via popup notice.  Before this update invasions where a real challenge and to survive on easy setting you still had to prepare defense structures and have at least 3 armies pretty early in the game.  This beat me down a ton but I learned as I lost and adjusted accordingly.  Now the invasions seem totally pointless as I never lose them and suffer no consequences for the battle, a battle it should be noted again that I never get to see.
Also of note is that getting a notification every time a new trade route opens or a current one ends does not serve me much in terms of usage.  At least compared to how frequently they occur.  I check trade routes regularly as is and don't need to be remind.  However, it would be really nice to be able to jump to the spot on the map where my citizens are being killed!  Nearly every game I have played has put me in the spot of scowering the map over and over trying to find where a citizen or merchant has been killed.  It can be something as silly as a sewer monster hiding behind a build (and hard to see even with the transparent building setting on) and completely ruining my towns reputation.
Population growth is still off balance imho.  It seems that my town rep never becomes positive no matter what I do.  Have a walled in, protected town with a booming economy and no enemies on the map?  Still terrible rating.  It either is a flaw in the game or I'm too dumb to figure out something right in front of me.
As usualy my complaints sound ungrateful considering how much I absolutley adore this game.  It truly is a hidden gem of the citing building genre and I can't stop playing it for too long.  I hope the end game content sharpens up as the devs continue to tweek.

I am up to my ears in complexity when it comes to covering games, and it is nice to take a break from those games to a simple puzzle game. The game isn't super difficult, and I never found myself taking more than 5 tries on each level. The levels are designed to be easy to complete and make you feel smart after you beat them.
The graphics are also simple, not making use of flashy or particularly great art, but the ambient sounds and associated music are fairly chill and fun to listen to while you solve simple puzzles.
The physics in Art of Gravity isn't anything new, and we have no shortage of physics games, that being said, these physics are pleasant to watch. I'm not sure if it's the slow motion, or the pretty patterns the voxels create; but either way, it is incredibly fun to watch. This alone helps the game be fun, as it helps you gain a sense of completion after you beat each stage.
Overall, Art of Gravity is exactly what it says, it's all about gravity. It is an entertaining game that gives you a solid stream of content throughout its levels. The art is basic, but the music and sound effects are good, and the levels are all unique, and I can see myself coming back to this game. With this in mind, Art of Gravity earns itself a 7 out of 10 with a label of "Satisfying".

Lots of replayability (from achievemnts and unlockables)
supports a great indie game developer! (I wanna see more stuff from you Sean!)

Rocket Racoon
Fun RPG elements.
Great multiplayer.
Procedurally generated levels gives an interesting twist to your gameplay.
Cons:
Still not completely polished, still some bugs (although not gamebreaking) that could throw a good run.

This game is, in my opinion, as good a sidescrolling 2D action-platformer as you'll get. Here are my reasons:
The character creation has enough variables, even at the beginning, to offer a unique run to everyone, though through minutes upon minutes of clicking and a whole lot of luck, you can produce the same character every time. You can basically play however you want, with various races, styles, companions and, of course, hats to choose from, each having an effect on the character.
The levels are randomly generated, sometimes screwing you over horribly at the beginning and sometimes waiting until you've sunk a good half-hour into the playthrough and got some really nice items before doing so. It's almost always difficult, but a challenge worth taking. It's rewarding to beat the game, not only for the first time, but every time, and there are lots of different challenges for those better than myself, those too good at games in general. Replay value, need I say it, is high.
The game is split into levels, each themed to a biome or region. Each area has its own monsters and, in some cases, mini-bosses. Some may have more ore or trees, or more glowy bug things to hit, so depending on strategy, different places have advantages and disadvantages. At the end of each level, you can choose one of three doors to go through, determining the next area's biome, though towards the end, expect a crater or three to appear. You have twenty levels: nine 'wilderness', ten towns and the Scourge Lair (The lair of the Scourge). In true RPG fashion, you must conquer the nine and get your skills as high as possible to defeat the badguy.
The multiplayer, though initially faulty, is now working pretty well, so playing with friends is a possibility for social butterflies and other such people with friends. It's not essential to the game, so don't fret if you're missing, y'know, friends. Who needs 'em, right? Anyway, the multiplayer adds a new dynamic: sharing loot. If you're against that kind of teamwork or just really like your stuff, it may not be to your taste. If, however, you don't mind sharing that one herb or extra ironite, or if you really enjoy the results of your selfishness, multiplayer will be at least as fun as singleplayer, if not more so.
Finally, the music and artstyle are gorgeous. Like, this game is charming to play, with pulsating, dynamic pixelated backgrounds and one of the best soundtracks my ears have encountered. Except the forest: its music is merely great. The rest, however, are amazing. I'm still holding out for its appearance on the store page.
EDIT: Oops. I forgot to mention the crafting. It's good. You can look up crafting guides if you want, but figuring things out yourself is much more fun. So is figuring out what to do with that drum you made while clicking things. I've played for more than thirty hours and still don't know how to use it. Such is life.
Basically, you hold shift and click things, 1+1-style. Pretty simplistic.
EDIT 2: Since 1.4.5, multiplayer can now also have PvP, so if you really like screwing over your companions and watching their pixelated corpses wiggle on the ground, you do that. It also adds yet more challenge to the co-operative side of the game's multiplayer.
---
I highly recommend the game. It's just brilliant.
Other products are available.
---

Medieval II: Total War is one of the three best Total War games, the other two being the original Rome: Total War and Total War: Shogun 2. M2TW improved on the mechanics of its predeccesor RTW as well as introducing its own, slightly better visuals (2006), bigger battles, more complex diplomacy, improved siege battles, town management and religion.
The campaign starts in the year 1080 AD, and as in all Total War games you must expand and maintain the faction of your choice and build a mighty empire! There are only five factions to choose from though (England, Scotland, France, Holy Roman Empire, Venice, Spain) it might be possible to unlock more factions by completing the game, but I wouldn't know because i've never managed to complete a campaign, the shame...
Obviously it is wise to establish an alliance with one or more of your neighbours, before anyone starts eyeing up your lands.
The diplomacy in M2TW is much more complex than in previous games, if you have a bad reputation with a faction they won't give you the time of day. However, if you have built up relations with them then they will be highly unlikely to betray their most trusted ally (unlike RTW when your Gallic allies invade you on your 40th aniversary...)
Religon plays a larger role than it did it in RTW Barbarian Invasion, The Pope will keep an eye on all the factions, and you will receive missions from him like you do from the Senate in RTW (you also receive missions from the home team, the Council of Nobles). These missions range from build a chapel in X settlement, recruit a priest in Y settlement, to the pope launching a crusade, where you are required to send a crusading army to the specified settlement, usually somewhere near Jerusalem, or Jerusalem itself. Its quite jarring to be going along nice and easy expanding into eastern Europe to then suddenly have to sail an army to the other side of the known world not knowing what enemy forces await you there, and even if it is a successfull crusade, the Muslim forces might retaliate with a Jihad to retake the land. What ensues is basically the movie Kingdom Of Heaven.
New agents include the priest who converts the population of the settlement he is stationed in, to his religion, the Merchant who can be sent to resources on the map to trade them (Total War just became Monopoly), princesses who can be used as diplomats, or you can marry them off to a genaral to ensure his loyalty, or to someone in another faction to cement an alliance. Also assassination video's are back in this game (yay!).
It's also possible to be excommunicated from The Church if you upset The Pope too much, leaving you fair game for invasions from other factons. When The Pope dies however, the slate is wiped clean and you even have a chance to influence who the next pope is. Each christian faction has one or more cardinals who vote on who the next pope will be
so you can influence your cardinal's decision. In one play through were I played as England, I always did what The Pope asked (Conquer Egypt) I was awarded many cardinals, which means that whoever I chose was almost guaranteed to be elected. If you vote for a Pope who becomes elected you're in his good books before you start, choose poorly and The Pope will be most dissapointed with you. It makes you feel like you are part of a huge power struggle over the control of the Holy Land.
In addition to regular settlements you can convert a town into a castle, which is a lot easier to defend and allows you to train advanced infantry (Knights!!!). However, castles produce half the amount of income as regular settlements so you have to get the balance right so you are making enough money for your cities to support the armies being supplied by the castles.
Castle sieges are more difficult than regular city sieges, towards the latter half of the campagin castle defences are so high that more often than not it is literally impossible to get past a castles walls without losing half your army. Siege towers and the like are so easily reduced to matchwood that sending them up against anything but a wooden wall is a suicide mission. Meaning catapults aren't just optional, they are required while taking a citadel.
The acctual RTS side of the game is very similar to RTW, the Ai is slightly better than in RTW but will still regularly do something silly, espesially during siege battles (Units facing the wrong way while being hit by volley after volley of arrows, to name one of the more severe, though rare, cases). For some reason the cavalry charges in M2TW don't feel as powerfull as they did in RTW, neither do archers who do less damage and are less accurate than in the previous game (if you have about five units of archers firing at the same target they tend to eventually get the job done).
M2TW Isn't as glitchy as it could have been (certanly not as glitched as newer Total War titles) but occasionally bugs occur ranging from mild to severe, one time a unit from my reinforcements got stuck outside the map on a piece of scenery. Sometimes during sieges it can be extremely clunky to move units on walls, they completely stop responding when going into a tower. One time I broke through a gate with a Ram, "once more into the breach", I ordered my knights, and instead of using the gate (which was ajar and unguarded) they ran to a pair of ladders on the wall next to them and started to ascend while spear infantry positioned themselves in the gateway blocking the entrance. During the campaign I also managed to exploit a major mistake on the part of the Scottish Ai, they left their settlement
Inverness completley empty of soldiers. I just sailed round landed a small battalion and walked through the front door.
These major glitches were few and far between (for me at least). The most common problems in this game are path finding issues during siege battles. For the most part the AI is just fine, (you want to see some real messed up AI play Empire or Rome 2)
The reason why Medieval 2: Total War is so good is that it improves on everything that Rome: Total War did and introduces some of its own mechanics that add even more depth to an already deep strategy game. The Total War series is my favourite strategy series of all time and Medieval 2 Total War is one of the best of this series. I'm surprised that a game this old runs so well on a modern computer, it runs perfectly, (by contrast Total War: Shogun 2 crashes whenever I turn on V-Sync). If you like strategy games, or have never played strategy games and are looking to give them a try, this game is one of the best in RTS.

Because it's based on player choice, it's usually quite easy to find at least one way to do an objective, so it's not that traditional old game thing of "what the hell am I supposed to do". The game has a handy journal which keeps all important information (codes, usernames etc.) which you find in the levels, so you don't need to remember any of these things. Your objectives and sidequest objectives are also stored here. Sidequests can be found in each individual level, usually off NPCs. Completion of these sidequests gives you Exp, items or tips on ways to complete the main objective.
Each level is like a mini open-world, with people to interact with, paths to discover and sidequests to find/complete. The paths are mainly straightforward and the levels are designed to cater to any playstyle. I enjoy how NPC interactions, particularly debriefings, change depending on what you do. This is to be expected from this type of game, but not to this level. For example, I shot a barkeep to get some free beer (no, you have an alcohol problem) and I was rebuked for it afterwards, with the boss-man even referring specifically to the bar. It extends beyond even this level. At one point I was rebuked for visiting the ladies' toilet. Now that's attention to detail.
Also, becuase of the fact that the main character is voiced by a dev not a voice actor, the lines are very montone and there is a kind of sarcastic humor (I'm not sure it's intentional) which I just find wonderful.
Important tips:
Don't go non-lethal on your first run, as I tend to in stealth games. It's much more difficult than in most.
Don't do a ghost run on your first run
Think before you apply weapon mods
There is a ctrl + c, ctrl + v function that works in the journal so you can copy/paste info.

Even if it's not the best game ever made (and you can make an incredibly strong case for it), Deus Ex is, in 2016, without a doubt the most influential when it comes to modern game design. It was the first game to well and truly demonstrate the potential of "immersive sim", a term that you'll read a lot when researching this game. And it's just a fun, breathtaking game. Bold and ambitious and sprawling and surprising. And by God, it holds up.
Have you played a game in which you come across an overheard conversation between two guards? Or read a newspaper article or character diary laying around? Or experienced an unexpected consequence of an action you took? Or found a starting-level combination safe with the key containing the letters 0 4 5 and 1? That game owes a heavy debt to Deus Ex. System Shock had audio diaries in '94, RPGs had choices and consequences, but the vision of Deus Ex is a living world, a world that is not just a playground for the character you control but a place where people have to live while you are out busting heads.
Combat can and will break out in any setting, but the game shines in Hell's Kitchen. Return from defusing (or detonating) a few hostage situations and you're dumped on the streets of Manhattan, where people are walking around, trying to survive. It feels like a shell of a city because it is - a plague is spreading, jobs are drying up, people are giving up. The game doesn't come out and tell you this in big block letters, you just have to look around and you know (environmental storytelling is old hat in big-budget 2016 games, it was unheard of in DX times). Go to the bar and buy a cold beer for a guy on the job, try to get the bartender to open up about her cyborg implants. Go to the free clinic, where people are talking about the ongoing civil war and waiting to die of sickness. Break into a random apartment and find the bodies of overdose cases. Hack into ATMs and steal cash. Talk to vagrants on the street about how their friends have been vanishing in the sewers...
Most of the game is like this - you play as JC Denton, rookie counter-terrorist, who stumbles onto a global conspiracy. Every "hub level" (Hell's Kitchen initially, but there are others) has a central objective, something you have to learn or someone you have to deal with, but you're not given direct instruction on how to accomplish it. You're dropped on the curb and left to figure it out, by helping people who live around it or gunning down resistance or just studying the levels and finding the air ducts (thank Deus Ex for how common they are now) and trapped back doors, and using your skills or your superpowered jumping legs to access them, then go in guns blazing or in and out like a cat burglar. And Deus Ex's most celebrated innovation, so imitated in later games, was the ability to go non-lethal, by sneaking past or using tranquilizer darts or knocking people out with a baton (the last is much harder than the first two). If you don't kill anyone, the game will notice and react, at least in the early-to-mid game.
Gameplay-wise, there are some learning curves - Deus Ex uses an RPG system for its combat, meaning if you don't invest in a rifle skill (using points earned from completing objectives or for finding things off the beaten path), you're going to have to sit and steady your aim for a few seconds if you want to hit anything closer than arm's length. The stealth system is functional but rudimentary - it's mostly about line of sight, but sound and light levels factor in even though you have to play them by ear. It is possible and even advisable to stick with a pistol through the entire game (the pros, however, choose the GEP Gun).
Flaws? There are some. The voice acting is horrible (and eventually, vaguely racist) but at a certain point, it loops around to being great, one of the game's charms ("what a shame"). Some skills are less useful than others. Knocking someone out with a baton requires a head hit from behind which is remarkably frustrating to achieve. And the story, as it expands into epic scope, loses reactivity and some of the Immersive Sim qualities that made it so revolutionary. But it is indeed epic in scope. They sold the demo on CD at Target back in the day, and there was so much stuff in it that I was convinced for awhile that I'd bought the whole thing for cheap. The game is never less than incredible, always showing you new things, throwing dramatic plot curves and more formidable challenges at you. The soundtrack is pure MIDI synth and befitting the cyberpunk setting, with some wonderful (if proggy) tracks.
And the replayability? Believe the hype. The game takes choice more seriously than nearly any other game does, and by extension, more than most players do. There is a scene in which you are cornered by your enemies and a friend tells you to run while they stay behind - when I first played, I thought "this is a game and a well-worn action movie trope, clearly I'll die if I don't do what they say". I left, and later on I found the friend's dead body. Five IRL years later, I decide to replay the game for the nth time and think "You know what? I'm going to take down as many as these mooks as I can before they kill me." So I didn't run, and I killed all the attackers, and the friend lived to show up again, hours later, in a spot where every single playtime before I had run into a conversation about the dead friend. When people say they're still discovering things in Deus Ex, believe them.
Deus Ex very slowly came to become the most influential game in AAA development. Games that once would have taken after straight-up shooters like Doom or "atmospheric" shooters like Half-Life have slowly begun to emulate its storytelling in key ways, jump-started by Bioshock's evocation of DX environmental storytelling. Many games have tried, in their own ways, to pay tribute to Deus Ex. Dishonored and Dishonored 2 probably come the closest in terms of going whole-hog in recreating the magic, but they don't quite get there, as good as they are. Alpha Protocol takes its bravery with regard to choice and consequence to new levels. And the Square Enix prequels, well, they're love letters, but they lack the fundamental boldness of spirit, the risk-taking, that make Deux Ex what it is.
This game costs you almost nothing now, and once you acclimate to the controls and visuals and rhythms of gameplay, it will reward you, and if you're open to it, you will join its considerable cult. It is an undeniable achievement, a grail of design but also a hell of a game to experience. If you haven't tried it, try it. Choose the albino JC, take the computer skill, and walk into the ladies' bathroom when you get back to base. You will become a believer.

I urge you to nominate Deus Ex for the "Test of Time" Steam award in 2016!  I'm thankful that Steam is running these awards, as it's pushed me to write a review.
Deus Ex expanded and built upon early gaming concepts in a way I've rarely, if ever, seen since its release 16 years ago.  It can be seen as a culmination of a variety of games from the 90s, including Thief and System Shock, allowing for unprecedented player choice in handling objectives and masterful world building.
Given the technology of the time, Deus Ex gave players a stupendous level of control in how they wanted to play through each level of what is a surprisingly lengthy experience.  You can dump points into guns and upgrade armor and go in guns blazing, wiping out all opposition - remember, a headshot is a lethal takedown.  Or focus on stealth takedowns with crossbows and stun prods and quiet footwork.  Or perhaps avoid direct confrontation altogether and hack everything you can.  Yet again, maybe you've found an access panel and are now sneaking through hidden areas of the level.  The early levels provide some subtle (and less-subtle, in fairness) hints on what options you have.  Later levels assume you are smart enough to actually investigate and explore if you wish, a pleasant difference from many modern games that continue hand-holding until the very end.  All that said, the flexibility prevents you from feeling stuck in the later levels - there is always an alternative.  Particularly impressive is that the game has truly been built to support this, even from a narrative standpoint.  Objectives completed in odd orders, or simply left incomplete, will trigger differing dialoges and general sotry experiences.  While 2000s tech didn't allow for the level of branching storytelling now possible, it is very impressive for its age.
The overall experience also presents a very skillfully crafted narrative.  Deus Ex came out before high end graphics required high end art budgets, and you can tell that time and money went into writing and narrative design instead.  Never rushed and never too slow, Deus Ex builds an atmosphere of global conspiracy and fear within a cyberpunk world, revealing and opening up its player driven story much like a good novel.  I really cannot emphasize how effectively the Deus Ex team told a story through their game - I have seen this repeated maybe 3-4 more times since.  Deus Ex provides the groundwork for real thought and discussion, from a rapidly developing surveillence society to the human need for structure and order.  As such, Deus Ex winds up being an interesting, deep narrative experience coupled with excellent, robust gameplay.
This game is a bargain at almost any price, let alone the pittance asked for these days.  It is also still a top-notch experience, having stood for 16 years with little true competition.  I ask for your nominations for the "Test of Time" award.

It's an odd way to start a video game review, but I'm convinced NieR: Automata ought to be viewed as an artistic achievement and perhaps even a manifesto. Unquestionably, it is a love letter to practically every genre of video game--and this particular game demonstrates an unshakable confidence in a certain idea: that video games may exist as an art form without sacrificing any of the sheer joy that comes with playing a great game.
The problem with many "artistic" video games is that the people creating those games don't understand how to properly tell a story in this kind of medium. Developers who want their games to be viewed as an artistic accomplishment try making games the same way as somebody would make a novel, a film, a comic book or a TV series. Video games, of course, are none of these, nor do they follow the same rules. The medium that video games could maybe be best connected to is a choose-your-own-adventure novel, and the two forms are still distant cousins at best--ones who haven't really spoken to each other since the early '90s, at that.
Once video games began to attract big budgets, game companies tried to make games follow the same conventions as big-budget movies and TV shows. Worse yet, game companies tried to make games that could serve as good art, but in doing so imposed the rules of movies and television; they imposed rules in a medium which so defied them that an Italian plumber could quite easily serve as a superhero without any supernatural accident (like Spiderman), unique birthright (Superman) or any fortunate series of prior events whatsoever--and this simple plumber mascot's image would go on to sell hundreds of millions of games over recent decades because the company who created it understood the unique freedom of the medium.
What Yoko Taro and Platinum Games apparently never lost sight of while making NieR: Automata is that the best way to tell a story through a video game is by no longer imitating television and film. The video game is its own art form and this art form has found its own voice. Unlike most major forms of media--though television is a debatable point here--video games have only ever existed in the postmodern era, and are perhaps the best vehicle to express postmodern ideas and running themes, such as:
-fragmentation, especially of the self.
-subverting the search for meaning.
-black humor and irony.
-magical realism.
-temporal distortion.
-poioumena (the process of creation).
-asking huge questions without an expectation of big--or even coherent--answers in return.
-transhumanism.
Playing the game, you might notice that NieR hits every single one of these ideas over and over again. Even as it piles cliche after cliche on its surface--zombies? robots? adam and eve? aliens? post-apocalyptic future? sure, why not all of them!--there runs a game as deep as a sword plunged through an android's heart. And this, perhaps, is where the strongest case can be made for this particular game being not only one of the great games of 2017, but being one of 2017's great works of art. NieR: Automata starts with ideas that we all thought had been explored as much as they ever could, yet still manages to discover a way to breathe new life into them.
Even more remarkably, it does this in a way that could only have worked as a video game.
So, go on. Go have some fun with the 26 different endings.
