I can't recommend this game enough. The PC port is a bit wonky, with some driver issues for AMD gpus and resolution issues on all systems, but this game is worth it if you have the patience to deal with looking for fixes and workarounds. The combat is smooth and satisfying, with skills that can be modified to suit your preferred play style and weapons that can be swapped around to alter your combos and movesets. The open world is a little small, but that works to the game's benefit as it becomes much easier to memorize the layout of the areas. The game also switches seamlessly between standard open-world action-rpg segments, 2d side-scrolling segments, and top down twin-stick shooter segments. Last but certaintly not least is the story. In fact, the story is damn near the most compelling part of this game in my opinion. I won't spoil anything here, but the full story requires multiple playthroughs, each of which adds new layers of information and context to the story and the characters in the game. I highly encourage you to experience the emotional roller coaster of Nier: Automata's story.

I enjoy the combat, but that is about as far as it goes for me. The UI, inventory system, quest structure, and short playtime are my biggest quips. The game is painfully short, which is a shame considering how fun it can be. This is justified in the idea that you can play the game over and over again and each time its slightly different, and you achieve a different ending. Personally, I have no interest in playing a game Ive already finished numerous times to see a few new things. I just dont get how that would be something anyone would WANT to do. The different ending and a few new side quests arent enough to renew my interest. Mainly because the side quests Ive encountered are terribly mediocre. The majority seem to be time trials/minigames where you do some simple activity like running toward a finish line or killing X amount of robots in X amount of time. All of which are unimaginative and shallow, and they only get more difficult, that is the only difference for each stage of those quests. Some of the story quests are crap too. Go ask the resistence leader about this. Go ask the robot mayor about that. Go back and ask the leader about this other thing. Fetch quests, and go here and collect this quests. I was not a fan of backtracking to a previous zone simply to ask someone about a plot point. I mean what they dont have phones in the future? Cant they just contact those people over radio like you do with Yorha operators? It seems like they stuff those boring parts in just to buffer and fill the game to make the playtime longer. Considering how short it is, and the amount of filler quests, the game ends up seeming rushed and feeling a little light. But I can say that I am glad they didnt make everything a crap fest like Andromeda, where 90% of all the quests are mind numbingly boring and mundane tasks. A lot of the quests in this game ARE great and fast paced. There are some great bosses and moments. There are also some very interesting plot points, and ideas like can androids like 2b and 9s have feelings and how would they react to various scenarios. Its also awesome how 2b and 9s interact. But since they are mostly emotionless androids, it also means that they are sadly boring and shallow characters. They have no depth, fittingly. Yes I know they are basically robots but that doesnt change the fact that they are one dimensional black and white characters that are extremely unoriginal. As fascinating as the idea of a robot pondering emotion is, its been done SO MANY times, and its somewhat of a cliche now. It is still an interesting concept despite the unoriginality.
Overall the game is a lot of fun, and has great moments. But for $60 it was definately not worth it for me. I am no fan of hack and slash beat em up games though. I heard that this was an RPG of sorts so I got it, but sadly there isnt much RPG stuff in the game at all. The game is not crap, its a solid 7/10, but for myself personally, the $60 would have been better spent on a game that would hold my attention and interest longer than a mere 20 hours.

Although WildStar has had a few rough patches, the game is vastly better than it was at launch 2 years ago. The game is currently celebrating its 2-year anniversary throughout June and also tends to cycle through weekend events such as XP bonuses or for targeting specific forms of content. I've spent many, many hours on this game and loved every moment of it!
Despite what the doomsayers would like you to believe, the game is terrific and certainly does have an active community - that hopefully potential Steam gamers like yourself will come to expand it! The game is certainly capable of being played quite extensively solo, but it is vastly more fun with friends - and you are much more likely to find groups by forming them yourself rather than silently waiting in a dungeon queue.
The Free-to-Play model is incredibly generous, one of the best models I've ever seen in an MMORPG. There are very few (if any, depending on what you consider crucial) "must-haves" in the store, all of which are cheap, and nothing that's pay-to-win. As you play you earn a currency called Omni-Bits that are used to purchase almost everything that you could alternatively buy with real money. Although there are a couple of social restrictions for truly free-to-play players, they're minimal and can easily be negated with a small purchase or by investing in an optional subscription. If you enjoy the game as I do, you'll be looking for reasons to spend a little bit of cash to help support them. At no point will you feel like you're being robbed, like other F2P games are guilty of. I cannot stress enough how satisfying their F2P business model is as a customer.
I'll refrain from an in-depth analysis on gameplay, there are countless other reviews that can give specifics. I will say that there's enormous potential to express your creativity through the Holo-Wardrobe and, of course, the incredibly in-depth Player Housing system. Roleplayers rejoice!
The art style is gorgeous and has a wonderful soundtrack. Artistically, I cannot oversell this game, it's beautiful and the environments are creative. Don't let the bright colors confuse you - this game has plenty of adult humor and a rich story that captures a full range of emotions. Just you wait until you reach Isigrol...
The only major negative about the game itself would be its interface. While it's a nice style, it's horribly lacking in functionality and often gets in the way. Simple tasks, especially regarding auctionhouse/commodity exchanges, are cumbersome. A few addons will address most of the issues, but the interface will still be a bit of a hindrance. Everything else about the game makes up for it.

The game is good, I just think it didn't cater to my taste as much as DWU cause it doesn't allow you to snowball to victory like DWU by putting in a lot of diplomatic obstacles and cause of the economy being way too simple.
If you like a game that doesn't require a lot of micromanagement but has kind of repetitive elements , you will like this.
End of tl;dr;
________________________________________________________________________________
The good:
Graphics = nice
Politics and population-interactions = well-implemented, you have to act according to your populations beliefs if you don't want to suffer adverse effects (like separatist movements contesting your government or having them run off your planets).
Some funny features like observation stations that allow you to do abductions on primitive societies or worse.
Species traits influence how you handle business in space and respond to other empires. You can't play pacifists and claim enemy planets for yourself, for example.Or better: You can but it requires a change in policy that would make your population unhappy.
Diplomacy and warfare = There are multiple approaches depending on your policies in handling aliens. You can go guns blazing on everything and enslave/kill incompatible populations, or you play a more good guy type that will require you to follow several steps until you can claim a part of the enemy cake in a more peaceful, indirect manner (liberate, then vassalize). Liberation doesn't make much sense as it essentially spawns a bunch of alien citizens that follow your same ethics, but they had to be implemented for this to work. It does make you feel like you are pulling the strings and it's nice.
What's missing is more trade options. I never found a use for my stockpiles of strategic resources which I would have liked to use to dissolve defensive pacts before attacking. Sadly you can't trade with diplomatic measures.
The bad:
AI = bad at times, and forced upon you. See below.
Control over your stuff = limited. You may manage 5 planets, the rest you have to hand over to an AI "sector" that sometimes just leaves your planets unattended or builds things you really don't need. You can give them a focus on one of two currencies or science, and restrict their options. I kept a balanced focus and it ended up in having too much of one currency, while the other currency I had to pour in manually on a regular basis.
UI = Inefficient for the following: You need to actively go look for buildings to upgrade or mining resources to claim. So you'll be looking for white icons you didn't build something on in this huge universe. Easy to overlook later on.
Battles = Chaotic. Doesn't matter what weapons you equip, the fleets just charge at each other. You can't order your fleet to keep distance and kite when you have more range on your weapons, for example. But. That's cause the ship type dictates how they fight, not the weaponry. This isn't that big of a deal, the battles are still really nice to watch but sometimes you wish you could actually issue a strategy.
Research= dumbed down, random outcomes (no you can't follow a path you want, you get 3 random options), minuscule percentage bonuses on various policies and options since the numeric scale for research is way too low. Also: The bigger your empire, the more research you need, making it not a bonus to build more labs and stations and having a bigger empire, but a necessity.
So you can be the biggest empire in the galaxy, have more labs and population than the others combined. And somehow still not be ahead of them in research.
And sometimes you will keep missing a really basic technology that you really need to progress.
Economics = You build science vessels and click every single system to survey it (or trade maps with others who did that), then you send a construction ship to a system. Want minerals? Mining station on minerals. Want Energy credits? Mining station on EC. Very simple, but the UI makes it tedious.
Ship design = Kind of redundant. More range and damage usually means less accuracy. You can't do much wrong just putting as much medium stuff on the ship as possible.
Pirates = Laughable singular quests or random fleets just sitting around in some system waiting to be attacked. It's like they stopped working on them after designing their ships. When you start out as empire in DWU, the universe belongs to pirates and if you defy them without any defenses, they will make your life hell and raid all your planets and facilities constantly. They might as well not have implemented them in this game.
Later in the game you will encounter random fleets for no apparent reason.
If you like a more casual game with fancy graphics and easy controls, but that might make you realize that it's a grind behind a fancy illusion of complexity, this might be for you. I must commend the political options in this game cause they force you to adapt to the demands of the population which is a nice level of immersion and it does give you some thinking to do. But this game still has features that are rather rough around the edges. I hope that some expansion will be released reworking or adding some things, which would be nice.
For now, I prefer DW:Universe and would reccommend it over this if you're looking for a more complex 4x space game where you're willing to afford a steep learning curve and simple graphics.  Still, a good game.

Played Borderlands 2  for 234 hrs, bordelands 1 for 137h + a playthrough on Xbox360. I played 31  ish hours of this game and I have been having a hard time being motivated to finishing them, but  buyer's remorse, and the hope things would get better helped me power through the rest of the sludge.
At moments I wish the whole experience be erased for ever from my memory along with Alien 3 and 4 and the dungeon and dragon movie. yeah, it can be that crappy.
It had it's moments, but you will get more " oh ...really ? " , or " damn this is really bad ", "it's like this game was made by internet trolls" moments.
As usual difficulty spikes are all other the place trivial, one second, to "over the top yolo burst damage, fight for your life ! Out of the blue" the next (pretty much like BL 2 let's not test our game, let's just yolo it ).
The secondary quests for the most part are as boring, if not worst than the first vanilla borderlands ones a step back from borderlands 2. Some do shine like diamonds in the rough, like flowers surrended by shrapnel and stuff.
Main story missions often overstay their welcome, everything extends way past it's due time and streches out way passed the point of tedium, way past the point of irritation,  getting you to the point where you are numb and you don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about anything.
The new caracters are fine (real efforts were made), yet they are not as memorable as the older ones and  huge character bending liberties have been taken with most of the fan favorites. (mild yet permanent damage was made, a lot of purist will say this one is not canon)
The one voice actress for all females wears thin (athena has the same voice as lielith).
The eye of Helios (turning off the lazer) mission is god awfull, "just on more step" and the more steps you do, the more steps you'll have, like a Mirv grenade. It's a never ending chore. The dev try to joke about it, have Jack share your frustration, they try to let you in the joke, but ultimately you feel trolled, and no comic relief is ... well relieving at this point.
It's kinda like listening to a stand up comedian tell the exact same joke over and over again for ever an hour and a half.
It drags out for so looong that it makes the optional quests look attractive. This part was a horrendous experience.
The whole last mission is actually quite decent, lots of stalling going on still. And the 4 phased boss is manageable and not too long and tedious as was his predecessor.
Gameplay is solid (played as athena), Cryo weapons are an awesome addition I much prefer them to slag.
Clap trap claptrastic voyage DLC, is the only content DLC this 3 rd itteration has to offer setting an all time low in terms of gameplay.
The DLC is actually really good, it's better than torgue and hammerlock DLCs for BL2 (even if that's
not saying much), quite inferior to Scarlet's booty and Tiny Tina DLCS.
Very decent indeed despite it basically revolving around "stalling you through that one objective" joke you had to endure during the turning off the eye of helios. And the Indying boss that simply won't let see the ending cutscenes you have to fight 3 damn times.
I'll be perfectly honest the second I realised I'd have to fight the last boss 3 times. I said ♥♥♥♥♥ it,  alt F4, watched the ending on youtube, because Ultimatly I'd just drop a legendary weapon I'd never use since I ain't going through the main game again.
I was tired of the recycled joke, underleveled and desesperate for the whole experience to end.
And boy, am I glad I am through with the whole thing.
All in all, it's sad sad note to end this franchise on.

Cons:
--Tutorial isn't so great, and could benefit from a more guided approach instead of reactive context-sensitive dialogues.
--Economic breakdown isn't as detailed as I'd like.
--The labels for ships/resources/etc could be organized better so they don't overlap each other in the GUI.
Pros:
--High degree of polish in the art assets, voice acting (when you can find it), and smoothness of controls.
--Forcing the player to hand off control of large swaths of the empire forces unusual strategic choices which may not have normally been considered.
--The R&D system keeps players from instantly min/maxing, which makes the game more interesting.
Final word:  Buy this if you're a fan of 4x games, it won't disappoint.

First off, only get this game on sale. Even though I recommend it, I don't for $13. It's more of a under $5 game. Also if you are looking for a really creepy game that keeps you on your toes, and/or have balls of steel, then this game might not be for you. This game has a few good jump scares but for the most part you end up losing the fear until the jump scare puts you back into it. And if you are pretty comfy with most horror games then the jump scares will make you jump a bit then be like "Meh." Finally, if you want a 'simple' game that is easy to play, then this isn't for you either. The puzzles are hard and for most of the game me and my friend had a guide we would go to every time we couldn't figure what to do.
With all the said, Me and my friend enjoyed the game. The surroundings were spooking, the story was interesting. Hell the main reason we didn't want to stop was because we wanted to figure things out. Why was he there? What were those statue? The Voice acting is pretty bad though, I remember asking my friend if they just pulled some guy off the coding crew to voice the main character. I think that might be my biggest complaint, that the voice acting was horrible. It really pulled you out of the game whenever they spoke, especially the main character. But I've dealt with worse.
If you are easily creeped out and good at puzzle games, I recommend the game. If you are more into being chased and always having to be on your toes, then maybe you should go look somewhere else.

Hexcells is a logic puzzle game with a really simple concept: fill in all of the hexes on the screen. You do this by looking at the clues already given to you in the form of numbers and arrangements. For example, if you have a hex that has a number 2 inside it, that means 2 of the neighboring hexes will be blank blue ones and the rest will be other numbered ones. As you go through the different combinations and solve more of the puzzle, more clues and patterns will become apparent to you, until you're able to fill up everything.
The strategy is simple and intuitive, with easy to understand instructions whenever a new rule is added, so you never feel like you don't know what you're doing. It's very satisfying when you solve a super complicated puzzle and see how it all fits together like an equation. There were a couple of times when I felt like I wasn't given as many clues as was necessary and just had to guess, which is annoying, but these times were few and might have been simply my own incompetence.
The graphic scheme is obviously very bare-bones but it's very visually eye-catching, in my opinion, which is nice. There are only a couple of music tracks but they're very serene and help get you into the mood while you're puzzle solving.
Overall I think Hexcells is a pretty good game, challenging but not frustrating, and one that will give you a good 3-6 hours of play-time, and for that price it's definitely worth it. If you're a puzzle fan, I urge you to check it out.

You probably already know why you should buy this game.
The branching story.
The endless gameplay choice, allowing players to leap between genres from stealth to FPS to hacking simulator and so much more, as well as allowing you to merge these together.
The size (this game is huge!).
It's cheap and everyone loves it, so the thing preventing you from buying it is probably the barrier to entry that old games often have. I was cautious about this too but, too my surprise, it's not that bad.
I would reccommend installing Kentie's Deusexe alternative launcher as it fixes pretty much every problem with modern PCs.
Now.
Because it's based on player choice, it's usually quite easy to find at least one way to do an objective, so it's not that traditional old game thing of "what the hell am I supposed to do". The game has a handy journal which keeps all important information (codes, usernames etc.) which you find in the levels, so you don't need to remember any of these things. Your objectives and sidequest objectives are also stored here. Sidequests can be found in each individual level, usually off NPCs. Completion of these sidequests gives you Exp, items or tips on ways to complete the main objective.
Each level is like a mini open-world, with people to interact with, paths to discover and sidequests to find/complete. The paths are mainly straightforward and the levels are designed to cater to any playstyle. I enjoy how NPC interactions, particularly debriefings, change depending on what you do. This is to be expected from this type of game, but not to this level. For example, I shot a barkeep to get some free beer (no, you have an alcohol problem) and I was rebuked for it afterwards, with the boss-man even referring specifically to the bar. It extends beyond even this level. At one point I was rebuked for visiting the ladies' toilet. Now that's attention to detail.
Also, becuase of the fact that the main character is voiced by a dev not a voice actor, the lines are very montone and there is a kind of sarcastic humor (I'm not sure it's intentional) which I just find wonderful.
Important tips:
Don't go non-lethal on your first run, as I tend to in stealth games. It's much more difficult than in most.
Don't do a ghost run on your first run
Think before you apply weapon mods
There is a ctrl + c, ctrl + v function that works in the journal so you can copy/paste info.

Even if it's not the best game ever made (and you can make an incredibly strong case for it), Deus Ex is, in 2016, without a doubt the most influential when it comes to modern game design. It was the first game to well and truly demonstrate the potential of "immersive sim", a term that you'll read a lot when researching this game. And it's just a fun, breathtaking game. Bold and ambitious and sprawling and surprising. And by God, it holds up.
Have you played a game in which you come across an overheard conversation between two guards? Or read a newspaper article or character diary laying around? Or experienced an unexpected consequence of an action you took? Or found a starting-level combination safe with the key containing the letters 0 4 5 and 1? That game owes a heavy debt to Deus Ex. System Shock had audio diaries in '94, RPGs had choices and consequences, but the vision of Deus Ex is a living world, a world that is not just a playground for the character you control but a place where people have to live while you are out busting heads.
Combat can and will break out in any setting, but the game shines in Hell's Kitchen. Return from defusing (or detonating) a few hostage situations and you're dumped on the streets of Manhattan, where people are walking around, trying to survive. It feels like a shell of a city because it is - a plague is spreading, jobs are drying up, people are giving up. The game doesn't come out and tell you this in big block letters, you just have to look around and you know (environmental storytelling is old hat in big-budget 2016 games, it was unheard of in DX times). Go to the bar and buy a cold beer for a guy on the job, try to get the bartender to open up about her cyborg implants. Go to the free clinic, where people are talking about the ongoing civil war and waiting to die of sickness. Break into a random apartment and find the bodies of overdose cases. Hack into ATMs and steal cash. Talk to vagrants on the street about how their friends have been vanishing in the sewers...
Most of the game is like this - you play as JC Denton, rookie counter-terrorist, who stumbles onto a global conspiracy. Every "hub level" (Hell's Kitchen initially, but there are others) has a central objective, something you have to learn or someone you have to deal with, but you're not given direct instruction on how to accomplish it. You're dropped on the curb and left to figure it out, by helping people who live around it or gunning down resistance or just studying the levels and finding the air ducts (thank Deus Ex for how common they are now) and trapped back doors, and using your skills or your superpowered jumping legs to access them, then go in guns blazing or in and out like a cat burglar. And Deus Ex's most celebrated innovation, so imitated in later games, was the ability to go non-lethal, by sneaking past or using tranquilizer darts or knocking people out with a baton (the last is much harder than the first two). If you don't kill anyone, the game will notice and react, at least in the early-to-mid game.
Gameplay-wise, there are some learning curves - Deus Ex uses an RPG system for its combat, meaning if you don't invest in a rifle skill (using points earned from completing objectives or for finding things off the beaten path), you're going to have to sit and steady your aim for a few seconds if you want to hit anything closer than arm's length. The stealth system is functional but rudimentary - it's mostly about line of sight, but sound and light levels factor in even though you have to play them by ear. It is possible and even advisable to stick with a pistol through the entire game (the pros, however, choose the GEP Gun).
Flaws? There are some. The voice acting is horrible (and eventually, vaguely racist) but at a certain point, it loops around to being great, one of the game's charms ("what a shame"). Some skills are less useful than others. Knocking someone out with a baton requires a head hit from behind which is remarkably frustrating to achieve. And the story, as it expands into epic scope, loses reactivity and some of the Immersive Sim qualities that made it so revolutionary. But it is indeed epic in scope. They sold the demo on CD at Target back in the day, and there was so much stuff in it that I was convinced for awhile that I'd bought the whole thing for cheap. The game is never less than incredible, always showing you new things, throwing dramatic plot curves and more formidable challenges at you. The soundtrack is pure MIDI synth and befitting the cyberpunk setting, with some wonderful (if proggy) tracks.
And the replayability? Believe the hype. The game takes choice more seriously than nearly any other game does, and by extension, more than most players do. There is a scene in which you are cornered by your enemies and a friend tells you to run while they stay behind - when I first played, I thought "this is a game and a well-worn action movie trope, clearly I'll die if I don't do what they say". I left, and later on I found the friend's dead body. Five IRL years later, I decide to replay the game for the nth time and think "You know what? I'm going to take down as many as these mooks as I can before they kill me." So I didn't run, and I killed all the attackers, and the friend lived to show up again, hours later, in a spot where every single playtime before I had run into a conversation about the dead friend. When people say they're still discovering things in Deus Ex, believe them.
Deus Ex very slowly came to become the most influential game in AAA development. Games that once would have taken after straight-up shooters like Doom or "atmospheric" shooters like Half-Life have slowly begun to emulate its storytelling in key ways, jump-started by Bioshock's evocation of DX environmental storytelling. Many games have tried, in their own ways, to pay tribute to Deus Ex. Dishonored and Dishonored 2 probably come the closest in terms of going whole-hog in recreating the magic, but they don't quite get there, as good as they are. Alpha Protocol takes its bravery with regard to choice and consequence to new levels. And the Square Enix prequels, well, they're love letters, but they lack the fundamental boldness of spirit, the risk-taking, that make Deux Ex what it is.
This game costs you almost nothing now, and once you acclimate to the controls and visuals and rhythms of gameplay, it will reward you, and if you're open to it, you will join its considerable cult. It is an undeniable achievement, a grail of design but also a hell of a game to experience. If you haven't tried it, try it. Choose the albino JC, take the computer skill, and walk into the ladies' bathroom when you get back to base. You will become a believer.

I urge you to nominate Deus Ex for the "Test of Time" Steam award in 2016!  I'm thankful that Steam is running these awards, as it's pushed me to write a review.
Deus Ex expanded and built upon early gaming concepts in a way I've rarely, if ever, seen since its release 16 years ago.  It can be seen as a culmination of a variety of games from the 90s, including Thief and System Shock, allowing for unprecedented player choice in handling objectives and masterful world building.
Given the technology of the time, Deus Ex gave players a stupendous level of control in how they wanted to play through each level of what is a surprisingly lengthy experience.  You can dump points into guns and upgrade armor and go in guns blazing, wiping out all opposition - remember, a headshot is a lethal takedown.  Or focus on stealth takedowns with crossbows and stun prods and quiet footwork.  Or perhaps avoid direct confrontation altogether and hack everything you can.  Yet again, maybe you've found an access panel and are now sneaking through hidden areas of the level.  The early levels provide some subtle (and less-subtle, in fairness) hints on what options you have.  Later levels assume you are smart enough to actually investigate and explore if you wish, a pleasant difference from many modern games that continue hand-holding until the very end.  All that said, the flexibility prevents you from feeling stuck in the later levels - there is always an alternative.  Particularly impressive is that the game has truly been built to support this, even from a narrative standpoint.  Objectives completed in odd orders, or simply left incomplete, will trigger differing dialoges and general sotry experiences.  While 2000s tech didn't allow for the level of branching storytelling now possible, it is very impressive for its age.
The overall experience also presents a very skillfully crafted narrative.  Deus Ex came out before high end graphics required high end art budgets, and you can tell that time and money went into writing and narrative design instead.  Never rushed and never too slow, Deus Ex builds an atmosphere of global conspiracy and fear within a cyberpunk world, revealing and opening up its player driven story much like a good novel.  I really cannot emphasize how effectively the Deus Ex team told a story through their game - I have seen this repeated maybe 3-4 more times since.  Deus Ex provides the groundwork for real thought and discussion, from a rapidly developing surveillence society to the human need for structure and order.  As such, Deus Ex winds up being an interesting, deep narrative experience coupled with excellent, robust gameplay.
This game is a bargain at almost any price, let alone the pittance asked for these days.  It is also still a top-notch experience, having stood for 16 years with little true competition.  I ask for your nominations for the "Test of Time" award.
3 sequels later and this game still shines, head and shoulders above them all.

I love FPS games - I'm awful at them, but I still love them. What's not to love about shooting and blowing things up??
With that said, I love this game! It's in black and white (except for the blood) resembling a 1930's or 1940's film. And you can shoot  and blow up just about everything. Fire a gun at a car and it blows up, hopefully taking a lot of zombies with it. Shoot boxes and you might find money (used to upgrade your weapons), shells, or other goodies.  As a matter of fact, you have to blow up everything you can to find hidden switches to get into hidden areas. There are secret areas that can be accessed if you can find the switch that lets you in.
Both controller and keyboard are supported. I like using the mouse for aiming and shooting (I'm a complete spaz with the controller on shooting), so I have to live with the keyboard for movement (total spaz there, too!).
An excellent feature (and a way to know that you're just about ready to die!) is the auto save.  The game will auto save just before a big battle where you could (and I generally did until I figured out the right strategy) die. That's the other thing I love about this game - there is strategy involved. If you use your resources wisely, you can get through even boss battles.
If you like shooters, blowing things up, or zombies, you'll love this game. Recommended for beginers as well as more experienced players.

Although WildStar has had a few rough patches, the game is vastly better than it was at launch 2 years ago. The game is currently celebrating its 2-year anniversary throughout June and also tends to cycle through weekend events such as XP bonuses or for targeting specific forms of content. I've spent many, many hours on this game and loved every moment of it!
Despite what the doomsayers would like you to believe, the game is terrific and certainly does have an active community - that hopefully potential Steam gamers like yourself will come to expand it! The game is certainly capable of being played quite extensively solo, but it is vastly more fun with friends - and you are much more likely to find groups by forming them yourself rather than silently waiting in a dungeon queue.
The Free-to-Play model is incredibly generous, one of the best models I've ever seen in an MMORPG. There are very few (if any, depending on what you consider crucial) "must-haves" in the store, all of which are cheap, and nothing that's pay-to-win. As you play you earn a currency called Omni-Bits that are used to purchase almost everything that you could alternatively buy with real money. Although there are a couple of social restrictions for truly free-to-play players, they're minimal and can easily be negated with a small purchase or by investing in an optional subscription. If you enjoy the game as I do, you'll be looking for reasons to spend a little bit of cash to help support them. At no point will you feel like you're being robbed, like other F2P games are guilty of. I cannot stress enough how satisfying their F2P business model is as a customer.
I'll refrain from an in-depth analysis on gameplay, there are countless other reviews that can give specifics. I will say that there's enormous potential to express your creativity through the Holo-Wardrobe and, of course, the incredibly in-depth Player Housing system. Roleplayers rejoice!
The art style is gorgeous and has a wonderful soundtrack. Artistically, I cannot oversell this game, it's beautiful and the environments are creative. Don't let the bright colors confuse you - this game has plenty of adult humor and a rich story that captures a full range of emotions. Just you wait until you reach Isigrol...
The only major negative about the game itself would be its interface. While it's a nice style, it's horribly lacking in functionality and often gets in the way. Simple tasks, especially regarding auctionhouse/commodity exchanges, are cumbersome. A few addons will address most of the issues, but the interface will still be a bit of a hindrance. Everything else about the game makes up for it.

I've been playing the game since launch, and have stuck around since. While the road to this point has been rocky to say the least, but the game has seen massive improvements since. I've played plenty of MMOs, mainly WoW, but I've played GW2, ESO, and a few others. I'll split the rest of this review into sections.
Combat:
The combat system for this game is telegraph based. Essentially every ability has a telegraph similar to classic AoE abilities in other MMOs. Most abilities have a cap of enemies/allies they can hit listed on the tooltip, including healing abilities. Enemy mechanics also rely of mainly telegraphics. While not all damage is avoidable in every fight, DPS tend to take little to no damage if they avoid the telegraphs in a majority of fights. Telegraphs are also part of PVP. Combat-CC is a major mechanic of many boss fights and world encounters. If you hate tab targeting, this game may be worth a look.
PVP:
PVP as a whole tends to have balancing issues. Many of the tank classes cannot be killed, healers are essential to winning matches, and DPS should know their roles. There are 3 Standard PVP maps (1 CTF, 1 Sabotage, 1 Point based), arenas, and Warplots. Warplots are essentially raid-based PVP, similar to old AV on WoW, however, it tends to be difficult to find a group for this without a premade group and scheduled time being planned. Arenas are fairly dead at the moment. BGs are sporadic.
Raiding:
The raiding in this game tends to be the biggest strength. There are 2 raids, each with interesting mechanics that require the group to be awake, unlike say, WoW's LFR. The raids tend to be rather difficult, especially at lower item levels. The raids do require heavy coordination, mainly in Datascape. For this reason, Pugs tend to be rare for Datascape, and pugs for Genetic Archives do happen, but likely don't full clear. Generally speaking, you need to join a raid guild for raiding. One minor issue (or benefit depending who you talk to) is the lack of guides for raiding, especially Datascape. There are a few good guides floating around, but no where near as many strategies as WoW's community may have. There is a 3rd raid in the game that is a single boss raid, but it tends to rarely be done due to lack of adequate loot.
Non-Raid PVE content:
There are 4 types of PVE content: Open world, Dungeons, Adventures, and Expeditions. Dungeons tend to be run to gear up for raids, as well as prepare you for raiding. Adventures are easier minidungeons that have very little purpose aside from cosmetics. Expeditions are solo content that can scale for up to 5 people, and tend to be interesting casual content. Open world offers a few daily hubs which offer things to alleviate some of the Pre-Raid preparations if grinded. Arcterra provides gear better than dungeons, and tends to be the most efficient way to gear if you can't get a dungeon group.
Housing:
Probably one of the better bits of content in the game. This housing system provides more flexibility than SWTOR's system, while having a simple enough UI so that anyone can build a masterpiece. The Roleplaying community in particular takes advantage of this system, and has made some pretty amazing stuff. Housing provides a very good variety of content at endgame, and increases relevance of some older content.
RP:
The roleplaying scene is pretty good on both factions. Exiles have a higher population, but the Dominion community still goes on very strong. For more information, I'd recommend checking out the Wildstar Roleplay Enjin site.
Population:
The game's biggest weakness at the time of writing. Queues tend to be rather slow, especially for PVP content. Many of the daily hubs are barren. Keep in mind, this review was written the day of the steam launch, and will likely get better with time. It's also worth noting I am a Dominion main, and the Dominion has a smaller population than Exile. At the time of writing queues are faction locked, but the devs are working on a system to merge the factions for PVE content.
Bugs:
The game tends to suffer from a lot of bugs as well. All the bugs tend to be fixed within a months time, but a couple of them take a tad longer to get fixed. It's overall not too huge of a problem if you play other MMOs.
Cash Shop:
Cash shop isn't too intrusive. The only thing most people tend to be salty about is the service tokens. Otherwise, the store is rather empty at present. A decent chunk of items are on the store, all of which are cosmetic or boosts. Service tokens are your average "Speed Up" currency which can be used to reset transport cooldowns, take instant flight paths, and make runecrafting (similar to gems in WoW) easier. You earn a currency "omnibits" while playing which can be used to buy most items on the store. Some items in my opinion tend to be a little pricey, but that is a pure personal preference. The subscription for this game is not required in any way, but tends to give very nice boosts.
Costume System:
You can wear any armor any time for cosmetic purposes, and can purchase up to 14 costume slots, with redying. Weapons cannot be redyed. Weapons are the only thing class restricted costume wise. There is a way to decustomize your character in game for gold or service tokens.
Closing:
This game is certainly worth a try, if you like MMOs. Since it's free to play and doesn't have any "fee-to-pay" elements to it, I would advise getting to 50, trying out the content, and making your own decisions from there. Hope this helps.

This title is a game that became very popular for something really silly: 2B's appearance. Though it probably has to be expected, the design is very appealing, and so that's what people encounter first. But one shouldn't forget that this game has some substance to it. To be completely frank, this title was my first in the setting, and the first game from Yoko Taro. So both my knowledge regarding the lore and history of previous games is non-existent.
I actually had to upgrade my rig in order to play this game, and visually it was worth it. Perhaps not the best looking game out there, sometimes the texture fading makes certain locations look not too impressive, but there also are moments where the mere visuals are captivating (enough). Overall I myself am not too critical when it comes to graphics, I more follow a "good enough works just fine" route, so take my opinion on this with a piece of grain.
The combat itself is based a lot around dodging, especially during bullet hell sections. Having to double-tap a movement key to dodge is rather unhandy, but the true problem lies within the default keybinding: I have died several times because a simple action like using a heal item takes a (comparably) complex key combination that most likely will require you to use both hands unless you re-bind some of the keys. It gets even worse when you want to use an item you didn't previously used, for example switching from a small recovery item to a medium one; at times you even accidentally switch to another item, which can lead to possibly infuriating results.
Another problem is that during certain bullet hell sections of the game (during hacking for example) aiming with the mouse is next to impossible which drastically restricts the angles you can shoot at targets and through that increases the difficulty of these sections.
Nevertheless and despite it possibly being infuriating at times, I personally find the combat and port sufficing, again perhaps not the best or most innovative, but it remains fun for the most part.
I won't spoil anything. There is just a single thing I want to point out here:
Let me actually try something different here, namely try to figure out to whom I would not recommend this game. You need some endurance for this game, both physical and mental. You need to be open. Sometimes a mere NPC can toss up a question that can very well stick to you for a while, something that's not just rather random, but that has a deeper philosophical meaning to it. Such questions often don't actually have an answer, and the game rarely (perhaps not at all even) tries to give you one. So I believe that to truly enjoy the game to the fullest, you need to be open to think about what is going on. Like mentioned above, the combat mostly is alright, but nothing ground breaking. Most should be able to enjoy it alright for a bit, but if that's what has to keep you fully entertained in this game, this maybe isn't the right title for you.
I decided to write this review directly after I received ending E. I want other people to see and enjoy for themselves, too.

This is my favorite 4X game ever. It has the right mixture of depth, gameplay, graphics, and fun! I love creating an empire and building it from nothing, and conquering my enemies among the stars. I'm still just getting started in this game, but have played enough to see its strengths and weaknesses compared to other titles.
It has more diplomacy, economy, and depth than Sins of a Solar Empire. It is easier and prettier than Distant Worlds. It has more depth and customization than Hegemonia (an old standard I use for space strategy games). It is realtime (with pause and time acceleration) instead of turn based! This makes the game flow much better for me. The combat is more engaging than Endless Space.
The mod support is good too, for any gameplay elements you want to tweak. The only thing I don't like is how the tech tree works. You can't work through a linear tree path of research, but more frustratingly, if you make a choice of one option over another, sometimes the other option won't show up for the next research cycle (you get a selection of several random items you can elect to research within that field). So I'm going to fix that with a mod once I finish a few more Vanilla games.

Namely I think the DLC we've had so far has helped to bolster the originally dull mid-game, and expect more to be done in relation to all the other phases of the game as well. I look forward to seeing where this game goes. Now should you buy it as is? That depends. Logic puzzle game, similar to minesweeper but without the need to guess any moves.
I really enjoyed playing through Hexcells while short. Every puzzle (30 to complete) in it is fully solvable using logic, no guessing is required. It gradually introduces you to different clues as it increases in difficulty as you progress through the levels.
It is forgiving there is not punishment to making mistakes or guessing other than being unable to “perfect” the level which is completing it with a limited amount of mistakes, which is also the only real reason to reply levels.
One negative is that puzzles can’t be saved mid game, so you lose progress when you exit.
Even though it can be quite quick to get through the 30 available puzzles I still recommend Hexcells as; one on sale it is very cheap, and two it’s a good starting point to ease you into the series.

One of these games that anyone "should have played at least once". Played through this for the first time back when I was a kid, played it again some 15 years later - for nostalgia's sake I thought - and just taking my time reading through all the lore, books, newspapers, etc. discovered so much more than I had in my original playthroughs. And I am sure that I have missed quite a few secrets and hidden paths along the way.
Deus Ex is a piece of art. Gameplay-wise, you can customize your character and weapons to suit your style, and there are always several ways to reach an objective; which also gives the game great replay value. You may go for the silent approach, lockpicking your way to vents to complete your objective unnoticed, but you could also just walk through the main door facing the alarmed enemies with a rocket launcher. You may also just hack automatic turrets to kill your enemies or booby trap the building...
On top of that, choices do matter and change the way the story unfolds. The atmosphere really takes you in, the characters have depth, the general story is challenging and thought-provoking.
The game is simply a timeless must-play.

This game does well to create atmosphere, the imagery is hauntingly beautiful  (apart from character models and some items) and the sound design is spot on, unfortunately the immersion is ruined a little due to this frustratingly slow and clunky way in which you move around and interact with things. There is a lot of puzzles and most of them are really nice, but the controls can be awkward to use and some puzzles are pretty difficult or annoying because there doesn't seem to be any clues as to what you should do. The game's story is convoluted and I don't really learn much from it, I'm not sure if this is intended so that the player can interpret things, but I was left pretty confused. The ending is also very anti-climatic, there are two endings and they are pretty much the same and they are both very cliché endings. Despite the negatives, I do recommend this game but probably not at full price. As a person who enjoyed what I managed to play of the old "Dark Fall" (before it became incompatible with my operating system), it was a real novelty to go back to Dowerton Station and re-experience interaction with some of the more memorable characters from the first game -- and ultimately bring closure to the wandering ghosts.
The story is fairly mediocre and predictable this time (it also fails to explain what the "Dark Fall" is, which will confuse any who hadn't played the first two games), but what was outstanding about the first "Dark Fall" carries over into this one. The puzzles are clever, original and solvable. There is plenty of exploration and the environments are very well rendered (granted, it takes you forever to move from place to place). The game provides a few really effective scares (only 2-3 jump scares), and a tense atmosphere. There is also enough surrealism to make any survival horror veteran uneasy.
By far, the best part of this game is the sheer amount of time you spend scissoring things. I don't think I've ever used so many pairs of scissors so many times and so consistently in an adventure game. I personally feel the scissoring makes up for most of the very bad plot devices. Completely.
All in all: Don't play for the story. Play it for the puzzles. Stay for the scissoring.
Would have been nice as a fully free game, but the payed section of it makes its message very cynical about what it tries to mock (capitalism).

Deus Ex, along with Arma and just about every decent flight simulator is a game that illustrates why PC Gaming is a great platform. It is a deep, rich game that is rewarding on multiple play throughs. It doesn't have the best graphics and, if we're being honest, it never did. It tries hard to be an RPG but falls short. It's not even that great on action given its subject matter. However, none of those deficiencies hold it back from being one of the, if not the best PC game ever made. Now of course Deus Ex was ported over to consoles but never very successfully. Its successor was very much more focussed on being successful in the console realm and, as such, didn’t live up to the original. The question is, why didn’t it live up to the original? People cite the poor story, weaker characters and so on. I believe it was because it door locks.
What?! Door locks?
Well, okay, door locks and a whole host of things that invested you in the original world that, by being console focussed, the subsequent games have never been able to adequately capture. But, let’s focus on door locks that had keypads attached for a moment. Deus Ex is famous for having multiple routes to a goal and even multiple outcomes based on the player’s interpretation of the goals. To get past a locked door may involve you getting to the room via an unlocked door covered by a camera and using your multitool to disable it. Alternatively, you may be able to get into the room via vents. Those that didn’t like to sneak could blow the door off its hinges if it was vulnerable to such attacks. However, my favourite way was to be observant. Hacking into emails sometimes gave you door code as did listening to conversations and so on. The main point is that when you tried the door, you entered the code using the mouse on the screen keyboard or using the numpad on your physical keyboard. You’d have to remember the code, or spend time looking through logs to enter it. I used to physically write notes as I played and on the later missions I still do this.
I remember playing Deus Ex 2 and finding a locked door, I found a code went back to the door and didn’t have to type anything, the door just opened. The rest of the game was as numb and uninvolved. Just run around and ‘listen’ to every conversation, try all the doors and hope you had ‘heard’ the next secret to allow you to continue. Faster, easier and forgettable. I only played Deus Ex 2 once, I don’t remember the plot at all and I don’t remember the characters.
Deus Ex Human Revolution was much closer to the original. I loved the cinematic moody feel of it but it still never had the depths of the original. So, I’m nominating Deus Ex for “Test of Time” award. It’s a truly brilliant narrative that future game makers should look at to build upon because very little has come close in over 16 years!

A fun little arcade space game that has quite a lot of different types of ships and customization. The story and dialog is pretty weak, but there's still enough here for a few hours of fun.

For a game that tends to focus on trading, they didn't make it very intuitive. There's no way to store goods, so you either have to get a ship with LOTS of cargo space, or just sell anything you get right away. There's also no economy map. You can look at the highest\lowest known prices for each item; but prices change a lot, and so you have to constantly check which turns into a click-fest. If they just added an economy map all this could be remedied.
AI is mediocre, usually the only challenge is being outnumbered 10-1. Fighting a couple ships at a time usually isn't a challenge once you get some better weapons and items. But watching AI battle each other can be painful.
Graphics look decen't, but for some reason the background stars look blurry and washed out. Planets and special fx look really sharp and crisp, overall they get the job done.
I'd highly recommend a controller, and to get the game on sale ($20 seems a little steep).

What happened between Borderlands and Borderlands 2? Well this did.

This game functions...as both a sequel and a prequel. It's a prequel because the events and story that are told are the events that predated Borderlands 2 but came after Roland and his crew defeated the Destroyer in the first borderlands. If you were paying attention to the audio logs you would've learned some crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥happened between now and then...but what started all that crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥that happened between now and then? That's what this game tells. It's all told by Athena, a former assassin by the now defunct Atlas Corp captured by Lilith and the remainder of the crimson raiders. The timing of her capture by Lilith is after the fall of Handsome Jack and this is why it's also a sequel.
All controls and gameplay pretty much play the same as BL2 but someone thought Zero-G, airboosting with a slam attack, and Oxygen breath meters would be cool. It's not...it's really not that fantastic really.
The maps on the moon surfaces felt like they weren't tested very well. You'll be driving your vehicle to what will look like a ramp for a jump to another little chunk of land but instead you'll hit a piece of land that stood higher than your ramp jump's angle and then inevitably crash into either instant-death lava or a bottomless pit. Yeah that's real fun, considering these maps are pretty huge.
Helios Station is even worse. There's whole hubs that can only be traversed via the jump pads. The map itself feels useless in there.
Here's another fun thing no one will enjoy: One of your earliest enemies, scavs, they can airslam you just like you can but it does 3 things at once. First all it's ♥♥♥♥ing fast when they do it so you can't just trace them when they take off and come back down to airslam, secondly it pushes you back and third...best of all...the blast from the ground splashes dirt on your screen so NOW YOU CAN'T SEE!
That's high speed attacks and crowd control all thrown at you at the beginning of the game along with the fact they keep coming out of nowhere. That's just gamebreaking. Thank god the attacks are pretty weak but if two or more of these guys are doing this to you it's ridiculous.
There's very little DLC in this game and only 1 new character. I've yet to get to trying her or the DLC but after what I've been through it's hard for me to recommend it but also not to diss it but it's not a complete failure either.
There's still some humor in this game but it's mostly aussie nonsense coming from the big bosses. You can't really hear most of what the bandits in space are saying because...well you're in space...but enough of that detail. Marcus somehow managed to get guns to work out here so let's not debate it too strongly.
Purple and orange weapons/gear are much easier to come by and you can even make them using the new grinder machine in the game...however I have no idea how you're supposed to make orange weapons or even other orange gear. There's no “recipe manual” or whatever anywhere in the interface so I have no idea what explanation said that I had to know a “recipe” to make said gear.
Honest to god, it felt like 2k Australia was trying rush this out without thinking about how the moon mechanics worked and if they were actually fun or not. This game isn't terrible but it's far from being amazing while at the same time it's not the most frustrating thing out there. Coming from it's legacy it should have been much better than this...
But hey..it could always be worse.

I really wanted to love Nier: Automata. I was a huge fan of the original Nier and I never thought we'd get a sequel, much less one by Platinum, who seemed like the perfect studio to bring exhilerating combat to the game. It really seemed to have everything going for it, yet other than the soundtrack I struggle to think of anything I felt Automata does well.
The combat is grossly dumbed down Bayonetta, where there are no combos (save for one, sort of) and there's no drawback to spamming dodge and being invinsible 99% of the time. The game's difficulty curve mostly seems to come from giving the same three enemies progressively more absurd health bars and throwing them at you in ever more baffling numbers. The upgrade mechanic is abusable in the extreme and within 90 minutes you can accidentally make yourself effectively invinsible.
The plot is impossible to care about, and people returning from Nier 1 will already know one of the main twists
. The characters range from "stern" to "generic whiney male anime protagonist who's bland enough for whiney anime fans to project themselves on to", and when the game is really trying to pull emotional punches they fall completely flat because you don't care about who these people are or what happens to them because they have no personalities at all. Several times they bend the characters over backwards just because the plot needs them to suddenly do an about face on their stance on robot-genocide.
Thematically, Automata is basically a pile of existentialist ideas for you to pick over at your leisure and say "Yep, I remember reading Camus." It has nothing to actually
though, it's more like it's recommending you go read about existentialism on your own because forming views is hard.
Automata wants to do what Dark Souls 1 did in keeping fast travel away from you so you can admire the dramatic decaying scenery and feel the scale, but the landscapes are bland and muted, and you just end up skipping across them looking at the same five ugly grey buildings over and over again.
Even the act structure is broken, with the first and second playthroughs being 90% identical, there was no reason to pad the game out so grossly before finally letting you have the second half in NG+2, 3 and 4.
That said I'm glad this game got made, I'd rather Platinum take big risks and end up with big failures than keep pumping out Bayonetta forever (as much as I love Bayonetta), because that's how we end up with the really special games like Nier 1.

It has more depth and customization than Hegemonia (an old standard I use for space strategy games). It is realtime (with pause and time acceleration) instead of turn based! This makes the game flow much better for me. The combat is more engaging than Endless Space.

This game is a very well-executed take on the city-building genre.  At its core, it plays similar to SimCity, but it takes the concept in new directions.
It's easy to get into, and there's a lot of depth.  The tutorial is straightforward and quick, which is nice; it doesn't hit you with unwanted dialogue like many tutorials do.
The gameplay is set up in a way such that new concepts are introduced at just the right pace: after you've produced enough food for your townspeople, they start asking for other luxuries like alcohol, furniture, and boots.  Amusingly, they put alcohol at a higher priority than everything except food.  Once you have a production line set up for the resources they want, their houses automatically get upgraded, and you continue onto their next wishes.  The pacing is great.
As time goes on, AI-controlled opponents will start to interact with you.  This gives you some options for trading, so you can get rid of excess resources in exchange for the resources you want.  They also apparently attack you, and you can build weapons for defense, but I haven't experienced that yet since I've only played for an hour so far.

Genius.  I haven't had this much fun since "Sim City 2000," and this game is superior.  Better than "Banished" as the end-game isn't pointless economic tedium, but RTS / TD feudal city building.  I love this game.  I have spent 100s of hours playing before launch testing and on Desura, & still can't wait to play again.  The progression from city building and farming to battling graveyard ghouls feels right.  The pacing is pleasing, not overwhelming like an RTS.  One can actually get to know their villagers a bit before they are destroyed years later.  "Hearthlands" also lets the player design their city a bit more openly, providing awards for evironmental prowess and properly spaced villages.  The restrictions are still there, but the player has room to add a few trees and such without it hurting the economy;  it in fact boosts it.  If you miss the good old days of simulation cities but don't want to deal with the new age bullsh!t being pushed by the AAA publishers, this is a great game and company to support.  Very few games make me smile, give me glimmers of happiness... this game does just that by evoking my childhood imagination for sim cities once again.  "Hearthlands" is the perfect compliment to my other work -art- as it inspires & amuses.  Just how many little villages didn't make it?  How many millions slaughtered just so that we could survive on?  This is a great break from the intensity of "Crusader Kings" yet still one can entertain the same novel characters & events in their own storybook style sandbox.   --  Oldschool Respect -- Critics of the graphics should understand the homage to the early era of sims & keep in mind the appeal to a generation which utilized their imaginations more than their eyes.  Tolkien's favorite rendering of his books was of the Hobbit and Golem doing riddles in the dark, an abstract with few details.  Tolkien said he loved it because it left more to the imagination of the beholder.  That is why I love "Hearthlands," how it inspires me to a better state of mind.

I bought the game on July 27th with the intention of playing it then and getting some video, but I wasn’t able to due to time constraints. I played it the next day, finished chapter zero and played a bit of chapter one. I intended to sit down today (Sunday), take a video and play it fully, but after a recent update, I now can’t. Whenever I try to start a chapter, it puts me into some weird looking water. I try swimming, but get nowhere. Blood slowly takes over my screen because I’m clearly drowning, I die, then the game crashes to desktop with two errors.
From my little time with it a couple of days prior, it was interesting, albeit very rough. Chapter Zero has you playing as a security guard in a university library. You need to check out six specific areas, which you can roughly relate to collecting notes in Slenderman-type games, while avoiding a mysterious figure who doesn’t ever seem to walk toward you. If you get up behind him, he’ll continue walking away, and as long as you don’t touch him, you’re safe. If you’re in front of him but not directly in his path, he’ll go right past you. I checked the six areas, proceeded to the basement, found a ritual sort of thing, then the game crashed.
Upon restarting, I tried out chapter one, which is where you play as the rookie security guard who was talking to you in chapter zero. You’re supposed to monitor a bank of cameras for an intruder, while occasionally getting up to walk around the area and check it out. Unfortunately, once the other guy stopped talking, I was “stuck” on one of the screens, and couldn’t switch to another camera or get up to investigate. After pressing all the keys the game told me to use for that chapter, it crashed.
I didn’t bother with chapter two. Apparently there are more chapters coming, but it would be fantastic if the developer fixed what was wrong before adding new chapters which will inevitably also be buggy.
The only thing I can say with certainty is that the game looks fairly good, and for something that’s running on CryEngine, it should.
has far too many flaws for even early access. It has potential, and the few minutes I played before the developer broke it was interesting enough that I had intended to play it some more. Unfortunately, their hotfix broke chapter zero (I didn’t test the others), and they’re already talking about another game using the proceeds from a game that doesn’t work. When many issues of the game extend to simple UI functionality that doesn’t work, or is flat out broken, it doesn’t bode well.
It has potential, and I’d like to see how it pans out in the future, but at the moment, I can’t recommend this at all. I will keep it installed and will RSS the news feed to stay on top of updates, and will gladly change this review when, or if, things change for the better.
To the devs, good luck with the game. You do have an interesting premise, it just needs a lot of work.

Hoo boy, where do I even start.
Well, I'll begin by saying I've played every major MMO out there and none have made me fall in love with the game as much as Wildstar did. - You begin your journey in the planet Nexus, free to explore, study, settle and protect this new-found planet. - The game is free to play in every meaning of the word. You can buy cash shop items just from playing the game, so you don't need to spend a cent. But by the end of the day you just have that urge to pay just to support the people who made this game so awesome.

I highly recommend giving this game another chance if you haven't yet done so.
- The starting area and tutorial/introduction has been streamlined.
- The Esper class is tweaked so it feels more active.
- The Challenge reward system is different and gives you points to level up towards grab bag rewards and currencies as opposed to grinding for that specific housing item and hoping your RNG is good.
-------->Instead of having to grind for specific housing items, you grind for a specific currency.
- F2P! The system is very good and NOT P2W at all. Everything that can be bought in the store can also be bought just by playing the game.
- The dye system reminds me of GW2, in that you can dye different sections for each piece of armor and there are different dyes to collect and unlock for your character.
- Previous items that were "per character only" are now account-wide.

- The soundtrack is amazing. Probably one of the best game OSTs I've heard in awhile aside from FFXIV.
- Don't let the visual style hold you back. I mean, people are going crazy over Overwatch and that has some pretty cartoony graphics. Don't be a hypocrite and use the art style as an excuse to dislike the game!
- The housing system is one of the best! It's especially fun to visit other people's housing plots. Some people get really creative and you wonder just how they did what they did.
- The crafting mini-game is a nice breath of fresh air from the usual crafting in other games.
I've been cutting back on FFXIV and playing Wildstar more often. I'm thoroughly enjoying the leveling experience without the pressure of a subscription, going at my own leisurely pace.

Okay; so, I love this game and I think it's hilarious. I got it on sale, and I have enjoyed it well over the normal price of ten bucks. This game, like a lot of the other reviews are saying, is better with friends. It's also incredibly difficult in singleplayer at times as if you die, you restart kind of thing. I thought the game's best parts were at the first few chapters, and then my experience slowly degraded from there. The fights went from fun and unqiue to just kind of frustratingly hard enemies being thrown at you for the whole stage/area thing. In the first half of the game, the game has really casual-type gameplay, with you not really being punished (Note, I am not saying these chapters because you don't get punished) and you being able to cast new, creative types of magick and just messing around. However, shortly after, the game just expects you to know all of the best castings, so it's very linear and repetitive from there. And, after a while, you'll eventually figure out some of the absolutely broken castings (Such as the "steam-beam-supreme", (I had the displeasure of being a part of the naming process with my friend) which does incredibly high damage per second) and just eliminates all of the creativity of casting spells. Some of the magicks (Lightning Bolt comes to mind) are also incredibly powerful and spam-able; they're all you really need for the whole game. I also got kind of bored after beating this game, but I generally do that with games, so it doesn't really count. It may also be because I logged ~60 hours in the week.
TL;DR, very fun, worse singleplayer, bad fights, creativity diminishes after roughly halfway through.

PROS
-The STILL magnificent combat that is the same as other Borderlands games.
- Great playable characters (Especiallly Claptrap!!) that have awesome special attacks that give even more variety to the gameplay.
- Creative Weapons that influence you to level up your character just to use that AWESOME Rocket Launcher or Rifle.

- Good Story (Story is not as creative and interesting than Borderlands 2 but WAY better than original Borderlands.) with great characters that are from previous Borderlands characters. Also has some funny new characters. (Nurse Nina replaces Dr. Zed in this game and is in my opinion a better character/
- Pretty cool, fun, and tough boss fights especially in the end. (Again, not as good as Borderlands 2 battles, but still fun and creative.)
- A good variety of enemies to fight. The aliens towards the end of the game were really tough and fun to fight.
Cons
- The story antagonists were sort of bland and generic (Especially Zarpedon, the mayor was a little better but not so much.)
- The laser weapons seemed underpowered compared to other guns  (A level 24 laser gun seemed less powerful than a level 22 assault rife.)
- The checkpoints and save points sometimes did not work unless you completed an objective or side quest (During the end I was spawned back in an area that I have already completed  many times.)
- The main story was sort of shorter than Borderlands 2 (I completed Borderlands 2 in 23 hours and I completed Pre Sequel in 14 hours.)
- It seemed like some of the boss battles in the game seeemed unecessary to have (The RK5 battle was kind of annoying.)
- The side quests did not seem as fun as the other Borderlands games.
- It is almost impossible to beat this game unless you do the side quests or kill enemies for hours to level up.
- The skill tree did not seem as creative and seemed more geared towards cooperative players.
I very well enjoyed this game since I am a fan of the other Borderlands games.  The game is very similar to the other Borderlands games in the series but does have some new elements to appeal to Borderlands fans with the zero gravity on the moon, creative elemental/new types of weapons, and the new playable characters. If you are new to the Borderlands series, play Borderlands 2 first to see if you would like this game. If you were not a fan of Borderlands 2, you may not like this game either. But I still think this is a great game that I will replay at least once.

While some may argue it's less polished in storyline compared to BL2, I subscribe to the Doom philosophy where storyline is expected but I don't really care. They also argue it has less endgame raid content, but overall I think the Pre-Sequel improves and polishes the gameplay quite a lot.   In addition, the setting is much more fresh and interesting than BL2.
(These are compared to BL2)
Pros:
- Classes are way more intricate; Lots of mechanics that weave together very well. (Played Aurelia the most so far)
- Cryo subbed in for Slag.  Late game Slag in BL2 felt required, and detracted from the game, imo.
- Less robots.  BL2 had way too many armor mobs which made corrosive too mandatory.
- Anti grav mechanics add a lot, and give it a unique feel.
Cons:
- You get too many points for the size of the class trees.  This is offset a bit by the fact that MOST of the options are very desirable, which lead to hard choices despite.
- Less content?   I guess the studio shut down?  I'm not here for some WoW-style endgame raiding, so this doesn't affect me too much.  I don't expect to be playing this game for years; It's doing its expected job well.
Overall, I feel more engaged with the mechanics of this game compared to BL2, and I'm loving the mass effecty atmosphere.   I'm having a great time.  (If you can't tell, my hours played aren't logged on steam)

If you like the idea of a post-apocalyptic, reclaimed by nature world populated by the machine life-forms, you should consider getting this game. I'd say it's well worth the price of admission, given the quality of the storyline, the engaging and fun combat systems as well as the sountrack and so on. Rant:
Let me begin by saying that I personally am very interested in the field of AI, and that some of my favorite movies include Ex Machina, I,Robot, etc etc.
Hence, the concept of Nier enticed me and I ended up buying the game, with not that much of an idea of how the game would be, I liked the idea of a post-apocalyptic world reclaimed by nature and populated with machines sort of thing.
And then I started playing, and I've been absorbed by the world platinum has created. There are no humans as such so far in the game, but the machines and the Androids(The ones we play as) have such interesting characters, and the tale that's told is very captivating, and also emotional. I personally got very invested with the characters and the world as a whole.
The combat in the game is pretty nice, it's hack and slash, but your customization comes mainly in the form of your pod. The pod can do stuff like auto-use health items, that makes one less thing for you to have to worry about. You can also put in upgrades like evade range up, etc etc to suit your playstyle. The pod is very useful, and there are a total of 3 in game, one that you get by default and another two that are hidden in the world.
And now to the world. The world looks amazing, although it feels empty at times, but perhaps that was intended. The whole ruined city that's reclaimed by nature, falling apart is pretty well done, and the music really really complements the game very well.
Buy the game.

Let's start with the most important thing that I see alot of people overlook. If you play and beat your first run. DO NOT STOP. I won't say why for the sake of spoilers, but if the real experience ended there, the game would be very mediocre.
NieR: Automata had a story that takes you by storm. When you are truly done... you will know. I approached this game with an expectation of a typical action hack 'n' slash game, and by the first ending, there was a few neat twists. The twists were really nothing to write home about. I was about to dismiss the game as "alright", but I decided to push through because there seems to be alot of craze about "different endings". I feel that's a little bit of the wrong term. It's not so much as "different endings" as playthroughs that expand what you know and make the world as truly fascinating as it is.
The soundtrack is fantastic, almost every single zone, town or boss has a theme that really sticks with you. It is definetly not a forgettable sound track. Infact, the soundtrack was something that really convinced me to try this game in the first place.
The visuals are also phenominal, though I can only imagine how much greater it would be if some people didn't run into resolution issues (which aren't gamebreaking by any means, just a small damper). I'm not sure how common these issues are however =/.
Overall this game is an emotional roller coaster. I was thinking about how beautiful the whole story was for days after. It took me a long time to soak in every bit I could from the characters and their developement. It is possibly one of my favourite stories presented by a video game ever. Yoko Taro, you are something else pal.
