This title is a game that became very popular for something really silly: 2B's appearance. Though it probably has to be expected, the design is very appealing, and so that's what people encounter first. But one shouldn't forget that this game has some substance to it. To be completely frank, this title was my first in the setting, and the first game from Yoko Taro. So both my knowledge regarding the lore and history of previous games is non-existent.
I actually had to upgrade my rig in order to play this game, and visually it was worth it. Perhaps not the best looking game out there, sometimes the texture fading makes certain locations look not too impressive, but there also are moments where the mere visuals are captivating (enough). Overall I myself am not too critical when it comes to graphics, I more follow a "good enough works just fine" route, so take my opinion on this with a piece of grain.
The combat itself is based a lot around dodging, especially during bullet hell sections. Having to double-tap a movement key to dodge is rather unhandy, but the true problem lies within the default keybinding: I have died several times because a simple action like using a heal item takes a (comparably) complex key combination that most likely will require you to use both hands unless you re-bind some of the keys. It gets even worse when you want to use an item you didn't previously used, for example switching from a small recovery item to a medium one; at times you even accidentally switch to another item, which can lead to possibly infuriating results.
Another problem is that during certain bullet hell sections of the game (during hacking for example) aiming with the mouse is next to impossible which drastically restricts the angles you can shoot at targets and through that increases the difficulty of these sections.
Nevertheless and despite it possibly being infuriating at times, I personally find the combat and port sufficing, again perhaps not the best or most innovative, but it remains fun for the most part.
I won't spoil anything. There is just a single thing I want to point out here:
Let me actually try something different here, namely try to figure out to whom I would not recommend this game. You need some endurance for this game, both physical and mental. You need to be open. Sometimes a mere NPC can toss up a question that can very well stick to you for a while, something that's not just rather random, but that has a deeper philosophical meaning to it. Such questions often don't actually have an answer, and the game rarely (perhaps not at all even) tries to give you one. So I believe that to truly enjoy the game to the fullest, you need to be open to think about what is going on. Like mentioned above, the combat mostly is alright, but nothing ground breaking. Most should be able to enjoy it alright for a bit, but if that's what has to keep you fully entertained in this game, this maybe isn't the right title for you.
I decided to write this review directly after I received ending E. I have tried multiple times to beat the final section completely on my own, my screen was almost completely filled messages from other players. I refused to give up until I have wasted something between 1 to 2 hours. Then I accepted the help from a stranger, and realized..it was never meant to be beaten alone. It perhaps wasn't virtually impossible, but all odds were stacked against you a million to one. That means I literally only could do this because of someone else. This ending basically has reached a meta level that goes beyond the game itself, and going through that experience rendered me with a hollow feeling, the kind of state you're in when you just have finished something amazing, something you genuinely enjoyed; may it be a book, a series, a VN..or a game.
I want other people to see and enjoy for themselves, too.

Ok, for a seemingly simple looking puzzle game, this one is surprisingly addictive.  It feels kind of like minesweeper, but with different ways of visualizing the pattern instead of just the number of "mines" surrounding a block. My wife even enjoys this game quite a bit, and she doesn't play games often.
My main gripe with this game is that the controls feel backwards from minesweeper in that you left click the block that is part of the pattern (a mine), and right click an empty block.  I have played a good bit of minesweeper in the past and right click for mine and left click for empty was a very hard habit to break.  I had to restart many puzzles due to click confusion.  Unfortunately the game doesn't make you restart when you make a mistake, but it does keep track of the number of mistakes.  If you want to go for the perfectionist achievement, you have to beat every level without mistakes, and it doesn't seem to tell you which levels you made mistakes on if you choose to complete the stage with mistakes.  I get around this problem by restarting the level when I make a mistake.
Overall, this is a great addition to the library!

Party Hard is one of those games that satisfy one's lust for challenge, style, and music. I originally bought Party Hard after seeing it's wonderous concept mixed with genocidal Hotline Miami feel. It's kind of a stealthy version of Hotline Miami I guess you could say. Either way the game is really quite fun.
Party Hard has a relatively untouched concept which is really great because I've always loved stealth games. While the mechanics can be a bit weird such as people spotting you through the open door despite it being hid off to the side, or cops becoming stuck unable to catch you thanks to their chase A.I. becoming breakable with certain objects, the game still plays great. Strategy is another key feate of this game. Maybe you spread force the crowd to disperse by dancing like a pro or maybe rig some speakers to blow up half the crowd.  The are various ways to deal with the people and with each map being randomized with different traps each time, adding replay value.
This game also leaks style. From the design of the Party Hard Killer and the characters, to the jamming music on every level, it reminds me alot of Hotline Miami with pixel characters and pixel blood and beat you can jam to whenever you feel all while in an 80's esque setting. The story is also pretty nice with a neat twist but is a bit predictable.
The game's major flaws come from the AI and RNG. While the RNG is neat mechanic that makes you think on your feet and adds replay value, it also make clearing out crowds or dealing with near impossible because sometimes the crowd would rather jam to your dance moves or beat you up than actually leave the area, making it hard to find isolated kills. Not to mention some traps and body dumping sites act as great hiding spots to perform kills. Not to mention that Guards are near impossible to isolate and kill without a trap. Navigation bugs also exist that actually can cause you to get stuck in spots that for some reason you could walk into but not out.
Despite it's flaws, the game is actually really fun and rewarding when you beat that one level that seemed impossible to beat but you fought through and found a way. The style is also very appealing with nice bright neon colors and 80's esque design choices that really give it that touch of beauty that I and many others seek so much for in games.

I've only put a few hours into this game, but can already tell there's a mountain of possibilities here. Definitely BUY this, support the developers and follow it closely!
If you like classic RTS games like Settlers, Majesty or the Anno series, this is a very well-produced hybrid of those in progress. You build a city, manage resource production / distribution, train a military and fight off monsters / other cities. There's also a roguelike, sandbox element in that your city exists on an overworld map with other cities who will trade with you, invade you, or be subject to invasions/raids.
Though it's not complete yet, it's clear that the developers have done a good, solid job of building the engine and foundations -- that is to say, from here it seems like a lot of the groundwork has been done and the rest will simply be adding content and features.
Features I would like to see implemented in the future:
- Greater varience of buildings/skins, or random rotations (at present there is only one "look" for houses, for example, which can make blocks of houses which you need lots of, look somewhat bland or boring)
- More supply/demand dynamic for trading. Resources often have a relatively set cost that hardly deviates at all. I would like to see something implemented where resources will fluctuate more heavily in price, even between other cities. It makes trading more exciting/dynamic, as currently if two other cities want to buy your resource, they will both largely offer an identical price. I would like to see this fluctuate, so that a player would have to pay attention to trading -- and could even mean that a player running a "trading village" could be economically viable, as buying resources low from certain cities and selling high to others at a profit could potentially work.
- More permanent overworld map changes as the game progresses. i.e. other cities going to war and "taking over" rivals, which would in essence form small "kingdoms" (say, a certain NPC city will then own 2 or 3 cities). Also perhaps something like "invasions" of other cities from monsters, so that cities would become "monster citadels" or "lairs" if they are taken over.
- More military options (siege weapons, different units (perhaps using shields and swords as resources as well))
- Better "fortification" options. Right now there are stone walls and stone gatehouses, but only wooden stockades and no wooden gatehouses. This would be a valuable addition.
- More monsters, though I think the devs have already mentioned wanting to do this. Goblins, orcs, dragons, etc. etc. etc.
Overall though, great game, one of my most favourite in recent memory, and I can't wait until the content starts being more fully fleshed out. There's so much potential here.

This is probably the best indie title of the genre for years to come. Splatter is an incredible dense and atmospheric top-down zombie shooter with a unique Max Payne noir style. Everything in this game has so much artistic detail put into it. The latest version is fully voiced, the voice acting is decent and supports the atmosphere.
Animation, lighting and effects (especially the splatter) are great, the noir-storytelling is awesome and the gameplay offers despite its linearity a lot of variety that keeps you motivated. Besides ammo and health you collect money to invest in upgrades for different weapons (genre typical pistol, shotgun, AR, flamer,  RPG, ...).
Be warned though, the medium difficulty already gives you a taste of survival in a zombie apocalypse:
You run blindly into the streets, you'll die.
You rush into a room without checking your six, you'll die.
You let yourself get surrounded or cornered, you'll die.
You rush into a corridor without thinking of a emergency exit, ... guess what... you'll die.
There are a few things you have to set up in the options though:
First, turn down music and effect volume and turn up the voice volume.
Second, set the control style to 'cardinal direction' or you'll be moving like Jill in the first Resident Evil game.

With an assortment of top-down shooters to choose from, Splatter is a gem.
With the exception of one level segment and (to my knowledge) a bug only I've encountered thus far regarding the final boss, there aren't many flaws to be found in the game beyond those that are minor (occasional spelling errors in the dialogue and item texts being the only thing that stands out readily and even then they aren't hindering enjoyment of the game overall).
Dreamworlds has managed to nail exactly what makes this particular type of game fun to play vs. turning it into an interminably difficult chore. The dialogue and art-based cutscenes don't drag on longer than they need to, leaving plenty of time to enjoy soaking multiple parts of a level's floor with the blood of enemies.
The game's story is one that, whether intentional or not, is reminiscent of the best "worst" B-movies of all time (with voice acting to match). Going in expecting the plot to make sense is not recommended, to say the least. It's not confusing but it certainly doesn't have a strong foothold on logic either (which is a good thing, since a game like this would only be hurt by taking itself too seriously).
Gameplay is rather typical for the type - you run and gun down hordes of monstrosities, with the occasional boss or arena-styled fight thrown in for variation. A difference in the formula comes in the ability to toss a flare to the ground which will act as a temporary repellent for a majority of the creatures that want to tear you to pieces. There are also a small number of collectible items to be had for those looking to explore the levels, mostly extra cash to be used to upgrade existing weapons in your arsenal (which is generous but not particularly extensive beyond essentials like a pistol, shotgun and flamethrower to name a few) but there are others such as pieces of a flak jacket and a weapon upgrade that negates putting all your money into upgrading the starting pistol.
The environments, each containing destructible elements, are varied enough that you aren't left looking at a parade of the same color all the time (though eventually you'll be looking at red and green frequently once the bodies begin to drop) and the lighting in the game affords it some nice tricks in terms of enemies that remain stationary until the player comes into their line of sight.
Splatter also has a medium element of replay built into it. Beyond the collectibles, there are branching story points that can be taken on subsequent plays. While they aren't as in-depth as those featured in more story-focused games, they do serve as a nice and simple way of extending the time one spends with the game. Dreamworlds has also included a survival mode, complete with leaderboards, which should satisfy anyone looking for an arcade-style experience.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough, especially if you're the type who has enjoyed any top-down shooter made within the last decade or so. It certainly isn't the kind of game everyone can enjoy but if you're willing to give it a chance, it just might surprise you (as it did me).

Splatter – Blood Red Edition is a top down twin-stick shooter set right at the outbreak of a zombie invasion.  The game begins as you, Max, wakes up in his apartment with the sound of gunfire and havoc outside...
The story while not particularly original, science goes wrong and the result is zombies, is told very well through a series of old school Max Payne like panels and all characters are fully voiced.  The VO is decent and the English translation could use some work, but there is an awful lot of style here in the story-telling.  The best part of the story is there is no Mr/Ms Exposition to be found, all the characters you meet along the way are in as bad a situation as you, knowing very little of what is going on, they are just trying to survive.  The game takes place across more than a dozen levels with optional sub quests and boss fights mixed in.
As said, the view is top down and the graphics are very good for the price.  Light plays a huge part in the game-play and is translated very well here, how is bends round corners and through doorways.  Very early on in the game you find yourself overwhelmed and here the primary mechanic comes into play, using light to scare off the zombies via either from ambient sources, or from thrown flares.  Charging head long into a darkened area full of zombies ensures a quick death.  Vehicles also play a part in the game, from riding shotgun on the back of a truck with a machine gun to mowing down the zombies in a combine harvester.
There are many guns to pick up, from the initial pistol with unlimited ammo, to grenade launchers, Laser guns, shotguns, flame throwers and more.  All the weapons can be upgraded up to 4 times and the extra damage and abilities will become vital to your survival.  Upgrades come through purchasing them at work benches with cash you collect that is lying around the levels, or inside destructibles.  You can also collect pieces of a golden pistol that eventually provides an extremely powerful upgrade to the pistol.  Since the pistol is the only weapon with unlimited ammo and you can't purchase ammo, only pick it up, the pistol will quickly become your best friend.
Things can get very hectic at higher levels and will provide a very good challenge to even the best players.  All in all this is very good example of the genre at the lower price scale and the story will keep you interested to the end.
7.5/10

Splatter is a brilliantly crafted top-down shooter that mixes the best of the genres game mechanics with a solid story straight out of a (purposefully) B-grade zombie movie. It operates on a simple concept; did you ever want your top-down to be less pure action and more gloomy ambience and storytelling? If you said yes then Splatter is for you, but if you said no you should probably move on as a large part of the game is devoted to telling a story and building an air of tension.
- Tight controls.
- Varied Weapons.
- Progressive weapon upgrades.
- Incredibly rich and engrossing ambiance.
- Deep story (for the genre) that even includes optional bits.
- Solid length (around 6 hours) with extensive replayability (and achievements for those that care) .
- Good soundtrack.
- Leaderboards (again, for those who care).
- Dumb enemy AI is dumb (but made up for with intelligent level design that takes advantage of their usual blind charge).
- Some weapons are blatantly better, meaning some sit about and are never used.
- While the graphics themselves ARE nice, I’m not fond of the film-noir filter that grey-scales your surroundings.
- Unstable difficulty flailing between painfully easy and crushingly difficult (mostly notable on the hardest difficulty during “defense” missions).
In short the positives the game has are far greater than its negatives and it’s definitely worth your time. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys the genre, especially if they’re also fans of the super cheesy but fun classic zombie movies. With good gameplay, a fun story, and a high degree of replayability anyone with a passing interest in the genre will get their monies worth and an experience to remember.

I really wanted to love Nier: Automata. I was a huge fan of the original Nier and I never thought we'd get a sequel, much less one by Platinum, who seemed like the perfect studio to bring exhilerating combat to the game. It really seemed to have everything going for it, yet other than the soundtrack I struggle to think of anything I felt Automata does well.
The combat is grossly dumbed down Bayonetta, where there are no combos (save for one, sort of) and there's no drawback to spamming dodge and being invinsible 99% of the time. The game's difficulty curve mostly seems to come from giving the same three enemies progressively more absurd health bars and throwing them at you in ever more baffling numbers. The upgrade mechanic is abusable in the extreme and within 90 minutes you can accidentally make yourself effectively invinsible.
The plot is impossible to care about, and people returning from Nier 1 will already know one of the main twists
. The characters range from "stern" to "generic whiney male anime protagonist who's bland enough for whiney anime fans to project themselves on to", and when the game is really trying to pull emotional punches they fall completely flat because you don't care about who these people are or what happens to them because they have no personalities at all. Several times they bend the characters over backwards just because the plot needs them to suddenly do an about face on their stance on robot-genocide.
Thematically, Automata is basically a pile of existentialist ideas for you to pick over at your leisure and say "Yep, I remember reading Camus." It has nothing to actually
though, it's more like it's recommending you go read about existentialism on your own because forming views is hard.
Automata wants to do what Dark Souls 1 did in keeping fast travel away from you so you can admire the dramatic decaying scenery and feel the scale, but the landscapes are bland and muted, and you just end up skipping across them looking at the same five ugly grey buildings over and over again.
Even the act structure is broken, with the first and second playthroughs being 90% identical, there was no reason to pad the game out so grossly before finally letting you have the second half in NG+2, 3 and 4.
That said I'm glad this game got made, I'd rather Platinum take big risks and end up with big failures than keep pumping out Bayonetta forever (as much as I love Bayonetta), because that's how we end up with the really special games like Nier 1.

You might be thinking, as I did, "but it's more Borderlands. How can that be bad?". The answer is The Pre-Sequel. Few characters. The higher-jumps/low-grav is pointless because the level design took it into account so everything is just higher/further away. The jokes are poor. Story meh. Loot abysmal.
If Borderlands 2 is The Empire Strikes Back, then The Pre-Sequel is Attack of the Clones.

Wildstar is the MMO that I can't put down. After my stint of hardcore raiding in WoW from Vanilla through Cata, I thought I would never enjoy an MMO the same way. Nostalgia kept me playing WoW far longer than I really loved the game and I was very turned off by the style and feel from the initial advertisements I saw for Wildstar (WoW clone, anyone?). However, Wildstar not only surpassed my expectations, but blew me out of the water with its unique personality and how fun the game is. It is something I have kept coming back to since playing it in beta.
Other reviews here go into the bits and pieces of where it is great a lot more thoroughly than I will, however, the PvE experience is something that holds up and even surpasses my favorite raid in WoW (Naxx40). The challenge is more than, hey lets add an ability or two from normal mode and make everything have more HP and hit harder... the game demands that you adapt your character for each encounter (you can change 'spec' and abilities on the fly) and that you master game mechanics. A few good healers, tanks, and dps won't carry you. You **** up, you die. Wildstar raiding is the Dark Souls of MMOs. And with that comes the same satisfaction with taking down a boss or mastering some mechanic that was murdering your face.
The story of Wildstar is something that I have also greatly enjoyed and am excited to see unfold more. But, be warned, they do not hit you in the face with the story. Sure, they have the questline to follow for region/zone/world that will get you the bare bones of whats happening. But, read, explore, and collect. Items in the game fill in so many blanks and are actually enjoyable to read as they are filled with the quirky personality that pervades Nexus. Datacubes quickly became one of my favorite lore devices as the voice acting for them is phenomonal and over the course of leveling, you begin to feel as if you know the Eldan who created them. They pull me into the scope and full impact of the lore in the same way the story of Gascoigne's family does in Bloodborne (if you get that reference, I like you a lot).
All that being said, there is plenty of content at max level for people who have no intention to raid and the housing system is amazing along with costuming and other customization systems. The barrier to entry isn't as high as a Dark Souls game (if that worries you from above comments).
TLDR: I highly recommend giving Wildstar a shot. It has its quirks and isn't for everyone, but its worth the time to figure out if its a fit for you, because if it is, you're in for a wild ride, Cupcake.

Now that this game is Free-to-Play, I'd say absolutely try it out if you're looking for a new MMO.

Many of the negative reviews are correct: this game can be hard, frustrating, and arbitrary.  That said, it is also fun, quirky, and endearing.  Let me explain.
The good parts of this game are the simple, rewarding gameplay, interesting level design, and good, if repetitive, soundtrack.  Levels mostly seem well thought out and death has no real consequences, which makes the occasional arbitrary arrest less frustrating.
The bad is that, especially in early levels, it can take many, many tries to beat a level.  The poison in particular can take some getting used to as if you're spotted near a dead body it is automatically assumed you committed the murder.  This is also true of NPCs, and cops are frequently seen hauling them off to jail.  That said, with the exception of the Miami level, evading capture is pretty easy.  Also the less said about the terrible voice acting, the better.
One problem stems from no real tutorial.  You get some info from newspaper clippings on the ground, but generally the first time you see a bouncer, you're going to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked and have no idea what just happened.  Reading the clippings and just checking the pause screen for controls helps too.  Be curious and try new things.
Difficulty peaks in the Miami level and the rest of the game falls pretty quickly after that.  According to Steam I've played it to completion in about 5.4 hours, and that sounds about right.  I immediately bought the DLC and look forward to playing it too.
The game has some replay, as the traps are random so every play through a level is a little different.  Also apparently there are extra characters to unlock and a co-op mode.
I'd call it an interesting diversion and well worth picking up on sale.   Maybe even at full price?

I love this game. Hexcells takes the classic game of Minesweeper and pushes it to a whole new level. Instead of squares, you get hexagons - this sounds more difficult, and some of the levels are pretty challenging, but it was a great improvement. There's no guessing, either; you're always given just enough information to complete the level with zero mistakes. You can listen to the ambient, relaxing music as you test your brain with these 36 levels.
Not only are there numbers on the hexes, but once you get far enough there are also line headers (numbers above rows or beside columns) as well as counters on some of the blue tiles that tell you how many blue hexes are within the highlighted area. I think this game is unique, intuitive and overall very satisfactory. I got it on sale for less than a dollar, but I would have purchased it at full price. It's worth it.
If you're looking to test your puzzle solving skills, this game (and the entire series) is something to try out.

Hexcells is the first game of its' series.
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're minimalistic. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio.
There is no difficulty mode option that's assigned. But each of the puzzles has their own difficult.
Hexcells is closely similar to mine sweeper game. So the objective is rather simple to figure out which cells to make blue and which cells to make black.
There are total of three slots with six world that has twenty-four puzzles to solve. The first world for each of the three slots are automatically unlocked. Completing one world will unlocked the next one. All of these puzzles can be replayed after the first go around. Please do note that the puzzles in the other two slots are the same as the ones in the first slot.
There's no time limit in this game. Allowing the individual take as much time that they want to solve each of the puzzles.
There six achievements for this game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
Final thoughts, it's an neat game to play and enjoy. As for the game's replay value it's low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

"Here i find myself in the midst of chaos,but everything breaks if exposed to enough pressure" listening to that and watching the static cinema that came with it i thought i was in a "MAX PAYNE" game,but no i was in the rather enjoyable and action packed shooter that is "SPLATTER : BLOOD RED EDITION".
Ok when you start to play you wake up in your house and after some rambling to yourself wander of outside,*BANG* bullets everywhere and the army telling you to get of the street you follow them and then you get to find your first weapon the obligatory hand gun (which has infinite ammo,of course it does DUH).
As the game progressess you gain acess to more powerfull and impressive weapons (shotgun,rocket launcher ECT) and trust me when i tell you,you are going to need them as some of the boss battles and even some of the normal battles (you do get over run at times) get quite hard and the enemy can overwhelm you if you use the wrong weapon.
Now the most easiest and best way to help from getting overcome is to throw a flare,see the dark abomination's you face have a fear and total dislike of the light ("wonder where we have seen this game play element before" "i dont know ALAN,WAKE up") which can give you time to re-gather your thoughts and blow them away whilst they scuttle away from the bright and painfull light that encompasses them.This game play mechanic is one that you will use to your advantage on numerous occasions and will save your neck more than once.
As the game plays on you will encounter some puzzles but they are usually of the push button variety and are allways easy to overcome and you will never feel lost as to what to do next and this is a good thing as the action should (and does) take a front seat to all else in game.
The graphics in game do a good job and for this sort of game handle really well with no lag no matter how many enemies are on screen (shouldent be in this sort of game),the music in game is good but at times you do find that the spoken dialogue is overshadowed by the music or the gunfire happening in game (minor quibble but i did miss out on some conversations due to this).
The story and script are both good and at times you do feel like you are in a different game (MAX PAYNE anyone),but at times it does feel all a little B-MOVIE but actually this is not a bad thing and does suit this game right down to the ground.
Will you play this game and would you want to even buy it,well enjoy a game that is all bang for its buck and want something that will itch those trigger finger blues then i would say yes,if that doesnt sound like you and you want more from your game than gun blasting action then i would say look elswhere.
In my humble opinion this is one enjoyable blast and i would fully reccomend it just dont expect it to be one of the best games you have ever played just one of the best blasters you have ever played and enjoy it for what it is "ONE HELL OF A BLASTING GOOD TIME"

GOF2 was originally an IOS game released in response to rising popularity in it's predecessor GOF.
GOF2 proceeded to expand upon GOF1's features and add new ones, attempting to turn the game from a linear space dogfighter into a more 'open' 'explorable' map of different solar systems, where you choose how to progress.
Before I proceed, please understand that this game is the vanilla GOF2 ported onto PC with supposedly better but easily ignorable visuals. NO further DLC has been added, nor will it ever be, given the developer's (FishLabs) abhorrent attitude to the PC community.
You play as Keith T. Maxwell, a space 'soldier' who is whisked several decades into the future after a malfunction in engaging his hyperspace drive. Keith is now stranded in an unfamiliar section of the universe with no money, no ship (now obsolete and damaged beyond repair).
Thankfully he is rescued, and brought to the nearest space station. Here you start with a basic ship and no money. To begin with you must slowly make money by mining asteroids to pay off your saviour. Then you are let loose to follow the storyline of trying to re-assimilate yourself in this new sector of space.
You learn of a hostile alien race known as the Voids. They control wormholes between their homeworld and any parts of the universe to attack various other space stations, wreaking havoc and causing distress to all of the resident alien factions. It is up to you, with the help of others, to defeat the Voids and restore peace to the universe.
Thus the storyline is linear, predictable and rather boring. If you value this aspect of game design, you have nothing to find here :P
The whole 'universe' as such in the game is from Keith's POV a previously uncharted sector of the universe. It consists of 22 Star systems. Each has an un-visitable star surrounded which is surrounded by several un-visitable planets. (all gameplay takes place either in space surrounding the space station or within the space station itself)
Orbiting (more like next to) each planet is a space station which one can enter (not seamlessly - loading screens are key) within which various functions may be performed:
- Automatic ship-repairs (armour bar fills up - yay)
- Automatic Updating of Steam Achievement Progress#
- Space Lounge (talk to different people for side objectives)
-
:
- Shop (sell/buy resources, equipment, weaponry)
- Ship (equip equipment, weaponry)

The higher-jumps/low-grav is pointless because the level design took it into account so everything is just higher/further away. The jokes are poor. Story meh. Loot abysmal.

Rant:
Let me begin by saying that I personally am very interested in the field of AI, and that some of my favorite movies include Ex Machina, I,Robot, etc etc.
Hence, the concept of Nier enticed me and I ended up buying the game, with not that much of an idea of how the game would be, I liked the idea of a post-apocalyptic world reclaimed by nature and populated with machines sort of thing.
And then I started playing, and I've been absorbed by the world platinum has created. There are no humans as such so far in the game, but the machines and the Androids(The ones we play as) have such interesting characters, and the tale that's told is very captivating, and also emotional. The combat in the game is pretty nice, it's hack and slash, but your customization comes mainly in the form of your pod. And now to the world. The world looks amazing, although it feels empty at times, but perhaps that was intended. The whole ruined city that's reclaimed by nature, falling apart is pretty well done, and the music really really complements the game very well.
Buy the game.

Thanks to Steam, I was finally able to finish this game last year.
I started playing this game when I bought the game of the year edition box in 2002 and I still have the save files to prove it.  I played the game being completely immersed in a world that was just so cool and the ability to solve problems in a multitude of ways.  I fell in love with the characters and I really cared about what happened to them.
I was playing the game until the time that I flew to Japan on September 11, 2002, a year exactly after 911 and carrring my cat that died two years ago.  So not only has this game made a huge impression on me as being the best game of all time but it also brings back memories of great change and turmoil in my life.  The one big big big point was that I was not able to finish the game before I left.
After I came to Japan, I had no time for several years to play any PC games at all.  Trying to be a good English teacher, learning Japanese, dealing with living with my Japanese-in-laws (who I lived with), watching a dying mother-in-law from dialysis and how to farm for the first time all accumulated in having very little time or mental consideration for games.  This is from someone who constantly played games from when my family bought a commodore 64 maybe in 1982.
It wasn't until years later that I was finally able to think about buying a PC, let alone playing computer games.  Once I finally bought the computer and I transferred all the files off the hard drive that I brought with me from Canada.  I realized that it was maybe too late to play the games on a new computer with the old spec games.  So I played the limited amount of games that I was able to buy over the internet and ship the boxes to Japan.  It wasn't cheap either.
That all changed after I found Steam.
I was able to buy games old and new so easily and without waiting for the boxes to be shipped overseas.
I also noticed that Steam took care of some of the problems of playing old games on new computers.
Because of Steam, I was able to buy Deus Ex again and use the old save files that I brought from Canada. So I started to play Deus Ex again and finish it.
I cannot thank Steam enough for my ability to not only finish Deus Ex but finally being able to bring some closure to my life in Canada and also being able to finish one of the greatest games of all time in my opinion.
Thank you very much Steam.

I think the developers added some things to the game to make it feel like things like Hotline with high-octance action, but it's designed to punish the player for reckless behaviour, even going as far to add a variety of enemy that is capable of knocking you out for standing close to them in some situations.
Essentially, I think it's interesting enough to consider a purchase when on sale, but it doesn't really do anything new or interesting enough to recommend otherwise. It descends from strategy and pseudo-stealth elements into 'wait in this room until another six people enter then start murdering them from the exit of the room toward the back, stabbing them as they run past you'.

Let's start with the most important thing that I see alot of people overlook. If you play and beat your first run. DO NOT STOP. I won't say why for the sake of spoilers, but if the real experience ended there, the game would be very mediocre.
NieR: Automata had a story that takes you by storm. When you are truly done... you will know. I approached this game with an expectation of a typical action hack 'n' slash game, and by the first ending, there was a few neat twists. The twists were really nothing to write home about. I was about to dismiss the game as "alright", but I decided to push through because there seems to be alot of craze about "different endings". I feel that's a little bit of the wrong term. It's not so much as "different endings" as playthroughs that expand what you know and make the world as truly fascinating as it is.
The soundtrack is fantastic, almost every single zone, town or boss has a theme that really sticks with you. It is definetly not a forgettable sound track. Infact, the soundtrack was something that really convinced me to try this game in the first place.
The visuals are also phenominal, though I can only imagine how much greater it would be if some people didn't run into resolution issues (which aren't gamebreaking by any means, just a small damper). I'm not sure how common these issues are however =/.
Overall this game is an emotional roller coaster. I was thinking about how beautiful the whole story was for days after. It took me a long time to soak in every bit I could from the characters and their developement. It is possibly one of my favourite stories presented by a video game ever. Yoko Taro, you are something else pal.

This title is a game that became very popular for something really silly: 2B's appearance. Though it probably has to be expected, the design is very appealing, and so that's what people encounter first. But one shouldn't forget that this game has some substance to it. To be completely frank, this title was my first in the setting, and the first game from Yoko Taro. So both my knowledge regarding the lore and history of previous games is non-existent.
I actually had to upgrade my rig in order to play this game, and visually it was worth it. Perhaps not the best looking game out there, sometimes the texture fading makes certain locations look not too impressive, but there also are moments where the mere visuals are captivating (enough). Overall I myself am not too critical when it comes to graphics, I more follow a "good enough works just fine" route, so take my opinion on this with a piece of grain.
The combat itself is based a lot around dodging, especially during bullet hell sections. Having to double-tap a movement key to dodge is rather unhandy, but the true problem lies within the default keybinding: I have died several times because a simple action like using a heal item takes a (comparably) complex key combination that most likely will require you to use both hands unless you re-bind some of the keys. It gets even worse when you want to use an item you didn't previously used, for example switching from a small recovery item to a medium one; at times you even accidentally switch to another item, which can lead to possibly infuriating results.
Another problem is that during certain bullet hell sections of the game (during hacking for example) aiming with the mouse is next to impossible which drastically restricts the angles you can shoot at targets and through that increases the difficulty of these sections.
Nevertheless and despite it possibly being infuriating at times, I personally find the combat and port sufficing, again perhaps not the best or most innovative, but it remains fun for the most part.
I won't spoil anything. There is just a single thing I want to point out here:
Let me actually try something different here, namely try to figure out to whom I would not recommend this game. You need some endurance for this game, both physical and mental. You need to be open. Sometimes a mere NPC can toss up a question that can very well stick to you for a while, something that's not just rather random, but that has a deeper philosophical meaning to it. Such questions often don't actually have an answer, and the game rarely (perhaps not at all even) tries to give you one. So I believe that to truly enjoy the game to the fullest, you need to be open to think about what is going on. Like mentioned above, the combat mostly is alright, but nothing ground breaking. Most should be able to enjoy it alright for a bit, but if that's what has to keep you fully entertained in this game, this maybe isn't the right title for you.
I decided to write this review directly after I received ending E. I have tried multiple times to beat the final section completely on my own, my screen was almost completely filled messages from other players. I refused to give up until I have wasted something between 1 to 2 hours. Then I accepted the help from a stranger, and realized..it was never meant to be beaten alone. It perhaps wasn't virtually impossible, but all odds were stacked against you a million to one. That means I literally only could do this because of someone else. This ending basically has reached a meta level that goes beyond the game itself, and going through that experience rendered me with a hollow feeling, the kind of state you're in when you just have finished something amazing, something you genuinely enjoyed; may it be a book, a series, a VN..or a game.
I want other people to see and enjoy for themselves, too.

First thing you have to know about Wildstar is that it has changed a lot since the launch. A lot of dirt is thrown at the game because of the #hardcore philosophy at the beginning. That is in the past. The game is quite casual-friendly now. There is still a picture in the heads that Wildstar is a very hard game, since it might seem so at first sight, but it really isn't THAT hard. There is some challenge in the gameplay (mainly in it's endgame, not talking about leveling), but it comes in the form of WASD, not farming the best gear. It's not an asian MMO, there are a lot of shortcuts for casuals to enjoy the content fully, you'll discover those in time.
Second important thing is that the game is free. Never mind those DLCs at the main page, those are not for new players, when you will know the game you will know the meaning of those. Those include subscription time and vanity items. You don't need them to enjoy the game. With a free account you got the whole content. You are short only in convenience things like character- and bank slots and receive ingame currencies a bit slower, which is no big deal. In this game you don't pay to unlock parts of the game that are behind walls, and it's not pay to win, in this game you pay (mainly for vanity items) because you like the game, and you want to support it. So there's no reason not to try out if you're interested, you have nothing to lose.
Third and most important thing. There's no denying that Wildstar has a small playerbase at the moment. Because of this, the old community is tight but passionate. They are patient people. There might not be droves of players everywhere, but if you're looking for group content, you'll find it. Look for a guild. Join global channels (I cba to list them but you'll find them in other reviews, or just ask ingame). Socialize, like in a real MMO. It was passion that kept this game alive so far. I'm not gonna say it's the best game ever, but it's a damn fine little game and it's definetly worth a try.

I have fallen face first in love with this game the day I joined at F2P and cannot get up. Take my thoughts as coming from someone who doesn't play many MMOs, Wildstar is more the exception than the rule. I think this will be probably friendly advice if anything, to new players.
As someone who draws for fun, I am extremely partial to art in a game, and Wildstar will deliver a thousandfold on that note. It has a quirky cartoon-animation style that is unlike you have ever seen before. You will either hate it or love it to bits. If you love a good scenery, there will be many times when you just cannot help but stop and say, "Wow". The music will stun you speechless and make you shed many tears in the variety of your desired gender.
If you loved scaling impossible mountains in Skyrim on horseback, play Explorer. If you have an itch to pick up everything you find, love to help other players, and love to have everything at your convenience, play Settler. It's the hardest, but most useful too. (Need a vendor? How about you summon one? Need a taxi? How about you BUILD one?) If you love reading about the lore and getting special buffs from your environment, play Scientist. (Scientists will also be the one to summon groups when you are doing veteran content.) I haven't played Soldier yet, but I think it involves killing even more things, so if neither of the previous ones float your boat, just go with this one.
I will wager, Housing is what you will love the most. People like to call it the "real endgame". The most wonderful money sink ever created, it will be your eternal bittersweet purgatory. For those who are familiar with Fallout or Elder Scrolls games - imagine a completely flexible modding tool like the Creation Kit, in which pretty much every asset is made available to you in some way or the other, either dropping in game or to buy with ingame gold. Some decors are also craftable if you choose that profession. I've seen people build entire towns, spooky underground sewer networks, and forests.
You will have a lot of fighting abilities that you'll have to learn how to use in combos in order to get by. This wasn't an easy process for me at least. Fellow players will gladly give you advice or point you in the direction of a good guide though.
A lot of the content is designed in a way that you will NEED other people's help. Don't be afraid to ask.
In general, you will NEVER find a better community than what I have encountered in this game. People are extremely helpful and kind, no matter what you need help with. Not only ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are rare, but people will go out of their way to help each other and work together.
If you like something from the in-game cash store, you don't NEED to spend real money. If you keep playing, so-called Omnibits will drop which can be used for the same thing. Signature status is also available to buy with ingame gold. (Legally. There is a market for it in-game.)
There are a lot of different currencies in this game used for different purposes. If you feel extremely confused by this, I can assure you, we probably all do.
I haven't played PvP, but many people swear it's amazing. Large-scale PvP group content is organized every Saturday on the Entity server, ask around for it if you are interested.
People call it a dead game, I think for two reasons. One, because most of the current players have moved on from the levelling zones by now, probably decorating the houses on their plot, lol. Two, because they are not joining the right channels. Talk in the zone chat is rare. Start with /chjoin lfg, and you will have more people to chat with than you need.
There is a HUGE RP community also. If you like RPing, look us up.^
Get yourself a hoverboard as soon as you arrive in the main city. That ten gold will feel like a wealth at first, but soon you'll be making money left and right and ten gold will feel like nothing. Hoverboards are both extremely cool, and useful if you have to cross a long distance in an area you haven't explored or are not used to.
Have a look at what mods are available. If you like taking pictures of your character, look up Character Shot. Perspective or EntSpy will help you find things as you level. If you like building on your plot, Katia Builder Toolkit is a must.
Which reminds me: if you see someone called Katia Managan call out in the housing zone "Who wants to play golf?" Drop everything and go. Katia is a programming witch and a goddess. You will learn to worship her in time.
It might happen your character will have an out of body experience in which they are thrown a thousand miles up the sky above "Uncharted Waters" and die on the way down during the fall. Treat it as if it were a nightmare, resurrect at the nearest holo-crypt and move on. Consider it an omen of good luck.
Sometimes devs come to hang with us and/or hand out free stuff. It is highly recommended to follow them on Twitter.
If you want to play on Exile side, consider making a Granok. They are beautiful creatures that need some love. If not Granok, create a Mordesh, because they are clearly the best (absolutely unbiased opinion.)
Enjoy levelling. The lore is amazing, the world is full of unique creatures, a certain self-consciously cheesy and pulp fiction-like humor permeates the entire game as a whole that still makes me laugh to this day. Though I wouldn't know who to credit for it, I've heard it being described as something along the lines of "as if Borderlands and Firefly had a baby baptized by Star Wars." It also has a grain of fantasy mixed in. In space. Such a beautiful, amusing mess of everything.
10/10 would drop over the mysterious Uncharted Waters and die again, as often as it needs be, for this game, and the amazing community it has.

Deus Ex is a Diamond. A largely flawed one. With scratches everywhere. But that's the wonder about Deus Ex.
Play this game.

There's so much stuff in this game that people were still finding new things about a decade after release.
Seriously, if you haven't played Deus Ex yet, you owe it to yourself.

Nowadays, most games are well-polished updates of old games: Beautiful or retro graphics, good stories, new environments, well-rounded gameplay - but without new ideas, without invention, without creating anything of their own.
Deus Ex was different.
Its developers created something never seen before, something fresh, giving players a degree of freedom and choice in accomplishing their objectives that was unprecedented. They got the graphics, sound, story, and other elements on a par with or better than others at the time, but they did more than just that. The game did not fit into an existing genre, it defined its own, took that evolutionary leap into the unknown that has become so rare in the industry.
By now, many other games have followed in its path. But Deus Ex was a groundbreaking title, it was the first of its kind.
+1 for taking that leap:  11/10
“Without leaps of imagination or dreaming, we lose the excitement of possibilities.” (Gloria Steinem)

tl;dr A weeb game with big booty androids fighting around in DESTRUCTABLE maid costumes made me more of an emotional wreck than any video game I've ever played
It's a shame that this game released when it did, because otherwise more people would be able to enjoy it for what it is, a complete masterpiece, the best game of 2017, and possibly the most important piece of work to really challenge the limits of video games as an art form since the original Metal Gear Solid over 20 years ago. As a longtime fan of the Drakengard games and the original Nier game, Automata exceeded every single expectation I had going into it, and there was a lot of hype believe me, but somehow the game overdelivered to the point where I have a literal void after completing it.
Yoko Taro has always been known for his very quirky, but very emotional, thought provoking stories but until now the gameplay element of his works have always hindered otherwise amazing stories. Automata on the other hand was a literal match made in heaven with Platinum who know a thing or two about making great combat systems combined with Yoko Taro's mindblowing game and story ideas. Combat is very enjoyable, if a bit too much on the easy side, however that's easily forgiven because mowing down endless amounts of robots with a combat system this fluid is so much damn fun.
Normally in an open world game you have the map littered with pointless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because the devs think very lightly of the attention span of the average gamer, but with this one every bit of the map plus all the sidequests and all the areas to explore are very tightly crafted with every square inch serving its own purpose. This is the first game in a long while where I've been compelled to actually go around 100 percenting everything because of how beautifully the top tier side stories are crafted into simple things like weapon upgrades having mini poems or stories about their past, or report files on lore that are hidden around the map to really help flesh everything out better.
The biggest issue with writing a review for this game is that the story is something that you really should go into as blind as possible for maximum emotional impact, and lemme tell you this♥♥♥♥♥♥is ♥♥♥♥ing heavy and you will come out of it feeling completely drained of your soul. It doesn't break any new ground in terms of themes or whatnot but the execution of it is spot on and will stay with you for days. The white phosphorus scene from Spec Ops pales in comparison to the crap the player is put through in this game.
And of course, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the god tier soundtrack. When I played Nier all those years ago, I never thought that any video game would have an OST that matched this, but like everything else in this damn game I was wrong and my expecations were exceeded. This is the kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥you will immediatly want to just buy and download to listen to it outside the game, it's that good. The dynamic music shifts depending on situations and locations are ♥♥♥♥ing dope as hell like everything here.
If I had any complaints, it's that the first two chapters drag on a bit too long for my liking and the performance of the PC port is very shoddy. I'd expect for a game that looks like this(decent looking but nothing that demanding) to run fine on my 980Ti and i7-4970k but I kept getting massive framedrops and stuttering until I installed the godsend FAR mod to fix the performance and I've been running it at 1440p with no issues whatsoever. Other than that this product is the best thing I've played in a long, long time.
Please buy this game, I implore you. There are a lot of very good quality games coming out around now, (Horizon, Zelda, Persona 5), but honestly this one is the best out of all of those. When people argue for video games as an art form, they should look to this game. As Jim Sterling said, if history forgets this game, ♥♥♥♥ history.

Medieval II: Total War is a Medieval strategy game developed by The Creative Assembly and released 2006. Medieval II: Total War is full of country-micromanaging with strong emphasis on historical context, strategies, and battle planning.
There is a Campaign where the player takes on the role of the selected nation, and develops said nation militarily and economically. The story is generally trying to follow historically accurate events, foes, allies, and important key leaders.
There are two game modes in Medieval II: Total war
: Battle Mode, when it's opposing armies clashing against each other. The other mode requiring just as much skill as battle strategy
is World Mode, where you navigate the map, edit city construction, politics, religion,  army movement, and much more.
There's a lot to learn going into Medieval II: Total War, if you haven't played any of the previous franchise games.
The game starts out with a tutorial campaign explaining basic combat concepts to battle warfare and gives the player a rudimentary introduction to camera movement, and unit controls. While the tutorial is effective at helping you learn, there is far more information to learn about the franchise inner workings, and for that: your best friend is the in game advisers
.
There are no steam achievements for Medieval II: Total War. There are historical battles that you can try your hand at, and in my opinion winning a historical battle that is usually lost, is a huge achievement.
Medieval II: Total war is priced at $19.99, most strategy games eat up time like it's nobodies business, I personally like to spend an hour for every dollar I spend and Medieval II: Total War will do just that, and then some.
Story: Emphasis on Historical facts and events
. Gameplay: Difficult to learn if you haven't played any other Total War games. Achievements: None, however there is no lack in difficulty. Price: Fair, almost all strategy games are worth their weight in game hours played.
I recommend this game to Gamers who enjoy either History and/or strategy games. Generally it takes a fair amount of time to learn how a strategy game works, after you learn the mechanics then the game goes faster and it's very easy to get sucked into it.

- The tech progression system is very easy to understand and come to grips with
My one issue with the game is that the tutorial doesn't offer much help. A lot of this you have to learn yourself. It will come to you naturally in time however

This is a fun program to use.
I would not call it a game. I would not call it a puzzle game. To cut it short, I would not call it a video game.
My point can be summarized as the following:
If my experience from a 'game' does not decrease with printing out a screenshot and try to solve it on the table with a pen, what is the point of purchasing a videogame for the mentioned experience? There are billions of good puzzle newspapers, magazines which are much cheaper (per puzzle basis), and most of those even includes more than one type of puzzles.
What I am talking about? There is no save in the middle of a mission. So if u are bored with a specific puzzle, you must start from anew. Paper and pen solution is better in this case. There is no undo for moves. While it is a good exercise for mistakes and incentivize perfecting things, sometimes I just misclick and got a correct filling. Since I am a bit obsessive about doing things without any hints, I really try hard to ignore that extra hint in the aftermath of the mistake. Again. Pen and paper approach is still nicer. Ok, not pen, but a pencil would do the job. Music is not outstanding, it is not even a music, just ambience sound, mostly I muted the game and opened some music of my own. Pen and paper approach is not worse in this aspect as well. It has no options, no metagame, no seeing how long your other friends took for solving some different puzzle. It has no occulus rift support :)So again, pen and paper approach is not inferior.
To summarize my point, I am not declaring this program is not fun to use. It is. It is a good mixture of minesweeper and griddlers, and especially as a fan of griddlers I enjoyed my time solving the puzzles. But I would also enjoy my time with solving them from a newspaper. While I mostly enjoy minimalistic setups in puzzle games, this one was too extreme in that. I really cant point out what is the difference between this program (I am insisting on not calling it a game) and a published puzzle thingy except it lets u know when u did a mistake instantly.
Since puzzles are much easier in this compared to Hexcells plus, having no save feature is not that devastating in this first title. It still is annoying though.
Needs much polish before I can call it a game. Since all of the puzzles have a unique solution, I dont think we need a programmed thing for this kind of puzzle even.
TLDR: Did I enjoy using this program? Yes. But I also enjoy my time solving some sudokus, or griddlers online, and this one does not stand out that much from some best voted griddlers in
. So I dont think paying for this is well legitimized, especially after considering its short gameplay time.
PS: Some of my points are taken care of in Hexcells Infinite, by saving feature, a few options, and infinite puzzles thingy. But since those changes are not retroactive, they are not relevant reviewing of this game.
PS2: Most of the ones who check out for hubs of older games are fans of it. That is why, a negative review for an old game will most likely be heavily downvoted, since the ones did not like the concept already will not wander around that much. So, take possible downvotes with a pint of salt.

Well, let's start with the good.
-As you can probably see from the screenshots, the game looks nice.
-Fairly large, open universe.
-The filler parts of the game are well designed and somewhat enjoyable.
-It runs at a solid 60FPS
-The voice acting is ok.
Now for the bad:
-The campaign is really short. I've clocked just over 7 hours and I've spent at least 3 of them mining and doing freelancer missions. The campaign itself is somewhere between 2 and 3 hours at best.
-You don't get any advanced ships or weaponry during the campaign. All of the rewards from the story missions combine to about 100k which is the price of a single high end piece of equipment. Top of the line ships meanwhile cost upwards of 2 million. Thus you'll spend most if not all of the story flying a starter ship or one marginally better and if you want the end-game stuff, you'll have a lot of grinding to do.
-While we're on the subject of the story, it's quite mundane. Without spoiling too much, it boils down to some gibberish-speaking aliens popping up all over the universe and stealing cargo and we have to stop them. Who are they, why are they doing this, is there more to this? Who cares, just shoot them.
-The universe is underdeveloped. There are 4 different factions but I only noticed that when one of them started shooting me because I got friendly with their enemies. Who are they and why are they fighting is a mystery. Naturally, you can't affect the wars (which incidentally would've made for a much better campaign than what we got)
-The combat. It feels like a poor man's Freelancer combat and that game is what... 10, 15 years old? I think it suffers from being developed for mobile devices.
-Lack of support. Apparently the developers were very surprised (and quite unpleasantly so) by the fact that PC players didn't throw twenties at them for the 2 hour experience and they've decided to essentially take their ball and go home to the iOS crowd that has more money than brains. As a result this is all we're going to get. No patches, no DLC, no modding support, nothing.
-The developers themselves. Looking over a few of their replies to their customers, reveals them to be quite arrogant and obnoxious.
-The price. Frankly, the game is overpriced for what it is. If they had bundled the DLC with it, MAYBE it would be worth 20 bucks. As it stands, it most certainly isn't.
In conclusion, while the game has it's moments, I can't recommend it at it's current price. If you can get it on sale 70% + off, go for it. Otherwise, stay away

Wildstar is a great game that suffers from poor marketing on NCsoft's part.  They only have a western release, ignoring the huge asian mmo playing population, it's like they want this game to fail.
Yes it's an MMO.  No it is not WoW.  I play WoW too.  This game is silly and irreverent, with a lot of voiceover, animated cutscenes, animated characters and expressions, and it's very different from WoW in gameplay also.  Sure basic get quest collect random stuff turn quest in is there, but your gameplay experience is drastically different.  Wildstar is faster paced, it's an action style combat system with outrageous attacks and you run and double jump and roll out of the way of enemy attacks.  There's no standing there while your pet takes everything out (unless you're a lazy low level engineer, but that doesn't last all that long) or standing there taking hits cause you're a tank.
Each class has a dps role and either a tank or a healer role.  You can mix and match in some healer or tank skills in while you level, and indeed even at end game there's a bit of mixing, no one's a pure build all the way really.  Think WoW a la bc and wrath.  Are there cookie cutter builds out there? Well sure, but given that the play style is so precise you may want to use different skills here and there and be more effective.
I know a lot of raiders who enjoy it, and pvp is sluggish right now due to people never queuing at lower levels, but there is a looking for group player channel at least on exile side (and probably dominion too) that wil help find people to hang out with.
Where this game shines more than any other MMO on the market at the moment is the roleplay community.  Because player housing is very very customizable there is a lot of room for players to make their own stories and homes and even event plots.  One player even made a working mini-golf course with the help of lua scripting. (They have to be present for it to work.)
The devs can sometimes be found in game willing to chat, attending player run events, or just handing out promo item codes.  The are also very responsive on twitter.
Either way, if you played at the beginning, check it out again to see what's changed.  If you've never played it, it's free.  What do you have to lose?

This is a fun program to use.
I would not call it a game. I would not call it a puzzle game. To cut it short, I would not call it a video game.
My point can be summarized as the following:
If my experience from a 'game' does not decrease with printing out a screenshot and try to solve it on the table with a pen, what is the point of purchasing a videogame for the mentioned experience? There are billions of good puzzle newspapers, magazines which are much cheaper (per puzzle basis), and most of those even includes more than one type of puzzles.
What I am talking about? There is no save in the middle of a mission. So if u are bored with a specific puzzle, you must start from anew. Paper and pen solution is better in this case. There is no undo for moves. While it is a good exercise for mistakes and incentivize perfecting things, sometimes I just misclick and got a correct filling. Since I am a bit obsessive about doing things without any hints, I really try hard to ignore that extra hint in the aftermath of the mistake. Again. Pen and paper approach is still nicer. Ok, not pen, but a pencil would do the job. Music is not outstanding, it is not even a music, just ambience sound, mostly I muted the game and opened some music of my own. Pen and paper approach is not worse in this aspect as well. It has no options, no metagame, no seeing how long your other friends took for solving some different puzzle. It has no occulus rift support :)So again, pen and paper approach is not inferior.
To summarize my point, I am not declaring this program is not fun to use. It is. It is a good mixture of minesweeper and griddlers, and especially as a fan of griddlers I enjoyed my time solving the puzzles. But I would also enjoy my time with solving them from a newspaper. While I mostly enjoy minimalistic setups in puzzle games, this one was too extreme in that. I really cant point out what is the difference between this program (I am insisting on not calling it a game) and a published puzzle thingy except it lets u know when u did a mistake instantly.
Since puzzles are much easier in this compared to Hexcells plus, having no save feature is not that devastating in this first title. It still is annoying though.
Needs much polish before I can call it a game. Since all of the puzzles have a unique solution, I dont think we need a programmed thing for this kind of puzzle even.
TLDR: Did I enjoy using this program? Yes. But I also enjoy my time solving some sudokus, or griddlers online, and this one does not stand out that much from some best voted griddlers in
. So I dont think paying for this is well legitimized, especially after considering its short gameplay time.
PS: Some of my points are taken care of in Hexcells Infinite, by saving feature, a few options, and infinite puzzles thingy. But since those changes are not retroactive, they are not relevant reviewing of this game.
PS2: Most of the ones who check out for hubs of older games are fans of it. That is why, a negative review for an old game will most likely be heavily downvoted, since the ones did not like the concept already will not wander around that much. So, take possible downvotes with a pint of salt.

Party Hard cues you in on what to expect by its very name.  A calculated and unforgiving time warp into the 80's, it's a game for the patient person. The levels are simple in graphics with a gorgeous 8-bit palette...but don't be fooled by it--the game takes a moment to really get the hang of it.
A few things really make up the main mechanics of the game. One, the environmental traps. You can go around and poison the punch, call in guests (a personal favorite), electrocute, explode...all in the hopes that you'll knock down the numbers of attendees a bit. The levels also sometimes introduce an item to the mix which makes for fun and diverse gameplay.
Two, is the cops. If someone spots you do something shady, kill someone, around poisoned people or bodies, someone else will freak out and call the cops. They'll had already clocked your face, so the police will come kicking down the doors. They come in extremely fast, so you tend to position yourself for a short run. What this game does well is the timer in which the law actually does chase you before they give up. It feels fair.
The story is a really fun, typical 80's dark cop scenario. Sounds somewhat oxymoronic, right? Well, we must remember we're all playing a game about lighthearted mass murdering. The art style is absolutely amazing and completely on point. Something that caught me out though was the voice acting. For me, it was on that fine line of not knowing if the deliveries were supposed to be funny and cliche, or if this was the hardest the actors were trying. But the writing. The writing surpasses. It's extremely well done and entertaining.

All that being said, I found myself glued to the monitor far longer than I usually sit for gaming bouts, really trying to stab everyone on that yacht. Especially the security chaps. Go quick on the draw or extra clever with those guys, or you'll be finding yourself well punched up. The music was good, but quickly became a footnote for me when it got a bit repetitive for the amount of time I was spending on each level. The DLC breathes some new life into it after you're done with the main game, which is always a huge plus.
It wasn't a bad game, not at all, but not the easiest game to master. The key is patience, and much at that. But if you like tearing down the house at a party (quite literally) or anything 80's really--you'll enjoy this unique title.

Even if I disregarded the games that came before this one - which is admittedly difficult, given how much I enjoyed 2 - I can't say that I would recommend this game on its own. It's nothing special, in my eyes. If others enjoy it, I'm glad for them! In my case, however, I wish I had saved my money (and I bought this on sale).
Here are a few things to consider, if you're looking to purchase this game and combing through reviews for some outsider input. I'll start with the objectively nice things:
-It handles just like Borderlands 2, which is to say very nicely. It also looks great, keeping with the signature style of titles before it.
-The new cast of characters are diverse and provide some neat expansion of the previously explored areas of the Borderlands universe. There is a feeling of many more possibilities moving beyond the given playable experience.
-While it sticks largely with the Borderlands 2 system, there is enough 'newness' in here that it provides a very different experience. The unique location, the Grinder, the new gun type, and the new element are enjoyable.
-The new vehicles were pretty cool.
-It was interesting to have to manuever in the new environments in the given way (even if it was slower). The need to interact with the oxygen vents on the surface could go either way for me. It made travel somewhat more difficult, which made the otherwise slow hops across the surface more exciting.
-The new playable characters and abilities are pretty fun.
Unfortunately, for me, that just about ends the good things that I can think of to say about this game. I was trying to be generous, honest.
I seem to be in the lower bracket of opinions on this, and for the life of me I can't figure out what I'm missing out on. I really wish this was something I could enjoy. It just doesn't cut it for me, though. I see people redeeming this because in some way you could try to think of it as a DLC and not what's supposed to be its own game, but I can't even accept that. It just.... wasn't fun. Here's why I thought it wasn't fun:
-From right off the bat, there were some ridiculous bugs causing the models to pop in and out of reality, especially in Sanctuary 2.0. Kind of breaking the diversity there.
-The characters were so, so, so unfortunately samey. There were attempts to diversify them, and it helped that this team had characters to build off of from games before, but overall it was just.... bland. They were not at all belonging in what has been established in the fun and quirky Borderlands universe. They were often not more than ushering you down the questline with little other individuality or redeeming qualities to their name. ♥♥♥♥ing Pickle.
-The main quest was so boring I refused to do side quests to avoid doing but the bare minimum. Consequently, I found myself severely underlevelled. I joke with my buddy that the script for each and every quest went this way: "Give player objective across map, player attempts to proceed by completing objective, something breaks, give player new objective all the way backwards through the map to fix whatever went wrong with last objective, repeat". There was SO much backtracking and loss of progression. It's NOT fun.
-The characters being queer were cool. The characters having no other qualities I could tell you about other than them being queer are uncool. It felt just like the team wanted to include their sexual orientation just so they could say they did. That's the end of their work. Everyone pack it up.
-REALLY forced attempts at resurfacing character qualities from previous games. Example, quite early on Torgue makes some comment about friendzoning and then something something about ladies and whatever. I think it was an attempt to relive what was actually kind of a cool moment for his character in his DLC, but it was just.... harsh.
-Speaking of harsh, just about every dialogue bit in this game is harsh. It feels like the team played the previous games and only got "insert joke into EVERY LINE POSSIBLE" from them. They're not good. They're not subtle or clever, definitely nowhere near the beloved Borderlands standards. They're so forced, and it's painful to witness potentially neat characters being funneled into (now it is time to make a JOKE!). It's bad.
-Also on the dialogue line, a lot of the dialogue was way too much, very cluttery and overwhelming. There were a couple times the ol' Borderlands dialogue came through, and it was a breath of fresh air, but it wasn't often enough.
-This would only be an issue if you disliked this game the same way I do, but the replay value on this is seriously 0 for me right now. I replayed BL2 close to 10 times at this point, so I was really hoping for something else I'd be able to waste my life on, but I'm afraid it's not here.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this even as a DLC. Especially if you've played the games before this, I just don't find it up to par. If you consider yourself someone who especially enjoys characters and quests, then I'd be especially cautious. If you're just in it for the gameplay, then go for it!
