Tron Evolution is a wonderful movie world experience built into a terribly executed PC video game.  If you can get past its myriad of flaws, the game itself is at best an “ok” experience.  4/10
-	You are a tough as nails rogue program on the Grid with cool parkour abilities and a disc that probably says “Bad Mother*%&@)^” on it in Hexadecimal.
-	The world is recreated quite well, which is a treat for Tron fans.
-	Light Cycle levels while being shot at  – WOOOoooOO!
-	The platforming is one of the best examples I’ve ever seen on how *NOT* to make parkour controls in a video game.
-	Tank controls are excruciatingly awkward.
-	Combat gets repetitive after a few levels.
-	Meh storyline that is easily forgettable.
-	A good chance you may never be able to run the game, and even then you will need to edit the .ini file.
Get your Daft Punk helmet ready.  You know the one that looks ultra amazeballs with LED’s flashing twitter memes across the front.  You’ve been eyeing this game for a bit, and feel like it’s time to strap a disc to your back, fire up a  lightcycle, and headbob to that awesome Tron soundtrack.
Oh, but wait.  I forgot to mention – the game may not run at all.  Oopsies.  That’s right.
The first thing you need to do is get Game for Windows Live to work.  Good luck with that.  I managed to get it to work, but a good chunk of folks could not. So, be prepared to ask for a steam refund because it could be unplayable.  There is a guide in the Community Discussions that is quite helpful for what it’s worth.
If you manage to get the game to run, then you also have to edit the .ini file in WordPad to get a resolution that works on your screen.  I typed in 1920X1080 on mine, turned off the intro screens, and disabled that annoying intro cinematic from starting each time.  Good to go, right??  Um…sort of.  It didn’t recognize my Xbox controller at the beginning; you have to turn that on in the settings.  NOW, I can play.  Really, man, after all that hassle this game better be good.
It’s not.  The beginning is quite nice and you’ll be wowed by the slick looking monochromatic world of Tron in all it’s 60 FPS glory.  But early on you realize a major issue. The platforming is a little off.  Run up to an edge to jump and – nope.  For some odd reason you did not jump off correctly, but plummeted to your de-rezzed death.  Try again…okay.  Now I am speed running on wall when I didn’t want to.  Try again, and YES got it.  But once I landed the character ran along the wall again without wanting to and jumped off the edge.  REDO.    This happens pretty much all game long, from the first chapter to the last.  There were a few nice areas in Levels 4-5 where I didn’t jump to my death 50 times in a row, but overall the controls are absolutely bonkers.  It astounds me.  Can you imagine if Shadow of Mordor had controls this bad?  It would be the fail of the year.  Yet, somehow the mediocrity of Tron Evolution lets it slide.   You can get better after time, but even then there are bad spots where you spend more time trying to get the parkour controls to work than fighting bad guys, including the bosses.
:
The game is linear without any real missions, just level chapter to level chapter. You fight with your disc weapon and a variety of good combos such as electro-poofing someone away or slamming the floor really hard to make them fall down.  Rarely did I get stuck on a boss or swarm fight.  I could disc slam or explode the floor with relative ease. The gameplay itself wasn’t bad, albeit repetitive.  But wait, some rather good games are repetitive, correct?  So, why complain?  The rhythm of the fighting is basically the same over and over.  There are few bosses and the ones you do encounter are not a giant sweatfest of stress to get past.  Not that it’s a bad thing, but expect bosses to be slightly different variations of the standard tough bad guy you’ve been attacking the whole time or dozens of swarms attacking at the same time.  On top of that, you can just spam the special moves over and over.  It’s *fun*, but just so-so.
There are tank fights. And this is where you cue some derpy circus music because it’s sort of like a grown man driving a little monkey sized tricycle.  Just play the controller with your nose, it’s about as accurate.  Wiggle-move that tank across some bridges and blow up other tanks, etc, etc.  Let’s get ready for a snails paced bit of action and excruciating maneuvers through a few tight corners.  I could have made a gag reel of that.  Somehow, I didn’t die: go figure.
Next up, we have light cycle action sequences!  Right here, is the best part of the game.  You on a light cycle, zipping around and driving through mines, tanks, exploded data bits, and gunfire hailing from the sky.  AWW, YEA. Yet, it’s not what you’d expect.  What I wanted – what I think we ALL would want – is to be able to kill baddies with my light cycle in a maze like mission level.  Instead, you get an almost rails-on sequence where you just avoid pitfalls.  Not the best, BUT, you are on a light cycle.  How cool is that?  A light cycle!
Lastly, we have online battle arenas.  Except no one is there, ever.  But the nice thing is that there are bots who are surprisingly fun to play with.  In no time I was leveling up and getting all sorts of unlocks.  I think I may have more fun here than in the entire game.  It’s a total battle royale of tron inspired multi-player havoc.  I put in several hours with the bots and enjoyed myself immensely.
I can’t really say much about it.  You are a random program just minding your own business when Tron and Flynn get their butts in trouble. You have to find Flynn while the evil Clu decides to kill all the Iso programs and take over with his new color coded minions.  Quorra is there ( her face looks weird ) and she guides you for a bit until you have to rescue her.  That’s about it.  Add some baddies and cut scenes  - viola.  Voices are well done, I’ll give them that.
I found the look of the game to be gorgeous.  Frankly, it’s the eye candy that keeps the player from just quitting.  If it was janky looking or didn’t have that Tron vibe, I doubt I would have bothered to keep going.
It could have been so much better!  Just slap on some better controls from another game and get rid of Games for Windows Live.  Then, it’s more like a 6/10.  As it is, this game is a hassle to set up and a so-so game experience.  I just shake my head at what could have been.

Think I got this game from a bundle or something, so it was utterly out of chance that I installed this little gem and actually played it.
First of all, when people say it's easy to grasp, they're not lying at all. If you can w+m1 on TF2, you can do it here with a lot more reward.
Pros:
- Mostly easy to understand, has a few quirks on how the UI works that it didn't seem to explain such as how buying/selling works. It didn't take long for me to find out though. Simple and therefore mindless to play.
- As basic as the environments are, the artistic value of some of the scenes are awesome such as the Void planet.
- A lot of ships and upgrades to buy.
- New areas to find, even after the main story.
- Allows you to take your time with the objectives as long as you don't enter the system your objective is currently based.
- Has a basic economy system to allow players to establish their own trade routes to make a profit on goods from system to system.
Cons:
- No DLC.
- Gets repetitive later on after the story aside from unlocking new areas.
-  Short storyline, again, without the DLC.
- Turrets are mostly useless as they are manually controlled. A turrets moment would probably be as you are docking to a station and have locked your course otherwise you may as well just use your primary weapons.
- Blueprint crafting requires you to enter each and every single piece by mashing a button til it hits 70 tons of whatever it is your need to complete the recipie, wasting time rather than just crafting on confirmation once you have the supplies.
All in all, I do recommend this game if you're looking for a quick pick up whilst you're waiting for some of the main games of the year to release. It's fun, easy and visually interesting.

Lots of games punish you hard for being a wizard. At the start of the game, you get your one or two spells, and then you have to pretend you're a fighter or run away useless.
This is not one of those games. In this game, you actually feel like a wizard. The only consequences for letting off as many of your most overpowered spells as you can is that maybe one of your friends gets caught in the blast. But you're a mother effing wizard, so resurrect the poor sucker and keep going.
There is a story, but the game doesn't really expect you to pay attention to it. You're a murder hobo on a quest to save the world by killing whatever happens to be in your way. But that's not the point of the game.
The point of the game is the magic system. It's by far the most unique way of handling magic I've ever seen. It takes a bit of getting used to, but once you get the hang of it it is supremely satisfying to let of a huge string of different spells in quick succession, subtlety tweaking your spells to suit the situation.
Or you could just spam QFASA over and over, if that's your thing.
Final note: the game is really designed to be played in co-op. You can play single player, but you're missing out on the full experience.

Does Adventure Capitalist need a review? Sure why not; I review everything else on Steam, lets get into it. As with most games like this, there are plenty of unfunny joke reviews that will fill up the front store page for this game so I'm hoping to beat the trend and give some points about the game.
First of all, Adventure Capitalist is a game, about, well capitalism. You are an investor setting out to make your fortune.  This game is very similar to the likes of Cookie Clicker, which first came to fame in 2010, is still a mega popular game today. You start off buying lemonade stands, each click on the lemonade stand generates money, with that money buy another stand, so on and so on. Eventually you have enough money to hire a manager for your lemonade stand. The manager acts as the clicker, so you can leave the game running (or close it down) and you will still generate money. You then work up to other investments following the same pattern, and no sooner have you started, you will soon be a millionaire.  With your millions you can also purchase upgrades to your investments, such as increasing profit by 3% or something similar.
This is where AC is different to other clicker games, you no longer actually need to spam click in order to make progress, since you have your managers working over time for you. What I really like about AC is that you can close the game down, and you will still be generating money, meaning you can let your funds mount up for a couple of days, log back in, spend it all, and watch your money roll in for a bit, then log out.
The UI is so brilliantly displayed, you can work your way around all the menus with ease, and you can find all of the information you could ever need either on the main screen or within 2 clicks.  Be warned, this game not only has highly addictive gameplay, the soundtrack is almost just as addictive. Once that song gets in your head, it just will not leave.
AC is not hard at all, it just seems to be a time-sink, and one that keeps you logging back in on a daily basis. You can see just by the amount of hours I have in this game already just how easy it is to loose yourself in a really simple game. I would say I am not in the game for longer than 15 minutes on a daily basis, but it does keep bringing you back just so you can see what made up number of money you have made over night.
The developers are always adding new content to this game as well; recently there was an update which allows you to continue making your fortunes on the moon! This runs along side your regular empire back on earth, meaning twice as many investments to manage and oggle at crazy sums of money.
Given that AC is a free to play game, you have no harm in trying it out. I would say that even if you just load it up every couple of days to check it out, you will still get a lot of enjoyment out of it. There is also an iOS version of the game, but unfortunately it does not link up with your game on Steam; that would of been just too good if it did. Maybe it's a potential possibility in the future.
I really strongly recommend AdVenture Capitalist; its a simple, yet horribly addictive game, that allows you to pop in and hour of the game with ease for ten minutes at a time. Play in small doses to get the full effect!

NieR: Automata tells the story of equipments 2B pencil, iPhone 9S and A2 size paper and their battle to reclaim the machine-driven dystopia overrun by powerful machines.
Overall Score: 9.5/10

Of course this game is not perfect so I will start out by listing some of the issues:
- The PC port has problems with fullscreen resolution (the FAR mod can help with this)
- Dodging when using K&M controls is clunky (I recommend playing with a controller)
- I experienced a bit of "popping in" of environmental-assets
- The hacking mini-game that becomes very prevalent later on in the game can be frustrating
- Some of the sidequests are rather tedious (a certain quest in the desert comes to mind)
- No auto-save, remember to save often
However these are in my opinion massively outweighed by the positives:
+The combat is crisp and feels very statisfying when you get good at it
+Most boss battles feel very epic
+Shifts seamlessly between different gameplay styles (Hack&Slash, Side-scroller, Bullet-Hell)
+Beautiful and varied scenery
+Tackles philosophical questions without coming off as pretentious
+Intriguing setting and fleshed out world that ties into Yoko Taro's previous works
+Main characters are likeable and have good development
+The plot is interesting and gets quite emotional
+Multiple endings
+Absolutely phenomenal soundtrack
+Final Credits are ingenious
Overall NieR:Automata was an incredible experience and one of the best games I have ever played.

A very average Hidden Object game that is very light on puzzles, HO scenes and story.
Once again, like 90% of HO games, you are a parent looking for a loved one who has disappeared due to supernatural forces, in this case your daughter has been taken by a ghostly madman.
As the story is set on a train, it is very linear as you progress through the train, occasionally stopping at stations along the way. While there is some backtracking required, it is usually no more than 1 or 2 scenes.
Overall, the game is short, easy and not much of a challenge. The story is tired and there are few if any voice-overs. The conversations are text based. As you progress, the game seems to get even easier. There isn't anything bad about the game, but nothing good either. I would probably avoid it unless you've picked it up cheap and/or a fan of the genre and are looking to kill a couple of hours.

This game is a bit sick, very dark and greatly entertaining. One of the best aspects is the randomly generated dungeon, so every game is different. The artwork and aesthetic combine monstrous subject matter with cutesy cartoon style to produce something pleasantly disturbing. The nightmares that go through Isaac's head between levels echo the deepest darkest fears of every child; fears that never truly leave us even as adults. I found myself instantly sympathetic to Isaac's cause, and highly satisfied when, through my control, he became more and more powerful and able to destroy the demons that attacked him from every corner of the dungeon.
When he eventually became powerful enough to face and defeat his biggest enemy, I felt like somehow I myself had emerged from the dungeon with Isaac, having overcome not just countless hostile beasts and grotesque giants, but also a darkness in my own soul, and in doing so, became truly a man.

The story serves as a prequel for Tron: Legacy, helping set up the events of the movie and giving you new insight into the plot of the series. Gameplay-wise, Tron: Evolution is decent. It's not the best game I've ever played, but it's not the worst either. It's a third person action game that has a high emphasis on combat and parkour. I personally found the controls to be a bit awkward, but I was using a keyboard and mouse. I recommend playing with a controller if you have one.

Even without its interesting plot and setting, Deus Ex would be a classic sheerly for its open-ended level design. A wide variety of skills, augmentations and tools allow a player to approach most problems in a variety of ways, allowing them to develop their own strategies for progressing through the large, complex maps.

A lot can be said about Deus Ex. One could mention its fantastic soundtrack or its incredible atmosphere/worldbuilding, but that would barely be scratching the surface. Deus Ex's story, in my mind, delivers a powerful message which actually puts itself forward well, and without using the incredibly flawed comparison of augmented individuals to represent oppressed groups which later games in the series tried. It is truly a story of conspiracy, class division and espionage at the highest level of government that really isn't to be missed.
Deus Ex is the definition of cyberpunk, and to this day I've never seen a game pull that theme off with such grace and faithfulness to the originators of the genre (namely William Gibson's excellent novel Neuromancer, which I would reccomend to any fan of Deus Ex). I'm not here to write an in-depth pros and cons list about this game, just to sing its praises along with so many others really. Looking past its semi-wonky gameplay and the incredibly dated graphics, Deus Ex is a classic which everybody deserves to experience at least once. If you've ever even passingly considered yourself a fan of cyberpunk, be it from Shadowrun, the Matrix or anything else, play Deus Ex. If you've ever seen somebody playing it and thought to yourself that you might enjoy it, play Deus Ex. No matter who you are, there are very few circumstances under which I would not advise you to play Deus Ex. One of the most deep, interesting, complex stories I've ever experienced in a video game, and all for £5, even when it's not on sale.

This is coming from a person who adores pixel games, just not this one. When I saw this game, I was estatic and immediately purchased it without really thinking. Unfortunately, I was incredibly dissappointed. While the visual design is something I adore, the gameplay is absolutely atrocious.
Every level revolves around some procedually designed area with different traps and slightly different room themes. These levels have a main section with other rooms that are chosen based on RNG. This would be fine and dandy and all except for each room has its own set of those aformentioned traps for you to use, which can sometimes be critical to winning the level. I understand that the whole goal was to make each time you play a unique and it encourages quick thinking, but the system becomes incredibly frusturating because an area which would've been critical to your victory just isn't there. Not to mention that there are other RNG-based elements which range from actually helpful to actually hindering and just wasting your time. Speaking of wasting your time, a majority of levels is spent waiting for one unlucky victim to waltz out of sight of the other partygoers, killing them, and then hiding their body. Rinse and repeat until you finish the level (or get screwed over somehow and start over).
The AI also adds to the incredibly unforgiving gameplay (and not in a good way). The AI for the different partygoers is oftentimes broken and flat out irritating. I'll have npc's who can't see two feet in front of them at one point and others who are omnipotent and spot me doing my business clear on the other side of a dark parking lot. Remember when I mentioned waiting for them to come to a secluded area? Well, some of them have set patterns, and never actually leave the rooms they're in unless something forces them to. You can't directly force them to do anything because they'll suspect you and call the cops on you faster than you can even react. You can, however, indirectly influence them, but those methods rely on RNG and oftentimes don't even help. The cops are also a massive nusance. When one is called on you, they'll immediately rush to wherever in the house you are to arrest you, even if you're past multiple doors or within a crowd of people. If they get to you, all of your progress is over, and you have to restart the level ad infinitum.
I can't stress how much I wanted to love this game to no end. However, the heavy presence of RNG and poor AI makes the game just unfun to play. I hate to say this, but I cannot recommended this game at all.

Ill take it from the top.
Pros: PvP, Friendly community, Dungeons, Raids, Housing, Chill F2P system
Cons:Crafting sucks,leveling kinda bad after you doit more than once, bugs (but what game doesnt have bugs right?), Small population
From the top PVP:
PvP is the reason I started playing this game. Some people call it a zerg fest which in a lot of cases is right but there is skill involved. You can be the guy that stands in all the telegraphs or you can be the guy that positions himself to not get flattended like a pancake. The worst part about pvp is maybe the gear grind. From a fresh 50 to full amps/abilties to getting all the gear, runing it out, imbueing it to make it legendary. It takes a longggg time to make all that happen. But the telegraph combat system is what makes it great and its the main reason i stick to wildstar as my main pvp game. Once you get really good at it theres almost no playing another mmo for pvp. ive tried to go to other mmos to pvp and its just so hard because of stuff like not being able to double jump, dash, sprint, aim all my abilities and such. Sadly the pvp is like the black sheep of the game. Need some of you steam folks to come in and pvp :P
The community:
The community is also a big reason I stick around. I made so many friends in this game that I genuninly enjoy talking to. Wish I woulda met some of these people sooner and I probably wouldnt have given wildstar a break. Overall the community is really close knit. As in both factions talk to eachother alot to organize stuff. I have plenty of friends on both factions that make my time on wildstar that much more enjoyable.
Dungeons:
I didnt give much thought to dungeons until recently. I was strictly a pvper for months and months. After the pvp died down a bit I turned to the pve alas dungeons were one of my regular things to do. At first they were really challenging but extremely fun to learn. When you are learning with other people is when its most fun. They ARE hard but not too hard. Over the years they have been nerfed to make them more do-able. Over time I got really good at dungeons too and I do them to pass time now.
Raids:
They are like the dungeons but much bigger and much more challenging. The raids are the best wildstar has to offer. If you are looking for a game to challenge yourself in raiding than look no farther. Honest wish I would have started raiding much sooner than when I started because it feels rewarding when you kill a boss. Genetic Archives was an enlightening experience for me, it wasnt too hard to learn but also not too easy. Datascape was a whole different beast to learn for me. LOTS of trips to the holocrypt. The telegraph system works really well in the raids too because it makes you learn through trial and error xD. I learned what I can touch and what not to touch. New raid coming out with the next big content patch so nows the time to start your raiding.
Housing:
The housing is also really ridiculous in this game. There are some things that people make that make you wonder how they even thought of what to combine to be able to make it. There are people that literally just house in the game. Housing is their end game. There is fights over decor drops in raids lol. Than theres people like me that cant build anything and pay people to make a fancy plot. There are definitly some jaw dropping houses and plenty of creative people to make amazing custom decor items.
F2P system:
When compared to other f2p systems like swtor, Wildstar has one of the best f2p systems on the market. Its not p2w, and you can get anything out of the cash shop without spending a dime in game.
To the cons
Crafting: Honest most of the crafting just sucks. I only took on one of the professions just so I could craft certain potions and stuff for pvp. Aside from that profession the other ones seem to feel a little on the useles side  considering how fast the gear gets replaced. The coordinated crafting is also one of the worst parts lol.. A lot of people just dont understand it because its clunky. I get it but a lot of people dont want to figure it out.
The leveling:
Well as of late if you are choosing to level nows a good time because of the influx of new players leveling. But before steam it was pretty lonely. The low level pvp doesnt happen sadly and its hard to get people to queue up for lower level stuff in general. But with the new people low level stuff could possibly be a thing again so learning dungeons can be done while leveling :)
Bugs:
Some bugs have been around forever but they are hardly noticable as in they dont effect my every day life on wildstar. The bugs really were the downfall of wildstar the first 2 times though. However, most of them got ironed out now and you dont really encounter all that many bugs anymore.
Overall the game is worth trying. Im not gonna live in some fairy tale world saying the game is perfect because its not. You probably will find bugs but none that are game breaking. Steam is helping Alot and theres a bunch of good stuff comin out shortly so would I recommend the game? Absoluetly.

Maybe you remember when this game came out, or when it went free to play. Maybe you even played it for a little bit, left for one reason or another, noticed it on Steam, and are wondering if it's worth coming back to. Maybe you've heard predictions from doomsayers, claiming that the game is dead and that you should leave it to rot, or maybe you're just seeing it for the first time. In any case, sit tight and enjoy the essay, 'cause  there's a lot to go over. I'm going to try and explain to you everything you need to know.
Basically:
Wildstar is a free-to-play sci-fi WoW-style MMO focused on endgame PvE with a pretty cool player-owned-housing system. The manual aiming telegraph-style combat works really well for an MMO, and the game's core and endgame are really pretty good, but sometimes you have to trudge through some bad stuff to get to the greatness.
Monetization:
The game is 100% free to experience, from character creation to endgame raiding. There's a cash shop for cosmetics and convenience and a subscription plan for what basically amounts to more xp/currency drops. Thing is, you can buy almost everything in the cash shop with in-game currency, too, including subscriptions. I'm honestly not sure how they make money.
PvE:
With that out of the way, let's start with the good. This is a PvE focused game, and its dungeons and raids are the best on the market right now.
Carbine (the devs) have shrunk away from their ULTRA-HARDCORE stance since launch, but even in the 5-man dungeons you still need to know about one or two unique mechanics per boss in order to not die. It's not too scary; just ask your group, and 95% of the time they'll be happy to explain and you'll have a wonderful time in what are essentially mini, queable raids.
If you want a more passive or grindable experience a-la WoW dungeons, the game has you covered. Expeditions are basically spammable instances that scale to support 1-5 players, and slower-paced Adventures offer branching paths for a party of 5.
Raid attunement has been massively simplified since launch, now requiring only one step: get bronze medals in 4 of the dungeons (which is almost guaranteed for completing them) before you enter the first 20-man instance, and boy, is it worth it. The combat system was made for raiding, and (most of) the fights are just designed well, utilizing their settings to the fullest extent. I won't be too detailed, this review is cumbersome enough as is, but just for example there's a fight where you grapple between platforms as they crumble behind you. You can even grapple your teammates, which, believe me, turns into a fantasticly amusing waste of time.
For the interested, there is currently one 6-boss raid, one 15-boss raid, one boss-in-a-box with optional hardmode and an incoming 7-boss raid with optional hardmode next patch. They're all great, and from what guilds who've tested it say, the upcoming one is hands down the best yet.
World bosses drop some neat loot sometimes. There's usually a big group on the "wubba train" you can join at any time going around killing them in some order.
The holy trinity is present. Every class is either DPS/healer or DPS/tank.
PvP:
If you're looking for a PvP focused game, look somewhere else! It's there, and warplots are cool (big customizable battlegrounds), but most people don't even bother (including myself, which is why I don't have much to say here) and if it's all you're looking forward to, you're gonna have a bad time.
Housing:
The ultimate blank slate. In my (apparently rare) opinion, it's not as perfect as everyone says it is. Sure, you can rotate and resize everything to absurd proportions and make it all float in midair, and there are some AMAZING things people have done with this system (ask around in-game, you'll be blown away), but for the average player who just wants a nice place to live, there's not a lot in the way of templates. You get a big flat rectangle with a house of your choice in the middle and 6 surrounding slots about the size of the house for what the game calls "plugs." They can be mining plots, low-gravity pads, minigames, portals to (sometimes housing-exclusive) instances or just decorative, which is all great, except the system for getting them there is kinda of awkward, and the slots are in the same places for everyone, unable to be rotated. Skyboxes, music, lighting, floor texture etc. can all be changed out.
I'm not saying the system is bad, it's definitely as "best-in-class" as they advertise, but without putting a lot of time into it, most people are going to have basically the same house as everybody else.
Other Customization:
Pretty thorough. There arent a ton of options for character appearance, but you can fine-tune all the face options and whatnot. Armor is much more versatile, able to be saved to the "holo-wardrobe," sold, and still worn cosmetically, dyed all sorts of colors. Naturally, the cash shop provides a lot of options here. You can even customize the mounts and hoverboards to some extent.
Leveling:
Pretty standard MMO questing. There aren't a lot of options when it comes to choosing a zone for your level, which is a pain for the altoholics out there, but you can get to max pretty quickly if you push it, and endgame is totally worth it.
Presentation:
Graphics are great! Music is great! Voice acting is great! Unfortunately, the game is about as optimized as Minecraft with shaders and chances are you'll have to look at it through a screen door to make it run at 60 frames. It sucks, and I'm convinced it's why the population is as low as it is. It's a stupid reason, since it has little to do with the gameplay, but you can't really blame anyone for not playing because of it, either.
Universe:
Like a lot of video games, the lore is neat but the story is pretty eh, though still enjoyable as long as you don't go in expecting anything amazing. Wildstar does a pretty good job of building a universe for being a new IP.
Professions/Crafting:
Professions are pretty standard. Everyone gets 2 plus cooking and runecrafting. There's miner, armorer, alchemist, etc. Actually doing the crafting involves moving targets on various grids to align with whatever variant you desire via various methods, so it's a bit more involved than WoW's system of clicking a button.
To be perfectly honest a lot of people don't like the system and I'm not quite sure why. Maybe I'm not involved enough to see the flaws?
Also sort of related, every character chooses a playstyle-based "path" at creation that determines some of their available side content and their non-combat abilities.
The Not-So-Good:
-Like I've mentioned, it runs horribly. Recomended specs are totally a lie, my 970 doesn't pull 60 on ultra in raids.
-Confusing at first. There is a new and improved tutorial, but the game still tends to throw everything at you.
-The world design (physically, not lore wise) is kind of incoherent. There are some cool areas, but a lot of teleporting between them, too.
-Bugs. It's cleaned up since launch, but stuff still goes wrong. I haven't crashed too much, but others haven't been so lucky.
-The UI is kind of bad. Fortunately, there's robust addon support. You'll need a good few of 'em.
-Not necessarily a negative, but it's hard. If you can't put time in, there isn't much in the way of progression raiding for you.
-Population. The game isn't quite dead, but there's literally only one server. To be perfectly honest, Steam is basically the game's last hope. Don't let that stop you, though. You, potential player, can save it!
TL;DR: If you like endgame PvE and/or player housing, Wildstar is your best option, but you'll have to deal with a few issues.

I'm putting this as "recommended" not because it's good but because it's a decent way to pass some time.
There are a lot of better HO games out there, but there are a lot that are far worse. The artwork is basically what can be expected of HO games. There's nothing spectacular there. All of the puzzles and their required pieces are constrained to being in the same general area, so there is no map in the game: it doesn't need one. None of the puzzles are particularly difficult, but you can easily skip past any that get annoying. Although the game doesn't give achievements, it does give Steam trading cards. I'm  not sure what achievements would give you anyway because they would all have to be story related. So everyone would be guaranteed to get all achievements anyway.
There is no voice-over so you don't have to worry about the typically horrendous "actor" quality of most HO games. Most (definitely not all) of the puzzles at least make some logical sense and keeping everything localized to within a few screens certainly beats having to run all over using a map.
If there is any weakness, it's the story. I know that HO games very rarely have intriguing plots, but this one was really weak. It fell into the old cliché of magical hocus pocus to explain the bad guys without giving any kind of story of how he came to acquire such magic or how it all fits together. It's just ... there, which is annoying.
The game also does a very poor job of explaining why some characters are there. Near the end, a ghost is locked up in a shed. (I'm not kidding.) I got no story popups or dialog regarding the ghost, his story, or how an incorporal being is locked behind wood. He was there and somehow your character knows that he needs an amulet to be freed. She just knows. I've played many HO games that at least put a background behind its characters. This game is very lacking in that regard.
Still, it's not awful. I don't recommend paying full price for this. You can get more quality from cheaper HO games. But if you can nab this on a Steam sale, you will probably find it an easy-going way to spend a few hours.

The best way I can think of to describe Hexcells is not as a puzzle game, but as a "meditation game" and a sort of mental massage.
The gameplay follows on from Minesweeper, you start with the same rules, identifying blue hexes by the non-blue hexes telling you the number of adjacent blues.  But new mechanics are introduced which pushes it toward the realm of Sudoku.  I never found it frustrating or confounding, because the rules are simple enough that you only have to look for the next step, not make crazy leaps of logic.  Also, while you don't get a full score for making several mistakes, each mistake you make at the same time serves as a hint and moves you closer to the solution (a nice parallel with positivity in real life!)
So the gameplay requires you to be active and logical mentally, but not so much that you can't relax or have to get stressed.  And the rest of the game with its simple visuals and procedural ambient soundtrack works to make one of the most relaxing experiences I've seen in games.  The puzzles and music are in a nice area between idleness and frustrating which lets you slip easily into a meditative state while playing.
I highly recommend this game, especially if you turn off the TV, turn the lights down a bit, kick up your feet, turn on a humidifier, lay a damp washcloth on your forehead, and just completely relax while playing.  For anyone dealing with excessive levels of stress or anxiety, this game could be outright therapeutic!

The story takes place on Earth millenia after the first NieR. Humanity was driven away from the planet by an army of machines sent by aliens and humans found refuge on the moon. All hopes to win back the planet are placed in the organization YoRHa, which sends battalions of androids to lead the front against the robotic invader.

You are playing as 2B, Android Combat Unit. You will be sent on missions to take back strategic positions. You will be accompanied by 9S, a reconnaissance unit. They form a really endearing duo and give some very interesting insights, sometimes philosophical during their dialogues. While being androids, they manage to create emotions and are developing a rare humanity. They have their own identity, sentiments,
As soon as you will launch the game launch, you're embarked on some sort of identity crisis, it looks like an action-RPG, sometimes Shoot them Up, with platformers actions...  Camera angles are being as smooth as possible and make these changes as fluid as possible.
The variation of game styles added to the choreography (because it is a dance), everything is incredibly smooth and fluid in the NieR: Automata experience. The fighting revolves around a beat' them all but induced simple handling of the fight to just enough technicality making it enough pleasant. Gameplay is an undeniable success.
The mechanics transform each confrontation into a deadly dance where your ability to dodge will be rewarded with a few invulnerability frame and a powerful counterattack. The player will also need to develop the POD (your assistant) to acquire new defense or attack mechanisms. Fights are not clumsy. Ever.
NieR Automata also offers the player to make himself a tailor made interface. You can equip and modify your OS (understand here your HUD and details) at your convenience. Removing parts to focus on speed, defense or attack. This system was very innovative making the game an entirely customized place.
Death is also something integrated in the game, the death of your characters equals the transfer of his data to another body identical to the previous one. Making it possible if you encounters your body (or another) to rise them to fight for you, or simply to pick up the missing add-ons you installed on yourself.
The game is also an open world filled with NPCs and quests, merchants and some secrets to find! But do not expect a immensely big universe, there is a handful of open zones articulated around a ruined city filled with enemies. Every map has a different feel and fun stuff to do, desert surfing is one of those. While NieR Automata isn't a graphical beauty, the post-apocalyptic setup is charming.
Scenario is interesting and the encounters are filled with emotional, philosophical lines. Prepare to be immersed into the story and to feel it. The game revolves around a reflection on mechanical awareness, with his robotic figures capable of emotion, fear and love.
The Soundtrack of NieR: Automata is a wonder. High class soundtrack that really helps while playing. This is a jewel you should listen to even if you don't play NieR Automata.

Finally, it is sad that graphically the choice was on fluidity rather than graphical qualities. This weakness is compensated by artistic designs. One word of advice: don't forget to save, often. I can't stress this enough. The amount of time I a lost a lot of gameplay time, because I didn't save.

I really don't understand the appeal.
In this game, like minesweeper, you have to find the 'mines' with the number of adjacent mines of one tile. The difference are that few levels of Hexcell aren't randomly generated and more complex mechanics are introduced as you go on.
The first problem I have with this game is that it does not let you fail. Rather than failing a level for hitting a 'mine', it only count your mistake. It sound like a good thing, but it simply inadvertently spoils the game. I admit that I don't know what could be done to fix this, but nevertheless its the equivalent to trying to solve a math problem with the answer in front of you. You might do your best not to look, you still end up figuring something that you wouldn't have normally.
The second problem is related to the few inconsistencies of the game. It's a minor issue, but sometimes, it seems that the game take liberties with its own rules (or simply doesn't set them). For example;
Two mines in a row of four tiles are said to be next to each other? Turn out that 'next to each other' still count when the row is separated by a huge white space.
symbols like '--' indicate that mines aren't next to each other? It only mean that at least one mine is not connected to the others.
etc.
Like a said, this is a minor issue, but combined with a very short unpunishing game, it doesn't leave you anything worthwhile. I can't recommend this game when other interesting puzzle games are available for the same price.

The board is almost solved with no mistakes so far. With numbers and blue cells everywhere, all that is left is two yellow cells. It's unclear what cell's to be cleared, and what cell is to be marked. You look at the board, squinting your eyes as you make hypotheses about what would happen if either cell was marked.
And then, when you're as confident as an eagle swooping down for prey, you slowly but steadily bring your mouse cursor to the cell you chose. You're sure you can't be wrong; after all, you thought it all out. The numbers all add up. It's a calculated move. This cell just can't have a number below it.
And as the cursor finally lands on top of the cell, you click with your mouse.
But it turns out you pressed RMB.
11/10. Super Meat Boy for intellectuals.

First the positive: The game looks pretty and sounds cool, the atmosphere really puts you into the Tron universe.  The story ties in with the new movie with recognizable characters and scenes, although I didn't get far enough into the game to really give a valid opinion on the story itself.  As a big fan of the Tron fanchise, I was growing somewhat skeptical of where the story was headed before I quit playing.
Now the negative:  The game is an obvious console port.  It's definitely more difficult to play with a mouse and keyboard, there is a distinct advantage to using a controller.  This in itself is not a problem, but it detracts from the experience a little for me to think about how this is a game about living inside a computer that wasn't actually originally designed to run on one.  The gameplay itself is visually appealing and basically alternates between levels of psychedelic parkor and flashy combat, with the occasional crazy vehicle level thrown in.  None of the gameplay is particularly difficult or challenging however and it becomes a little rote after awhile - except for when it becomes ridiculously hard in random spots but for the wrong reasons.  A spot of particularly bad level design that led me to get frustrated and put this game down was a 'disc station' you visit for upgrades placed right next to a cliff.  You have to perform a jump combo off this cliff to get to the other side by first pressing A to jump, but you also press A to access the disc station.  The end result is I repeatedly ran up to the cliff edge, accessed the disc station instead of jumping, then fell off the edge.
Other thoughts:  If you're looking for a good Tron game, play Tron 2.0 instead.  It's older than this game and pre-dates the new movie but is a MUCH better game than Tron: Evolution.  I think Tron 2.0 had more thought put into an original and engaging story because it wasn't just capitalizing off the success of a new film, and the gameplay was both more challenging and rewarding.  Sure, it's not as pretty as this game, but is still an attractive game and still looks way better than the original Tron movie!

I was so ready to write a fully positive review on this but...  the last part of the game left a bit of a sour aftertaste which is a shame.
So firstly, I really enjoyed the game until the end. It reminded me of everything I liked about the Borderlands series, the humour, the elemental weapons, the lovely graphics and the lite tactics you need to employ such as choosing what weapon to use in what situation, for example using acid weapons against armoured enemies or launching into the air via the new low gravity we have in this version and then but slamming down to blast bad guys away, great fun!
However it also reminded of the things I dislike about Borderlands...  the endless Inventory juggling, swapping out one weapon for another all the time in a UI that is clearly designed for a controller, struggling with it usually mid fire fight but more than anything at all the worst crime this game commits is need to grind and it is this mechanic which stopped me playing.
Now to be clear, grinding is one of *my* big turn offs in a game, for me if you have a level up structure to your game and clear main line of quests that are linked by narrative, then they should be designed in a way that ensures the player gets all the experience they need to be the right(ish) level for the relevant story mission. I feel like I should only be asked to grind for levels if I want to complete side missions or challenges that demands that commitment. Borderlands the Pre Sequel seems to get this right for most of the game.... kind of.... but when I hit the final hours of the adventure that went out of sync.
I am literally at the end of the game, the last level, but I just cannot be bothered grinding levels to be strong enough to finish it, grinding is tedious and not fun at all in my opinion, it always feels like a waste of my finite free time and a huge turn off in a game.
So I just though.. forget it.... and watched the ending cinematic on YouTube and I'm done. If there was no grinding involved I'm probably an hour from finishing the game, which I know is ridiculous to give up now but I wasn't having fun anymore and being asked to repeat previous levels and zones to get my character to the level it needed to be was a chore I didn't want to undertake.
It is a good game, let me make that clear, but if I haven't got my point across already, being asked to grind and repeat content wasn't doing it for me.. and this led to the fact I wasn't enjoying it anymore so there we are. Maybe you don't mind that or maybe you enjoy that, if so... then you'll probably get more out if it than I did.
20 hours of fun, with about 4 boring crappy one's at the end before I gave up. The game is what it is, but I bounced off one of it's key mechanics and just something for you to consider before hitting buy.

My friends and I usually play board games during our annual holiday get-together. This year was different. As I go over our shelf of board games and debate between Catan and 7 Wonders, one of us blurts out, "You guys need to play this game called Don't Starve. I've been playing it together with D (her boyfriend) for weeks and it's so much fun."
Our party of four consists of a Blizzard gamer, a strategy gamer, a casual gamer, and a handheld gamer (me). I'm the only person in our who plays indie games and has heard of Don't Starve. I own the Vita (original single player) version and share my impression of the game: it's pretty challenging. I've never survived a full winter or summer.
"There's a co-op version," she says and immediately proceeeds to gift two-packs to us on Steam. We open up Steam on our computers, download the game, and completely lose track of time. Our first attempt failed because W burned down our base by mistake and M died trying to save our chests. Our second attempt ended with another base fire, this time started by M.
"Okay, let us agree to put away the torches when we're in base," I say, at the start of our third attempt which again ended with a base fire. This one was my fault- I killed a fire hound in our base by mistake.
Eventually, W says, "I'm starving."
"There's meatballs in the chest at camp," says J.
"No, I'm actually starving," he clarifies and we realize we haven't eaten dinner. We check the time and order a pizza.
After dinner, M suggests we continue playing. "Sure," says J. "30 more minutes?"
We ended up quitting after 3 more
at 4:00am when our base was again ablaze from someone brilliantly setting fire to a Treeguard.
Don't Starve is a survival rogue-lite similar to Minecraft and Terraria but with much better graphics (IMO) and a stronger focus on survival. You need to maintain your health, your hunger, and your sanity while accumulating resources and avoiding the dangers of the world lurking everywhere.
The single player version is a great game but it is much, much better played with friends in the same room or at least through voice chat. Being able to announce what you are doing, what you need, and hop over to view your friend's screen to show him where to find something or how to do something improves the experience greatly.
Is it worth getting? Yes- if you enjoy challanges, Minecraft/Terraria, and survival games. And yes- especially if you have a friend.

I played this game like crazy before it came to steam. I was worried that when this game went F2P, it would fall under the same treachery of other MMO F2Ps. Thankfully, this fear was cast aside, when I found that very little had been changed to the core game. The only change was that you were able to buy several cosmetics from the store as microtransactions. Aside from exp and currency boosts, there is no means of pay to win in this game, which is fantastic. F2P aside, I suppose I should discuss what makes this game great.
WildStar is basically a sci-fi/fantasy adventure, where two factions battle it out over a new planet. The gameplay is phenomenal, boasting action-based combat that you rarely see done so well in an MMO. Complete with dodging, stunning, combos, and ult-like abilities, each class feels fluid, and well thought-out. On top of that, each class can play two out of the three roles in the game; healer, damage, tank. This allows players to not feel so trapped when deciding on a class to pick, as there is something for everyone. Hell even the Medic class can make for a scary damage character.
The art-style of WildStar is great, very cartoonish and stylistic, something you don't see in too many MMOs. Albeit a bit tougher to run due to the level of design and the high-quality animation, it is something to be appreciated by anyone. The holo-wardrobe system is a great addition for those types of people who like the look of their current armor or weapons, but don't want to lose it to one with higher-stats. Thanks to this system, you can save the look of any gear piece, so you may turn it on whenever you wish. This doesn't just affect one character though, as it carries over to every character in your account!
Aside from cosmetics and combat, to keep players occupied is the Path system. Similar to jobs and crafting (which is part of the game), Paths are something you decide upon character creation. Each gives you a nice set of side activities in the world around you, granting you more experience, unique abilities, exploring uncharted areas, finding rare loot, and so much more. They serve as a great break from the regular MMO grind that you might eventually suffer.
On top of all this, WildStar includes a housing system, granting you a plot of land where you can build your dream-landscape. Complete with being able to fund your crafting ventures, this is a nice addition to those seeking something for end-game activities, as most of it will cost you quite a pretty penny in in-game currency.
A fantastic action MMO that deviates from the norm with both its combat and art design. Coupled with a good F2P system, and fun side-activities, this is a game that will even satiate those gamers that aren't MMO players.

Pros: Dungeons, Raids, Combat, Housing, Roleplaying, Battlegrounds, Class Balance/Diversity, Cash Shop
Cons: Leveling**, Crafting, Relatively small player base, Lack of fulfilling open-world content
This is my first srs review so apologies if formatting is horrible or it just turns into a bunch of rambling.
I’m going to try breaking the game down into the parts I think most people look at when deciding if this game is for them. I have been playing since beta and have poked around in just about everything, but most of my experience is in dungeons and raids.
Seriously, there is nothing better out there in terms of combat, dungeon, and raid quality. If you can find a progression guild that fits you, you are going to have a ton of fun. Anyways, here we go!
tl;dr: No P2W, can acquire 100% of the items in the cash shop without spending a dime
Probably one of the best F2P models we have available right now. All items are cosmetic/convenience like costumes, character slots, bank slots, mounts, etc. As you play, you’ll build gain currency called Omnibits, which can be used to purchase anything in the store you would otherwise have to use real money on. There is a weekly limit to the amount of Omnibits you can acquire, but it is something like the equivalent of $10 that you get for just playing the game! Additionally, the you can get the subscription benefits which includes things like increased XP, Omnibits dropped, currency gained…by purchasing C.R.E.D.D. from players off the market using platinum (like gold but better!).
tl;dr: Hurray for balance!
My first thought when trying out a new MMO is ‘what do I want to play and is it actually going to be viable’. Fortunately, class balance is pretty darn good! If you read up on a class and it sounds fun, you can be sure that you can top those dps charts/hold aggro/keep the party alive just as good as anyone else.
tl:dr: It gets better I promise!
Leveling really isn’t Wildstar’s strong suit, and for most it’ll probably feel like a chore and a grind.  Due to population levels, you probably shouldn’t expect to see sub-50 instance queues to be popping in any meaningful time, and for the most part expect leveling to be a solo experience. Fortunately, leveling is also pretty fast and it isn’t too hard to hit the cap in a few days, especially with friends.
**Edit: Steam release has brought quite a few more new players in than I was expecting so if you're just starting out, there is a good chance your leveling experience won't feel so empty after all!

tl;dr: Find a group of people to learn dungeons with and it’ll be the best thing ever
Now we’re talking! Dungeons were what sold me on the game when I started playing and if you manage to get into one while leveling you’ll probably see why. Dungeons have two modes: normal and veteran. Normal is just the sub-50 version where players are scaled (somewhat poorly) to match its level and the encounters are a bit easier with more forgiving/missing mechanics than you would find in the veteran versions. Veteran dungeons are where most of the action is at. Sadly, there has been a fair amount of power creep and it’s pretty easy to just steamroll everything and bypass all the fun mechanics with high enough gear. There are enough players out there that are still new to dungeons though that it shouldn’t be too hard to put a group together and experience it in all its glory.

tl;dr: Like dungeons, but better! And new raid releasing soon so we can all learn together \o/
Like I said, I’ve been around since beta and have even been in the same guild this entire time. And yet, despite being a raiding guild, we still haven’t downed the final boss in Datascape. This isn’t necessarily because we’re all terrible players (okay maybe a little), but raids are hard! In the good way! There are lots of other guilds out there who *have* cleared everything and are just waiting around for the next raid to release, but progression guilds still very much exist and if you can find one that matches up well with your schedule, you’re in for a lot of fun. And pain.
tl;dr: Mostly just battlegrounds, relatively balanced, usually limited to certain days and times
World PvP might happen here and there but is definitely not something you’ll see that often. Battlegrounds are where the bulk of the PvP is at, though even those tend to require coordination on queue times to get consistent matches. Arenas happen on something like 1 or 2 days a week through coordinated efforts. Warplots are even less common but tend to happen on same nights as battlegrounds if there are enough people.

tl;dr: Did I really just spend the last 6 hours on this plushie mountain?
This is something I personally have trouble getting into due to having the creativity of a piece of cardboard. For those more artistically minded however, you can create just about anything you set your mind to and make it look awesome. There is also a variety of ‘plugs’ you can install that serve as little minigames or instances with their own unique rewards, or teleporters to your favorite zone/raid, or your own garden because you can never have too much Heartichoke.
tl;dr: Fun to see/experience, but no tangible benefit to doing them
Expeditions are basically solo instances that you can do while leveling and have a veteran version at lv 50 as well. Adventures are also available as you level and have veteran equivalents, but are notably easier than dungeons. I grouped these together because aside from running them a few times just to see it for fun (and they definitely can be fun!), there isn’t really much point to them. At one point, the progression path looked something like Expeditions->Adventures->Dungeons->Raids. But today you can jump into the open world content like Arcterra or world bosses and get gear that blows anything you’d get from expeditions/adventures out of the water.

tl;dr: Large amount of content with (mostly) low replayability
Once you hit 50 you have quite a few new open world zones/objectives available to you. You have your standard daily zones for gold, some zones that feel a lot like leveling zones but are more story driven, a constant event-driven zone that gives some decent gear and gold, some events that happen every hour or couple hours that tend to require a raid to complete, and there is usually a group somewhere farming items to summon world bosses which gives the best pre-raid gear. It is actually quite a bit of content available but I still consider open world to be a con in this game. Most of it is enjoyable for the first round or two, but things get a bit repetitive after a while. As a result, most of the open world players stick to farming world bosses and keep the event-driven zone going, with other time-based events going largely ignored.
tl;dr: Armor/weapon crafting largely unnecessary. Consumable crafting remains viable but unrewarding.
Most of the new content that gets added seems to make it easier and easier to get solid gear, and as a result the crafting professions that produce gear/weapons don’t have much use except for those at the raid tier (though even those are fairly situational). Consumable crafters are still a necessity to provide boosts and food for raids, but it isn’t the most exciting or rewarding job. Crafting materials are also pretty endless in supply with gaining them through item salvage, housing plugs, and natural abundance in the world.

Well, it's kind of a crude attempt to put a roguelike/ASCII styling on a rudimentary FPS game. You run around in extremely repetitive and hard-to-read levels, you can shoot randomly named letters and collect arbitrary clues that further your believe in some kind of truther thing. I guess it's supposed to be some kind of big joke or meme, but it does a pretty bad job of conveying it. The heavy-handed "Wake up, The Man is always watching" theme drips of fedora cliche, which would be fine if the gameplay were smoother.
Visuals are an odd combination of ascii symbols and simple 3D models, the latter of which reminds me of that old 3D Windows maze screensaver. I found myself wishing this game stuck with a single one of these art styles, or at least fully committed to using ascii only for important objects. This seems to have been done to some extent, but only enough to cause confusion when you can't intaract with something that looks like you should be able to.
That said, I must award points for including a toilet that I can both flush and kick into pieces.
Menu navigation is clunky: To use an item, press I to open inventory, Enter to use it, X to continue after having used it (why?), then I again to close inventory. This doesn't sound awful, but X is only ever used to dismiss these messages, and Esc doesn't close the inventory or stat menus, which means you have to move your hands out of the standard WASD + Mouse location to do anything in the inventory. This may be picky, but it's just more unnecessary button presses for simple interactions.
Enemies all have perfect accuracy, which means that you've probably already taken damage from anything nearby if it sees you first. This can be especially frustrating when you're up against a wall and find that they can see and often hit you through solid objects.
Randomized wall/structure locations sometimes put doors right up against other buildings, which makes navigating those spaces confusing and awkward. In a few cases, I think the only entrance to a building was blocked by another building, so I wasn't able to get into it and find what I presume was the location of the last clue I needed to beat the level.
There are some interesting ideas here, but Illuminascii lacks a certain polish that keeps me from recommending it.

Trains! I like trains! The game really has nothing to do with trains other then the fact the gamer gets to play in, through, across, and over the top of several different trains which makes this game worthwhile just for that.  The psycho is Trainman, who causes train accidents.  As a villian he is petty, warped and evil minded.
Storyline: A mother and daughter board a train which is in an accident caused by (inferred) a demon possessed psycho known as the Trainman.  Trainman steals the girl and the mother gives chase, more like hunts down, Trainman.  The mother starts on the train that was in the accident (and it is still moving), gets off at a station, takes another train, stops that train before it crashes, nearly rescues her captive daughter, commandeers Trainman's own train (which flies, so cool), ends up in a train graveyard, and finally confronts Trainman.  Of course the player gets plenty of help along the way from various souls who do not like Trainman.
Gameplay: Linear gameplay that plays more like a hunt then a chase, and depending on one's point of view can take on a philosophical air.  There are creepy aspects and mild horror.  I call this a hunt, rather then a chase, because the mother has to find out where Trainman went with her daughter and she get helps from various disgruntled souls to go after him.  Plus Trainman is the one running away from her.
There is a good combination of point and click, hidden object and puzzle elements all intermingled together.  Need something to pull down that ladder, sort through that pile of debris (hidden object scene), need a code, puzzle it out with a mirror, need to break a curse - where was that pickaxe again? The whole game intermixes these three game genres very well and seamlessly.
Really enjoyed this game, especially because when I thought it was going to end, it suddenly kept going (and not in a boring or forced way).  The little pause was like a small intermission then off to play some more to the final conclusion.

I am writing this review because this game deserves more than the measly 83% on the store page. This game is a masterpiece that I would compare to the likes of The Witcher 3. I get that from the trailer, this seems like a typical Japanese hack and slash, with random bullet hell elements or 8 bit sequences, but ALL the gameplay mechanics fit in so well that every fight is a fight for my life. The story progresses at a phenomenal pace and at times I found myself doing side missions just to let what transpire in the main quest to soak in. The characters are very well fleshed out and every playthrough (and do play through it all!) I found myself more entranced in the character's relationships, motivations and hates. The environment and music is what made this game. The scenery is stunning, and the areas in the game are unforgettable because they evolve and progress with you as you proceed. The music is hauntingly good and meshes in well with action set pieces. Actually, to do the music justice, I happened to hear the game music in a random stream and my heart raced with nostalgia.
To sum up, I realised this has turned less into a review but more of a love letter... and I am OK with it. If nothing else, put it on the wishlist or watch a stream of the gameplay, because as far as gaming experiences goes, this is one of, if not the best gaming experience.
TL;DR My experiences with Nier Automata is nothing short of amazing.

I was so ready to write a fully positive review on this but...  the last part of the game left a bit of a sour aftertaste which is a shame.
So firstly, I really enjoyed the game until the end. It reminded me of everything I liked about the Borderlands series, the humour, the elemental weapons, the lovely graphics and the lite tactics you need to employ such as choosing what weapon to use in what situation, for example using acid weapons against armoured enemies or launching into the air via the new low gravity we have in this version and then but slamming down to blast bad guys away, great fun!
However it also reminded of the things I dislike about Borderlands...  the endless Inventory juggling, swapping out one weapon for another all the time in a UI that is clearly designed for a controller, struggling with it usually mid fire fight but more than anything at all the worst crime this game commits is need to grind and it is this mechanic which stopped me playing.
Now to be clear, grinding is one of *my* big turn offs in a game, for me if you have a level up structure to your game and clear main line of quests that are linked by narrative, then they should be designed in a way that ensures the player gets all the experience they need to be the right(ish) level for the relevant story mission. I feel like I should only be asked to grind for levels if I want to complete side missions or challenges that demands that commitment. Borderlands the Pre Sequel seems to get this right for most of the game.... kind of.... but when I hit the final hours of the adventure that went out of sync.
I am literally at the end of the game, the last level, but I just cannot be bothered grinding levels to be strong enough to finish it, grinding is tedious and not fun at all in my opinion, it always feels like a waste of my finite free time and a huge turn off in a game.
So I just though.. forget it.... and watched the ending cinematic on YouTube and I'm done. If there was no grinding involved I'm probably an hour from finishing the game, which I know is ridiculous to give up now but I wasn't having fun anymore and being asked to repeat previous levels and zones to get my character to the level it needed to be was a chore I didn't want to undertake.
It is a good game, let me make that clear, but if I haven't got my point across already, being asked to grind and repeat content wasn't doing it for me.. and this led to the fact I wasn't enjoying it anymore so there we are. Maybe you don't mind that or maybe you enjoy that, if so... then you'll probably get more out if it than I did.
20 hours of fun, with about 4 boring crappy one's at the end before I gave up. The game is what it is, but I bounced off one of it's key mechanics and just something for you to consider before hitting buy.

All-in-all this is a good game and I recomend it, it will give you 20-25 hours of good gameplay.

What is there to say, besides that this has to be one of my most favourite games ever? It wasn't really love at first sight, though. When I first tried it many years ago, my English wasn't all that great (there's still LOTS of room for improvement), but anyway, since I couldn't really understand what was going on, I'd still have some fun typing some cheat codes and slaughtering everything that would move in my sight.
Time passed by, and I had the opportunity of playing this game again. I was actually afraid that I wouldn't really enjoy the experience, by thinking that it would already be outdated, but I was actually surprised to see that I was completely wrong. Of course, this game can be really hard in the beginning, especially because you start with some terrible skills and equipment, but it doesn't take too long for you to get used to it and surpass the difficulties. By the way, me and my friend would use to laugh about it, after all, we're talking about an experiment that it's worth billions of dollars and doesn't even know how to shoot properly.
Ok, now for an overview: The graphics are somehow outdated, but tolerable. Either way, if you still think that they could use some improvement, there was a fan-made mod that was recently released which kinda helps in that way (it even adds some achievements to it).
The sound effects are great, I still laugh when I hear those ridiculous death screams. The music, no comments. Alexander Brandon is an awesome composer, and in my opinion, he really managed to make a perfect match between the game's climate and the soundtrack.
The gameplay takes place in a first person perspective, and there're also RPG elements involved, which allows you to improve your character's skills through experience points that are received, and also to make some choices throughout the way.
As for the story, it's a full plate for fans of cyberpunk and conspiracy theory enthusiasts (Illuminatis, Templars, Majestic-12 etc). In the year 2052, there's this deadly disease called "Gray Death", which is killing a whole lot of people in the streets. It actually has a cure called "Ambrosia", but only people of a high echelon have access to it. Then, there's this sudden bombing attack in Liberty Island, which completely explodes the Statue of Liberty. After these events, you get to know your character, who's an agent of this recently created terrorist combat unity called UNATCO, and your main directive is to recover the vaccine that was stolen by the NSF (through whatever means it takes). Everything else besides this premise, is much better to discover while playing the game.
It's really a shame that there're no achievements nor trading cards for this game. Besides, it would be really cool if they'd make a remake of this game in the future, but I wonder if that'll ever happen.
Overall, this game of the best titles that I have in my library, and that I would easily recommend it to anyone.

If you are reading this, you have propably heard that Deus Ex is one of the greatest examples of game design ever to grace our beloved thinking machines. Many will begin from praising the layout of the opening levels, others will make their point by admiring it's rich story and complex plots. But the true, undiminished value of this game is actually the fact that, after a decade and a half, it's still one of the geatest ways to dive into the american psyche. From countless remarks about the jewish overlords of the UN, through self-proclaimed confedarates fighting with "fascist pawns of the global banking establishement", up to the FEMA camps - Deus Ex is a grimm picture of a fractured and schizophrenic society struggling to connect the dots and recreate it's grasp on reality, as shown in the pulpiest, and, unfortunately, most accurate way possible.  We can laugh about the idea of JC Denton actually being a fascist pawn of the Jews, then launch a random broadcast by Alex Jones and suddenly realise, that a great many people actually deem such a story not only realistic, but factographic.
A perfect classic stealth game, it only needs the malkavian mod integrated and it'll definitely be the one and only.

Getting this game gifted to me on Steam last week was the best thing that happened to me this month game wise, and those are some big shoes to fill and I’ll tell you why. Magicite is a piece of procedurally generated genius, packed with hours of fun and intuitive game play. If it wasn’t for DOTA 2 I would have jumped on this game months ago, but that was consuming all of my time along with my Steam wallet. I saw this game in the Steam Greenlight forums and investigated further and found a very generously funded Kickstarter.
I was attracted by Magicite and its pixel graphics immediately, hard for me to compare, leaving Magicite in a field of its own. Since my affair with Terraria, these 2-D platformer games always seem catch my eye. Much like Terraria but even more like Castelvania: Symphony of The Night, Magicite is addicting like that first bite of sriracha covered chicken. Rougelike, with a crafting system and the ability to build weaponry and utilize merchants in town to make armor or melt ore, this semi-sandbox game is brilliant.
“Explore, craft, and survive in this Multiplayer RPG Platformer with permanent death. Featuring many Roguelike elements, Magicite randomly generates each underground dungeon for you and your friends to delve deep into. Chop trees, mine ores, and hunt beasts in order to collect the resources and materials you need to survive in the harsh and unforgiving environment. With a ton of character traits, stats, companions, and classes, players will have a different experience each play through. Be prepared to die… A LOT.” – Magicite
Each world and town being randomly generated along with your characters starting stats keeps this game fresh. Before you begin each game, you decide what character you want to play. Depending on which hero you choose, you’re given select attributes that go along with that characters race. Another thing keeping Magicite fresh and new is the unlockable item system. The more you play, the more races you unlock, the more items and companions you unlock.  Each of the unlockable items have a boost attributed to them, so when equipped to your hero it stacks with his stats.
For every item you craft and enemy you kill, you gain experience points and levels. When you level up, like most games your stats are buffed, and every 5 levels you are able to choose a magic ability. These abilities are divided into 3 different categories; Melee, Magic and Ranged. With 5 special abilities per category every 5 levels offers something new aiding in your quest. Certainly a complex game, you must keep track of your health, weapon durability, and much like real life you need to stay fed. In early game, you will find it hard when trying to attack enemies, so focusing on gathering materials before engaging in a fight is usually a good strategy. Enemies can be as easy as a pig or murderous as a toxic lava ball spitting dinosaur, and everywhere in between. But watch out for the scourge, they leave no one alive in their wake, and are only summoned after spending too much time in a stage.
Magicite is a fast paced game, and its good for hours of fun, or a few minutes trying to kill time before work. One of the best things about a rougelike is its ability to pull you in for hours and watch you fall violently from grace after building an epic hero. Even more fun is the multiplayer aspect of Magicite, easily its best feature so far. Playing with your friends and sharing finds is even more fun. My first play through was with one of my former DOTA 2 team mates, so it was a blast from the start, as he was able to give me a few pointers to ease me into the game. A money system is also present in Magicite and certainly serves a purpose. The gold is obtained from killing enemies, found in treasure chests, or when selling unneeded items in town. Town is where you will craft your gear and cook your food, but if you choose not to, you can save up enough for some gnarly sword that does serious damage.
When you die, and the game ends you are given score. This also is a layout detailing your gameplay from kills to potions brewed. I love games that do this, because after 45 minutes of gaming you find yourself looking to improve and get better for the next round. Their is no word that describes this game other than fun. With every character having his own back story, all the different biomes and unbelievable imagery; it’s like I always say, the little things make a game as truly awesome as it is.

In a game where most everything you encounter is randomized you're left with just that and not much else. While I can see why someone may enjoy trying to pull of a flawless run or even just go through and try to become a buffed out child tyrant, it's entirely in the hands of the game deciding wether or not that would be possible. The feature of this randomness is both Binding of Isaacs strengths and flaws. The first few times you go through the game its pretty entertaining and interesting. Though, latter on as you repeat from the beggining over and over because some measely fly killed you, the experince just becomes repetitive and bland. You begin to look for specific items and know exactly how to take on an enemy or boss in the most efficent ways possible. The rooms also become tedious to run back and forth through. With pleanty of back tracking to specific rooms just so that you can spend that extra penny you happened across into a betting machine or in a game of guess where the item is just to see if you get anything good, or anything at all. It just becomes a waste of time, which is hard for me to say about any game really. The art direction in this game may be the only thing this game has going for it, in my opinion. They did a great job at really making me feel like I was in a dreadful scenario and was faced with nasty creatures. Thats cool.  I feel like their may just be something missing in me that doesn't allow me to fully enjoy this experince but the game isn't perfect either.
