in short: It's good. Tetromino puzzler mixed with music mixed with a bit of Qix.
You place tetrominos on a grid to try and create quads, blobs that cover up part of the grid. Ideally, you want to cover as much of the level as possible, make as many quads as possible, etc. It works similarly in some ways to the old Atari classic Rampart--minus the whole Army/Castle minigame stuff, of course.
The neat variation is that there is a beatline sweeping left to right across the grid, which plays a basic music track (and they're good--well known electronic artists like Moby and Philip Glass) but then layers elements into that track based on the position of your quads. So you might get an EDM track where vocal elements or percussion suddenly show up because you've created a quad in a new area. Pretty nifty.
I'm sure some reviews will say it's zen-like but it really isn't... there's prety good pressure throghout the game to rush the tetromino placement, but the gaem does offer a 'free' mode to play around in as opposed to just the timed (3 min, 6min, 9min) modes.
Pleasant game, well worth the minimal time investment.

Party Hard is an interesting take on noise enforcement laws executed via serial killing, starring a guy who just wanted some peace and quiet. Throughout the game you will crash parties in a variety of locations, and kill single person on the premises.
Each level will have a randomly generated assortment of items and traps for generating as much murder and mayhem as possible. As partygoers are killed, some of the less-dead ones will inevitably notice the dead bodies and ring for the police. If you are spotted killing someone, or close to the body of a fresh victim, a handcuff icon will appear over your head to indicate that the police are actively trying to arrest you. However, if you are sneaky enough you may avoid detection entirely or frame a nearby innocent guest. Keeping alerted guests from reaching a phone is also essential, and you can even use said phone to call in some “guests” of your own, depending on the stage.
The game itself is a pretty simple concept stretched over 12 stages (not counting extras/DLC) so by the third or fourth level you will have seen just about everything the game has to offer. Some levels will be incredibly frustrating if you don’t get certain randomly generated items and you might find yourself restarting just to get a better loadout. One particular item I found to be almost game-breakingly overpowered was the smoke grenade which lets you clear out entire rooms through a flurry of stabbings inflicted on a crowd of blind guests (not to mention you can use it twice!). It’s so powerful that it makes a lot of the other items not even worth using, save for maybe the spare clothes which allows you to escape from police if used out of sight.
Party Hard usually goes for about $12 on Steam and that makes it kind of hard to recommend at that price. While the whole 80’s aesthetic is catchy and fun, the music gets a bit repetitive and the game is not without its bugs.  It’s pretty short too, only about 5-6 hours to do the main storyline (albeit there is a free DLC and some extra levels to pad things out). That being said, if you wait for it to drop to its usual sale price of around $4 you will find it hard not to enjoy Party Hard.

I hesitant to makr this game as a recommendation for ANY one running Windows 7, but it seems to run fine in Windows 10.

In terms of a port I must admit then Tron:Evolution is a bit of a nightmare, if you wanna get 1920x1080 resolution you're going to start using .ini files with mixed success and, while it works for me on windows 7 I'm hearing a lot of mixed things in terms of what works for who, so while one can hope the modding community will work on all this it is by definition a bit of a mixed bag.
The thing is (having completed the x360 version) what hide behinds that nightmare is a fun game. Clearly inspired by the 3d Prince of Persia games it's a fun romp through the early world of Tron:Legacy with more information on Tron's corruption, the birth and death of the ISOs, Clu's purge, and how Quorra made it out in 1 piece. Even referenced in the film itself this game actually feels relevent to the universe and canon of Tron in a way few license games ever do.
The campaign itself is pretty basic and standard fare for this kind of game, lots of free-running, lots of combat (that is basic but nice and flashy and with a few interesting mechanics like disc varients and damage multiplayers depending on if you are free-running while attacking encouraging moving while fighting), and some scripted light-bike sequences; it's functioning if uninteresting with some stand-out levels and some amazing visual nd sound design that keeps you going through an average experience as Daft Punk music tends to do (and yes there's a lot of Daft Punk).
However this game has one big trick up its sleeve....The multiplayer (once you can find people) is absolutely beast! Now while you can do a single bot match in the standard arena mode before it transfers to an online lobby (there's a few odd decisions regarding bot availability) the main multiplayer only maps that allow people, light-cycles, and tanks can create some truly unique experiences with people jumping out of bikes to parkour into health pickups while throwing disks at oncoming traffic. It is truly amazing if there are people on, and thus is the biggest problem...
Tron: Evolution is a dead community with noone playing, the games best component's rely solely on people and they are genuinely worthwhile experiences that essentially define why I do recommend this game as opposed to saying that one should be indeifferent to it unless a tron fan in which case you should already want this! With that in mind I have created a steam group that I plan to add weekly play-sessions so that we can all bring back some of that light together. The multiplayer is something that makes this game so unique so one can hope that this gives life back to it even if only once in a while. If you're okay for an okay to good game with the risk of boosting it up to a great one again together then buy it and join me, because this game is great together, we just got to bring that together bit back!

There must be something I'm not getting. Don't Starve Together seemed by everyone else's metrics to be a very good game. Don't get me wrong, I can see why it is so widely liked. The art style is fantastic, the music is great, the atmosphere, characters and enemies are so well designed, it's fantastic. I like everything about this game other than the one thing that I have a gripe with and it's pretty fundamental. It's the gameplay.
Perhaps I'm just burnt out on survival games and this is my own prejudice affecting my judgement, but the gameplay was just a big slog. The game is very difficult and going into the game knowing nothing, there is a steep learning curve. I ended up dying a whole ton, not really getting to see much. Having to babysit your hunger, sanity and especially health was a massive pain to me. This being the majority of the difficulty of the game, if you find any of these features annoying or frustrating, you will not like this game.
Respawning was a big issue for me. The game's methods of reviving a character in the beginning are so limited it might as well not have the feature in the first place. The "Touch Stones" are few and far between and the other methods don't come into play until way past what I ever got to. Even with game settings where respawning is automatic, the lack of a concrete respawn point was annoying. Having to trek back slowly to your base camp was boring and sometimes you would not make it back in time for nightfall and die all over again.
Learning how to play this game and survive is key. Unfortunately, this game has one of the biggest bad habits that most survival games have. The game itself does not adiquately teach its concepts through playing. The only way you will know what to do is through dying or by looking at a wiki. I found myself struggling to figure out what I should be doing not only in the way of progressing in the game, but merely doing enough in it to keep from dying. The game gave me no obvious indication how to manage or upkeep my resources and I would constantly run out of them, which to me, was more exhausting than fun. On top of that, the crafting system was iffy for me, being hard to read the way the menu was designed. Trying to figure out what to craft and how exactly to craft it was just another thing to worry about on top of the other stressors in the game.
In my humble opinion, there was not enough to discover in this game that was worth the constant nagging of the survival elements. I must concede, most of my problems with this game was because of the fact that I could not "git gud". If I could have gotten over the anxiety of constant "starvation" I may have ended up liking the game. There was a lot of love put into this game for sure, but it is definitely not for a person such as myself. If none of these factors seem like problems to you, then like most people who have played it, you will probably like it too.

I'd vote this more as a neutral in my opinion. Perhaps I ruined the experience with the DLC items but I just don't feel I can recommend this game.
GAMEPLAY:
The game is rather lengthy which was nice, except that it was also repetitive. There's about 2 dozen different dungeons and you can expect to visit each at least 3-4 times through a single play through. They aren't long, no puzzles to solve, and the layout never changes. There's also no "Repel"-like feature in this game, so even if you're level 400+ you'll still have to fight some useless battle with a Lv 2 Bee or a Lv10 Robot that you could probably line up 300 in a row and still have left over damage. The enemies don't scale in New Game+ but you can carry over everything from your previous play through, including characters that you had before.
The outfits/accessories for characters felt lacking and you could only really equip an Accessory and an Armor piece. Everyone's weapons were locked. There are 5 different types of "weapons" you could use in battle, but most are outclassed by another type (Launcher weapon was by far the best but luckily it stays locked until nearly the end of the game). I'll get back to this a little lower in the BATTLES section.
DIFFICULTY:
The game has 5 difficulties ranging from Amateur to Hell. There's an achievement for clearing the game on Hard. You won't get the achievement for clearing on Hell. Quite irritating that the game was already relatively simple but now I had to replay it on an easier setting.
BATTLES:
Most of the time I found I was just spamming the same skills over and over. Either basic attack chains with dozens of hits to build Morale, or just using the strongest skill I had (which usually was also the widest AOE). Remember how I said certain weapons were outclassed? Essentially you just focus on the attacks that have the most hits because your basic attacks are typically worthless otherwise. Occasionally I'd transform my characters for more damage or a stronger skill but outside of certain bosses this was never really needed. The original game allowed using 3 characters, ADF allows 6. At some points I felt that they didn't balance the game properly for the larger party. Most of my play time was on Hell with 2x Damage Furies active all the time because it just made bosses less of a drag. I suppose this also helped chew through the weak enemies in the dungeon but whatever. (The 2x damage affects both you and your enemies, which usually don't get to attack anyway so I guess that just made it easier? idk)
ANNOYANCES:
I've almost finished all the achievements except for the one requiring 40 hours and the one requiring 10,000 monster kills. Both require about 8 hours of needless time waste now. Also every time a team mate leaves the party they unequip all their items. There were many times where a party member would leave and practically rejoin again within 2 minutes, thus resetting their Fairy and Equipment. The annoyance is solved in NG+ because even if the character leaves in the story you still have them in your party.
If you want to save yourself the headache of playing the game 3 times you could do the first play through normally then on the 2nd run only pull out the required single Fury (I suggest something that offers Damage x2 to make the "boss" battles that much quicker) and speed run up until Cavarre Desert first shows up. Then save your game in 2 different slots and each will become one of the endings you can only get on NG+. This will save you about 1-2 hours of skipping dialogue and trying to avoid battles while mindlessly droning through the same dungeons you've been through at least 8 times before.

Party Hard is an interesting take on noise enforcement laws executed via serial killing, starring a guy who just wanted some peace and quiet. Throughout the game you will crash parties in a variety of locations, and kill single person on the premises.
Each level will have a randomly generated assortment of items and traps for generating as much murder and mayhem as possible. As partygoers are killed, some of the less-dead ones will inevitably notice the dead bodies and ring for the police. If you are spotted killing someone, or close to the body of a fresh victim, a handcuff icon will appear over your head to indicate that the police are actively trying to arrest you. However, if you are sneaky enough you may avoid detection entirely or frame a nearby innocent guest. Keeping alerted guests from reaching a phone is also essential, and you can even use said phone to call in some “guests” of your own, depending on the stage.
The game itself is a pretty simple concept stretched over 12 stages (not counting extras/DLC) so by the third or fourth level you will have seen just about everything the game has to offer. Some levels will be incredibly frustrating if you don’t get certain randomly generated items and you might find yourself restarting just to get a better loadout. One particular item I found to be almost game-breakingly overpowered was the smoke grenade which lets you clear out entire rooms through a flurry of stabbings inflicted on a crowd of blind guests (not to mention you can use it twice!). It’s so powerful that it makes a lot of the other items not even worth using, save for maybe the spare clothes which allows you to escape from police if used out of sight.
Party Hard usually goes for about $12 on Steam and that makes it kind of hard to recommend at that price. While the whole 80’s aesthetic is catchy and fun, the music gets a bit repetitive and the game is not without its bugs.  It’s pretty short too, only about 5-6 hours to do the main storyline (albeit there is a free DLC and some extra levels to pad things out). That being said, if you wait for it to drop to its usual sale price of around $4 you will find it hard not to enjoy Party Hard.

Who'd have thought? a literal "Murder Simulator". Heh.
Okay but seriously I want to recommend this but with something of a caveat. This review is based on the normal version of the game, not with the free DLC that's just released, as I haven't yet played that bit.
What we have here is effectively a face paced puzzle game where the puzzle shifts about dynamically and somewhat randomly. The puzzle is "bunch of people are partying too loud". The solution is "kill everyone without being taken out".
Your stock character has nice easy to understand mechanics. Stab people, drag their bodies around, or push people into environmental hazards, or heck just interact with parts of the environment to make things happen, like distract people with pizza, or summon zombies, or aliens, or a swat team or a chainsaw murderer, stuff like that. You know, normal things.
Guests react with horror at seeing dead bodies, so you will want to deal with that. or maybe not. depends on your strategy you're going for. Maybe the police and ambulance showing up could be a good thing. maybe you can pin the blame on someone else if you're quick and lucky enough. and that's a few less guests to deal with. Get spotted near a dead body and someone will try to call the police to get them to show up and arrest/kill you. Evade them long enough and they'll get bored and go back to their station or whatever (swat don't seem to though, nor do FBI), but each time the police are called it gets tougher to evade.
The game has multiple characters you can play, each with their own mechanics and each challenging the player in a different way. This helps things not get too stale, which is good. Though certain characters are just plainly awful to play as in certain situations unless you really want to challenge yourself.
As for the story (yes this game has one), I would say that it's actually rather interesting; perhaps a touch pedestrian and predictable, but enjoyable nonetheless and it kept me interested all the way through despite calling it right near the beginning as to what the twist was. You probably will as well, but even so it was an enjoyable, kind of silly game.
I'm not sure what the dlc changes or adds, but it is free so there's no worry there. Fan response to it seems divided however. Luckily, it's free. and it doesn't change the core game. only adds to it.
There's also a level editor as welll so you can design your own parties and such. I got several hours out of this game so I don't regret getting it really, and I'm going to recommend it wth the sidenote that the game really doesn't give any incentive for replaying it, kind of a "One-and-done" sort of game, and the gameplay can get a touch repetitive, and frustrating, with luck due to random dynamic movement of guests around the parties causing some odd situations, sometimes favourable, sometimes crippling your run.
So basically, yes it's fun, but maybe not fun for everyone, and maybe its issues will turn you off the game before you can get far enough in it to complete it. Honestly in terms of "the puzzle is dudes need to die, the solution is kill everyone" type gameplay, I feel the Hotline Miami games do it far better, and they have a better story too, but then they have a very different type of gameplay to Party Hard.

This is an interesting concept that needs a lot more to make it a good game. But for a couple bucks, meh. It's not a bad game, it just has some...issues.
The concept is that you place pentaminos in an effort to make large quadrangles. Music is playing behind it and beat bar sweeps across the field. Different sections of the field, once covered by a quadrangle, respond to the passage of the beat bar by playing a portion of the music that had been previously muted. If you've ever worked with a DAW, then you have a rough sense of how this works.
Of course, this means that in the beginning, almost none of the song is playing. By the end, if you've bothered to play, you'll likely hear most if not all of the song. This is great when the song is something worth listening to. The nature of the play though, lends itself best to repetitive electronica of some stripe, and that's what you get. The reason it lends itself to repetitive electronica is because repetitive electronica is extremely repetitive with gradual changes to a phrase you hope is more than eight bars long.
The repetition of repetitive is deliberate. If you found the repetition of repetitive grating, you'll also find it the repetition of the repetitive music grating.
If you play it more than once, the grating will also be repetitive.
Some songs are worse than others. The Moby track is bad, but it isn't the worst. The best, of course, is "Still Alive", but this version of it is pretty stretched out even if you play the three minute version.
You can see everything this game has to offer in an hour or less. There are leaderboards, but like most leaderboards, may as well be considered set in stone, and probably involved and exploit of some sort.
If it had more than six levels, I'd play them once or twice, so I'm recommending it. Just don't expect a lot from it.

Chime is a beautiful puzzle game that seemed to give Lumines a run for its money when I first played it. You have to place pentominoes down on a grid and create rectangles with them so the line that sweeps through in time with the music can play the sound they produce (changes depending on the shape of the rectangle) and then delete them from the board, highlighting the area that they covered. Your goal is to highlight the entire board to get a point bonus, start fresh with a clean board, and repeat the process. Each of the six songs sound wonderful and I really love both the mechanic of the music getting more
the better you do and the mechanic of different-shaped rectangles making different sounds makes each play session feel fresh, similar to Lumines.
Sounds great, looks great, plays great, I'd recommend Chime if you're a fan of puzzle games, musical games, or a mixture of the two.

I'm frightened for the future of this game and its community.
Despite my fears I most definitely recommend this awesome game.

11/10, buy this game. It's even better than everyone claims.
Mechanics:
This game mixes genres seamlessly. You play as an android and run around with 3rd person perspective. You can jump around, evade and have weak and strong attacks with your melee weapons. Additionally you have a little "pod" following you. It can shoot in any direction. So you mash through some robotic enemies when suddenly the camera changes and leaves you with a 2D sidescroller. Still using all the mechanics from the 3rd person perspective. Then again, the camera goes to ceiling view and you maneuver in a
through a huge amount of enemies and bullets.
The action is written and presented so well, it almost hurts. Later in the game there is a hacking mini-game introduced. It's an 8-bit asteroids version on steroids, a quite refreshing change in gameplay (Edit: It becomes a bit much later during the game tho. If you can't stand this minigame at all you won't enjoy the game fully).
You can also upgrade your weapons as well as yourself. You, being an android, can be enhanced with plug-in chips. They give bonuses like attack power or movement speed. Space is limited tho so you cant use all you like. It's a neat system.
Story:
It's as anime as it can possibly get. I wont even try to summarize it. It's quite philosophical, a lot like the "ghost in the shell" setting.
The game features 26 different endings, 5 of them being main endings. Once you finished the main story (after about 10 hours) you can start a new game+ but play as 9S, the sidekick from first playthrough. His hacking abilities give a lot more insight to whats happening during the game. After this the whole storyline continues and the game lets you decide between two characters.
After the third ending you get a "chapter select" option which lets you jump to any point in the story to finish all the sidequests and do the collecting of stuff you missed out.
Sound:
Best music ever made for a videogame, hands down. The themes used for certain areas etc are so well done (
), it's a pleasure to listen to.
Controls:
Crisp. And yeah, it's a gamepad game. People report it's playable with keyboard/mouse, but this was clearly designed with gamepad in mind.
Issues:
Personally I had ony slight issues. When setting the game to fullscreen it applied some downscaling as well. I found
which fixes it. No crashes. (System: i5-4690@4,5, 8gb ram, gtx970)

With the MTs removed it is a massive grind fest to progress. The controls are of course half done, with very noticable "you had to tap here, slide there, or finger this" all over the place. (And they still include the facebook/twitter for gold phone tactic..lmao ) With the lazy mobile and console market being so prevalent (It's a lot cheaper you see to make a console game and even cheaper to make some silly phone app) since they require less depth, less graphical quality and less work, many of these cheap indie companies choose to go that route, then as an afterthought cash grab, since the PC market is smaller in their opinion, they half-bake a port and send it to the PC, usually through the biggest "cheap junk, scam early access, and barely betas are welcomed  because we have no quality control and could really care less as long as we get a cut" platform that exists...a company called Valve and a platform called Steam! This game is amongst them, with the typical formula that goes like this,, interesting game, acceptable graphics and something new for your library, EXCEPT we are gonna spend as little as possible to make it just playable enough to garner a few fanbois to defend us in the hopes of grabbing a bit of "Side cash" from the PC market.
Anti-Squad is right on track with that formula. You'll take WAY longer than you should to progress and upgrade, endure VERY repetitive levels (Which you can expand of course by buying our "Use to be micro-Trans" content that we'll call DLC. This game is fun for a short while, but I very quickly realized it was not even close to being worth its full price. Reasons are below:
(
)
Mediocre gameplay.
The crafting system is decent at best, and leaves a lot to be desired. The fact that you have no idea how to get what you want to get until you experiment for 2 hours or just give up and search the answer online is NOT what I call a good learning curve.
The combat is okay, but nothing to be amazed at. Melee is timing so that you hit stuff and don't get hit. Ranged is... too easy. Have a bunch of arrows, shoot them at enemies until they flop over. Which leads to the next point:
Bad balance.
The game doesn't even seem to be trying to give players viable options. There is no multiclassing here, unless you want to end up super weak compared to pure characters. And even then there is only one good choice. It's a pain in the butt to regenerate any health in the game, and magic doesn't recharge fast enough to be useful. The result? Archery is the most OP  path to choose. As soon as you get a bow and enough arrows (which doesn't take that long) you can steamroll pretty much the whole game without getting hit once.
Lack of content.
Magicite attracts with its glowy effects, cool-looking dungeons and spells, etc... but in the end there just isn't that much in it. Enemies have like 2 attack patterns - charging straight at you or shooting projectiles. The few that attack sort of differently appear rarely, and even then they're not really a challenge as long as you use OP archery. Melee weapons and tools progress in straight tiers, and there are only two types of melee weapon that you can craft. Magic? There are three staves and they're rather boring. Ranged weaponry? There is literally just a bow. That's it. It doesn't even upgrade.
If you must get it, don't get it at full price.

Party Hard is a pretty bad stealth murder game.  The concept itself is solid if rather twisted. The neighbors are having a loud party and you simply have to murder everyone to have some peace and quite.
Overall the pixel art is decent and the levels often have a lot of cool details. The human sprites look pretty bad, however. The game also has an annoying soundtrack and some of the worst voiceacting I have ever heard.
The gameplay is rather tedious and repetitive. Using the few traps on each level is fun enough, but usually you can only finish off a few of your targets that way. After that you are stuck either waiting out for single targets to leave groups or going on short murder sprees and then hiding from the cops that arrive to the scene.
This is where the game really falls apart. The police act extremely randomly, sometimes they give up the chase just as they are about to catch you, other times they will keep chasing you even when they should have no idea where you are hiding. Everytime you get caught you need to start the level from the beginning and this gets tedious extremely fast. After a few levels I simply decided to give up, as I didn't find this kind of gameplay enjoyable at all.
Party Hard was a good idea but the execution leaves a lot to be desired. Not recommended.
The good:
- Good concept
- Levels have some cool details and traps
The bad:
- Relies too much on luck and repetition
- Tedious gameplay
- Annoying soundtrack
- Extremely bad voice acting

Deus Ex is easily one of the very best games I've ever played. Sure, it's old, the graphics look horrible by now and the game mechanics have been massively improved upon by many games that came after it. But still, for its time, Deus Ex was brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. And frankly, it still is. I can't count the number of times I've played the game on two hands anymore. And during most of those playthroughs, I discovered new things. New ways to tackle problems, new texts, new locations. The game world is huge. Except for RPGs, they don't make such massive games anymore. Which is a real shame.
Deus Ex has an extremely rich story and plot twists are abundant. The script is as near to perfect as it could possibly get. Sure, the voice acting is cringe worthy at times, but don't let that get in your way to enjoying the game.
But enough talk. This game needs to be played. And if the graphics seem like too big a hurdle for really appreciating the game, I suggest downloading the Deus Ex: Revision. It completely overhauls the game and manages to squeeze every last bit out of the Unreal engine, graphics wise. A brilliant, beautifully made mod, created with much love for the original game. And hey, it's free!

Over, it is so-so from what I have played so far. The gameplay itself is pretty decent and the story looks like it might be pretty good too given what I have seen so far. But major glaring issues.
- To say this is an Australian game is an understatement, this is austrailian to the point they parodied themselves. Everyone but the main characters from the other borderlands sounds like they took speech classes from Crocodile Dundee with a majority of the humor done the same way so you will miss a lot of what was said unless you know a little about their humor. This game is Australian to the point that if a US based company had tried to make this game, they would have probably caught some legal trouble for making fun of them. I am playing as Nisha and her melee attack is a friggin whip.
- The game itself has been fairly easy so far, you die more to jumping in lava or chasms (Even died once where I tried to jump on what I thought was a path only to find out it was just for show at the edge of the map and fell through)  than you do from enemy fire it feels like. Also, I hate the oxygen aspect of this game even more than I hated Slag in part 2.
- The Grinder, while a decent idea, just doesn't seem fleshed out enough to me, you will understand when you use it.
- The Skill trees just feel like they are all over the place to me for all the characters but Nisha (whole reason I chose her). The old games the skills had defined ways to play and it showed, these feel all over the place and too much emphasis on skills that wind up and cool down after combat with 20 different names for the stacks of the buff or debuff. You can pull up the talent calculator if you want to know what I mean.
- The butt drop attack honestly feels a little awkward for the game and tacked on to me.
The main reason why I still give this a thumbs up is it still plays like Borderlands and is at least somewhat entertaining but the humor is getting old rather quick. This game is not worth full price by any stretch of the imagination, get it on sale if at all.
This game makes me wish they had a neutral decision on if you would recommend or not as I couldn't really recommend it to others outright unless they are just played out of the other borderlands games and want another and I can't really say it isn't worth playing at all as the storyline itself kinda makes it seem like it is worth the first playthrough at least. But I am still working my way through it and can't so for sure whether it will be truly worth it for the storyline. This honestly feels it should have been a DLC for part 2, not a full on game.
UPDATE:
I have tried to give this game every chance, I have left and came back to it and still can't get myself to get into it. Changing my thumbs up to a thumbs down. Even to a borderlands fan, I just can't find it worth the value.
The game play mechanics on it overall aren't that bad minus the oxygen and butt drop mechanics. It is a little easier than i would like but otherwise fine. But the storyline just isn't there from what I can tell so far, the humor isn't there, and the talent trees just don't seem right to me. And dear god the voices get grating at times, especially that little boy Napykins Lunestalker when you kill his dad. Makes you want to mute the whole game.
At this point, I am kinda hoping they figure out a way to remove this from the borderlands storyline entirely and write it off as Athena lying to the vault hunters or losing her mind or something. Overall feels like they ruined a lot of potential in a what could have been a very good backstory. Still going to finish at least one playthrough though just see what all is going on before I move onto the Tell Tale game.
UPDATE #2: Finished the main story and have to definitely give this a thumbs down.
This takes place after Borderlands 1.
It tries to make it look like Handsome Jack is actually a good guy at the beginning but ends up going bad after being repeatedly betrayed and screwed over by others including Lilith and Roland. The problem with this is the Echo on Borderlands 2 already prove he was an evil person with how he locked his own daughter up and how he talked to her while doing it.
It  also tries to make Lilith and Moxxi much more evil than they really are. Tries to turn Lilith into a stone cold backstabbing killer and while she is a killer she still had morals to her in the other games which was thrown out the window entirely for this one to the point Brick was telling her to calm down and she wasn't acting like herself.
Then the ending which I won't spoil doesn't fit the Borderlands theme at all.
So as my final update and verdict. The story doesn't fit the Borderlands them in both style and has the continuity error for when Jack went bad which ruins the premise of the whole game, the other characters don't fit their types in this game and the overall game just doesn't fit.
It honestly feels more like a 1980's movie's themed fan fiction than an actual Borderlands game.
Sorry, but I just can't recommend this game and I hope they wipe it out from the official borderlands storyline as well.

This is easily the absolute worst game I have ever sunk so much time into. But I'm done, I give up. This game is domestic abuse. You're desperate to play what you want this game to be, and it will keep punching you in the face with bad design on every level.
The first thing you'll see is the UI. Don't be fooled, it's terrible. While functional enough on first introduction, like everything else with this game spending time with it results in constantly having to struggle with utterly amateurish problems. Fleet control is non-existent, thanks to having access only to a 'split half' button, and splitting off a new fleet via a list...and clicking every single individual ship. There's no shift click, drag click, zero functionality whatsoever. One click, ship moves. And if you click too fast it bugs out, registers a click outside the box, declares you must be done and goes with whatever was moved. Oh, and after every click the list scrolls back up to the top. So if you want to split off the battleships at the bottom of the fleet list in your 300 ship fleet, you need to scroll down, click, scroll back down, click, scroll back down....this is the quality of life the Stellaris UI consistently delivers to you. It creates frustrating micromanagement tasks where even the slightest degree of sci-fi strategy game experience and savvy would have resulted in none.
So you're playing the game, you got some planets. You probably lost some science ships and leaders to 'lolrandom' RNG event failures that are the antithesis of strategy and risk management (you can't manage risk when there's no feedback on risks, so design like this is poor in any game and, again, amateurish), but whatever. Now we're up against the 'core systems' limit. See, for some reason this game was intended to be a macro scale grand strategy game, so obviously they put in absolutely tons of micro-intensive planetary tiles all with individual population and buildings. Because that's good design. Macro game, add loads of micro features. Genius. So, seeing this problem of an ever increasing micromanagement burden on the player as they expand, the designers added a solution! A planetary planner, so you can simply lay out what you want the planet to eventually look like and it'll develop itself towards it!
....that's a joke, the actual solution is to force you to give the planet over to a 'sector', which places it entirely under the control of the AI. See, having introduced all these population and building mechanics, the designed solution is to then *force you to watch the AI f*** it up on your behalf*. As a result, the entire game consists of nothing more than you personally administrating a handful of planets, the research, and your fleet, while any other planet in your empire operates as an almost entirely untouchable (remember, terrible UI) AI controlled resource feeder that you have to spend highly limited influence points to regain control of for any reason. THAT'S the solution. Introduce tons of micromanagement features into your macro game, then force you to not interact with it. Oh, and remember, since playing around with your space navy is one of the only things you've got to do, because diplomacy is a shallow + and - numbers affair you usually have little power to affect (or care about), you have to recall back to the terrible UI for actually controlling your space navy. Yay. Fun.
Since the AI is consequently such a powerful focus in the game, what with it controlling even the majority of your own empire, it is, obviously, top notch.....yeah, no, that was another joke, it's terrible. The AI will, with it's own empires and with your sectors, often fail to develop planets at all. The result is, oh my look at that, intensive micromanagement as you try to properly set up a world so the sector AI won't screw up with it after you hand it over, and a staggering degree of incompetence by opposing empires, who will all invariably be Space North Korea thanks to their patiently expanded military fleet and facepalmingly weak economy.
The Steam review section simply doesn't allow the word limit to go over the flaws in Stellaris. The problem is that they're not immediately apparent. My assertion that Stellaris is like domestic abuse was, putting aside the inevitable 'triggerings' I'll get posted to me, very carefully chosen. You're going to be drawn into the idea of this game, you're going to want to play it. And then there'll be problems. It'll be shallow. Poor design will get in the way. But you're still invested in the idea of Stellaris....we all are, we want a cool sci-fi macro strategy game that's less opaque and nicer on the eyes than Distant Worlds: Universe! You'll buy the DLC. One is an overpriced cosmetic. The other adds a few bits of content that should have been in release and don't do enough to add life to a sterile galaxy of RNG anolomies and mining stations. You eagerly await each patch. They're supporting the game! It's expanding, getting better! ....except it isn't. The core experience remains *exactly the same*. Shallow. Dull. Frequently demanding of cookie cutter approaches. Sectors have been a failing so prevalent and consistent since launch that they....declared them to be fine, forced everyone into a single thread for it, then ignored the thread entirely.
It took 288.9 hours for the endless stack of Stellaris straws to turn the back of my camel into a thin paste, and admit that I was working far, far too hard to try and get something, anything of what I WANT Stellaris to be from the pitiless, cold hands of the reality of what Stellaris IS, and will always be given the current direction and attitude of the developers,  judging by the forums.
Hell, people can look at my review history and conclude I just ♥♥♥♥♥ about big games everyone loves, but I'll tell you this; I'd flip every single damned thing to recommended in comparison to Stellaris. Yes/No is a binary state. In a more granular world I'd have put Fallout between 50 and 60. Stellaris I'd give a 40, and that's a rating that can be achieved by anything that runs stable. Big whoop, well done. That's my Stellaris recommendation: "It didn't crash." Feel free to f***ing quote me on it.

I really like Chime conceptually. I wish that the game included more songs, and that even more songs were available as DLC. I bought Chime on the 360 a while back, and I enjoyed it. There isn't a whole lot of content, so I burned through it pretty quickly. I felt mouse controls would be faster and more precise, so years later when I saw it on Steam, I ended up buying another copy. Unfortunately, mouse controls feel very clumsy. I never feel like I quite have control of the position of the current piece, and I end up locking it down in the wrong spot way too often. Ages ago, I played a lot of Puzzle Pirates, which includes a somewhat time-sensitive pentomino placement minigame, and in that game, I never felt like a misplaced piece was the game's fault. With that in mind, it's definitely possible to have tight, clean mouse controls in a game like this.
That said, the game is still completely playable with other input methods, and even with its relatively limited content it's worth a play.

After playing through the tutorial missions it's easy to say that:
- Sniper movement cost is too big, he will be too much behind rest of the group even though his shot does high damage.
- Ability costs are unbalanced early on.. the fk you want me to use movement speed boost for 2 turns on sniper if it takes a full turn away?
- It costs too much to upgrade abilities to make the characters good enough
- Because of high cost of upgrading characters, you have to grind a lot for later missions to make the game feel playable
- You have very few abilities you can use per character and movement uses up bit too many action points. Trap skills are hardly useful when the enemy doesn't even come to you unless you run away from them to make them take damage, making the gameplay feel slower and much too boring
- There is no dodge chance, critical chance, cover, destroying obstacles or anything like that so you are taking out simply laid out enemies 1 by 1 with your squad in each mission, typically by moving once and shooting once per character turn.
That and how it feels slow overall. The game looks good, but it should be more than just slowly moving and shooting with aoe or single target attacks on 3 (up to 5?) units. I guess I just don't like most turn-based games. They usually need that something more to be enjoyable.

Having played the original FFF I got this one on sale expecting a sequel. What I got was a remake with minor differences in gameplay. Essentially this is the same as the original. Of course there's some change in story and some additions to its battle system, but most of them are very minor.
The change in the amount of characters on the field from 3 to 6 is pretty big but is countered by the number of relative enemies you face so the point is moot. What's funny is there's still the switching mechanic even though so far there's no more than 6 playable characters at a time. From what I remember the combat itself and the upgrade system stayed the same. Same skills, or similar enough to not really matter, same basic attacks, same furies. Most if not all the enemies and bosses so far are the same, or different but minor enough to not be a big deal. There's a new, I think, dashing feature that's slightly faster than running but it's hardly important.
I've heard that there's now 3 diverging storylines with their own endings but so far I haven't noticed anything different. I'm mostly just skipping the story anyways since I already watched through it in the original one.
The areas you visit and the dungeon layouts are exactly the same so far including enemy placements, types of enemies, and most of the items littered around.
The graphics and animations are all the same so nothing special there. The music they use during special actions and events are also the same.

Party Hard is a game published by tinyBuild and about "cleaning up" partys from bikers, party addicted, aliens and more. Trough carefully prepared sneak attacks, fast assasinations, traps and phone calls you have to clear each of the 12 levels (+7 bonus levels) and, if you feel the need several workshop created stages.
About the Story: the protagonist, a young, honest citizen (with a little personality problem) cant fall asleep. The reason for this are a bunch of neighbours having a loud party. Fastly you decide to get rid of the excessive noises and "convince" your neighbours to stop the fuss. After clearing local problems, you decide to widen the purge over all of Las Vegas...with success.
Gameplay: all of the 12 original levels have unique design, theme, NPCs and events wich makes almost every level a new and different experience. As already mentioned, there also exist 7 bonus levels you can unlock and many, MANY workshop created maps. There also are 4(+1 DLC character) alternate characters you unlock through the game or by getting specific achievements (these however are hard to get and the 2 chars you unlock through simply playing you only get after finishing the main story). Controls are simple, you can move up, left, down and right, give yourself a little sprint boost that drains your stamina, stab, pick people up, use items and traps or show your hot party moves.
Every level is randomized (in a specific frame), for example:
1. time next to the entry there stands a zebra
--->you get "busted " or die; you restart
2. the zebra is gone, instead you can see a little white car at the end of the road
Sadly, the amount of given traps runs out very fast and often doesnt take many people out, so the second half of most levels starts to become a kill-hide-repeat game, wich, in my opinion, takes a bit of the fun away, especially, when you have so few traps, that you basically have to wait until someone leaves the group to be able to kill him without noticing. When then suddenly a random NPC decides to call the police, after you killed 75% of party harders and you cant flee or dodge the cop you feel rather f*cked. This is, what the game makes hard, however, if this happens several times to you in one level it just gets annoying.
There also are some weird mechanics, that seem rather stupid. For example, a cop tried to arrest me, so I hid behind a little bus. Suddenly the trusty officer decides to "screw it " and leaves. I also found several bugs through my play through, too  (mostly graphical).
So...what is GOOD, what's BAD?
Pros:
-unique levels
-workshop
-choice of different characters (mostly after playtrough!)
-interesting story
-you can party
-free DLC with extra level and special mechanics
Cons:
-after all traps of a level are gone it might get boring
-soundtrack gets annoying, since it starts anew once you died
-bugs
-AI sometimes feels weird
-unlockable characters you only get after playing story mode or through hard achievements
In my opinion this game is fun to a certain point. Story is interesting with a nice little twist and the DLC is fine (however it isnt free without reason...). Should you play this game?
Only if you have good determination.

Without a doubt one of the best Call of Duty games of all time. The campaign is set in the Cold war era allows you to fight in Cuba, Vietnam, Laos, Russia, Kazakhstan, Hong Kong, America and the Arctic circle, allowing for the experience to never get boring. That alongside the great storyline means that the campaign in this game is without a doubt one of the best campaigns in CoD history. The multiplayer is well balanced and one of the hardest multiplayers in Call of Duty, if you're good at Call of Duty multiplayer, it'll show in this game. As for zombies, Black Ops 1 features some of the best maps ever created, such as Kino der Toten, Ascension and Call of the Dead. Out of all the Call of Duty games we've had, Black Ops 1 has my favourite zombies exerience by far, and features all of the World at War zombies maps
Unfortunately the community is small, which is to be expected for a Call of Duty game on PC, finding games of Team Deathmatch is still easy, but finding public matches for zombies can be difficult, and almost impossible if you're looking for a DLC map.
Overall, if you're a Call of Duty fan I'd strongly advise buying this, as it's one of the best Call of Duty titles ever released, especially if you're a Zombies fan.

At first, I thought that this game is all about fanservice and gimmicks.
Then I've decided to play this game. And I have never been so wrong in my life.

This game’s story is rooted in previous game, NieR (also known as NieR Gestalt/Replicant). Nier was not published on PC and was, unfortunately, extremely underestimated on consoles. Most people made their opinions based on critics’ reviews. For some reason, most critics
and, based on most reviews, dropped the game at the very start. But NieR has wonderful story which is strongly connected with plot of Automata. Honestly, I would recommend anyone to
watch all cutscenes from NieR. The amazing story of Automata becomes even deeper if you know previous game’s story.
Nevertheless, NieR:Automata’s striking plot even on its own allows you to make links to all three main characters and almost feel them. Through this link, you can feel their emotions – happiness and sadness, joy and infelicity, love and hatred almost like you ARE the character of this game.
I really shouldn’t discuss plot in this review because it should be experienced. not told by someone else, to avoid ruining impression it makes on uninitiated. All I can say is that is combines emotional and logical influences to make you feel the situation.
Gorgeous soundtrack – literally every one of them is great. I am a huge symphonic metal fan, but I have to admit that soundtrack is awesome. I would like to even go further and say that quality of Automata’s soundtrack is beyond reach of most artists. If you don’t believe my words, listen for yourself:
or
They are the same, yet different.
Furthermore, every track can dynamically change to represent your current situation. For example, almost every track has a 8-bit version that is played during hacking mini-game.
Maybe visuals are not so great, but they fit right in and you forget about it after an hour or two. Design is astoundingly good and every detail is placed right where it belongs. Still, I have to say that
. Some people just can’t find a giant diamond covered by thin coat of dust.
Gameplay is also great and variable. Transitions are smooth and every gameplay type in this game is marvelous. Whether you are playing a bullet-hell stage, or 3rd person slasher, I bet you will enjoy it. Nevertheless, let me tell about it. Gameplay can be divided to three types: air battle, ground battle and hacking battle. In air battle you have flight unit and you are shoting enemies. Pretty simple, huh? Still, this mode splits to two - when you are flying forward (and shooting forward) and when you are flying slower, but can look to any direction in 2D space. Ground battles are... well... ground battles like in other hack'n'slash games. However, sometimes camera is forced to be at certain angle (side or top). Hacking games can be separated to three categories. First, simple, just shoot black sphere. Second is speed run to black sphere and eliminate protecting system. Third – plot driven hacking. All these modes are combined in different ways, thus gameplay requires you to always tune your strategy according to the situation.
But the thing is… you can’t judge these aspects of the game separately. The key to beauty of this game is it’s…
. All these aspects together create a unique experience, when you think that everything fits right in. They are, if one can say, tightly linked to each other, thus creating something new, that I can feel but can’t describe. In most games, you can turn off music or ignore landscape. This will affect your experience, but only in that field. On the other hand, in Automata, if you disable at least one aspect, other will be affected. Everything is linked together and the plot of the game is really reinforced by landscape design, music, gameplay…
Surely, I have some final words toward this game’s plot and game itself, that should be written at this moment.
Thank you for reaching to my soul, to my… gestalt, through protective layers of cynicism. Thank you for breaking it apart only to make it whole again. This game lets you experience being a strong person facing overwhelming odds. This game surely lets you taste the bitter sweet taste of pyrrhic victories. Of course, we have won… but what was the price?...
The one and only problem of this game is optimization. But this problem will definitely fade as new generation of videocards appears, so it's just temporary. Many games had similar issues at start (remember Witcher 2 ubersampling?). And come on, real-time calculations of water vaporisation are not that simple. Road for the next-gen!
Thus, comes an end to my review. But, I think,

"Hitman meets Hotline Miami" is probably the best way I can describe Party Hard. Like any game featuring a certain bald-headed assassin, it's got open-ended levels with a wide variety of traps and accidents to trigger to throw a wrench into the game's social stealth-based AI, and like Dennaton's ultra-violent duology, the whole thing is presented with a kitschy 80's aesthetic featuring 8-bit graphics and synthwave music that is earworm-y as hell.
There are a ton of ways to go about your murdering sprees, but it's best to stay as subdued as possible, because your knife is slow and extremely short, and you can't sprint for very long if someone catches you carving into an innocent bystander. It seems like your movement and attacking are made intentionally crappy in order to prevent the game from being too easy, and this is compounded by certain assets and items in each level being randomized every time you play, so you'll always have to think of a new strategy when you replay levels because that one really useful trap isn't going to be there every time you replay it. It does make the game a little difficult, but I'm having so much fun just trying new stuff every time I replay a level that I don't really mind it so much. It's not perfect, but it's really fun, and for such a low price, you'd be crazy not to at least try it.

Deus Ex is foremost a unique game in its field. It is really quite unlike any other game I have ever played. It shares territory with titles such as Half-Life and Tomb Raider, but also takes inspiration from some role-playing games as well. It seems to have carved out or invented its personal little niche in the game market, by mixing two normally contrasting game essentials. It manages to successfully combine puzzle, shooting and RPG elements to create a really exceptional atmosphere. While it may have several middling faults which will occasionally make you cringe, it is mostly an extremely fun and thought-provoking game, inspired by both modern conspiracy theories and philosophy.
The storyline is based in the near future, and revolves around nano-augmented (basically this just means technologically enhanced) Agent J. C. Denton, who works for the United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition (UNATCO), based out of Liberty Island, New York. As is normal, the world of the future is not a safe place to be, and UNATCO must protect the citizens of the Earth from various terrorist plots and evil denizens. Primarily in the first mission of the game, you must regain control of the Statue of Liberty and Liberty Island, which has been seized by an organisation known as the NSF (National Secessionist Forces). The plot is far to complex to go into detail, and it would also spoil the game, but save to say that the basic premise is that Denton must work to solve problems relating to deadly viruses (which has the lovely sounding name Grey Death), corrupt governments and world domination attempts. The plot is really the best aspect of Deus Ex, as without it, it would not have anywhere near the same novelty value. The game is also extremely long, taking often upwards of twenty hours to complete, and if you were to go hunting for all the many hidden locations, objects and side-quests it will take much longer. Luckily, there are only a few dull moments during this, as you will be visiting New York, Hong Kong and Paris on the globe-hopping crusade. It can however become slightly annoying when you must retrace your steps several times in order to return to previous locations in each city. During this epic journey Denton talks to literally dozens and dozens of other characters, all of whom have a great array of responses, and can be conversed with many times. However, this leads me to probably one of the largest faults of Deus Ex: the character voices.
Although every character talks a great deal, and the scripts themselves are very good and involving, the voice acting is frankly rather below standard. Absolutely no characters (with the possible exception of arch villain Bob Page) seem to have any genuine emotions in their voices at all, and instead inhabit a world where emotions have seemingly been destroyed, or at least mainly forgotten about. Denton and his brother Paul both speak like they have walked out of the Terminator films as reincarnations of Arnold Schwarzenegger. Even when people are hurt, they shout or scream only in a vaguely half-hearted manner. Listening to all of these emotionless and mainly blunt conversations can sometimes get a bit tiresome; although you will often be too engrossed in the subjects they are discussing to notice this. On top of this, mainly the musical score is also rather dull, and mostly sounds very similar and unremarkable (though it will inevitably slowly grow on you anyway), apart from the classic main title theme. However, general sound effects and ambient sounds are quite good.
Thankfully, gameplay itself is consistently solid throughout. It is theoretically possible to get through the entire game without killing anyone (save from one or two characters who must be incapacitated), as you are given a wide range of both lethal and non-lethal weapons with which to take on enemies. However this can get extremely difficult (as you will be frequently running out of non-lethal ammunition) and furthermore, you are given no incentive to do so (apart from the honour). It is much easier (and often all the more fun) to go in with all guns blazing, although this may not always be the best way to handle a given situation. Shooting and targeting is relatively easy, although it can be tricky earlier in the game when skill levels are lower. Graphically, the game isn't much to look at today, but that just gives it the much sought after "classic" feel.
A nice touch is to give Denton the various abilities to learn skills such as lock-picking, hacking computers, swimming and making aiming easier, through the reward of skill points, which are earned by achieving certain goals or fully exploring the different maps. This can make your own version of Denton able to complete certain tasks much easier. At first, this system seems overcomplicated, and to be frank it often is leading to an RPG-ish feel, and could have probably been implemented more simply, though the scheme is easily workable. The gameplay also has several nice problem-solving virtues, and situations can be resolved through a number of ways. The game makes use of a detailed inventory menu, from which you can see objects picked up, check health and review known information and objectives. Also, you handling of situations will influence other characters views and opinions of you, subtly changing the storyline. Due to this, it is very unlikely you will ever replay exactly the same story.
Deus Ex is simply different from anything else, and stands out from the crowd on its own plinth. It is a welcome change from the more stereotypical action-adventure, and blends many different elements almost seamlessly together. Although it does have some minor faults, I still highly recommend it to anyone, as everyone should be able to overlook the mediocre voice acting and still thoroughly enjoy this game, in all its "cyberpunk" glory. In retrospect, Deus Ex has to be looked upon as a worthy contender in any “Greatest Games” list. The true value lies in the morality, philosophy and conspiracy themes the story focuses upon, which help to stimulate both the mind and psyche.

Hexcells is a simple logic puzzle game. While it starts off very easy, it later on can get a bit more complicated, often taking me a while to "see" some clue I was missing.
I've had this on my library for a long time, and only recently have I decided to play it, after Kami.
This is more up my alley. The game can be very formulaic, perhaps, as there's never the need to "guess" any move. If you observe the board carefully, you'll have everything you need to make the next correct move. Initially, I didn't think it was that good, most levels being rather short and obvious. Thankfully, things got more complicated, levels bigger, and the game proved very satisfactory!
It's very similar to minesweeper, although there's no losing. You won't touch a bomb and restart. Instead, you'll have +1 mistake, that later affects how many gems you get, for completionists' sake.
The game also has various sets of puzzles, introducing a new mechanic between each one, keeping things interesting, without overwhelming the player with everything at once.
Puzzle-wise, it's alright. I enjoyed it, but it's nothing mind blowing, in my opinion.
What makes it stand out, for me, is the audio design. It's amazing! It's very minimalist, but it works really well!
With most puzzle games, I just have my own music on... in the case o Hexcells, it felt rather out of place. There's an ambient track constantly playing in the background, but your actions in the game produce sound-effects in sync with the background track and create a great sense of "atmosphere", even in a puzzle game!
It's something I rarely see in videogames that aren't music related. They tend to ignore how sound and music is important, so Hexcells is a breath of fresh air, to me!
For that reason, above all else, I'll recommend this game. Looking at the developer's games, it seems indeed that sound always plays an important role, so I'll definitely be looking out for me!

This is an early impression review.
I'm 6 hours into the game and rather disappointed. I've played the dickens out of Borderlands 2, so when Borderlands: The Pre-sequel went on sale for $20, I decided to finally take the plunge.
Cons:
Political correctness and censored vulgarity seem to be the new order of the day. Mr. Torgue's censored speech was always good fun in the previous game but now all characters eschew bad language in odd ways. Darn, dang, etc. It rings hollow. It seems like Gearbox and 2K were trying to make this more family friendly in the hopes of turning Borderlands into a wider media property and in doing so betrayed a portion of the game's heart which had previously made the game stupidly fun. You fail when you need to preach at and brow beat your audience into submission rather than presenting a multi-dimensional situation which allows the player to decide what, if any aspect, is right.
Writing & voice acting are limp and seemingly inept thus far. These areas were always great in previous incarnations yet they are amazingly bland in this game. I know the actors can deliver great performances, as we've all heard before, but they seem to have been given terrible or careless direction when performing, then again, they weren't given much to work with from what I've heard so far. Some characterizations seem to have entirely changed. Moxxi isn't flirty, she seems annoyed or disinterested in everything at best, etc.
Humor, or lack thereof. This goes to the previous points, writing, voice acting, and characterization. I don't need meme-laden reference humor all the time, and that is absolutely in here, but there doesn't feel like there is any meat here. The wit, zing, and bite of the previous jokes are gone. We're left with something barely tepid.
The game engine is virtually the same, not that I expected them to overhaul the entire thing but there isn't much in the way of new visual wizz bang doohickeys.
Items, including moon rocks, seem to disappear entirely. I'm not sure if this is a bug or a "feature". In BL2, items seemed to stay put until you got round to collecting them. Items do disappear from crates you've opened, if they are vented into the vaccum of space. Also, be prepared to lose a lot of items when killing bad guys, especially when they're flying over the inummerable areas you can't get to unless you want to instakill yourself.
The moon buggy is horrid to drive. Get ready to repeatedly kill yourself when trying to make some radical jumps, dude. :P I'd compared it to Mass Effect's Mako, but at least the Mako could jump over obstacles properly.

Seemingly less content overall. The hard disk footprint is about 6GB smaller than BL2, that's with all DLC for both installed. Some have complained about the story, I assume length is a major factor, I'm not far enough to judge that or narrative.
Pros:
The music is pretty great.
Some grindy challenges seem to have been done away with, finding vault symbols, collecting all echo recorders in odd locations, etc. I could be wrong as I'm not too far into the game but it seems slightly less grindy in this area.
Moon rocks seem more plentiful than eridium was, thus slightly less grinding.
That's about it so far.
Conclusion:
There is no polish to be found here. Borderlands: The Pre-sequel is little more than a quick buck cash grab, or so it seems at this early juncture. Add a new location, and a couple new elements, then mix it up with all the old BL2 concepts, reskin it, and they have a "new" game. They had a hit with BL2 and tried to remake it as fast as they could for another win on the scoreboard, it didn't work too well.
This would have been more fitting as a large expansion pack for BL2. DLC outside of the Season Pass, for that game.
It seems like reheated cafeteria food. You can eat it but I'm not sure anyone is salivating for it.

Low Desert Punk is a high octane single player free roaming driver where your only real mission is to stay alive by not crashing.  Enemies however have a different goal in mind and will swarm you relentlessly trying to crash you up.  Definitely a lot of hand/eye coordination required here.  Combined with the catchy music, this small Unity value game delivers some fun!
Controls couldn't be simpler.  WASD used on the keyboard, no mouse required.  W to go, S to slow, A & D to swirve your truck left and right.  The Space bar gives you a Nitro boost but is limited by a cool down.  Hit the targets, and use Nitro to allow you to get some revenge on the swarming enemies.  Hitting more targets faster helps get you a bigger multiplier to get bigger score totals.  The game keeps track of the top 9 Steam scores so you'll always have a target score total to aspire to reach, which is nice for a game like this.
Game has two modes, both single player.  One gives you 3 "hit" points or 3 lives if you would, and you'll gain a life every level you advance, and the other mode gives you three times the points but only one chance to wreck and your game is over.
You can play with a controller, but WASD and Space worked just fine for me with fluid, responsive controls.
My only gripes were there are ZERO options available.  No sound settings, no resolution options, no key mapping, and not even a full screen/window option.  Bare bones in the options department.  Also there was no cursor on the main screen and selecting a mode and hitting start was tricky for me.. not being able to see a cursor, but that might be because of my dual monitors and might not be an issue for most players.
My Score for Low Desert Punk is a 74%, mostly hurt by a lower then you might expect "value" score.  Even at the price tag under a dollar, I think the game is addictive enough to make most people want to play it a few times, but that will likely only add up to a half an hour for most people.  Good game and fun while it lasts however!

This isn't a normal JRPG in my eyes. It has something about it that kept me playing to the end of the campaign but no further. It is unusual in many ways, both good and not-so good...
Characters: Personally, a decent chunk of them seem a tad generic. Some are truly special and are will forever more be remembered even with the game being no longer played for a very long time. Still, this is far between and I counted 3 ish main characters like this. Although the rest do not fall under general stereotypes, they are typical for games of these types. Still, for the first 10 ish hours of gameplay, they were all bearable. Then, later, their "interesting" personalities do fade quickly and you'd wish for some development in personality. I felt no sympathy with some of the characters.
Music: One of the best parts of this game by far. Every song that I have heard from this game is rememberable in their own rights. From the epic transformations, to the cheerful and humourous exposition. Every point has this music. Music that I shall remember due to the fact I have a playlist of 'em on youtube now. Never shall get rid of them. The only real problem with the songs is that there are too little of them. Towards the end, they'll be played more times than the top charts. But, it isn't too bad to counter their quality. Quality over quantity.
Plot: This was a little too generic in my eyes. This story could be placed into numerous other games, or another story's plot could have replaced it, and not too much difference would be made to be honest. The characters may drive on and on about how the world is in danger, but I never felt engaged to the story too much. Even the parts you would be crying over. I did not. Just simply because sometimes, their death or brink of death did nothing to develop the plot nor characters. But, at least it is linear and can be easily followed until half way (no spoilers).
Graphics: In a nutshell, its the Neptunia game engine used for the exploration of dungeons, monster designs, combat and everything really. This isn't too bad, these graphics are a little dated, but that's because these are ported from the PS3. The dungeons are not great nor too bad. They are reasonably large with many monsters and nice scenery in the background. Up to a point anyway. Some of the dungeons are repeated multiple times, and are visible from first sight although on other sides of the map. These maps are well designed though, I just wished they added more maps for each dungeons. This goes with the the monsters too. The monsters, even some of the bosses are of the same basic design. Moreover, some of these repeated monsters are extremely similar to the monsters from Neptunia. Too similar... But, the battles and the mechanics involved are the same of the neptunia. So, they are very good and you can grind for many hours, in which you will even with DLC, without getting too boring.
Conclusion: This game I would class as a "one-trick" pony. It does what it is meant to do, but nothing more nor less. Nothing surprised me and parts were predictable. But, I kept playing because what a pony this game was! Yes parts were annoying. Yes parts were predictable. Yes parts drove my head in. But, I played it till the end. Further more, I feel like I kind of benefitted playing fairy fencer F advent dark force. I would say this game is worth the money once an offer of 30% or more is on. Just because with the normal amount this game is worth, you might as well buy neptunia and have a better time. Still, if you have, then go ahead, knock yourselves out! The vile God awaits...

Every action requires far too much clicking and fussing, and every moment spent with the game is a reminder that Antisquad was designed for mobile devices rather than the PC.
UI and control gripes aside, the gameplay itself doesn't measure up to what you'd expect from a Tactical TBS game on the PC. There isn't even a cover mechanic in the game -- everyone simply stands around out in the open, exchanging gunfire. If that wasn't bad enough, you'll also need to grind for gold coins in order to upgrade your mercs and open lockboxes. Because mobile port.
I have to be brutally honest here... Even Jagged Alliance: Flashback was a better Tactical TBS than Antisquad. Just think about that for a minute before you spend any money on this.

Nier: Automata came out at an unfortunate time. 2017 is quickly turning into 1998 part 2 as one of the best years for videogames and Nier: Automata has come out amidst killers such as Persona 5, LOZ: Breath of the Wild and Horizon. Nier: Automata would've been a clear winner for GOTY any other year but it has stiff competition this year. However, even if Nier is not the "Best" game of 2017, it's probably one of the most important games to have come out this generation.
Nier: Automata is a milestone in Videogame storytelling. It's the greatest achievement in this field since Metal Gear Solid 1 and Final Fantasy VI before that. It's difficult to explain without spoilers but the amazing story that is told by Nier is something special that would be impossible to replicate on any other Medium.
The gameplay is fantastic, utilising a mixture of character action, bullet hell, 2D platforming and twin stick shooting. You may think that these mechanics are diluted by the sheer numbers but each is masterfully crafted, fun and flow into one another smoothly.
The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in years and the music is used for fantastic effect, making epic or truly heartfelt moments all the more impactful.
I loved every character. Despite being Androids these were some of the most human characters I've ever had the pleasure of meeting. Every hardship they went through affected me personally and there were few moments during my playthrough where I wasn't completely invested in their plights.
The game does have some cons, like performance is a bit rough, it's not terrible but it's not exactly smooth, with strange stutters every once in a while, especially when entering new area's. The game is also not exactly great looking, graphically. These shortcomings though are easy to ignore compared to what this game does right, and what it does right, it knocks completely out of the park.
While games like Horizon or Persona 5 will be remembered as some of the best of 2017, Nier: Automata is gonna be remembered as one of the best and most important videogames of this generation as well as for the industry as a whole. Thank you to Square Enix, Platinum games and Yokotaro for crafting this masterpiece.

+ Interesting and fun gameplay elements.

A fun, simple little game, with an interesting, brightly colored art style.  The monsters are ALL very tricky at the beginning, but after a few hours, you should be able to master them without taking damage.  The level design is very repetitive, although I somewhat like that you can see the entire world, top to bottom, and don't have to explore up and down at all.  Crafting is MEH, there need to be a LOT more items, and more unique ones... you can pretty much make identical, albeit more powerful items depending on the materials used, which isn't interesting at all.  The inventory menu needs to be made larger, and the only way to get gold (which is, at last in the early/mid game, the only way to get decent armor) is to monotonously chop down every tree in every level, since all items have the same $2 selling value, you may as well load up on 99x wood in each inventory slot.
I think this game has potential, but needs to be greatly expanded upon.  I'd recommend it if you've played through other, more polished games like Terraria, Risk of Rain, Don't Starve, but honestly, the quality and depth of all those games eclipses Magicite by so much, it'd be tough to move on from them to a strict downgrade.  That said, I'm looking forward to what the creator has in store for Magicite, there's a lot of room for improvement, and sometimes it's nice to have a "lite" version of Terraria to play.

Still worth it all these years later. The game is amazingly clever, letting you control a secret agent through a sci-fi/semi-near-future world fighting against all sorts of conspiracies. It's technically a first person shooter, but run-and-gun gameplay does NOT work unless you put in a lot of effort to building your semi-customizable character toward that goal. Instead, you're supposed to sneak around and talk with a variety of interesting characters.
What really sells it is how responsive the game is to your actions. Kill too many people? The acquisitions officer will stop giving you ammo. Sneak into the wrong sex's bathroom? Your commander calls you out on it. Faced with a moral quandary on how to handle a surrendering enemy? You could carry out the execution you're ordered to do, or... blow up your field supervisor if you feel this is just that unacceptable.
