I'm something of a Picross nut, having played and near-beaten most of Nintendo's Picross games. When I saw Hexcells on the Steam New Releases section, I was quite happy; I have always thought these kinds of logic puzzles were better on a platform with a mouse. A few bucks later (thanks to Steam trading card sales - this game doesn't give out cards, btw), I had Hexcells in my library.
The actual logic of Hexcells is not difficult to grasp. If you've played Minesweeper or Picross 3D, you'll be right at home. You'll be following numbers inside of hexes, with symbols indicating whether the surrounding blue hexes will be consecutive or split, and later you will find numbers on rows or columns as well, with similar symbols. These symbols are, admittedly, not as easy to remember as I'd like (a problem that even Picross 3D had). I've made a few mistakes in puzzles because I misread the symbol in a given hex. In a related note, it's also somewhat easy to forget which mouse button performs which function, causing stupid mistakes that get recorded in your level score. Hexcells does not have a time limit of any kind, so you are essentially free to brute-force your way through a puzzle if you so desire, but making mistakes reduces how many hexes you receive as a reward for that level, and Steam Achievement nuts will probably want to avoid doing that if possible, as there is an achievement awarded for getting a perfect score on every level.
Presentationally speaking, Hexcells is simple and pleasing. The visuals are extremely minimalist (hexagons, and only hexagons); the only visual effects you'll be seeing are the tiny animations for shading or breaking hexes. The music is electronic ambience, in the style of Solar Fields (i.e. Mirror's Edge or Capsized), with the added effect that in-game sound effects are played on rhythm, a la Lumines or Rez. If I could complain about the presentation in any area, though, Hexcells does not provide a color-blind option (though I am not color-blind, I am unsure if the game's use of blue and orange would cause problems for those who are), and the low-contrast nature of the backgrounds makes the "Menu" button difficult to find.
I am pleased to report that Hexcells performs admirably on both Windows and Linux, owing to its nature as a Unity game. I would presume that Macintosh support is also good, as a result. Both of my test machines (no slouches, admittedly) ran the game with no obvious slowdowns or graphical glitches. I'd wager most machines made in the last half-decade will work just fine; I suppose netbooks may be feasible as well, but as I do not have access to one right now, I cannot say for certain, so Your Mileage May Vary.
About the biggest complaint I have about Hexcells, though, is that there are just not enough puzzles. Hexcells offers 6 "worlds," with five puzzles each, and the last puzzle essentially acting as a credits reel. I finished the game in a little over an hour, though I have not achieved Perfect on every puzzle just yet.
All that said, though, at $3 or less, Hexcells is certainly not a waste of your money. I'd like to see more logic-puzzle games like this on Steam.

Chime is a block dropping game in which not quite Tetris pieces are randomly given to you to place onto the board. The main goal is to create quadrilaterals using the slightly unfamiliar pieces. I should mention the blocks do not actually “drop” You can place them anywhere on the board and as such the possibilities are greater so the game demands your combos and coverage to be better than traditional “falling” block games.
This game takes from Lumines more than the others. You build quadrilaterals and then a timer starts until it becomes solid in which you must add to it before solidification for more points and combo scores. Once solid, a bar that sweeps the screen collects the solid stuff you have made. And this continues until you have amassed enough to unlock the next stage. Its unfortunate that even in free mode you cannot even preview what the next stages song will be as unlocking new stages requires play in the timed mode.
The reason I say it borrows from those games is because of how the gameplay is integrated into the music. The more elaborate the combos the more flare is added to the music; and the music is phenomenal.

Antisquad looks like a pretty fun little squad based tactical game. However, before you start playing, there are some differences between Antisquad and other quality games which you should know about:
First and foremost, excessive clicking is required. It appears that this game was made for phones or tablets. Now, maybe this is only true during the lengthy tutorial, but I wouldn't know. I never got past the game holding my hand as if I were a semi-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child.
Duuuurrrrr...I mean secondly, the tutorial. During the tutorial the game will only allow you to do exactly as the game instructs you. Even if you click somewhere else, nothing happens. I will note that Antisquad does a very adept job at telling you how the game works during the first mission, but after that I firmly believe they should leave you alone. Instead, going into the second mission the game is still like that creepy uncle that just hangs around and wants to hold your hand. I did not make it past the second mission because, personally, I prefer to figure games out on my own, at my own pace, and am not afraid of failing miserably once or twice while doing so. Though, with the simplicity of Antisquad, I doubt even the most mentally challenged gamers will fail to complete missions successfully from what I've seen.
In conclusion, the game is graphically appealing and may even be fun. I just can't help but feel a little violated after all of the excessive hand holding and whisperings of sweet nothings in my ear as I attempt to play.

So, I've finally beat the game.
After many tries and around 7 hours, I've finished the final level of the main campaign.
And what do I think about this game?
Well, you know how Hitman games or the stealth playthrough of Dishonored make well planned murder feel satisfying? You stalk your target from the shadows, wait for the perfect moment and then take out your weapon and strike. You hide the corpse and vanish without a trace. No one seen anything. No one heard anything.
Now imagine that you have 50 people on a small, crowded map and have to kill them all without being caught. Murder becomes a chore. A grind. You're thinking to yourself "Jesus Christ, I still have to kill 20 people, help...". You don't need a plan of any kind, just wait for someone to go to a place where no one will see them, go up to them, press the button, walk away, do it 59 more times. Also, don't even bother about hiding the bodies. You get no penalty if a body is found, unless you're standing next to it. So feel free to cover the map with corpses.
The music? Everyone says that it's good, but after walking away from the computer I don't remember a single song. Meanwhile I keep humming songs from Bastion, Hotline Miami or Undertale. I'm tapping my feet to songs from Patapon or Crypt of The Necrodancer. But this game? Meh. It's not bad, but it's just there and doesn't cause you to feel suicidal.
Story is extremely dissapointing and lazily written. You can tell what the plot twist will be after the second level. They tried too hard to make it serious and edgy, but I just killed a clown with a exploding bubblegum machine.
In short:
No. Just no. Don't waste your time on this game.
I don't know how you can make a game about murder that makes you think "Man, killing people is so grindy", but congrats. You did it.

At first, I thought that this game is all about fanservice and gimmicks.
Then I've decided to play this game. And I have never been so wrong in my life.

This game’s story is rooted in previous game, NieR (also known as NieR Gestalt/Replicant). Nier was not published on PC and was, unfortunately, extremely underestimated on consoles. Most people made their opinions based on critics’ reviews. For some reason, most critics
and, based on most reviews, dropped the game at the very start. But NieR has wonderful story which is strongly connected with plot of Automata. Honestly, I would recommend anyone to
watch all cutscenes from NieR. The amazing story of Automata becomes even deeper if you know previous game’s story.
Nevertheless, NieR:Automata’s striking plot even on its own allows you to make links to all three main characters and almost feel them. Through this link, you can feel their emotions – happiness and sadness, joy and infelicity, love and hatred almost like you ARE the character of this game.
I really shouldn’t discuss plot in this review because it should be experienced. not told by someone else, to avoid ruining impression it makes on uninitiated. All I can say is that is combines emotional and logical influences to make you feel the situation.
Gorgeous soundtrack – literally every one of them is great. I am a huge symphonic metal fan, but I have to admit that soundtrack is awesome. I would like to even go further and say that quality of Automata’s soundtrack is beyond reach of most artists. If you don’t believe my words, listen for yourself:
or
They are the same, yet different.
Furthermore, every track can dynamically change to represent your current situation. For example, almost every track has a 8-bit version that is played during hacking mini-game.
Maybe visuals are not so great, but they fit right in and you forget about it after an hour or two. Design is astoundingly good and every detail is placed right where it belongs. Still, I have to say that
. Some people just can’t find a giant diamond covered by thin coat of dust.
Gameplay is also great and variable. Transitions are smooth and every gameplay type in this game is marvelous. Whether you are playing a bullet-hell stage, or 3rd person slasher, I bet you will enjoy it. Nevertheless, let me tell about it. Gameplay can be divided to three types: air battle, ground battle and hacking battle. In air battle you have flight unit and you are shoting enemies. Pretty simple, huh? Still, this mode splits to two - when you are flying forward (and shooting forward) and when you are flying slower, but can look to any direction in 2D space. Ground battles are... well... ground battles like in other hack'n'slash games. However, sometimes camera is forced to be at certain angle (side or top). Hacking games can be separated to three categories. First, simple, just shoot black sphere. Second is speed run to black sphere and eliminate protecting system. Third – plot driven hacking. All these modes are combined in different ways, thus gameplay requires you to always tune your strategy according to the situation.
But the thing is… you can’t judge these aspects of the game separately. The key to beauty of this game is it’s…
. All these aspects together create a unique experience, when you think that everything fits right in. They are, if one can say, tightly linked to each other, thus creating something new, that I can feel but can’t describe. In most games, you can turn off music or ignore landscape. This will affect your experience, but only in that field. On the other hand, in Automata, if you disable at least one aspect, other will be affected. Everything is linked together and the plot of the game is really reinforced by landscape design, music, gameplay…
Surely, I have some final words toward this game’s plot and game itself, that should be written at this moment.
Thank you for reaching to my soul, to my… gestalt, through protective layers of cynicism. Thank you for breaking it apart only to make it whole again. This game lets you experience being a strong person facing overwhelming odds. This game surely lets you taste the bitter sweet taste of pyrrhic victories. Of course, we have won… but what was the price?...
The one and only problem of this game is optimization. But this problem will definitely fade as new generation of videocards appears, so it's just temporary. Many games had similar issues at start (remember Witcher 2 ubersampling?). And come on, real-time calculations of water vaporisation are not that simple. Road for the next-gen!
Thus, comes an end to my review. But, I think,
, whether they are real or not.
This is the first game in my life that made me actually cry. And it did it a bunch of times. I didn’t want to cry. I just couldn’t stop tears from running from my eyes at some moments in this game. Not a single game in my whole steam library could put me in this embarrassing situation.
And this game can make you feel characters (and what’s more important - yourself) alive.
Still, this game has a very strong message to everyone.
Farewell 2B, 9S, A2, Adam, Eve, Commander, 6O, 21O and all other androids and machines, whether they were introduced as developed characters or not. I will miss all of you. I can’t stop tears. But these are good,
, tears.
11/10, 12/10, all these scores are way too low for this game.
Let me give it MASTERPIECE/10. This is how games should be made.
P.S.
P.P.S. If this review will make at least one more person play Automata until the very end, it was worth it. I really hope that if you decided to read my review to the end, than you will at least give NieR:Automata a chance.

I simply had to nominate Deus Ex for the Test of Time award for it has given me some of the best gaming moments of my life. I suppose it was destiny that I received the game along with the Sound Blaster sound card that I purchased right after my final school examinations. At this point, I might be drunk on nostalgia but that is barely impairing my judgement. If nothing else, Mankind Divided has made me realize how far ahead of its time Deus Ex really was and that it still epitomizes the peak of user driven story telling. The graphics were not up to scratch with the Unreal 1 engine but boy, did it capture the ambience, be it the cathedral, chateau, bar or Area 51. The context-aware and location-specific music spearheaded by Alexander Brandon was simply epic and I carry the OST with me to this day.  In fact, I have devices bearing the names Daedalus, Morpheus, Helios and I can tell you that my inspiration for doing so doesn't come from Greek mythology. Most of the titles in my Steam library are crying to be played but I am pretty sure I will always find time for another playthrough of Deus Ex.
P.S.: Steam just made me launch the game and wait for 5 minutes to post this review and I loved every moment listening to the theme song and "spilling my drink".

Aside from the obvious aforementioned, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel excels in many other areas. The leveling progression seems to follow at a fairly steady pace, rarely dumping you into a place that is high above your level. Since leveling is much more balanced, the weapons that you'll use through your vanilla playthrough seem balanced in return.
The new zero-gravity is really a hit-or-miss. Some people have complained that it ruins the game, but others have praised it and even said that it's hard to come back to Borderlands 2 without the maneuverability of this game. Personally, I enjoyed the zero-gravity mechanics and soon throughout your playthrough, it'll become second nature.
The dialogue is, as usual, just as hilarious as the previous installments. A helluva lot more cursing (it's Australian, after all!) and great voice actors can get you really invested in the story and characters. It's not a Borderlands game unless every character and enemy has a unique personality that will have you quoting them to your friends!
Lastly, the Grinder adds a new aspect to the game. Other than selling all your worthless junk to vendors, you can plug all your crap items into the Grinder for increased rarity. Say you have white items; putting them in the grinder will offer you a green item. So on and so forth. It's a very great way to earn a lot of really great items in a fast amount of time without grinding the same area.
While the new enemies are really enjoyable to fight, sometimes they can be overwhelming and even annoying. A particular enemy that comes to mind is the Shuggurath. You'll meet these enemies when you get about a quarter through the game, in Triton Flats. While easy to kill, they have a huge draw-range and pin-point elemental damage. This can become a huge nuisance and can sometimes force you to fight several at time just to proceed with your quest.
Backtracking is a big issue too - at least for me. Many of the optional questlines force you to traverse through miles of a specific area to complete said quest. Since you're on the Moon, these areas can be quite big and without properly spaced out fast-travel systems, you'll be backtracking through the same area frequently. This can make an otherwise cool location very, very stale.
I also feel that I have to bring this up because many people in the reviews seem to compare this game to Borderlands 2. If you are comparing the story, mechanics, and systems of this game with it's predecessor, you will find more flaws in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel than you might like to admit. However, if you cast aside your differences and play it as an entirely new game with a new storyline, you'll be pleasantly surprised at how engaging this game can actually be.
If you're a die-hard Borderlands 2 fan and you're looking for something that will be your Borderlands 3, then this game isn't for you unless you catch it on a good sale. The story and replayability in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is vastly shorter than anything that you will get in Borderlands 2. Not to mention, downloadable content with this game is scarce considering the developers that made it (2K Australia) shut its doors.
On the flip side, if you're someone like me who loves the Borderlands series and can be really invested in a new story: you should buy this game. Although it may not be as long as Borderlands 2, it still has it's fair share of new content, loot, characters, and classes that will keep you busy for several hours.

A nice little game, which reminds me a lot of freelancer (in a way smaller version).
You're taking control of a space-pilot, who is accidentally jumping foward in time and finds himself faced with an alien threat.
Don't expect anything groundbreaking or new from the story, but it serves it's purpose.
The characters you meet are kinda clichee/flat, but the dialogue is good enough to keep you going.
Apart from doing the main quest, you can do in between whatever you like. Trading, fighting off pirates, doing escort missions, mining asteroids for ore etc. pp.
You''ll earn money from doing so, which you can invest in a new spaceship and equipment. There are quite a lot of ships to choose from, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. More cargo, better hull, more slots for primary weapons...
Depending on how man equipment slots you have, you can choose to install mining lasers to mine asteroids, getting different sized cabins to transport passengers, getting a shield, a cloaking device etc pp.
There is also the possibility to buy trading goods and sell them somewhere else for a higher price. Though the economy isn't really complex or deep in any way.
The main storyline isn't very long and also the systems/sectors aren't that big, they basically consist of an asteroid field, a space-station and a jumpgate.
So, if you don't mind a rather small space, repetition in quests after a while (to get money) and a relatively short main storyline, this might be for you if you liked Freelancer, Starlancer and similar games.

Battle strategies can be somewhat complex, but once you get the hang of them you will feel like a 5 star general. Not to mention the fact that you can even modify the game to play as the papal states, which has influence over most European factions. I haven't tried any big mods for this game yet, but I've heard about many of them, so it's nice to know that there are options out there in the unlikely event that I ever get bored with the main game. If you're looking to buy anything on Steam, this is a game you should seriously consider adding to your library. Happy warmongering!

Objectively, I must admit that Galaxy on Fire 2 shouldn't really standout from any other game in the genre.  There are games with much more in-depth economy systems, games with more advanced flight simulation, and games with a better storyline.  Like I said, it shouldn't stand out.  But it does, at least for me.
Something about this game just does it for me.  The atmosphere is handled so beautifully.  The game has a really immersing vibe, and the way everything comes together into an overall experience is just fantastic.  Particularly when starting a new game, I get really into the look and feel of the whole game.  It also has fantastic graphics and art; the ships have some really cool designs, and the stations have really sexy interiors when you're docked.  There's a lot of nice touches in the presentation as well, like difference in audio when talking to somebody in person vs over radio.
From a gameplay standpoint, this game is better viewed as a more casual entry in the space combat/trading genre, but what it does it does well.  If you're a hardcore player, you may want to look elsewhere, but for everyone else this is simply not a game to be missed.

A strategy/tactics game with nice graphics, decent story, and somewhat stereotypical characters and situations representing various countries. If you're not willing to grind out old maps for gold, then this game isn't for you because replaying maps for gold is pretty much mandatory to make later enemies easier. If you're not good at tactics games or don't like taking things slowly, this game isn't for you because there are enemies that can easily kill your characters if you aren't prepared because they have enough Action Points to move large distances and shoot many times.
Right now I'm up to the third campaign, Morning Star (if you include the first tutorial campaign).
The english in the beginning is pretty awkward and poorly translated, but it gets a lot better later on. There are still some mistakes/oddities ('Eliminate the elite forces. None of the squad should not perish.' and 'Above the rate of fire!'), but the dialogue between characters is acceptable.
After the tutorial maps, losing a map after clearing some enemies nets you ~3-10k gold, while clearing a map gives ~25-40k. The costlier upgrades cost ~27k-40k and opening the tier 2 reward boxes requires ~15k each. You will probably want to clear Normal stages first and ignore higher difficulties until you upgrade your characters enough. Since you don't get much gold, try to concentrate your gold on upgrading a couple core characters that you use (upgrading Teddy's Guard Ability to grant 2 shields is pretty useful). Buying items can save your run, but they cost a lot of gold which (in the long run) is better spent on permanent upgrades. You have to take things slowly and carefully, use Guard right before an encounter to absorb any fire they get in, and try to disable anyone you can't finish off.
---
Edit: Beat all stages I own in the Antisquad Original on hardest difficulty and cleared all stages I own in Antisquad Tactics. All the missions I had in Tactics were tutorial-like, so you might as well play through those before playing the original game. It plays pretty much the same but everything is cheaper, characters have less upgrade tiers, and the stages are a lot easier (at least on normal difficulty). The two versions don't share anything (gold, items, etc.).
In Original, I found a small stage that gave decent gold that I could clear quickly and easily. I ground that level for gold for key upgrades until I could beat it on higher difficulty levels (it gave ~60k normal, ~130k highest difficulty). After that, levels were mostly a cakewalk. You unlock new weapons and armor to buy when you upgrade your character's stats enough to increase their rank. It can be very effective to increase damage through a better weapon and start with more armor from a better outfit.

So... I don't often write reviews, really, so bear with me. I have mixed thoughts about this game, please don't just take the thumb up as final judgement. Read, and form your opinion.
The game 'Party Hard' is a little arcade-like game of killing all people on a party across several locations, with several characters, items, traps. It is a concept similar to games like Werewolf or Mafia, except for the fact that you're always the killer, and being found out isn't the absolute end as you can always find ways to flee from the police or other harmful entities, or, in the worst cases, just restart the level.
So... what makes this game fun? Really, it is like a very fluid, small puzzle. Each level is. It feels satisfying to set up a trap that goes just as planned, killing a lot of people at once, and marking you the ultimate victor.
However... And here is where this review might get confusing, because I am now going to get into the negative aspects of the game.
And they are. So. Plenty.
The game... it's probably bug tested well. I don't want to insult anybody that worked on it. But it's by no means bug-free. In fact, you need to put in little to no effort to find bugs, clipping, forgotten walls (visually there is one, but you can pass through, usually roped off areas), glitching graphics etcetera. It isn't too much of a complaint, really, I don't think I ever ran into a game breaking bug, but it... takes you out a little bit, as weird as it feels to say that, regarding a pixelated top down game.
The gameplay is repetetive. Very. Very. Repetetive. The levels at times feel like masks, but it's still... very much so the same game. You will find new traps, but they don't change the gameplay much, because you'll still end up running around, activating everything you can find in a frenzy, to then see how many 'enemies' are left to kill with actual strategy, and this is where the positive point sadly falls a bit mute, because... well... what can I say, it felt good to set up traps and plan them, when I was doing that in the beginning, but... I kinda stopped doing that, because it was less effective than spamming everything I could.
On the topic of the traps - here is another part of the game that bothers me, a great deal. Every level has some random positions for traps. While you'd think that makes for replayability, it just kinda... doesn't. It really kinda doesn't. What it does is completely throw off the difficulty curve of the game, which is ♥♥♥♥ed as it is. The game puts the easiest level right behind the hardest, or that is my opinion anyways. It starts out easy, goes to mediocre, to hard, to easy, to hard, to mediocre... etc. I don't mind hard games as long as I feel in control of the difficulty, most of my favorite games are on the harder side, as I am a sucker for roguelikes, yet... this game's hard levels merely annoyed me, and did nothing else for me.
So... what this game does to me is one thing, it leaves me wondering why I played through it. It's only roughly 5.30 hours long (I had it open in the background for a while), the story really is nothing amazing (though it IS nice to have one in the first place), and... overall it annoyed me. The game was fun at times, but for the most part starting over and doing something again because I rng ♥♥♥♥ed me annoyed me. Starting over because I made a mistake - that I'll gladly accept, but it all too often felt like I merely had bad luck with the placement of traps that can kill more than one person.
I played through the main storyline for this review. I gave the new dlc level a shot, but have to admit that the mechanic introduced in it reminds me of the rest of the game, as it is - annoying.
Now... why do I still recommend it? I don't. I can't. It feels wrong to recommend it for the price it has. But I can't not recommend it either. I personally got it for free through a couple of circumstances of a friend who already owned the game being gifted it. And for free - obviously, I could have stopped after I had my fun, and wouldn't have had to face the annoyances of the game. But I think I would not be happy if I had spent 13 bucks on it, and saying that makes me feel bad, because 13 bucks is not a lot for the effort that goes into a game.
Overall my final verdict is to buy it when the game's reduced, or if the concept really grips you. You'll have your fun for a while, and the steam workshop support makes sure you'll never really run out of content, if the arcad-ey repetition does not bother you. So... if you can get it cheap, I can wholeheartedly recommend it, support the developer, maybe they'll read this review and others with similar gripes, take into consideration which parts of these were intentional game design and which weren't, and well - all I can say is that I'm looking forward to seeing what direction they will take in the future.

Nier: Automata came out at an unfortunate time. 2017 is quickly turning into 1998 part 2 as one of the best years for videogames and Nier: Automata has come out amidst killers such as Persona 5, LOZ: Breath of the Wild and Horizon. Nier: Automata would've been a clear winner for GOTY any other year but it has stiff competition this year. However, even if Nier is not the "Best" game of 2017, it's probably one of the most important games to have come out this generation.
Nier: Automata is a milestone in Videogame storytelling. It's the greatest achievement in this field since Metal Gear Solid 1 and Final Fantasy VI before that. It's difficult to explain without spoilers but the amazing story that is told by Nier is something special that would be impossible to replicate on any other Medium.
The gameplay is fantastic, utilising a mixture of character action, bullet hell, 2D platforming and twin stick shooting. You may think that these mechanics are diluted by the sheer numbers but each is masterfully crafted, fun and flow into one another smoothly.
The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in years and the music is used for fantastic effect, making epic or truly heartfelt moments all the more impactful.
I loved every character. Despite being Androids these were some of the most human characters I've ever had the pleasure of meeting. Every hardship they went through affected me personally and there were few moments during my playthrough where I wasn't completely invested in their plights.
The game does have some cons, like performance is a bit rough, it's not terrible but it's not exactly smooth, with strange stutters every once in a while, especially when entering new area's. The game is also not exactly great looking, graphically. These shortcomings though are easy to ignore compared to what this game does right, and what it does right, it knocks completely out of the park.
While games like Horizon or Persona 5 will be remembered as some of the best of 2017, Nier: Automata is gonna be remembered as one of the best and most important videogames of this generation as well as for the industry as a whole. Thank you to Square Enix, Platinum games and Yokotaro for crafting this masterpiece.

Before I begin the review I have one simple question for the developers: HOW THE ♥♥♥♥ COULD YOU LEAVE THE PET MONKEY OUT OF THE GAME?! There's countries in the world where people are thrown off buildings for lesser "crimes".
Now that those unpleasantries are out of the way, I'll review the quality of the actual product on sale here. First up, it's a mobile app which doesn't appear to go full screen, so getting used to the somewhat "windowed" presentation is a bit of a pain. It also doesn't "save" or "bookmark" the last page you were at, meaning you have to remember this for yourself, then use the Contents page to fast-track back to it. Not exactly ideal.
There's some novel interactive touches, like polls which feed back instant internet-based survey results, and photos you can pan around 360 degrees; a spirit of innovation which is regrettably sullied by the videos which lazily link out to YouTube, meaning you'd better have some extra bandwidth up your sleeve if you wanna get the full experience.
This said, the content is nice enough, and of evident interest to anyone who either adored the game or plans on making games of their own. Is it worth two bucks? Guess so. Half that price on sale, easy. Though the more penny-pinching among you could probably save yourself the money by just Googling and Youtubing much the same information. For the rest of us who don't mind paying a small price for the quasi-convenience of it all, it's a nice enough package, if quite a ways from "essential".
Verdict: 6/10.

I'd really only suggest buying it if you like platforming roguelikes with invisble timers. The crafting here is not much of a selling point.
The game does quite a lot well. The graphics in the game are nice and colorful. The enviroments are lovely. I like the array of enemies. The game also offers a good varity of options for customzing your character to suit your playstyle. It also randomly drops underserved loot into your lap, which is always a treat. I don't really dig the combat, but it's alrght. The game has a huge ammount of replay value. The biomes are randomly generated which means that the layout and the enemies will be different every time. The game also has lots of items, races and cosmetic options to unlock.
I really want to like this game more than I do. It's not a bad game, but some things were implemented really poorly.
The hunger system doesn't seem to have any point. The reason it exists in turnbased roguelikes is to keep you from exploring the entire floor and getting all the loot/hp. It's supposed to make you decide if you'd rather continue or stick around and hope you find something useful. Here? It's a minor annoyance. I've never once died of hunger. Being able to get a good supply of food is dead easy. All food does is provide an alternate way to get HP back.
I don't like that I had to read guides to find out what the stats did. The traits are explained, but for some reason the stats aren't.
Speaking of annoying things, the invisble timer. It  isn't a blight on the game, I just don't like timers and want to warn others who might feel the same way. You only have a limited ammount of time to make it to the end of the level before big scary demons come to eat your face. Normally I found that it doesn't get in the way, but when it does, I feel really cheated.
I also find the inventory and crafting system to be awful for this type of game. In roguelikes you have limited inventory so that you can't stockpile cosumables for much harder levels. In this type of game though, it doesn't make sense.
The inventory size feels way too small for a game with a crafting system. It doesn't need to let me hold every single item in the game, but more space is needed. You also need to have at least one slot empty if you want to do any sort of crafting while out in the field. I could even tolerate this stuff, if it provided a easy way to destroy items to clear up space for the stuff I actually want. Instead you have to drop them on the ground where they will follow you like a sad puppy before giving up. This makes crafting kind of time consuming, which could but THE SCOURGE HAS INVADED! GET OUT!!!!!!

Aside from the obvious aforementioned, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel excels in many other areas. The leveling progression seems to follow at a fairly steady pace, rarely dumping you into a place that is high above your level. Since leveling is much more balanced, the weapons that you'll use through your vanilla playthrough seem balanced in return.
The new zero-gravity is really a hit-or-miss. Some people have complained that it ruins the game, but others have praised it and even said that it's hard to come back to Borderlands 2 without the maneuverability of this game. Personally, I enjoyed the zero-gravity mechanics and soon throughout your playthrough, it'll become second nature.
The dialogue is, as usual, just as hilarious as the previous installments. A helluva lot more cursing (it's Australian, after all!) and great voice actors can get you really invested in the story and characters. It's not a Borderlands game unless every character and enemy has a unique personality that will have you quoting them to your friends!
Lastly, the Grinder adds a new aspect to the game. Other than selling all your worthless junk to vendors, you can plug all your crap items into the Grinder for increased rarity. Say you have white items; putting them in the grinder will offer you a green item. So on and so forth. It's a very great way to earn a lot of really great items in a fast amount of time without grinding the same area.
While the new enemies are really enjoyable to fight, sometimes they can be overwhelming and even annoying. A particular enemy that comes to mind is the Shuggurath. You'll meet these enemies when you get about a quarter through the game, in Triton Flats. While easy to kill, they have a huge draw-range and pin-point elemental damage. This can become a huge nuisance and can sometimes force you to fight several at time just to proceed with your quest.
Backtracking is a big issue too - at least for me. Many of the optional questlines force you to traverse through miles of a specific area to complete said quest. Since you're on the Moon, these areas can be quite big and without properly spaced out fast-travel systems, you'll be backtracking through the same area frequently. This can make an otherwise cool location very, very stale.
I also feel that I have to bring this up because many people in the reviews seem to compare this game to Borderlands 2. If you are comparing the story, mechanics, and systems of this game with it's predecessor, you will find more flaws in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel than you might like to admit. However, if you cast aside your differences and play it as an entirely new game with a new storyline, you'll be pleasantly surprised at how engaging this game can actually be.
If you're a die-hard Borderlands 2 fan and you're looking for something that will be your Borderlands 3, then this game isn't for you unless you catch it on a good sale. The story and replayability in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is vastly shorter than anything that you will get in Borderlands 2. Not to mention, downloadable content with this game is scarce considering the developers that made it (2K Australia) shut its doors.
On the flip side, if you're someone like me who loves the Borderlands series and can be really invested in a new story: you should buy this game. Although it may not be as long as Borderlands 2, it still has it's fair share of new content, loot, characters, and classes that will keep you busy for several hours.

This game is much shorter than Borderlands 2 (I have not played the first Borderlands). There are fewer side quests and a much shorter campaign. There are also a huge lack of DLC expansion packs and unlockables. While this is a new game, and Borderlands 2 is quite old, it is seriously lacking DLCs. Hexcells is one of the best puzzle game experiences I've had.
It starts off with a simple Minesweeper-like premise. After a few levels, the game begins its brilliance by adding new types of clues beyond "three of the surrounding hexes are empty," turning the game into something resembling a nonogram-like puzzle (the kind of puzzle featured in Nintendo's Picross games). These mechanics are backed up by excellent puzzle design and an ambient soundtrack that keeps players relaxed and focused as they work their way through the puzzles.
The only serious flaw in the game is that there isn't any replay value. There is still quite a bit of skill in repeating the large puzzles without making a mistake, but gradually players will remember the patterns and can cheat by learning from previous mistakes. Smaller puzzles also suffer as they can become simple exercises in trial and error.
Yet that flaw is a minor complaint. Anyone who enjoys logic-based puzzles should give this one a go. After finishing it, check out Hexcells Plus for an even greater challenge or Hexcells Infinite for an endless amount of content.

One strike is wonderful wonderful game about 6 samurai fighting eachoter in ancient japan. This is achieved with a measely 6 buttons to make your character move across the screen, block and slash up your opponents. The name "One Strike" comes from the mechanic that once you're hit, you're dead; this makes the game ever more tense as you are trying to down your foes and save your own life.

One strike is a two dimensional fighter with a one hit, one kill mechanic. Your primary objective is to kill your opponent, this is done by hitting them with whatever weapon your character has; this varies from character making the ways you fight and fight every enemy more thoughtfull and gives the game more depth. All of this is supported by the games amazing soundtrack that puts this game in my book as a "Good Game" as i know i will play this game many times because of how much fun i have with it.
This the most important part of a 2D fighting game and it does it very well, not that it's perfect however it is near to perfect. Each character has the ability to: move forward, backward, dash forward and backward, block and attack. The movement, although having different animations, are practically the same for every character. The block and attack are very different, each character has a different weapon, this ranges from a simple sword to a throwable knife with a chain attached to it so it can be pulled back. Each character has their own weapon and utilizes it in their way, one character may use his sword to block directly while the other swings around his staff so fast he blocks enemy attack with them. These blocks last for a few seconds after which you are vulnerable until you press the block key again; this is done on purpose so that someone cannot sit still blocking for the entire match so that the enemy still has a chance to cut your wang off.
Attacking can be done during the times your enemy isn't blocking, this does leave you vulnerable if you do miss and not being able to block instantly makes you think wether you should attack now or later in order to main your enemy. This level of depth is something that i had at first not expected from a game like this, being as this is a one hit one kill system the combat system is not like street fighter where you mash the same button and eventually win.
The addition that every character has it's own weapon and blocks is also very important, this makes you as a player change the way you play the game according to your character and to your enemy, that means that there are 216 different ways to play the same game; which is pretty impressive.

The soundtrack of this game is also phenomenal, it's fast paced and has an almost japanese theme to it. It's very nice to listen to and it accentuates the great combat of One Strike. I cannot stress enough how important the soundtrack is to this game, it is absolutely amazing and one of the best i have heard in a long time. I find it accelerates a little slow however when it's going it's absolutely wonderful and i feel like a japanese samurai 800 years ago fighting for my life. dashing across the landscape in intense combat.

There are 4 different was to play One Strike, One life; where you have one life and have to beat 5 other characters. Arcade where you have to beat 5 characters however you both have 5 lives. Team deathmatch where you need to beat 5 teams each 3 characters with one life each. and Tournament where 8 characters figh in a tournament grid, so 1v1's until the finale, all these gamemodes can be set on easy, medium or hard which brings me to my next point
The AI in this game is quite good, it knows how to play the game and does so with supprising accuracy, often it was ammusing to see the hard AI fight ittself just because of how good it was. I have heard complaints about the easy AI being too simple however there's a reason it's called "Easy" if you want to easily win then that's the gamemode for you. To me only the "Hard" bots prove a real challenge that i struggle to beat.

There are minor technical problems such as in tournament mode both players being called "P1" in the finale etc. These are all very small things that i see other reviewers heavily criticising however this is not a gamebreaking aspect in any way so i'm going to leave it at this because it is not important.

One strike is a wonderful game with combat that feels rewarding, the sounds not being overused and nice to listen to; all supported by a masterful soundtrack that i'm still listening to while writing this review. For it's relatively low price this is a game i recommend anyone that likes video games to play; I myself don't like 2D fighters too much and i was able to enjoy it all the same.

One Strike is a great example of one-day games. Gameplay is pleasant, and the graphics do not irritate the eyes, the music is suitable, and in appearance - a good game. But there is no distinctive features to make the game stand out against the background of others. This is a two-dimensional fighting game in the setting of medieval Japan with pixel graphics and retro aestetics. In total, the game has 6 characters, several arenas and game modes.
In such indie games, in a limited budget, it is important to maintain a balance in the graphics - to make a unique design and fit into a low budget for development. Unfortunately, only the result of the fact that the developers saved money. Sprites are made so-so, and on the backs of only plain-looking dull pixel art. Artists fighters are also very strange, we have the same retro aesthetics, so why make the interface of the main menu and the choice of the character pixel, and the background and sprites of the characters to draw the usual? Arenas are not something that would be ugly, but you could do better - at least the overall composition should be built according to the rules, not at your discretion. I also did not like the dim color palette, you can add a little brightness to the colors and contrast. And so, basically - the usual pixel indie-graphics, nothing new.
Music does not convey that atmosphere, but it does well with the ambient function. An incomprehensible Chiptune, or even ordinary tracks recorded in FL Studios using effects - it is not as expressive as you would like.
The gameplay in the game is the main feature. In total there are 6 characters and 5 game modes. Battles take place on the condition of "one hit - one kill", where the enemy and you die from one hit, and it's great - thanks to this condition the game got rid of tiresome fights like in the other fighting games - they pass very quickly and vigorously, you will not get bored here. The simplest control, only 6 buttons, four of which are responsible for control, and the rest are for the block and attack. Accustomed to instantly - there really is nothing to get used to, and it's cool. Each character has his own blocks and attacks, and this results in different tactics for different heroes. The modes "Tournament" and "Local multiplayer" are incomparable. If with multiplayer on one keyboard everything is clear, then the tournament is something new. Up to 16 players can compete with each other and find out the relationship with the leadership in the tournament grid, it's something new.
A good indie fighting game with the ability to play with friends, a variety of game modes, nice gameplay, and an excellent price - why not play it? Especially, it is clear that the developers tried, although in some aspects the game did not come out very well.

One Strike - это отличный пример игр-однодневок. И игровой процесс приятный, и графика не нагружает глаза, музыка подходящая, да и по виду - хорошая игра. Но нету никакой изюминки или отличительных свойств, чтобы игра выделялась на фоне других. Это двухмерный файтинг в сеттинге средневековой Японии с пиксельной графикой и закосом под ретро (мы этого ещё никогда не видели, инфа сотка). Всего в игре есть 6 персонажей, несколько арен и игровых режимов.
В таких инди-играх, в условиях ограниченного бюджета важно соблюсти баланс в графике - сделать уникальный дизайн и уложится в низкий бюджет для разработки. К сожалению, здесь виден только результат того, что на графике сэкономили. Спрайты выполнены так себе, а на задниках только невзрачные тусклые пиксель-арты. Арты бойцов тоже весьма странные, у нас же ретро-эстетика, так зачем делать интерфейс главного меню и выбора персонажа пиксельным, а фон и спрайты персонажей нарисовать обычными? Арены не то что бы некрасивые, но можно было сделать лучше - по крайней мере общую композицию нужно строить по правилам, а не по своему усмотрению. Ещё мне не понравилась тусклая цветовая палитра, можно добавить слегка яркости краскам и контраста. А так, в основном - привычный пиксельный инди-графон, ничего нового.
Музыка не передаёт той атмосферы, но с функцией эмбиента справляется хорошо. Непонятный чиптюн, или даже обычные треки, записанные в FL Studios с использованием эффектов - она не выразительна настолько, насколько хотелось.
Геймплей в игре - это главная особенность. Всего есть 6 персонажей и 5 игровых режимов. Бои проходят по условию "one hit - one kill", где противник и вы умираете от одного попадания, и это здорово - благодаря этому условию игра избавилась от утомительных боёв как в других файтингах - они проходят очень быстро и энергично, здесь не заскучаешь. Управление простейшее, всего 6 кнопок, четыре из которых отвечают за управление, а две остальных - за блок и атаку. Привыкание происходит моментально - тут толком не к чему привыкать, и это круто. У каждого персонажа свои блоки и атаки, а из этого вытекают разные тактики боя за разных героев. Режимы "Турнир" и "Локальный мультиплеер" просто бесподобны. Если с мультиплеером на одной клавиатуре всё понятно, то турнир - это что-то новенькое. До 16 игроков могут соревноваться друг с другом и выяснять отношения посредством лидерства в турнирной сетке, это что-то новенькое.
Хороший инди-файтинг с возможностью играть с друзьями, разнообразием игровых режимов, приятным геймплеем, и отличной ценой - почему бы и не поиграть? Тем более, видно, что разработчики старались, хоть и в некоторых аспектах игра вышла не очень.

This game is oddly charming. This might have to do with the fact that the game's pixel art and normal art combined with its smooth gameplay and enticing soundtrack is rather well done. As far as I can tell, there isn't many bugs and I haven't tried out all the modes yet, but from the base game alone, I can tell it's very well done. I have achieved all modes of the One Life except for Very Hard which I haven't unlocked, so I'll base this opinion on those quirks alone. Every character is balanced in a specific way. The first one, The Swordsman, (I couldn't really get their names as the font is really hard to look at,) is basic enough to learn the game with. He has a guard that is activated with H and an attack that swings outward with G. He can also dash backwards and forwards with the T and Y keys respectively. I personally like The Chain Swinger as she has zero guarding, but can easily attack targets from a distance with her G attack and can swing faster in close quarters if she is that close with her H attack. It's not too bad of a game as it reminds me of others such as DropKick and Mortal Kombat. It is simplistic enough that it isn't too hard and not too easy. It's balanced just right to where you feel a sense of accomplishment when you make a finishing blow on a target and don't feel annoyed as much when you lose.
Pros:
-The gameplay is well done. No character feels out of place here. Each have their own strengths and weaknesses that make them strong against certain targets and weaker against others.
-The pixel art is very good for the time. It is reminiscence of older japanese cultures as what I picked up was that all the characters in the game use a specific type of japanese weapon. While I may not know the specifics of the swords, I do know that the last character, The Sai Wielder, uses double sais in her tactics which I believe was used in old japanese lore.
-The soundtrack and sounds are all approriate for its timeperiod. They don't sound completely off and instead enchance the game's overall appearance making you feel like you are fighting others somewhere in older Japan.
Cons:
-I found a weird bug that happens specifically with The Sai Wielder. If she dies and the opponent dashes to her before the revenge and other buttons appear, she can glide across the ground back to the other side. This isn't too deterimental as it doesn't happen a lot, but I found it odd that it happens at all.
-Another wonky thing I found is that the hitboxes for some abilities are rather...quirky, I guess. For example, if you use Sai Wielder's Attack just before The Chain Swinger uses her G attack, you can get the hitboxes rather unresponsive to an attack to the Chain Swinger unless you dash into her again and attack. This is also a weird bug that occurs, but I have no idea how it works. It also happens really frequently, but it's activated by player response to AI reactions. It's not too bad, but I've had a few times where the attack should of hit her and it goes right through. I'm not sure if it's even truly a bug either, it might just be how the Sai Wielder is played.
-The controls take some time to adapting to. I don't like that you can't change them because I only used a keyboard to play the game as it was all I had. It's just weird, that's all.
Overall: I'd give it a solid 7/10 or 8/10.
Comments: The game works well with what it has. Although there are some random bugs that may occur, they don't detract too much from the presentation overall. The gameplay, soundtrack, and pixel art all work well and together they make a charming game that doesn't require too much from the player.
Edit to the current review: Found another bug, but it's only purely visual. Somehow, on the final tournament battle, you end up with two 1P. The battle is the same as it should be from how it looks on the tournament screen normally, but when it says who is fighting who next, that shows up instead of your actual opponent. I'll see if the glitch happens in other modes other than easy in tournament. This will happen even if your opponent is the same as you. A similar glitch that happens is if you are in the final stages of the tournament and then quit, the profiles from the last match that would of happened get overlayed with the profiles from the current match. Specifically, this seems to do with the other glitch of the 1P getting overlayed with the actual opponent. This also happens even if a CPU wins and takes your place as the opponent. The person on the right is always refferred to as Player 1 even though Player 1 can't even be over in that bracket. I found another such glitch that happens if a CPU wins. If they win, their profile gets overlayed with where they were in the last tournament. So you might end up with a Staff Wielder background combined with a Swordswoman foreground. Luckily, this only happens in the first round as the background of the previous winner stays there and only the foreground moves up.

(The below video is of my FIRST first impressions of the gameplay, the review after more time spent with it follows)
A novel one on one fighter in the vein of Bushido Blade, Dive Kick and Nidhogg where the key to victory is not with insane complex combos or special moves but with quick timing and anticipating your opponent's own moves because as the title implies, it only takes ONE STRIKE to down a combatant.
While it appears relatively simple on the surface, each fighter has their own unqiue movements and attacks, making for a variety of match ups and thus strategies. In the mold of "easy to learn, hard to master", it actually makes it a sell for both casual and hardcore players as multiplayer with friends can easily add as much depth as you are prepared to give it in return. Full disclosure, I was only able to play a sizable amount of the single player only, yet the appeal of verses mode is clear.
Against the AI, it did provide a good challenge, with multiple difficulties and modes including arcade and tournaments. While there is a great variety to each fighter in terms of both movement and attacks, adding further to different strategies, I did find some easier to play as than others. In one case not only was I able to stream roll through arcade with ease, when the AI played as the same character, they also did the same to me. As a result, I do question some balance. Granted, there may perhaps be a strategy to it but when the AI also struggles I am left wondering. However this is far from a deal breaker, rather something I personally noticed in single player at the time.
The presentation is an interesting mix of 8-bit graphics yet 16-32-bit music that will not be for everyone but I'll argue it is fitting with the simple but effective gameplay and overall charming style. There is also very well hand drawn art that somewhat clashes with the pixels but it does add character to each fighter. Despite the pixelated visuals, there is variety and distinct colour, with really only a couple of level and character combination blending a tad more than the rest. The music though is pretty stand out and nails the vibe it is going for, a particular point of praise!
Overall, it does effectively combine an retro-presentation with well crafted timing-based fighting gameplay, making it perfect for enoyable bursts and no doubt more fun with friends, potentially with even more depth and length. At a very low price point, I would recommend trying it for yourself and supporting this developer.

One strike is similar to that of Samurai Showdown.  You are given 6 characters.  Each with their own weapon and fighting style.
I tried both the team mode, the arcade and the one life modes just to see what they did.
The game is fairly simple.  You have two variety of attacks and depending on who you use, those attacks vary between offense and a few that are defense.
So let me put out the scores.
For visual graphics I give the game a 6.0 because it does have backgrounds though the faces in both the models on the fighting portion, and in the background are fairly pixelated with zero facial features for the most part, save for a beard. The clothing designs are semi-stylish but again there is a fair bit of pixelizing.
For the music, the simplistic scores are pleasing to the ears and they represent the game well.  I give the music a 9 out of 10.
The fighters:   The fighters at least on the full menu show actual visualization of their faces.   But that is not what you see once you start the matches.  you see blank faces.  The fighting moves and styles are somewhat interesting and so i give the fighters a score of 7 out of 10.
The game mechanics in terms of keyboard controls are a little..... strange.    For example, my mouse did not work in the game's menu or fighting area at all. I had to use my keyboard.  And I did. i was using  the arrow keys for left/right, but i was using G and H for the attacks.   Which was a little weird but I got used to it relatively fast.  The game controls get a fair 7.0 from me because even if they are a little odd, you can still casually play the game.
The overall fun factor stands at a solid 7.0.   I had some fun the first time around but after a short while I found my attention for enjoying this game waneing a little.  I would have liked more characters, maybe a few facial details besides the beard and clothing to identify better with the characters.
I would recommend this game to a friend, and I will say this.  The game is so casual in and of itself, that pretty much everybody from little kids to adults can play it with relative ease.

where do i start with this amazing game... with the good points
1)The soundtrack and voice acting: The creator of this game created a completely new laungues out of nothing for it, which is used in the songs and for writing on walls around the world. The sounds which play as you travers the beutiful scenery and battle your way to your current objective are amazing, fromt the songs to the precise and perfect voice acting.
2)The view: The game can run at 60 fps, with the cutscenes limited to 30. The shadows, the player models, all show the amount of time, money, and sweat that went into the game. You can see the hair and frills of the clothings sway in the wind. The sun reflecting from pools of water. The unique art style this game posses is one of it's subdle, yet impactful assets(A small tip from someone who 100% the game: use self destruct when playing as 2B)
3)The gameplay and action: Some of the best live rpg combat i have ever seen, allowing new players to quickly learn the mechanices and how to dodge the seeminlgy infinite amounts of bullets sshot your way, and how to perfectly stack up your combos with your  firing pod, or the melee attack gear(swords, spears, fist weaons, heavy swords, the list goes on). The boss fights feel satisfying, the mobs are fun to hack and slash(and shoot) through. The exploring is highly rewarding, finding weapons and materials to upgrade your stuff. And moving around feels smooth and natural, the controls are tight.
4)The story: With the possible execption of bioshock 1 and infinite. This might be the best story mode i have played thorugh. Each diffrent ending(from the 5 true ones and the 21 bad ones. For a total of 26) provids either a new perspective of the story, or a joke on your expense on the cause to the ending(for example ending K, caused by  eating a fish) The story has a way to grab you and not let you go to sleep. As you watch the characters develope in such a realstic fashion you actually grow attack, at least i did.
Now to the few bad points:
1)Grinding for upgrade materials and chips can get tiresome, it's a core part of RPG's, but it's the prominent in this game, i'd recommend checking online for the grinding spots
2)the Fuse system, used to uprgarde your chips(which are your skills, for example the "offensive heal" chip will let you heal some of the damage you deal to enemies, can get a tad confusing, but it's important to pay attention to the instructions. And quickly get it. Another importnat anacdonte is that chips with a little black square next to them have the smallest possible space cost.
Overall I'd greatly recomend this game. It's more then that. It's an experince and it's definitly worth it's price

Summary: A great idea in theory: combining interesting storyline with the frenetic action of shoot-em-up, and adding simple-to-use support for player-created levels. But the game is deeply diminished by a wide variety of bugs and some questionable UI and input design decisions.
Pros:
+ Includes level editor that makes for pretty robust shoot 'em up level creation
+ Better story-telling than most SHMUPS
+ Customize your character
+ Some controller support
Cons:
- Controller support is immensely patchy: many oft-repeated actions still require a keyboard (such as progressing through the extensive dialog sections), and sometimes the controller buttons suddenly won't work the same way (like using items)
- Steam screenshot go-to button "F12" always seems to just trigger the console in my browser (etc)
- Steam overlay doesn't seem to work at all
- Frustrating controls and overlapping UI decisions mean you may do a lot of what you didn't intend (example, it tells you to chat which probably requires you press the space bar, and yet the space bar is also how you progress through the tutorial, so I missed a ton of guidance while trying to explore something they asked me to do)
- Settings menu sometimes won't detect buttons or keys, or will tell you a button is already in use when it isn't
- A lot of grammar mistakes: not a HUGE deal, but enough to be obvious
- A wide array of bugs (one easily repeated example was just trying to close the game, it wouldn't respond, I needed to alt=tab and close the window from the task bar)
- Likely more: I stopped playing after the first hour and am unlikely to return

*********************************************************************************************************************************
This is a fun game if you like upgrades and destruction. The main campaign was completed within 4 hours of gameplay. After that there is a survival mode taking you up to level 100. I can predict roughly 5-12 hours of gameplay.
There are a variety of weapons that you can augment with upgrades you can find. The game is fun when you start with a tiny ship with a single machine gun and eventually progress to a flying fortress of doom equipped with 5 rocket launchers and 3 laser guns. It does get extremely repetitive after a while. However, it can prove to be quite fun if you like this type of game.
*********************************************************************************************************************************
Disclaimer: I have only been playing this game for a few hours but have reached level 55 in the game. I am in no way an expert at this game. I am simply giving a bit more information about the game because there are zero guides at the time of making this review.
Looting: Looting happens at random when you kill enemies or complete maps.
> Weapons can drop in the following rarities. I don't see much of a difference between them too be honest. Each weapon is generated with random stats. One might come out of the box with extra projectiles or one might come with pierce already built in.
- Common
- Uncommon
- Rare
- Epic
> Upgrades appear with a given level. The higher the level, the greater the applied effect is to the weapon. For example, a level 10 Projectile Upgrade will add 5 projectiles while a level 1 Projectile Upgrade might add 2.
- Appears to be capped at 3 upgrades per weapon.
Weapons: To my memory...
Blaster - Shoots plasma blasts in a straight line.
Rocket - Fires a rocket that explodes on impact.
Laser - Fires a continuous beam for a duration followed by a cool down.
Boomerang - Fires blades that reach out to a distance and retract backwards.
Flamethrower - Fires flames at a short range for a duration followed by a cool down.
Rifle - Fires a high powered bullet.
Acid - Fires a blob of acid at a downward arcing curve.
Drones - Fires a drone that shoots at target briefly.
Upgrades: To my memory...
Projectiles - Adds extra projectiles. Seems to cap at around 5 extra projectiles at level 50. It may go higher though.
Damage - Adds a bit of damage. It seems extremely useless to use these mods as it might increase damage by 10% where any other upgrade can improve functionality by 2-3x.
Range - Increases the range your projectiles travel.
Speed - Increases speed of projectiles or duration of beams, flames.
Piercing - Allows your attacks to travel through targets a series of times.
Splitting - Allows your attacks to split upon impact.
Targeting - Allows the weapon to auto target within a degree cone.
Special - Adds a unique bonus to each weapon. For example, it can increase explosion size of rockets.
Strategies:
I personally find lasers to be among my favorite along with rifles and rockets. The lasers can be upgraded pretty quickly with extra projectiles. Upgrading their special ability makes them do a lot of damage as the laser is held on an enemy. This is extremely useful for tougher enemies. As far as I'm aware, projectiles are by far the best mod to add onto any weapon! There doesn't seem to be a damage penalty for adding projectiles.
The rifle was also super strong from my gameplay. They excel at single target damage. Most of the gameplay will be strafing around while your weapons destroy most trash enemies pretty quickly. The tough ones are usually the ones that fire back so it's nice to have rifles to take them out quickly.
I personally feel like rockets are also very good especially with homing on. They can easily fly around and travel towards enemies leaving a satisfying volley of explosions in your wake.
*********************************************************************************************************************************

This game has potential. The combat is fast paced and is a flawless bullet-hell style game. The level creator is easy to use, bosses are fun to build and experiment with, and it's easy to share / play shared levels.
The reason I wouldn't recommend this game is because there's not nearly enough content to warrent a 15$ price tag. At the time of writing this review, with the game having been out for nearly 2 months, there was only a tutorial and less than 20 shared levels. Until the development picks up and adds a campaign, or the community grows and more levels are shared, I wouldn't pay more than 5$ for this game.
The developers also ignore small mistakes that shouldn't have been missed. Menu items that won't highlight but can still be clicked. Screens you can go into but there's no easy way to get out of. The leaderboard will update with your name and score but won't update your profile image. Small problems, but unacceptable considering the size of their team. When a developer overlooks small issues so that they can rush to release a game in early access it destroys any hope that this game will be anything more than a cash grab. This game shouldn't have been released yet.
I'll continue to have some faith that the game will be fixed and become worthy of it's price tag, but until it does, I can't in good faith recommend this game.

The arena genre is one that has faded over time, with titles like Quake or Unreal Tournament being some of the best shooters of their time. It isn't all that bad, with some great tries at revamping the genre with names like Gears of War, but since then it has been nothing but a move to more "realistic" shooters like Call of Duty and Battlefield.
While these games aren't bad - in fact they fill a playerbase that adores that style of shooting genre - it does stiffle the communities need for a third-person fast-paced action shooter, and this is where Loadout comes in.
I've long sought after a game that I can easily jump into for a good four to five rounds, enjoy my time and not feel burnt out. This is Loadout. It is chaotic, it is fun, it has great artstyle and does the free-to-play tag justice. Nothing is "OP" or "pay2win" like the usual supects, and freedom is granted through the stupidly awesome weapon crafting system.
Character evolvement wise it goes beyond ridiculous. From taunts to shirts to hair-do's, the customisation allows you to really make your character you. Of course, this is where the real world payment system comes into play, and only in this situation does it rear the ugly head of paying real dollars. For these fluff items you do need to purchase a bundle of cash, be it anywhere from $5 to $50, its up to you. Most items in the store are reasonably priced, and they offer the fluff you want if you want it.
Now, don't get me wrong in that I wish the developers would have made more fluff items freely available, or at the very least affordable through the in-game cash system, but you have to make money where you can. The freemium tag is put across a lot of titles, and to have one that is so well balanced in its hunger for your wallet just makes me not bat my eyelids at the pricing structure of the fluff in-store items. Go nuts, spend your cash, but I'll continue to be happy that I can still play on a level playing field thanks to the chosen system.
Overall, Loadout is a great game. With a well-balanced shooting system that makes every match an adrenaline-pumping good time, what is not to love about a game that really tries to bring back the fast-paced arena action. Kudos to the developers for not taking the easy road and charing an arm and leg for unlocking items, and actually sacrificing profits over freedom to play how you want, when you want.

This game is very fun, charming, and addicting all in one package. I loved the animations and art style, the game it self is very unique. You basically keep moving to the right slaying monsters, chopping trees, and minging rocks, after you complete an area you come to 3 doors the color determining what the next area is like, the areas alternate between dangerous, and town. At the town youre able to buy, sell, and use special facilities (Ie: Blacksmith, Leatherworker, clothing maker). The Blacksmith will smelt your minerals into bars, and craft armors out of them for you if you desire. The Leatherworker will infuse metal with leather to make it stronger, and to reinforce it, which you can then have him craft into armor. Finally, you can have the clothing maker infuse minerals with cloth to make better magical clothing.
In this game there are 3 different skill sets, attack, magical, and dexterity. Attack is all about doing the most possible damage with your melee weapon or using it for special abilities, although there arent many skills in each tree and you arent able to pick them, it doesnt really matter, because you can only have 3. The magical tree is all about summoning things to fight for you or adding magical damage to you, and your allies weapons. And the dexterity tree is all about doing the most damage with bows, or using special arrow abilities.
Also, in Magicite, there are many things for you to unlock. There are 9 races to play (You start with the Peon, then there is Noble, Orclops, Dwelf, Crusader, Remnant, Trogon, Earthkin, and Pigfolk) each race spawns with their own specific items, and special stats. There are also 24 different hats to collect each having its own special attributes or abilities. And there are also 6 different companions you can get (Regen Fairy, Ancient Bat, Haste Beetle, Gadget Gaurd, Gorgon Eye, and Floaty Slime) Each has its own special attributes, and way of unlcok (Most require beating or getting really far in the game)
There is a wide variety of items you can find or craft. In Magicite there is permanent death, so youre forced to be much more careful then in any other game youve played. When youre starting your game you are given two traits and randomized stats (Attack, Health, Dexterity, and Magic) There are 18 different stats that are given in pairs of two. My two favorites to get are Potion Brewer: "You have a 50% chance to create large potions with basice items" and Healthy: "+ 2 Health"
When yo ustart the game you will always spawn in a forest area where you will fight (In order least to most threatening) Pig, Slime, Bee, Boar, Bee Hive, Tyrannox, and Percyl (Percyl is a boss that has a small chance to spawn)

It's not as good as Borderlands 2, but it's still a fine game. It has a lot of things that you can't get in BL2, but unfortunately the good is balanced by a lot of annoyances and irritations. Since I do recommend the game, I'll start with the bad:
1) Level design -- The combat does not flow very well, there is a lot of downtime, and it's easy to get lost. I felt that the environments were inconveninecing me much more than enriching my experience. The larger maps are mostly empty, requiring lots of tedious travelling. This is especially disappointing since Borderlands 2 had such good level design.
2) Combat -- The low gravity adds much more verticality to the combat which can be fun for the player, but it also makes combat much more confusing and haphazard. The problem is that we can only view the game world through the tiny field of view of our monitors. The verticality in the Pre Sequel means that much of the enemy movement is happening off-screen. This makes it difficult to maintain your situational awareness. Borderlands 2 did an excellent job of keeping the battle mostly within the confines of your monitor, so that you could get all the information you needed by immersing yourself in what you could see. In the Pre-Sequel it's much more difficult to find enemies in the first place, since many of them are flying around out of your field of view, and the mini-map doesn't do much to help. Besides, who wants to spend their time staring at a mini-map during combat?
3) Aesthetic design -- The environments and enemies are generally bland and colorless.
4) It takes itself a bit too seriously -- To me, the story in a shooter serves one function: to enhance immersion. One of the reasons I love Borderlands 2 is that it acknowledges that what we're doing is fundamentally absurd: we're running around shooting psychos in the face with shotguns that are on fire. The tone of BL2's story made me feel immersed in this type of action. The Pre-Sequel has it's head up itself telling its story (which is admittedly pretty good for a video game), but it breaks the immersion more than it enhances it. This is really exacerbated by the amount of pointless waiting, listening, and button-pushing that you're forced to endure simply to move the story forward and access new areas. Also, the insane phrases that the enemies in BL2 screamed at you are replaced with either silence or bland phrases like "For the Legion!"
5) Replay value -- This is mostly related to level design; there are really no areas that I would enjoy running through multiple times. BL2 offers a LOT more end-game content.
6) Loot -- There is not nearly as much decent loot compared to BL2. They have replaced chests and enemy drops with vending machines and the Grinder, but this is a terrible choice in my opinion. It's like a very slow and inconvenient way of using a save editor. Instead of rewarding us for playing the game, they reward us for sitting in town pushing buttons and endlessly hitting "Save and Quit." I think this was their idea for the end-game: that everyone would pick up a bunch of terrible weapons and then spend hours at the Grinder hoping they would turn into something good. I'd rather actually play the game, and be pleasantly surprised when I find something decent and fun to use.
The Good:
1) The combat: I have had a crazy amount of fun playing as Nisha using her dual-pistols, shotguns, and her lightning-whip melee attack. (Her action skill is unbelievably lame, but I simply never use it.) When it works, the combat in the Pre-Sequel is a LOT of fun.
2) The Claptastic Voyage DLC -- Pretty much all of my complaints above are remedied in this DLC. It's better than any BL2 DLC in my opinion. Unfortunately, it is only the length of a DLC.
3) It's more borderlands.
It's not nearly as polished or consistent as Borderlands 2. I do not recommend it over Borderlands 2, but I do recommend it as a fun game.

It's more a grand strategic thing throwing entire fleets around, and then watching them duke it out in epic, eye candy firefights where you can zoom in until a single ship fills your entire screen. With all those red, blue and violet laser beams glittering in the darkness it's quite atmospheric to watch. What the game needs more of 'tho is different shipsets. There's only six different ship and city styles. One per species. (or seven if you get the DLC). Now you can build endless amounts of subraces within those six species, all with different racial looks and perks, but additional shipsets and species would be welcome. For example i miss being able to play a robotic civilization. But overall great game! Most fun i've had with a 4x game in some time now. Last two i played were Armada 2526 and Endless Space.
