After so long of not palying this game, I went back and played as both the Holy Roman Empire and England. I had completely forgotten just how much content depth this game has as well as the amazing dynamic combat and cavalry charges. Nothing beats watching your heavy mounted knights charge to the rear of enemy troops being held in place by your men-at-arms. There's always something to do in the game. Whether it's building up your empire with the constant upgrads to cities and castles, to you participating in crusades or squashing rebellions. And those general speaches are absolutely amazing. This game isn't without its faults. The ai can be quite stupid at times, but that's the case with all TW games so it isn't too bad considering it's not broken. The game itself (the campaign) has no real story but the one you make with whatever events unfold during your playtime. The game has 2 phases: one is a turn based campaign map where you manage your empire. How you manage your empire is really up to you but keep in mind that this isn't Rome 2 or Attila, there are consequences to your actions. Too much war mongering against other factions that share your religion and you'll be excommunicated by your religious leader meaning that you could find yourself in the middle of both a Jihad AND a holy crusade. Your generals are also EXTREMELY important! I cannot stress that enough! You need generals not only to lead your troops in battle, but also to build up your empire. If a city or castle doesn't have a governer (a general either a family member or just some general in your family) you cannot choose what to build or what units to recruit. It will be automanaged. One of the downsides to this game though is the annoyance of having to hire a diplomat in order to take diplomatic actions with other factions. It may be a bit more immersive, sure, but it's still a pain. that's one of the things newer TW games have done right. The game also has missions that are sent to you. From taking certain cities or castles to joining crusades, as stated before there's always something to do. However, some missions can be absolutely stupid and won't benifit you in any way or are nearly impossible to truly accomplish and it sucks because if they're not done, you lose reputation. be it with other factions or with your respective religious leader. But other than that, this game really doesn't have much to complain about. The 2nd phase is the real time battle map with thousands of men under your command. The best trategy here is the best strategy in any TW game: Take the high grounds and if none are available, use the "hammer and anvil strategy. It works extremely well in this game because of the powerful heavy cavalry. Overall this is a phenominal game and has earned all its praise and love. It's not perfect and has some glaring flaws, but they're easily overshadowed by the sheer amount of content and high quality of the game.

The game's too short if you just want to finish the missions and call it a game. TL;DR: If you like the simple fun of a game like Dive Kick and wouldn't mind more of that same pure simplistic fun, this game is exactly what your looking for. This game does a great job of making you want to get into deeper fighting games and you'll come to appreciate it as the gateway drug/game to more complex fighting games, just as Dive Kick is considered.
Pros:
-Simple Controls
-Local multiplayer is always a plus
-Different characters have enough difference to them, to make you find a one tailored for your gameplay style
-CPU is an actual challenge to fight
-Teaches basic fighting game tactics
Cons:
-No configurable keybindings
One Strike, joins Dive Kick perfectly on the list of games that builds the bridge for causal gamers seeking to go from games like those to heavier fighting games like Street Fighter, King of Fighters, or even Mortal Kombat. These games need to be praised more but honestly maybe these games are the unsung heroes of the genre because with these game are literally the gateway drug/game into fighting games for casual gamers. Fighting games these days are filled with systems and set-ups that many people including myself don't care to invest in, honestly its just to complected or intimidating. One Strike and Dive Kick goes back to the roots of what makes these games fun, by simplifying that tense moment in a match where both players are on edge and one hit can end it all.
Story/Gameplay: No story, but i can tell this is just a simple old school idea of an Japanese warriors tournament. There are different modes for solo and local VS, and even an local tournament mode. One mode (Arcade) specifically gives each fighter 5 hit-points (its still 1 Hit-point kill per round) after losing all 5 you will lose the match.
-The combat is simple and fast paced just the same as dive kick. You can move left or right (No jumping in this game), and two buttons for attack or block, and two for dodge forward or back. Now the special thing here is that each button triggers a distinct style of move for each character, for example for one character a dodging backwards might be a simple backstep but for another its a swift retreating attacking. With this the game becomes more than just a simple wait to attack game because your while you are worried about taking the first strike, your also worried about whiffing (Missing an attack) and whether its on purpose or not. If you play on harder difficulty you'll see the CPU whiffing on purpose alot to trick you into attacking and they will punish you for it.
Controls- The controls are simple but i do wish you could configure the keyboard bindings. I also tried to connect my controller to this game (In the options it states there is controller configurations) but i just couldn't get it working at all.
Visuals: The pixel art is well done but I'm not going to lie, I would love to see a great game like this have a more detailed art style. The fighting Arenas are artistically well done, my favorite is the cliffs above the sea-level.
Sound: The music is unbelievably good, like crazy catchy. The chippy tunes reminds me of music from games like Street Fighter 2. They really pull you into the fights and gets you hype.
Conclusion: I gotta admit I love this game, because an non-fgc gamer such as myself can be taught fighting game tactics like whiffing, countering, and canceling without realizing it, that's what games like One Strike and Dive Kick does; it teaches you fighting game basics. After a while you'll what to play a game with even more complex fighting game tactics to learn more.

We find a 2D game with a retro and 8 bits style with the mechanics that the first to hurt the opponent is the winner. In the story we get into various characters of medieval Japan with the intention of become the best warrior.
-A wide variety of characters to choose from.
-Each character differs from the others by their weapons and fighting styles.
-There are a lot of scenarios where battles take place.
-Some scenarios have effects that make you put more in it, like the winter scene where snowflakes fall from the sky.
- Collection system of your victories called '' Accolade '', is a tree where your victories are shown in all modes, difficulties and characters.
-A simple control and easy to understand.
-A HUD, artwork and beautiful setting with many details that give it that oriental touch.
-An extensive amount of game modes: 2 main game modes, single player and versus. The singleplayer mode is divided into 4 (The only life, Aracade, Team duel and Tournament) and the versus mode is divided into 3 (Arcade, Team duel and Tournament).
-The system of choice of characters team duel mode is very well achieved, so they will make you remember old fighting games.
-The One Touch One Death system manages to make fast and simple games.
-A simple background story but that gives you enough to have a role.
-The characters have only one suit and this does not change unless you are against it.
-Many difference between the difficulties, the '' Easy '' is very easy, the '' Normal '' is difficult and the '' Hard '' is impossible. (This obviously is going to be noticed less with practice).
-It has some bugs, like the tournament mode, in this same when you reach the final in the box of who fights against whom, your character appears against your character (p1 vs p1) instead of your character against the machine (p1 vs com).
In the end, is a game that will give you a lot of hours of fun to complete it 100%, and for only $ 5 worth much more than the price that have. Game completely recommended.

I think that this game has great potential, but there are two core elements that are wrong with this game that makes the game very frustrating. The first and most obvious is the planet cap that you get and will keep throughout the entirety of the game. Because you have no tech tree, you assume as a new player this cap will expand as you develop more social technologies. You might think you can create a futuristic government based off the government you selected at the beggining of the game. Instead, you are expected to meet the planet cap and then basically vassalize any other planet you want to inahbit, making the map of your empire look distracting and unappealing while you deal with the amazingly terrible AI in the new vassal states you created. Its completely normal to have buggy AI within the first year of a launch. The issue here is the core elements of the game force the bugs in the products to center stage. Its acceptable for a game like Civilization to have bad AI because the competition for winning the game is a small portion of an experience that's really more about defining what you want to do. However in this game, the core elements force the bad AI directly into your own decision making process, making the entire experience completely frustrating and irratating. The AI govenors starve populations and waste land tiles like their names were Comodus, Coligula, and Coligula's horse. Its amazing how a team of game of devolopers can put months of care into creating a game and fail to see this enormous a monumental flaw.
The second game breaking problem is the tech trees, or the lack there of. I'm pretty sure the developers were going for a realism theme with this format. Because you don't know what new technology is, how could possibly tell what your going to study hundreds of years into the future? Its sounds great and thematic on paper, but in reality it becomes an obnoxious and stupid design flaw. See, when your playing a game for like 6 hours, and your still waiting for the mid game to set in, you can tell there's a problem with pacing. Grand Strategy games can be really, really long, especially when they come from Paradox. But the thing is, Games like Crusader Kings 2, Europa Universalis, and Hearts of Iron all begin with telling you the begining and end of the game. Without this, Stellaris has an issue showing the player where he or she is in the game, especially the player has no idea how much content is left in the game. This may seem like a small gripe, but not knowing where you are in the game means not knowing what to do in that given time. Should the player already have amassed an army to prepare for interstellar wars? Could the competing AI be at the halfway point in winning the game? The player does not have the resources available to even make assumptions on these question, therefore he has no idea what to do in the game at all. If you have no understanding of the time left in a game, you won't understand the rewards or consequences of your decisions.
These specific issues will likely not be changed because the developers might feel that its what makes there game unique. If these two things in the game I have labeled as problems weren't present, I would likely be praising this game and dreaming of its depth and potential. The race creation is better than galactic civilizations or any space strategy game ive seen, and the developers efforts to help you personalize your tech and your ships are very charming. What's really missing here is the challange and reward you get from acheiving something through a complex and difficult situation. This game will likely never give me the same challange that EU4 or Crusader Kings 2 gives me. So I cannot recommend it.

Antisquad is a turn based tactical shooter strategy game along the lines of X-Com: Enemy Unknown. There is a lot of style and personality to the game with its characters. There is a bit of skipable dialog before and after each mission. A lot of the fun and challenge comes from the combat. It is a game of chess, 3 troops of your choosing vs a small army. Your troops are just as frail as the enemies. You need to be smarter than their numbers. Enemies become alert when they spot your troops or see their allies die. It feels like a port of a mobile game. Everything is a mouse click, so it feels very click heavy and if you can overlook that, its a great game for its customization and combat.
You have five troops at the start, but you can hire more. The troops are basically a sniper, a scout, a explosives expert, an assaulter (armored weapons melee expert), and a heavy gunner. Each of these troops has two of their own special abilities. One is a special attack like a dart to slow enemies, a knife to break through enemy armor, a grenade to do area damage and the other is a passive skill that lasts a few turns and has a cooldown, such as a smoke screen to hide allies, armor increase to increase the armor of everyone around and so on. Everything your troops do cost 'action points' and all characters start out with the same amount of AP. Moving, attacking, using skills and reviving fallen allies cost AP, but for each character, every action costs a different amount of AP. So the scout's movement costs 6 AP, her attacks cost 12 AP and smokescreen costs 54 AP vs the sniper's 40 AP attack and 30 AP dart skill. The only thing that doesn't cost AP are items that you find or buy in the store. If one of your troops has AP remaining after their turn, and an enemy attacks them, they will fight back if they have enough AP. This allows you to let enemies come to you.
Since it is turn based, everyone on your team gets to use all their AP and then everyone on the other team gets to use all of theirs. The game does a good job of showing the distance you can travel with the remaining AP, but shows how much you'll have left when you're done traveling and even what distance you need to be in order to attack someone. You will need to double click for most every move, because the first click is just to show what you'll be doing. Click on an enemy to see their stats and what things you can do to them, double click to attack them. One click to see where you'll move, the AP you'll have left and how the enemy will react and double click to move there. You get the idea.
One way the game seems shallow, there's no sort of hit percentages, fog of war or height advantages like in other games. Its all just flat terrain with objects and walls for cover. There are no destructible environments. Again, its not as deep combat strategy wise as other games. There's still a lot of depth in upgrades.
Before a mission begins, you can buy items, guns, gear and upgrade each character for a cost. Upgrade their attack damage, movement, armor and so on. Every layer of armor is just an extra hit they can take, such as someone with 3 armor can be shot 3x before it'll drain their health. Once they're out of health, they're down. When they're down an ally can revive them, but if they aren't revived in X amount of turns, they're gone from the mission, but not forever.
The missions have simple objectives, get to here, kill all enemies, blow up this or that. Sometimes you'll have to push buttons to open doors or operate things to kill enemies. Some of the areas are pretty straight forward, but others allow for flanking and different routes. Each mission feels like a healthy amount of gameplay. Not just that, but when you head into each mission, you chose your difficulty from four difficulties. Its a nice feature and adds replayability to missions when you need to grind for gold to buy upgrades.
So when I say port of a mobile game, to me that would send up red flags of 'pay to win' or microtransactions. There seems to be none of that here, all of the gold you get in the game comes from winning (or losing) missions, completing challenges, killing enemies and clicking on them. Yes that's right you need to click on dead enemies for whatever reason. I guess that prevents wasting turns from touching each one. Some enemies can drop power ups for the mission that you need to have your troops physically collect. Enemies know to collect them instead of you to power up themselves. Other times, you get crates that when you are between missions, you can open them and have random loot. Some games charge you $2.50 to open crates.
In all, the game feels simpler than other tactical turn based games, yet still a lot of fun. The depth comes from the customization. Its a beautiful game to look at and that adds to the enjoyment of the game. It feels polished for a $6 game and I got a lot for my money, even if it is click heavy.

Having played only ten minutes of Ricochet I can assure, without a microgram of uncertainty, to anyone of any background, that the interactive experience known as "Ricochet" is the cornerstone of Human achievement in the arts--nay--the peak of man's consummation itself! I see myself to be perpetually indebted to whatever deity unfurled the momentary lapse and position in which not only is this masterwork accessible, but also that I dwell in the juncture of living among the virtuosos who gave birth to the interactive marvel. How might a single mind solicit to inspect such a transcendent monument? Be forewarned, dear reader, that I, nor any man, could possibly hope to dissect a work of this calibur by his lonesome. Hell, I refuse to consider that an array of one thousand strong could decipher it! However, similar the prodigies that created it, I can only hope to muster the copious amounts of genius pouring from this work and cram it into the confines of the english language.
Upon initiating "Ricochet", you are greeted with so much symbolism to consume that most average citizens of our realm would choose to exit such a dense and meaningful screen. It is too much to the man with an anemic consciousness. I hardly know where to start when considering bringing this knowledge to the common people. I shall begin with how the work addresses the aboriginal of life and nature itself--birth. The anterior screen showcases many images, one of which tends to dominate the human's attention, as it is the most leviathan icon currently viewable. The gargantuan circle adorned by futuristic glows and structures is a symbol for the birth of the individual, as well as the birth of man into the technological age. Allow me to elaborate. The neo-digital ring depicted is an obvious allusion to the birth canal that nature devised each human to pass through. "Ricochet" proves this by how close up to the circular (or rather, somewhat polygonal) shape the art goer is. The moment is almost demonstrated as if your head is about to pass through, yet you are not quite out yet. You, dear reader, may be asking "Well, if it were the birth canal depicted, why isn't there a light on the other end? Isn't that usually how the birthing process is shown?" Well dear reader, you are absolutely right! Keen observation of yours, if I do say so myself! However, this is clearly intentional coinciding the entirety of "Ricochet"'s premise. You see, "Ricochet" proposes that in a rapidly advancing digital age, you are born into as much shadow as you were conceived in originally, hence the futuristic design of the configuration. Whether or not the craftsmen of this piece intended to imply that we are merely headed in that direction or we have already lived this concept is entirely disputable. There is much, much more to discuss about this object, but for now the picture requires more context, so I shall leave it at that. Moving on to the next point of interest, another image stands out. Yes, the icon associated with the game's title (to be discussed later)--the feature's logo. On first observation, one may assume the logo is but a relapse of something straight out of a 1980's film--font and all. Be that as it may, the visual holds a profound connotation. When the logo is rotated 180 degrees, the image appears to imitate the lower section of a triangle! Of course! Now, as you would assume from such a work, this holds a variety of nuance. However, I will discuss my interpretation of the logo's meaning. You see, the bottom of a triangle can be associated with the masses. The largest in number, yet trampled upon by its aristocratic counterparts. A classic case of the proletariats versus the bourgeoisie. The logo attaches itself with the work--"Ricochet". Clearly, the masterpiece's author's intended to represent the common man. Not only that, but the logo suggests something more, as it is rotated so the bottom of the triangle is at the top, The rotation confronts the idea that this piece will give the proletariats the power to overthrow the few that control them and restore power back to mankind itself. While this has not happened, I presume that the craftsmen who administered "Ricochet" assumed that would happen. That is one of the major reasons for the game's futuristic settings, after all. "Ricochet" shall not bring light to the people until technology and the people have collided with one another, allowing the work's true power to disseminate. Such tenacity bequeaths my soul optimism for our posterity. What beauty to behold, the day "Ricochet" provides its rightful nectar to the dry third eyes of the public! Excuse me, I got a tad passionate there. Yet, the principal still stands. I digress, there is more to discuss, and so little allotment for one lifetime! The next immensely abstract element of "Ricochet"'s title card are its four options. Of course, an important element to any interactive piece: choice. "Ricochet" insinuates that any choice you make can be boiled down into four simple decisions: "Find, Create, Options, and Quit". Allow me to elaborate on each of those phrases. Find--discovery, you choose to make a journey of some kind to quench your nature-given curiosity. You may not only find what is on the outside, but also evaluate what is on the inside. Create--to craft, to make something of your own. To use your abilities to craft your own solution to any problem. To create is to show yourself to others, much like the artists of "Ricochet". Options--to alter or change how you will solve a problem. You may not solve the solution in the most efficient way, but by changing how you operate, you can avoid any negative feedback one may receive. And finally, quit--to cease, to make null any progress of your heart and mind. To stop evil, or to stifle good. The most threatening and harsh choice of them all. Each of these choices can be intertwined with one another, yet they each build a unique experience. Moving along with my simple observations, the first two options specifically state the word "Server", along with "Find" and "Create". It's my humble opinion that the word "Server" serves as an opportunity for the creators to manifest a dissection of religions and their deities and how they are found by many people, and how each and every one of them was also created by many people. A "server" is someone who, well, serves another man. Many look to gods as mere reflections of mankind, showing them as forgiving or blessing, rather than a lonesome creator of all. The authors of "Ricochet" point out the obvious irony that humankind tends to worship themselves when establishing religions based around gods. These deities, while on a surface level they are higher than humans, are merely there to serve as a torch to show man its way. "Ricochet" shows these two options alongside one another to demonstrate how comedic and silly the concept of religion seems to be. While you may not personally agree with those statements (and I may not as well), it is the view of mankind that the work builds. True or not, the work still stands. While there are many more avenues of the starting screen, one man cannot possibly see them all. I, for one, cannot hope to understand every concept displayed. Therefore, I must continue my analysis.
Without getting into the still immensely compact consequences for selecting one of the phrases, the systems of "Ricochet" hold a host of implications. First off, you, the player, control a clearly hominoid individual. You represent a member of the public. A representation of the base of the triangle of class, as discussed earlier. In this future, you are pitted against another bipedal combatant, to serve as entertainment for the bourgeoisie. There is no other explanation of the ridiculous colours you are adorned with. It's an allegory for a sport, two opposite teams compete against each other to entertain--

I dreamed a game like this for ages. Now it's real.
It's the perfect mix for both casual and hardcore players: fast matches for casual, much depth/longevity for pro players.
There is a hall with a global chat, a friend list, your faction, your upgradable stats, your inventory (which contains materials and upgradable weapons), and a couple of panels to start Custom player scenarios, or the editor, to build (test and share) your levels. Here you can spend the points earned by playing, to unlock new drones, modules, parts, bosses, weapons, etc... these ones are used to make your custom levels more challenging. Every drone unit has a different ability (example: Mandible units are able to drop black holes, which attract you), so the gameplay is extremely fun because of the unit combinations. The editor is very easy, everyone can build something through endless possibilities. Also, they are going to add many other game modes.
As 2D shooter game, starting a match is fast and not stressful, but in the meanwhile, there is a RPG part if you want to farm, or a leaderboard dedicated to every single scenario, if you want to improve your scores and beat the other players like a pro!
In other words, this is A GAME FOR ALL.

This game is not something I can describe in normal gaming terms. It's not a technical masterpiece as it has its share of bugs, it doesn't have the prettiest graphics or require a state of the art computer, and the story comes off as generic. At first. First off, this game has 26 endings, A-Z, but worry not as some of those endings are not "true" endings. A lot of people are refering to them as joke endings, but I feel like that takes away from the impact of these endings. I would say it's more appropriate to call them non-canon but still important. Secondly, the fact that some reviewers stopped reviewing this game after route A is, in a word, insane. You basically quite after the tutorial. In order to get the full impact of this game you have to play until at least route C, but don't worry too much about it as almost every mission from route A carries over into route B. This makes all the difference.
This sounds pretty normal, but the way in which all of this is presented is what makes the game special. Unfortunately all of this is tied into the main story so I can't go into much detail about it, but let me just say that this game is memorable in a very special way.

I'm writing this review @ roughly 30 hours in...
I bought this game because everyone and their mum was going on about how this game was some auteur masterpiece that tugged at the heartstrings and destroyed their expectations.
Before I say anything, I will say that the game is smoooooth as butter in both optimization and character animations. it may be possibly the highest quality animated game ( combat and movement-wise) that i've played. I also REALLY enjoyed the surprise bullet-hell sequences, especially in the hacking mini-game context.
I've gotten the ABCOG endings and I have to say.... it's a bloody slog. It's not a JRPG (it's a hack'n slash), but it suffers from all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that has always held the JRPG genre back; such as grinding for experience, utterly boring combat, ambiguous item gathering/ upgrading systems, and a npc-world dissonance that rivals final fantasy XV.
It's like this game attempts at all angles to defeat itself (maybe that's the entire bougie point) and put it's own ideals in front of the player's connection with the world, characters, or mechanics.
I want to experience this badass emotional rollercoaster of emotions that people are talking about, but I just can't go though all these counter-intuitive obstacles. It requires a modest devotion of bland gameplay inbetween every story moment.  Kind of like Metal Gear, but not immersive in the slightest.
This game should have been an anime.
Please, buy this game because you enjoy the platinum games mechanics and smooth experience, not because you're craving story.

This game has a huge learning curve, one that you most-likely won't ever get over. The control scheme is meant to be a bit disorienting to make the game much more difficult, whilst easily playable, for the player. Don't lead this disuade you though, this game is incredibly unique, and a brilliant concept.
The premise of the game is that you must shoot powerups at the colored circles located in the middle of your quadrant. Once you shoot one with a powerup, the powerup will move to the quadrant corresponding with the color of the circle that you had shot. You may not regularly shoot at other players, as you must use the portals in the middle of your area. Other players also have the ability to halt your powerups, for example... one powerup spawns some enemies within the area that you should it to. The player in that area may shoot and kill the enemies of course, so that they will not remain taunting the other player for the remainder of the game. As I stated previously, and you most likely could already tell... I would highly reccomend this game to anyone that enjoys local, splitscreen party-like games.

Good game mechanics

Cons:
Few levels and no player-created or periodic content, and thus little replay value.
Summary:
If you like puzzle games, snag this on a sale for about $1. It'll last you about 2 hours.
After looking around, it turns out the game has two sequels which expand on the game mechanics and add randomly-generated levels.

I wish steam gave a more helpful metric than "do you recommend this game." BtPS isn't a terrible game, it's just disappointing after Borderlands 2. There was a lot of opportunity to fix some of BL2's problems but most were left while 2K Australia added a new story with some hit or miss gameplay gimmicks.
Since it's a Borderlands game it seems reasonable to start with the loot. BtPS introduces a number of new weapon types including Cyro elemental, Glitch (with DLC) and Luneshine. Of these the Cyro feels the most natural in the Borderlands world along with the other elements (fire, shock, etc). Hitting an enemy enough with it freezes them solid rendering them highly vulnerable, leading to some nice balance decisions. It basically takes the place of slag in that it's helpful to have at least one person on the team using it to weaken enemies. Glitch and Luneshine (the latter of which I didn't even know existed in my playthrough) are... well, they exist. I didn't really find them compelling. Glitch ads a semi-random effect that cycles and I'm not even sure about Luneshine. I think it just adds a modifier. Feels a bit tacked on.
The game also introduces O2 kits and the delightful ability to have a jumpjet fire on every jump. There is also a 'slam' ability when mid-air to crush enemies and a new vehicle that takes advantage of these features. I like being able to hop-jet across the map faster than running, but the addition of another category of loot (the O2 kits) is beginning to make the system feel overburdered.
The new characters are fine. None can replace my loved melee-built Zero from BL2, though. It's a shame that one of the DLC characters with an interesting skill-set, Aurelia, has such an annoying voice\personality (don't get me started on Claptrap).
The story is good (if a little confusing with the 'flashback' elements), though the quests are bogged down when they send the player from one side of the map to another for tediously thin reasons. It is nice to see more of Hyperion and Jack, a great character who is well balanced, plot-wise. He's not so psycho that it defies belief to work for him (until the end) but he's not portrayed as a particularly good guy, either.
The maps are poorly designed, unless they are meant to cause frustration. Remember Opportunity from Borderlands 2? I liked the aesthetics but hated how easy it was to get turned around and lost even when there was a map with the objective displayed. Almost every map is like that in BtPS with maze-like areas that you have to check the large map to figure out (which is okay in single player, not so good in multi). Worse yet, there are way too many hazards on the maps. I died more due to falling in lava than I ever did to enemies. In BL2 these existed but they were rare or around the edge of the map, but in BtPS they're everywhere! Including places where it looks like you're supposed to go.
I guess this is a bit biased but I disliked much of the NPC voice acting in BtPS, particularly the fact that everyone sounds like they are hamming up their Australian accents as much as possible. I wanted to throw that pickle kid off a high tower into lava as soon as I heard him. It makes the game seem apart from the others in the series and just ends up sounding too goofy.
Things that SHOULD have been fixed, but weren't:
- The dialogue system is still crap. It's way too easy to miss lots of dialogue because one character moves two feet and triggers another line that cuts the first off.
- The duel system could have been upgraded to have options for a 'free for all' or vehicle dueling. Not a big part of the game but it would give a new shine to the mechanic.
- Not enough Tiny Tina.
All in all, BtPS is fine but seems like a wasted opportunity to explore an interesting moment in the Borderlands world. It wisely centers a lot of the action around Handsome Jack, one of the few interesting NPCs in this game (Moxxi makes a too-brief appearance as well). Its gameplay is more of the same and it mostly works, especially in multiplayer.

Party Hard is an enjoyable party game. Now you can’t play with your friends in this game, however your friends can watch you fail at being a murderer. This game is based around you as a murderer going to different parties and killing people without being noticed.
Gameplay
To begin this review, lets discuss the main aspects of the gameplay. For the most part you will be going around stabbing people in the back with a knife, the game also has a dance mechanic which allows you to lure people away from the crowds surrounding them. This mechanic was very unreliable; you couldn’t control where the person moved to so on more than one occasion that person would walk off to another group of people making it very difficult to kill them. You can also find and pickup heavier weapons which allow you to kill more than one person with a single swipe. Overall it seems that there were a lot of missed opportunities with the gameplay, every time I went to set up a trap it would earthier fail or just not work entirely which was a real shame.

Offen enough I would see that I was being chased by the police so I would set up a trap only to have the trap not go off when the police walked past it. This produced many frustrating moments as progressing on to the next map became more and more of a chore rather than a fun. experience.
Music and Visuals
As for the music and graphics, they are both relatively good. The music fits the theme of the game insanely well, with each map containing a slightly different song from the last. The graphics also melded with the games concept fairly well, with flashy colours and lights that represent what a party should look like. The graphics contain a colour palet of a TRILLION COLOURS......no really, it feels that way as every party contains flashing lights which seem to change every level. The rich colour scheme of this game, makes Fallout 4 look like an elderly's funeral.
Performance
What can I say? Much like hundreds of other games on steam, this game utilises that 16 bit like art style, so obviously the performance section of my review becomes pointless. But since this is the performance section I might as well point out the obvious and say...YES it runs well. A few additions I did notice were the options to turn down the lighting and turn on/off different stylistic effects. These are good options to have as they allow the player to cater their personal taste to the game.
Map Variety
However, what I really liked was the map variety, there are many unique party locations in this game, this keeps the game fresh for longer periods as the maps are always changing their location and environment. There are always new events that occur which livens the game up quite a bit. You can go from having the swat team called on you, only to realise that when they leave a bear will be sent in.....yes a bear, but don't worry he's a petty chill bear, great at dancing too!
Conclusion
In conclusion Party hard is a very fun game for the extensively cheap price. It contains great music, visuals and map variety, only to be slightly let down by a few mechanics that are extremely unreliable like the dance and trap systems.
TO DISCLOSE! Yes I recieved the game key for FREE, however I would like to maintain that these are my honest opinions on Party Hard.
-JoshuaUpham

Chime takes me back to the days when Lumines on the PSP was massive... possibly in some small sections of the PSP Puzzle Strategy community.
Ok, so Lumines probably wasn't all that well known outside of the PSP, but essentially you had 2x2 different coloured squares come down, much like tetris. You'd clear the board and score points when you build up 2x2 blocks of the same colour, when a line would slide across the screen and take them out.
In Chime, you don't need to worry about colour, but the pieces are all different configurations of 5 squares connected, much like tetris' 4 squares. You can move, rotate, and place them anywhere on the grid. The 'beatline' will move in time with the music, setting off events when it hits the shapes. If you have a solid blocks of 3x3 or more, they will disappear after a short while, give better music samples, and stamped down a completed section on the grid. The aim is to get 100% coverage on these grids before the time runs out.
This game is great if you want to fill in time, or if you're into mixing a few tunes with samples based on how well you play. Probably a small cult following for that. In the end, since there are only 6 or 7 level/songs to play, it only becomes a grind to try to get 100% coverage on each level, not really much more than that.
Pretty good if on sale, not really something to put in a wishlist though.

Nothing is explained particularly well (although thankfully with this little gameplay there's not actually much to explain), and you're thrown straight into a 50-person party with little to no idea of what to do. Spoiler: walk slowly from person to person and press X to perform a two-frame animation to murder them. If other partygoers see you, you'll get a visit from the police, who will channel the yeti from Skifree and chase you down to your inevitable death (unless you reach a window, which will cause them to ignore your multiple homicides, as climbing through a window is a lot of effort).
All in all, I spent 20 minutes with this game, and had no desire whatsoever to spend any more time with it. If there were other mechanics, they were so poorly explained that I had no idea they were even there.
The game desperately wants to be the kid brother of Hotline Miami, but where Hotline Miami crashes the party, steals the booze, punches the host in the face and makes off with their girlfriend, Party Hard turns up an hour early, gets drunk on two bottles of light beer, throws up all over itself and has already passed out on the couch by the time the other guests arrive to draw dongs all over its face in sharpie markers.
Avoid.

This game frustrates me to no end, because it starts off great. Act One is easy, but makes great use of the mechanics and has some decent drive to it. Sadly, the translator and play testers for the game appears to have quit the second they saw Act Two and Act Three, because everything after the intro is a trainwreck. The levels are boring, the interface has no idea how to click the right spot on the map (and misclicks are harshly punished), Act Two's difficulty is just adding hitpoints to the bad guys, Act Three instead just gives them suicide bombs, a million movement points, and the ability to instantly know where you are, while the writing goes from vaguely forgettable banter to nonsensical gibberish. (I'm convinced that the "witty" banter is bugged and it's only supposed to be playing one or two lines at a time and instead plays all of them. It's the only way to explain this, unless everyone contracted Parkinson's disease in between Act One and Act Two.)
Oh, and it's a port of a mobile game so you'll want to use Cheat Engine to bypass all of the grinding. It knocks off most of the playtime this title has (it's amazingly short), but there's no reason to replay the same missions over and over again just to get around the obstacles they intended you to pay to bypass.
All told, if you can get it super cheap then you'll probably get some good fun out of Act One. If you enjoy trying to decipher Russian to English Google translations then the stories Act Two and Three might amuse you as well, but the gameplay is awful.

Nier: Automata came out at an unfortunate time. 2017 is quickly turning into 1998 part 2 as one of the best years for videogames and Nier: Automata has come out amidst killers such as Persona 5, LOZ: Breath of the Wild and Horizon. Nier: Automata would've been a clear winner for GOTY any other year but it has stiff competition this year. However, even if Nier is not the "Best" game of 2017, it's probably one of the most important games to have come out this generation.
Nier: Automata is a milestone in Videogame storytelling. It's the greatest achievement in this field since Metal Gear Solid 1 and Final Fantasy VI before that. It's difficult to explain without spoilers but the amazing story that is told by Nier is something special that would be impossible to replicate on any other Medium.
The gameplay is fantastic, utilising a mixture of character action, bullet hell, 2D platforming and twin stick shooting. You may think that these mechanics are diluted by the sheer numbers but each is masterfully crafted, fun and flow into one another smoothly.
The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in years and the music is used for fantastic effect, making epic or truly heartfelt moments all the more impactful.
I loved every character. Despite being Androids these were some of the most human characters I've ever had the pleasure of meeting. Every hardship they went through affected me personally and there were few moments during my playthrough where I wasn't completely invested in their plights.
The game does have some cons, like performance is a bit rough, it's not terrible but it's not exactly smooth, with strange stutters every once in a while, especially when entering new area's. The game is also not exactly great looking, graphically. These shortcomings though are easy to ignore compared to what this game does right, and what it does right, it knocks completely out of the park.
While games like Horizon or Persona 5 will be remembered as some of the best of 2017, Nier: Automata is gonna be remembered as one of the best and most important videogames of this generation as well as for the industry as a whole. Thank you to Square Enix, Platinum games and Yokotaro for crafting this masterpiece.

A brilliant hack and slash JRPG! But in no means perfect. I do feel many reviewers gloss over some of the games faults.

- A little to excessive fans service. Not really necessary and doesn't add to the experience.
- Pretty poor graphics for a AAA title. Feels like the game was originally developed for the PS3.
- Despite being "open world" it certainly has a lot of immersion breaking invisible walls.
- No auto save. Save system is neatly integrated in the world building of the game but leaves a lot to be desired.
- Poorly optimized PC port, especially if you're playing in ultrawide.
- Cutscenes are pre rendered video files. They are rendered in 16:9 and plays at 30fps. In-game actually looks better if you are playing on a high resolution monitor!
Pros:

+ Very interesting and well designed characters.
+ Interesting and fun gameplay elements.
+ Combat is tight and rewarding.
+ Amazing soundtrack.
+ Story and sidequests are very well paced.
Overall I loved this game and cannot recommend it enough. But please be aware of some of its faults before buying!

Pros:
- Based on classic Minesweeper, but more forgiving
- All levels are solvable without guessing - lots of satisfaction when you complete one!
- Nice atmosphere, albeit maybe distracting
Cons:
- Becomes rather bland after a while
- Quite short
I find Hexcells cute - it's basically an interesting iteration on classic Minesweeper. The basic mechanics are pretty much the same, the difference being that squares are now hexagons. It's also a lot more forgiving, although you'll likely find yourself restarting games just because you want to complete each level without any mistakes. Besides, all levels are solvable without guessing, and  completing a difficult level will often fill you with satisfaction. The atmosphere is quite enjoyable, although I found myself switching off the sound because it could be slightly distracting.
However, there is some criticism to be made. Once you get the grip of the game mechanics, which should happen quite soon, the game becomes rather limited. The most challenging levels become a time for staring at the screen, wondering "what am I missing?". You'll often get stuck and resort to carefully scanning the screen, trying to find out which is the next tile you can click on. And that is why I'd game this game a mixed review if I could - it can become a test of patience rather than one of cleverness. Although fans of Minesweeper will not probably be bothered much. ;)
The game is also quite short, considering that I beat all levels with a perfect score in just two hours. However, if you can get this one in a bundle or in an offer (I got it for 0.89 Euro), then it's likely that you'll have put your money to good use.

Fans and gamers were spoilt with Tomb Raider - the rebooted origin tale of the titular Lara Croft - and this wonderful behind-the-scenes digital book companion will offer great insight into how it all happened. Veteran journalist Geoff Keighley provides a relatively comprehensive look at the design process, showcasing many concepts that never made it to the finished game, as well as artwork, sketches, interviews and reports on how Crystal Dynamics recreated the video game icon.
This well designed application is best used on a tablet computer, but can be enjoyed just as easily on a desktop. Additionally, there are interactive elements, such as panoramas of the developer's studio and a music mixer. Much of the video content is actually streamed rather than downloaded with the application, but I found the content both new and good quality.
While everything is well designed and easy to navigate, I found the content lacking. The whole book can be read in just over an hour, and there is little beyond the abandoned concepts that proves truly captivating. For those who have followed previews, the content could be considered lightweight. And for those who haven't, there isn't a great deal on offer to make this a must-buy.
For Lara Croft fans, this is a fine addition to a wonderful game, and for those interested in the development process, Tomb Raider - The Final Hours offers a glimpse behind the curtain into the industry and the pressure to reboot gaming royalty. Overall, however, this is just an optional add on that offers little value for money and should only be purchased as part of a collector's edition. There just isn't enough content to justify its asking price.

This game is an immediate disappointment for me. I thought the idea of combining a shmup with loot grinding sounded amazing, but it's really not very much fun in practice and the execution here is more boring and frustrating than addictive and fun.
The first thing that strikes you about this game is how bizarre the difficulty balance is. There is a ridiculous amount of difficulty levels, which is cool, but they only scale reasonably for the first half of the list or so, then the enemy damage/health rises so quickly that it becomes immediately apparent that you can't beat those without high-level gear and that it's a challenge for your gear and not so much for you as a player, so you have to resign yourself to the lower difficulty levels. And, man, is that difficulty ever low. We're talking Baby's First Shmup here. On the default level, I think there was something like 5 bullets fired at me in the first stage. Five. I'm not kidding.
However, when the game does start throwing bullets at you, you start to understand why they were so careful with them in the beginning. It's because your ship and hitbox is possibly the largest ever seen in the entire genre. It's gigantic! There is no artful dodging here, just throwing your clumsy titan of a warship around the screen, dodging equally ridiculously large bullets in extremely loose patterns (because, of course, intricate patterns don't work when your hitbox is planet-sized).
When you've played a few levels, found some loot and started getting into it, you notice the next annoying problem... The game has both ground and air-based troops, but for some strange reason, they've designed it in such a way that you can never see both at once and have to scroll the screen by moving your ship constantly. There are supposed to be sound cues played when ground-based enemies show up, but half of them don't make any sound at all and most of the others play the sound way too late and when the vehicle is halfway across the screen. The reason this is a big deal is because there's a money train that shows up, which is where you will get most of your cash for upgrades, so you absolutely have to keep track of the ground. But then your rating for the stage is based on your kills and your health, so you can't just hang out on the lower half of the screen to make sure you get the money, because then you'll miss that S rank. Why would you do this? Horizontal shmups have avoided scrolling the screen for 30 years for a reason, and this is that reason. It's just obnoxious not to be able to see and/or hear all enemies when the game expects you to kill everything for a good score and rating.
Furthermore, they've done some pretty serious stretching of limited resources here. The game has the typical 5 stages, which is common for a shmup, but they've milked each stage by dividing it into 10 substages where each substage just adds maybe a formation or occasionally a harder enemy. These substages are actually fairly lengthy, for what they are, and they are treated like proper levels with a score/rewards screen and an option to back out to the upgrade shop between each. It's like you're playing versions 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and so on of the same stage until you're finally granted access to the actual 1.0 version of the stage and can move onto playing 9 beta versions of level 2 before getting to play the real level.
But, above all, the major problem is the basic idea, like I touched on earlier. A shmup where the barrier to success is what gear you're wearing just isn't as much fun as one where your skill carries you the whole way. Winning in the highest difficulty level without proper gear is literally impossible in this game. It cannot be done. That's boring and artificial and creates a grinding situation that just feels hollow and insincere. I thought this idea sounded great when I got the game, but it's just really not much fun in practice. At least not in this game.

Hello.
This isn't a big game, but it's a pretty cool game with a lot of good replay value. This is the kind of game that is easy to get into, but takes longer to master.
Anyway, I know some people would say that the crafting is a bit tedious but when you get the hang of it it's about as simple as they could make it. You craft most items by mixing 2 of the same together using shift. The only thing is, for example,  if you want to make an axe handle (stick + stick), if you split your stack of sticks in halves and then mix them together you will get a ton of axe handles you don't want. Instead left click the stack of stick to pick it up, right click another inventory spot to place only one there, place back the stack, then mix them. I have to agree it does sound a bit tedious, but it takes like 2 seconds in games really.
Inventory tend to fill up quickly too, but people need to realize that they actually save inventory space by mixing(crafting) items ONLY as they need them. If you have 5 stones, it takes only 1 spot. If you turn them into bars (stone + stone) you wll have 1 stone and 2 bars, which takes 2 spots. Even if you had 4 stones and turned everything into bars, the next things you will grab will be stones, not bars. Also, there comes a time that you know what to keep and what not. There's a lot of items that you won't really use depending on your build, so that can help clearing more of your inventory as you go.
Also, some people seem to complain that the game is too unforgiving with the permanent death thing. Just keep in mind that this isn't skyrim or anything like that, you could beat the game in about an hour or less so saving the game really isn't needed. The whole point is to see how far you can get. Allowing restarts from check points would be just silly.
The only thing I don't like is that all the items can be unlocked in single player OR in multiplayer. While it sure makes it easier to get them all, it takes away from someone who obtained them alone. Here's an example: Unlocking a specific hat requires you to beat the game without talking to any npc. This means playing with little to no armor, which is the main issue you have to deal with. Meanwhile, if you are playing in multiplayer, you can unlock the hat easily by having your friends buy you armors and such, which defeats the idea of not talking to npcs.
Oh another thing, it's really a shame that there is no servers to match players together or anything like that. The only way is to get players to host the games for themselves and send IPs to people found in the magicite chat room (or personal friends of course). You may have to use hamachi to get it to work too. I guess it gets the job done tho, can't ask too much from a small game like this.
Well, thanks for reading and do give this game a try, it's pretty fun.
TLDR: It's a good game, inventory management isn't great but is actually fine, anything else than permanent death would be silly for a game like this and multiplayer can be fun, but somewhat tricky to get to work. You get plenty of fun for your 10$.

Pros:
-Runs well on most hardware (cheap laptops included)
-Robust but understandable customization
-Further customization through items during matches
-Champions can't be switched after match lobby, loadout cards can't be switched after first round starts, which means you always know what you're against (unlike other games where you don't know until it hits you, or until you see it)
-Very fast matchmaking in first few hundred hours of gameplay
-Mounts and quick respawn times keep the action going
-Frequent updates, champion roster increases quickly
-Free real-money currency is awarded for consecutive daily logging in, which means you can have a couple of premium skins without actually paying money for them
Pro/Con:
-Meta changes quickly
-Free to play (everyone can play for free, but that includes hackers as well)
-Sometimes Patch Notes are like watching Game of Thrones, your main character could die for 2-3 patches (but you quickly realize others are fun/great to play as)
-Lots of nice skins, some of which are inside chests which contain many items so you may not get instantly what you wanted and unlucky people have to go through all the chest contents till they get to what they wanted
Cons:
-Lately server instability causes dropped games once in a while (doesn't negatively impact your win/loss, it just wastes your time) - devs say they're working on it
-Matchmaking sometimes makes a very one-sided match
-It takes a while to unlock all gameplay features (you play matches to earn gold and chests, you spend gold for unlocking champions and buying more chests, chests are used to get cards for loadouts) - a currency called "Essence" which is rewarded for duplicate drops and disenchanting cards you don't want is used to unlock specific cards that you yourself choose, which helps with unlocking things
Overall 8.5/10, would nerf Skye again.

Review for Galaxy on Fire 2
----------------------------
It's a nice 1st/3rd Person Shooter set in space with ships and the like. You travel from sector to sector, defeating ships, taking their loot, mining, whatever tickles your fancy. Each Sector is comprised of a varying amount of planets, usually no more than around 6, and each planet has a space station that you can visit.
Now, that doesn't meant the whole sector is one huge map you can fly around. The entire game is a series of small to medium sized maps. Each space station is a small-medium map you can fly around in. I'd say it'd take 40 seconds to 1.3 minutes to fly from one side of the map to the other.
Each space station has a Commodities Market that you can buy and sell goods at, meaning you can spend your time buying low in one sector and selling high in another if you wished. It even tells you where you saw the specific good, or more importantly, where you saw it selling for the most and where you saw it being sold the least. It's a nice feature. You can also mine asteroids and make a fair amount from that too. Each station sells different Ships, Weapons, Missiles, Commodities, and Miscellaneous Equipment so you'll have to travel around a bit to find what your looking for sometimes.
Speaking of ships, there's quite a number of different ships, each having it's own unique appearance(though not always). They each have different amounts of health, armour, shields, weapon slots, equipment slots, speed, etc., so it's quite possible to find a ship that meets you play style perfectly. There's a fair amount of weapons too, and they all have reasonably different effects and stats from each other too.
Each Station also has a 'Lounge' where you find people offering a small variety of things: 1) They can offer you a mission for an amount of money dependent of the missions difficulty. 2) They can offer to become you're Wingman for a certain amount of time for a reasonable price. 3) They can offer to sell you a varying amount of Commodities or Equipment at a reduced price, so you can sell it for profit later. 4) And sometimes they don't really do anything but chat with you, though sometimes they'll tell you which sector is selling what and sometimes at what price.
The combat is fun, and you're not required to do the main story for too long. You start with nothing really, and you'll slowly be given more equipment as the story goes, until you eventually get the ability to jump to different sectors freely. It doesn't take long until you're allowed to do as you wish, so just hang in there.

Anyway, this is a pretty fun game at a pretty low price. Definitely worth it.

Let me start off saying, this is a really short game... If you let it be. However, after having played for about 5 minutes, I was contacted by a friend on steam who saw what I was playing, and told me to take my time as the game was really short if I just followed the storyline.
As it turns out, he was right, and I'm glad I listened, because what I got was a really good experience instead of a mediocre one. The ingame timer says I completed it in 11 hours, 45 minutes, and I'd estimate the main storyline would take about 3 hours or so. That's not to say I was extremely thorough, because there's a lot more systems to see and more expensive ships to buy than what I saw, and purchased, but the game did end rather abruptly, and after it finished there was really little reason to play on (though it's a possibility as it's open ended).
Now, the game is probably the closest you'll come to playing freelancer again, and it's not really in the same league at all. This is a much more simple version of the same style of gameplay, but it's not without its charms. The voice acting is appalling, but you quickly learn to just smile at it, and completely disregard it (at least that's how I coped with it).
So what makes this game fun? Well, it's one of those sandbox type games, where sure there's a main story, but you don't really care so much, as there are lots of star systems to visit, with even more planets to dock at. Each planet has a space lounge, where you are offered side missions for money, or good/bad deals in terms of merchandise. These missions range from the typical defend this convoy, or destroy the pirates, to scanning out a traitor at the local defense force, and getting shot at by everyone else afterwards until you dock, or transporting goods, or passengers to other systems. It's a good idea to do these missions, as it sets you up with a base currency so that you may buy a better ship with more equipment slots.
The real money making doesn't start to roll in until you get a so called Khador drive, which lets you travel to star systems without using a jump gate. This is part of the storyline, and won't take long to get. Once you have that, you're able to sort out what's profitable to sell where, as long as you have been docking at all stations in the system you've visited (it'll give you system name for where it's most profitable to sell a certain item at), but enough about that. Another way entirely to make money is to mine. You do this by outfitting your ship with a drill and getting a scanner, and then just drilling astroids outside the various stations. It comes with a minigame of its own, but it was rather boring, if you ask me, so I didn't really get into it.
You also have to be careful who you do missions for, or against, because there are 4 "friendly" factions in the game, and they are paired up against each other, so doing missions for the Vossk will decrease your Terran reputation to a point where they will outright shoot at you, and refuse to let you dock unless you bribe the station chief. You can fix this by paying a diplomat which sometimes spawn in space lounges if your rep is low enough, but it'll cost you a pretty penny to do so.
The story itself is nothing new. Start out with nothing and find out it's up to you to save the world.
There are many different ships to choose from in this game, and they are all different in terms of weapon/equipment slots, armor, the way it handles, and so on. You can outfit you ship with a wide range of modules, including shield, armor, tractor beam, cloak, booster, agility mod, warp drive, passanger cabins, and more. This allows for a great deal of flexibility. The weapons comes in form of primary and secondary. The primary slots are for your autocannons, blasters, lasers, and what have you, and the secondary is reserved for missiles, rockets, or emp bombs to disable enemy ships (this will also allow you to steal their cargo if you have a scanner and tractor beam for example).
You'll see combat almost everywhere you go, so some good advice would be to get a shield and an armor mod and equip them on your ship as soon as possible, and go from there.
Actually.. I will finish the review off with a couple of things I thought were a great shame.
You can't really play this game with a controller. The game allows for it, but this being a iOS port, it wasn't designed for it, and even if you are using a controller, everything ingame will be listed with keyboard commands on the HUD. The keyboard/mouse works well enough, so it's not a big deal, but I thought it was weird.
Two expansions were released for the iOS, which supposedly made the game a lot better, and introduced new mechanics (upgrades) and ships to buy along with a new storyline, but that will never make it to the PC.
I could ramble on, but I suppose I've written a lot already.
Overall I really enjoyed the game, and if you can live with a less than stellar experience, I'd recommend you get the game while discounted, and enjoy the ride. There are a ton of achievements you can chase to keep you busy, and if you want the best ships in the game, you'll be playing for many more hours than I did, so in terms of bang for buck, I certainly got mine.

This game has the potential to be great, but only if:
1)- You have the patience to give the developers the time to mould and hone it. The complexity and scope of this kind of games require it. It's simply not possible to "get it right" at the first try. You need the feedback of thousands of players to make things work. The game is far from perfect at the moment, but it would be unfair to start blaming the developers right now. If in a couple o years the game will still have major issues, then we'll have every right to be angry. But at the moment, I'm perfectly satisfied with what I've got. I'm having a lot of fun with it, and I see that the developers are listening to the players feedback, making changes that they believe will improve the gaming experience.
2)- You do not approach every new game with an "I've got to win" attitude, but more likely with "I will do my best in the situation I'll find myself in". Winning may simply not be possible, if you get unlucky with your initial hand. But it doesn't mean that you can't have lots of fun, even in the worst situation. In the end maybe you'll be crushed by some fallen empire, get stuck in some remote arm of the galaxy or simply conquered by a stronger opponent. So what? It's part of the realism of the game. I expected it. I would have been disappointed otherwise.

Party Hard (or "Try Hard to Enjoy the Party")
I looked forward to getting this game. I did. It has a retro-feel to it, techno-beat music, mindless glorious violence, a lot of good things to look forward to. Likely inspired by games such as Postal and Hotline Miami, it had the potential to do well in this dark genre.
That being said, it was quite a bit of a let-down, having considerable problems where there shouldn't have been.
Concept & Story:
The concept is fair enough. It isn't particularly original, but it doesn't have to be. The player controls a psychopath on a murderous rampage, bent on killing everyone at a party. Good enough an excuse to spill gallons of blood. For this genre, it works.
This premise could have been left on its own. It should have been. It wasn't.
The player is forced to endure some of the worst dialogue writing that I've witnessed since high school. Yes, forced. You aren't allowed to skip the cutscenes. Additionally, the voice acting is simply awful. Not even the sort that is so bad it can be celebrated (eg. Castlevania - Symphony of the Night or Resident Evil). It just makes one want to stop playing. The voices and writing are not convincing or entertaining. Even the word, "f*(<" seems half-hearted, as if the writer was just trying to show the world that they can swear... and no other purpose.
This game would have greatly benefited from having *no* dialogue or cutscenes at all.
Concept & Story - 3/10
Gameplay:
Control is fairly simple and straightforward, as it should be. That being said, an ability to remap controls would have been nice.
Your inventory is limited to a single item (outside of your Attack). This works out fine and demands a player's choice of priorities if and when another item shows up.
Each level features traps to lure victims into grisly deaths. While this is a great idea, every level feels like there should have been more. It's as if each stage was started and then forgotten about around 80% of the way through.
The player has the ability to run, limited by a simple endurance bar. Great idea, but the speed gain is marginal and very short. It is exceedingly rare for it to provide any practical benefit and, if anything, becomes frustrating in its deficiency.
The most glaring issue is inconsistency of game mechanics and really, really bad hitboxes. These are the game-killers here. Police can occasionally see the player through multiple walls, even without witnesses to tip them off. Guards can work there way through some small portions of walls while the player cannot. Players can be caught when using Escape Routes, even with police being more than a meter away. Enemies can reach farther in attacks than players. The player can even be arrested by a police carrying off another suspect... without the player being pursued!
(As a side note, when Swat Teams arrive, they take forever to leave, and become a significant hindrance to the game. They seem less of a challenge and more like a game glitch.)
It makes the person playing suspect that the game wasn't tested for more than a few hours before publishing. There is no excuse for this.
Gameplay – 3/10
Graphics:
The game visuals work very well. It's pixely, blocky, and reminiscent of 90's computer games. Many of the level designs stand out from one another. They're unique and offer a good selection of “hunting grounds”. Sometimes they feature traps that are only found in that level.
This is the game's shining point and is where the real creativity of the game is shown. Animations are appropriate to the genre and the style works well. Lovers of pixel art and retrogaming will not be disappointed.
It would have been nice to have a bit of variety in how the Protagonist kills his victims as well as more unique traps.
Graphics - 8/10
Sound & Music:
The sounds of this game are simple, but work. Nothing remarkable, but nothing to complain about either.
The music tracks fit in quite nicely. The two bones of contention is that they are very limited in number and that, in several cases, the music cannot change to another track. When dealing with the afore-mentioned gameplay issues and repeating stages, this becomes a real pain.
While the, perhaps as many as five, tracks are well composed and executed (no pun intended), it's the same five... or one track, over and over and over again. After a couple of retries, you may find yourself turning the speakers off.
Sound & Music - 6/10
Enjoyability & Replay Value:
The ghastly failings in gameplay really did this in. It's difficult to enjoy a game that just pisses you off. It's worse when you know that it's game problems and not just a matter of meeting up to the game's challenges. The thing is broken and should have been fixed before release.
Replay...the game offers some post-game content, which is nice, however, the rest of the experience makes one not want to play it. It's not good when “more levels” feels like an unpleasant chore instead of a welcome encore.
If anything, the replayability is really from user-created levels. These have been more fun to play than the developer's levels, despite not having the same visual creativity.
Enjoyability & Replay Value – 4/10
Final Thoughts:
I wanted to like this game. I really did. On the surface, it offered many good things that shouldn't have been hard to provide. But... those awful cutscenes and the faulty game mechanics were just too much. After finishing, I didn't feel accomplished, just sore for having paid for this and annoyed. This wasn't, “Yay, I beat it! Rock on!”, it was, “... it's finally over. Finally.” sigh
I can see the reason to play this, I can see why others would like it. It's a fine enough idea and it has the right look for what it is, but I simply cannot recommend this game.
Overall - 4/10

Reign of Bullets is a side-scrolling shoot ‘em up where you blown up everything you meet, collect drops and scrap and use them to either upgrade your ship or add new weapons to it; it has a simple yet effective gameplay that's especially fun in short bursts backed up by quite interesting loot and customization systems.
-nice cartoonish graphics
-frantic gameplay with many enemies and bullets flying around the screen
-tons of loot to gather with different rarity levels amongst the various weapon classes
-great weapon customization
-quirky sense of humour adds to the game's charm
-several difficulty levels to choose from let you make the game as easy or as harsh as you want it to be
-basically no story, both hero and villains are paper-thin and forgettable
-sounds are simple and tend to get a bit droning
-can get a bit repetitive in the long run
-requires some grinding to properly upgrade for certain harder areas/ bosses
If you strip Reign of Bullets of its loot and upgrade systems you'd be left with a fairly standard and somewhat dull shoot ‘em up: thankfully said systems truly help the game stand out and deliver an engaging, somewhat addictive gameplay experience.
The loot is Borderland-esque, you get many drops belonging to different weapon classes and ranked by rarity; each weapon will have slightly different features such as number of bullets fired, range, piercing potential etc and these can be further altered by modding it. Each mod drop will also have a rarity level with rarer mods having stronger effects and costing more to apply thus driving you to clear a few more levels to see what you'll get and/ or gather enough scrap to mod your favourite weapon. Last but not least you can decide exactly where to place each weapon and at what angle to point it, want some weapons firing directly upwards or downwards? Just rotate them and you're set: in fact certain enemies or bosses might be easier if faced with an unconventional setup.
Reign of Bullets has enough original concepts to make up for its lack of story or straightforward gameplay, it might not hold your interest for as long as titles with more depth but it is a good game nonetheless and a great way to spend a few hours shooting stuff up.

Reign of Bullets is a fun addition to the SHMUP-genre. Despite the name, this isn't one of those Japanese "1 hit 1 death" bullet hell games, and that is a good thing. Although the amount of bullets flying at you at certain times is pretty high, the game still provides you survivability with upgradable health meter and shield.
The challenge is good on lower levels, but if you want to test your skills to the max, you can always up the difficulty level (which this has about 10 to choose from). This also increases your chance for better loot. The loot consists of different weapons, weapon upgrades and scrap, which you use to upgrade your ship and weapons. The loot system is nicely done and I felt like most of the weapons have their purpose.
The story isn't a story at all, but you don't really need it, since this game clearly focuses more on level and grinding type of gameplay (clear the levels as well as you can -> better rank). Also the music is really bad and bland. I was hoping for a more pumping and epic soundtrack for this, but you might aswell just mute the music and play your own.
All in all it's a nice SHMUP "snack", but not worthy of a "dinner" -status. Still, in my opinion everything was done right in this type of game except for the music and level variation.

Side-effects of playing Magicite are undocumented in the wake of the recent planetary invasion, please disregard any and all negative symptoms in favor of overthrowing your new rulers.
