I have had my long share of time on this game, played for a team, and still play it. I no longer reccomend it, for the reasons below~
Positives-:
A great F2P model with only characters needed to buy, which you can earn very quickly (Which I have learnt over my 3 accounts)
Very unique character design, with a few cliques here and there, other than that it is very unique for how much Overwatch fans give it grief for how it looks. Even if, yes, someone like Fernando looks similar to Reinhardt or Evie // Inara looks similar to Mei, it is completely different with unique kits and cards, something I will come onto next.
There are cards in this game. Ones which you buy once per game to counter enemy Champions, removing any need to change Champion, although you cannot change the champions in the middle of a match, anyway. These consist of doing more damage to shields, slowing down healing on enemy targets, getting more healing from your teammates, running faster and much more. You earn credits to purchase these in game by capturing points, killing others, tanking damage etc.
And, then there are card decks, and card legendaries. You can choose your deck at the start of the match and every character comes with one basic legendary and one basic deck, which isn't usually very good, so a player always has this artificial advantage. I will get onto the negatives of this in the next section. The Legendary cards can completely changing your characters kit and playstyle. This makes the game more fun and makes the game feel like it has more characters, artificially.
The game has a few maps, with mostly good flow and balance, especially how the maps are mirrored.
The game recently added a new pre-game UI, which tells you if you have a lack of a certain Champion subclass. To add to that; most characters are sorted into subclases. Some don't fit, as e.g. A flank in the game, named Zhin, has a lack of movement in his kit, especially vertical movement, so he could most likely be classed as a damage, but for instance, a damage named Willo, could be placed in the Flank subclass for her movement ability and ultimate.
Negatives-:
The games F2P model is hindering for the first few levels of the game no matter how easy it is to earn the champions. Most of the base characters are quite weak, and can lack. When someone has paid money on the game, they will have mostly, the upper hand when it comes to character selection and what you want to play.
The card system, the card DECK system to be more specific, is quite unbalanced. You can pay for chests, and then use those chests to get a currency called 'Essence' The game does not start you off with enough essence when it comes down to you only have enough to make a good deck for around 2 characters. When a character can afford enough for a good deck for almost all of the characters, -Keep in mind the chests that give you essence also give you cards and basic customisations which don't really effect your character unless you pay more of the in game paid currency, crystals-
The games competitive gamemode is difficult to unlock **Speaking of ranked 1.0 of the time of this review** And is a very player lacking system. You are more lucky to find players under a rock. The system is also broken on how it works, but most of this will most likely be fixed in the 2.0 patch coming later this week. With this lack of players the matchups are usually unfair, especially for new players or players who lack skill. The communication system is also dodgey.
The game also houses many, many toxic players. You are very likely a prime target to be flamed if you are new to a game and only own a basic deck for your favourite character because you have not spend money on this free game and cannot afford a loadout for this character.
There is a quest system with this game, which you only unlock at level 7. These 4 quests refresh weekly and reward essence or gold. Level 7 is a drag, I personally think you should earn them at level 5, after the bot games have finished.
To add onto that, the bot games are there for players to learn new things about the game, but that isn't very helpful when the bots have aim better than most players and can detect stealth and other things.
The daily login system has improved, but still needs a few changes, you get incresed gold throughout the week and then you get essence then a few crystals on the 7th day. I feel you should earn more from these.
Now, the main reason I do not recommend this game, is its rapidly declining playerbase, and toxic community, as mentioned earlier. This game has a lot of potential, but needs to be found by fixing the games many bugs, balancing the Champions to their best extent, and making this game fair for all skill levels.
This is Paladins, the game which is an Overwatch ripoff, so to speak.
Thank you for reading and I appreciate all feedback.

It is based on the classic and bombproof ELITE fight & trade & mine & explore & upgrade & save-the-galaxy formula and shares all the good and bad sides of the late followers like Freelancer or Darkstar One. It has pretty visuals and fast engine. In the case of space sims it comes from the technical realisation, there are less polygons to move than in most of other genres so game designers can use the extra processing power on speed and lights that look really good here. Considering that originally it is a mobile game (first I saw it there, it is pectacular on mobos) the HD graphics in the PC version that I played is quite decent too. The overall atmosphere is really nice and space-y LIKE IT SHOULD, you get into the feel in seconds. The ship flies and shoots well, the mouse drive function gives me no desire for attaching my game controller. It is a nice working space fighting engine.
Where it lacks is where its buddies Freelancer and Darkstar One do: the content that fills the big space with life. The side missions become repetitive after a while as if there was a big book of space sims with patterns to follow, e.g. you get the missions in the bar the same way as in many space sime games before and the skeleton of the missions share that, too. The beautiful big star system feels to be empty after a while and the main story is rather predictable with no real depth. If you fly by the storyline you can finish the game rather soon.
Apart from that, it is an enjoyable space shooter and developers did everything to enhance the experience and reduce unnecessary time burn. The time speedup function is one of the friendliest around and it has the best planetary nav computer programming I've seen so far in any space sim. Due to its mobile origin, flying commands are simplified to the bone and they work pretty fine. Minigames (like asteroid mining) are fun and dialogs have a good sense of humour. Also, the game contains one of the best supporting game character names I've ever seen: Mkkt Bkkt the intergalactic drug dealer whose one single trade can render the whole crew of a space station useless. The name alone sells. All in all it is a fun game that is quite entertaining during the main mission but it doesn't start a revolution. Maybe a space trade sim doesn't need a deep story line like Mass Effect, who knows. As a gamer, I'd just happily see a space sim that changes the almost 30 years old Elite formula more boldly.

This game has the potential to be great, but only if:
1)- You have the patience to give the developers the time to mould and hone it. The complexity and scope of this kind of games require it. It's simply not possible to "get it right" at the first try. You need the feedback of thousands of players to make things work. The game is far from perfect at the moment, but it would be unfair to start blaming the developers right now. If in a couple o years the game will still have major issues, then we'll have every right to be angry. But at the moment, I'm perfectly satisfied with what I've got. I'm having a lot of fun with it, and I see that the developers are listening to the players feedback, making changes that they believe will improve the gaming experience.
2)- You do not approach every new game with an "I've got to win" attitude, but more likely with "I will do my best in the situation I'll find myself in". Winning may simply not be possible, if you get unlucky with your initial hand. But it doesn't mean that you can't have lots of fun, even in the worst situation. In the end maybe you'll be crushed by some fallen empire, get stuck in some remote arm of the galaxy or simply conquered by a stronger opponent. So what? It's part of the realism of the game. I expected it. I would have been disappointed otherwise.
---------UPDATE--------
After playing a campaign with 1.6 patch, I still feel we're not there yet. I love playing diplomatically in my strategic games, and I still feel there's not much to do on that front in stellaris. Diplomacy still feels rather hollow and simply not a viable way to successfully play a campaign. Hope that will change in future patches. Loved the mega-structures, though.

Gameplay wise there are a few new features like O2 kits since you're on the moon, less gravity, new vehicles, laser guns, but at its core it feels very much like Borderlands 2; the way quests play out, enemies being reskins or analogues to enemies from previous titles, and the cel shaded look which is just hiding some gnarly texture issues. This game feels like what Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon was, and yet it was not; it was released as a full price game when it feels more like an expansion in Blood Dragon's vein; A standalone game in and of itself that was fun but didn't really need to be done. If you're looking to grab this i'd wait for a sale as usual, grab it with the season pass for $20 and it makes that $20 worthwhile. If you're looking for innovation this really isn't the title, it's more for the Borderlands fan who is already familiar with the previous games and just wants a little bit more.

Despite this, Hungary, which at this point was the most powerful nation in the world,( the HRE being second despite endless attacks by also Milan, Venice, France,Denmark and the Moors, which also all lasted 50 -100+ turns without any peace seen except with the Moors) continued to attack ME, even though it was clear that I could always barely irk by despite my desire for peace and my many attempts to SEE peace through acts of goodwill by releasing their endlesss armies of men only for them to attack me once anew.
That being said, when I chose Very Hard Combat mode, I expected a challenge, not in that the enemy forces would just have superior forces and troops, but that the enemy generals, atleast when it happened to be a unique character with good command, would be at all competent in their decision making, and not that they would just let my cavalry always destroy their artillery and missile infantry as they were never in a position to defend them.
Having played CK2 for 100s of hours, I can say that the diplomacy system and the general decision-making of other nations is not only extensively dumbed down(which is not that big of a deal since Total War is mostly centralized around battles) but also completely unreasonable. I did not ask for every major nation around me to declare war on me, I asked for a diplomacy system that would present an intriguing challenge, like in CK2.
I still give it a 9/10, minus the serious AI and diplomacy issues it is still one of the most entertaining games I've ever played.

This is one of the more entertaining spaceship action games of its era. It's not groundbreaking, and it's not the caliber of Wing Commander, but the tone is always fun and the quality is consistent throughout.
The space sim aspects are a little weak in places. All systems draw from the same power source, and they're balanced in a way that makes most ships slow and vulnerable if you try to keep all systems partially powered. Most zones feels like large enclosed rooms rather than small sections of open space. Missions can be fairly long, and it can be difficult to locate or stay on top of victory conditions. Large enemy capital ships are easy to dodge and very slow to kill. But despite the limitations, the universe feels large and diverse, with colorful characters established purely through voice communications to your ship.
Speaking of voice, Bruce Campbell. Your character is the usual roguish Han Solo type. There aren't very many outright funny one-liners in the script. And that doesn't hurt Campbell's performance in the slightest. He brings all his talent to the role, throws in plenty of asides, and is a large part of the appeal of flying long distances to advance the game.
There are two competing factions to join near the beginning, offering opposing missions and storylines. It's essentially two long games in one package. Each faction has its own distinct lineup of ships and equipment. The corporate side is easier to use but both are quite playable. Each ship has its own unique balance. Not all are worth using. There are lots of upgrades to purchase for your ships, some offering tradeoffs rather than straight improvements. You can hire useful wingmen as well, though there isn't much interaction with them.

This is an interim review which will give my initial impressions.  I hope it will help with those making a decision to purchase.
In Antisquad, you will be in-charge of a group of mercenaries who basically fight for good.  You will start with about 5 or 6 and you can add another 3-4 to the team via purchase.  The game is turn-based and attacks always hit, there is no random chance to hitting something with an attack.  It is your attacks, skills, and special attacks versus the enemies.   In that regard it plays a bit like chess or Stratego or a board game without random chance.  The most important thing is to choose you moves and actions carefully, in the right order, and to consider what the consequences are before hand.
Gameplay itself is sort of a mix of chess and XCOM EU.  The setting is much like Jagged Alliance 2 or similar tactical strategy games.  There is banter between the characters.  Each character has unique skills and attacks, but are mostly of one class.  Classes include a scout, assault, demolitions, so on.  But each character within a class has some different special abilities.  Characters not only can upgrade their attacks and skill, but attributes,  personal weapon and outfit (armor) (which is  only useable by that character), and additional items that are useable by anyone such as medkits, stims, grenades, and armor power ups.
The game advances through missions.  Each mission is part of a series of missions that make up a chapter, I suppose.  I'll have to check on their lingo a bit later.  I believe only some of the chapters are advancing the story, others may be selected as you wish.  To her experience and gold to purchase things, you can replay these missions over and over, at any difficulty you choose, once it is available.  Or just proceed to the next mission as you wish.
The game was first made for tablets, is very colorful, the AI is good, the game is entertaining and makes you think.  But you finish each individual mission in a chapter at easy or normal difficulty, in about 15 mins to an hour.  However this is early in the game in the first three chapters at easy and normal.  It gets more involved later.  The point is that you don't have to plan a whole evening around playing it.
The game on the pc is user friendly.  While on the Title screen tips will come up, you can click on these pop-up boxes daily and receive some gold, a nice touch.  You can equip items in your personal backpack of each character depending on the outfits pockets, you can even have them airdrop some items from the store during a mission but for extra cost.  There does seem to be a character with a personal item that if purchased reduces these airdrop costs also.  Fantastic!
The key concepts to remember for newer players are:
1) All attacks and skills hit.  2) If you kill it during the action, the enemy cannot counter-attack  3)Read the help and learn from the tutorials and tips.  It is all accessible in-game as you play.  3) There is an icon that explains if someone can counter-attack or not.  See the help etc   4) The mission will have drops that can benefit you, both placed and as enemies die.  5) Learning when a unit can counter-attack or not is important in the game.  You need to have enough enery, enough range, a trait, or a power-up or other bonus that overrides the lack of stamina or action points.
The game is well polished, looks great, runs on an Intel HD 2500 gpu smoothly.  It runs on Win7-64 bit no issues.  I recommend the game as long as you don't see it as a fully fleshed out Fallout, XCOM, or Jagged Alliance type game.  It is more like Chess meets XCOM-EU missions.   It's like Stratego or a bit like Sid Meier's Ace Patrol, it's not a simulation or full RPG like Arma or Jane's Fighters would be in comparison to those.
I think that will do for now as a review.

So if your starting out and either getting shot down, or are just barely making it through, don't fret, your guys will get stronger pretty quickly if you spend your money right.
Also I was only compairing Antisquad to Wasteland and Xcom as they are all turn based strategy games, but really the simularies all end there. I could pick it all apart and say where Antisquad excells and where it fell short, but that would serve no real purpose. If your reading this, your wondering if this game is right for you. A few simple questions will answer that for you.
1) Do you enjoy turn based strategy games? (If yes, then this is a good match for you)
2) Do you prefer your games to have a sense of humor to them or do you prefer them to be more serious? (If you like a bit of humor then this game is a good match for you.)
3) Do you want your games to have good soild graphics, or do you think the graphics don't matter as much in a strategy title? (If you like graphics and want your games to "look good" then this game is a good match for you.)

The arguement of whether or not videogames are art or not is a popular topic in today's society, I believe there are a lot of distractions from an original experience and well sold formulas only make it tougher for original ideas to come to fruition.
Some of my best game experiences have been no name creators with a vision of something new, these are the people who deserve your money more than anyone, people who are willing to take risks, and believe me, the payoff is incredible.

Music/sound:
Nothing caught my attention, but everything was constant throughout.
Storyline:
Not applicable to this game. Just advance through all 6 levels!
End Impression:
I loved this game so much that I played and completed it in 3 hours. I also loved it to the point where I had to complete each level perfectly, no mistakes allowed.
Parting Words:
If you love minesweeper, get this game. The complete pack (3 games in one) is on sale for $2.69 until June 22, and in my opinion very much worth. (I got gifted the $0.89 one)

When I want to unequip a weapon, I either sell it off, or click the "(un)equip" button and wave my mouse around the screen clicking for a few seconds, before it returns me to the menu and the item isn't equipped any more. Still haven't figured out what I do to make that happen.  Weapons have upgrade slots, you can rotate them any direction, and are in a list of easy-grab menu boxes. But there's no drag and drop. Some cynical people like to describe modern roleplaying video games, particularly those in the mmorpg style, as systems that exist solely to entrap its players into a skinner box of increasing stats and digits. Where context and story are set aside as its players become more and more efficent in the pursuit of ever higher numbers. I'm not here to prove or disprove that arguement. But something that is true is that a part of being a human is a feeling of satisfaction when our efforts cause numbers to increase. All sorts of games across all sorts of genres are essentially efficency machine skinner boxes, addicting players through the well documented process of operant conditioning, enthralling through the joy of watching digits tick upward incrimentally.
Some games provide story or gameplay context for their systems of increasing numbers, some don't. Clicker games wear this fact on their sleeve, games that admit to being about watching numbers go up with none of the "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" so to say.
If you were to boil down your typical clicker game into their most core elements...you wouldnt get adventure capitalist, you would get a game where you click the space bar and a number goes up by one.
But if you were take your typical exploitative clicker game and add a cup of humane design, and a tongue in cheek sense of humor, you would get Adventure Capitalist.
Adventure Capitalist has perhaps the most basic theme you can think of, making money. you buy buisnesses and upgrades for those buisnesses in order to have them generate the most money possible, which allow to you buy more buisnesses, so on and so on. Making more money means attracting more investors, angel investors that is, heavenly buisness partners who give you a 2% efficency each when you sell your buisness and start from square one. The time between restarts is typically a half hour to an hour of actual gametime, but really equates to once or twice a day if you stay vigilent. In a great design decision, you dont have to be there clicking on your buisnesses the whole time, hell you don't even need the game open, as you can buy managers who click them for you, even when the game is off.
That fact alone elevates this game above your typical clicker. You generate profits with the game off, and can accomplish in only a half hour of actual playtime what would take several hours of having the game open in a typical clicker game like cookie clicker.
Is this game fun? I have to answer with a resounding yes. It is pleasing and enthralling to watch the dollars tick up with greater and greater speed, it is always a great feeling to restart and watch your money generation spike with the influx of new investors. It  is a great moment when you find yourself at the point you last restarted at in only fifteen minutes instead of the hour it took you last time. You will find yourself loading up the game a couple of times a day to eagerly check up on your buisness.
So it seems that a game that exploits our inbuilt desire for efficency and progress is fun to play...who would have guessed?

A casual and light weight space-conflict/exploration that can't hide its roots as a Android/iOS game
Rating 5/10
The first thing you'll notice about Galaxy on Fire 2 is that as a game developed for tablets and phones it's very easy to pick up and is far less bloated and complex than other recent games in this genre such as the X series.
The game is broken down into a main plot that runs alongside freelance missions, open ended trading and mining. The first thing you'll notice is how easy it is to control and play, even with a mouse and keyboard it's easy to pick up and master in a matter of minutes.
Combat of which there is a lot is rather predictable and shallow, pirates will appear at most hubs and you'll soon find them a minor annoyance rather than a serious challenge. You can be helped by station defence fighters and by hiring wingmen to protect you although even on the hardest difficulty they are rarely needed. You are able to outfit your ship with up to four primary weapons depending on how advanced your ship is and four secondary weapons. Primary weapons constitute a selection of different laser based weapons whilst secondary are rockets and bombs.
In order to afford these upgrades you'll need to make money and you can make money quickly, easily and in a number of different ways. Completing missions is the fastest way to make money and these can be picked up from various talking heads in the bars of each space station. However they soon become repetitive and lack depth, you'll be offered a variation of defence missions, clean up missions, escort missions, retrieval and transport missions. The only thing that differs between the missions on offer is the location.
The next best way to make money is to trade goods between stations or mine for materials from asteroids from asteroid fields outside each space station. Mining is a mini game of keeping your cursor within a circle whilst it moves erratically as the circle becomes smaller. Once you've mined enough ore you can sell this on for a minor profit. Trading is a simplistic affair as you buy and sell a wide range of goods from station to station.
The worst part of the game however is the awful dialogue and amateurish voice acting, another of those occasions where just text instead of bad voice acting would have improved the game. If you can't afford good voice actors it's sometimes best not to have any. The protagonist is Keith T. Maxwell, yes you read that correctly, they named the main character Keith. The name Family Guy mocked as being the "most unattractive male first name in the English Language". Not to be outdone by such a terrible character name they follow that up with characters called 'Mkkt Bkkt' and 'Erkkt Uggut'. The plot itself isn't too bad if not clichéd. It centres on a mysterious race called the Voids who are striking at outposts across the Galaxy from wormholes and it's up to Keith to save the day. However the terrible dialogue and voice acting makes you want to avoid it or rush through it and to play the game as an open sandbox world instead.
Even with all these criticisms I would however just about recommended the game. It is extremely easy to pick up and looks pretty in places. It also doesn't require a big time investment or more than a few minutes to learn the game mechanics. A lot of people have described it as a poor man's Freelancer which it is but it still enjoyable enough for fans of space-conflict games and there isn't a great choice out there at the moment. Obviously this will change with the upcoming Elite Dangerous and Star Citizen.

An occasionally funny game with a decent concept but terrible execution.
Do you enjoy spamming the same exact spell over and over again?  Then this game is for you.  So many spells you can cast, so little reason to ever cast more than 3-5.  Combat often becomes frantic with many enemies coming at you, so you don't have the time to remember and input some of the larger combination spells.  Why bother anyway?  In the time it takes to cast the FQFFQFFQ spell which does 300-500 damage to enemies in front of me, I could spam SDF and launch it out 5-6 times and do 1000+ damage to the enemies in front of me.  Here is combat in a nutshell.  Spam one spell over and over, heal if hurt, put fire out if on fire, occasionally melee attack enemy that won't get away from you.  Rinse & repeat every level.  Gets old and boring quickly.  Occasionally the game changes it up by putting armored enemies out there that SDF won't hurt, so you spam SD or S until their armor breaks and switch back to SDF.  Brilliant!
Navigation is annoying as well.  Instead of being able to click somewhere and walk there, you have to hold down the left mouse button to move around.  Let it go and your character stops moving.  This is especially cumbersome when looking around for items to interact with.  The game will not highlight objects with the cursor if you're currently moving around.  So you have to stop moving, swing your cursor around to see if anything is interactable, move a little further up, stop and swing your cursor around to see if anything is interactable, and repeat ad nauseam.  This game would benefit tremendously by having a point & click to walk to that point without having to hold in the mouse button.
Not much else to say.  Might be decent with other people, but solo play is mind-numbingly terrible.  Don't do it.

I bought this game for 1$ and was quite amazed about how interesting it was. Basically, you play Isaac and have to defeat ennemies and bosses in various rooms. You kill ennemies by shooting them with your tears or by "bombing" them.
This game is a "rogue-like" : you go through doors, not knowing what you'll get, and have to find the bosses in the various different floors, along with the "item-rooms" that level-up your tears or give you new abilities.
The whole game is RNG, every floor is always randomly generated and this is the main point of the game : no playthrough will be identical, ever, and that's what offers a great replay value.
Another important thing : permadeath. If you die in this game, you have to start back at the beginning  (with another layout of course, since everything is RNG), and trust me, you'll die often. But each time you die, you learn from your mistakes and make better the next time. At the beginning, you'll be happy if you reach level 5, but at the end, reaching level 8 is quite normal. (Note : if you unlock new item, death doesn't affect that)
[Pros] :
+ RNG all around the place = infinite replay value
+ 2 minutes to get the point of the game and the controlls, 200 hours to fully master it
+ A ton of items and stuff, you will learn something new at each playthrough and get better and better
+ Items have synergies and can be "combined" for powerful results
+ Awesome price for awesome game (under 1$ in sale)
+ Will train your reflexes, strategy and learning abilities
+ Cool graphic style
+ You can make it work smoothly even on a potato computer
+ Simple controls : WASD to move, Arrows to Shoot, E to Bomb, Space to Use Item, Q to use Pill/Card ; that's all.
+ A ton of "secrets" to master to get better
+ "Humoristic" items with Internet Memes References (Lemon, Hoop de Loop, Forever Alone, Super Meat Boy...)
[Cons] :
- Hard at the beginning, can be very frustrating if you don't like the "learn by mistakes" approach (=/= die and retry)
- The game engine can lag sometimes, the game isn't fully oprimized
- Don't hope beating the "last" boss with under 60 hours of /played (but the game is fun even if you never finish it)
- RNG land, sometimes, you'll get f*** up hard by bad RNG
[Conslusion] : Anyone that is ok with games that involve reflexes should try this, at least if it's in sale for less than 1 buck. 10/10

is an addictive twin-stick shooter that rejuvenated the roguelike genre and gifts players with a memorable gaming experience, though it is thoroughly hampered by technical flaws, creative limitations and the existence of a wholly-superior successor.
In
, you play as the titular character, a five-year-old boy, fleeing from his homicidal mother throughout the realms that exist beneath his basement. Isaac uses his tears as bullets to fire at enemies. He's aided by items, trinkets, pills and cards that he finds along the way, which further disfigure him until he is almost unrecognizable by the end of the game. The full game can be beat on average in under an hour - this is the staple element of the "roguelike" genre, which developer Edmund McMillen implemented in
, effectively resurrecting the genre among the indie game market. Roguelikes are exceptionally short, but are also permadeath, meaning that a character's death is absolute. Finally, each playthrough of the game is randomly generated, with no two playthroughs featuring the same items, bosses and floor layouts. This all effectively means that
is infinitely replayable, for there is always the motivation of finding undiscovered, superpowerful item combinations to keep players coming back.
The unique thematic styles that the game contains provides an experience that can be quite subjective and polarizing, though those coming in with open minds find that they enjoy
's charm over time. The game has significant connection to the Christian faith: the title of the game, the names of the characters (minus one) and many items contain references to the contents of the Bible. Though these references are not explicitly sacriligious, considering the context of the game (surrounded by a naked crying child and rooms full of poop) and its lore (with divine intervention driving Isaac's mother to hunt him down), those who are deeply devout may be turned off by the game's subject matter. The music is somber and melancholic, underscoring Isaac's desperation throughout his journey. Overarching visual presentation possesses an air of artistry, due to the models of characters and enemies being hand-drawn by developer Edmund McMillen, then being directly transplanted into the game. The wide variety of sizes and styles for enemies and item effects allows players to internalize what certain things do, which in turn paves the way for strategic deveopment and improved play upon practice.
The issues that this game faces are great in number, and cannot be solely attributed to the game's genre. Technologically, the game has faults that could even lead it to being described as "broken". The limitations of the Flash medium the game was designed on is often attributed as the cause of framerate issues, as well as cases of the game freezing while loading certain levels, the latter of which has become so well-known in the community that it even has its own name ("the Pink Glitch"). The in-game stat screen on the pause menu is known to misrepresent the actual stats of the player, and either way is too vague to be useful. Some item descriptions outright lie to the player, and at least one item and one trinket are known to either do nothing or solely harm the player. There are some interactions that allow the player to fall to negative health. Though these facets harm most players, there is an interesting metagame that exists in the
community that calls for exploitation of known bugs and synergies to literally "break the game", by getting every item available or forcing the game to crash while trying to get there. What is arguably more dissappointing than these technical issues are the ample lack of synergies. Though some basic tear modifiers can stack on in large numbers to create crazy effects, the strongest items in the game that change your attack from tears to another format largely cancel each other out upon pickup, with invisible stat changes the only possible outcome. The game punted its opporunity to become great by neglecting to implement synergies to so many combinations.
Despite the aforementioned issues,
was still the standard-bearer for the roguelike genre and was a phenominally popular game. However, it has been dethroned by its own reimagining:
. This recent successor was developed by a new development team and has addressed the numerous technical and synergistic issues noted above. Though the game is not perfect, it is far superior to the original
on virtually all levels. Therefore, in consideration of buyers' finances, if you're new to the franchise then get
. However, on its own, this is still a brilliantly-conceived title with engaging gameplay and an indefinite lifespan. Considering the price for the original is often so low on the Internet, it may still even be worth purchase now.

This is a turn based action game in which you control a team through various missions achieving various goals.
The graphics are very nice and the music (mission impossible-like-ish) and sound effects are great too.
The controls are simple and easy to understand.
The game-play is turn based action with each character having Action Points available they can use for movement or special skill and attacks.
The game uses the term contracts which contains several missions. Each contract is a story which progresses through each mission.
Before each mission you can select your 3 team members you want to take along. You have originally a choice of 5, each with unique weapon skills and special skills. During the course of the game you can hire additional members as well.
Each member has 1 unique special skill + item slots you can pre-populate before each mission.
Each Mission can be played in one of several difficulties: Easy, Normal, Hard and Hell. Each raised difficulty level gives bigger rewards along with the raised risk or death.
During a mission you navigate your team through a map using your characters action points wisely. Inspecting your enemies and their stats, skills, visibility and shooting range can help and give you an advantage when planning where you are moving your team member to and how many Action Points to leave for special or counter attacks.
After you kill an enemy you can click the dead body to reveal item drops, which can be anything from extra cash to item boxes you can open between each mission or temporary attribute perks that can be applied immediately to a team member when walking over them.
The game has tons of STEAM achievements as well as in-game challenges, such as "Use 4 Special Skills in a single Mission" or similar.
I personally find this game very entertaining and would certainly recommend it.
The price definitely is more than fair for this title.
The scripted dialogue from the characters during each mission that progress the story reads nicely and make the game feel more like a story you play through rather than just mindlessly playing each mission.
The characters have entertaining personalities and each have a unique feel when played.
Great value for money for sure.

Fantastic little game. If you like tetris then you will most certainly like this game. It isn't quite the same, the blocks don't fall out of the sky, and most of the shapes are not tetrominos.
This is a very fun and addictive little game. I wholeheartedly recommend it. The only major con is that there isn't even -more- of it! However, as you see with my play time so far you will likely get many hours of enjoyment.
Plus of course I must mention that there is a Portal board.
The idea is to place each shape on the board and fit them in like a tetris game. Your goal is to "colour in" the entire play area (defined by the white borders). As you create squares of blocks that are 3x3 or larger, they form an area that begins to time out. You can either add more blocks to increase the size of this area, or let it time out to clear some more space on the board.
Yes, there are only six boards, and each has a specific song (no customization of the music) but each board has as many levels as you can keep going for. It's a fair challenge just to get past the first level of any given board, which is done by "colouring in" every square on the board before the time runs out. Your goal is really self-inflicted to get as big a score as you can.
There are also achievements to this game, and some get you to explore a different way of playing. For a less stressful play there is also a timeless mode. Each board has a different set of shapes that you must get used to and learn how to most efficiently place.
Entirely mouse driven. The shape is essentially attached to your mouse pointer. It will move when you move your mouse. You then click to place the shape where you've positioned it.
No storyline, doesn't need one!
There are six different songs, one for each board. They are a bit techno for my liking and I found a couple of them to be extremely irritating - to the point that I would call them noise, not music. However there is an epic board which I can play almost endlessly for the sheer joy of listening to GLADOS singing.
Regardless of my opinion of the actual songs, I found it very interesting how the music builds up in reaction to your level progress. If you're doing well then you get more music (different layers of sounds) and if you aren't doing so well, or its the start of the level, the music is more subdued.
Nothing spectacular. I would say the graphics are functional. They support the user's understanding of the game and how to play. The colour schemes are pleasant. This isn't a section that I'd say is bad, the graphics just aren't remarkable, and nor do they need to be.

Outcast 1.1 is a great game. I'm enjoying the hell out of it, with a few exceptions. If you follow the advice above you will limit the only real issue I have with this title. There are many hours I've lost between my own negligence as well as where the game decided to shaft me. Below are a few examples of what I'm talking about.
1) When I 1st started the game. I played for about an hour, never bothering to save. I accidentally aggro'd a group of enemies that overwhelmed me & forced me to start from the beginning. (I thought I had learned my lesson)
2) After many hours of play without issue. I got complacent. I went 3 hours & made a ton of progress. I had finally reached Okaar & did a fair amount of wandering. It finally dawned on me that I had not saved in a while. I quickly saved & continued exploring. Shortly after making that crucial decision, I died. You may think I dodged that bullet, but you'd be wrong. You see I made 3 mistakes here. 1st I neglected saving earlier to another file slot. 2nd I had about 50% health. 3rd when I did save, I was standing in what I thought was a safe spot in a blow dart maze. I thought it was safe because when I stood up to save I wasn't being shot at, after I saved I still wasn't being shot at & I even made my way out of the area before I died. However when I loaded my game I was immediately hit with a dart & killed. This happened every time I tried to reload that game.
3) Every now & then the game randomly closes to desktop.
----------------------------------
With all that said, I recommend Outcast 1.1. Sure it's a bit on the ugly side & there are uncanny valley violations everywhere you look. But due to the age of it's source, this can be forgiven. The gameplay is still rock solid. The BGM & voice acting is pretty damn good. The SFX not so much, but passable. The story is very Stargate-esque, but enjoyable nonetheless. Yet with all it's flaws Outcast 1.1 is scratching all the right itches. I haven't come across a game in a while that could make that same claim.
This is well worth the $5.99. Even more so if you get it on sale.

This Game is a Masterpiece.
The World gets quickly very immersive, the Story is fantastic and the Gameplay makes a hell lot of fun and is rich in variety.
That, for me at least, is a very important point, because many RPG these days lack heavily in said variety. Sometimes so hard that it just gets too boring to even listen to the Story anymore. Or it just gets a real hassle.
But Nier:Automata just does everything right. Everytime you could get to the temptation thinking: "Oh not this again"
the Game just changes the Gameplay ever so slightly. Not so much as it has a total new Gameplay, more that you see the same Gameplay in a new perspective or in a different way, so that its a lot of fun again.
I know some of you may argue now "So what? Its still the same Gameplay!" but just try the demo first and get a Tease at what I am hinting at. And trust me it gets even better.
And to avoid any misunderstandings, the Gameplay on its own is already really good and really challenging, especially on harder difficulties. In case you get bored just try the hardest difficulty, there you get instantly killed after one hit.
Interestingly the hardest difficulty also changes the way how you play the Game, so that is also a complete new experience you get there. But enough about the Gameplay, the Game has a lot more to shine about than its Gameplay.
I dont want to spoiler you guys so I will try to keep it short from here.
Thats because it is a lot fun just to dive in the game and explore it.
Lets talk about the World first. The Game has an open world there you can roam around, do some Quests, kill enemies, find secrets and so on. What I really liked about it though is that they tried to keep a suitable scope to it. The World is large enough to encourage you to explore it, but not too large so you get bored after a while running around and find nothing to do.
But what really got me is not the World itself from a gameplay aspect, rather more from a narrative aspect.
The Protagonists of the Story are Androids! A lot of the Characters you meet in the game are Androids! These Androids have many human characteristics and also emotions, because they are pretty damn advanced and of course were modelled after humans. But they are ultimatly not humans and that is seen in the World. The Characters in the World dont call themselves Androids and then just completely act like humans. No! They act like Androids! They dont have human problems, they have Android problems. And this fact is integrated in the whole game, not only from a narrative viewpoint but also heavily from a gameplay viewpoint. But I wont go in any Details, just play the game and see it for yourself.
(And no that doesnt mean you need to run to a recharge Station every 10 minutes or something annoying as that.)
Furthermore I would also like to mention the soundtrack of Nier:Automata, its just so good I cant even put it into words.
For the ones around here that like music, you will probably love this game a lot.
The background music never fails to catch the atmosphere of the particular moment you are currently in the game.
It just is fantastic.
Puh, so normally I would now start to ramble about the Story and the Characters, but everything I could tell you would probably be a Spoiler soo.....
Just let me say that the story and the characterization are pretty awesome.
If you want to get to know some of the Main Characters, play the demo. But let me also tell you that the demo only scratches on the Surfaces. Its just a tease like a demo should be.
At last I would like to talk a bit about the prequel of this game: Nier.
Or more precisely how the general connection from Nier to Nier:Automata looks like.
First and foremost, you dont need to have played the prequel to play this game. It explains everything you need to know and if you really want to know more, you can find reports around the game world explaining the most important stuff.
Basicly there will be some moments in the Game, if you have not played the prequel you will probably think "Hey, cool!" and if you have played the prequel you will think
"Hey, thats because of....." or you will just start crying again. :D
But the amount of these moments is pretty low. Nier:Automata is basicly its own game, but it does rewards players who have played Nier.
Thats it from me and like I said at the beginning in my opinion this game is a masterpiece in every aspect and is totally worth the money and time you invest in it.
Edit: Some people are complaining that the Game has poor Performance and is a terrible Port to PC because of that. I have an Intel I5 of the 3rd Generation and an Middle-class Graphic Card that is from 2010 and played the game with 1920*1080 in 1080P. I had no Issues with performance!

Deduction and puzzle game lover, here's a perfect game
for you!
Hexcells is the first one of the series. In Hexcells the game area consists of hexes, each having zero to six neighbours. Hex is either blue or black with a number. Mechanics familiar from Mine Sweeper (MS), the number states how many blue hexes are next to the black hex. Your job is to reveal for all hexes whether they are blue or black.
Unlike in traditional MS, everything can be deduced - guessing is not required at all if you know what you are doing. The controls are similar to MS, with left- and right-clicking determining whether you think the hex is blue or black one. Also, in case of a mistake you don't need to start at the beginning, though if you do more than one mistake, you have to start again if you want a "perfect" score (and ultimately an achievement).
The learning curve is very smooth, the challenge rising gently towards later, larger puzzles. As you get further, new mechanics are introduced, with similarities to nonograms/hanjies: a number will state that a column or a diagonal will have certain number of blue hexes. There are two special cases to this that either say that all blue hexes will be interconnected or that they must have a break in-between. All mechanics naturally introduce new ways to think and deduce through the puzzles.
Music is ambience like "glowing crystals", and when you make right moves there's a distinct "ding!" sound echo that adds fluidly to the ambience.
All the 36 puzzles are well-designed and fairly interesting. This is also its biggest drawback: there is little replay value after beating all the puzzles, a task that takes just a couple of hours. The other drawback is the lack of a save feature (for single puzzles; game obviously remembers if you have beat a puzzle before), so you have to complete each puzzle fully or either leave the game running or start the level again later. If these features are a bottleneck for you, both of them
introduced in
, the third part of the series.
If you're left craving for more,
is the de-facto sequel. You should really play Hexcells first and only then go to Plus though, for the sequel is way more challenging and introduces all the mechanics from early on and even adds one new one.
is a good alternative to both: it has its own puzzles and all the mechanics and features from Hexcells and Hexcells Plus, but the challenge curve starts from easy like Hexcells and goes to difficult like Plus. In that respect it's more stand-alone than Plus sequel.
All three are nevertheless good puzzle games. As for challenge, Hexcells is the easiest one and therefore the natural place to start. Also, it's a fairly cheap investment.

Paladins is mostly comparable to Overwatch (which I haven't played) just without the big price tag. Anyone can download and play this game, but not everyone will be able to enjoy it - at least, not to start with. You only have a limited amount of starting characters to choose from with some new ones coming in weekly rotations. To unlock all of them, you can either use in-game gold to purchase the characters which you specifically like, or purchase the founder's pack to unlock them and all future characters. To put it bluntly, if you want to have the best early-game experience possible, this game is $20, not free. However, the founders pack is worth it as it will save you thousands of in-game gold, as well as providing even more benefits such as extra gold, essence to craft cards etc.
As stated before, Paladins is similar to Overwatch, but it is also similar to Team Fortress 2; in that the gamemodes, weapons and certain characters are closely similar. This does not take away from the game as it is quite individual in its own right. There is a wide variety of character who each have their own unique playstyle. Currently, there are four different classes with a mix of characters to choose from: Front Line (High-Health characters that stay on areas to capture the objective), Support (Healer), Damage (Dealing as much damage as possible), and Flank (getting around eneimes and attack from behind - preferably at low health enemies). Each class, and each character plays slightly different and no two characters are too similar to be repetitive. Some characters can only attack at close-medium range and deal significant damage; others deal fast, rapid damage; others are fast moving, low-damage characters etc. You can play Paladins to suit your own playstyle.
Each character has their own attacks, abilities, ultimates and card sets. Each of these are vastly different from each other and is too much to go into detail here. Simply: A character has a Q and an F skill. As well as a right click, alternate attack and an E for an Ultimate Attack. The Ultimate attack (again, is varied amongst each character) will have different effects; ranging from massive healing, damage, movement or other things. Some characters' ultimates are grately better than other characters'.
The community is a great mix, like most online multiplayer games. You will be spending most of your time playing casual (in the early-game, anyways), and you will meet a great variety of people. This can range from the amazing, know-what-they're-doing players who will play their specific roles, to salty, yell-at-you-through-chat people. You can encounter these people almost every casual game.
It would be more than wise to try to get as many friends as possible when playing Paladins, so you don't have to run into any problems.
Paldins is still in its beta, so expect some bugs and glitches whilst playing. These can range from minor inconveniences (like having the enemies' health bar remain stuck on your screen and Kinessa's ultimate skull being also stuck on your screen or Lian not having a reload animation) to match / game-breaking bugs like Buck's constant reload glitch,
Games crashing randomly, Games randomly ending yielding no experience or gold etc. Occasionaly you may play a game and go to the end-screen to find you do not get any gold or experience (this has only happened to me once in a casual game).
Hi-Rez does its best to fix as many glitches and bugs as possible with each patch and it's great that the developers are listening to the community. The problems listed above have happened to me in the past week (besides the Buck reload glitch).
There are currently two forms of in-game currency that are Coins and Crystals. Like most multiplayer games, Crystals are worth much more than Coins and can only be collected through daily play, rewards, referencing friends or purchasing them with real-life money. Coins are easier to come by as you can earn them by playing daily, rewards, referencing friends and after every game based on your performance. Crystals and coins can be used to purchase chests and skins. Skins are simply an aesthetic feature for your characters' and weapons' looks. Skins do not change or alter the performance of your characters or their weapons. Chests will simply reward you with skins; however, purchasing chests is more of a dice-roll. You may ask yourself "Why not just buy the skins." Chests are there for two reasons:
From my experience, I have not unlocked that many skins as I keep getting the same ones (I got the Buck triggerman epic skin 3 times out of around 6 champion skin chests).
Cards are certain alterations to a specific loadout for your character. Each character has their own set of cards for each skill they have. These alterations will affect the game you play and which skill(s) you prefer. These cards are also vastly ranged and are not limited to effects such as: Faster cooldown, higher damage / healing, faster movement or reload speed etc.
Choosing the right cards for the right loadout is essential to making your character better than its base 'stats'. It is recommended that when first trying a character, you play with the basic set to begin with and then branching out into your own custom loadouts that fits your playstyle. Collecting all the cards can take a long time, and can be done through crafting them or purchasing the standard Radiant Chest. Currently, the Radiant Chest is the only chest you can purchase using gold - every other chest must be purchased with crystals as they contain more valuable items.
When creating a loadout, you will choose 5 different cards (which, initially, have one point each) which you can then scale (with a max of 4 points per card) until you get the maximum 12 points. For example; say a level 1 card increases your health by 50 points. By increasing this card to level 2, you will gain an additional 50 health points, totalling to 100. This can go until 200 additional health points which is the max card level of 4. (this does not apply to every character). Of course, this is just one example; other examples include life steal, damage output, health reduction rate, movement speed, damage multiplers etc.
Cards come in four rarities (similar to Hearthstone): Common, Rare, Epic and Legendary. It can be assumed that the higher the rarity, the better the effect. This is not always true as some cards can be an epic (for example) and not be as good (to you) as a Common card. As stated before you can collect cards by opening chests; however, you can also craft them. Crafting is a system of selecting the card(s) you want and making them yourselves, which will save yourself the chance-roll of getting your desired card in a chest (similar to skins). You can use Essence to craft the cards you want and it will scale in the amount of essence required to craft the cards depending on the cards' rarity. Common: 350; Rare: 1,000; Epic: 4,000; Legendary: 10,000.

Well this one was (un)surprisingly awesome!
Let's from the beginning. The game had really good reviews and almost cult following. It also had a really neat idea of the spell combining. And as every game does it wanted to tell a nice little story. Where most games\game companies struggle nowadays is making getting all those components into a nice polished package... Not the case with Magicka though - it manages to pull it's weigh all the way through.
Let me start by mentioning that I played it to arounf halfway with a friend and then did a full solo run from start to finish. So I got a taste of both worlds. To sum the experiences up, I would say that I enjoyed the solo a lot more (I am more of a singleplayer guy with games that have  an exploratory side and an actual story), but I see how this could be a great fun. Be warned though, you really need to partner with person(s) who don't ♥♥♥♥♥ about you making mistakes (cause they finished the game already and know certain combos an mechanics you have no idea even exist), has the same level of taste for level and exploration and don't try to skip every cutscene and then afterwards try to fill you in on the details as you go... and preferebly don't be overly drunk yourself. In my case I did all the wrong decisions here... :/
In any case, this game needs to be experienced: the story is nicely crafted, even thick at some points; chuck full of jokes and references, but they all went straight for my funny bone. I mean not just smirking - full out laughter at some points. The characters are nice with their own personalities and quirks.
The combat\spellcasting might seem a bit daunting at first but as you go, experiment and get more experience and are gradually introduced to Magicks (special uber powered spell combos) you start the feeling of control and pride in what you can achieve at that point. For me as a decent DOTA Invoker player wanabee Magicka really hit the home run with the main game mechanics.
The game is also full of secrets, with secret items, references, rewards for doing good in certain battles, and is really nicely crafted all the way through.
So do I recommend playing this game? Ab-so-lu-te-ly  YES!

NOTE: I am writing this review on a very early version of this game.  It's possible that it may have changed by time you play it.
If I had to describe this game in one word, it would be over-the-top.  Yes, that's one word.  The weapons are crazy, the violence is extremely gorey, and best of all, the game doesn't take itself seriously at all.  I know when most people see "free to play" they immediatly thing "pay to win," meaning you can just pay for the best weapons in the game.  In loadout, the only way to get weapon parts is through playing the game.  Granted, you can buy bonuses that allow you to earn more in game money, but you still have as much access to weapons as someone who hasn't paid a penny.  Which is good.  The main profit from this game is from cosmetic items.  Hats, outfits, taunts, etc.  Not a single one can be bought using the money earned throughout the game.  You're given three different characters, and while you are free to choose between them, you cannot change what they look like without paying.  It's a bit annoying that everyone looks exactly the same, but it's better than having to pay for weapons.
In my opinion, there isn't that many options when it comes to building your weapons.  There's still plenty of options for building your guns, but for a game whose entire focus is about building your loadout (hence the name), I would have expected a few more choices.  It feels like they spent a lot of time on adding extra options for more weapon types rather than others.  For example, there's a rediculous amount of options for making the perfect rocket launcher that suits you, but you can barely customize the beam weapons.
I really, really hate the names for all the game modes.  It would have made things so much simpler if they used the typical names for the game modes, for example "kill confirmed" or " capture the hammer" instead of things such as "extinction."  I don't have a problem with reusing popular game modes, but just call it what it is.  It would make picking a map so much easier.
Other than these minor problems, I did find the game enjoyable, though.  It could use a few more game modes, and maybe a few more customization options, but other than that it's pretty good.

Overall, the game is kind of like a single hot passionate night of love with a beautiful woman, only to wake up in the morning and find out that woman was your mother. It is fun and fufilling when you first play it, but then you wake up a few hours in and realize it is nothing but a pile of shame.
I'd also like to emphasize that, because the addons aren't available on PC, and never will be, the game is incredibly short, with half it's content, and ships, missing as a result.
The developers previously used the excuse "Sales weren't good enough on PC". Of course, with a $20 pricetag ($15 more than the mobile phone counterpart), its a wonder why, on top of the fact that most negative reviews about this game stem from the fact that none of the DLC has been, or ever will be ported to PC.
I hope this helps anyone looking into this game. There are better space games out there. This is essentially a non-multiplayer version of Star Conflict with worse controls.

Tachyon: The Fringe is a nostalgic look into an older era of space and flight sims. If you enjoyed the Descent games, this is right up the same alley. Sure, the graphics haven't aged well - but I found by about an hour into my playthrough that I hardly noticed this any more, as I had become so involved with the actual play of the game.
There are certainly things absent from Tachyon that I would expect to see in modern games of this type - greater customization, some balance tweaks with the weapons, ways to better group and utilise multiple mounted weapons... but this is not a modern game, and despite these deficiencies Tachyon is still absolutely worth a playthrough or two - even in today's market.
I do feel obligated to mention the voice acting, as well - it's a little contrived in places, but I found that the performances and the writing definitely contributed to the sense of joyful abandon that I experienced during my playthrough.
If you're reading this, chances are you're the kind of person who would get enjoyment out of this title, and I say go for it. I doubt you'll be disappointed.

When your one and only objective is to stealthily murder a whole lot of faceless victims, you want different, fun ways to complete it in. You don't always get what you want, though, and such is the case with Party Hard.
Despite the game claiming to offer different and unique ways to off people, you have very few options, none of which requires planning or cleverness of any kind. In fact, most of them are spelled "wait two minutes for a guy to leave a crowd, stab said guy, hope you don't get spotted by another guy who suddenly grew a pair of x-ray vision eyes in the back of his head, and go back to waiting for the next guy to wander off". You can use the environment and set a couple of traps in every level, but they all just require you to activate them with space and then sit on your pixelated ♥♥♥ and wait. Oh no, that disco ball exploded and killed one generic person, oh the humanity. Let's not hope the same happens with the other two disco balls in the room.
Were you unlucky enough to get caught in the act of crime? (And by "caught in the act of crime", I mean that someone saw you standing 20 feet from a body and decided that you and only you and not any of the 5 NPC:s in closer range were the murderer) Well, keep your fingers crossed that the cop with the arbitrary AI coming to arrest you won't get stuck in a table or a wall and spend the rest of his evening doing his running animation there. Because that happens a lot. It might be good for your murdery character on his massacre mission, but don't try to tell me it isn't stupid.
To summarize it: You wait patiently. You stab someone. You activate a trap. You wait some more. You stab someo... nope, another guy entered the room, back to waiting. So you wait some more. You stab someone. You wait. And this goes on and on for the rest of the game. Even if you have the ridiculous amount of patience it takes to sit through every level, the only thing you're rewarded with is some cut scenes with the worst and most cringey voice acting ever heard of. Oh god, I never mentioned the voice acting until now, did I? No, please, my PTSD is kicking in. Make it stop.
You could get Party Hard on a HUGE discount and maybe enjoy a level or two, but you could also get Hitman: Blood Money (R.I.P, last good Hitman game) instead and set a personal objective of clearing every level of every NPC without being spotted. Is that an objective of that game? Absolutely not. Do you get penalized for doing so? Absolutely. And yet, it's still more satisfying, fun and clever than the experience with Party Hard where stealthily killing everyone is the actual freaking goal of the game.
But, uh, the art and soundtrack is really nice. So there's that.

What on the surface seems like an interesting stealth/puzzle murder game quickly becomes a mess. The level design becomes an unfair pile of bull, obsessed with psychotic Bouncers and big crowds.
Rather than a game that has you think like a serial killer, planning, prepping, and laying traps, Party Hard is instead a waiting game. You spend most of your time sitting in a killzone, waiting for somebdy to plod over, hoping that the AI won't see fit to give them 40/40 eyesight.
I mentioned the Bouncers earlier. The Bouncers are possibly the most poorly designed enemy in video game history since the Physics Engine from Sonic 2006. In a perfect universe, seeing a Bouncer would make you think "Oh, that part of the level is a V.I.P area, I shall have to be clever about how I enter!", but this is not a perfect universe. This is the universe where Pi is three and a bit, and the Bouncers are violent, sociopathic clints with serious personal space issues, who are capable of instantly killing you. In the Campus level, they will attack you for standing outside of a window.
Graphically, it looks like every indie game ever, and the strings are chock full of broken english.
If you intend to purchase it, purchase it at a 60% discount minimum.

There's a small number of games which I've revisited numerous times, and Outcast is one of them. When it first came out, it was a gorgeous game - but the graphics were highly reliant on a powerful CPU, which meant that a lot of people couldn't actually run the game, even at its ridiculously low resolution (even at the time). As a result, the game didn't go on to become a commercial success despite being widely praised otherwise.
By the time I first laid my eyes on this gem a few years after it came out, the average gaming PC had become able to comfortably run the program with no real issues, and boy, it wasn't just a gorgeous game (despite the tiny resolution), but also an incredibly immersive one. In this game you end up exploring what was at the time a vast and expansive world with several different regions, inhabited by the Talan - an alien species - as you try to save both this world and your own (the Earth) after an experiment has gone terribly wrong.
The world is immersive, the lore draws you in, the characters are memorable and the story is satisfying. It is not a flawless game - movement can feel a bit clunky (especially jumping/climbing), there are a few ways in which you can cause bugs which prevent story progression (most notably by going to areas you're not supposed to go to early, though that's fairly difficult to do) and there are a few (very rare) situations in which you can be stunlocked until you die by some of the most elite opponents (though good planning can avoid this). However, all in all, this game was (and still is) a tremendous success, and comes highly recommended.
With Outcast 1.1, a number of the bugs related to CPUs have been fixed (a too fast CPU could break certain parts of the original game) and it's finally possible to play the game at a decent resolution. Be aware however that this game is very demanding on the CPU (even now) when played on higher resolutions. It's voxel-based graphics are rendered by the CPU, not by the GPU, so if your game is underperforming, consider lowering the resolution a little.

Can One Cereal Box Video Game Sway the Political Leanings of an Entire Generation? – the Pajama Sam Effect
Humongous Entertainments’ 2000 point and click adventure game “Pajama Sam 3: You Are What You Eat from Your Head to Your Feet” is nothing short of a masterpiece. Through a complex and layered narrative, the player is guided through child-friendly lessons on nutrition and anatomy, with the added dimensions of allusions to geopolitical conflict, diplomatic relations, freedom of expression, the complexities of the legal and penal systems, as well as to the Marxist master-slave dialectic fundamental to the capitalist mode of production.
This is made absolutely evident in one of the opening scenes of the game: our protagonist finds himself in the candy-cane jail, to await trial which is set for the next month; an obvious symbol for the consistent failures of the justice system, due in no small part to its bureaucratic inefficiencies. Sharing his jail cell is a broccoli named Florette, a delegate for the food group peace conference (a not-so-subtle allusion to the United Nations) who is being held as political prisoner. Florette asks our protagonist to help her escape imprisonment, and to rescue the other delegates so they may safely reach the peace conference. Clearly, the antagonistic Sweet State has as motive to keep the delegates (each representing an essential food group) away from the conference so as to maintain a nutritional hegemony without sanction.
In the much cited section on estranged labour in Marx's 1844 Manuscripts, he posits four dimensions of alienation suffered by the proletarian class as a result of the capitalist system: alienation from the object of production, from the sum-total of labour activities, from his species-being, and most importantly, from fellow men. Following the fourth dimension of alienation of man from man, workers see other people the same way they see their own labour; as being alien to them, and therefore hostile. In PS3 (Pajama Sam 3), our hero must free the delegate Bean #47 trapped atop a girder in a quarry, overlooking a workers uprising due to internal factionalism between the Jelly Beans and the Kidney Beans. This conflict is orchestrated and clearly a result of greed and negligence on the part of the foreman, who represents the capitalist bourgeois proprietor of the means of production. This section of the game is a not-so-veiled representation of this fourth dimension of alienation. The Jelly Beans and the Kidney Beans see each other in the same light that they their own labour: they are estranged from it, and therefore confront it with hostility. When spoken to, the foreman shows little regard for the plight of his workers, but rather claims repeatedly that he has counted them, while shuffling through a number of blank documents; he is putting up a front of a caring boss, but his reluctance to provide any useful information until the third interraction with Pajama Sam shows that his care is only on a very superficial level, and that he still sees his workers in terms of their commodity values, and means to an end.
One by one, the player then helps Pajama Sam find and save the other delegates and sends them on their way to the conference. In the final scene of the game, the six delegates, all in the peace conference (strongly resembling the United Nations Security Council), begin to bicker and argue with each other over which food group is better, rather than continuing deliberation with decorum. In response to this, Pajama Sam gives a rousing speech in which he implores the delegates to remember the original spirit of diplomacy between food groups: to address the concerns of human physiology, and to ensure their continued prosperity and collective autonomy.
Many children across north America that enjoyed the many Kellogg's breakfast cereals that included the game in one of their boxes was then exposed to the leftist rhetoric overlaying the themes in PS3. Could these quasi-subliminal messages have influenced the political leanings of millenials? As was made evident from the last presidential election in the United States with the overwhelming support for candidates like Bernie Sanders by youth, this could very much be the case. The evidence points to this, and given the right statistical analysis of distribution and demograpgics related to PS3 and its players, it can be claimed that this is all due to the Pajama Sam effect.

Spectacular game, but not absolutely perfect.
The story, the characters, the music, the gameplay, are all excellent. The combat is satisfying once you get used to changing up your range, and the amount of customisation available is pretty interesting - though a tad overwhelming to begin with. I don't think I can possibly fault the story, as it's engaging and keeps you in the dark for a lot of the time, leaving you desperately wanting to uncover more secrets about the world. The music is superb -  I even purchased the official set of 3 CDs!
There are some issues, however, that would keep me from thinking of NieR: Automata as a "10/10" game. Subquests are somewhat difficult to keep track of sometimes, and chapter progress limits which subquests are available and can be completed. It's a little too easy to go too far ahead and be mostly unable to go back and finish off something that may have seemed simple when you first talked to an NPC. However, the game mitigates this to an extent by way of... a certain feature... you unlock that means chapter progress isn't an issue.
The biggest gripe for me, however, is the technical side of things. I've played this game to N̶i̶e̶R̶ near completion on a machine with an i7-6800K, a GeForce GTX 1070, and 16 GB of RAM (can't recall the double data rate type, sorry), at a nice 1080p. Some users have reported upscaling issues in gameplay, but as far as I know, the game has run properly at the resolution I've told it to. That isn't the issue for me. My issue is the cutscenes: they're unbelievably choppy. They're seemingly upscaled from 900p and don't even make it to 30fps a lot of the time, which is something that shouldn't be happening on my rig, and a lot of others. Right now there are mods that adjust them to run smoothly and at 1080p, but they're not 60fps. I know outright asking for fresh cutscenes rendered at a full 60fps might be too much to ask... but at the same time, I'd expect the devs to roll some kind of patch out to fix the choppiness. Full 60fps cutscenes would be great, though.
Overall: Very solid game, but technical issues stop it from being absolutely stellar.

This is a... weird game, one of those games that is equal parts joy and misery...
Advent Force is much better than the original Fairy Fencer, no doubt about that, but just as the original Fairy Fencer was not for everyone, Advent is also not.
If you ever played one of the Neptunia games, Fairy Fencer's "elder sister" series of jrpg games from Idea Factory , you should have a good idea about the general tone of the story and gameplay.
Most of the story follows the light tone from Neptunia series, its not a game that takes itself too seriously, it makes some goofy jokes that sometimes hit the mark and sometimes are just cringy, the dialogue have both hilarious and face-palming moments. The plot works but falls deep into the generic category, it is the kind of plot that uses a bunch of ideas that were used to exaustion on many mangas and other rpgs, but it works if nothing else. The characters follow the same rule and all of them fit into some kind of manga stereotype. Not a game that surprises you.
Until the "true", evil godess, ending route that is...
Avoiding spoilers, that route follows a much darker tone, the story gets much heavier and more serious. Much of the cast have a drastic different fate and the story, imho, holds much better... for some time... as the story progress, it feels more and more forced, like they took the dark tone a bit too far, or maybe just were plain not sure how to fill some gaps or how to develop some characters, and ended with many anticlimatic moments. Its that weird kind of story that manages to makes you interested but ends with you looking at the screen saying "thats it?". Ultimely it feels weird, they changed the tone very drasticaly(almost dont feel the same game, really) but ended in a similar place(with an ending just as flat as the original Fairy Fencer).
The gameplay also resembles the Neptunia series, it is turn-based with some elements of positioning on it. They did a better job at the combo system than in the original Fairy Fencer and positioning can be a big factor in some fights. Some cool things from the original game like the weapon upgrades, the option to give the characters a fairy to increase some stat and the divine revival mechanics are back. The problem here is that the team behind the game did not give any tough into escalating the old mechanics into the super late game that you will be when you play the new storylines(one of the new storyline is literally impossible to reach if you are not in new game+) and by the time you are playing the fresh story, most of the mentioned mechanics will be maxed out well before you reach the midle of it. The new fights are nicely done for the most part, but the way many mechanics were just copy-pasted and will be rendered obsolete for a very large portion of the game is dissapointing.
It is ultimely a game that have some great ideas, but feels incomplete and not because it was rushed, but rather, because the developers just ran out of ideas after some point. The many mechanics untouched with no regard on how they would escalate into the now mandatory new game+ also gives the impression that they focused a too much into fixing the negatives of the original game and forgot to improve what was okay. It is better than the original game, but is still just as flawed, if that makes sense...
Do i recommend this game? Welll... not for a random person. This game is VERY hit or miss, maybe watch some gameplay video or try another rpg from Idea Factory first.
