It wasn't terrible?
There's not many companies out there that can make decent games like this, and Artifex Mundi is one of the few.
I care about three things in these games: Story, puzzles, and exploration (new ideas, scenery, resulting in mood).
If you like story, try Clockwork Tales: of Glass and Ink.  Much better story, and continuity is good.
If you like puzzles, try Parallels Cross.  It is a good puzzle game, but still mostly HOG. (or ASA: A space adventure, for serious puzzlers)
If you like exploration, ?
If you are sick of Artifex Mundi, and want something different except the same, try Frankenstein: Master of Death.  They made a good game.
Honorable mention: Dark Arcana: The Carnival -- good plot, good mood, decent puzzles.
Honorable mention: The Emerald Maiden: Symphony of Dreams, cohesive, good mood, decent puzzles.
Honorable mention: Nightmares from the Deep series. imaginative and cohesive. OK puzzles, good mood.
But back to Myth Seekers: The Legacy of Vulcan.  The plot line got destroyed.  This seems like a production issue.  Big dreams, didn't spend enough time/money getting the narrative to fit the graphics and gameplay.  High resolution graphics is there, if that is a big thing for you.  It's pretty obvious when they added text to try to make the animated scenes make sense.  Hi-res graphics? check.  Puzzles? a bit above (Artifex Mundi) average, I think.  There were two puzzles that made me stop and think for a bit, so there's that.
One thing that Artifex Mundi does heads and shoulders above all the rest: I know the game will work.  No show-stopper bugs.
*shrug* Doesn't really stand out otherwise.

The introduction hints at a new series on myths with this first game which leads the player into Greek mythology.
The game starts out as a hunt for the Vesuvian Codex, which had been in the possession of Phillip Miller, an agent with the myth seekers agency. We have the year 1929 with Mussolini ruling Italy. He is searching for the codex, as this is the key to Vulcan’s hammer, a powerful artifact. You play as Amelia, agent at the MS agency as well. As Phillip is missing, your task is to get hold of the codex and prevent it and more so, Vulcan’s hammer, from falling into Mussolini’s hands.  The hammer’s power is immense, having belonged to Vulcan himself. After getting hold of the codex, Amelia is struck down by a strange woman, who takes it and leaves. We will learn later, who this woman really is and why we have to hinder her, to get hold of the hammer and use it.
In order to get it back, Amelia begins her search in Rome. But this is only the starting point of the sub-plot or – in my eyes – the real story of the game. It is the tale of Vulcan, whose mother Juno threw him out of Olympus only after his birth, but survived the fall and was adopted by nymphs. Though crippled, he became the smith of the Olympus, forging armors and weapons for the gods. Later he sought revenge and tricked Juno… We will learn more about him, his marriage to Venus, who betrayed him with Mars and his dealing with her infidelity, that lead to his imprisonment, which is on the verge of ending in these days, when the Vulcanalia festival will take place.
In communication with several Greek goddesses and gods, we step closer to our opponent and Vulcan’s hammer and in the end succeed in overcoming our opponent.  In the course of the game you will be equipped with powers, which are bound to a talisman. The first one is a cornucopia, later you will get Mars’ helmet etc. These powers will help you in defense and fulfilling tasks.
The graphics are beautiful and crystal clear. There are morphing objects as well as Roman gods and goddesses as collectables. In the Extras you’ll find achievements, screensavers, you may replay puzzles etc. Puzzles in the game are varied, not too difficult but neither too easy. Loved the HOS, many of which were creative: you find your item by interacting with the scene. The game is quite entertaining, even humorous e.g. when Amelia uses her cornucopia, several rocks fall on her fellow agents’ car – her comment: “Well, things may be a little rocky with Lorenzo, after this…”
All in all a wonderful playing experience.

If you love Space Games where you are not overly rushed to perform any action, then Galaxy on Fire 2 HD is for you. GoF2 combines all the best elements of past Space Exploration, Trading, Combatting games into one. The graphics are stunning and will leave you wanting to explore new systems for hours on end.
Ship control and firing is done through using your mouse. The system is identical to freelancer in a lot of ways and I find to be the best way. The story mode is engaging and well worth the play. Character voices have been meticulously developed for all of the missions and really fit within the game quite well. You have many options while playing GoF2. You can either do all the story missions, or if you get tired of those, you can go trading, mining ores, doing side missions you can pick up from the Space Lounge which include cargo delivery, pirate hunting and killing, transporting people from one star system to another, and you can even find great deals on rare items being sold at times.
Combat is pretty straight forward. Depending on your ship (and there are a great deal of different ships to buy), you can have a number of different types of weapons equipped. Ship movement is handled by moving your mouse. Ship speed is handled by your mouse's wheel scroller and firing primary and secondary weapons are handled with your left and right mouse buttons respectively.
The only downside to this game is that there is no online or Co-op multiplayer. It would be great to play with other people around the world and team up in fleet's to go exploring and pillaging deep space. However, having said that, in one way its also good that its not online, simply because if it was, it would more than likely be the standard PVP style that leaves you without the option to opt out of PVP battles which is a trend in online space exploration games.
If you love space games, Galaxy on Fire 2 HD is one you should not live without. It is by far the best offline single player space game I have ever played!

You play a ****ty slasher film from the 80's or 90's, complete with awful acting, a non-sensical plot, and unrealistic behavior - all set to an awesome soundtrack.
I see a lot of negative reviews from people who tried to do perfect stealth instead of exploring how to effectively kill people in this game.  I'll put the blame squarely where it belongs, though: the tips/tutorials.  If you make the mistake of treating this like a stealth game, you're going to have a bad time.  You have to treat it like you would Hotline Miami - it's an action puzzle game where the pieces are acts of violence.
* If all you're doing is waiting endlessly for people to wander off alone or to stumble into a trap, you're doing it wrong.  One of the best ways of clearing a map is to cause a panic.  The tips warn you not to do this early - ignore them.  The earlier you cause a panic, the better.  Fully panicked people will sometimes attack people for coming too close to them, give false reports to the police (being arrested counts as a kill), or spread out to other areas (eliminating a lot of that endless wait).
* Using traps exclusively on party goers is equally pointless.  Traps can be used to take out cops, SWAT, and the feds.  You should be saving some of them specifically for when you expect to become wanted so you can escape capture. Having the option of surviving a chase means you can take out people when stealth is impossible, take a chance when you're pretty sure you can wipe out most of a group, or for not having to restart when you feel like taking a stupid risk for the fun of it.  (Pro Tip: Horses are the most useful trap in the game for taking out someone who is chasing you.)
* Do not attempt to play this game like you're some kind of real life ninja and will have to kill yourself for behaving in a manner not in keeping with the teachings of your ancestors.  You're playing a slasher move - it's not supposed to make sense.  Carry sleeping people over to a punch bowl before you poison it.  Get yourself killed/beaten repeatedly learning how the AI really works (particularly the plumber who interferes with the escape hatches).  Party-goers run for a phone when they see someone die; you can use this to make small groups run into you instead of having to chase them.
TL;DR:
Pros:
* Gameplay
* Soundtrack
* Humor
* Afterparty Explansion was free
* Surprising amount of tactical options once you know the AI and traps (I beat Miami Party *before* Katie was changed to knock people out)
Cons:
* Everyone moves faster than you except walking party-goers
* Your sprint duration is an absolute joke
* Occasional bugs
* Enemies concealed by doors (level design mistake)
* Level design does not work with some unlocked characters
* Tips/Tutorials are random, sometimes unhelpful

That was pretty good. I'm glad Humongous got back on track for Pajama Sam.
I don't think companies should stick to a solid formula if they create a franchise. Nintendo has managed to evolve the Mario franchise over the years, but with very few distinct changes. That's honestly one of the biggest problems with series. How far do you go to make a sequel distinct and different, while also keeping the same general formula of your previous installment(s)?
I think Pajama Sam 3 did alright. I liked what it did. It was different, but it was still distinctly a Pajama Sam.
The story is similar to the other installments, where Sam has a problem and some supernatural imaginative event carries Sam to a separate world where he learns the error of his ways. Although, this is the first time in the series where Sam doesn't deal with a fear: it's more or less a personal flaw of overeating.
The world, much like the Land of Darkness from the first game, is incredibly imaginative. It's a massive rendition of Sam's body, as he goes around and "restores balance" to the food groups. There's no B.S, random conflict that comes out of nowhere. No random World Wide Weather business complex. It's simple imagination- like the first Pajama Sam.
But, despite what good things there are, there are still plenty of bad things. The mini-games are absolutely awful. I hate the bean-sorting game and the ski slopes. And some puzzles were a little vague, especially if the game was made for kids. Like specifically finding the sand castle for the bag to fill for the Cheese Delegate guy. And, the voice actress for Florette the Broccoli sounds like she's just reading a paper in front of her face.
However, the game follows the original Pajama Sam formula, without using the first game as a crutch, like Pajama Sam 2 did. It tells a new story with new characters, while keeping the charm, subtle humor, small symbolism, and story of personal growth that the original game created. And I enjoyed the time I spent playing it. I'm giving this one a 7/10.

NieR: Automata’s strongest qualities are its narrative and characters. What pushes Automata’s story to greater heights in which people will be talking about it for a long time is how Automata visually and mechanically through unique game play represents the story. While Platinum Games does a commendable job on the basic free world combat, it’s the hacking mini game that comes into play that escalates the story into another level. You play as an android and Automata knows it. How it tackles representing thoughts and concepts of the android mind is nothing but fascinating and uniquely fun. I will concede though, it does get repetitive at times.
Hacking aside, the characters of 2B, 9S, and A2 stories are wonderfully told. Never have I wanted to fight for a bunch of inappropriately dressed video game characters for a long time. Equally as good are the boss battles. The music and the ever-changing game play all come together for some memorizing and engaging boss battles. The side quests are a hit or a miss though in terms of being fun, but at least they contribute to the overall world building.
Wrapped around an amazing story and characters is the godly music of Automata raining straight down from the heavens themselves. Awe inspiring and euphoric at times, I can be driven to do anything with this OST playing in the background, it’s just that powerful. Not since Chrono Cross’s OST have I been infatuated with a video game soundtrack.
It’s just a huge disappointment Automata isn’t getting the full attention it deserves. Most reviewers obviously never completed the game to its ONLY ending, ending E. The other 25 endings are either gimmicks or not real endings, calling these “endings” is what hurts the game the most, it gives the false impression you’re done. It would have been best if the credits never rolled in all honesty for ending A where I’ve seen many players stop and called it for the game. As for the rest of us that’s completed Automata to its final closing, we know we have a masterpiece here, faults and all.

What can I say? 10/10 would buy again. This little gem has been a classic and to my knowledge no space fighter game has been able to live up to this, unless somebody would like to make a recommendation.
The intuitive nature to this game is beyond compelling, I've taken down multiple capital ships, overcome insane odds, all while strategically being able to manuever my craft and manage my shield and energy/ammo reserves. The ability to turbo and then slide is exactly something a space simulator should have, I'm not sure how I could play any other without it. The way the physics are set up are awkward, but make sense to how true space physics would be.
While I am extremely attached to the gameplay, everything else is top-notch. The explosions aren't amazing but still satisfying, voice acting is great and while limited the playful banter between you and your wingmen is just added fun. The only thing missing? A second game, more missions/ships, whatever else. I might check out Freespace 2 eventually and see if it can truly live up to this legend.

This is a story driven space combat "simulator". A basic one, in fact. More like Freespace than Elite. You click on the next mission(escort, destroy, defend, deliver, etc.), equip your ship, hire of fire wingmen, and launch to kill some bad guys in space. That's it. There are shield/energy management mechanics, that many other games of this type have.
The story will branch at some point and after choosing a faction to fight for, you'll have access to ships and weapons specific to that faction. Different ships have very different cockpit interface, requiring some time to adapt, which is a nice touch.
Graphics are ok, for 2000, but nothing spectacular. Sound design is decent, voice acting is good, synth music somewhat repetitive. It only supports 4:3 aspect ratio with max resolution of 1024x768, which is expected.
If you are easily irritated by ocassional sexist jokes you may want to play a different game.
Anyway, this game is not a masterpiece, but if you can't get enough of space dogfighting, try it.

I'm not really a fan of JRPG's. Obviously got caught up with FF7 back in the day and I occasionally try these things just to see if I can recapture that magic. I had high hopes for this one. But... Nope. In short, I’m sure fans of this genre will have fun but I got bored of the repetitive gameplay.
So far as JRPGs are concerned, Fairy Fencer is kind of OK. It's pretty enough and the gameplay is that traditional combination of grind and skills development, but the lack of diversity of monsters and incredibly repetitive gameplay just isn't offset by the lack of story. I never felt invested in the characters and wasn't even bothered when a character or two are removed from the party for "story" reasons. I also found the partially voiced character interactions only served to act as a distraction; one of the other would have worked so much better.
With that said, the Earth Forming ability is a really cool feature and permits the player to use multiple swords to change the statistical impact of a dungeon; making the creatures easier or increasing the loot drop rate for example. It adds a dimension to the game that I’m sure JRPG fans will enjoy.
Overall not my type of games. I really did try very hard to get into it, but when I’m looking around a dungeon and I find myself fighting the same group of monsters for the umpteenth time I'd had enough. It did keep my interest for a little while though and I’m sure if you are a fan of this style of game, you’ll have some fun.
I don’t want to mark this game up or down but since it’s not my thing I’m going to give it a thumbs down.

As someone who didn't play the early access, I have no opinion on wether the game has improved since then.
The game is amazingly good fun, and I'd reccomend it to anybody who likes rogue-like combat-based games.
The combat is a nice touch, simply left clicking (or right clicking for some effects) is very cool and it allows you to enjoy the game to the fullest. There are many unique mobs, and enough to fit nicely. You always start in the relatively friendly forest/jungle and have to run through various levels. After that level is complete, you get an option of 3 different rooms, some of these (or sometimes all) can be biomes you already visited or a completely new one. Every time you die in the game, you have to start from the very beginning with nothing on you but the starting gear of that character and the traits you used last time (if you press the play again button, cancelling out resets the character's traits and stats). You may sit there for a couple of minutes trying to get the perfect stats with the perfect traits your character suits.
I've discovered 4 different types of "classes", Warrior : The basic and most easiest to start with, using swords. Ranger: Using bows and arrows, focuses on the dexterity skill (DEX). Magician: Using magic staves (which are quite limited at the current time) and Barbarian: using Giant axes and Zweihanders, dealing MASSIVE damage. The easiest and most common is the Warrior, as the other 3 are pretty hard to set up early on, and by the time your later on in the game, you already have the best sword... Odviously, you can mix and match these, but these are the 4 main ways of dealing damage.
Even though this game is amazing and has no glitches (that I've found, at least), the game has a lot of area's lacking in content. the game is really fun to play, and there are quite a few unlocks, but there's not enough content to make you play over 40 hours, as at that time you've already had everything there is. Not saying 40 hours worth of content is bad, but the fact that there is not a lot of unlocks limits the replayability of the game without having to completely start over, and having a lot more hats, minions, customization and characters would be nice.
Overall, the game is great for it's relatively cheap price, so get it if you like the look of the game!

I finally played it through again, and I must say I still enjoy it, even after all these years. But I am not really sure that would be the case if I hadn't such big nostalgia for it. It was a bit like visiting old friends *sniff*
But I would never expect new players to enjoy Outcast as much as I did, even with the improvements the developers added. I still recommend it, of course, as it is one of my favourite games. My personal pro points regarding Outcast are the atmosphere, the fact that you can do a lot of quests, the music (oh, that music!), the nonlinearity and often the humor. And the music.
But yeah, the combat is a bit halfbaked, the story doesn't always make sense (although it's very immersive) and you will do a lot of walking to get to the different places, but luckily there are shortcuts if you use your tools right. And I wish the developers wouldn't have added so many achievements, as they tend to negate the atmosphere and immersion a bit.
Overall, Outcast is a rewarding experience, if you can ignore its shortcomings.

EVE's mission system (pre-EVE, by the way) coupled with the zero-G flight mechanics of Freespace form the core of an often-challenging and generally fun space combat sim with a sound and engaging campaign. The control scheme is daft and requires memorization of a full-size keyboard layout (the boxed version shipped with a huge trifold reference chart, which you may still be able to find if you're exceptionally good at Google searches). Also, If you don't have a joystick with twist/rudder support you might have to hit up Ebay for one before you start playing. BUT, if you've got the time and feel like playing a genuinely satisfying and entertaining starfighter game, this is one of the best there is.
There is a multiplayer mode, and while the online servers are quite likely dead these days, I had some great times trying to match my wits, skill and ship upgrades against opposing pilots. The real draw, however, is the campaign. Based around jobs and for-hire missions, it'll have you chasing down troublemakers for private shipping magnates or joining up with the enlisted military against common enemies, all as a mercenary pilot voiced by none other than Bruce Campbell. The voice acting is substantial, in fact, and serves the story in a way that invites you to root for the Nathan Drake-esque protagonist's otherwise short and unremarkable journey from self-interested freelancer to potential 'good guy' with a cause. You can save your earnings to buy new ships, improve your weapons payload, and add new functionality to your ship's capabilities (lateral thrust, for example).
On the downside, the learning curve is substantial, and if you want to play this game right you're going to need a flight stick with rudder controls. But smooth and enjoyable space combat and a broad range of available unique ships and environments to fly them in may have you coming back for more. Good 'ol Bruce Campbell.

I rushed out to the Steam Store to buy every expansion I could find - but they aren't here!
Apparently, the developer decided it wasn't worth their time or effort to release the DLC / Expansions to the PC version.  Note I said "PC version" specifically, because the develeoper has released the DLC to ALL OTHER PLATFORMS (Android, iPhone, and Mac).  I can't even begin to tell you how frustrating that is... The Binding of Isaac is similar in a number of ways (difficulty, room layout, enemy types) to the original Legend of Zelda for the NES. The main difference being of course that this game is top-down shooter with largely random item/power-up drops, which changes gameplay considerably. I HEARTILY recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a serious challenge, wants massive replay value, and is not going to be driven away by the rogue-like elements and the clever, but unsettling art direction. I've laid out the most pertinent pros and cons below to give a better understanding of whether you'll want to play this game.
Pros:
Huge replay value (randomization, a number of unique playable characters, additional levels unlocked after beating the game)
Great level and enemy design (despite being somewhat derivative of the original Zelda)
Medium/High difficulty level (you have to work for it)
Brilliant and meaningful achievement system (every achievement unlocks a new item to be obtained in-game)
Cons:
Occasional fps slowdown when a number of enemies are onscreen (can be fixed by reducing quality settings)
Freezes occasionally when loading later levels (simply needs time to fix itself)
There are a number of bugs related to ahievement unlocks in Steam, but seems have almost everything right in-game (playthroughs with one character count as wins with another, for example)
Art style makes frequent references to abuse and other somewhat taboo themes and can be very unsettling at first
The sheer number of items available can force a decision between on-the-fly play (with weird item interactions) and having the wiki open in the background to understand your items

Outcast is a game released in 1999.  Expect 1999 graphics.  But if you can get past the graphics, you'll experience a fantastic game with a solid storyline that doesn't take itself too seriously but still manages to be compelling.  The amount of content in this game for the price is staggering, and the world draws you in easily.  This remastered version fixes several bugs and blatant issues that were present in the CD release (like some obvious missing quests and the SLNT-B upgrades), and makes it play smoothly on modern systems.  It's a lot of fun, and for the price, definitely a lot of bang for your buck.

Dystopia is seldom as gorgeous and compelling as it is in NieR:Automata (though I'm somewhat embarrassed by the fetishistic goth-loli character designs). The worldbuilding is great, though the story seems to wallow in tragedy at times. Yoko Taro is a bit too fond of kicking the protagonists when they're down, but that seems to be the standard for the Nier/Drakengard series.
Combat is pretty smooth. I barely made it past some of the endgame stuff, and basically got laughed at by some optional missions and secret bosses, but it all feels dynamic and well-balanced. It can get quite grindy in some parts, though not like Dark Souls' level of ridiculous difficulty. I'm not sure what gear actually made a difference, other than max leveling one good sword and spear. I pretty much had to keep fighting bosses over and over, until I learned their patterns and finally beat them.
There are at least 3 "endings" (the first two are more like ends of act 1 and 2), and you will definitely want to keep playing until you see them all. Try to read as little as possible online about this game. It works better when it comes as a surprise, and there's eventually a newgame+/chapter select that lets you go back and finish collectibles and optional missions.
Loading times are pretty substantial. They teach you patience. The game and story are good enough that you'll want to burn through it in a few days, but you should definitely pace yourself IRL. Eat, sleep, take bio breaks, shower, work, walk, don't die of blood clots in your legs. That sort of stuff. The broken but beautiful world of Nier will still be there when you get back.

Picture a game that will make you have fun, but it'll make you sad. You'll laugh one moment and cry the next one, and it'll all make sense, because that's how good this story-telling is. We're getting into an emotional trip here so you can skip the first three paragraphs if you just want to know about Automata.
I remember when I found the original Nier back in 2010, and although I'm not getting into details (because I'm hoping they'll do some remastered versions of Nier and Drakengard for us with Automata's success, where I'll review them instead), I can say that I got my mind blown: everything was beautiful. The characters were great, I loved every single one of them, the story was awesome, every dialogue was worthwhile, and the music was absolutely insane, the best soundtrack I've ever heard in my life. After that, I played Drakengard 1 and 2 and guessed that was it. They were a small company with no money, how the hell would they make something new?
A few years afterward they made Drakengard 3, which I played as well, and although I was still amazed by the story, soundtrack and characters, I still didn't think there was any hope for the franchise to really grow and conquer new fans... the ideas were there, but combat was still clumsy, there were some silly technical issues, and the ambience still felt a little dead. All in all, you had to really be a fan and like their work if you wanted to get into it.
Well, after that, if someone told me they'd make a sequel to Nier of all games - a game born from a "joke ending" from the first Drakengard -, I'd have laughed at them, called it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t... but well, here we are! I still remember my excitement when I saw the announcement, but I feared that it wouldn't be as good as the first one. Yes, it was way more polished, and knowing Platinum Games' work, I knew it'd at least be a fun game to play, but I still feared that everything else would be watered down so the public would enjoy it a little better... and, to my surprise, we got the best of both worlds.
Everything from the first Nier was "corrected"; every idea that didn't work well because of the low budget got polished, and now it works 100% well. I remember people complaining in reviews about how the original Nier travelled from an Action RPG to a shooter, then back at RPG, then a top-down action game, and then it turns into a novel reading game. Well, they repeated this here, and I'm so glad that they respected the original game's ideas and brought them over, and I'm even more glad that people seem to find it interesting now, because it has so much to offer. It's new and it feels fresh.
As for the combat, it got the Platinum Games style, which is always fun: you can try different kinds of combos with different combinations of weapons, and also different builds with their respective side-effects, opening a lot of room for experimenting, which was something that was lacking in the first game (all you needed was the Phoenix Spear and a pattern of rolling, attacking and pressing triangle and that was it). You can make it fit your playstyle along with the plug-in chips and pod programs, which give you specific buffs and new powers, so there's a lot you can do, really - combat never felt stale to me.
Now, the highlight that turns this game into a masterpiece: the story. As I've said, I've thought they'd water it down, or make it easier to sell with some silly plot twists and whatnot, but instead I found a perfectly crafted story - exactly the kind of story I'd expect from Yoko Taro. If you've played the original Nier and/or the Drakengard series, you won't be disappointed. The side-quests also have interesting stories - some are funny, some are cute, some are depressing. I enjoyed most of the side-quests from the original Nier, so I was expecting something like that in this one. Ah, and of course: Keiichi Okabe's wonderful music, which is the best thing that ever happened to me in a video-game, is as powerful as ever.
As for the down-sides: I liked that they brought the "Tokyo Drifting Boar" from the original game (along with the mooses you can ride), and they also included the fishing (which wasn't something I was very fond of at all, but still, as I've said, it's just nice that they respected the original game's content), but I felt like they didn't explore the wildlife as much as they could've with side-quests. The fishing also grew more tedious, since it's completely based on luck: you just toss your pod in the water and hope for the best, whilst the original Nier gave you the option of buying different kinds of bait to catch specific kinds of fish.
The difficulty is also something that could've been planned better: I played on Normal at first, and in the beginning the game was challenging enough for me, but after I got some plug-in chips and managed to upgrade my weapons, it slowly started to become a bit too easy. I tried setting the difficulty up to Hard then once I finished the game's first part and reached Route B, and once again I felt challenged... but suddenly, around Route C, the challenge became way too much: I was getting killed with one hit from enemies way too often, it almost felt like I was playing on Very Hard (which is where this is supposed to happen). By the end of the game, after I completed everything and reached Lv 99, there wasn't a single enemy who could actually damage me anymore (since they only go as high as Lv 60-something, aside from two optional bosses), and it was either that or Very Hard's one-hit kill madness, there was no in between. I feel like the problem here is the leveling system, and if the enemies became as tough as you once you started the game all over again (for exemple: Lv 99 enemies appearing in Route A once you're Lv 99), perhaps they could offer a fair challenge.
Of course, none of this gets in the way of making Nier the masterpiece it is, and I really hope this series as a whole - Nier and Drakengard - starts getting the praise it always deserved now so we can get more of this awesome content in our lives!

I first played this game more than a decade after it was originally released and at first I regretted my purchase. The combat seemed stiff and the voice acting was laughable. The more I played however, the more I loved it. The game excels at giving the player their choice of how to proceed, and the amount of options you're given to complete many of your objectives is amazing. For certain levels, it's possible to ignore sections of the level completely and still complete your objective. This is possible due to the augments system which gives the player the choice to fill an augment slot with one of two augments. You can't switch between the two whenever you want, so you'll probably choose the one that fits your intended playstyle.
It's possible to complete the entire game without killing anyone (even bosses) if you know what you're doing. The story is far better than the modern prequels and will have you seriously weighing the consequences of your actions by the end. The music doesn't take a back seat either. In modern games, the music is often atmospheric, but entirely forgetable or unnoticeable. That is not the case here. This game's music is very noticable (I had the Hong Kong and UNATCO themes etched into my memory after my first playthrough).
Overall, I would seriously recommend this game. If you don't often play older games, it may take some getting used to. The controls will likely need to be rebound (the default flashlight key is F12, which Steam uses for screenshots).

This is an amazing game, if you're into any kind of Space games I'm confident you'll love this one.
I'll give a summary of individual features (some opinions);
Story - Actually engaging. You want to read everything and listen to the characters voices, it's really well made and you find yourself remembering names and places that in most games you skip through. Not only that, the story is optional, there are some benefits from it that I have experienced so far but nothing says you can't fly off and do what you want.
Customisation - You can buy multiple ships with different benefits, some with more weapons, cargo space, equipment slots etc.. Multiple weapons can be equipped, including different types so you can mix and match to suit your playstyle. Equipment slots let you equip enhancements like Shields, Armour, Speed boosts, Mining equipment and more. You can turn your ship into what you want it to be.
Freedom - As I said above, nothing stops you from going anywhere, earning Credits(currency) how you please. You can go to safe Systems and mine rocks in comfort, sell them at stations to pure profit. You can buy/sell commodities to and from stations. You can complete side missions for NPCs, involving Pirate killing, transport, selling items to them and many other activities. Or go hunt down enemy factions and take what you want, then sell it off. Much to do!
Graphics - I think the graphics are great. The Systems in the game all look spectacular and the Planets are superbly well made. You see the screenshots, I need say no more.
Other stuff;
Travelling is very well made and navigation help is quite minimal.
Scanning / Lock on system is also really cool. No simple button to instant loot, you have to aim your tractor beam at your loot and allow it to fully activate, same with auto navigation, you must lock onto your target before auto navigating. Both can be improved by buying better equipement.
There are only very minor niggles for me. Firstly the AI sometimes seems a little lacking, they'll fly right through asteroids and sometimes I have exited a Station inside one. The asteroid generation is also similar, sometimes you get asteroids clipped into the Station / Jump gate. The Auto navigation is also a bit silly, It will fly your ship directly into an asteroid, it doesn't fly around objects. Again not too big of a deal but it could be improved.
Overall the game is worth it by far for space sim lovers and anyone alike.

I started playing this game before I hit double digits and it doesn't matter how old I get or how many times I play it. It remains as one of the best games ever created. It's a classic that other classics are and will be built on. And the great thing about it is that no one had to tell me that, that Deus Ex was a classic, a game-changer for future games. I played it over and over again, blown away each time, subconsciously figuring that out for myself.
My favourite aspect of this game is the rich, multi-faceted, complex storyline that turns and twists and takes you to different corners of the world, reimaginging each space into a bleak futuristic representation of itself. I'm a player that likes to be entranced by story and if there is ever a game that could do that, it would be this one. The way that your choices in approaching the levels shapes the story as you progress creates a beautiful experience, ensuring its own longevity by providing a different gameplay experience as you explore other options when you play it differently.
The music was also absolutely a wonderful part of the experience. Beautifully written and created pieces of music jazz up the ambience of each level, getting downright creepy and giving you anxiety in some of the stages. A work of art in itself. This Game of the Year version, however, is missing the music track for the final Hell's Kitchen level, which leaves you blind in a sense because it serves as a good indicator of whether or not you've been spotted and trouble is brewing. Not fun to think you've not been spotted and then suddenly, you get shot. The track is a particularly adrenaline-pumping piece at that, so it's a shame to have lost it in this version.
I'm not going to measure up on graphics because I wouldn't know how to give a fair assessment of that in 2016. I didn't know how to give a fair assessment of it when I started playing it years and years ago, to be fair, so I'm not going to do that now. What I will comment on is their use of colours. The greys, browns and blacks of the game truly give the feel of the futuristic, almost apocalyptic setting being used. Not your traditional thing of beauty, but absolutely effective for its intended purpose.
Gameplay gets a bit tedious sometimes when you find yourself running up and down and up and down in some of the levels, but I suppose I can appreciate the sentiment behind a little legwork leading to the biggest rewards. Wouldn't be much fun, I figure, if everything was easily within reach and you didn't have to search for things. It makes for a meticulous player.
The stealth aspect and hacking are my favourite attributes of the game, as is the proper support for both lethal and non-lethal approaches. I appreciate a game that allows me to play according to my own moral code and preferences, allowing me to take a walk on both sides if I feel up to it. The multiple possibilities in each layout gives you freedom to engage or avoid as you'd like, which I really love, plus the hidden boons that can be found if you explore the levels well.
Overall, great, great game. One I will endeavour to hold on to as long as computing devices will support it and maybe even beyond for sentimental purposes. One that helped me bond with my older brother, in fact. Word of warning however: when you grow up on the best, it's hard to branch out afterwards.

I really tried to enjoy this one. The art and presentation are incredible and the music is fitting although not nearly as memorable and creative as Hotline Miami. That's where all possible praise ends, as gameplay quickly devovles into a waiting game where you slowly cull a ridiculously excessive crowd while hoping the arbitrary AI coupled with the basically non-functional run button don't screw you over, forcing you to start over in a newly randomized level.
The entirety of gameplay offered here is waiting for people to separate, then walking up to tap X and back away. If you get lucky and don't get spotted - or don't get randomly designated as the killer by a cop on the other side of the map that may or may not end up being impossible to outrun - your reward is more waiting for your next faceless generic victim until you eventually wipe out the other several dozen party goers. Knife swings don't connect far too often and there are countless visual bugs and strange hitboxes. The bouncers can sometimes spot you across a room and kill you from outside of your own attack range, other times you can walk right past them or they'll miss an attack despite your sprites literally overlapping. Events and character behavior are so erratic that any possible strategy goes out the window in favour of capricious trial and error.
There are about 1-5 traps per level, often implied to be a core feature. Some are interesting but all require you to mindlessly sit on your♥♥♥♥♥until someone wanders close enough, netting you a grand total of one kill each and forcing you back to the idiotic knife mechanics to kill everyone else. Timed and explosive traps take so long to activate that the AI will have wandered off from the explosion.
-Good art
-Decent music
-Terrible story bordering on cringe worthy
-Horribly amateur voices to the point where they'd be better off silent
-Thoroughly unenjoyable level designs with excessive amounts of enemies
-Levels that only get more repetitive and offer less room for creativity as it goes on
-Idiotically designed traps
-Arbitrary AI and often random, unavoidable failures
-Glitches
-Even when functioning correctly, the AI of cops and guards feels very random and their methods nonsensical
-The SWAT teams are even worse, as far as making any kind of sense in their actions
-Very shallow mechanics with no experimentation
-Even with enough patience for all the waiting you will not find a rewarding experience
-Barely lines up with its own description and promised features
-Boring, above all else. Don't buy it.

Ah, the nostalgia! What a classic of its time, unfortunately not successful enough for Infogrames (now Atari) to finance a sequel. I gladly remember being addicted to the game and being a regular member of the Infogrames forums back in the day, being part of an awesome community and helping a lot of people with the many secrets and and complexities Outcast had to offer.
The voxel engine was and still is a curiosity, resulting in a natural, non-blocky environment. While the textures are quite low-quality compared to today's standards, it is still a decently looking game. The high resolution of the remake helps with that. I am still stunned by the music and find myself regularly humming it while traversing the beautiful landscapes.
I would claim the AI is still up to today's standard, the enemies seem smarter than in Skyrim (that's not saying much, but it's something). And the population with its diverse day-to-day routines make up for a believable world, which was revolutionary back then and holds up to this day.
The remake has been well done and deserves - unlike other so-called "remakes" - its name. The developer did a good job and even fixed some long-standing bugs. The introduction of the achievements was a really good thing: It highlights not-so-obvious sidequests that many people missed when the game was orginally released.
If you can live with a few quirks here and there (the game is 16 years old after all!), I can recommend Outcast 1.1 from the bottom of my heart. A dirt cheap price for an atmospheric experience many modern games aren't able to deliver.

What a strange and wonderful game this was.
The story is painstakingly detailed and impressively realized. I've heard that this is actually a sequel to about three or four other games that I've never played, so I imagine that I am missing out on about 50% of the details here. Black Scrawl? Gestalt Project? Aliens? Psycho Mantis? These are details that will be lost on the newcomer, but they nevertheless give the impression of a world with a rich and nuanced history.
What's more important however is that the game sets out to make characters that are deliberately flawed and go through several coherent character arcs. Even better, the game isn't shy about letting characters die and taking bold steps to advance the plot, rather than lingering on in a comfortable status quo. I wouldn't describe the game as being a complete downer, but the game does its damn best to make you feel sorry for the robot dudes you constantly are killing. It's a unique approach that reminded me of Undertale of all things and that can only be a good thing.
For gameplay, it's one part hack and slash of the Metal Gear Revengeance variety, then another part bullet hell shooter. That's a strange combo, but it's done pretty seamlessly. Heck, I think the ending sequence of the game where you are constantly switching between the two modes amounted to one of the most effective bits of gameplay drama I can recall.
The game does have a few flaws however:
- The subquests often involve a lot of running around looking for♥♥♥♥♥♥ One quest where you scan for things in a desert stands out as being a complete and utter ♥♥♥♥♥torm.
- The game doesn't have a good middle ground difficulty. I played most of the game on 'hard' because normal for the most part is baby mode. But then all of a sudden I'd run into a boss that just would go ahead and literally kill me in one hit within 3 seconds of the fight starting. A middle ground between these extremes was needed.
- You have to play the first half of the game twice in order to get to the good stuff in the second half.
- The hacking minigame that  you do gets pretty old after a while and is basically cheating mode for every fight.
Nevertheless, in spite of all that stuff, I think this was pretty great. A solid purchase.

I was surprised that I enjoyed this game as much as I did. It feels like DmC (Devil May Cry reboot) mixed with Metal Gear Solid V, both games that I thought were great. It's open-worldy, but not excessively so. It's easy to keep track of the things you need to do and to look out for at all times. The unique twist that this game has, is that it's not always third-person fighting; the game will often switch to a top-down bullet hell shooter mode, as well as a side-scroller mode. The transitions work well, and isn't really confusing at all. I played with a controller, but have heard that keyboard+mouse is a bit more clunky.
The UI, soundtrack, story, and combat are all top-notch. The characters and voice work are superb, although not all the dialogue in the game is voiced. The story was both interesting and compelling, and seems to extend through additional playthroughs, which the game really needs, as there is a ton of fresh, additional content. You really aren't playing the full game unless you do, although additional playthroughs I hear don't take as long, as you get to keep you level, inventory, etc.
The environmental designs often have more invisible walls than I'd like, but it's consistent, so you eventually figure out where the game isn't going to let you go... you just have to get over that limitation. The environments are very pretty, in a worn-out, post-apocalyptic sort of way. Many areas tend to not have much of the "fluff" and "clutter" that you'd get in modern games, but I appreciate the clean style here.
There's a lot of things that this game does with the combat that cannot really be explained quickly, but I'll just say there's a variety of things you can customize in order to change how you need to play in order to be effective. I personally never found the larger, slower weapons to be very useful during combat, as you almost always have multiple enemies grouped up and attacking you at the same time, forcing you to evade. Faster weapons just made the combat feel much more fluid, and allows you to weave in evades, making the combat feel elegant. Perhaps there's a way to make the slower playstyle work, but I haven't messed with it. Also, the combat lock-on system often behaved very strangely for me... it would often target smaller enemies that were off-screen and further away than what I was trying to target. It didn't happen much, but it was noticeable when it did. The game feels like it plays better without locking on to an enemy, unless you are specifically trying to kill something at range (with your POD), but it's not even mandatory.
There's a ton of attention to detail in this game, and you can tell the developers really wanted to provide a great experience. Most notably, the animations are pretty great, and there's a lot of them for different interactions.. simply going up and down a ladder is made more exciting than we're used to in videogames. The pacing felt perfect, and I never felt like I was grinding, or ever had to grind. The boss battles were challenging but extremely fair on normal difficulty. There's a ton of memorable moments, both serious and humorous.
NieR has been a great experience so far, and my first playthrough took 17 hours, with a lot of exploration and side-questing. Most of my issues have been technical problems which are pretty common and known about, and can be fixed with a patch. Any other complaints I have are really nit-picky, such as having to stand at the front of a chest to open it... it can be finicky at times, especially at extreme camera angles.. it's one of the few things that slows down an otherwise fast and fluid-feeling game.

The voice acting is highly reminiscent of early 90's animes, bringing back a sense of nostalgia for some players. A mesmerizing soundtrack, the soundscape is fluid, filling the space in the more open environments, and heightening immersion in others.
NieR is worth your time, paying you back with great combat, spellbinding soundscapes, and fourth-wall breaking moments which somehow pull you in further.

First things first, let's make my feelings on this game clear: I place Outcast among my favourite games of all time, right up there with Deus Ex, Fallout 2, Half-Life and other classics. It's a masterpiece, and it still holds up incredibly well. The graphics may have dated, but the gameplay is still really solid and to this day very few games have managed to match the sheer amount of depth and effort Appeal poured into the alien world they created, which feels like a genuine place with its own culture and language. Even the score is excellent and it's one of the very few orchestral scores I rate.
But Outcast 1.1 is a little problematic. The little improvements it does on the technical side of things are fairly negligible compared to the sheer amount of issues it presents. It's glitchy as hell: during my playthrough I encountered various bugs from the minor (achievements being triggered by cutscene actions) to the genuinely bothersome (certain sidequests were impossible to complete due to critical items vanishing, while others simply never triggered). These issues were never present in the original or the GoG release a while back, so I'm a little hesitant in calling the Steam release wonderful.
My advice? Unless you're really hardcore about Steam or really want those trading cards or achievements (some of which require you to do some really stupid things you would never dream of doing otherwise), get the GoG release. It's smoother and stabler. The positive recommendation is for the game itself.

I remember way back when, when I was a small, foolish child who could barely understand english. Even though all I had was the demo version of Outcast, I knew it was a fantastic game, and I'd play it day after day. And now, here I am, happy to say it still occupies my slot of #1 favorite game of all time.
The world is the most alive I've ever experienced, even moreso than any modern games that boast having a living world to this day. The characters and story are interesting, there's so much to discover about the world of Adelpha, and everything has an interesting or funny in-universe reason for being the way it is - right down to why the keys only work once before they break.
And the combat is just plain fun! Every weapon firing relatively slow-moving projectiles means you have to run and jump around, making fights really active, and even encouraging laying traps for the enemies trying to get behind you. And if that's not your cup of tea, you can sneak around, and even do objectives that weaken your foes, so there's really something for everyone.
The voice acting is excellent, the music is gorgeous and perfectly fits the atmosphere, and the whole game feels so expansive and organic.
Outcast is a very old game, yes, but Outcast 1.1 has made many, many improvements. It was nigh impossible to get it to run properly on modern computers before, and even the GOG version caused me major issues. The screen's flickering, Cutter walks too slowly, I can't get up on this platform I absolutely have to reach, etc.
Now, it's fixed, and every little problem that the game had has been solved, and the problems that it still has are getting quickly taken care of day by day.
Outcast has always been perfect in my eyes, and now that the developers are back and actively improving it, it's even more so.

In the year 2000, while some people were playing games like Counter-Strike, the real hardcore gamers – my five-year old self included – were playing Pajama Sam 3. Every time our ignorant parents would accuse us of rotting our brains away by playing video games, we could point to the latest Pajama Sam title and show how we were teaching ourselves about balanced nutrition and international negotiations simultaneously in Sam’s latest adventure. Pajama Sam 3 is as good as it gets: featuring a quest to unite all the food groups and prevent total war (take notes, world leaders: diplomacy does work), a sidequest to collect enough box tops to win a Pajama Man action figure (does anyone else remember collecting these for school fundraisers as a kid?) and a cameo of everyone’s favorite hippie anarchist carrot (the diehard Pajama Sam fans will go crazy for this one), Pajama Sam 3: You Are What You Eat From Your Head to Your Feet is a masterpiece from beginning to end. Even if you aren’t a lifelong Pajama Sam fan and can’t experience a jolt of nostalgia like everyone else, you at least owe it to yourself to play Pajama Sam 3 today so you can at least pretend to be as cool as we were fifteen years ago.

You know, I have to be honest with you. This is my first written review of any computer game. I have never been compelled to do so before now, however Stellaris has invariably resonated within me; the chord being struck a mere 15 minutes into the gameplay. Though I have not reviewed games before, aside from forming my own personal opinions and critique, I have played strategy games nearly my entire life. I was born in the year 1989, but even at an early age I recall the glory days of Master of Orion, Civilization II, Sim City, and countless others. Perhaps my egocentric hubris is to blame, but I have often found myself playing God, at least in the harmless environment of positronic computer screens. Such a rare gem of a game it is, when you are given complete and total control over the actions and decisions you make; A title such as Stellaris does indeed bring order to a disorderly world. Stelleris delivers on so many fronts, in many of the same ways as the timeless classics aforementioned in this review. When every decision you make has enormous ramifications on a galactic scale, you know you have a good strategy game. I won't go into the very minute, mechanical structure of this game, as that is not what a review should strive to do. There are plenty of "let's play" video reviews and tutorials scattered across the internet, and I would highly recommend checking those out if you want to know how this game plays exactly. That being said, allow me to break this game down into the things I absolutely love about this game, and things that could use more improvement.
The Good:
* Gameplay. Exceptionally balanced mechanics, paired with a wide variety of custom race creation options, allows for a plethora of opening strategies and open-ended gameplay. Random chance is done very well, allowing for meaningful risk vs. reward decisions.
* Graphics. My God, man, the graphics. Such stunning visuals, while not overly important in strategy games, adds a rich level of immersion the likes of which have never been done before in a galactic empire building game.
* Player-driven story. You are in the driver's seat as to how you want to progress through the game. If it is in your imagination, it most likely can be done. Whether you are a die hard roleplayer who wants to act their part, or a mere science fiction enthusiast who is just along for the ride, you will not be disappointed.
* Soundtrack. I was completely surprised by the audio in this game. I am usually guilty of muting my games, only to listen to background music of my own supplementation. However, this title is one of the few where I find myself not doing this. Beautiful "space opera" tracks, that add yet another layer of immersion.
* Modability. Maybe you're like me, and find mods to be an important aspect of the games you play. Whether you like to make your own mods, or play total conversion scenarios, Stellaris is amiable with its Steam Workshop integration. There are hundreds, if not thousands of mods currently available to make this game your own.
* Optimization. This game, for all its bells and whistles, operates as smooth as butter on my PC. There is admittedly a somewhat lengthy loading screen when you are first seeding your game, but during the game itself, I have never experienced any kind of stutter, crashes, or otherwise poorly developed software. I play on max graphics settings on my main gaming rig, and medium-low setting on my laptop. Neither of which have ever caused me problems.
* Price point. At a mere $39.99 USD, this game is a bargain in and of itself. Let alone if you're able to grab it during a sale. With this level of quality that only Paradox can deliver, one might expect to shell out $59.99 or more. Even at that price point, it would be well worth the investment, but at $39.99, it is absolutely worth every penny.

The Bad (Or at least the "Meh.)
* User interface. The UI in this title can definitely take some getting used to. With such a massive level of depth and scale, it is hard to avoid using convoluted tabs and windows and charts and graphs and be able to make sense of it all. I have certainly played games with worse UI's, and the "quick bar" feature helps a lot, but all in all the interface could use some improvement.
* Not for the casual gamer. A good game of Stellaris takes time; on a good day you can finish a game in perhaps 8 hours, though even this figure would be with a small map and won't do the game justice. If you want a strategy game where you can play start to finish in one setting, Stellaris is not for you.
The Ugly
* Learning curve. As I have stated earlier, I have played countless strategy games throughout the years. And very few have offered this level of complexity. It will take you hours upon hours to learn every nuance this game has to offer. I admittedly only have about 80 hours logged, but even after all this time, I am still learning new things in terms of how the game flows. To me, this is a good thing, but for the vast majority of folks, this can pose a challenge and intimidate them from trying to learn how to play. This is further compounded by the fact that the in-game tutorials are nearly non-existent.
In conclusion, would I recommend this game? To someone like myself, who views gaming as a lifestyle as much as a hobby, absolutely. Would I recommend it to the science fiction enthusiast? Again, the answer is yes. Would I recommend this game to someone who has never played a strategy game before? Yes, but with a caveat. Make sure to take the game slow at first, and ease yourself into it. This is hands down the best game released for PC this year. It sits in my top 10 favorite PC games of all time. And at a modest forty bucks, it will not let you down.

In the game you will take over the role of the intergalactic adventurer and war hero Keith T. Maxwell. Catapulted 35 years into the future by a malfunction of his hyperdrive, he suddenly awakens at at the far end of the galaxy, where he quickly finds himself fighting for his life against a mysterious alien armada that is wreaking havoc on the warring races occupying this volatile sector of space. Despite his efforts to return home, Keith is drawn into a deadly plot to investigate and stop this alien menace. Along the way he must fight space pirates, trade cargo, explore new territories and negotiate with shady characters to uncover the truth about this powerful enemy and ultimately find his way home. Old friends and new enemies join forces as Keith takes command of a dangerous intergalactic mission that sends him deep into enemy space, bringing the war to an explosive conclusion that will set the entire galaxy on fire.

With fully customizable controls for mouse, keyboard and gamepad, Galaxy on Fire 2™ Full HD brings the finest outer space adventure to your PC - bigger and better than ever before!

I bought this short but sweet game when it was on sale for 50 cents. I didn't expect much, so it was a pleasant surprise to find a true logic game.
Though Hexcells borrows elements from several different puzzle games, I was most reminded of nonograms, also known as Picross or Hanjie, which I've solved hundreds of by hand and in video games. As with nonograms, the game's beauty lies in the fact that the rules are are simple and it is purely logic-based (instead of relying on gimmicks or time-limits). That means that even in the later puzzles, which can be a bit challenging, you never have to resort to guess-work and anyone can solve them easily with enough focus and time.
It's true the game was far too short (you can get 100% completion in a few hours), but now that I've tried it I would recommend it even at full price, though of course preferably wait for a sale. Apparently, the third installment has a random puzzle generator, which soundss like exactly the kind of thing this kind of game needs, but I will have to try it to see. Regardless, this game has proven the concept amazingly well and given my brains a few solid hours of work to do for the price of a cup of coffee.

If you enjoyed any other Platinum games then this is definitely a must buy.
For everyone else, I'd wholeheartedly reccomend getting it if you're looking for an interesting and strange experience in terms of story and world. It might seem like a by the numbers modern JRPG (in terms of story) with hack and slash combat in the beginning, but it slowly builds into a heartwarming, feels generating game. The art direction on the characters is excellent in terms of style, thematically its weak but its easy to look past it once you settle into their personalities. Though I can see why the character design can put some people off. Main story is excellent, it will drive you with intrigue as there is something new around every corner to ponder about or discover. Side quest (from the ones I did) had interesting enough hooks to pull me to them, some however can feel bogstandard (mostly just collectathons), while others will make you chuckle as they make fun of tropes from gaming and other media. The world can feel dull in some places, areas like the desert, the theme park and the forest and strong and distinct, while the city is dreary and boring (which may be the point honestly but it stil could have used a defining feature). Combat is very smooth and intuitive like most other platinum games, but it lacks the depth in comparison other games in the genre like bayonetta or the old DMC's. It's fun but don't expect to be reading through an expansive moveset or exprementing with many different combanations. There is the addition of the POD which is a nice touch of utility and ranged combat that can spice things up sometimes.The upgrade system uses chips that can be inserted to add different benefits to the character. The idea is cool and well implemented as each upgrade actually gives new dynamics to the combat instead just [INSERT PERCENTAGE STATS HERE] though some do fall under that category. For the love of god though play the game on HARD, its very easy to break on normal with certain chipsets that practically make you an unkillable god (looking at you auto and deadly heal).
Pacing can feel off in the second part of the game but it solves that in the third act.
Overall, this things a 9.5/10. If you can look past the character design (if you hate that sort of thing) please play this, I gurantee you won't experience what it gives you in any other piece of media that exist or ever will exist.

I bought Outcast in 1999, shortly after release and it has been one of my favourite games of all time. Perhaps, nostalgia is one of the main factors but one can not deny Outcast is/was a solid adventure game.
Outcast takes you on a sci-fi journey in a parallel universe in which you are on a quest to save not one, but two worlds. The world filled with strange creatures and inhabitants and a rich story with romance and deceit.
Back in '99, Outcast was way ahead of it's time using technologies which haven't (often) been seen in other games. Technologies like: Lip Sync and characters would actually look you in the eyes. Outcast was one of the first 3D Sandbox games (as far as I know) with beautiful graphics. The world is amazing and fun to explore and every npc has his own role in the game. The CGI also was ahead of it's time and pretty well done combined with the terrific orchestral soundtracks. Due to this, the game's production costs were very high, which should not be a real problem if it sells.
Sadly, Outcast did not sell well, even though almost every game magazine gave it a perfect rating. A developing attempt was made for Outcast 2 but this never happened. The kickstarter for an Outcast remake failed aswell, so the only way we ever get to see an Outcast 2 is if the classic sells well.
Obviously, Nowadays this is not the prettiest game anymore and the controlls are a bit wonky. Still, Outcast remains a great sci-fi experience and it's still well playable. I recommend this game to anyone who is not afraid of aged graphics and just want an amazing experience playing one of the best games ever made.

... utter genius.

There is a real sense of charm and wit to the world design. Occasionally self-aware, usually always surprising.
The boss battles are the most poetic, balletic, multi-staged, beautiful experiences... If Dark Souls wants to terrify you again and again and again with ever grander hideousness... this game wants to visually delight you, surprise you, provide you with an indelible memory that's unlike anything you've seen before.

In the third installment of the Pajama Sam series, Sam eats his way through several boxes of cookies in order to collect the right amount of box tops in exchange for a Pajama Man action figure. Right when he opens the final box, all of the cookies come jumping out and storm into the kitchen. Sam knows they were up to no good and decides to trial them as "Pajama Sam". Upon entering the kitchen Sam soon enters yet another world of his imagination inside the kitchen storage room which is a gateway to a food world. All six food groups of the world aren't in peace with each other and the only ones who can stablize peace are the food delicates of each food group. It's up to Sam to prevent a war from breaking out. Unlike in the previous two games, Sam isn't over coming any fears in this game, instead it's about preventing war and learning about the food groups as he progresses his mission. The story is just as inventive as the previous installments and the characters and jokes once again are clever and well thought out. If you love the last two Pajama Sam games, then you can't go wrong with this one.

This game is ambitious and falls flat. It is gorgeous, with some really interesting mechanics, good soundtrack, etc. and is frustratingly unplayable.
It tries to be simple, which in a game of this magnitude is just poor design. Take trade. Trade is core to the game, has interesting mechanics, etc. The problem is that you have, short of counting tiles, literally no way of knowing whether your trade network growing in size will get you more cities in it, let alone if those cities will generate more profit than not building a trade network. With a few simple UI adjustments (like saying what cities a market will reach, and how much will be generated) it would be fun. Instead, it's a blackbox of build markets everywhere and just assume it's good money.
Combat is also a blackbox. There is a huge amount of city building that can get you cool advanced units. Short of siege weapons necessary to pierce even the most trivial of defenses, I am not sure any of it is worth the investment. Huge battles between hordes of peasants versus elite troops resolve with comparable losses, and drag out over 10 or 20 turns. The combat reports don't help to explain that, just let you know that. Sieges can take anywhere from a turn to 20, with no real indiciation of progress or explanation for why. Even EU4's notorious siege percentage system is more informative.
Fun fact, naval transports are useful, but can only be put in stacks of 4. Since armies are in stacks of 8, you need a whole whack of micro to cross a river system without looping through a ford. Not to mention loading, unloading everything manually. See a feature, see it poorly/half/frustratingly implemented.
Fun fact, if your moves cause a One Army Per Tile conflict, guess what they do? Both armies sit there, with no notification to you. So two armies can be stuck, literally forever, both trying to go to the same tile. This happens a lot of with armies set to autoexplore.
Fun fact, sometimes your tax collectors just don't. No warning, no explanation, just rolling over a turn to discover that you incurred all your expenses with 0 income... So welcome to however many turns of debt, twiddling your thumbs.
Even the victory conditions are opaque. Conquest seems impossible with the city limit system, so short of literally razing all of China to the ground, you can't. The diplomatic victory is impossible unless you cut everyone down to size, see conquest problem. Plus, sieges take literally forever, and moving across the landscape is tediously slow. What doesn't take forever is accumulating a lot of money and spamming temples for a culture victory, which is at least achievable if boring. There is also a score victory condition, which is basically cultural victory but slower.
This game is probably a diamond, but it's still in the ground.

This is a great game!  I have been playing games in this genre for more than 25 years now and I am pleased that a game like this has finally come along. People seem to have quickly drawn comparisons to the total war series and civilization series of games, and it is understandable, I will have to add in the romance of the 3 kingsdoms games to that list and equally so. One thing I would like to point out is that All of those games have been around for more than 20 years, they all carved a sort of niche for themselves in the style of game they were going to deliver and are sort of stuck on a set of rails to deliver a similar experience through progressing titles. What I absolutely love about this game is that by combining many of the elements of these games together so well, it sort of allows you to play any and all of them at once and get to do some of the things that you always wished you could in the other games.
I had always wished I could explore more, and build my own cities in the total war and romance games and this allows me to do that, also the combat system in this game while simplified yes compared to total war still has enough to it that it is more immersive than smacking the auto resolve button which 80 percent or more of those battles have come to in that series, in this game it is taken as stretegic planning and you cen set how you want each individual unit to behave and more or less perform as during the anticipated engagement. I like this because it it is more personal and also allows a game in which running an empire with hundreds of engagements and small unit actions is viable and more meaningfull as opposed to three or four doom stacks like some of the other games encourage.  This one of the ways that it breaks hard from rock paper scissors combat in the civilization games and I had always wished that game had just more involvement with the troops.. I think this game has a good balance.
The city building in this game is meaningful and forces you to make choices which help you stay immersed in the actual running of your faction. so many of us have been trained by these other games to just build whatever we want wherever we want it and to be honest we have been spoiled. I like that this game makes individual cities matter more as whole by making each one defined and integrated into how your faction balances its budget and need for proper troops as the game progresses.
There is alot of ways they can move this game forward where be it in more user familiar interface functions or to choose elements that either help to immerse the player more into the era chosen or thoose the path of simply expanding the game outside the region and peoples that are already in game.

This is probably the best balanced 4x game made in recent years. Game appears barebones at first, but game mechanics and rules work very well. Offers more ways to play than seem immediately apparent. Can viably play as a typical empire builder, pillaging horde, mountain hermit kingdom, or colonial trade tycoon. Game rewards planning and harshly punishes carelessness. Each faction in the campaign presents you with different challenges simply based on their geagraphic position. Would like to see more options for espionage, sabotage, and tile improvements. AI seems unable to use boats.
Money is scarce so you'll have to manage your expensive armies carefully. Trade routes absolutely must be defended and are not just bonus income like other games of this type. Two other empires might be fighting each other but if one was a big trade partner poverty is a real motivator to get involved. Sell pots. Upgrade the markets for the multipliers.
Farms are valuable so turtling in the city is never an option. Put those things where you can defend them. Peasants are morons and will revolt if they work too hard making farms but will then revolt when there's a food shortage but will also revolt if you overdraft the militia to defend the farms from the pillaging Huns so no one starves and revolts. But a drought hits anyways and now there's a food shortage, the lord dies in battle, causing the nobles to get uppity and now your vast empire is torn apart by a civil war and peasant uprising at the same time because your timing was bad. What's a lord to do?
True to the Warring States era, AI is extremely aggressive, backstabbing, and reasonably fair. Will attack if you show weakness. Does not seem to be getting free resources on harder difficulties. Will sometimes forget to bring archers to burn your gates down and will instead squat dozens of giant armies of peasants outside your gates, pillaging your farms, causing famine and revolts.

TL;DR: Read the Conclusion at the bottom of this review!
2265 A.D. - 3 Collective (meaning Slavers) alien races declare war onme.  They have a combined strength of 15K-20K. Me, playing as the human United Nations, had overstretched. Too many planets, and a navy with only 2K strength to fend off 3 enemies with 10 times my military size. There was no way I could win, so I cede. I negotiate a peace treaty with 2 of the alien races and give them 2 of my planets
They then proceeded to enslave every human on the 2 planets I gave them. I had abandoned my own people to slavery on the promise of colonial riches. I actually felt bad for abandoning them :'(
But I also went into a fit of rage. I was still fighting 1 alien enslaving empire. Despite still being outnumbered, I fought a war of attrition, getting them to attack my space stations to decrease their strength, despite losing some of my space stations. My economy went into overdrive, every planet was churning out ships and I was running a government budget deficit.
2281 A.D. - After 16 years of war, I defeated the alien bug race with whom I had was still fighting against. I had smashed their military and economic strength and my allies, who initially didn't send fleets in, eventually sent them over and helped me defeat my enemy.
But the other 2 empires still had control over my 2 planets that I ceded to them. Worse yet, the humans they enslaved there were running out - THEY WERE FORBIDDEN FROM BREEDING :'(
There was still much work to be done.
2291 A.D. - After the 10 year ceasefire was over, I went to war again with the alien race I had smashed earlier. I won in 3 years, although I failed to successfully capture their capital planet, their homeworld, I still managed to take out the rest of their planets and establish a Vassal State which eventually integrated into my empire.
Initially, I purged some of the aliens living in the vassal state that I made once they integrated, but my people didn't like that since they were very individualistic and as such, I went back on my purge policy. Purging is a combination of ethnic/species cleansing and genocide.
But the 2 other empires still had my 2 planets where there were still a few humans left.
2309 A.D. - A few years before, the 2 empires that still had the 2 planets with humans enslaved in them had gone to war against another, powerful empire. This was good news, all I had to do was wait. Eventually their military would wind down, they would become weak, and then I could strike, reclaim the 2 lost planets with whatever humans were still left there after over 5 decades  of slavery :(
in 2309, the time came.  I negotiated help from a different empire that I had good relations with. My plan was, I can't go after both the empires on my own, but if I can keep one empire distracted by fighting a war with my ally, I can focus on the other one.
2325 A.D. - The plan worked. After another 15 year war, humans were once again united everywhere. It had been almost 3/4ths of a century since those planets were lost in a peace settlement which saw them abandoned, so I decided to give them their own independent state, but I also sent them a guaranteed monthly economic aid of minerals and energy credits to help them themselves back up on their feet. It comprised almost 25% of monthly government profit. Within 2 weeks they asked to become a vassal so they could be protected properly. Soon they will be re-integrated back with the rest of humanity.
So what happens next? I don't know, but I now enjoy having the most powerful military in my region of the galaxy, and a healthy economy capable of growing my military into twice or even 3 times the size it currently is.
CONCLUSION: This game gives you amazing stories. Let your imagination go wild and run free,  it's the best way to enjoy this magnificent work of artistry that Paradox has produced =)

If you're new to the series I'd say start with BL2 and if you're turned into a fan BL:TPS is definitely worth your time and $20.
