Ok so actually about the game. I've clocked 40hours and considering ive only had the chance to finally play it in the last 2.5 days i'd say thats pretty evident to how truly addictive it can be.
Day 1 - plan to play for a couple hours at most before bed being 8pm at this point... ooohhhhhhh look something shiny on the map *bammm* its 7am. Where did me life go so wrong!!!
Day 2 - ok ok so i'm so im not going to play so long today, im not gonna play so long *mantra continues*, finally work out how to own more than 5 planets and start to catch up with the map (although by this stage it was already to late to grow anywhere) and guess what 7am came around to soon
Now - *must resist the temptation to play more*
Thats the life in this game. You start playing, you admire the depth of detail, start learning the basics whilst staying ahead of the map, next minute you know you're now trying to keep up with the AI as you didn't know the basics after all.
What makes this game great is the fact its not using a turn based system, i'm usually use to that more. But I thought I would give the game a go anyway due to the reviews here. Being "real time" it just makes the game run much more smoothly without thinking what to do each turn, instead being constant time you have to think non-stop or risk falling behind (which is so damn easy to do). The ship design option is great, i keep playing with it and still learning which works best. I also like the fact you are restricted to 5 planets (until research), it makes you think tactically, what I wish I had realised sooner was you need to then create sectors in a tactical way to then expand and colonise more.
Ok it has its flaws, there's not much events after a certain point or the events that do happen overwhelm your forces so much you just feel like curling up in a ball and crying. But i believe more things are planned to be added into the game in the future. I would also reiterate what others have said, if you last a long time on one map out of nowhere you begin to get lag, mid battle for example the ships just freeze, or you click to upgrade something and it takes 5seconds to respond, and this is  using a high end spec computer. It can be frustrating but to be honest for me it does no detract from the beauty of the game.
Overall 10/10 the devs and paradox have really done well here and it truly is amazing

The only words I can think of to describe this game are " B-rank cult classic."
The story is cheesy yet entertaining; for example, you travel to another dimension (interesting), but the dialog is hilarious (like the reason for doing so is because the world is facing a “diamond-level threat,” apparently). The made up alien language sounds silly, and they somehow also speak English (or at least it seems that way). But it’s entertaining. It’s one of those things that are so cheesy they’re lovable.
The same can be said for the animation; it’s basically a lower-resolution version of Team America. The forehead wrinkles and eyebrow movement must have been new at the time, because they certainly spared no expense in using them. The price of admission is worth it just to watch the hilarious expressions the characters make.  And the mouth movement is pretty much exactly like Team America, because of the limited jaw movement available for the character models.
And the controls! They’re just as amusing as the story and animation! They’re just so weird. For example, when you first start and if you haven’t drawn your weapon, the left mouse button is a jump button. It’s completely weird and doesn’t really work, but it’s so quirky that it’s entertaining! Also, the screen text read, “Press the Space Bar to crawl,” but that also made me jump. I just messed with the buttons until I figured out that C was to crawl.
Character interaction was amusing too; I was trying to figure out how to stealth in the game for a quest, kept failing because of the weird buttons (was slowly getting it), and apparently the character took pity on me and then gave me an item to help me out…and the item wasn’t even remotely useful for that one quest haha. Anyway, failed again just because the funky controls (was my first quest and apparently was supposed to be the “hard” quest), and rather than make me do the quest…the character was like “Don’t worry…a lot of the young warriors can’t complete this quest…” Basically, I received the ultimate gaming insult, an “A for effort.”  I also found this amusing, because what game does that?!
If you want a silly, quirky game and you don’t mind learning odd controls, I would recommend this game. It’s just too unique to pass up.
Also, I wasn’t actually even going to play this game for a while (too many other ones to play), but almost every time I turn on Steam, there’s an update to some part of this game. Usually it’s only a few mb, but so many updates. I haven’t ever had a game that was so well-supported, and based on that level of customer service, I would buy this game again in a heartbeat. Thank you, caring developer! While I may not have the time to finish this little gem for a while, I notice and appreciate the effort!

If you want to support sci-fi silliness, love, and B-rank goodness, this is a good purchase. If you don’t like all of those things, just be warned that it’s not gonna be some open-world Star Wars game. If you don't mind the controls, you still might like it for the unique experience.

Hello everyone,
First off, I have only owned this game for two days and have only had a single playthrough so far. This playthrough has been immensely successful as I neither found the game hard to understand nor difficult to learn your way around. But when I came out to look at the reviews on the store page, I was utterly stunned by the number of thumbs down for this game.
First off, this game is positively beautiful. The landscape, the music, the detail put into everything from background artwork to little figures running around constructing your empire.... all of it builds to a world you can, and I regularly do, get immersed in for hours as I forget I live in the 21st century rather than Bronze Age China. Each faction has a distinct style of play, and should be played as such. This is NOT a game you can just pick a faction and expect it to work like another faction you may have tried in the past. Some call this unbalanced, I call this realistic and therefore REFRESHINGLY WONDERFUL in my book.
Each playthrough is organic and a learning experience, you start off with one city and build where you like, when you like. Contrary to what others have said on these reviews, placing your towns strategically makes ALL THE DIFFERENCE between a lost campaign and one in which you are on your way to becoming Emperor of China. You cannot expect a mountain town to have tons of food, and you cannot expect a plains town near a body of water to not get flooded sometimes. Learning factional quirks will help you understand how to approach each of them. Some factions are cowardly and prefer to stab opponents in the back when they arnt looking, others are ferocious and come full force, some are loyal to a fault if you befriend them. Also, that is another thing, this is a game that you cannot go through without learning how diplomacy works in the real world, just like you cannot go through it without learning how actual economies work. Trade flourishes in times of peace and dies in times of war, building farms helps with food but unless you tax it you wont make any income on it, I could go on and on. This game gets two BIG thumbs up from me as being one of the most expansive, interesting, and wonderful games I have seen in a long time. Please do not listen to those who did not take the time to try to learn it, or expected it to be like various games they have played in the past. I am a veteran Total War player and found this reminicient of a lot of concepts I have seen used in the past, but unlike in Total War, every playthrough is different and every faction is utterly different from the last.
Played the Han who were supposed to be wiped out by too many enemies, made friends with half of them, now on my way to becoming Emperor of China on my first playthrough. 10/10 would be used by my Chu vassals to wipe out half the map before realizing they were playing me again.

Verdict: Nier is slightly above average, carried mainly by the story and amazing soundtrack. However, in a world that has a ton of games that are well above average, many for less than $60, Nier doesn’t cut it. It’s worth a play for the story, but I’d hold off until it goes on sale, unless you really have absolutely nothing else to play.
Pros: Amazing music, great story, and cool theme.
Cons: If you don't have a controller you probably want to skip this one.
Performance: Running the game on a GTX 1070 FTW, Skylake i7, and 16GB of RAM at 1080p. Even when I ran the game on lowest settings I still experienced some pretty major stuttering problems throughout the game. V-sync also completely tanks my performance and stops me from getting even a solid 30fps. Unfortunately, without v-sync on there is very noticeable and frequent screen tearing. Luckily there are some community mods out there that help with these problems, but it seems unacceptable that these problems are still persistent after almost 2 months for a game with a $60 price tag.
Load Times: I’m guessing this also has to do with the poor port, but for whatever reason a lot of the time loading screens are upwards of 30 seconds. This wouldn’t be so bad if it wasn’t for the fact that the vast majority of the games quests are fetch quests which require you to teleport around quite a lot (and by proxy sit through a lot of loading screens).
World: All this time running from point A to point B for fetch quests wouldn’t be so bad if the world was interesting. Towards the end of the game some pretty cool areas unlock, but for the most part the world just feels super bland and empty. Even after unlocking the teleporter you still have to do a ton of running around to actually get anywhere- it almost feels like they tried to prolong the game this way. At least 10-15 hours, if not more, of my playtime was spent just holding forward, waiting to get someplace, or waiting for loading screens.
Combat: It's not terrible, but it's not great either. Combat definitely looks cool, but outside of that it feels very basic. After you get used to things the game basically has two difficulties: so easy you'll never die, or dying if you get hit once by anything on very hard. There's a happy medium a lot of good games strike, Nier doesn't get there.

If your child has played beginning level software and is ready to move on to more advanced gameplay, Humongous Entertainment's Pajama Sam series (and Freddie Fish and Putt-Putt as well) are an excellent choice. These titles take the cognitive tasks up a notch as children must accumulate specific items, navigate a number of locations, and use their problem-solving skills to help new friends and achieve larger goals. Along the way, funny and lovable Pajama Sam will meet a number of nice characters, visit a variety of interesting locations and play mini-games as he completes the larger task of getting a representative of each food group out of a pickle so they can get to an important meeting. Along the way he will solve a lot of smaller puzzles and click on many objects that dance or act out funny events. Specifics change if you start a new game, and you will want to play with your child a few times before they'll be able to enjoy it on their own, so each game is good for hours of fun.

It's great to back in Saxton! The series debut
rates among one of my alltime favourite point n' click games. The tones and nuance of the atmosphere throughout the games memorable scenes, the extremely accomplished and artful use of fairly lo-fi graphics, the eccentric yet sincere English regionalism of the setting and cast, intelligently written puzzles and mysteries and a haunting soundtrack lifted that game above so many other ghostly themed titles. This is a short point and click game that follows The Lost Crown.  It is set in the same town with many of the same characters but is a much smaller game.  I finished it in about 8 hours playing very leisurely but an experienced adventure gamer may finish in just a couple of  hours.  There are only a few puzzles and they are not very difficult.  There are lots of things that seem important but don't lead anywhere, and you can sidetracked on them. There are no steam achievements for it.
During play it can seem like you're stuck and not making any progress.  You'll perform some action and it isn't immediately clear sometimes that you've done anything.   There are choices that will affect the outcome if not the main story line.  I saw questions in the forums asking whether or not the game was bugged.  I played through without any issues at all and I think it plays as designed.  My advice if you're stuck is to look around thoroughly, talk to everyone multiple times, do actions multiple times (even if they don't seem to do anything), and don't forget outside.  There are only a few areas in this game so there really isn't that much to check.  I would not resort to a walkthough because there are very few things to solve here and you'll probably regret it.  I'd recommend this game to anyone who likes point and click adventure games.

The Last Crown: Midnight Horror is not up to the quality of the previous games. It was often the case that I had to do something I didn't expect in order to trigger the next thing to do. I ended up using a walkthrough to help me complete the game. If you don't play this one, you're not missing anything.

I have just completed, a "special Halloween stream" of Midnight Horror. It was a lot of fun, as well as spooky!
Compared to the last game (The Lost Crown), this takes place in a smaller area but has smoother animations with improved fluidity; the quality of models and textures are also better. The game is meant as a fun filler between The Lost Crown and upcoming Blackenrock, designed to be completed in just a few hours. The gameplay is a lot less serious too, and there are some funny moments: eggings, Nigel hanging around outside pub toilets trying to listen in on discussions about "legal highs", and a drunk bloke trying to chat up a skeleton.
Sadly, to progress in the game sometimes requires the player to hit arbitrary triggers, e.g. looking at a family tree triggers someone to leave a room, Nigel needs to consume exactly the right amount of cheese and alcohol to make something important happen; so following a walkthrough is mandatory, unless you enjoy brute-force trying everything (with little or no hints) until something works.
Final thoughts: it's not a well designed game, it's not a technical masterpiece, but there is something hilarious about playing a flatcap wearing, down-and-out, keptomaniac man who stinks of PROWL and insists ghosts are real. Play it with friends, you'll probably have a laugh.
Can't wait for Blackenrock!

Party Hard is a strange indie gem that is more of a methodical and evenly paced dark twisted relative of Hotline Miami, with stealth and it's dark sense of humour adding to the majority of it's charm. The storyline is based around it's slasher-film-esque main character, who simply wants to get some rest, but as his acts of violence escalate, so does his story.
Taking alot of inspiration from previously mentioned slasher films from the 80s, with elements of The Guest (synth music and murderous vibes) and murder methods dreamt up from something you'd read in Tyler, The Creator's early lyrics, Party Hard is a great time killer, as well as a great party killer.
The game has some issues too, but these are minor. The bugs are mainly in the achievement section of the game, the final achievement will unlock itself at a random part of the game, and the Engineer achievement no longer works on the Party Bus level, so instead, I recommend completing the game first, and going back to the first level in the Cop uniform and completing that 3 times instead. But apart from that, nothing else really negative to say.

TL;DR: Read the Conclusion at the bottom of this review!
2265 A.D. - 3 Collective (meaning Slavers) alien races declare war onme.  They have a combined strength of 15K-20K. Me, playing as the human United Nations, had overstretched. Too many planets, and a navy with only 2K strength to fend off 3 enemies with 10 times my military size. There was no way I could win, so I cede. I negotiate a peace treaty with 2 of the alien races and give them 2 of my planets
They then proceeded to enslave every human on the 2 planets I gave them. I had abandoned my own people to slavery on the promise of colonial riches. I actually felt bad for abandoning them :'(
But I also went into a fit of rage. I was still fighting 1 alien enslaving empire. Despite still being outnumbered, I fought a war of attrition, getting them to attack my space stations to decrease their strength, despite losing some of my space stations. My economy went into overdrive, every planet was churning out ships and I was running a government budget deficit.
2281 A.D. - After 16 years of war, I defeated the alien bug race with whom I had was still fighting against. I had smashed their military and economic strength and my allies, who initially didn't send fleets in, eventually sent them over and helped me defeat my enemy.
But the other 2 empires still had control over my 2 planets that I ceded to them. Worse yet, the humans they enslaved there were running out - THEY WERE FORBIDDEN FROM BREEDING :'(
There was still much work to be done.
2291 A.D. - After the 10 year ceasefire was over, I went to war again with the alien race I had smashed earlier. I won in 3 years, although I failed to successfully capture their capital planet, their homeworld, I still managed to take out the rest of their planets and establish a Vassal State which eventually integrated into my empire.
Initially, I purged some of the aliens living in the vassal state that I made once they integrated, but my people didn't like that since they were very individualistic and as such, I went back on my purge policy. Purging is a combination of ethnic/species cleansing and genocide.
But the 2 other empires still had my 2 planets where there were still a few humans left.
2309 A.D. - A few years before, the 2 empires that still had the 2 planets with humans enslaved in them had gone to war against another, powerful empire. This was good news, all I had to do was wait. Eventually their military would wind down, they would become weak, and then I could strike, reclaim the 2 lost planets with whatever humans were still left there after over 5 decades  of slavery :(
in 2309, the time came.  I negotiated help from a different empire that I had good relations with. My plan was, I can't go after both the empires on my own, but if I can keep one empire distracted by fighting a war with my ally, I can focus on the other one.
2325 A.D. - The plan worked. After another 15 year war, humans were once again united everywhere. It had been almost 3/4ths of a century since those planets were lost in a peace settlement which saw them abandoned, so I decided to give them their own independent state, but I also sent them a guaranteed monthly economic aid of minerals and energy credits to help them themselves back up on their feet. It comprised almost 25% of monthly government profit. Within 2 weeks they asked to become a vassal so they could be protected properly. Soon they will be re-integrated back with the rest of humanity.
So what happens next? I don't know, but I now enjoy having the most powerful military in my region of the galaxy, and a healthy economy capable of growing my military into twice or even 3 times the size it currently is.
CONCLUSION: This game gives you amazing stories. Let your imagination go wild and run free,  it's the best way to enjoy this magnificent work of artistry that Paradox has produced =)

This game truly is a masterpiece, and the best roguelike on Steam. Whether you're looking for just a short bit of fun or an intense and extrmeley challenging experience, The Binding of Isaac can offer both with very rewarding outcomes. Everytime you play this game, you will fight new enemies, pick up new items, see new things and generally have a whole different gameplay experience than the last time you played. I think that's where the magic lies in this game. The game encourages you to keep playing so you can see all it has to offer. Even with my 100 hours sunk into this game, I still have not unlocked all the game's secrets. Isaac is a different kind of game altogether, and what I once thought was a ridiculously simplistic game of being a naked baby crying on enemies in an attempt to escape from your mother proved to be a deep and altogether engaging experienceof a game. Yes, Isaac Rebirth has been released already and many have moved on from the original, yet I still think the vanilla game still holds some charms that the remake does not. This truly is the best roguelike game you could ever wish for, and at five dollars you'd be doing yourself a great disservice by not purchasing this fantastic gem.

Ok so actually about the game. I've clocked 40hours and considering ive only had the chance to finally play it in the last 2.5 days i'd say thats pretty evident to how truly addictive it can be.
Day 1 - plan to play for a couple hours at most before bed being 8pm at this point... ooohhhhhhh look something shiny on the map *bammm* its 7am. Where did me life go so wrong!!!
Day 2 - ok ok so i'm so im not going to play so long today, im not gonna play so long *mantra continues*, finally work out how to own more than 5 planets and start to catch up with the map (although by this stage it was already to late to grow anywhere) and guess what 7am came around to soon
Now - *must resist the temptation to play more*
Thats the life in this game. You start playing, you admire the depth of detail, start learning the basics whilst staying ahead of the map, next minute you know you're now trying to keep up with the AI as you didn't know the basics after all.
What makes this game great is the fact its not using a turn based system, i'm usually use to that more. But I thought I would give the game a go anyway due to the reviews here. Being "real time" it just makes the game run much more smoothly without thinking what to do each turn, instead being constant time you have to think non-stop or risk falling behind (which is so damn easy to do). The ship design option is great, i keep playing with it and still learning which works best. I also like the fact you are restricted to 5 planets (until research), it makes you think tactically, what I wish I had realised sooner was you need to then create sectors in a tactical way to then expand and colonise more.
Ok it has its flaws, there's not much events after a certain point or the events that do happen overwhelm your forces so much you just feel like curling up in a ball and crying. But i believe more things are planned to be added into the game in the future. I would also reiterate what others have said, if you last a long time on one map out of nowhere you begin to get lag, mid battle for example the ships just freeze, or you click to upgrade something and it takes 5seconds to respond, and this is  using a high end spec computer. It can be frustrating but to be honest for me it does no detract from the beauty of the game.
Overall 10/10 the devs and paradox have really done well here and it truly is amazing

First thing first, there are two reason why I don't like Magicite: first, I've notice an overwhelming amount of thumbs up, which might gives potential buyer an overly-exagerated positive impression. Secondly, the game is targeting a very specific player, and only that specific player, i.e: only people who enjoys challenges and speedrunning - which some might even argue it's a matter of taste. However, if you're a big, big fan of rogue-like games such as Spelunky (which I like more than Magicite), Rogue Legacy (of which I like more than Spelunky, way more than Magicite), or The Binding of Isaac (a game I played less than I would like due to fear of addiction) then the best way to describe Magicite is this: if Spelunky have a fling with Terraria's crafting system, the end result would be Magicite. However, if you're still on the fence I'll elaborate a little more.
As mentioned earlier, the problem I have with Magicite is that even though I like the game, the game doesn't like me back. The permadeath system I'm not a fan of, but if I could tolerate that in Spelunky, Rogue Legacy, and Isaac I could certainly tolerate that in Magicite. So what has changed? The answer is immediately obvious, Magicite utilizes a unique crafting system that's usually a common component of sandbox games, a decision I found questionable. In most sandbox games, you can take all the time you need to google it or even just look up the in game recipe book, browse through all the stat and decide upon which build you like; you have all the time in the world to plan out your build without having to worried about monster chasing you, if you camp in a safe area. Such luxury isn't available in Magicite, if you take too long in the map, the scourge ( a  group of monster that can K.O player in one hit) will hunt you down Mafia style unless you exit the map quickly. I frequently have to pause and look at the recipe, unpause to open the inventory before crafting because otherwise the game time would flow and the scourge will be that much closer to me, which hampers the flow of game somewhat. While some might enjoy speeding through the game world and crafting on the fly. I personally do not find that enjoyable, my crafting persona and my rogue-like speedrunner persona reside in different area of my consciousness and I prefer to keep them seperate. Had the game either includes more equipment loot so that I don't have to worry about crafting my own weapon on the fly, or not rush me with the "Scourge" so that I can take my time with crafting, Magicite would be far more enjoyable. At this point I wouldn't recommend paying the full 10 dollars for Magicite. Wait for a sale of at least 50% off.

Pros:
-Lot of good ideas for mechanics
-Devs did their homework in flavor text and historical settings.
-Good time killer
Cons:
-Lots and lots of bugs
-UI a bit stiff
-Fixed identities, e.g. if your political entity is X you get fixed buffs/debuffs. You can reform, say, from nomad to agriculture like you can in Paradox titles. I get this is a civ inspired game, but the devs seems to have done a lot of history homework so I would have expected more. An eu-styled decision/reform system wouldn't be hard to implement and would have made the game experience much better.
-Mod support
-Lots of micromanagement
In the end I think this game has a lot of potential and there are lots of things I like about it. But in the end, it might be worth it if you're really into 4X, but at present the micromanagement and bugs in mid/late game make the overall game experience poor.

I'd like to start by saying I had issues with this game crashing on start, but I came back to this game after I had to install old versions of Physx for a different game and I wondered if this game would also be fixed. Turns out it, that fixed it. I played through the whole game on Win 10 x64 after I installed old versions of physx manually.  It never crashed and ran great.
Next I'd like to give some advice, don't use a controller its just way too hard to control.  This game is best played holding the forward button on the keyboard, and use the mouse to "steer" the cat.  Once you get this down, you can actually do some pretty good moves with the cat. There was a steep learning curve, but when you get the hang of it, the control can actually be pretty fun.
Next Advice is that you should use the F5 quick save all the time, at least for the jump puzzle type parts, so you won't have to re-do any of the skill jumps.
OK, so back to the review.  I really liked this game.  Sure, at first i was super frustrated with the control, but you get good at it if you keep trying.  Its true this is an indie game and almost everything seems a little ruff around the edges, the jumping and physx engine being the worst part.  If you get used to the quirks, the artwork, music, voices, story are all entertaining.  The gameplay is varied enough to keep you from getting bored.  A bonus is that there is a poetry reciting minigame, that acually teaches you some poetry from Alice Through the Looking glass. I love indie games and this is a great example of why, where else are you going to  get game content that is actually something new.  Anyway, the game is the right length, about 3hrs.  At about that time they either needed to have a new mission type, or just end the game, and so it seemed like a good place to stop.
The artwork is just great (minus the animations) and it even has correct 5.1 surround sound support (even many non indie games get that wrong).  If you like cats, every kind of cat, and if you want to hug all of them, then this game is for you!

I've said before that fans of space trading/combat sim fans have waited for years for a decent game.   Elite, Privateer and Freelancer have not had any particularly brillant successors.
Galaxy on Fire is good, and does still belong at very the end of that list.  The ship designs are excellent, weapons fire, local stars and nebula look beautiful.  The sounds are great, and the music is awesome even if it gets repetitive after a couple of hours.
I found the overall experience astonishing on ipad, because of what the developers were able to run on such  a weak gaming platform, but on PC it's a lot less impressive, even with the higher resolution textures.  Visuals are better than Freelancer, not as good as X3.
The combat is simple, but fun, and very reminisent of Freelancer.  Upgrading your ship is rewarding and will keep you cracking through the game despite the lacklustre storyline and it's cheesy cartoon characters.
The trading is very simple, with no real economy to speak of, so if you're a fan of X3 or Eve Online because of the economy and empire building aspect of the gameplay, then this won't be enough to keep you interested for very long.
The DLC availble for the ipad version is not availble for the PC release.
My advice - if you spend a lot of time gaming on an ipad - then get it FREE in SD (or very cheap in HD) from the app store.  If you want it for PC and the price isn't cheap enough for you, wait until Elite 4 or Star Citizen come out in 2015-onwards.  Good luck space sim fans, and hang in there... good stuff is coming, our long wait will soon be over.

Medieval 2: Total War is the 4th game in the Total War series and was released in 2006. It shows it's age a little when standing next to the newer games in the series, but is still fun to play. Medieval 2 is set in the latter half of the middle ages, between 1080 and the 1500's. Medieval 2, only allows you to play as 5 Factions when you first start out. All of these factions were the historically powerful factions of the age. Defeating additional factions unlocks them for play up to 17 different playable factions in total through campaign mode.
A mixture of real-time tactics and strategy, as well as turn-based gameplay, exploration and expansion, Medieval 2 is fun to play, but is starting to show it's age a little. I suppose we are getting spoiled in 2015 with games that have realistic looking characters; However, it is still fun and would be recommended to anyone who enjoys the Total War series.

I do not recommend this game, but, that being said it is one of my guilty pleasures.
Let me explain, I picked this game up rather cheaply a long time ago and by god is it bad. Holy moley, the graphics, the sound design, the gameplay, it's all so bad. But after the first five hours or so, a thought popped into my head, "Why am I still playing then?" This game held my attention for a glorious neigh on fifteen hours. Was it the fact that I was playing with my friends, or was the game secretly a gem? I'm not sure the answer but from all I could guess is that it had transcended horridness into glory, abysmal glory. When you get down to it I suppose I had fun due to the fact that you could send vehicles soaring skyward with a simple grenade toss, that using the jet pack to let your pitiful ground-locked friends to be eviscerated by the horde of raptors only to be one-shotted by those damn flyers was bloody hilarious. The fact that no matter the guns or tactics one of your friends would end up blowing you to bits with a grenade, or going invisible while you beg for them to save you.
I honestly think this is a game for a good few hours of laughs. Tragically after one play session too many, it just lost it's sheen. I think it was when me and my friend weren't cackling with laughter but just silently playing a bad game. When we both realized that this game would never be fun again. I've not played it since but maybe, maybe I'll return to the terrible wasteland of Orion and have another blast, but until that day, negative review for you my sweet summer child.

If you like Borderlands 2, then I would get this game on sale. It's pretty similar but there's also a lot of issues with it. Since it was made by 2k Australia, it almost seemed like they wanted a template to practice game development with. There's one or two vending machines on huge maps, the jokes are no longer cheesy but rather just freaking immature, and coupled with that, it makes me hate Australian accents. If you think any of the characters in Borderlands 2 are obnoxious, wait til you hear them with Australian accents and seemingly purposely trying to be obnoxious. A lot of the voice actors are reused and just plain bad which destroys joke delivery and any chance of them being funny. Around chapter 7/12 the game starts to become more fun but I'm pretty sure that's around when 2k took the game back because the format changed. There were less Australians npcs, maps became more concrete, and there was more than one damn vending machine available.
Now that I've explained just some of the issues here's some positives: I really like the introduction to laser and cyro weapons and if you wanted to get Jack's side of the story, then you're getting it. Borderlands 3 was also definitely confirmed in that ending. That's all I got. It's pretty easy to point out the negative. I don't really recommend it, but I don't not recommend it.

NieR:Automata™:
Summary:
Offering a fresh blend of action and RPG gameplay styles, NieR: Automata is the follow-up to the 2010 cult hit NieR, and combines the design talents of Drakengard designer Yoko Taro in collaboration with development team PlatinumGames. The game tells the story of androids 2B, 9S and A2 and their battle to reclaim a machine-driven dystopia overrun by powerful weapons known as machine lifeforms.
Invaders from another world attack without warning, unleashing their secret weapon: the machines. In the face of this insurmountable threat, the human race is driven from the earth and takes refuge on the moon. The humans develop an army of android soldiers to fight back against the mechanical horde, but succeed only in slowing its advance. To break the deadlock, a new breed of android infantry is sent into the fray: the YoRHa squad. In the forsaken wasteland below, the war between the machines and the androids rages on. A war that is soon to unveil the long-forgotten truth of this world...

This game. This ♥♥♥♥ing game.
First of all: I generally don't write reviews, but this is a special case. So please bear with me.
Secondly: with all due respect, Roger Ebert (may he rest in peace) can suck my less-than-average-sized left testicle because this game is a work of art.
Nier: Automata is in the same vein as games like Undertale or Pony Island (albeit more impressive and on a grander scale): to tell you exactly WHY this game is so great would be to ruin the whole experience. Suffice it to say that this game ticks all the boxes:
- great story,
- great characters,
- AMAZING soundtrack by Keiichi Okabe (which is itself as complex and intricate as the game as a whole),
- great combat system, which transitions seamlessly between multiple genres during even the same sequence - a concept that SOUNDS jarring and clunky but is executed remarkably by Platinum Games,
- unique and interesting world.
- some of the most heartening and simultaneously haunting and creepy explorations of the human mind I've seen... maybe ever...
All of this combines to create one of the funnest, most fleshed out and thought provoking experiences I have encountered in a game, atleast recently.
I could elaborate so much more on every element of this game but to do so would take far too much time, and as I mentioned before, I believe the best way to enjoy this game is to go in somewhat blind without spoiling any of the more intricate, obscure and interesting elements of it. While there have been many great games over the years, few are on par with Nier: Automata. A true masterpice. (Suck it BOTW, in Nier you can run more than 10 metres before running out of breath. And kill more than 1 enemy with a single weapon.)
Thank You Yoko Taro. Thank You Keiichi Okabe. Thank You Platinum Games.
P.S. This game made me appreciate Shakespeare on a whole new level :)

Outcast is certainly worth a playthrough, even today. After 15 years, there have been little to no other games following its game concept of an open-world third-person shooter where you don't just shoot everyone (OWTPSWYDJSE in short), and the "stranger in a strange world" setting concept is almost extinct because consumers prefer things they know.
This game will throw you into a strange world and force you to adapt to being called the Ulukai, to everything and its mother being or having a "Fandazma", and to saving with a "Gaamsaav".
The gameplay is solid third-person shooting with the ability to switch to first person, but it is sadly hindered by its technical nature.
This is because it uses Voxels. These are basically 3D pixels that face in a certain direction, giving the illusion of a 3D world. Everything except small objects and characters is made out of Voxels. When you turn around, you'll notice "scan lines" going through the world - these adjust the Voxels into a new direction. Overall it looks really weird, but I don't know if it would look better or worse if the game had used polygon technology back then.
Point of the matter is that there is no such "adjusting mechanic" vertically. You'll notice that when you talk to an NPC in an elevated position - the ground behind you or them vanishes. To prevent that in normal gameplay, your camera has a very limited vertical range, even in first person, meaning you can't shoot enemies from, say a ledge. Extremely frustrating.
To make up for this, in third person your character will auto-aim vertically, but that's not too reliable and auto-aim sucks in general. If this was fixed, the gameplay would be absolutely solid third/first-person shooting, unless you have a fetish for chest-high walls and bloody screens.
Something else I noticed is that the voice quality seems to be low. I always thought Talan voices were modulated to sound more alien, but even the humans sound weird, which leads me to believe that they're in a low bitrate.
Luckily, this doesn't affect the soundtrack. Which is spectacular, by the way. For one of the first games to use orchestral music, Outcast's is simply phenomenal. Incredible achievement by Lennie Moore, I would have backed the kickstarter for his involvement if nothing else.
The 1.1 improvements are good enough. The original Outcast had a highly limited resolution range (below 640x480) which could be modified to run at 1280x720 with terrible performance. This release updated that to a max resolution of 1920x1080. This is still a limit to some, but the game seems to be running with DirectX 8 currently, which has a max resolution of 2048x1536 (everything above 1920x1080 leads to problems though). The performance is still relatively bad, but playable. The game's probably biggest curiosity is that it runs entirely on the CPU, which even today simply is not made for graphical calculations. The multi-core support and updated compiler helped, but even on an Haswell-E it only uses 20% per core, resulting in a framerate of somewhere between 20 and 90 FPS.
To be blunt, just like the Kickstarter, the 1.1 Update has a certain amateurish vibe to it. The launcher has minor graphical glitches (and comes standard with an annoying Twitter panel that shows all Tweets mentioning Outcast), the setting menu has the standard Windows Forms icon and the intro video is played in Windows Media Player, and is stretched from 4:3 to 16:9. Still - it does its job, and the ongoing updates are laudable.
Overall, I'd say that Outcast 1.1 is worth its money, and moreso because unlike with other old games the money actually goes to the developers. I have followed Outcast casually throughout the years and saw how the devs tried to get their hands on the IP over and over until they finally got it in 2013. If that isn't dedication, nothing is.

Have you ever found yourself trying to sleep whilst your obnoxious housemate hosts, what seems like, the loudest party ever? Banged on the wall, screamed and smiled with satisfaction as the volume drops? Imagine taking this impulse even further and murdering each and every attendee. This is Party Hard. A pixel art, murderous puzzler where the party may last just a little too long.
Party Hard follows the story of a sadistic, serial killer attending gatherings across the country with the intent of being the last one standing. Whereas this is usually achieved with the consumption of energy drinks, Party Hard pursues a slightly more savage approach. You play as Darius who grows frustrated by a local party preventing his nightly routine. Armed with a small knife, Darius ignores the standard protocol of calling the police and systematically slaughters everyone from the bouncers to the DJ.
The narrative focuses on Darius’s increasing bloodlust, as he travels between parties, leaving a trail of bodies behind. Detective John West, who leads the investigation, has his own motivation for catching the perpetrator as his own daughter suffered at the hands of the maniac at the first party. The story gives context to the party locations and circumstances surrounding them. You are only treated to these small cinematic scenes during loading times though as participating in these massacres are why you will be playing Party Hard.
The first level is a standard, college party seen in teen films. Shady characters smoke around a bonfire, lightweights fall asleep in the bathroom and raunchy adolescents fondle around the side of the house. Approaching the party, you have a challenging task ahead of you as fifty or more people could be attending the rave. Killing these party-goers is as simple as pressing a button to quickly stab them. The obstacle is the witnesses. Armed with a small amount of stamina, chasing potential spectators can be impossible and soon, after a call to the law enforcement, a cop has a warrant for your arrest. Evading the pursuing policeman is an option, however, each time you allude them, they will return faster and more determined than before. Being spotted is not the most effective method to stop the party so you can either eliminate victims out of eyeshot or use other tools available to you.
Although the structure of the level remains the same, the activity within them will change each time. Aside from the numbers attending the affair, entire rooms can transform too. What was once a lounge room could become a meth lab. A group of dancers could be replaced by a drug deal which ultimately is raided by armed SWAT officers who assist you in reducing the number of victims. This diversity and unpredictability will have you adapting to your surroundings.
Regardless of the layout, the objective remains the same. Kill everyone. The ever-changing level will assist you with this perverse goal. A punch bowl can be poisoned, a gas canister ignited or you can even lure an advancing cop into a deadly bear trap. Utilizing these lethal weapons will drastically reduce the popularity of the party and as the numbers plummet, the level becomes increasingly tense.
As you reach the last dozen, opportunities are harder to come by. Thankfully, you are blessed with terrible dance moves so offensive, others will walk away from you shouting profanities behind them. Be careful though as annoying them too much may result in them beating you unconscious. As you stop the party with the exceptionally gruesome death of the DJ, you ironically dance alone like a maniac on the dance floor.
As you progress through the game, you visit a number of exotic locations and parties. Penthouse suites, executive yachts and even a party bus. Each has a brilliant soundtrack, which although on a loop, never outstayed its welcome. Each stage retains the random ethos with new haphazard such as wood-chippers, dancing bears and an infestation of zombies. Each level looks significantly different but I was shocked to see that, given the fact there are only a handful of stages available, one was a direct copy of a previous mission.
Sadly, the assortments of toys to play with can become dull and repetitive. Although at first, assassinating a large group with an explosion is fun, it soon becomes protocol. The majority of the killings are accomplished by the using the boring method of picking up a sleeping drunk, moving them to a secluded spot and murdering them discretely. The biggest frustration arises when the unfair AI can see you perform this act when seemingly behind cover. A particular level took me an hour to complete simply because of these frustrations which in turn found me becoming reckless to progress past the level. Party Hard is a game of patience yet instead of the meticulous nature feeling rewarding, it just became inattentive.
When the campaign is completed and depending on your performance, new characters can become available to you. Although they have similar skill-sets to Darius, they do differ slightly. A chainsaw wielding psycho can briefly decimate a number of people in a small radius whereas the crooked cop can accuse others of being the perpetrator. More bizarre levels unlock once the story has concluded too but the same formula remains.
Party Hard begins with an exciting concept. Being influenced by gory, pixel art games such as Hotline Miami; this mature, arcade slaughter fest has a lot of potential. Unfortunately, as in real life, returning to the same bar every weekend came become predictable and uneventful which parallels the issues within Party Hard. More diversity, modes and challenges could have reinvigorated this party but it should have called time a little earlier.

Galaxy on Fire 2 Full HD is a simple, but quite enjoyable little space game, offering a spread of different ships with unique characteristics, several primary and secondary weapon styles to choose from each with a progression through different tech levels, mining and trade opportunities and a nice little story.
It is far from the length, scope or complexity of say, the X series, but also way more accessible, owned to the fact it is primary developed for mobile OS, like iOS and Android. That also marks the biggest flaw: The mobile variants have expansion packs, DLCs and ingame-shops, all of wich are missing completely from the Steam version, so you really buy half of the game.
Another small flaw is the fact that you cannot lock-in a target lock, and also cannot except friendly units from being locked. Add to that the fact friendly targets are far easier to lock (i.e. in a quite bigger radius around the targeting reticle) and the property of any homing projectile to switch instantly to your current lock, and all homing weapons have something of a problem with friendly fire.
If you can stand those small flaws though, it is all in all an enjoyable nugget for the casual game in between.

Personally must buy for Strategy gamers I'm veteran of TW and Civ. Lets just say I'm over 40. Now this has been described as a hybrid of the two, i think thats fair discription.
Basically its scout, build, fight nothing new there. Age of Empires did that 20 years ago.
But whats  nice about this game is no silly Auto resolve 200 times per game. You give attack orders and you watch the battles, having no control, which is more realistic in an age without mobile phones but its actually fun to watch. Each faction has there own hair cut, different units give bonuses etc.
So its turned based like civ but rather wait (what can sometimes be like 5 mins in civ between tuns) you can watch your units battles, movements and that of enemies (or just fast forward).
That can lead to a heart in mouth moment when you've left your capital undefended to go all out to attack your neighbour and some previously undiscovered clan appears 3 hexes from your capital, but thats the fun.
Its not the finish article needs some tweeks i think. The interface is clunky. The build screen for example, click build on settlement screen, then a number in gold appears  at top of a desciption of building but this is not the cost of building but the mainance cost, you have to scroll down on mini screen to find the cost and build button. Annoying but minor. The devs look active though.
So before buying in the sale i read a few gamer reviews, i'll go through some their Cons here.
CONS
Resources - its not that clear (ive only played a few hours admittedly) what the value of resources are. Not yet found over all balance sheet, you can see a city's one. But you can have dozens of settlements. There is a copper resource but no tin but i dont think you need it in this game to make bronze? Bronze is important - armour upgrades etc
AI - this is what i saw a few people complain about. The AI is aggressive off the bat even on easy and doesnt let you turtle/ build up in peace which would be handy when trying to learn the game. But i went to easy level but even on medium its not too difficult. It looks like at the beginning of most games one faction will plant a settlement close to your capital, this cant be ignored they will wipe you out in the long run usually.
I just took it as it was undefended and fought them. Early on taking a enemy capital doesnt look easy like Civ but you can kill their settlers and stop them from expanding and build walls in yours. Then with other factions not trying to build settlements in your garden its easy to use a useful diplomacy system to make agreements like no attack 20 - 40 turns.
Soundscape - nice chinese background music little else seen that in the moans. yeah true but is that really important to you in a strategy game.
OK
Pro's
Tech tree - learn 4 techs  on 4 trees studying them all at once. So you can see how the game can take many different paths plus learning about chinese civilisation on the way . When starting a new game it defaults to games with 300 turn limit. This can be adjusted i clicked it up to 4000  and it goes higher. Are there enough techs for a game that long. Well it starts bronze age and on the trailer i saw that gun powder and other major events come in later. There is 3000 years of history to get through. Will it hold interest that long?
Factions - as mentioned each has their own quirks and bonuses. Noted that you have access to about 6 factions at beginning you have to play a game of 120 turns to unlock the others. But i know that at least one of those locked factions formed an emperor dynasty so they must have nice bonuses.
Raiding - people say this is a flaw. Yeah for carebears - only joking. A factions army can come pillage your farm without declaring war and upset economy when your armies off some where.  You can attack raiding army in your territory without starting a war. But i think this is good you have to use diplomacy screen - there are lots of options there i havent been through all of them and so far unlike TW they dont say no all the time.
Maps - its big and each civ pretty much knows hes got a potential enemy in each direction. Ive not seen a faction on coast rivers can be crossed early. The only natural barriers seem to be mountain ranges. So alliances and diplomacy look to play more of a role in this game.
Random encounters - they give bonuses and encourage expansion.
Floods i know this important and a feature it might knock your economy on its back side but i've not played that deep in to game yet.
In all i think TW and Civ missed trick by staying with tried and tested and these guys have come up with great, in depth and yeah funny strategy game.
Must buy for strategy gamers.

I would highly recommend this game! If you're looking for this game to be just like civ or a total war game in the aspects of the graphics and mechanics, you might be disappointed, but for half the price and with a very community involved developer this game has the potential to flourish with the help of the community. Yes there are some problems such as the tedious ways that seiges are done, the formations of troops can sometimes be annoying, but it isnt so bad that it is un playable. The replayablity of this game is what i like the most, if you have some friends you can spend hours and hours just playing a muliplayer game that will last you days or even weeks to fully complete. The various troops types are done very well, alongside the technology tree you have to prioritize what you want to get done first. you can rush superior troops and try to dominate your enemies or maybe go a more economics based game and focus on trade and diplomacy. The AI isn't terrible, they sometimes do some dumbs things but they arent so predictable that there isn't a challenge. There is so much room for further development, the devs are always asking the community for tips and suggestions and they actually listen!
Lastly, for the price of only 30 USD (18 while its currently on sale) you cant beat it. Most games of this nature run close to 60 dollars, for half the price this game is a perfect one to get.

Seriously underrated game. No, its not as good as Borderlands 2, and it is shorter, but I spent 10 more hours on this game than the first one, and that includes all the dlc of both games. Admittedly there isnt much dlc for the game, but I thought the claptrap one approached the same high quality as any from the first two games, aside from tiny tina's from Borderlands 2.

Note: Finished the game for the first time just recently (finally, right?). No nostalgia here. And I only used visual and graphics mods (try: New Vision and Project HDTP)
The good: It holds up. You play how you want -- stealthy, loud, merciful, lethal or a mix of different styles. The game gives you options for your chosen approach too (vents, hidden rooms, augmentations, discreet yet climable crates, FLAMETHROWERS EVERYWHERE, etc.) and it doesn't make a fuss about it. By that, I mean it doesn't hold your hand and lets you figure things out on your own, but gives you the tools necessary to do so without drawing attention to them and breaking immersion (like when in some games, some unfortunate soul had to paint red/white ALL the places the protagonist could interact with?). For example, there is no minimap. If there is, I did not find it. At best, you're given DIGITAL IMAGES or BLUEPRINTS of whatever you're infiltrating, which you have to access manually on your... manual? So you're the one who has to make sense of north from south, up from down. I like it. In a huge game like Witcher3, this would be very very irritating but in Deus Ex, with its impressive level design and "self-contained" maps (? I dunno, they're small enough to be manageable but large enough to allow a decent amount of freedom), this is a good thing. I did get lost a number of times but that was mostly due to the old and repetitive textures.
However, I didn't see much of a difference in terms of consequence whether you killed people or just left them unconscious besides opinions and comments of certain allies. I thought some would end up hating me at first if too many people were killed so I initially played the saintly route. Turns out, aside from a few quest rewards being different (accdg to your actions), not much of an impact. I guess that *can* be good; I find games that claim to be "choose-your-path" types then penalize you for certain actions very irritating, so I see the benefit of this too.
The bad: The tranquilizer darts for the crossbow are almost pointless. Score a headshot and the target can still get a decent amount of shots off (alarming others in the immediate area) or run off to pull alarms (or push? they have buttons instead of levers in this game). The only decent total, non-lethal stealth weapon is a cattle prod... really? With strength (or at least, that augmentation that makes you hit harder) maxed out, and aiming for the head with the baton, getting a one-hit knockout is still pretty random. (On the other hand though, non-lethal stealth should be hard, so... good?)
The good: Clichéd but entertaining.
The bad: Clichéd AND has a tendency for the highfalutin and pretentious.
To be honest, the game came out yeeeaaaars ago and far better stories have been written and presented since then. Some of those are likely inspired by Deus ex, too. There were times where I knew what I had to do but I just didn't know why - partially didn't care either. JC Denton isn't the most charismatic of characters but he fits his role. Overall, the story got me through just long enough to finish the game. Some characters live, some die based on your decisions. And some characters, for whom you worked SOOO HARD TO TRANQUILIZE, tanking their attacks using a stealth-based character! ... still end up dying (the game considers some characters dead no matter what you do).
ALSO: I was annoyed that the endings (there are multiple endings) are not majorly influenced by any prior decision. You only get to choose which one you want at the very end.
Buy it. It's not as "grandiose" as some make it out to be (probably the nostalgia), but for a game this old, it certainly holds up. I got it on sale and it was worth it.

Deus Ex was one of the very few games I went into without knowing a THING about it.
When i first got into it I really didn't think i would've gotten myself immersed into right away due to the age, but holy jesus was I wrong!
Deus Ex was made by a company known as Ion Storm ,Yes the same people who made Daikatana, and to come from that to this beauty of a game is amazing, The graphics are dated sure, but the audio design and music REALLY keep it up to today's standards. Coming from a game made in 2000 the voice acting is really good, even down right hilarious at times when the jokes pop up and the music, GOODNESS the music! its something that really takes my 1st place surpassing that of Doom.
The mixture of Techno and classical is a beautiful combonation that everyone should listen too! from the high-tech offices of UNATCO to the desolate streets of a worn-down Paris, it all sounds so pleasing to your ears.

Now, down to the real meat of this game, the Story (no spoilers) and Gameplay.
Deus Ex's story is handsdown one of the best I have experienced in a long time, rivaling that of Half-Life 2. the Multi-Choice endings are perfect on how it makes the player feel with the end result. the game can even let you kill off most of the story-important NPCS right off the bat and it seems like the whole story shifts around your actions. Dont expect a short playthrough with this game either, it took me a good 24 hours to beat it while looking in all of the corners of the maps to find secrets and hidden areas.
Gameplay wise, Deus Ex is a great experience, the combat system is totally unique and intuitive and the Inventory system is done really well and the Nano-augs you can get really shift on how you build your character and progress through the game.
the Skills system is a bit basic sure, but it will make you choose which you feel is more important, and trust me putting it all into Pistols and Rifles is something you DO NOT want to do first thing with each level offering on how efficient your character uses said items. It's always best to put points into the skills that help you rack up more ammo and supplies.
In Conclusion
Deus Ex is a down right masterpiece and it down right deserves to be called the "Greatest PC game of all time" in my books, everything about this game is done so right and if one can mod it so it works with modern machines, your in for one heck of a good time!

Our protagonist, Pajama Sam, is about to finish the last cookie box for his favorite action figure. As he reaches for the last box, a familiar voice calls out. "Sam, it's time for dinner!" Not feeling quite hungry for a meal, Sam notices something strange. The cookies come to life! As they flee, Sam searches for a logical place - the pantry. The door shuts, trapping Pajama Sam into a world full of scrumptious sweets, delectable delights, and tasty treats.
You play as Sam, a little boy looking to stop the general from declaring war. How does Sam do this? He needs to find members of each food group so they can hold a conference together. The only problem is...they've gone missing! Pajama Sam will need to consume candy canes to escape prison, drive on a donut, resolve balance between beans, and much more. The cool thing about this game (and the other Humongous Entertainment games) is that your second gameplay might be different than the first. The different food groups might be in different places next time, so replay value is actually fun.
I loved the creativity put forth in this game. Foods  of all sorts come to life with memorable personalities.
-Strong, beefy muffins draw cupcakes on the coast.
-Candy canes substitute jail bars.
-The names. Plums nicknamed "plummers." A granny smith apple named Granny Smythe. The sweet troops marching around.
Fans who have not played this game yet will love the cameo appearances. The carrot from the first Pajama Sam game makes a return. There's also Sprinkles the Donut who helps Sam travel. (It reminds me from Otto from PS1).
Not only is this a fun game, the name is definitely true. Sam makes a valid point at the end of the adventure. You are what you eat from your head to your feet.

A fun puzzle game with similarities to Minesweeper, where you must determine which cells are filled with blue hexes, and which are vacant.
2-3 hours
6/10
Hexcells a simple puzzle game, its closest companion would be Minesweeper, except it’s a bit more involved than that (also a lot better, and you’re not timed). The way the game works is you have a… let’s call it a board, filled with hexagons, which we’ll call cells. You need to determine which cells are occupied with a blue hexagon, and which ones are vacant (which will be grey). The vacant cells will also have a number inside them, indicating how many adjacent cells are occupied. You simply left click a cell to mark it as occupied, and right click a cell to mark it as vacant. If you’re correct, the cell will change accordingly. If you’re wrong, it’ll shake and mark you as getting making a mistake (more on this in a moment).
As you progress through the game, the puzzles will get more complicated, and additional ways to indicate whether or not a cell is occupied are introduced.  Sometimes numbers will be encased in curly brackets, indicating that all the occupied cells adjacent to the vacant cell are touching each other.  Where-as a number that has a hyphen on each side means that at least one of the adjacent occupied cells is not touching the other adjacent occupied cells. (Note for clarity: When I say the cells are touching each other, I don’t mean ALL the cells are touching ALL the other cells, but that they are connected like a line curved around the vacant cell. For the hyphenated numbers, some of the cells may be touching each other, but there is at least one break in the group. There may be two groups of two touching cells for example).
Numbers will also appear at the top of columns, or even at a diagonal, indicating how many occupied cells are in that row or column (reminding me ever so slightly of Picross). This numbers also will use the same additional mechanics as the vacant cells, with the curly braces and hyphens indicating if the cells are all connected, or have a break in them. The later stages will require you to use these different numbers in tandem to solve the puzzle.
Now, even in the later stages of the game, Hexcells never gets too difficult. It’s a fairly easy game, and you’ll be able to complete it in 2-3 hours without much trouble. After that, you’re done, there’s not much replay value (unless you try to perfect every level, which you might do just playing through it anyway).
The levels in Hexcells are divided up into 6 worlds. Each world consists of a couple of stages (4-6 stages, with a total of 26 stages). When you complete a level you are awarded blue hexes towards a total score of them. By earning enough of these blue hexes you unlock the next world. The number of blue hexes awarded for completing a stage varies depending on its difficulty, and you will be awarded less blue hexes the more mistakes you make in a level. (Don’t worry, you can redo levels do earn the blue hexes you missed).
The music in the game is fairly calm and simple, it’s not anything particularly note-worthy, but it fits with the relaxed feel of the game. (Both the game and the music are overall rather relaxing).
As for criticisms, they’re two main things I feel this game lacks. 1). There’s no option to save a level mid-way through, so that you can leave the game and return to it later. My work around for this was to take a screen cap if I had to stop playing for some reason, and then just redo my stage progress from there. 2). It’d be nice if there was a way to map out a potential solution (similar to Picross’ overlay feature), so that you can indicate which cells you think may contain blue hexes, and which you think may be vacant without selecting them. Though, this is less needed in this Hexcells game than it is in later ones where you must figure out how large swathes of a level work together to determine if a cell has a blue hex or not.
So if you’re into puzzle games, then consider picking up the Hexcells pack when it goes on sale (often you can get all 3 games for less than $3). If you already have the first Hexcells game and want more, Hexcells Plus is basically the hard mode for this game, and Hexcells infinite will also provide you with more puzzles to play. If you only want one Hexcells game, go for Infinite, it has some improvements over the other two, and a random level generator, so it’ll offer more play time, (see my review for Hexcells Infinite for more details on that). Whichever route you opt for, it’s a fun puzzle game.

So, I'm going to begin by stating what the primary collective of these reviews state as well, as you can probably tell by my profile in general I don't "do" the whole game review scene, however, in a game that has taken me through every corner of emotion possible, and absolutely blown my previously most loved game right out of the water, I felt that this is one of those once in a lifetime games that I had to leave a review for.
So, to start from the top on my personal experience with the game, some background, I, before being introduced to this game via the few youtubers I watch, had never heard of the Nier franchise, or had any remote interest. As a more middle ground gamer that prefers to vary slightly for new tastes but keep rather constrained in my section of primarily first person based action and ect, this game was a tad of a leap of faith for me, I jumped into the game knowing very little about Japanese style games in general aside from MGS which even then only ever getting into the series in its most recent installment.
With all my previous gaming experiences in mind, beginning to play this game, especially in the beginning and trying moments, worried me beyond belief and almost had me turning away 30 minutes in to refund it, but in the back of my mind, there was this nagging interest, something that only fostered and grew the moment I sat down and said to myself "lets at least give it a fair shot".
This nagging interest, this feeling in the back of your mind while playing through this game, even when faced with your first experiences of losing progress because of your poor adaptation to the save system early on, or when faced with the eventual "grind moment" that all games of this type usually have within a certain point, or evenwhen facing the loss of a character you've grown to learn and love, is something that I think I can fairly say all those that have played that game to its fullest have experienced.
This, almost "charm" of this game, cannot easily be put into words, once or twice I can easily reflect on a time when I sat back in my chair after my most recent time of being annoyed with a boss I couldn't beat, or a side quest that was just proving too difficult, and I asked myself, "What am I playing this game for?" and this question, although usually very easy to get a response, in this case I found, at least during my initial play of ending "A", was much more complex than I original thought. This "charm of the game" although beyond my personal comprehension, kept me playing, and gave me the chance to proceed through the initial story, the initial worries, a sudden and believed to be un kept, and loose ended ending, turned out to only be the very beginning of my journey throughout this beautiful story.
If there is one thing beyond all else that causes the current state of the game its major grievances, it is of course, the quality of its port, I myself, even though praising the game for its unique and near perfect complexity, cannot deny that the port is not currently at a stable state, even through my own game play on a computer that practically never has any issue with games, ran into two crashes in full screen that set me back on one occasion an annoyingly stupid amount, choppy cutscenes (the already capped 30 fps cutscenes not helping that factor {though of course not completely uncommon in video games}) and dropped frames.
After all I have experienced, learned, and loved in this game, if I were to speak to a previous me skeptical about this game, worried about the port quality, the new and unknown style of game play, the lack of any real way to experience the game in a multiplayer fashion like I have become so accustomed to in so many of these modern games, with all my knowledge about both the good and the bad I have experience through playing this game, even with the knowledge that I would have to go through hour after hour of a terrible port crashing, lagging, and making the experience almost completely unbearable, I would still indeed tell that version of myself, yes, you absolutely must buy this game, it will cause you worry, and doubt, and even anger at some points, but if you push through, and give this game a chance, the cons of the platform are heavily outweighed by the absolute pro's that the entirety of this game is and provides.
So, in closing, if you can even slightly relate on a level of anything I touched on, the doubts, the worries, the previous experiences, I stand to offer another voice in a sea of praise, this game will in no doubt go down as a classic, no matter your play style, expectations, and preferred game types, I humbly request that you, even at the games current state, purchase it, if you go in and give this game your attention, unlike the mass of games we are pelted with on a day to day basis, I promise you this, this game, its story, its narrative, will treat you not simply as "another customer" but as its audience, in its first opening night, on the biggest day of its career, the game will show with its performance, that it truly cares about your experience.

Verdict: Nier is slightly above average, carried mainly by the story and amazing soundtrack. However, in a world that has a ton of games that are well above average, many for less than $60, Nier doesn’t cut it. It’s worth a play for the story, but I’d hold off until it goes on sale, unless you really have absolutely nothing else to play.
Pros: Amazing music, great story, and cool theme.
Cons: If you don't have a controller you probably want to skip this one.
Performance: Running the game on a GTX 1070 FTW, Skylake i7, and 16GB of RAM at 1080p. Even when I ran the game on lowest settings I still experienced some pretty major stuttering problems throughout the game. V-sync also completely tanks my performance and stops me from getting even a solid 30fps. Unfortunately, without v-sync on there is very noticeable and frequent screen tearing. Luckily there are some community mods out there that help with these problems, but it seems unacceptable that these problems are still persistent after almost 2 months for a game with a $60 price tag.
Load Times: I’m guessing this also has to do with the poor port, but for whatever reason a lot of the time loading screens are upwards of 30 seconds. This wouldn’t be so bad if it wasn’t for the fact that the vast majority of the games quests are fetch quests which require you to teleport around quite a lot (and by proxy sit through a lot of loading screens).
World: All this time running from point A to point B for fetch quests wouldn’t be so bad if the world was interesting. Towards the end of the game some pretty cool areas unlock, but for the most part the world just feels super bland and empty. Even after unlocking the teleporter you still have to do a ton of running around to actually get anywhere- it almost feels like they tried to prolong the game this way. At least 10-15 hours, if not more, of my playtime was spent just holding forward, waiting to get someplace, or waiting for loading screens.
Combat: It's not terrible, but it's not great either. Combat definitely looks cool, but outside of that it feels very basic. After you get used to things the game basically has two difficulties: so easy you'll never die, or dying if you get hit once by anything on very hard. There's a happy medium a lot of good games strike, Nier doesn't get there.
Bosses: I’ve beaten all of the bosses (including the secret ones) and, while I think all of them were cool from a story perspective, there were only two that were cool from a gameplay perspective. Furi is an example of a similar combat concept that just does combat and bosses much, much better.
Graphics: Not terrible, but not great. they get the job done.

It was a promising game, great visuals, some stories, but:
1. Frustrating and fiddly UI (subspecies management, fleet splitting, army management). For example, to build a proper army, you have to manually click every unit and add an attachment, which is very low-cost and has no drawback. Only problem is clicking a lot.
2. No real depth to the game. No supply mechanics, just build anywhere. Only viable strategy for war is doomstacking. Fortificating is useless because even top-tier space defense station can be easily overcome by contemporary fleet, most it can do is shoot down unarmed transports being carelessly sent by AI.
3. Events are interesting, deep and varied, but all scripted and you get the same ones every game (mostly), Gets boring after first time.
4. Performance gets AWFUL from mid into late game. Game gets choppy and frustrating to look at with anything but five ships on the screen. Only one CPU core is ever used. Expect FPS-death.
5. AI is dumb, sending numerous unarmed fleets to their death. Only way it can win is via cheating which is called "difficulty setting".
6. Most of the game is spent micromanaging your planets, ensuring the best positioning of buildings. You have to process each planet manually to achieve good returns, but you can't keep them all under manual control so you have to give them out to "sectors". Having only small pool of planets to manage yourself results in frustrating fiddling with sectors. Otherwise you have at best sub-par performing planets, at worst AI "management" causes happiness to drop and sectors revolt. A lot of research is useless, a lot is must have and clearly they didn't think about balancing it much, just threw a ton of tech with +X percent to something in.
Free updates are ongoing, but while fixing stuff they kinda break game even further. They tack the shiny stuff like perks, quests, and carbon copy of Civ 5 culture perks on top without fixing basic stuff. Only year after release they FINALLY are contemplating adding drawing resources from sectors which everybody have been suggesting on forums from day 1. Certain overpowered ship parts were "fixed" by dramatically restricting your option for ships: every ship size is locked into its role and has very restricted options for weapons. There's still no any signs about adding some kind of espionage system (will probably be in DLC two years from now).
Stay away unless in far future they patch this mess up (unlikely, they will never abandon the sinking engine, like Bethesda).

If it comes down to a binary choice, I guess I can't really recommend buying this game.  It's a kind of shallow, but easy-to-approach space sim in the same vein as Freelancer, but way, way simplified.  While relatively bug-free, the gameplay is extremely repetitive.  The voice acting isn't awful I suppose, but the script is extremely cheesy and B-movie-esque.  The story is pretty much a cut and paste from Freelancer, without the length, wow-factor or plot twists.
The sandbox gameplay is lacking any inspiration and you'll find little reason to continue playing other than you can't currently afford the best ships in the game.
To be fair, the game isn't terrible, but I'm kind of past considering that praise.  I can no longer afford to waste time or money on games anymore that don't innovate in some manner.  And being an indie title is no excuse for making a mediocre game.  In fact, the lack of time constraints and publisher pressure should, if anything, improve one's ability to look outside the box and approach even a well-travelled game concept with original ideas.
Buy this game.
