I am going to compare this game to Rome: Total War, an older entry of the series.
Improvements I instantly notice:
Naval combat feels very rewarding! It is still autocalculated, but 2 ships will go up against 1 and you will probably win. 6 ship can go against 5 enemy ships, and you might just win a heroic victory with 0 losses!
Instead of the SPQR for Roman Factions, you have a Pope for the many different Catholic factions! This is a good addition in my opinion, as now more factions feel fleshed out.
Graphics are better here and there, but the way my settings are, I don't really notice major differences. Not that the graphics hold anything back!
Pre-battle speeches feel nice and Medieval-like! Though they are slightly repetitive, they're still a joy to listen to.
There is no balance issues that I can see, but the Byzantines/Turks and the Holy Roman Empire seem to have it easier early on when they're played by AI.
Crusades are a nice new addition as well!
For the most part, the Campaign map feels the same. However, a key difference is that you can swap a settlement between being a Castle or a Town. Castles offer military power, whilst Towns offer economic power. The choice is yours!
Agent system feels a lot more immersive.
There are tons of cinematics! It feels like an achievement just to have a Spy take a look at a few stray enemy units.
MP is still kicking, but Rome 1's MP is also alive.
It is also only worth $20, with a very cheap DLC! That is a complete steal for a game like this. That said, Rome 1 is cheaper.
Probably one of the best things this game has is the fact that the map is more immersive! There was historical events in Rome 1 like volcanoes and floods, but now you can witness the spawn of the Mongols, or contact Aztecs when you have been confined to Europe all this time!
10/10

I first voted NO, but I will give the developers the benefit of the doubt.
I am 46 years old. I have been a gamer since the first Atari consoles evolving through the first strategy games, 4x, RTS, you name it. That being said, I find the concept of this game to have incredible potentials. However, as it is right now, it is unplayable. Here are the reasons.
1) No room for different strategies. The early game is a rush game of survival. The enemy spam hordes of armies at your settlement doors, while you cant afford even a militia. There is no current way of escaping this trend—it is a constant in every game.
2) Not city-building strategy. For the moment, buildings instead of helping, become a burden (even economic buildings cost more maintenance than what they produce). The trade-off is not justified.
3) No Sun Tzu friendly. As far as offense-defense, the game does not distinguish the benefits of defense. In Civ, for example, if you want to take a settlement you better be ready to lose a lot of manpower. Here, the defense bonuses are unexisting (at early game at least)

From a good strategy game I expect to just start a game on normal level, and without help from any walkthrough, or forums, or guides, or formulas, to just intuitively play, as if I am truly the future Emperor, immerse in the game, find all the challenges and solutions and the FUN in the game itself - and here Oriental Empires delivered  and succeeded my expectations - more than 40 hours in just 4 days, "one more turn" lost night, did NOT happen to me for a looong time.
(2nd game was already on hard, and was FUN and successful as well ...without any extra web-searching)
I would NOT compare it as a Chinese child between civilization and Total War series - although this comparison would be a compliment .... but still I feel that the developers of Oriental Empires created  a UNIQUE space in the crowded "Historical strategy genre", and succeeded to draw me in this world, so I could already spend very entertained hours of game-play.
Oriental Empires is a mature, very solid beautiful game. It stands proud before us, as IT IS - FAIR and delivers the value for money!!
NO DLC SPAMMING, no "half game now, the rest you have to wait" (and spend extra money) for many more DLC policy, to deliver finally (or never) a solid game.
As I was playing, my wife passed a few times by, sat on the couch near me and just watched me playing commenting how relaxed she feels just listening to the atmospheric MUSIC - "like in the Chinese restaurant" ...she said :) ... and watching a visually very appealing introduction in the atmosphere and the "world of the East" for us "westeners".

And first I was Shocked by how different it was presented, and it appeared as too little! This fact, seems to be the main issue in the negative reviews. BUT actually meanwhile I like it very much, because, it invites You to dive into the game intuitively, to BE the emperor You are, and not to be a bureaucrat who searches the net for all the "perfect values". There are no exact formulas and values for the buildings You want to build, BUT before I build routine wise a bazar in every town I own, no matter how small it is and later complain (like many reviews) that they cost more money, than they earn, I build 1 or 2 and observe and compare the values of income and expense and on hand of real observation and intuition I slowly start expanding my trade network ( when the towns already grown a little). Actually in reality an Emperor never knew BEFORE he ordered something the exact consequence. You build this and that and observe, and than plan further moves.
The game has great mechanism to prevent You from routine spamming buildings or units, or new towns (due to the authority system). As buildings cost/per turn,  as an Emperor I will think twice before I build in every town a barrack or all buildings.  First, there is no room to build all, and You would go bankrupt and loose in a very frustrated way. You have to "specialize".
...so Yes, You have to act carefully and You have plenty of information for reacting. Actually it is an interesting strategy concept, where the emphasis is less on "theoretical detailed planing", but more on intuitively ACTING and observing given information and REACTING ... and that's how an ruler often has to live by.
Last but not least is the very interesting COMBAT phase! First, lets be honest ...how often did You have Your "perfect battle" in Total War or Civilization? How often were YOUR battle-skills in commanding every army in every way, crucial in winning a whole Campaign or game?
Most probably You will agree, if I state, that more often it was Your "great campaign" skills of tricking the opponent to fight where You prefer and at the time You prefer, with a bigger army, better equipped, and more advanced units ...maybe even add some surprise and trying to have as little casualties and protecting Your income, infrastructure and diplomatic relations.
And this is where Oriental Emires hit it exactly on the point. I sense a lot of strategy experiencing in presenting in the game this concept / battle phase where You DON'T have any direct control of the fight itself, BUT all important decision, between a clear win and a frustrating loss are at Your feet.
You save time by skipping micromanaging every battle, but still You are visually involved, You can jump from battle to battle who are fought simultaneously at different part of Your empires, You can stop, observe  and learn, and You can soon move on with the global campaign ... and that's what it is all about ... to be able actually to finish a game in a reasonable amount of time if You are a person with real life.
Again, in some reviews I read that there are not enough "before" information and predictions.
I, personally, am tired of the dumbed down "battle prediction percentages" in case of this or that stance in some other games ... and don't tell me that a true SHOGUN needs a computer, or formulas or percentages to issue orders. A true SHOGUN "knows by heart" which units will support, which will harass, which will charge and which will hold positions or flank. A true Emperor will be thankful for some losses in minor battles to learn about his men, about their skills and he WILL KNOW how to plan a battle and trust that further assistance is not necessary once the battle begins.
A true Emperor will not arrive without siege weapons, or at least some archer units in early phase ...and then complain that he lost his whole army in an endless and frustrating siege.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Fairy Fencer F Advent Dark Force is a turn-based combat JRPG. The title is actually a remastering of a title by the same name (Fair Fencer F), from 2013 with a PC port release in 2015. The title was developed by: Compile Heart and published by: Idea Factory whom are known for their acclaimed Hyperdimension Neptunia series.
The player takes control of Fang, a mysterious (and lazy) boy who finds himself pulling a sword out of the ground in hopes of free food. He instead ends up with his own fairy companion in a quest to revive the great goddess of light from her slumber by collecting more of these swords known as furies.
During this adventure the player will acquire different abilities and party members that can aid in battle. This newer version of the game introduces new story lines and choices for the player to make, as well as giving the player some previous DLC bundled into this remastered edition.
--------

The graphic assets are what you would expect from a game like this, and being a remastered title, the quality of the models and cut-scenes are sharper and more define than the original. Art is very subjective, especially when it comes to anime inspired titles, as some may love it and may not. That being said, an individual probably wouldn't purchase a game like this if they did not already enjoy this art-style. The art is very colourful and high quality, and although the character and environmental models seem very generic to other JRPG titles, they get the job done.
As in many games such as this, the player is able to customise the attire of each of their party members which is a nice addition in personalising the game. The different stages within the game are all quite different, even if some of the terrain models are reused. The backdrops and cut-scenes within the game are very high quality and pleasant to look at.
It seems that the game was optimised fairly well as it doesn't seem too demanding on any mid-tier system, and would run perfectly fine on lower tier systems with some graphical setting tweaks.
--------
There is a wide array of music tracks for the game, and certain tracks will change to match certain moods or situations that present themselves within the game. The opening theme of the title is very high quality (in addition to the opening scene that takes place). The game's sound effects are very standard when it comes to combat noises, though one of the aspects of the game that really shines is the voice acting. The game has voice acting from the very beginning to the ending of the game and in almost every scene and confrontation. In addition to this the voice acting is really well done. The Japanese and English voice acting are both very impressive and really add depth to each of the characters. Even the small side characters have a voice.
--------

The mechanics of the game can get a bit complex and overwhelming at times, as there's quite a bit. This portion of the review will go over as many of them that are relevant as possible, although there are other features to the game that may not be discussed.
The battle system mimics that of the unique real-timeish turn-based combat of the developer's other title; Hyperdimension Neptunia. Each characters act in turn order, though instead of being stationary, the player has the ability to move their character within a certain range in order to position them before attacking or using an ability. This alone adds a lot to the game-play, as not every character and enemy has the same range, meaning positioning is key to defend from enemy attacks, or even attacking multiple enemies at once. Attacks and abilities will also have different ranges, effects, and SP consumption. During combat the player can choose to fuse with their fairy in order to become much more powerful. This can only be done when the fuse gauge has reached a certain point in combat. In addition to stat increases, The player will then have access to certain abilities and attacks only available when fused.
Stats are increased via levelling, though stats can also be increased through other methods as well. An example of this is; Strength increased by a certain amount after striking a victory pose X amount of times, or running 1,000 meters will increase your agility by X amount. These types of stat increments will happen as you play the game and complete certain hidden objectives.
Like in most RPG titles, the player can outfit their party with a variety of equipment, though in addition to this, the player can equip different fairies and furies that can change their play-style dramatically, as each fairy can harbour different abilities as well as gain experience to level up further. Furies can also be powered up manually by accumulating weapon points and choosing which fury to assign the weapon points too. This increases the power of the fury.
One of the biggest aspects of this game is the "God Revival System". The basics of this system is that the player will offer one fury and one fairy to remove one sword embedded into either the Vile God or the Goddess of Light. The fairy used in this offering will return to the player with new abilities which can aid the player in combat. The second role of this system is actually more significant. Depending on how many swords are removed from each entity, the actually story of the game will change. This gives the game a few different routes to explore and gives it some replay value.
--------
This is actually the first time I'm playing a game with this sort of combat system. I've never played any of the Hyperdimension Neptunia games so I thought that the battle mechanics were actually quite unique.
There are a few aspects of the game I wasn't able to cover though I feel as though I covered  the core parts of the game. It is also a very story driven title so expect to be reading/listening through cut-scenes quite often. I did a little more research on the title and the story actually gets pretty deep at some parts of the game, though this is also heavily based around what god you choose to revive. It's neat that they added all these small, but nice features to this remastered version of the game and actually makes me want to try some of the developer's other titles.
The game is enjoyable and the story is actually quite interesting. I'm not sure how grind-y the game is, though there are some people who enjoy that.
Thanks to the devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

I want to recommend this game, I really do. However the amount of frustration it can deliver slightly outweighs the fun I personally get out of it, so it's got to be a thumbs down from me.
I'm a big fan of 4X titles and so the fact there was a game on a period of history that isn't widely covered seemed appealing to me. The devs do a good job of making the setting accessible to western audiences and the graphics, while by no means the best I've seen in a game of this type, are functional enough.
That being said, the main hurdles for me are a finnicky UI, a general lack of feedback that can make it difficult to keep track of everything that's happening, a boring soundscape (the number of sound effects are minimal and more often than not all you can hear is the music. Not much an issue with a game like this but it gives the game a very "empty" sound by default which doesn't really do it any favors) and a sense of balance that seems incredibly difficult to get ahold of without the use of a user guide; the game doesn't explain the intricacies of a lot of its systems to you and by the time you figure out you've been mismanaging part of your empire it's typically too late to avert the damage.
On the subject of difficulty, the AI is incredibly aggressive and seems to have no problem whatsoever in outpacing you, although it's entirely possible that this is due to me missing some crucial part of the game's balance that the game itself didn't really bother to explain to me. I'm not asking that the game should handhold me by any means, however I feel the amount of support and documentation within the game itself isn't really up to the task - if people need to consult fanmade FAQs to learn how to play your game, your tutorial isn't good enough.
If you're a diehard fan of these kinds of games you'll get something out of it, but if you're looking for a 4X game to compliment the big boys in the genre you're going to leave disappointed.

Pros
1-6 character battle system
2-Enhance battle system
3-enchance graphics
4-Dynamic character interactions/pairings
5-Comedic dialog
6-Dozens of hours of fun.
7-Customizable combat
8-New story paths are great and expand the overall experience
Cons
1- Cliche Character Personalities,
2-Linear, hallway like dungeons
3-Despite strong on simple levels, many character interactions fall flat due to lack of meaning on a broad scale.
4-Overly repetitive, bland side quests
5-Predictable stories (if you have play the original game)
For the fans of that series and its comedic tone, you will find the same style of comfort here. For newcomers, if you can put up with how contrived the story can be, it may be worth a shot thanks to the exclusive content. Fairy Fencer F: Advent Dark Force added much needed and requested changes, but not everything seems to have been addressed with this re-release. The different paths you are able to take add more depth to the already well told story. Though it more often feels like a Director's Cut than a true remake, 'Advent Dark Force' nonetheless turns a flawed PS3 RPG into a stronger experience overall, making it the absolute best way to play 'Fairy Fencer'. The story has been made a great deal more interesting, playing with concepts that the original only hinted at, and the combat has been given a big shot in the arm thanks to the expanded party sizes and rebalanced difficulty. The game's biggest issue is that it feels like it could've been improved a great deal more than it has, leaving us with a game that's good, but falls just short of greatness. Still, it's a worthwhile adventure that lays down enough strong groundwork that could lead to a truly excellent sequel.
FINAL VERDICT: 4/5
Advent Dark Force went all-out in order to make the most definitive version of Fairy Fencer F that it possibly could. This title should be a no-brainer for fans of the original Fairy Fencer F, and I would also recommend it to anyone in the market for a good JRPG. Fairy Fencer F Advent Dark Force provides enjoyable gameplay, memorable characters, and a branching story good enough to warrant multiple playthroughs – and hey, isn’t that all that matters?

As the original game was one of my very favorites, I was delighted to see this short interlude game appear on Steam.  I personally hadn't had a clue there was such a thing in the works!  But I snapped it up the minute I saw it, and I'm completely delighted by it.
As a caveat, you will want to have played The Last Crown (original game) before you play this, or you will lose a good chunk of pretty much everything in the translation.
Playtime runs about 3-4 hours depending on how much you lollygag around, or in my case, wander off to answer the phone and forget to shut it off.
From a technical standpoint, this game continues on the same atmosphere as the original; graphics, sounds, scenery, and character design are the same.  Nigel's slightly-odd voice mannerisms are also still there (but for some reason, I find his somewhat Shatner-esque pauses endearing rather than irritating).  It appears all previous voice actors reprised their roles.
From a plot standpoint, it's not particularly deep like it's predecessor, but it's not supposed to be.  As a Halloween short and interlude between main games, it's perfect.  Short and sweet, but leaving some questions which I suspect will lead into the next main game.
Gameplay is also the same as the previous game.  Inventory, navigation, dialogue, etc. are similar if not identical.  The ghost-hunting mechanics are very similar but have been souped up a little to give the player somewhat more control over the situation rather than taking static pictures and whatnot, and I appreciated that a lot.
All in all, this is worth it especially if you enjoyed the previous game.  I know that I, at least, am waiting impatiently for the next installment of this series!

Despite the obvious negativity from the Borderlands community, stating this "isn't a full game/feels more like a big DLC," this game has its charm. At first, I was disappointed as well, but I found as I played it again, I liked the energy it created. I could even so much as say I like The Pre-Sequel over Borderlands 2.
The one thing I love most about this game is that it establishes one major essence of the Borderlands series that I didn't fully comprehend until now: there are no "good" guys. Every character has flaws, every character has at least some questionable morals. And they all make mistakes! (A non-spoiler-ish example would be Mr. Torgue, who in this game has absolutely no respect for Janey or for females at all - but you hear present day Mr. Torgue butt in the story to say he apologized for his awful behavior back then. Because people can change, for either the better or the worse--)
All the characters, especially the playable ones, are quirky and lovable in their own ways. There are a lot of things in this game that I wished they did in Borderlands 2, either gameplay-wise or story-wise. I hope that they adopt some of the mechanics from this game into their next one (mostly the fact that the characters actually reply with spoken lines, which Borderlands 2 only did in their DLC, because I'm a sucker for banter).
Any fan of the Borderlands series should play this game, not only does it add more lore, it adds to the story, the overall gameplay, and to the cast of colorful characters in the Borderlands series. Play it, you won't regret it.

For the first few hours I was having a blast and laughing one hell of a lot at the black humor.  Than you discover that there's really not any more mechanics and it gets pretty boring and grindy.
-Each level you kill everyone.  That is the only objective.
-90% of traps in the stage can only be used once.  And a lot have really short ranges that npcs never get near so you will only use them when a cop is chasing you.
-Most levels boil down to picking people off one by one as they walk off by themselves.  Fun for a bit, but after the 20th one it gets pretty old.  And you will be doing this each mission.
-Only real difference from mission to mission is the different layouts (usually with less places to murder people unseen) and a few specific traps.  Feels very samey after awhile since the gameplay doesn't really get mixed up.
Honestly, I'd consider the game a really good base and just needs a lot more content to keep levels from becoming boring.  Specific targets, more dynamic things you can do to try to end the party, carrying multiple items and choosing which you can bring with you (unlocking them), and so on.  Really feels like a lot of missed opportunities.  I really don't regret buying it since I got it pretty cheap, but I can see it not being for everyone.
And yes the miami mission was the last I played.  I looked up how to beat it, just really have no interest to progress farther at this point.

The gameplay is fun, nowhere near amazing, but fun. However, the cons of this game far out-weigh the pros of this game. Weapon-crafting, which is this games foundation, while fun to experiment with is also it's downfall. The game gives you a total of two gunslots. While it does give you some more after you level up, leveling up is a slow process, and you'll have to play a lot to even start getting more gunslots and loadouts. Because of this, the incedible gun-crafting system is limited, giving a very small amount of room to experiment with. On the subject of loadouts, you'd think a game NAMED "Loadout" would give you more than one to start, but it doesn't. Like gunslots, you have to level up to get more loadouts, but you have to reach even higher levels to unlock loadouts. You can buy more loadouts and gunslots, but even small numbers of these cost more money than I personally am willing to fork out. The in game, real-world equivilent money source is called spacebucks, which sadly, unlike blutes which is the weapon-crafting systems currency, can't be found in game. You have to pay real money for spacebucks. I've never been a fan of having to buy money in a game, why can't I just buy stuff with money straight from my steam wallet. Spacebucks are expensive. While they offer inexpensive packages of spacebucks, anything worthwhile such as loadouts or gunslots are worth far more than those small amounts. And the variety of characters they show on the screenshots of the store page are just about non-existent. Every single cosmetic item costs spacebucks, and they aren't cheap. To add, I haven't noticed a system of trading within the game like other steam games, so there is no way but paying money to get any of these cosmetic items. Because of this the amount of variety in characters is very small, with most people sticking with stock leading to every character looking the same. In conclusion, although I've heard this game was amazing in it's paid beta, it's definately not something very worthwhile anymore.

The first 5 minutes are enjoyable and unique compared to other games I've played. After that, things get pretty boring.
Your objective is to kill anyone without getting caught. Seems simple, right? Yeah, it's WAY too simple. You either kill people yourself or hook up traps that do it for you.
Knife- This is your own weapon. It's pretty bad. It can kill only one person at a time, and if you try to silence any witnesses, it always seems to miss. If your default weapon can't even kill 3 people grouped up without any of them getting away consistently in a game where there are at least 40 people in the map, then that's pretty bad. Speaking of the amount of people...
Victim Amounts- Whose idea was it to put so many people on a single map? The best case scenario is having 40 people. 40 people! And you can really only kill like one person at a time without getting spotted. If you caught, then you have to go back to the beginning and kill the same 40 people over again. How exciting. This number only goes up over the levels, while nothiing like better traps or weapons compensate for the fact.
Traps- This is one of those things that's advertized to be a major part of the game, but it's really just a pain to use. When you first start playing, you will have no idea what some of the traps do. I mean, you'll see obvious stuff like "Poison Food", which conviently poisons food. Okay, that was straightforward. But then there'll be things like "Break Object". First of all, break what? In some levels, even when you listen to where traps are (BTW the tutorial misses this important feature for some reason) it show you a trap marker in  weird places so you really don't know what you're activating. So what does breaking an object do? Say you want break a motorcycle. Will it do the obvious and go Michael Bay on everyone around it? No. It just telepathically tells the owner that their bike is broken so they come to it. How exciting.
Traps (cont.)- I just can't get over this. Traps seem to have so much potential, but not only are they mysterious, but also competely underpowered. Remeber how I said there will be like over 40 people in a single map? Well there will be like only 6 traps. So what's the problem? First off, traps aren't reusable. Even those dinky 1 kill traps wear away somehow (well, there is like one or two traps that can be used a solid two times). And those explosive traps? Pff. If you activate one, you'll see a little loading circle that indicates when the trap will start. It's painfully slow, and even if you're not sprinting (another thing the tutorial forgot to tell you how to do), you can get away from it, kill a few people, hide some bodies, eat some popcorn, and dance a little before it fills up. Some traps activate faster than other, but they're all slow. And once it does fill up, it starts blinking. Like, what? The trap hasn't activated? By this point everyone's random AI has gotten them away from the trap. And it blinks for a long time too. Even if you time it perfectly you'll be lucky to get a trap to kill more than 4 people. And the cops? Don't even think about killing them with traps.
Cops- So these guys are pretty nice. One get called to help some innocent partygoers out. He arrests some dude solely based on what some drunk girl/guy told them, or if that dude happened to be near a trap that activated 5 minutes ago. He then beats the **** out of that dude, never allowing him to escape. Even if that dude happened to perfectly time a trap so it blows up when that dude is being carried away, the cop dies, but so does the person he's carrying! And all of this happens so that the player can happily restart the level and 10 minutes of their life to preserve the amount of gameplay time. Screw these guys.
Randomness- After dying a few times, you might notice your favourite horse trap is gone. Or that there's no food to poison. What happened? Well, welcome to this game's RNG! If you thought the partygoer's pathfinding or the way the cops arrest people was terrible and too random, then look at this! Some traps/items/special people will sometimes be moved or gotten rid of completely. I guess the developer's main thoughts were:
Change stuff around--> More variety--> More fun--> ???--> Profit
...or something stupid. But here's how it really goes:
Remove the best of terrible items/traps and put all the bouncers (people who target you at random and instakill you) in inconvienent locations--> Player dies more--> Player has to replay more of this crappy game--> Less fun--> Epic Fail of a Gameplay Mechanic
Story- This is the only thing that kept me playing for 5 hours. And it's not even good. I didn't finish it due to the game's horrendous difficulty, but it's just about some dudes talking about the player/serial killer, and yeah, it's bland. It does nothing new, it barely even segways the levels into each other. The only reason I played for so long was to complete the story and find out what's gonna happen for the sake of completing the story and finding out what's gonna happen. Good thing Google and Youtube exist.
Music- The only redeeming thing. It's good. It's lively. It set's the party mood. And it's completely ruined by the fact you hear it like 20 times over because of how many times you have to restart levels.
Final Words- There are other crappy things I could talk about, such as there only being one good item you can get, calling people, or that stupid Italian plumber, but if these reasons weren't enough to faze you from wasting your money, then atleast take my advice and be prepared to be disappointed.

It was a promising game, great visuals, some stories, but:
1. Frustrating and fiddly UI (subspecies management, fleet splitting, army management). For example, to build a proper army, you have to manually click every unit and add an attachment, which is very low-cost and has no drawback. Only problem is clicking a lot.
2. No real depth to the game. No supply mechanics, just build anywhere. Only viable strategy for war is doomstacking. Fortificating is useless because even top-tier space defense station can be easily overcome by contemporary fleet, most it can do is shoot down unarmed transports being carelessly sent by AI.
3. Events are interesting, deep and varied, but all scripted and you get the same ones every game (mostly), Gets boring after first time.
4. Performance gets AWFUL from mid into late game. Game gets choppy and frustrating to look at with anything but five ships on the screen. Only one CPU core is ever used. Expect FPS-death.
5. AI is dumb, sending numerous unarmed fleets to their death. Only way it can win is via cheating which is called "difficulty setting".
6. Most of the game is spent micromanaging your planets, ensuring the best positioning of buildings. You have to process each planet manually to achieve good returns, but you can't keep them all under manual control so you have to give them out to "sectors". Having only small pool of planets to manage yourself results in frustrating fiddling with sectors. Otherwise you have at best sub-par performing planets, at worst AI "management" causes happiness to drop and sectors revolt. A lot of research is useless, a lot is must have and clearly they didn't think about balancing it much, just threw a ton of tech with +X percent to something in.
Free updates are ongoing, but while fixing stuff they kinda break game even further. They tack the shiny stuff like perks, quests, and carbon copy of Civ 5 culture perks on top without fixing basic stuff. Only year after release they FINALLY are contemplating adding drawing resources from sectors which everybody have been suggesting on forums from day 1. Certain overpowered ship parts were "fixed" by dramatically restricting your option for ships: every ship size is locked into its role and has very restricted options for weapons. There's still no any signs about adding some kind of espionage system (will probably be in DLC two years from now).
Stay away unless in far future they patch this mess up (unlikely, they will never abandon the sinking engine, like Bethesda).

Despite some minor flaws in both the game and the port, this is a masterprice and one of the best games I've ever played.
Pros:
-Essentially flawless combat and a new gold standard for the platinum style action game
-Awesome story, both better and stranger than I expected
-Top notch art direction
-Truly excellent soundtrack that greatly enhances the atmosphere of the game
-Genre bending gameplay with consistent perspective changes as well as shmup and twin stick shooter elements. These serve to keep things exciting and never overstay their welcome.
-Very solid pacing
-RPG lite mechanics allow solid flexibility in play style
Cons:
-Largely grey scale color palette. Use of color here is brilliant and saved for effect, but sometimes the world feels a bit drab
-The "open world" is a little closed off and opens in stages
-Fair bit of backtracking
-Frame timing issues, particularly during cutscenes (gtx1080, i76700k)
-Locked at 60fps
Also, the game SHINES at higher resolutions and when super sampled, as long as you can hit the 60 fps cap.
The gameplay, music, story and art direction work together here in a way that turns the whole in to something really special. Highly recommended.

+ Nice cutesy but brutal art style
+ Gameplay is random with its roguelike elements, making it very addictive
+ A lot of different items and powerups to mess around with
+ Multiple unlockable characters to suit multiple playstyles
+ Plot has a ton of social commentary that will hopefully leave you thinking even after you stop playing
Cons
- Can be glitchy at times
- Difficulty curve can be very brutal for newcomers
Questionable
? If you're a pretty religious person, you may be pretty offended by the game's style, plot, messages and humor, but you may be able to overlook these things.
Overall, I would totally recommend this game to other people.

This 2001 graphics pixel precision jumping adventure set in the Russian countryside can't really decide what it wants to be. It may aim to be a quite jolly relaxing experience for kids, with some absurdly easy levels (that often turn into an exercise in how you can exploit the bazillions of bugs to finish a mission in 10% of the intended time)... but then, it typically is simply a ton of frustration from the barely functional controls and the many glitches. Considering a good lot of the game ends up being balancing your digitally controlled cat on a fence that's a pixel or two wide, I can't tell if that's intentionally designed like this or if none of the Russian developers actually tried playing their own game.
What stands out as a positive is the comically murky voice acting (with one character unable to decide whether to feign being very British or very French, and 'meow' always pronounced 'mee-how') as well as developers brave enough to use something else than the Unity engine, but it can't make up for the controls and the overall lack of game design.
Overall, not even the gratuitous use of cats can save
.

purposes, playing through the game once is enough, and that'll take between 2 and 3 hours depending on how often you fall off single pixels, get randomly tabbed out of the fullscreen game, or have your cat stuck jumping forwards in a straight line. For reasons i can't begin to fathom, this game seems to be a popular target for bashing... largely by people who have either never played it or only played for a few minutes. It may not be as complex as the X series of games, but personally i think that is one of many plus points about this title.
This game essentially plays as a slightly dumbed down version of the classic Freelancer, and is every bit as enjoyable as the title that clearly influenced the design. So, it's easy to pick up and start playing, plus it has an engrossing storyline which it also allows you to follow at your own pace (so you can put the story on hold while you raise enough cash to buy yourself a much better ship and/or better equipment and armaments, for example).
Visually the game is very pleasing, even though there are occasionally some very serious jaggied lines in clear view no matter how much anti-aliasing you're using. I run the game with 8x AA and 16x AF and yet they are still quite prominent, especially on the space stations. Incidentally, in the game configuration application it has the option to run 16x anti-aliasing but this option is always greyed out and i've never been able to select it... nor do i know anyone who has, no matter what graphics card they are using. This is one of only two negative points. The other is that stability could be improved. I've only had the game crash twice, but it is annoying when it happens during a mission and you need to start it from the beginning again.
The console versions of this game may have additional DLC which will not be coming to the PC version, and yes that is a shame that we won't be getting it, but don't let that sway you from buying it. The core game itself is extremely good and well worth buying, especially at the low price it's currently on sale for.

The Refund Gods stand before me asking: "Would you like us to take away Oriental Empires?  Is it not fun enough for you?"
NO!!
Oriental Empires is a simultaneous TBS with a complex between-turn battle system.  That's right - it's nothing like Civ or other TBS where battles take place during your turn, or during an enemy's turn.  Everyone plans their next move, and we all hit the "next turn" button at the same time, and if armies run into each other, battles take place that generate an outcome you have no control over, but is extremely entertaining to watch.  I don't know if they are deterministic or rely on RNG.  While at least some other TBS offer a default of "battles during my turn" with an option of "simultaneous turns" (I think Civ does), this game only offers simultaneous turns.  That means you always have to predict where the opponent might move, and it can sometimes feel like playing whack-a-mole - they might move out from under you and just take a city while they are at it.
Hint: Faster units will outrun a slow army trying to catch up, so hit-and-run tactics are a viable option, but also means you spend more time analyzing the board to see if your cities are within striking distance of enemy armies.
The simultaneous turns are similar to the game Dominions, but here if enemy armies are within 1 tile from you while either armies are moving to a destination, they will fight (they don't have to have the same tiles in their paths like in Dominions).
The battles that take place, out of your control, are "in real time", which means that units that have been ordered to move may do so unhindered behind other units that are in the heat of battle.  It's really cool to watch, and strategies can be developed related to the timing of when units will show up at a battle to maximize efficiency.
After 2 hours of playing, I've noticed that the game offers a new concept I've never seen before: authority.  This can affect city morale if leaders are percieved as idiots.  <I will refrain from making political comments, as tempting as they are to bring up.>
The atmosphere of the game is really dripping, oozing, bleeding richly with gorgeous artwork and cultural background.  If you are familiar with China it might resonate really well, and if you're like me, it's a really nice introduction, and just alien enough to pique my curiosity.  Part of that experience is the seamless map-view-to-ground-level-zoom.  This is a gorgeous trick and adds a huge amount of immersion.  The other part is that fields and cities have a ground-level view that is about the size of a football field, which adds realism (albeit slightly exaggerated) that I haven't seen in any other TBS.
The AI (it's a little early to tell) is relatively intelligent.  Or I'm just getting lucky with the board I'm playing.  Either way - there are interesting situations to work through.
The UI doesn't follow the (worn out?) standard "tasks completed in the right column" layout.  It does some new things that are intuitive enough that I didn't bother reading all the manual text - I could figure it out.  However, the tutorial help text could do a little more hand-holding for easing the learning curve.  In general I absolutely like the UI - it offers no drawbacks, and might be presenting a new standard for the genre.
After over 8 hours of playing (in one sitting), there are rebellions!  Cities break off to form their own country, and if you try to fight them, there's a good chance your own armies will desert to the side of the rebels.  There's this feeling like your whole country is being infected by a virus that spreads out of control.  This is insane!  It turns out the rebellions can be avoided (in small part) by giving the people a break from building new farms, new buildings, and serving in the military!  What?  They aren't just little robots for me to push around forever?  There are also nobles who can insite rebellion if they think my authority level isn't sufficient for the number of cities in the country.
Con:
- The game fails to show a clear supply-chain path of resources.  For example, bronze magically is produced by one of the buildings, but this isn't clearly documented, nor does the game make it clear.  You'll see copper mines, which implies you'd also see a tin mine, and combine those resources to make bronze - but it doesn't work that way, and this ambiguity can be confusing and increase the learning curve (as if there wasn't enough to worry about already).  [This confusion is because the game doesn't play like Civ - resources on the map are only catalysts to accellerate production, but any military unit can be built regardless of whether you control resources on the map.]
If you have played Civ, you may be wondering "what else is different?"  Well, in battles, units at full health going in almost never die.  Most of the time, units abandon a fight to stay alive, which means that you'll see enemies continue to hound you for a while until you have hit them several times to get rid of them.  This can drag things out a bit, but it adds to the immersion too.
I've read some negative reviews saying this game is a rip-off of <some ho-hum game that would never get my interest at first glance due to obvious lack of complexity and simplistic interface>.  Well if it is, I don't care.  This game stands on its own in its own right, with no need for comparisons.  This game brings way more to the table than I was expecting, as it is nothing like Civ, and adds a strange and refreshing new flavor to the genre.

Despite the obvious negativity from the Borderlands community, stating this "isn't a full game/feels more like a big DLC," this game has its charm. At first, I was disappointed as well, but I found as I played it again, I liked the energy it created. I could even so much as say I like The Pre-Sequel over Borderlands 2.
The one thing I love most about this game is that it establishes one major essence of the Borderlands series that I didn't fully comprehend until now: there are no "good" guys. Every character has flaws, every character has at least some questionable morals. And they all make mistakes! (A non-spoiler-ish example would be Mr. Torgue, who in this game has absolutely no respect for Janey or for females at all - but you hear present day Mr. Torgue butt in the story to say he apologized for his awful behavior back then. Because people can change, for either the better or the worse--)
All the characters, especially the playable ones, are quirky and lovable in their own ways. There are a lot of things in this game that I wished they did in Borderlands 2, either gameplay-wise or story-wise. I hope that they adopt some of the mechanics from this game into their next one (mostly the fact that the characters actually reply with spoken lines, which Borderlands 2 only did in their DLC, because I'm a sucker for banter).
Any fan of the Borderlands series should play this game, not only does it add more lore, it adds to the story, the overall gameplay, and to the cast of colorful characters in the Borderlands series. Play it, you won't regret it.

I never write reviews, but for this game I make an exception.
Outcast! A game I played when it was released in 1999 in a resolution of 320x240 on my pentium 3 450 mhz computer. Outcast had to compete with games like Half-Life back then. And one reason of why the sales numbers were so low, was because the game was using the cpu to render the game. People just didn't want to upgrade their cpu's or play on a low resolution and so the game didn't reach their goal of 1 million sales. Instead they sold around 400.000 copies. Outcast 2 was in development, but because of the disappointing sales, Appeal (the original developer) went bankrupt and Outcast 2 was never released.
About the game:
The game itself is absolutely fantastic. The story is very good! After I completed Outcast for the first time I was just overwhelmed by it's story. The developers did a very great job on it. It has drama, action, humor almost everything you can think of.
How does this 1.1 version run?
Well first of of all, let me show you my specifications of my computer:
CPU: AMD FX-8120 @ 3ghz
GPU: Palit GTX 770 2GB
Memory: Crucial Ballistix 2x4 GB
I'm running the game on 1920x1080 and i'm getting a nice stable fps of around 30 fps. Just enough to run it smooth.
Are there bugs? Yes there are bugs. For example: when the camera is facing Slate (the character you play) the surrounding disappear. After the camera faces a different direction, everything comes back. That's the only bug that I have found for now. Ow and also the recreator (a Talan that can produce ammunition for you) isn't in the village like he was in the original game but in the rice field near the mountain. Not sure if that was in the original too and that he moved later to village but that doesn't really matter imho.
I really recommend you guys and girls to buy this game. It's a very small price, and with the 1.1 update you can run it in a nice resolution. Oh did I mention that the music is also very great! Music was made by the Moscow Symphony Orchestra and adds so much atmosphere to the game.

Compared to something like MW2, it’s pretty direct and there are very few points where you have to worry about beating a super long level where all you do is go from one alley to the next slowly and being shot from every direction. Here it’s a lot more linear but it’s actually pretty fun. Plus, the AI for your teammates is competent so you can actually rely on them to be not idiots.
That being said, there are a couple of times that there were cheap deaths because it wasn’t super clear what the objective was and that whole sequence with the bomber was annoying and kind of pointless.

New vision also improves the textures, so the game looks slightly better. Otherwise you are stuck with low resolutions and some problems with the game being very dark.
When it comes to narrative and storytelling, the first Deus Ex is still on pair / actually better than Human Revolution (Mankind Divided is worse). When it comes to choices, it is on pair with Human Revolution. When it comes to action, it is a hair better than Human Revolution and much better than Mankind Divided. The game is playable with stealth (althrough it is very difficult compared to the later installments), you can run around guns blazing, you can go non-lethal and you can go melee. There are a lot of options and choices. The game doesn't really moralizes too much on decisions (like Mankind Divided), so the player can do as it likes.
I was actually surprised how good the game still is and how well it aged. Deus Ex is one of the best fps games ever made and I was suprised how well it still holds, after all these years.

TL;DR - worse Borderlands 2 that gets terribly frustrating and exhausting by the end missions. 4/10.
And now the long one. Let's just start with stating that this is still a Borderlands game, so if you enjoyed the previous ones you will most likely enjoy this one too, especially when playing with friends. For the most of it. Then you'll get frustrated and will want to just quit this god damn game.
Lets start with the missions. There are some nice ones, some quite unique and fun ones. But that's like 5 out of 40. The rest are all repetitive fetch quests that get unnaturally prolonged, because if not the game wouldn't be the half of what it is now. The worst part is that this applies not only to side missions, which are obviously always lower priority for production, but for main quests as well. Without spoiling, there was a mission that could be literally summarised to:
-Go to A
-A doesn't work,  you need to go to B then
-B doesn't work, ok C will for sure
-Well, C ALMOST works, you only need D to make it work
-Ok you have D? Now go back to C
-Ok C works now? ok go to B and then you'll proceed to the final part of the mission
Where story wise, it could very well and at B and be much more fun. Even worse, by the very end the WHOLE GAME feels like it is being unneccessarily prolonged, without an actual, reasonable explenation why. That leads us to writing.
The humor is worse. It's got to a level of stupidity that is actually cringe worthy and embarasing. The one part that they did well - Jack's change - is kind of destroyed by the fact that I can't state my point about it. Obviously, it's always like that in games like this, you have no dialogue choices etc, but the problem is, in other games your character doesn't make a change on it's own as well.
SPOILER STARTS HERE: I've started the game as a more or less good guy. I wanted to save the moon with Jack's help or as his help. Regardless, even though I might not be 100% rightous, I was still good. And that's the character I liked and I wanted to play as. Later, when Jack kills 4 scientist because he suspected that one of them was a traitor my character suddenly screams AWESOME. What the ♥♥♥♥? I mean, it was awesome in terms of building Jack's character, showing how voilence is changing him, but I never wanted my character to change with him, nor was I ever teased that it might happen. SPOILER OVER.
Next topic. Loot and character progression are both done terribly. Let's just say I've finished the game with weapons not higher than level 22, as a 26 level character, fighting level 28 boss. That's not how you balance loot. I've switched my sniper rifle 3 times during over 20h of gameplay. Also I have not seen a SINGLE legendary weapon, not to mention one I would actually like and want to use. Something that also didn't help with my gear progression is that I lost a TON of items by them dropping into abyss. You'd imagine they could write a piece of code that ensures loot lands on reachable place in a game that's heavily loot dependend.
Character progression can be summed up as: start with active ability, put 25 boring stat boosters after and then put an actually cool ability at level 26. Boring as hell. One thing that also needs to be mentioned here - main story balancing, combined with unrewarding loot system, pretty much makes side quests obligatory.
My last big issue with the game is it's optimization - on a GTX 780 i had very frequent drops to 30-40 even without maxing all of the settings and with turning off the PhysX. Another wierd thing with it is that even when it was running at stable 60 according to Steam FPS counter, there was TERRBILE screen tearing. G-Sync helped there, but not everyone can afford it. Then, when I switched to GTX 980Ti in the middle, it was still not achieving stable 60. What the hell. Witcher 3 runs at stable 60 in 2K, while also looking much, much better.
The other issues are not as big, but perhaps worth mentioning. Gearbox introduced a couple of new gameplay mechanics, for example oxygen in vaccum, lower gravity with booster jump and laser guns. Not a single one of those is actually fun. Oxygen is annoying, because for most of the game you don't care about it, only sometimes you are searching for O2 source nearby in panick. Lower gravity (which means higher jumps) would be fun if not the fact that level design doesn't seem to adjust to that correctly and multiple collisions are just a tiny bit too high to jump on them, even with perfectly timed booster. Laser guns are mostly useless (I found one that I was using for a bit, because it actually shot where I poitned it to, rest shoots wherever it wants).
There was also a lot of small bugs, like lacks of collisions or incorrectly placed ones, NPCs falling torso deep into terrain (mostly lunatics after their jump attack), problems with AI - NPCs walking past me peacefully while I'm in combat with their friends or launching a jump attack at a helicopter that's over lava in one of the missions, resulting in killing themselves, graphical glitches like some wierd, glowing mesh being left hanging in the air after killing one of the opponents.
To be honest it's hard to say anything good about the game aside from the fact that shooting is fun. But then the last two missions start, you have♥♥♥♥♥♥gear because of unrewarding loot system and you just want this to end, but it doesn't. It goes on and on and on for no logical reason other that boosting the number of hours neccessary to finish the game. I do not recommend this one.

The Last Crown: Midnight Horror is a nice short thematic point and click adventure game that is a direct sequel to "The Lost Crown" and a prequel to the upcoming Blackenrock game from Darkling Room Studios. Like most of Mr. Boakes' games, there is a lot of optional activity and superfluous items you don't need. I carried arround that Hot Dog from beginning to end for example.
The adventure places you once again int he role of Nigel Danvers as you try to solve what appears to be a haunting at the local pub. The game oozes with atmosphere and style and I love that the came has kept the mostly black and white graphics which made the original game, The Lost Crown, so striking. The music, mood, visuals and atmophere should keep fans of TLC and the Darkfall games happy from beginning to end. You'll also find that events are somewhat more randomized than in most adventure games which tend to be extremely linear. An event with the police didn't occur with me until the very end of the game, while for most people I've talked to, it happened at the very beginning.
Now that said, the game is far from perfect. Although it took me 4.1 hours to beat, half of that time was reloading the game due to crashes or stalls. There's a well known bug that occurs when you hand in the DJ Voucher. Thankfully this is not necessary to finish the game so just don't do anything with it if you get it.  I was surprised the game crashed on me four different times. Once after the seance and three other times in different rooms. I could play Batman: Arkham Knight without the slightest hiccup when it first came out yet this adventure game crashed on me several times. So remember to save regularly so you don't have to repeat things like I did!
Another thing to remember is that the game has some very small hot spots and, unlike some other modern adventure games, you can't just click the space button to see all the available locations. This does mean you'll be huting and pecking for things that you don't see or just outright don't trigger right away. Some of these include the wall by the rotting fish, the pots int he kitchen, the keyhole on the fourth door in floor two you gain access to towards the end of the game and so on. So be prepared to be thorough and don't be shy in asking for help in the community boards if you get stuck. TLC fans are a great lot and already people have been helping each other out left and right here on the game's Steam board.  There will be times you get frustrated. Then once someone helps you along, the solution will make a lot of sense in retrospect. Just remember to pass the help along.
Overall, Midnight Horror is a fun but flawed game. I love the artistic style of the game and the story told here. It's a nice classic ghost story in the vein of some great Victorian writers andf it was the perfect game for the Halloween Holiday season.
BUY AND PLAY DIS GAIM.

One of the best games I've ever played. In the past I liked the concept of exploration in a game called Spore. Finally, Stellaris fills the niche I've been looking for. I think many of the system scan events can dive deeper, but for now it's ok. I like that we can scan debris after a battle to learn techs the other race has and improve our own arsenal. I like that AI is smart enough to wait until I leave a system to flank my own planets. I don't like how one puny species with its final planet on the brink of my conquering can ally itself with the entire galaxy and tell me that if I attack it anymore, I have to wage war with all the races. Where did they get the leverage to make a protection pact with every race in the galaxy? Even races that don't like them. It made no sense. Sometimes this game makes you angry enough to switch from exploration to a dictatorship warmonger. And you can do that! That's what's great about it. The level of options and detail at your fingertips. Oh, and don't pick lasers as your starter weapons if you want to hit things. 50% of the time the tracking is too slow and so your hit rate is in the fifties. They sure look awesome though.

I really liked the concept of Party Hard, but the execution is fairly♥♥♥♥♥♥
Basic premise - you're a guy who hates parties, so you go to parties in various settings and murder everyone there. If someone spots you killing a dude or standing near a corpse, they'll call the cops, who are far faster than you, but will generally give up if you manage to elude them for 20 seconds or so. If they spot an unhidden dead body without you being near it, they'll call the cops just to have them switch the body for a bodybag. In either scenario, the party goes on until you're dead / arrested, or the last party goer is dead.
You get a number of randomized Hitman-ish traps scattered throughout the party, and a number of random events can help or hinder you (robbery, zombie attack, the FBI drop by, aliens fly around). Still; with all that done, traps and random events will account for 10 to 20 party goers. Parties generally have 40 to 70 guys hanging around. The rest you'll have to kill with your trusty knife, one at a time.
You can't actually control where party goers wander, and you can't outrun a party goer trying to reach the phone, so most of the game consists of waiting for people to wander into a location where you won't be spotted while stabbing them. Then you hope your 1 second (literally!) sprint bar will get you there before someone joins them / they wander away. Multiply this by 30 or so, until the party goers are thinned out enough that you can just murder them where they are. No checkpoints, each level is restarted and somewhat randomized when you fail.
All that - constant waiting, randomized failure states, lack of explanation for abilities and elements of the environment - would have been bad enough if the game wasn't glitchy and poorly translated. Every third body you toss into a hiding spot will stand in place, like a living NPC, but still triggering the "saw a body" reaction from party goers. I've been chased by a zombified cop trying to arrest me. I had to figure out why "overboard" was too complicated a concept to translate.
Check the guide section. I'll be you 5$ that most of these were created by the game's staff, as the grammar / spelling / translation errors are nearly identical. But hey, I have the advantage of speaking Russian, so I can just play the game that way, right? Oh, the writing is actually even more awkward and annoying that way. Welp.

OK, you can set high resolutions, but textures and models are still very low quality. Sound? Music - atrocious BGM. Voice - medicore at best, but passable, sometimes even funny. I could recommend this game only as a bargain bin purchase for 1 buck. In other cases you will feel like ripped off, because the boredom will quickly get to you. But dont get me wrong - its not a bad game. Its just not a good one.

This is quite simply the best 4x strategy game I've ever played in terms of immersive, detailed, balanced game design.
You literally are the leader of a powerful clan in bronze age China, settling the yangtze river valley and building an empire not just with warfare but with diplomacy and careful economic planning.
You can't build a doomstack and stomp the map in 20 turns, because each settlement you control above your "authority" rating causes unrest with your nobles, eventually leading to civil wars.
You can't just infinite build farms and clear forests and conscript millions of peasants into your army, as the peasants will grow wearing of your taxes and forced labor and revolt!
Oh and these revolts/civil wars don't just spawn a pathetic stack which can't hope to take your city wall or garrison on, NO! It instantly turns the city against you, and any force you lead to take it back might turn on you unless led by a family member.
The combat system leads to no overpowered, easy to win any battle armies (like in total war) but with a heck of a lot more hands on control than any other non-TW game i've ever seen.
It's just so well designed, you've gotta play it.

Deus Ex is fun. I played through of this because I like Mankind Divided, then went back to play through Human Revolution, and the next step was naturally to play through the original game again, to see how it holds up.
To begin with, on a modern machine (assuming you have an 1080p screen), get New Vision. It doesn't change anything when it comes to gameplay, but it makes sure that you can read the books as the scaling isn't really working with the original game. New vision also improves the textures, so the game looks slightly better. Otherwise you are stuck with low resolutions and some problems with the game being very dark.
When it comes to narrative and storytelling, the first Deus Ex is still on pair / actually better than Human Revolution (Mankind Divided is worse). When it comes to choices, it is on pair with Human Revolution. When it comes to action, it is a hair better than Human Revolution and much better than Mankind Divided. The game is playable with stealth (althrough it is very difficult compared to the later installments), you can run around guns blazing, you can go non-lethal and you can go melee. There are a lot of options and choices. The game doesn't really moralizes too much on decisions (like Mankind Divided), so the player can do as it likes.
I was actually surprised how good the game still is and how well it aged. Deus Ex is one of the best fps games ever made and I was suprised how well it still holds, after all these years.

TL;DR - worse Borderlands 2 that gets terribly frustrating and exhausting by the end missions. 4/10.
And now the long one. Let's just start with stating that this is still a Borderlands game, so if you enjoyed the previous ones you will most likely enjoy this one too, especially when playing with friends. For the most of it. Then you'll get frustrated and will want to just quit this god damn game.
Lets start with the missions. There are some nice ones, some quite unique and fun ones. But that's like 5 out of 40. The rest are all repetitive fetch quests that get unnaturally prolonged, because if not the game wouldn't be the half of what it is now. The worst part is that this applies not only to side missions, which are obviously always lower priority for production, but for main quests as well. Without spoiling, there was a mission that could be literally summarised to:
-Go to A
-A doesn't work,  you need to go to B then
-B doesn't work, ok C will for sure
-Well, C ALMOST works, you only need D to make it work
-Ok you have D? Now go back to C
-Ok C works now? ok go to B and then you'll proceed to the final part of the mission
Where story wise, it could very well and at B and be much more fun. Even worse, by the very end the WHOLE GAME feels like it is being unneccessarily prolonged, without an actual, reasonable explenation why. That leads us to writing.
The humor is worse. It's got to a level of stupidity that is actually cringe worthy and embarasing. The one part that they did well - Jack's change - is kind of destroyed by the fact that I can't state my point about it. Obviously, it's always like that in games like this, you have no dialogue choices etc, but the problem is, in other games your character doesn't make a change on it's own as well.
SPOILER STARTS HERE: I've started the game as a more or less good guy. I wanted to save the moon with Jack's help or as his help. Regardless, even though I might not be 100% rightous, I was still good. And that's the character I liked and I wanted to play as. Later, when Jack kills 4 scientist because he suspected that one of them was a traitor my character suddenly screams AWESOME. What the ♥♥♥♥? I mean, it was awesome in terms of building Jack's character, showing how voilence is changing him, but I never wanted my character to change with him, nor was I ever teased that it might happen. SPOILER OVER.
Next topic. Loot and character progression are both done terribly. Let's just say I've finished the game with weapons not higher than level 22, as a 26 level character, fighting level 28 boss. That's not how you balance loot. I've switched my sniper rifle 3 times during over 20h of gameplay. Also I have not seen a SINGLE legendary weapon, not to mention one I would actually like and want to use. Something that also didn't help with my gear progression is that I lost a TON of items by them dropping into abyss. You'd imagine they could write a piece of code that ensures loot lands on reachable place in a game that's heavily loot dependend.
Character progression can be summed up as: start with active ability, put 25 boring stat boosters after and then put an actually cool ability at level 26. Boring as hell. One thing that also needs to be mentioned here - main story balancing, combined with unrewarding loot system, pretty much makes side quests obligatory.
My last big issue with the game is it's optimization - on a GTX 780 i had very frequent drops to 30-40 even without maxing all of the settings and with turning off the PhysX. Another wierd thing with it is that even when it was running at stable 60 according to Steam FPS counter, there was TERRBILE screen tearing. G-Sync helped there, but not everyone can afford it. Then, when I switched to GTX 980Ti in the middle, it was still not achieving stable 60. What the hell. Witcher 3 runs at stable 60 in 2K, while also looking much, much better.
The other issues are not as big, but perhaps worth mentioning. Gearbox introduced a couple of new gameplay mechanics, for example oxygen in vaccum, lower gravity with booster jump and laser guns. Not a single one of those is actually fun. Oxygen is annoying, because for most of the game you don't care about it, only sometimes you are searching for O2 source nearby in panick. Lower gravity (which means higher jumps) would be fun if not the fact that level design doesn't seem to adjust to that correctly and multiple collisions are just a tiny bit too high to jump on them, even with perfectly timed booster. Laser guns are mostly useless (I found one that I was using for a bit, because it actually shot where I poitned it to, rest shoots wherever it wants).
There was also a lot of small bugs, like lacks of collisions or incorrectly placed ones, NPCs falling torso deep into terrain (mostly lunatics after their jump attack), problems with AI - NPCs walking past me peacefully while I'm in combat with their friends or launching a jump attack at a helicopter that's over lava in one of the missions, resulting in killing themselves, graphical glitches like some wierd, glowing mesh being left hanging in the air after killing one of the opponents.
To be honest it's hard to say anything good about the game aside from the fact that shooting is fun. But then the last two missions start, you have♥♥♥♥♥♥gear because of unrewarding loot system and you just want this to end, but it doesn't. It goes on and on and on for no logical reason other that boosting the number of hours neccessary to finish the game. I do not recommend this one.

Despite some clunky mechanics, Deus Ex is definitely a great game, I can see why it is one of the, if not
highest rated game of all time. Great nonlinear leveldesign lets you find your own solutions to problems that can be tackled in multiple different ways. Music by none other than the composer who already made Unreal a feast for the ears.
But rather than go over the good things that already have been stated a thousand times and list them a 1001th time, I find it appropriate to inform about some drawbacks you won't see mentioned nearly as often:
Deus Ex is quite a challenge to run on modern PCs, and this is coming from an old Unreal Tournament veteran who knows how to edit every setting of every config file in his sleep.
You'll have to spend some time fixing the game before you can even start playing. It suffers from a number of issues, like uncapped framerate which leads to it running too fast, prematurely cancelling ingame cutscenes/dialogue, screen tearing, crackling sound/music and mouse/cursor issues.
There are a number of fixes available for some of those problems, some of which work better than others. The best renderer is a newer, fan-made OpenGL renderer, which you'll find on the net and requires the 1112fm update, also available on the net. This OpenGL renderer makes the game look just like it did back then, and has some important features like a framerate cap. I've also tried the often recommended DX10 renderer, and found that it makes rather drastic changes to the way lightning is handled in the game, usually for the worse, so I cannot recommend it.
There's a 3rd party launcher for Deus Ex that apparently fixes many issues, but I don't like running additional software so I did most other fixes by manually editing the .ini files. Unfortunately, I have not found a solution for the mouse behaviour, particularly because it's the cursor in the menus rather than the ingame sensitivity that is way too high, with no way to change it. This makes going through the inventory, the logs and everything else you do in the UI a downright painful experience. And you
spend a significant amount of time dealing with the interface.
Going through all that trouble is worth is though. When you're done pulling your hair out trying to get Deus Ex to run properly and scavenging the internet for various fixes, you're left with a great game that has a decent amount of replay value.

I usually satisfy myself with mindless clicking at things that move, clubbing zombies and “flamethrowing” aliens enough to make a batter-happy Flintstone giddy. After a while the repetitive slashing and gouging puts a strain on my steadily numbing mind and I need a break. Brainiac games like Hexcells provides that pause from the world of action titles that many gamers find soothing from time to time. The minimalistic interface calms you to the core like entering your hotel room, the first day of your sunny beach-filled holiday. Easy-peasy controls and rules, as most strategic puzzle games tend to excel in, are explained through directions (though for Level 1 I felt the couple of trial plays planted in the beginning of each rule change, would have sufficed). I’ve seen plenty of reviews exclaiming it as comfortably easy to finish, which isn’t quite true as new rules are added regularly and consistently starting at Level 11. This lessens repertoire and makes Hexcells highly entertaining for a puzzle game of its kind. It calls for the elimination and deduction tools we have honed through countless hours of playing games such as Sudoku and Minesweeper. There is no timer so in a sense is closer to a Sudoku that’s pleasing to the eye. Hexcells adds the “chic” that Sudoku lacks and the logicality which Minesweeper is deficient in through functions which allow no room for the guessing games and visuality to match. No function is lacking or overdone in Hexcells. As Goldilocks would say, “It’s just right.” It is one of the most accessible and convenient game I have ever played. The UI looks fantastic for touch screens and as I’ve been marooned on my laptop for a few months, it’s always heaven to play low spec games that won’t freeze mid-play and still provide high quality content to keep me amused for consecutive hours. It is also a great game for a few minutes here and there as an easy to start, continue and leave at any time type game that doesn’t bore. For example, the widely loved classic, Peggle will have me dozing off in a few minutes flat although it’s a sweet little thing.
The intermediate level starts around Lv. 18-19 and I started finding it mind boggling beginning at Lv. 22. After that point some are comparatively easier than others which didn’t reflect the actual order or the levels. Thank goodness because the couple of easier levels here and there let me hang on to my sanity!
Most of the reviews I’ve read stated plenty of appreciation towards the needlessness of guessing the answers. There is 0% need to speculate and everything must be calculated if you want to play the game to its maximum. Keep in mind that if you mess up once you’ll end up with the obvious answer which means it’s extremely easy to use trial and error to pick through the games effortlessly. This sucks all the fun out of it so I suggest you aim for 100% accuracy each time you play or try and forget the hex you just wrongly clicked and move on to something else so you won’t end up getting everything easy. Another tip I have is to try playing it as fast as your mind will think and fingers will click because the music sounds better that way. It has one of those almost interactive tracks so that what and how you click will determine a different sound that in turns melds into the original score underneath it.
In all honestly, the aspect the feature I enjoyed the least was the music in Hexcells as it is repetitive and some parts sound like an orchestra of mobile phones with annoying, monotonous ringtones. (Note: I understand that there was only so much the developer could do and it wasn't that bad, I'm just used to better soundtracks is all. ;D) Which is why I eventually turned down the volume and even then I still couldn’t quite stand it. It wasn’t the relaxed ambience I was hoping for but it wasn’t as noticeable when playing at a faster pace (clicking hexes in acceleration) for reasons already noted above. A better example would be Duet, the strategic arcade game by Kumobius (iOS/Android). The music is directed via the player’s fingertips as they go through the puzzles and it is scored in a way that’s surprisingly meditative for a game of somewhat high difficulty. The fluidity of a game’s soundtrack influences a massive portion of its play mood in any genre. Other than that, I’m interested in buying the other two as well for a rainy day and hope the background music is a tad better than the first one.
