NieR:Automata is a tale that truly captivated me from the very beginning. Seeing the credits roll past me by a few times in a flash within the first hour of me trying to get past the prologue, struggling through the bullet hell parts, and getting absolutely smashed by a gigantic robot, was a sign to me that I was in for a one of a kind ride. For me NieR is so far the GOTY of 2017. Here are my reasons why:
- PROS -
- The story is masterfully written, it is presented in a somewhat vague way, so you're literally going to be in for a hell of ride, because you never know where the story might progress. Just be sure to not leave the game at ending A, as the other routes bring so much new content. It's not a new game plus, rather the story is sometimes told from a different perspective and later on continued from one ending.
- The main protagonists, 2B, 9S and A2 are all likable and their character designs are very well done. Towards the end, I grew to care about each of them, and how their stories might end.
- The combat is so fluid, as expected from Platinum Games. I really never grew tired of the combat or any enemies thrown my way. Smashing enemies up with various weapons and skills always felt so rewarding.
- The Plug-in chip system allows for some very neat combinations, so you can play around building a set that best fits your playstyle.
- The side quests, although a bit repetitive perhaps in their gameplay at times, really excelled in their writing. Each quest had a story of its own to tell.
- The soundtrack of this game is in my opinion perhaps one of the best scores in gaming. Keiichi Okabe really created a stellar work, with most of the scores featuring beautiful vocals sung by Emi Evans, and the tracks also have an 8-bit tune accompanying them. The songs seamlessly transition from quiet to dynamic to 8-bit.
- The english dub is really amazing. The actors manage to convey the feelings and moods of the characters very well across the whole game.
- Graphics in this game are perhaps not the best, the color palette is a bit brownish, but it fits the atmosphere, and everything feels stylish still.
- CONS -

- There were sometimes a little bit too much loading screens between relatively short sequences in the game which kind of broke the continuity.
- The semi-open world at times can feel a bit desolate, although filled with many quests and enemies.
- There's alot of quests and things to do in the game, just that I wish there was a bit more, a few more areas to explore and a few more bosses, but that's probably what everyone would want from such a compelling game.
NieR:Automata to me is a 10/10 game, Yoko Taro's storytelling really captivated me, the gameplay just felt so tight that I just had to keep coming for more.

Overall: a fresh, ambitious, uneven game that isn't approachable enough for everyone but is deeply rewarding for those who stick it out.
The good:
-Not just a Civ knockoff; brings unique mechanics and strategies to the table
-Unique and thoroughly-researched setting that matters for gameplay
-Great art, music and visual design
The bad:
-Bare-bones manual and tooltips make getting started difficult
-Lack of building/unit browser, sometimes difficult to tell what the prerequisites are for a tech, etc
The game takes you from the early Bronze Age, ruling over an agrarian society with minimal taxation or infrastructure and fighting wars with short-term levies, through the Warring States period of centralizing governments and growing professional armies, and into the Imperial era of larger, more stable kingdoms growing rich off of trade and industry. Gameplay is tied closely to the historical setting as technologies and Edicts (all based off of their in-depth research) shape your options. The design philosophy leans more towards simulation than balanced gameplay, for example with trade only becoming profitable organically through the growth and specialization of cities- there is a general lack of "pay one-time build cost, get per-turn income" type buildings as everything ultimately ties back to your food-growing, tax-paying agricultural workforce. Likewise your military units behave much more like troops in a combat-focused game like Total War (cues were definitely taken from Medieval II's recruitment pool system) than like the boardgame pieces that are typical 4x units.
The most serious shortcoming is that, for a game that takes such a unique approach to so many basic elements of gameplay, it has a totally substandard Help function, manual and in-game tooltips. For me, learning the game well came down to about 150 turns of pure trial-and-error and numerous restarts (and I came into things at least knowing Chinese geography and what to expect from "the Well-Field System"). Various opaque bits of the UI don't help much either. After going through all that effort I still think the game is absolutely worthwhile, but it's not doing itself any favors by making players dig to learn these things.

A very fun and aesthetically pleasing arcade-style space shooter.
is a fun little game.  It's not very deep at all, and beating the main game can likely be done in an afternoon or two (but much more if you want to get all achievements).  Furthermore, there are plenty of little missions and variations of things to do which should hold your interest as you play through the game, so it doesn’t grow stale.  Sometimes you have to dogfight in space against various ships, sometimes you have to escort cargo frigates, sometimes you have to smuggle some goods, and sometimes you just need to mine some minerals so you can buy a better ship or weapons.  If you like the idea of flying around the galaxy as a
-esque character, in various spaceships which you can upgrade and customize, then you will probably enjoy this quaint little game.
The gameplay is pretty simple and straightforward at its core, but surprisingly offers a lot of possibilities.  As I mentioned, there is a decent amount of variety to your missions and you also have a decent amount of freedom to choose how you want to progress. It actually is pretty engaging once you get sucked into the thick of it.  And right when the game may start to feel a bit repetitive…
you’ve reached the end of the campaign anyway.  Additionally, if you find yourself really into the game, after saving the galaxy you can embark on infinite side-quests of various types in an effort to grow your riches beyond your wildest dreams.
What also helps the overall experience is that the graphics and animations are pretty nice.  Anyone who appreciates the aesthetic allure of the vast and vivid void of space will enjoy the scenery and special effects in
.  I’m not saying it’s the prettiest game ever, but for a simple arcade game, it looks pretty dang sweet.  Things have come a long, long way since the
game I used to play as a kid on my SNES.  Now you can not only enjoy the gameplay, but also immerse yourself in the ambiance of space combat.
So
is a good game; but it is undoubtedly a simple and relatively short one.  But if it sounds like something you would like, it is worth considering picking this up at a price you feel comfortable with.

This is an ambitious game for such a small studio, set in a time period that's too-often ignored by the genre. Unfortunately, the game doesn't quite live up to the potential.
The graphics and music combine to give the game a really wonderful atmosphere. It really sets the scene of the dawn of Chinese civilization for the player, though a bit more variety in the music tracks would be nice. There were a couple of pieces that I seem to only hear once or twice in ten hours of playing, while others played repeatedly.
The main play screen is a birds-eye (or perhaps a bit higher than birds-eye) view of a China divided up into hexes and covered in virgin floodplains, forests, hills, and mountains. Zooming in and out is seamless, with the level of detail shifting appropriately. Special resources (the usual 4x fare -- gold, copper, fish...rhinoceri. Apparently Ancient China was lousy with them.) are indicated by simple, clear icons. As the game progresses, cities appear, land is tilled into farmland, and roads gradually link cities together.
So far, so good. Everything on the map is presented in a neat, aesthetically appealing manner. The first hour or two of gameplay might get sucked into simply enjoying watching the player's civilization grow and expand across the map as seasons change.
However, problems quickly become apparent. In nearly every facet of the game, trying to dig past the surface results in either complete bewilderment or the gnawing sense that whatever mechanic is at play was either not really finished or is exceedingly simple. The combat, fought out by "stacks" or armies presented on the game map by detailed soldier models and in the UI by simple yet attractively made unit cards a-la Total War, turns out to mostly rely on sheer numbers. Once battle is joined, the fighting is entirely in the hands of the game's AI, leaving the player to watch haplessly as chariots run around in circles aimlessly or as generals charge alone into huge masses of enemy soldiers.
It seems there is some sort of rock-paper-scissors model intended by the developers, but it's never really explained well within the game and it frequently doesn't seem to pan out in actual battles. There is a wealth of information on the unit cards, and the player can pick from a large variety of "battle plans," but the plans seem to have little effect on the AI's actual behavior once battle is joined.
Combat is but one of two primary functions of military units in-game. The other is suppressing revolt. Here, the developers seemed to have invested much time and energy developing a sophisticated mechanic where players must finely balance their demands on peasant labor with military suppression of dissent and carefully timed imperial edicts. Unfortunately, the whole thing is undercut by the game's other major flaw, a complete lack of useful tooltips or explanation in critical areas. What should be a highlight of the game is instead an opaque system full of random variables that ends up being more frustrating than fun. Raising a unit of peasant light spearmen in one settlement reduces the odds of revolt, while mustering one in another town sends the mobs into the streets with torch and pitchfork. Clearing a hex for farmland infuriates peasants starving to death. An advisor helpfully reminds that letting construction idle for "a few turns" will eliminate peasant unrest due to demands on their labor, only to have idle turns pass by with practically 0 drop in unrest.
Trade is another problem. The trading system is nowhere explained, leaving the player to fumble through with trial and error. Eventually, they'll realize that even though many of the basic trading techs are available on Turn 1, trade is actively harmful until a third of the way into the game because the trade buildings cost far more than trade can hope to yield. Of course, it makes sense that people only a generation or two removed from hunter-gatherers, living in straw huts on the Yangtze River floodplain, would not have much wealth to spend on buying jade figurines. But it's strange that a large chunk of the early-game tech tree is devoted to developing things like merchant networks for selling jade figurines, and that there's no way for the player to tell there won't be any buyers for his exquisitely carved figurines for another few hundred years.
The game was in Early Access for a while, but the product in full-release now feels more like Early Access than anything else. If the devs are attentive, they can still end up with a really fine game. None of the game's problems are truly fatal flaws. With some work on things like basic balancing issues, fleshing out mechanics like combat and diplomacy, and in-game explanations or even basic helpful tooltips for extremely important concepts like trade, unrest, and peasant labor, the game could develop into a true 4X classic.

Don't waste your money on this game, devs are only interested in making a game that can survive 2 hours so you won't return it.
1. See those promotional vids of units fighting against units? You have ABSOLUTELY no control over them (other than setting their initial formation), they just ram into each other on the map. Eventually you end up pressing spacebar just to fast forward the combat because it's all the same. Oh and did I mention that if there are too many combats on the map, it lags out the game? Total War this is not.
2. The tech tree is so boring, after a while you just get the AI to sort it out for you. Everything is +15% to trade income, +10% to happiness, unlock a building that gives you +10% to happiness, culture +1, authority +1 yadda yadda. If you like spreadsheet simulator 101, this is the game for you. Nothing changes, you just build your spear/archer/cav armies, and then slightly better spear/archer/cav armies and then hurl them against each other (see point 1). Civ this is not.
3. Getting sniped by AI. Within the normal game length I doubt you can conquer the whole map, because there is a hardcap on the number of cities you can have (authority). So games come down to points. You can be conquering half of China for the whole game, but guess what there is an AI hiding in the other half that you haven't encountered, there is no way to check their points total (unlike Civ V) so guess what? You have no idea if you are 2 or 200 points behind, so you don't know how much you need to tryhard to catch up. Maybe you want to alpha strike them, but see point 2? You still have the crappy spear/archer/cav armies trundling along the crappy roads at 0.1 km/h, what are you going to strike them with? This is not Civilisation, you can't send in the nuclear bombs for a Hail Mary stroke.
4. Weird bugs. Somehow 5 archers in a city held out for 20 turns against 5 armies. Weird mechanics. So what if you are recognised as the one true Emperor by a faction, you get nothing and good luck getting everybody on the map to recognise you as Emperor within 300 turns. This is not even Spreadsheet Simulator, because that would make sense.
Unfortunately, you don't realise any of this till > 2hours into the game, because everyone knows the first 2 hours of games in this genre are build economy, fight some local wars and these issues do not become apparent until mid-late game. So don't buy this game, because you will end up like me trying to return the game with 5 hours playtime, only for it to be denied.
TL:DR - would have made better use of my 20 bucks if I had rolled it up and set it on fire. At least I would get to do something that works and I haven't done before.

Fairy Fencer F Advent Dark Force is an "expanded version" of the original FFF.
For those who never played FFF, you can start with this. And a bit of a warning, similar to Hyperdimension, the game plays like a Visual Novel. You can still explore dungeons freely, but if you're expecting an open world mechanism and cutscenes such as Final Fantasy or Tales of series, I suggest rethink about buying this.
The most appealing change at first glance is the graphics, which looks better.
But there's some kind of..."bloom" thing that can't be disabled (if you ever played Megadimension, you know what I meant. I think this thing is already in the original as well).
The only graphics settings available are: Resolution, Outline Render and Shadow Render or something like that. So yeah, it's not really that specific, which is kinda meh for me.
The story is still the same as FFF, but more refined. Nice and fresh as usual.
With the addition of few more routes which I haven't unlocked.
As for the gameplay, it plays almost the same as the original FFF, but now you can use 6 characters at the same time!
And no, it doesn't mean that we're overpowered. The battle itself isn't that boring, especially at higher difficulty, which makes you pray everytime it's the enemy turn, so that they won't deal critical damages. (Personal experience, their crit multiplier at times is x10).
Character customization varies only costume and accessories.
Known issues:
-Glitching graphics at the world map (Not to major, since we don't spend more than 10 minutes in the world map).
-Harley's Bullet Storm causing to crash (Shame, but the animation can be skipped for temporary solution. Hoping for patch).
-There are times where the game just stopped for a few seconds, but it doesn't crash. Consider it lag of some sort.
These issues doesn't really affect my own gameplay experience, but I really hope it can be fixed with some update patch.
All in all, if you like simple JRPGs, buy. Or wait till bigger sale.

Loadout has brilliant art design, great levels of crazy gore, and tons of irrevent humor.
The gameplay, however, is really lacking.
The main selling point of Loadout is the customization of your guns. Now, this would be a brilliant thing to have, but the fact that many of the parts are completely overpowered and that you aren't required to use specific parts makes the game very unbalanced. You could argue that you can make shotguns, snipers, and healing weapons, but if everybody else is just going to be making high rate of fire and damage weapons then 75% of your weapon options are uneffective. The only credit I'll give to it is that it allows you to actually have some diverse loadouts, not "pick a gun, pick a grenade" loadouts like in Call of Duty.
Speaking of Call of Duty, that's pretty much how the gameplay is. No, there's no health regeneration, but the gameplay is just the same uncontrolled mess game and game again. The first problem is the 4v4 combat on large maps. You'd think that with the chaos of the overpowered weapons you could have some close quarters action, but instead I found myself running around maps for 1-2 minutes at a time before I get killed by enemies that I didn't even see from across the map. Couple this with the fact that teams don't have to play specific roles, so you'll find yourself outnumbered and under-prepared many times.
The game modes are horribly uncreative. There's a Capture the Hammer mode which is basically a CTF mode but instead it's with a hammer that can get instakills. You can argue that it's fair because it has only 5 uses, but 5 uses is more than enough to wipe out the entire enemy team and get back to base with no hassle. Death Snatch is Team Deathmatch except you have to pick up items enemies drop and Blitz is Battlefield style Conquest that doesn't work at all because you can respawn and get back to the point within 30 seconds anyway.
But by far the WORST game mode is Extraction. One person from each team has to collect "Blutonium" pieces scattered across the map and drop them off at an extractor. The problem here is either A. you can effectively split a team of 4 to both protect you and kill the other collector and B. you can pick up all the Blutonium in a small radius of an extractor and by the time you're done all the Blutonium you just picked up respawns anyway.
For the first few plays, Loadout is stupid fun. After that, you realize it's just stupid. Quality of free-to-play games is usually determined by your willingness to spend money on it. Believe me, if I spent money on Loadout, I'd be extremely disappointed.

Hexcells is a fun if very short logic puzzler.  The objective is to reveal the number of blue hexes in each puzzle level.  There are only thirty or so puzzles to beat and the game can be completed in a few hours.  Early levels are relatively easy to complete but as you can imagine the last few are pretty complex to overcome without making a mistake.
Each level begins with some hexes providing some initial clues as to where the first blue hexes may be found.  Numbered hexes reveal the number of possible adjoining blue hexes.  Additional elements such as connected or unconnected chains, blues in a row providing additional clues.  Together with these assisting functions the player must use their powers of deduction to complete each puzzle without making a mistake.  Though each puzzle is entirely solvable, trial and error is possible though making a mistake with affect a "perfect" completion.
If you arent a whizz with logic or deduction then you will become frustrated on these harder levels.  The fun though is completing each puzzle entirely through deduction rather than through trial and error.

I love this game. The combat is fast and fluid (though a bit barebones compared to the likes of Platinum's other games, like Bayonetta, for instance), the characters are great, and there's a lot of existential themes going on. There's also a lot of humor and the game can be incredibly meta and self aware at times.
There's a bunch of different endings, and the game is highly replayable, with a sizeable overworld. There's a nice enemy variety, a bunch of cool weapons to unlock, good progression systemns for customizing and upgrading your character and abilities through implants. These implants actually affect the gameplay in a meaningful way, and make your advancement feel instantly impactful when you equip them.
You can also upgrade each weapon giving it a special ability at it's final upgrade stage, and each weapon has slightly varying movesets, though every weapon in the same weapon class plays primarily the same.
There is a missed opportunity for cosmetic unlockables though. I was hoping that for a game with so much replayability there would be a large variety of outfit and clothing customization for the characters, but this is sadly not the case. Save for some head accessories, like a bow, an alien head, a machine mask and some valves, that's about all the cosmetic customization options available, period. Though I guess my prior experience with games like Lollipop Chainsaw has heightened my expectations.
The story is good, and the way it's told has you asking lots of questions, this keeps you invested until reveals, twists and plotpoints.
Graphically the game looks fantastic, although the overall color palatte is a bit dreary and lifeless for my taste. Though I suspect this is by design considering the themes and content of the game. There are some issues with the port, most of which can be solved through a fan patch found in the forums, or a 3rd part program. All the other issues were present in the game's playstation counterpart.
Overall, I'm more than impressed with this game. I love it. And I'm glad more games are getting the PC love they deserve, and that this game has sold so well.

Purely a Singleplayer point of view here.
Stellaris,  An Empire building RTS on a galactic scale brought to you by Paradox Studios.   This game ooze's production value goodness from its fantastic immaginative artwork too its innovative yet sutely inspired soundtrack.  The first thing you need to do in Stellaris is essentially create your own Empire template which will be used when you start up a new game.  Within this process there is quite a variety of options to make your empire unique and feel like your own, Options include Race, Race appearance, Race Ship designs, Starting weapon tech like lasers, Empire name choice, Home planet/system name, Ship Prefixs i.e TNS (Terran Navy Ship) thats one of my favs its a nice touch and just adds to the many layers of immersion.  Perhaps the most important part of creating your fledgling empire is argueably the Ethics system.  You will choose from many different types of Ethics for example Militarist, Zenophile, Individualist and Spiritualist.  Each Ethic will dictate how your empire will operate, how your citizens will behave according to your actions and how you are perceived by other empires in the galaxy.
So...
We start off looking over the home planet, The year is 2200 and your civilisation has just developed FTL travel and has finaly grown the balls to leave the home system.  This distinct first phase contains the wonders that Stellaris has to offer, From your civilisations first discovery of other life in the galaxy and remmebering the reports of your people rechoicing or  recoil in horror in the thought they are not alone, coming across a long forgetten research facility of unknown origin that yields technological treasures. Really good stuff that keeps you intrigued throughout the mid game.  Managing your diplomacy with newly discovered and long standing empires comes in many variations and with long term strengthened ties, these relationships allow Federations to be born.  Powerful coalitions working together with similar goals in mind.
The mid game takes an interesting shift that i like to reffer too as "The Age of Aggresive Expansion" where in it becomes a necessity to aquire beyond the 2 or 3 planets in your area of influence. By looking at surveyed systems with habitable planets and deploying some colony ships, This is quickly remedied.  More often than not, Diplomacy can be truly tested by encountering empires who you may deem "in the way".  Your actions reverberate through your empires people, your rivals people and most importantly, the empires all over the galaxy who curiosly watch to see how you handle the situation.  Empires with more Democratic ethics may find it easier creating and maintaining friendships and therefore finding ways around obstacles such as empire expansion obstruction.
The game contains a research mechanisim thats nicely laid out, nicely paced and gives the feeling of research actually progressing your empire, making it stronger..better.  Technology progression and aquisition is usually at its peak (as it is in real life) during wartime as you use science ships to scan the wreckage of destroyed enemy ships for its tech, often propelling your empire further down the tech tree saving many many years of research.
The Ship Designer section gives the player a wide variety of choice regarding ship types in the civilian and military sectors.  Depending on what research is done new ship types and attachments can be deployed.  Shield generators, Weapons, Armours and specials can be added in all types of variations of ships to your liking with the possibility of upgrades down the line.
What we have here is one of those titles that you think ill have a little play and save after a few hours before bed and come back it, but end up playing it through out the night with no regrets.
It keeps on giving each time your attention wonders something happens to bring you back into the galaxy of colourful blobs.
My only real gripe with Stellaris as a whole is a small one but its still one that gets me everytime.  For context let me say that i was very fond of Sins of a Solar Empire and its addtion Rebellion.  Infact 2 friends and i loved Sins so much we had a  LAN day called "Sunday Sins".  And for those who have played particular game will notice in the mid to late game systems are buzzing with trade between stations and allies alike which made the game feel so alive even when you were literally doing sweet F all giving atleast some sort of illusion to a moving economy.  Bringing it back to Stellaris,  You would think when owning a medium sized too well established huge empires would be brimming with activity more or less passively as you go about your business between empires but this doesnt occur unfortunately it feels rather empty rather desolate.
To sum this up i would definately recommend Stellaris even at full price.  Theres alot of content here and with Dlc's likely more will come for some time. 9/10

Deus Ex is showing its years, particularly in the graphics department, and I had an issue with the high-def mod I tried, in which everything else was fine but having water anywhere onscreen would slow everything to a crawl. But I'd still recommend the game. I already have three different character builds going, so I can try three different skill builds without knowing yet what I might need or not need later on in the game: a hacker, a sharpshooter, and a Thief-style lock-picking, head-bonking, hug-that-shadow-like-it's-his-girlfriend version. I'm pretty sure I'll be way past three before I'm done.
I like the comments NPCs make, both idly and about some of the actions I take in the game. It's fun fluff. Also fun is that there are multiple ways to proceed to goals, and multiple ways to deal with trouble encountered in getting there. I've gone at the game stealth-knockout style, or guns blazing, or avoiding combat (or sneaky head-bonking) as much as possible, and all three ways were fun. There's occasionally things I wish I could try to do and can't-- like offer an NPC asking for thing A if thing B would be an acceptable alternative-- but there always will be.
Speaking of that, let's talk nitpicks: I'm not a fan of the crouchwalking-to-sneak part, the sneaking part is fun, but the crouching feels awkward. The grid-style "realistic space usage" inventory (necessitating inventory-fussing to make a space of the right shape for an object I want to pick up) is as annoying as it always is, although not quite enough so to make me mod it out. I'm not crazy about the hack-o-meter countdown either. I was hoping there'd be some way for Denton to download the documents for a more convenient read, given that this takes place in a world in which cybernetics and nano-augmentation exist, but if there is one I haven't noticed. They don't seem to be showing up anywhere in the ingame logs the way conversations do, which seems a bit backwards to me.
Well, as far as that last one goes, it is a game that was made before USB or wireless goodness existed... So, given that augs are a thing in Deus Ex and those things probably should be too, and that I was getting really annoyed by this nitpicky detail, I went to a game wiki for the text of documents I discovered while using the Hack skill. I now read them that way as I find them ingame, waiting until a point when "Denton" reasonably could stop and check out what he'd found, and it's much more fun now.
Minor irritants aside, I'm having a lot of fun with Deus Ex, another title I didn't get to enjoy when it was released. Definitely better late than never.

The best way to describe this game is Tetris meets Qix with Music. Each level is considered a song, and each song has a beat which marches across the level as you fill the blank space with Tetris-like blocks. When you fill up at least a 3x3 space (called a Quad), it starts to fill and gives points. You can add to it while it fills, but once it's filled it's done. When the beat bar marches past, the Quad is added to the amount of space filled. 50% fill gives you access to the next level. It's a difficult game to describe, but if you like Tetris, Qix and Music, you really can't go wrong.

NieR:Automata is a tale that truly captivated me from the very beginning. Seeing the credits roll past me by a few times in a flash within the first hour of me trying to get past the prologue, struggling through the bullet hell parts, and getting absolutely smashed by a gigantic robot, was a sign to me that I was in for a one of a kind ride. For me NieR is so far the GOTY of 2017. Here are my reasons why:
- PROS -
- The story is masterfully written, it is presented in a somewhat vague way, so you're literally going to be in for a hell of ride, because you never know where the story might progress. Just be sure to not leave the game at ending A, as the other routes bring so much new content. It's not a new game plus, rather the story is sometimes told from a different perspective and later on continued from one ending.
- The main protagonists, 2B, 9S and A2 are all likable and their character designs are very well done. Towards the end, I grew to care about each of them, and how their stories might end.
- The combat is so fluid, as expected from Platinum Games. I really never grew tired of the combat or any enemies thrown my way. Smashing enemies up with various weapons and skills always felt so rewarding.
- The Plug-in chip system allows for some very neat combinations, so you can play around building a set that best fits your playstyle.
- The side quests, although a bit repetitive perhaps in their gameplay at times, really excelled in their writing. Each quest had a story of its own to tell.
- The soundtrack of this game is in my opinion perhaps one of the best scores in gaming. Keiichi Okabe really created a stellar work, with most of the scores featuring beautiful vocals sung by Emi Evans, and the tracks also have an 8-bit tune accompanying them. The songs seamlessly transition from quiet to dynamic to 8-bit.
- The english dub is really amazing. The actors manage to convey the feelings and moods of the characters very well across the whole game.
- Graphics in this game are perhaps not the best, the color palette is a bit brownish, but it fits the atmosphere, and everything feels stylish still.
- CONS -

- There were sometimes a little bit too much loading screens between relatively short sequences in the game which kind of broke the continuity.
- The semi-open world at times can feel a bit desolate, although filled with many quests and enemies.
- There's alot of quests and things to do in the game, just that I wish there was a bit more, a few more areas to explore and a few more bosses, but that's probably what everyone would want from such a compelling game.
NieR:Automata to me is a 10/10 game, Yoko Taro's storytelling really captivated me, the gameplay just felt so tight that I just had to keep coming for more.
Proposal: Do not miss out on this game.

This game ooze's production value goodness from its fantastic immaginative artwork too its innovative yet sutely inspired soundtrack.  The first thing you need to do in Stellaris is essentially create your own Empire template which will be used when you start up a new game.  Within this process there is quite a variety of options to make your empire unique and feel like your own, Options include Race, Race appearance, Race Ship designs, Starting weapon tech like lasers, Empire name choice, Home planet/system name, Ship Prefixs i.e TNS (Terran Navy Ship) thats one of my favs its a nice touch and just adds to the many layers of immersion.  Perhaps the most important part of creating your fledgling empire is argueably the Ethics system.  You will choose from many different types of Ethics for example Militarist, Zenophile, Individualist and Spiritualist.  Each Ethic will dictate how your empire will operate, how your citizens will behave according to your actions and how you are perceived by other empires in the galaxy.
So...
We start off looking over the home planet, The year is 2200 and your civilisation has just developed FTL travel and has finaly grown the balls to leave the home system.  This distinct first phase contains the wonders that Stellaris has to offer, From your civilisations first discovery of other life in the galaxy and remmebering the reports of your people rechoicing or  recoil in horror in the thought they are not alone, coming across a long forgetten research facility of unknown origin that yields technological treasures. Really good stuff that keeps you intrigued throughout the mid game.  Managing your diplomacy with newly discovered and long standing empires comes in many variations and with long term strengthened ties, these relationships allow Federations to be born.  Powerful coalitions working together with similar goals in mind.
The mid game takes an interesting shift that i like to reffer too as "The Age of Aggresive Expansion" where in it becomes a necessity to aquire beyond the 2 or 3 planets in your area of influence. By looking at surveyed systems with habitable planets and deploying some colony ships, This is quickly remedied.  More often than not, Diplomacy can be truly tested by encountering empires who you may deem "in the way".  Your actions reverberate through your empires people, your rivals people and most importantly, the empires all over the galaxy who curiosly watch to see how you handle the situation.  Empires with more Democratic ethics may find it easier creating and maintaining friendships and therefore finding ways around obstacles such as empire expansion obstruction.
The game contains a research mechanisim thats nicely laid out, nicely paced and gives the feeling of research actually progressing your empire, making it stronger..better.  Technology progression and aquisition is usually at its peak (as it is in real life) during wartime as you use science ships to scan the wreckage of destroyed enemy ships for its tech, often propelling your empire further down the tech tree saving many many years of research.
The Ship Designer section gives the player a wide variety of choice regarding ship types in the civilian and military sectors.  Depending on what research is done new ship types and attachments can be deployed.  Shield generators, Weapons, Armours and specials can be added in all types of variations of ships to your liking with the possibility of upgrades down the line.
What we have here is one of those titles that you think ill have a little play and save after a few hours before bed and come back it, but end up playing it through out the night with no regrets.
It keeps on giving each time your attention wonders something happens to bring you back into the galaxy of colourful blobs.
My only real gripe with Stellaris as a whole is a small one but its still one that gets me everytime.  For context let me say that i was very fond of Sins of a Solar Empire and its addtion Rebellion.  Infact 2 friends and i loved Sins so much we had a  LAN day called "Sunday Sins".  And for those who have played particular game will notice in the mid to late game systems are buzzing with trade between stations and allies alike which made the game feel so alive even when you were literally doing sweet F all giving atleast some sort of illusion to a moving economy.  Bringing it back to Stellaris,  You would think when owning a medium sized too well established huge empires would be brimming with activity more or less passively as you go about your business between empires but this doesnt occur unfortunately it feels rather empty rather desolate.
To sum this up i would definately recommend Stellaris even at full price.  Theres alot of content here and with Dlc's likely more will come for some time. 9/10

Very good game, unique in many ways. It made me interested in ancient Chinese culture and history. What impresses me about this game is how class conflict is built into it (you have to keep an eye on unrest of peasants and nobles). Military conflict is just an element, because your civilisation can easily crumble from within if you overburden, overtax and over-militarise your people. Over-reach is a real risk, the bigger your empire, the bigger the potential crisis when the people rebel. Nomadic civilisations, which you can only unlock after 130 turns of learning to play as an agricultural faction, are also interesting and have different style of play. I like the ambient atmosphere and music and the detailed level of graphical detail and art, seeing the peasants working in the fields, etc, usually not found in 'civ-style' games (you need to zoom in on the cities and landscape to appreciate it). Combat system gets complaints from other reviewers but I think that's just because it is unique and those who haven't grasped the tactics get frustrated. Hint: setting unit orders makes a huge difference to how they behave on the battlefield.

Oriental Empires is good.  Very good.  If you have been reading kingdom manga or are a fan of historical turn based strategy games this game is one of the best out there to simulate a very under-rated period in history (Warring States period, China).
The game has so much potential I could see an expansion or second iteration being close to a perfect game and that is a truly rare and remarkable thing.
What it does well: It plays and flows well, with a give and take in the battles that seems so much more deep than a system of rock paper scissors like in civilization.  It is very addicting in that classic 1 more turn mentality.   The battles, the tactics, timing, possibilities etc are awesome and allow a deep layer of strategic micromanagement that is balanced at the perfect level - you can go completely nuts down to the smallest flanking maneuver or rear attack etc or just smash large stacks together in a battle of attrition and numbers.
The graphics are excellent.  The style is perfect, everything looks and feels good when playing.  The UI is minimal and shows off the gorgeous map and game board.
The game feels and looks a lot more realistic and immersive than the vast majority of their better capitalized competitors.  Even the weather effects that block out part of the map are awesome.
Most importantly the game is really fun.  You need to set a timer or something or a day might just be gone the next time you look up.
I admit I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked in my first game when I overexpanded and many cities rebelled.  I had a heck of time clawing back my own lands and it was very fun and challenging.  The game does have a slight learning curve though and will punish you if you dont watch your class loyalty levels.  I reccomend players put on the automatic farming option so they can focus on more important things. like WAR.  It is the Warring States afterall!  We've got unification to think of!
What the game never explains is how the class system works and I think a lot of players get frustrated before they figure it out.  In general you use your upper classes to supress the peasants and the lower classes to keep the nobles in check, while your own professional soldiers and elites can be used against both.  Makes sense.  Once you understand this losing a city to revolt is very rare. So if you have a peasant revolt you will need to use armies made up more than 50% of nobles/professionals and ideally led by your king.
To prevent your king constantly dying it is helpful to set their individual unit ai to "withdraw".
Having played several thousand turns too I will say the AI is better than average and quite good in most respects.  I feel AI can always be improved in games, which leads me to the other side of the coin.  There were a few times where say Qin declared war on me with 100% of their cities undefended and not a unit in sight on the hardest difficulty.  Even when it took several turns to approach they didn't make a single unit and I captured the strongest foritified cities in the game unopposed. Silly.  Then a huge wave of Qin came in from the north and got obliterated on their own fortresses.  Bad moves happen in war, if I would have attacked them I would just be taking advantage of their weakness and that is a smart move - but they declared war on me!  Those Qin should mass up on my borders first, especially if I am their chief rival for hegemony.
The game badly needs a harder difficulty than "very hard."  Guys like me need more punishment, more collusion amongst the enemies.  Give them more gold and troops and make the ai more aggressive.
I also feel like the base authority rating should be higher or that very small cities shouldn't consume a point until they grow to a certain size.  The map feels unpopulated until hundreds of turns pass and even then there is still open land just begging to be exploited but you cant beyond a small number or risk a big revolt.  So you just cede it and burn enemy cities.  More points could just be added to the base rate or to some techs.  It just leads to some weird semi arbitrary points where you almost need to disband pissant settlements in order to keep giant cities happy, and forces you to always keep your kings and heirs crusading on the front lines to increase their ratings.  The rating itself is fine as a system to prevent overexpansion but having the rating reset to when your king dies of old age is more annoying than fun especially when the number of cities the kingdom controls isn't that large.  This is CHINA.
A large % of battles end up being sieges.  Nothing wrong with that, I actually really enjoy cracking a tough city and they should be difficult to take.  What I find immensely annoying though is sieging a city for 30 or 40 turns only to have a random guy come and take the city at the last second.  That is infuriating and it happens A LOT.  This leads to weird games were you try and time the last hit on the siege.  Obviously if I commit 3000 men and decades then a random guy comes and bypasses my siege lines and then takes the spoils that doesnt make any sense and is ridiculous. Without save scumming and trying to trial and error it you will lose the city, loot, resources, 1000s of men, time etc.
I also think that many of the policies/edicts are awesome and also stupid at the same time.  Many of these don't seem balanced or worthwhile.  A king appointing a general reduces his authority?  Okay, maybe, but what happens when that loyal general goes on to conquer half the world for you and becomes famous and feared? Still reducing your authority. In a way it kind of make sense he might get delusions of grandeur or something and revolt but overall most generals throughout history have stayed loyal to their homeland and cause. Maybe they could add a loyalty stat, but I do like the way it is now, simplified to a city's loyalty.  The penalties especially in authority in regards to edicts  usually lead to never chosing certain options and that is unfun/unintended. It also leads to a lack of generals/personality characters until very late game.  I think that is one of this game's weaknesses, the characters feels all generic and lifeless when say a simple family tree or random trait system layered on top would add a lot in depth.  I want to feel like a king and I want to know who my vassals and enemies are. If I want to be Wei and choose 5 elite generals and war in all directions that is my perogitive - even it backfires and leads to revolts or a large cost, whatever, I at least want the option.   Even at max authority/characters it seems a bit light for the scale of all of China.
I think they need a slightly better presentation for complex diplomacy.  Many games have a system where you click one nation and it reveals all the relations with coloured bars.  Would help organize a bit of the chaos in this chaotic ffa.
In the future I would like to see the player able to establish more historically accurate mods to their kingdom by undertaking customizable agricultural (irrigation/canal) improvements like the Zhengguo Canal and the Great wall of China.  They can add heavy fortifcations / castles that link together and maybe have levels since the QIn built a large defense against Chu even though it was nothing like the scale of the great wall.  They could even add river/canal diversions and dams etc to increase the usefulness of water/ship transport and similulate Qin's prepartion for their attack on the Yue.
Overall Oriental Empires is excellent and should by purchased by those who love history, strategy, and quality games.  It is actually far better in my opinion that many AAA titles like Civilization.   The Warring states is basically a 100 way ffa of small kingdoms duking it out in the most chaotic and ignored period of history in the west.  While Rome was fielding 1000s, these kingdomss were raising 100,000s and rising and falling in never ending waves of battles and bloodshed!  Come get a piece!

“Just one more turn and then another, until I’m nearly done.” That’s what we’ll all say, when playing a strategy game we're only starting to understand and enjoy. Few turn based strategies still have this effect on me though and I’m talking about the pure TBS genre, more like the Civilization series and less like the Total War hybrid. Oriental Empires reminded me of the first Shogun Total War even if it has surpassed that game in all regards. I know, comparing Feudal Japan with Ancient China, isn’t doing me any service since I’m a self-proclaimed, history buff. What do you want me to compare it to, the fairy tales from the  Romance of the Three Kingdoms series? Oriental Empires has no anime-style images and it is anything but romanticizing reality, so I was playing exactly what I was expecting. A stellar Steam debut from developer, Shining Pixel Studios!
Indeed the topics of China’s humble beginnings and its rapid blossoming into a great civilization, are rarely touched in general, not just in video games. I have fond memories with Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom, a  city builder that’s not on Steam (yet you can purchase it from GOG), which focused on a similar time frame as Oriental Empires, albeit from a 2D isometric perspective. What’s important to understand about the game I’m reviewing today, is that it makes very few concessions in regards to any inaccuracy about its historic simulation. One such compromise is the time compression, so to speak. It’s a TBS with 4 turns per “year”, but you’d be better off considering them as 4 seasons since climate change is noticeable. Can’t really say if it’s also related to story progression, but changing 5 emperors in 200 turns (shall we say 50 years?) seems closer to the Roman Empire’s instability than its Chinese counterparts. And glancing over my well developed (and overcrowded) 22 cities, it’s obviously not an achievement reachable in less than an in-game century.
Even if the passing of time may not be accurately simulated, pretty much every other aspect in Oriental Empires, has some historic meaning and potential for discovering new facts about Ancient China. There is no conventional story, not even a themed campaign following the exploits of Qin Shi Huang (the man who unified China as an empire, for the first time) and that is a missed opportunity, but not one on which to dwell a lot since the scenarios present in-game, compensate for the lack of a plotline. Both in singleplayer and multiplayer, Oriental Empires gives you the option to either develop a Chinese clan/kingdom in the Grand Campaign (spanning over 3000 years, from the Early Bronze Age to Imperial China), The Warring States (475 BC – 221 BC) or Custom Game, which provides players with some very creative maps that enhance MP matches and potential alliances.
One very interesting aspect that I hope more TBS games would use, is the option to set the total number of turns you wish to play before starting the game. They count towards the Victory Points you may accumulate during the scenario and you’re free to choose any number of turns from 1 to 9999. I suggest you pick at least 300 turns, if you wish to unlock the entire Tech Tree and still have time to put those upgrades to good use. By allowing players to set their own limits in regards to both the play style and expansion, Oriental Empires delves into an open-ended territory which has been thoroughly tested (and perhaps inaugurated) by the Civilization series.
Of course, you’re free to pick from some pre-existing Chinese clans and fulfill their ambitions until they’ve went from a single, defenseless settlement, to a true continental empire. Or a trade empire, if you wish. I went down that route of non-aggression and I found the gameplay to be just as intriguing in that manner. The Shu faction, protected and nurtured by the Sichuan Basin, will be a perfect start for new and veteran players alike. Rather than facing enemies from all sides, you have natural barriers in the form of mountains which shelter your farming-oriented faction from the aggressive horse riders/herders until you can develop your own military capabilities.
I had to dig through the game’s files since it’s not mentioned at the start, but this is definitely a highly modified Unity Engine project which shows once again, what can be achieved with the “indie/mobile gaming engine”, provided that it reaches skilled hands. With multiple levels of zoom, allowing you to see both the peasants working the fields and then planning your next settlement foundation or conquest from a top-down view that will make your empire stand out in the form of connections. A true network based on mutual trade, culture and urban development. The hexagonal map pattern can be disabled from the options, but you’ll still see its structural legacy when planning new farms, roads or troop deployment.
It looks beautiful, with detailed towns and cities that show incremental improvements which go beyond “this wall is now sturdier than the previous one”. Depending on what buildings you erect (since you may steer the settlements towards economic progress, military encampment or a mix of both), the cities will differ from one another. You can of course rename them, and you’re given a free hand in how you design the infrastructure and agricultural endevours. It’s not a button for “build farms/roads” since you’ll need to pay close attention to terrain type and climate. Rice paddies and terrace farming will allow you to take full advantage of adjacent hills, once irrigable flatlands have occupied their designated space. City development and population growth is logically tied to to the efficiency of the trade, crafting (mainly silk and porcelain) and last but not least, harvesting.
I wanted to emphasize on the complexity which is not that common in strategy games. Even Victoria II had a railway development mechanic that seemed far more automated when compared to the free reign offered by Oriental Empires. And you can automate some of the development processes in this game too, but I suggest you take an active role in your empire, since the learning curve isn’t very steep. Armies and individual troops are less detailed than the buildings and crops, yet they still look more than decent. I only had one issue with the graphics since the User Interface stutters and my otherwise stable 60fps on a 4K resolution, begins to drop close to 30fps. Only during the scrolling up or down on the Show Settlements tab from HUD’s left side. I’m sure that a patch can fix this. It’s only a matter of optimization since I noticed that many more players were complaining about the stuttering.
Though it’s lacking in voice acting, Oriental Empires compensates by offering a most relaxing soundtrack which is comprised of instrumentals. Chinese folklore, no doubt, even if I’m by no means an expert in the field. I played enough Shogun 1 and 2 over the years, so at least I can testify that it sounded different than their OSTs. Some audio cues and spoken instructions from the game’s advisor would have been welcome, but I’m no stranger to reading either, so it didn’t bother me by much. Also, there are no cinematics at all. Just the publisher’s logo when booting the game up. There needs to be some. A game of this production value, fully deserves them.

Great fun, lots of modifiers and thoughtful design features. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a more serious minded Civ, wants an experience that seems to try to emulate early civ development in a meaningful way, with the forced labour of the peasants as one of your currencies (their goodwill essentially). In my short-ish experience i found the rebellion system to be really gripping, with my leader dying in battle triggering breakaways at the edge of empire and the difficulty in reclaiming those rebellious provinces adding to the experience. Issues could be the lack of an indepth dynastic system, perhaps with marriages, a deeper trait system for leaders, but what the game focuses on, Intra-state rivalry and economic and cultural development. The bandits only seemed to show up at times of turmoil, so that was not an issue, as this fit with the identity of the game. Lots of fun for strategy types and well worth the price of admission with the size of the map, and on the whole competitive AI, this will give you hours of fun and maybe learn ya something on the earliest periods of development in China and all those "Hydraulic Despotisms." Lovely gem that came out of Early Access a polished product well worth your time and money. Thanks for the experience!

Full review:
Oriental Empires is basically what you would get if Civilization was set in ancient China. There are several similarities between the two, enough so that I was able to just jump in without issue, but there are also some key differences. Oriental Empires really sets itself apart with its combat system, but the economic and unrest features are also worth noting.
Pros:
The way the game manages economics. I love the way that finances are managed in Oriental Empires. Trade routes are automatically established with a given city once a bazaar is built. However, distance plays a huge role in trade, as cities are generally only able to trade with others within a 12-tile radius. This prompted me to place my cities in such a way as to have as many connections as possible, preferably next to resources on the map to give an extra boost to trade. There are several different buildings, each offering some different resource for trade, that can be constructed at each city. I ended up stacking these buildings in my trade centers, generating me a ton of money. In my first game I managed +3000 gold per turn at one point. It was refreshing to not have to micromanage economics, but still maintain a certain degree of control over that very aspect.
Peasant and noble unrest. While it can prove annoying at times, it is at least realistic in that a ruler must keep both the noble and peasant classes satisfied. There are numerous ways to both increase and decrease happiness for both classes, be that construction of shrines, overpopulation, or edicts (think Civilization social policies). If unrest rises to a certain point it may lead to revolution. This happened in my first game, with peasants taking over a few of my cities. I ended up getting them back, but it took some time and I learned my lesson! This area of the game was really well-executed overall.
Automation features. Later in the game when managing twenty or so cities is the norm, it can become quite tedious to build farms and such for each and every city. The game provides automation features to remedy this very issue, a welcome addition especially for a game of this scale. Want to automate farming, building construction, or even technology advancement? It can be done. I saved a whole lot of time by making use of the auto-farming.
In-game manual. Before playing the game I saw plenty of complaints about the lack of a tutorial mode. While there is no tutorial mode, I had no issues learning any of the game’s features as there is an in-game manual provided. Just press F1 and just about everything in the game is explained there. It was very useful during my first playthrough, although it probably also helps that I have played numerous 4X strategy games in the past.
Cons:
Awkward Combat and movement. The combat system has several cool features, but it felt as if half of these features did not even matter. The player can change the formation of each army (two columns, three, etc.), the battle orders (support, ambush, etc.), and the direction that the army faces. These are all really cool mechanics on paper, but it felt as if they had little effect on the actual gameplay. For example, I would set up an army to have archers on both sides of a spearman unit, with additional spearman behind the center spearman. The spearman in front would be set to “charge”, the spearman behind them set to “attack” and both archers set to “outflank”. Ideally, the spearman would charge in with the archers wrapping both sides and raining down on the enemy, but half the time it seemed that the units would run in circles, run through each other, or just do nothing at all.
It felt like the battle orders had no effect at all and it really just came down to numbers and the type of unit used. A lot of the time I just ended up defaulting to the standard “attack” battle order, as it takes quite some time to set up individual orders and I cannot tell if they even have an effect on the battle’s outcome. On top of that, the battles simply take too long, especially when taking a city. Despite having a clear advantage, friendly units will still pull back after a short while and it takes several turns to actually defeat an enemy unit or take a city. This was probably done so the player can assess if they want to continue the battle, like if he/she did not expect so much resistance and did not want to lose any more units, but being able to tell units to fight to the death rather than withdraw would be great (I imagine that such a feature would break multiplayer though).
Additionally, the movement of units was awkward at times as well. Units cannot be directed onto any tile in the fog of war, so I had to keep sending them to the edge of the fog before moving forward. This was especially annoying in the late game, when small patches of the map remained unexplored. It only takes a small amount of the fog to reroute entire armies around it, rather then just walking through it.
Confusing UI. I found the UI to be quite bothersome at times, especially when trying to split stacked units into separate groups. The unit list becomes a mess when doing so. The whole battle orders and formation mechanic is very cool, but the clunky UI makes it a bit difficult to manage. It is only really bad when managing units, elsewhere the UI is okay, but could use some minor improvements. Dismissing notifications that pop up on the right would be a start, rather than just giving them a check mark. This was quite annoying later in the game when I had a large list of notifications to scroll through. The game would just be a lot better if the unit UI was easier to navigate.
Oriental Empires is definitely worth taking a look into if you are a fan of 4X strategy games or Eastern Asia in general (of which I am both!). Although the combat and UI can be confusing at times, there is a lot to this game, a lot that I still have to experience myself. The game is heavily military-focused, so be ready to spend a lot of time managing armies, taking out enemies, and expanding as much as possible!
I'll be uploading a lot of gameplay to my YouTube channel, so be sure to check it out!

Recommendation - Minesweeper fans rejoice!!
Remember the free old Windows game Minesweeper? Remember how fun it was finding those hidden mines, and how you could feel your brain scream "NOOOOOOOOOOO" whenever a mine would pop its stupid head up and kill you? Remember how immensely frustrating it was when it was entirely impossible to solve levels without guessing?
WELL, NO MORE! Hexcells to the rescue.
Hexcells is very similar to Minesweeper in that you have to use various clues and reasoning to find the hidden blue cells on each level, but unlike Minesweeper, Hexcells' soultions can ALWAYS be reasoned, and if you're doing it right you will never have to guess.
The levels start out easy, with simple rules and puzzles, but new tricks are added just regularly enough to fully grasp, and before you know it, you'll find yourself scanning through 15 different criteria to find the 1-in-100 blue cell to start a level off. It's very satisfying.
Speaking of satisfying, the puzzles here never seem overwhelming or too tricky. Take my opinion with a grain of salt (since I have always loved games like this), but the level of difficulty in these puzzles was just perfect, and while some levels did force me to stare at them for a while, the solution was always there somewhere just waiting for me to grab it.
The Hexcells series is really 3 games: Hexcells, Hexcells Plus, and Hexcells Infinite. They each have different puzzles, and they are each worth getting, but Hexcells Infinite is the one to get if you're on a budget. It has the most advanced puzzles, and it includes a random level generator, so you can literally play to your heart's content. All 3 of them will slowly progress you through the mechanics of the game, though, so don't feel like you will be overwhelmed if you jump right into Infinite.
It's worth mentioning that the random levels in Infinite are mere pale shadows compared to the premade levels (they are often quite easy), but for fans that cannot get enough and don't want to go back to the guess-fest Minesweeper, they can be a lot of fun.
I highly recommend this game. If you're a fan of logic-based puzzle games, you can't go wrong with any of these 3 games. The prices are cheap, and the series is rather unique. If the devs could have just tightened up the infinite level generator ever-so-slightly, this game might be the only game I've rated to pass Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons.

This is the first of a trilogy of Hexcell games, and you should definitely play this one before attempting the others.  It sets the foundation for the remainder of the trilogy.
The way I'd describe Hexcells is that it's a brainy love child of Minesweeper and Sudoku.  The puzzles are all solvable, despite how frustrated you might originally get when attempting them.  There is a nice endorphin rush when you realize you've figured out which cell to click on next because you made a second-level deduction that isn't immediately obvious.  However, the first time you play you'll probably just accept that you made a mistake and keep going.  When you're done, you'll want to do it all over again, but trying for the "Perfectionist" achievement (no mistakes).  Even if you do make a mistake, you can simply start the level over again to try it mistake-free.
Hexcells probably has about 2-3 hours of game play in it, but you might come back to try again for that achievement...
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that enjoys logic puzzles or spatial puzzles.  When you are done, you'll immediately want to pick up the next game in the series (Hexcells Plus).

Nice puzzle game that feels like playing minesweeper, but the levels are actually designed rather than random, thus as you advance through you get coaxed into learning the various tricks and inferences you can make based on the clues already exposed and work your way through the level.
Each group of six levels tends to bring in an extra type of clue, such as a count of how many cells are "on" (bombs if you like) in each column/row/diagonal, or how many are within two squares of the clue, etc. The first couple of levels in each set then act as a kind of tutorial for how to solve puzzles with this new type of clue, then the complexity ramps up as the levels progress to 6, and then resetting back to easy for the next rule introduced.
This feeds into the main weakness: with 36 levels, pretty much half of which are easy/tutorial type levels, another bunch that are only moderately difficult, and you end up with only a handful of challenging puzzles (if you are relatively experienced at puzzle games). Still it all plays really well, and the levels have a really nice well engineered feel to them, and a few great moments where you have been stuck for a while thinking there must be a bug and that you have to guess the next step and then things finally click and you see the extra bit of information or logical inference you need to progress.

The game starts off well. It's Total War without going off the campaign map to do the real time battles. Instead, you watch them play out simultaneously after every player gives rather detailed marching orders. It does not have the depth of TW but if you love the strategic layer of TW more than you do the tactical then Oriental Empires could be just what you're look for.
Unfortunately the game has not been properly playtested, despite being in EA for a year.
I'll forego commenting on the lacklustre variatety of the game's many factions and the chaotic and unclear UI and go straight to where the devs really missed their mark:
The economic model comes with some really cool ideas - distance is a real factor and routes can be seen on the map. What the game does not tell you is that you should really only conduct trade for each good in a single town. If you build two pottery factories, each will only do 50% of what a single one would do. You're paying fully for the upkeep though. Eh... eh? Why doesn't the game simply disable these buildings? It's also completely unclear when and where you should upgrade your market or build the caravanserai to extend your trade distance. 40 hours in and I have yet to find a situation where building the caravanserai actually made more money than it cost. Oh, and why is the foundry a military building if according to the description its only purpose is to produce copper for trade?
The game could still be enjoyed even without trade being a modern day enigma machine though.
Sieging, however, takes that enjoyment away.
Battles can be a little confusing to watch but sieges are downright infuriating. When 1500 soldiers and 8 siege engines cannot break the walls of a city defended by 250 peasants for 20 turns there is something seriously wrong. I threw in the towel when I saw a totally undefended town with a wall withstand a full stack of units (8) for the 8th turn.
Without the trade and siege problems Oriental Empires would get a trong recommendation from me. With both there, it firmly falls below the recommendation treshold.

Very addicting and replayable game. Nice combat, smooth interface and a simple approach to gameplay that is very refreshing. This game is very fun with a friend or two but certainly has it's flaws. The main flaws revolve around 3 things; balance, crafting, and luck.
The balance is probably it's worst aspect. Damage and health values are all odd and there is almost no reason to stick to a melee weapon over a ranged bow or magic staffs. Too much risk vs low reward when using melee, even if you are skilled with it. Magic and bow wielders can inflict heavy damage from a distance with little to no risk on taking any damage. You can also hit enemies at a distance without aggroing them so there is literally nothing they will do to stop you. There are many other balance issues but I'll opt not to elaborate on those seeing as this one is my biggest gripe.
The crafting system is fun but loses it's spark pretty quickly. It doesn't have much depth at all and after a while most of the resources that you gather become obsolete.
Last but not least luck plays too big of a role. Randomized dungeons certain extend replayability but situations where you start off in a district and you're dealing with a big enemy blocking your path should be avoided. Also how lucky you get when gathering things can strongly affect how well you do.
I didn't go too deeply into what's wrong with the game seeing as there is a bit. With that said I still reccomend the game. It's highly addicting and very fliud. There aren't many gameplay glitches and everything moves relatively quickly once you get started. This review will attempt to be as spoiler-free as possible, although it may get a bit long.
Full Disclosure: I received the game for free for participation in IFI's closed beta testing, although I purchased the original FFF myself over a year ago.
For those who played the original FFF, this will probably be important.
The entirety of the original game basically exists within ADF as the 'Goddess' route, which you'll naturally enter unless you do some very specific things early on. There are some slight differences with respect to dialogue, event details, and character introduction timings in order to facilitate better story flow, but the overall story is exactly the same.
The 'New Stuff' is mostly the two new story routes. There are mechanical changes as well, with the most obvious being the doubling of the party size to an incredible six(!) characters, and a change in the way that Avalanche Attacks are triggered. There are also two new recruitable characters when you get to the third route.
The story routes themselves are all separate from each other. I thoroughly enjoyed each of them, as they forced you to come to terms with, and get used to things you may not necessarily be used to doing. Some may dislike the fact that character rosters change (temporarily,) but in my opinion, the new routes are best taken in as the game providing you with
scenarios.
Each route also has its own set of character-specific endings. They each contain their own set of dungeons; Some are new, others are 'new' with recycled assets, and some are repeats of earlier dungeons. The game has also been rebalanced a bit from FFF.
I enjoyed the game, but I cannot overwhelmingly recommend it.
For players who are familiar with other CH/IF titles (e.g.
series, or the original FFF,) you'll be familiar with how ADF plays out. For these players, I'd recommend it if you are interested in the story it tells, as I feel that the story is much better, and more coherent, than Neptunia's.
For players who are
familiar with similar titles such as the
series, it's tougher to recommend.
The problem is that this game (like most of their other RPG's) is not a very deep or complex RPG. If you are looking for a 'good' RPG for the 'RPG,' then I cannot recommend this game, as you will be let down.
This game, instead, plays much closer to a Visual Novel with light RPG thrown in between. The majority of the game time will be spent experiencing the story through dialogue/event sequences, before running off to clear simple dungeons, then repeating the process. Thus, the focus is much more on the telling of FFF/ADF's story, than it is about playing an RPG.
If this idea of a 'casual RPG' with a storytelling focus sounds appealing, then by all means, I would recommend the game.
Price, however, is a contentious point.
Certainly, there is enough content in ADF to justify being pricier than FFF; The new stories easily more than double the amount of content in the game compared to FFF. Couple that with the new visual upgrades, as well as re-hiring voice actors to voice entirely new scripts, and you come up with improvements that are more than trivial.
However, the price is still on the high end (comparable to
rather than the
series.) Whether or not these improvements are worth the extra cost is up to you, but I would definitely recommend it if you're interested in the game, and it's on a decent discount.
The required specs can appear to be fairly high, although that's the hardware IFI wants to recommend in order to reliably achieve 60+ FPS throughout the game. I have been running the game on an nVidia GTX-670 and i7-3770k at 1920x1200 with maximum graphical settings, and I was able to largely get 60 FPS almost everywhere. The exceptions were certain dungeons with heavy particle effects where I would dip to the mid 40's.
Ultimately, I ejoyed the game, and I helped to beta test the game because I thoroughly liked the original FFF's story, and really wanted to see the new stories present in ADF. Story-wise, I can say that I was not disappointed; I loved every minute of it.
However, I cannot provide a blanket recommendation because this game still hits somewhat of a niche audience, and you'll have to decide based on my comments above whether or not this is for you. If you are at all interested, though, I would say definitely!

This review pretty much mirrors what I've said in
of the original Fairy Fencer F game, with some more things on the plus side, hopefully. You'd probably want to read it first if you've never played Fairy Fencer F games before, otherwise just read below.
- True HD, say goodbye to the (720p?) upscale. It's extremely striking when you do a side-by-side comparison between
and the
. It's not just the textures, there are more flora and stuff overall. Colors are more vivid, and the world feels more vibrant. I won't post any more screenshots for now, I'll let you discover/enjoy the rest.
- 60 FPS, stable (if you care about that).
- Whole new story route, and slightly revised story routes for the old ones.
- New playable characters.
- Party size increased from 3 to 6.
- Menu interface slightly revamped (recolor mostly I'd say).
- New easier and harder modes.
- New dungeons & enemies.
- New story artworks.
- Tuned down gold achievement (was 100M in the previous series, which was ridiculous).
- The new, highest difficulty setting can be a challenge if you go commando.
- Fast loading times.
- Game still suffers from the "Mash the attack button and that's pretty much it" syndrome, albeit a bit less now. I still didn't feel the need to rely a lot on magic, although I recall using it more times than in the previous series.
- Criticals from enemies are a joke. Normal attacks = 300, crits = 3000. Logic?
When you're going for the 0 deaths/0 defeats/0 retreats stats, it's a real pain.
- Elemental mechanics are barely, if at all, exploited in this game, which is a shame. Same thing for the formation feature.
- No real incentive to play on high difficulties (higher than Hard especially), since the game doesn't provide any incentive to do so (higher difficulties do not give you more XP/Gold/BP, just "better drops"... apparently. Maybe.).
Enemies on high difficulties are just bullet sponges and all you'll be doing is wasting your free time pointlessly leveling to try to kill that boss that stops your progression. This is probably the aspect I regretted the most with this new iteration.
- You'll have to do
of new game+ iterations to complete the gallery.
Overall, the game left me with a positive impression, although I still feel that most mechanics are just an excuse for the story. But since the latter is enjoyable, I guess that's excusable.

I heard a lot of mixed opinions about this game from several different youtube reviews, so initially I was a little skeptic going into it.
Let me start with the good. The soundtrack is catchy, the art style is appealing, and the gameplay is fun. Each map offers a variety of different methods for disposing of your innocent victims, and combine this with the 5 available characters to play as, as well as the RNG decided layout of the map and movement of the npcs, and no two playthroughs of a stage will be the same. Sometimes having your victims get discovered can provide a tactical advantage. As the crowd devolves into chaos, you can strike more victims while the police is preoccupied chasing the wrong suspect, covering the bodies with body bags, or assisting paramedics.  Other times, its wiser to pick off the crowd one at a time until you narrow the numbers enoughwhere you can clean up. I consistently felt a sense of urgency and danger when an npc strolls into my area before I had a chance to hide my handiwork, and had to react quickly before they get a chance to notify the police.
This game isn't what you would call perfect though. Police sometimes arrest you through thin walls, sometimes you attempt to hide a body and despite the enviornment triggering that you hid the body (which has a cooldown before you can use it again) the body still remains in plain sight, and has ruined a run for me more than once. Furthermore, some stages/rng setups have no real method for disposing of crowds, which can lead to a painfully slow execution of the map, which is even further compounded when you lose with only a handful of victims left and have to start all over. As catchy as the soundtrack is, they are only about a minute and a half long, and loop on the stage. I found myself muting the game entirely on a couple more difficult levels. Lastly, its funny how no one bats an eye if you throw a sleeping victim over the edge of a building yet will beat you up for dancing.
Overall, I had some rough patches with the game but I really enjoyed it. It was difficult enough to stretch out gameplay, but rewarding enough to keep me playing. Took me about 8 hours to grab all the achievements, which are generally fun to go for, with the exception of the launch the game 100 times grind.
