This game took me by surprise.
I bought it the other day during the sale and I thought I would regret having bought this game.
I was wrong.
The game is simple. You are a serial killer who goes from party to party murdering an obscene amount of people who, for some reason, don't leave the party even though their friends' guts are laying at their feet. Hmm. The booze, codeine and Molly must have them ♥♥♥♥ed up.
The key to this game is to be stealthy, have patience and have a slight idea of how to control the crowd to your murderous benefit.
There is a varied amount of enviromental traps to off your victims in style. There are also a few items that will be really helpful (don't underestimate the power of the smoke granade).
The level design is good. Many of them have little easter eggs, extras or cameos/tributes to many films/characters of the 80s-00s era.
The game is set in 2000 if my memory serves me right, although it has a great 80s vibe.
The music is good (that was what really drew me into the game), but the tracks are too short and loop very quickly. Soon enough, you'll be focusing more on your murderous rampage rather than the music that loops over and over again.
It is kinda short. I finished the game in about 5 hours.
The plot is kinda cheesy, kinda meh, with meh/amateurish voice acting, but it was strangely enjoyable, specially the ending.
The game has a level editor which I haven't really messed with yet, but there many player-made levels and there are a few extra levels after you finish the game, as well as some unlockable characters -each with their unique abilities-.
I think it's a solid 7.5/10. It's a really good game. It can get a bit repetitive but it's hard yet not frustrating, and it can become really addicting!
The base game is good, but until they release the DLC that they had added to all the other game versions, I won't recommend this game.

Very addicting and replayable game. Nice combat, smooth interface and a simple approach to gameplay that is very refreshing. This game is very fun with a friend or two but certainly has it's flaws. The main flaws revolve around 3 things; balance, crafting, and luck.
The balance is probably it's worst aspect. Damage and health values are all odd and there is almost no reason to stick to a melee weapon over a ranged bow or magic staffs. Too much risk vs low reward when using melee, even if you are skilled with it. Magic and bow wielders can inflict heavy damage from a distance with little to no risk on taking any damage. You can also hit enemies at a distance without aggroing them so there is literally nothing they will do to stop you. There are many other balance issues but I'll opt not to elaborate on those seeing as this one is my biggest gripe.
The crafting system is fun but loses it's spark pretty quickly. It doesn't have much depth at all and after a while most of the resources that you gather become obsolete.
Last but not least luck plays too big of a role. Randomized dungeons certain extend replayability but situations where you start off in a district and you're dealing with a big enemy blocking your path should be avoided. Also how lucky you get when gathering things can strongly affect how well you do.
I didn't go too deeply into what's wrong with the game seeing as there is a bit. With that said I still reccomend the game. It's highly addicting and very fliud. There aren't many gameplay glitches and everything moves relatively quickly once you get started. Played with the right people this game is definitely a blast and I look forward to future updates that hopefully address  many of my concerns

It's a level design clinic.  The only other game that's in the frame is Hitman: Blood Money, but these levels are stronger because there are just so, so many ways to get it done.  By the time you complete a level, you've almost assuredly missed half of it.
Add to that meaningful character build choices and a wealth of freedom of choice, and you've got yourself a masterpiece.  Want to sneak around and bop everyone over the head with a baton?  Sure.  Prefer to go in guns blazing and use the GEP gun to solve the big problems?  That works too.  Snipe them from a mile out, brain them with a silenced pistol from behind...you've got options.  About all that's missing is Force Lightning.
Then there's the sheer volume of content, which is almost too much.  New York is about the length of a conventional game these days.  Then there's Hong Kong and the endgame.  It doesn't get much better than this, if it does at all.
Just mute the game, pull up BSG on netflix and play it in the background and you'll almost get a boner before you realize it's not a BSG game...then you'll turn it off and rewatch BSG instead.

I don't usually write reviews, and was like most, sceptical until I gave it a fresh look.
Gotta say though, this is not as boring as Civ VI, sean bean voice was nice yet he always dies anyways and not much help anyways.
Went in with a medium to steep learning curve expectation, simply for the fact that the game is stated as a blend of TW & Civ plus it's setting is chosen as China. The latter I know next to nothing about but have play many a game like these for over 30 years. So with that in mind I played a couple new games focusing on the mechanics, how each part of gwoing the population, how each aspect affects them and worked outward. Still no master of it, and currently learning how the various approaches to trade and diplomacy can affect my choices.
Probably the biggest surprise was how it's laid out, resource wise, so some areas have a certain bonus, and others have next to none but are good sized areas for growing the populations. Still alot of land to explore and find all the various resource types, but the bonus here even if you cannot find resources you're after, is that it's out there and you can take it or trade it. Both have their good and bad sides.
Military units are one of the key components imho, each Clan has it's special attribute Unit or other focus, so learning them all give a new perspective on how you might choose to play each one. When it comes to barbarians or revolting peasants, you can choose to crush them or apease them. Your choice :D
The hardest part of the Leader Character is knowing when you get one, or when you'll get another. Still learning how this works, I am liking the way it works so far. I send out a simple unit, army or leader, to explore the surrounding area to gather information, then when bandits show up, combine a couple with a leader to crush them and earn them a nice victory with xp so that when a neighbour comes to knock your door down, you can at least try to stave off losses. In my second game, most of the major players rarely send bowman, so simply creating walls, and ambushing these creates a stalemate where they can't take my towns.
The various tactics, formations, and so on have various benefits, often if you change the status of each unit and terrain with what they're up against will come in your favour if you play it right. This tends to be a hit and miss affair in the beginning as you learn how it works. Imho, this is a bonus compared to CIV as that seems to be more tech vs older units, yet in TW you get the zerg approach and out numbering tactics. This is a nice blend, and yeah sure, it could be improved upon, but liking the new approach honestly as it makes you think before each action.
So since this is new, there are things I believe can improve this even more, not a MUST have to currently play, but a nice vision of future updates and *cough* DLC *cough* that could expand it more.
Having a training scenario for each Clan, with an actual walk through of each as if recreating history. Even if this was only a small portion of what each is known in history for. That would then give you a "possible" guide to getting started with each special attribute of each to get things going. Without out it, you're trying to figure it out on your own, and for me atm, this will give more time to learn what does and doesn't work, but if added would help educate me on Chinese history a bit more and have fun while doing so.
Sadly it's named Oriental, so does somewhat limit future expansions imho to Japan and possibly other Asian countries surrounding China itself. On the plus side, this is a huge area that has many possibilities though. If they're like this game, then I'd give them a go as well.
My verdict, early days and alot to learn still, but I can see me sinking many hrs into playing all the factional clans and getting the most out of this in more ways than one. Pretty much shelved Civ becuase it's just downright dry, run out of something "fun" for me. Same goes for TW, it had it's moments, but in the end something seemed to be missing. Oriental Empires fills those voids and is interesting, fresh, and a different spin on things that makes you want to come back for more.
Maybe I'll come back when I have more hrs into the game and add further goods and bads to this review....

The storyline is fairly decent, and has some deep overarching themes. However, Deus Ex isn't some sinless saint. The game feels too long, especialy for one where there are so many methods to try out. I lost intrest about 3 missions away from the ending. There are also encounters with other augumented people which always seemed one-directional to me. They're immune to everything non-lethal, and they soak up bullets without missing a step. The only way I found to kill them was to just blow them up. Explosives in this game seem a bit overpowered too, since they basicly kill everything within 30 feet that has line of sight. Despite these flaws, Deus Ex is most definately worth 7 bucks. I was pleased to see Big Fish Games releasing more casual adventure games on Steam, though I'm a little disappointed to see that there is no achievement added. However, there are ingame achievements. Anyway, Dark Parables is a huge series in the casual world, first by Blue Tea Games before being developed by Eipix.
The series is a chronicle of investigations in the world of fairy tales: the fabled detective is sent to different kingdoms or fantasy worlds in order to find what evil is wrecking havoc and how to appease it. This game concerns the tale of the Little Mermaid and the Purple Tide (not really familiar with this one, as the only mermaid tales I know are the Disney movie, Lorelei and the ancient Greek myth - as for the tale itself, I've vaguely heard of it in the Wolf Among Us).
There is a temple undersea that suddenly appeared and a monster is terrorizing everyone. However, arriving there, a mermaid seems to want to help you while a cloaked figure (from a previous game if I've understood clearly as the detective was familiar with the voice) is also waiting to enter the temple and to find a lost kingdom.
The story is full of twists and questions: the mermaid is helping you AND also trying to slow you down, the cloaked figure is a suspect but his identity is quite shocking, the ghost you encounter is blaming himself but isn't opposed to your presence and the mermaids, well, some of them are also tied to other investigations (which is not really a shock as the fabled detective is acquainted with nearly everyone - however, as the game isn't the first in the series, it's making you wanting to play every Dark Parables out there).
The gameplay is standard: find objects, use them, combine them, solve puzzles and clear hidden objects scenes. Everything is quite easy, though you have sometimes an hard time to see some objects or to link them to an area of interest. Even these areas can be hard to spot. On the other side, you have the hunt for Parables (to unlock the whole background on your case), for Moons and even for cups of tea (a nod to Blue Tea Games I suppose). Achievements are also present ingame but they can be upgraded: you have to find a cup of tea, then 3 then the whole pack. Even the fish mascot (Felix I think) from Big Fish Games is present.
I'm not going to tell you every bonus in this Collector's Edition but well, there is a bonus chapter on Bluebeard, wallpapers, etc...
I loved the graphics as the general ambiance of the game.
Anyway, this game is really a must-have, though I would prefer Artifex Mundi's work (developped by them like Enigmatis or Nightmares from the Deep) but well, while I find the price tag a little high, Big Fish is now participating on sales, so, when you see a discount, go for it.

This game seriously needs more content and some balance changes. I beat it in about an hour, including the time it took just to learn how to play. I see so much potential in this game, really hoping the devs update it.
*EDIT*
So the devs do listen to the community and even had an update. I won't go into a full review about every single aspect of this game, but i will list some suggestions on how it should be changed.
1) What kept me from replaying the game is how terribly balanced it is. The guns themselves are usually pretty unique, like a spike ball cannon. But then how do you balance a gun like that? Well make it one shot of course. unfortunately that is like what, the second cheapest gun you can get? One shotting enemies in this game makes it incredibly easy. You could go on for a good 5 waves with just that one gun until you'd need a tower to defend your back. So its cost effiecient, and just efficient in general. The game loses all replayability when that's just the best strategy. At that point you'd need to limit yourself to make the game any harder. Rockets are useless since you need to hit things with the explosion, which would seem pretty nice if the blast radius was bigger than what it is now. The strategy for it is just shooting your tower and hoping the blast goes around it and wipes everything. Most "top tier" expensive guns are good at what they're trying to do. Unfortunately there are not enough enemies on screen to support it. Making it just another easy way to win.
As for towers, all low tier ones are trash. You'd expect that right? But they're so bad it isn't even worth spending anything on them. ESPECIALLY when it costs the same amount to upgrade them as it would for a higher tier tower, which is made even more ridiculous by just how worthless they are after upgrades. It almost seems like the devs just threw in some different cool looking towers (same with guns) and just did not know what to do with them.
2) I think what's holding this game back is the lack of different enemies. Because at this point its just about how well the guns and towers can handle multiple enemies instead of say, how well they can do against enemies with special properties like fire, ice, etc. But beside that putting actual different enemies in the game like skeletons or something that have different health would at least change it up a bit. Make enemies weak or resistant to certain guns or status effects. The game at this state seems like a work in progress really.
3) Gamemodes. or the lack thereof. There are three levels. forest, graveyard, and island. island is the hardest because its small and there are tons of enemies. So much so that it is (probably) impossible to not take damage in the first wave, seeing as how you cant get that one shot gun instantly. Of course that's a seperate problem entirely. There are (sorry if im wrong i havent played the game super recently) around 7 waves per level. That is way too short. Of course there isn't any incentive to want to keep playing more than what there is because you already have the best stuff. So it would just be the same thing each and every wave. Which is why a survival gamemode would get kind of repetitive. There just is not enough RNG to keep you on your toes.
Maybe having a level select and a campaign-esque "story" mode where you play through each level on a file would make it a bit more diverse other than just picking a level and throwing you into it. Of course if there were like 10 levels or something i'd see this being a great idea. But three seems kind of short.
5) If the gameplay was fixed and everything to make it not super repetitive and monotonous, then a good way to improve it even further would be to have different skills to change up gameplay. Sort of like Tower of Guns where you can choose a single skill that stays with you for your entire playthrough. That way it would make each game seem less like the last one you played. Of course i'd say this happens after everything is fixed.
Although, I don't think this game ever really wanted to be something spectacular. Just a little hour  of fun for $4. But it could be so much more than that. I'll be waiting to see what happens to this game in the future.

Borderlands 2 was the first "real" PC game I played. The first story-based one that could be sort of considered AAA, anyway. Playing it on my Mac with integrated graphics, I only got 25 fps on a great day. But I played it and loved it, especially when playing it with my friends. Unfortunately, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel doesn't give me that same feeling I got from Borderlands 2. I couldn't even be bothered to get through it properly, because I didn't find enough to get me hooked.
The antagonist is terrible. Jack in Borderlands 2 was awesome, and he had a character to him that was really interesting. Zarpedon, however, just seems far too forced. Like "Oh, she's trying to blow up this moon, ♥♥♥♥ her, right?" Jack was funny, interesting, and a great character, but Zarpedon? Nah.
O2 doesn't do enough. Many people liked this feature, but I felt it didn't really add enough to the gameplay, and what it does just takes away from the rest of the game. The butt slam, for example, just feels a little overpowered, and makes gunplay less viable. O2 allows you to boost as well, but the only time this is useful is to butt slam or do some unnecessary forced platforming. Also, it's way too easy to get. The game warns you about running out of oxygen and suffocating, but since almost every enemy drops a refill for your O2, it seems like the suffocating is an arbitrary feature that just irritates you at inconvenient times.
The characters are less... character-y. In Borderlands 2, every character had a unique personality and playing with them felt personal and fun, but TPS's characters are boring to me. The ones worth playing for their personality would be Jack and Auralia, and they're both DLCS you pay for.
Speaking of money, this game is horribly overpriced. It's way easier and shorter than Borderlands 2, except for the end where the difficulty rises incredibly quickly. But other than that, the whole game isn't worth the price. Borderlands 2 costs less and gives you more.
However, it isn't all bad. The story is interesting, and provided some nice information into the lore of Borderlands, particularly into the past of Handsome Jack and some of the original Vault Hunters. Also, anti-gravity can be fun to play around with, and I like the verticality it adds to levels. Player Characters speaking is cool too.
TL;DR Poor characters, especially the antagonist, not enough new gameplay features, overpriced for the shorter story (20 - 25 hours compared to Borderlands 2 60+ hours).
Conclusion: If you are a serious die-hard Borderlands fan, I recommend giving this game a shot. But if not, only buy it on sale; it certainly is not worth full price. Standing alone, this is not a bad game, but Borderlands 2 set the bar high, and apparently 2k Australia couldn't make the jump.

I can't compare the game to Freespace or Freelancer as I haven't played those, but for a touchscreen-based game going to the big times with controller support, this is still pretty good.  And the controls are great, barring that you annoyingly need to use the mouse for shops and menus.
The game is somewhat open-world, though each of the planets has roughly the same features (space station with varying degrees of "tech level" which determines what equipment and ships are for sale, asteroid field with different materials, faction ships, pirates, sometimes a pirate space station, etc.), and there isn't much variety for missions (help defend area against pirates, escort large cargo ships, ferry people or materials to area, etc.), and the story is nothing special.  But it's still fun.  You mine asteroids or destroy/disable ships for their cargo to sell to stations for money to buy better ships and equipment, and there's a Skip button for all the story bits if you really want to go that far.
All ships have a number of stats, being how well-armored they are or how many primary weapons you can equip at once, and there is a lot of equipment choices, so there is a lot for customizing and agonizing over which equipment to take this mission.  Combat is fairly basic, with three-dimensional movement, optional boosting, instant braking, throttle control, and strafing, so you won't have anything fancy like somersaults to get behind the enemy, or rolls to deflect enemy fire.
I overall recommend the game if you want a light third-person space shooter game, though I would say buy it only at $10 or so, as $20 without the expansion content the mobile devices have is a bit steep.

Sacrilegious as it may be to say but I don't like Deus Ex (Original). While I have already the ire of many devoted fans, let me preface this review with some info:
-I love the idea of DX games, and I like Human Revolution and Mankind Divided. I appreciate the importance of DX but that doesn't mean it's perfect.

-A game from the early 2000s is going to ask more from the player. Some of these aspects I like, such as the lack of handholding, while others I detest because they are aggravating or pointless.
-The only mod I used is a launcher to use modern resolutions and FOV.
-I have finished this game once after three restarts to better understand the gameplay. What convinced me to give this a negative review is that the game's quality worsens after you arrive in Hong Kong. Talking about its impact became more interesting than playing it.
-My specific issue is how the game becomes more viable to use exploits like your sword than your tools. The lethal playstyles have never won me over with subpar FPS mechanics.
And before anyone suggests I should have installed an overhaul, I like to play old games as true-to-form as possible. The only exception I'll accept is adding free-aiming to DOOM. I enjoy understanding each game's strengths and weaknesses, and when it comes to DX I find the weaknesses can only be accepted if the game scratches your niche.
If you like to go into games blind to enjoy learning as you go, I would suggest you avoid that habit. If you want to ignore my advice, then play the first few missions over until you find what works best; however, don't plan playing non-lethally for your first run.
DX expects you to know what skills you should invest into and where you can find augment-canisters to get your abilities quick. What makes it particularly more annoying than other games is how the mechanics are constrained by your skills. Aim-reticules take far longer to line up if you move or are not trained in a specific weapon, which some of them are not as obvious without reading their details (ex. handling pistols improves crossbows.) As for the other skills, all they do is improve the efficiency of a certain skill either by decreasing the time spent or by improving how many tools you need to use for an obstacle.
There is a common joke how you should never invest into Swimming; the same could be said for many other skills: Hacking and Health beyond untrained, and you forgoing Explosives and Environmental Training. This is because certain augments provide the same bonuses without items to take up your limited inventory space. Unfortunately, augmentations have an annoying issue: You have to play "red-light-green-light" with them, which is far too cumbersome to manage for what are passive buffs like combat strength. (They should still use energy but only when in context.)
The worst problem is how it hampers non-lethal playstyles by the game's inconsistency. As much as I enjoy the versatile items from pepper-sprays to stun-rods to tranq-darts, it's obviously not as balanced in the late-game. For example, tranq-darts are not an automatic knock-out to the head; it's based on what skill-level you are for pistols, and for some enemies they are immune to your whole arsenal. Your only option is to avoid them. This wouldn't be a problem if the stealth system wasn't as simple as it is in this game, so you will be save-scumming far too often as compared to pulling out your sword (regardless of your skill) for a one-or-two-kill.
Trying to go guns-blazing also has its own problems. As mentioned beforehand, the augments have to enabled/disabled manually, which is defaulted to all F-number keys. Even if you rebound the keys the fighting would be too cumbersome to move, turn augments on-and-off, and aim properly, and the AI doesn't account for that amount of time. And choosing to use the pause menu to enable/disable breaks the pace. There is simply too much going on for action to make it a viable means with guns--but running around a sword is a sure-win tactic.
I emphasize that sword's importance because it's one of the many game-breaking aspects fans come to love about the game. I don't enjoy breaking a game's balance so it irritates me more than others. The point of this is that by the time I got to the end all I needed was a sniper with a silencer, a sword, a shotgun for robotic spiders, and grenades and other consumables. (Some are too specific like fire extinguishers.) The extraneous tools quickly became forgotten because they were less efficient, and seeing how many tools I passed over made me aware of how often the amount of diverging paths are also illusions of choice.
There is a section that best illustrates however mechanically diverse the game handles situations it's often an illusion of choice. During the third mission from UNACTO of finding Ambrosia, you sneak into the tunnels and stop at an impasse. To the right you can use a lock-pick to access the valve, and to the left you can use a multitools to turn off the lasers. (Or you can make a stair-case of mines to hop over the lasers.) Every option will lead to the same room.
That moment epitomizes various things. For one, the only differences between using a multitool and a lock pick is how many of each item do you have and what skill-level are you. Second, whenever the game offers you a choice—to spare or to kill, to choose one side or action over another, etc.—it will always bottleneck to the plot. Third, once you see past the facade it's evident how the game is a linear set of missions with variables to play with.
For the time, DX is impressive and should be noted for its innovation. My issue isn't that the game lies to you about the impact of your choices; it's how the mechanics are superficial paths with no challenge. Perhaps it's because I enjoyed the hacking mini-game of MD so much that the loading bar for hacking in DX made me longing for mechanical complexity with my tools.
I don't even mind the endings because they have never mattered in DX games; what matters are the effects of the accumulation of your moment-to-moment choices. This quality is still in the original, but the effect I find lacks the impact of other games where there was more variety in how going about an objective changed the game.


Of all the things that disappointed me the most is the storytelling. This isn't to say the writing quality is bad; in fact, it's good in spite of the more glaring issue, the voice-actors. I normally enjoy hammy actors but the dialogue is so monotone that I couldn't even enjoy the sillier elements like the Illuminati factoids. (Jensen is no Shakespearean actor but he's more lively than Stonewall Denton.) I felt more attached to reading the emails to give more background on characters than listening to them.
I don't hear many people bring up that issue of immersion for such a serious game of prophetic visions of the future. Maybe I could have felt more attached to the storyline had I been exposed to this game at a younger age when 9/11 was more relevant, but I will say the themes underlying the story are still terrifyingly relatable. That quality is timeless.
All of these criticisms are not to disillusion fans but to illustrate the flaws that are in this "perfect" game. As for those who say I don't get it, I don't think it's healthy to ignore issues with a beloved classic and then lambaste the modern takes for having unobtainable goals. All DX games have their flaws, some have a greater fall than others, but we can all cherish the core of DX.
If that doesn't extinguish any flame-wars, just remember one thing: "What good's an honest soldier if he can be ordered to behave like a terrorist?"

8th game in the Dark Parable series.  (The Dark Parables series does have an overall series story arch which this game references.  However, it is stand alone as it.)  I highly, even passionately, recommend this game.
Storyline: In 510AD the palace of the Alexandros, King of Prasino sunk beneath the ocean waves ending a decades long war with King Bluebeard of Kokkino.  Centuries later the palace rises from the ocean depths causing a tsunami and a lethal purple tide.  As the Fairy Tale Detective you have been tasked with discovering the reason for this occurance.  Upon arriving you free a mermaid, Althea, one of the former King Alexandros's 5 daughters, cursed by the Sea Goddess, Thalassa for the father's betrayal and imprisonment.  And meet a mysterious stranger who has the key to everything.  Find out why the palace rose again, break the mermaid's curse, free the Goddess, and stop the purple tide - all in a day's work for the Fairy Tale Detective.
Gameplay: A mixed combination of Hidden Object picture assembly, easy point and click, find and use inventory, and a variety of puzzles with a built-in strategy guide.  Nothing overly hard and the sheer variety of things to do makes the gameplay smooth and effortless.  The lock puzzles are logic "match" games and logic "mazes" (move a ball of energy from point A to point B without losing all the energy).  There are sliders, picture puzzles, recipe, assembly, and a Master Puzzle (which is a puzzle with many smaller puzzles included).  There is a skip option on the puzzles, and a hint feature.  Also the inventory is interactive in some cases when assembly or disassembly is required.
There is a interactive fast travel map which shows the location of things that need done and the chapter objective.  (One of the few maps I actually use.)
There are the 3 usual modes: casual, normal and hard.  Though this game has a custom mode feature which allows the player to pick and chose how much or how little "help" they wish to receive while playing.

Extra finds: 40 crescent moons, 20 morphing objects which are the parable story pieces, and 2 sets of "secret" extra finds - 6 teacups and 3 Big Fish Game Felix the Fish mascot.
The 5 Parables tell pieces of the story line, a bit of back story and three tell the fate of the mermaid sisters Naida, Calliope, and Theresa.  Which is pretty impressive considering each parable is only 4 pages long and about 100 words each.
Extras: Lots and Lots.  Bonus chapter which recalls the events just prior to the palace of Prasino disappearing beneath the ocean waves, and tells of Bluebeard, King of the rival Kingdom Kokkino.  An extra game called collectibles, where the player goes back through every scene in the game to find a single item or object (easy and fun).  Replay feature of all HO scenes and puzzles.  Plus wallpapers, music, video, etc.
Achievements: In-game only but there are Steam trading cards.  The achievements are fun too and not the usual find everything in less then a minute variety.  There is an achievement for idling, over-clicking and watching cutscenes.  There is even one for watching the credits, which are really worth reading since they are so funny.
So the big question: Is this game worth the price?  Yes, and well worth FULL price.  The game itself takes about 4-5 hours to play and all the extra gaming that can be done probably adds at least another 3-4 hours.  So an 8 hour HO game is well worth full price.  Big Fish Games is not known for putting their games on sale either, and this is less expensive then the price in their web store.

Tungulus is a post-modernist subtle psychological horror game about a young man known as the Protagonist. The Protagonist visits a party, but they need to set up. So, the Protagonist is sent down to his friend's basement (said friend is clearly stated as the owner of the property on which the party is taking place on) to retrieve supplies. As you begin Tungulus,  you are given all of this information through, what I dare say is a masterfully well done cinematic slide. Already, before the gameplay has even begun, you are shown the amount of raw effort that was put into this game. So, as you begin, you are in the first room of the basement. The player is then introduced to what I will refer to as "The Paperman" or as the game acknowledges "him", the notes you acquire throughout the game. The Paperman will give you your first note about a set of keys which will assist you in going deeper into the basement. This first gameplay segment acts as not only a perfect anti-characterization of The Paperman but also a ♥♥♥♥ing BEAUTIFUL introduction to the main setting that is "The Basement". As you obtain the key from the Paperman, you head to its corresponding door and open it, leading you down to find a strange picture reading "Kuplinov Play" with an image of a surprised mature man on the front. If you will search the term up on google, you shall find this is a russian youtuber, and surprisingly relevant to the story. Kuplinov Play is actually, the protagonist. Kuplinov is clearly a master at playing horror games, so the Protagonist's natural reaction to going into a dark and scary basement and meeting the Paperman is more logical. Now, if you go deeper into the stairs, you will find a box. For the rest of the game, you will be collecting the supplies in these boxes, until you come to find the Tungulus. the Tungulus is a pale, chubby white man with no clothes yet no genitalia. If you enter the room which you originally view him in from a window, he will have disappeared. You drug yourself and pass out after being chased by the Tungulus shortly after. Kuplinov is sent into a mental hospital, and in the asylum he sees...
The Paperman.
Tungulus' story takes up a large fraction of this review, which shows how amazingly detailed and well-designed the plotting is in this game. The story is most likely Tungulus' strongest point, which is a huge accomplishment, as everything else also shines. The gameplay is fantastic, giving new objectives and incentives whenever I found myself starting to lose interest. The gameplay in Tungulus is often noted as the "Same old, repetitive and clunky trope of cheap horror games" yet I believe it is incredible. The graphical presentation within Tungulus is mindblowing, and compares itself to such amazing works as Sonic Adventure and Bubsy 3D. The textures are very high quality, and look almost as if they could really be there. Overall, Tungulus is a fantastical game about the meaning of life and what you choose to make of it, and how you should always party like it's the last day on Earth.
Tungulus is a MASTERPIECE, 10/10.

Tungulus is a breath of fresh air in the horror genre. Rather than more basal forms of horror like the jumpscare or the chasing man, Tungulus strikes at you on a deeper, psychological level. It is also a duel of intellects, as it provides you with mind-wracking puzzles to tungle with. Tumulus also has perhaps one of the most masterful, suspenseful storylines I've ever seen in a horror game, with characterisation the likes of which I've not seen since "Bendy and the Ink Machine" (2017). The voice acting is emotive and powerful, and is without parallel in the gaming industry, and only barely finds competition in the domains of Hollywood and literature. Its graphics are both stupendous and eye-watering, and are as much a treat for the optical senses as they are for the mind. The present price of 50 cents is a severe undercharging for a masterpiece of this magnificence, and serves as a tribute to the generosity of wunderkind creator magnamengine that he is willing to share such breathtaking, exhilarating games with us at such a marked down price.
Throughout Tumnus, there is no pointless distraction gameplay such as combat or survival elements, and in fact it masterfully parodies such extraneous horror game moments with its lone lockpick crafting segment. I'll not tell you more, as I do not want to give you any spoilers. This is an experience best experienced firsthand and first-time.
Overall, Tumulus stands head, shoulders and ankles ahead of a genre overbloated with forgettables like Outlast and Resident Evil 7, and provides a sophisticated, sleek and superior option to all three.

Think Commandos meets Postal meets Hotline Miami meets Hitman. Kill off the entire party without getting spotted, and if you are, either quickly get away or change clothes (if you have 'em). Party Hard offers a gameplay that's mostly suited for those that are patient and aim for perfectionism. For the most part you cannot be impatient, as the game will surely strike your attempts down in one fell swoop. You need to survey the land, find choke points (quite literally) and exploit crowd behaviour if you want to be successful.
Party Hard is at its core a stealth game, where you have to go about various locations killing off everyone. You do this by stabbing them in the face when no one is watching, shoving people into barbeques, torture chambers or off the roof, or letting a bull go on a raging stampede through vast crowds. What tools you have at your disposal on each level is for the most part random, even though some are set pieces that will always be there. Some of the later levels -require- you to make most out of the extra equipment on the level, or otherwise you'll stand no chance.
On the negative side the game has the occasional bug, like cops getting stuck, people reappearing alive when you throw their corpses off the roof or someone spotting you through walls. If you get upset easily by cheap deaths, this will tear on your sanity. I had to reset levels as much as 10 or 15 times in a row because of random events that was out of my control. For the most part though, Party Hard delivers on the stealth aspect, and unlockable characters allows you to further expand on the premise. For instance, the ninja is hidden when standing still against a wall.
The soundtrack featured is well composed and suits the game well. The voice talent and story is complete garbage. However, you're not here for that.
You are here to Party Hard.

A 3D, mission-based game with open, non-linear space travel, very basic real-time combat and no real exploration.  Initially on iOS, the graphics have been beautifully updated for PC.  Unfortunately, we don't get the DLC that iOS has, which is a shame since the story is so short.
Sadly, the game quickly becomes very predictable and repetitive: every system has planets; every planet has an asteroid belt; every planet has a single station; every station has a shop to buy/sell equipment, ships and commodities, as well as a lounge to pick up random missions and buy the occasional rare blueprint or coordinates to a hidden system, which is effectively the same as all the others. There's nothing else of note to discover or explore.
You can outfit your ship with weapons, armor, shields, cargo space, tractor beam, cloaking device, afterburner, repair bot, jump drive etc.  With only a few tiers of each, variety is lacking.  Ships are small and underwhelming.  Most content is procedurally generated and travelling gets boring very quickly.  I only recommend this to lovers of space games, and just barely.

Ticket to Earth is one of if not the best Indie Games to come out this year.
It takes the RPG Puzzler to the next level. Seemingly simple but soon enough it will have to questioning your choices and re-evaluating the strategies you used to get past the first clutch of levels. You think you'll have it sorted out but TTE (ticket to earth) does extremely good job in subtly shaking things up.

Unlike other Puzzle RPGs where skill trees feel linear and included "just because that makes it an RPG" TTE manages to provide a skill tree that won't overwhelm the RPG newbie but gives more than enough freedom for the seasoned RPG player to build the characters the way they want. I should also note there this a wide range of abilities for each character and a nice selection of weapons that have sockets. So yes it's every bit an RPG as well as a puzzler.
Everything about this game has been meretriciously crafted. The characters are fun and engaging, the story is brilliant with dialog cut-scenes that you don't just want to breeze through by clicking skip. The artwork style pops and is instantly memorable, the sound design fits perfectly, the soundtrack is awesome and compliments the various stages of the game well. The UI is crisp and intuitive and at no point have I become frustrated with the UI in any way which is massive as I am a UI/UX nerd, heck even the way in which the tutorials are laid out and paced quickly gets you familiar with the game without initially overloading you with mechanics.
TL;DR - Ticket to Earth is brilliant and you should buy it, NOW!

I went in without any expectations and was impressed. This is NOT a total war or civilization reskin, it does new and interesting things while being more realistic than either.
Noble and Peasant happiness are separated. They are appeased differently and their rebellions behave differently. You can create noble and peasant units for free although upkeep costs apply. Conscripting huge peasant armies is easy, but long campaigns will take a toll your economy. Professional soldiers require money to train and equip, but they won't defect to the peasant rebels and won't make your farmers unhappy when you throw them against your neighbors. This isn't a total war game where peasant levies are happy to fight with you forever, employing them in large numbers is for short term conflicts and emergencies.
The happiness of your empire isn't something that is static. To begin with, dissatisfaction will naturally fluctuate a little on its own and differ from city to city. Next, random events such as natural disasters, eclipses or omens can cause large swings in mood, the negative effects of which can be mitigated with research. Furthermore, the authority of your leader may vary. Send him out to win victories and your people will be less inclined to rebel. Lose battles and your authority will decrease. If he dies in battle or old age, his successor will have a temporary penalty to authority. It’s even worse if your leader dies without an heir. Messy power struggles after a king’s death are common in history, so it’s nice that the game reflects this with its mechanics.
Rebellions aren't easy to deal with. Nobles are more likely to rebel further away from your capital, and armies with too many peasants will join peasant rebellions. Creating and moving professional armies around takes time. Entire cities can defect to rebels. The AI isn't immune to infighting; It's satisfying to watch a large rival split in two.
Edicts are handled cleverly too. You can order your nobles to keep horses to transform them from an infantry unit to a chariot unit, create a central bureaucracy, force peasants to use a new farming system for increased profits or recruit officers to reduce unhappiness in cities or grant a bonus to armies they lead. Passing one usually means angering nobles or farmers in the short term or permanently in addition to requiring gold per turn. Therefore they require a bit of thinking before using.
People looking for total war style battles will be disappointed, but that doesn't mean the combat has no depth. Using various unit types, tactics and the terrain matters.
Since it's difficult to control a huge number of cities on your own without rebellions, you'll need to create vassals and convice other factions to recognise you as Emperor to control the huge map of China.
This isn't a game where you paint the map your own color. Diplomacy is important and internal weakness is just as much of a threat as external factions.

Often considered the greatest game of all time, I came into the original Deus Ex with high expectations. I played entirely unmodded, wanting to see what the game was like all those years ago.
Probably the most important factor in the enjoyment of a game is gameplay, and Deus Ex delivers in this department. It does take some time to adjust to the somewhat clunky controls and mechanics of the game, but when it all finally clicks for you after some experimenting, you feel immensely rewarded. All it takes is to find a style of play you really enjoy, and there are many different styles. For example, the first mission provides you with an immediate choice of weapons: Rifle, Crossbow or GEP Gun. Then you are let loose to blast terrorists or sneak around, or any mix of the two. So many different choices in every level, it would take me a very long time to describe it here.
I don't want to spoil anything, because the story is one of the best I've experienced in gaming. But here is the basic premise: You are the newest agent in anti-terrorist organization UNATCO and are sent to stop a group of terrorists called the NSF from stealing a cure to a virus...
The story unfolds from there...
The graphics are quite dated but still functional. There should be no real issues here; gameplay and story is what matters. The main issue is facial animation for me, and I did get some texture clipping, but mods and other things likely fix this.
The atmosphere is great, I felt as though I was actually there. I don't, again, want to spoil anything; it's best if you experience it for yourself.
The soundtrack is truly excellent; a techno-beat to most of the music, and a little bit of jazz sprinkled in here and there; brilliant stuff. I listen to it outside of the game it's that excellent.
If you have never played Deus Ex, then what are you waiting for? At least say you gave it a fair go, and you will have been able to experience what was once the height of gaming, and now is relegated to perhaps a lesser position, but is still truly excellent.

This review covers up until the end of episode 2.
This is not a bad game but I would say its mechanics are not deep and leave the player wanting more. Especially if you are expected to be replaying maps constantly in the pursuit of money, nitrium, and upgrade tokens. You generally feel trapped in a very rigid attack plan. You get two turn tokens per round and will generally always move once and attack once. You need to move because thats how you generate the amount of damage you can inflict and also how you charge your moves. Maybe im missing a huge game mechanic but that is the main strategy for the entirety of the game and you will do little else. I found when i had trouble with a battle it was just because of luck of the tiles or an underpowered character (bad weapon or move set) rather than me needing to alter my strategies.
Also dont bother mining Nitrium (which is used to create buffs for your weapons) as the amount you need vs the amount you pick up from battles is unrealistic for any of the buffs worth having.
As for the story, i pretty much fell out of interest in episode 2 though i did follow closely in episode 1. You can skip the story entirely and be perfectly fine gameplay wize.
Otherwise this is a decent little puzzle rpg. Despite its flaws its still fun to pick up and play here and there.

[review edited because the original was hastily written for the 2016 Steam Awards season]
Note: They've made this a little bit clearer since launch, but you only get credit for your achievements if you earn them during a game played in "Ironman" mode (autosaved on a single save file).
I bought this game at launch at the suggestion of an excited friend. It was a bit of a gamble: I don't typically buy games at launch unless they're tied to a franchise that I already enjoy. I don't have a lot of experience with RTS or 4X-style games. I've played some Civilization, but I'm rarely in the mood for competitive multi. I picked Stellaris up hoping for a solid single-player experience. The game had a bit of a rocky reception. The mid-game was really lacking in content, but subsequent free updates helped fill in the gaps.
It can be frustrating; I don't really like having to learn by failing and starting a new file, but I guess that's the nature of strategy games. You have to feel out the effects of the starting ideologies, you have to feel out resource-management priorities, you have to feel out the diplomacy options, you have to feel out your military needs. I enjoy the "Character creation" portion at the beginning. There's a wide variety of playable species with diverse phylogenetic backgrounds (though admittedly I nearly always play as humans). You can customize your species with various physical characteristics that will have meaningful effects on your game (above-average strength makes for better mineral output and tougher armies, for example). You also define your empire's starting ideology, choosing to emphasize things like materialism vs spiritualism or your stance on how welcome alien cultures will be. These choices confer additional positives and negatives and unlock access to various policies and forms of government. You also choose the starting weapon types and method of interstellar travel.
My only other worthwhile strategy experience comes from Civilization, and just as with that game I don't aim for conquest victories. Unfortunately, no matter what your strategy is, you have to build your military as though conquest was your primary goal. You might not get attacked by other empires often (especially on easier settings), but it happens, and if you haven't carefully balanced the strength and size of your fleet throughout your entire game, you may as well just start over.
I play for the exploration and expansion elements, and I enjoy the military component when applied against non-empire opponents. The custom mode I've enjoyed the most is to set a minimal number of rival empires and hope that they're placed far away from me so that I can enjoy the aspects of the game that don't revolve around border friction & opposing ideologies. If you're more interesting in interacting with your neighbors, there are systems in place for diplomacy, trading, and federations.
Exploration involves sending a science vessel into a neighboring star system to survey and catalog the celestial bodies. At the beginning of the game, you can view the full galaxy map to see the location of all the star systems and nebulae, but there is a sort of fog-of-war across all areas that your empire has yet to explore. Surveying new star systems will sometimes reveal natural resources, potentially-habitable planets, or anomalies which function as brief quests. These anomalies typically don't require much action or challenge beyond allocating one of your scientists for a period of time, but there are tons of anomalies to discover and only so many of them will appear in each playthrough.
A fairly tiny percentage of the galaxy's planets will be habitable by any species. There are nine standard biomes for habitable planets, and you begin the game only able to colonize planets that match your home world. In order to colonize other types of worlds, you'll need to research new technology and incorporate other species.
The borders of your empire are not limited to your inhabited planets. Your field of influence will reach out into other star systems as your population grows. You are only able to mine resources within your borders, which is a big part of why finding and colonizing new planets is so important.
Expansion brings its own set of drawbacks. Increasing the empire's population and number of planets owned will increase the maximum number of vessels you can have in your navy, but it will also hamper the speed of your scientific research. Increasing the size of your navy is important for survival, but every ship you own is a drain on your resources.
Ship customization can be a lot of fun, but it can also be frustrating and repetitive when it's time to upgrade. There are several different classes of ship, and you can design multiple sets of blueprints for each class, making use of the different offensive and defensive technologies you develop. Combat is a little disappointing to me. When one of your fleets engages an enemy, you lose control of the ships and the combat occurs automatically.
There is more depth than I can describe in a Steam review. There are customization options, leader characters, special resources, tradition bonus trees, unique buildings, and that isn't even counting the additions in the paid DLC. As of this writing, I haven't bought any of the DLC; it seems weird to pay for patches for a game that was so lacking in content at launch time. I'm told that this is just how Paradox operates, and if that's true, I have plenty of other games in my library already.
If you like the music in the trailers, get the soundtrack, even if you don't get the game. I'm not a big fan of the few tracks with lyrics, but even without those there's about two and a half hours of solid space tunes.

As a youtube comment somewhere so aptly put it, “Came for the booty, ended up crying.”
God, what can I say about this amazing game that would do it justice?
A Masterpiece, that’s what NieR:Automata is. A work of art that thoroughly drew me in, gripped my heart, filled me with joy and stabbed me with pain. Like a good book I felt I could hardly pause to catch a breath. I wanted to see the next part, wanted to feel the exhilaration of the next battle, wanted to-, no, needed to know what was to become of the characters I held so dear.
Even the pain was precious, because it meant something, it was real, it was deep, it was important, it was… I’m not sure….
All I know is that I have 198 games in my steam library, and have played countless others on consoles and PC over the years. I’m a pretty dedicated gamer. Games come in all shapes and sizes, from shooters to top down strategy, and It’s hard to compare apples and oranges, so in the interest of accuracy I’ll say this:
NieR:Atomata is the best action RPG I’ve ever played.
If you want an in depth description of game mechanics and play style I’m sure there are other reviews and videos better suited to providing you with this information, but I’ll go over the basics real quick:
Combat: A satisfying hack and slash system with a high skill cap which fluidly changes from 3D, to sidescroller, to top down depending on the situation. A wide variety of melee weapons as well as several range options can be employed throughout the game. Also included are arcade style bullet hell sequences both in 3D and 2D
Visuals: I’m sure you can see for yourself how good this game looks from a glance, but I should also note the special effects, character animations, designs and environments are very well done and interesting.
Music: I’m not one who usually pays too much attention to game music, but the ones in NieR really captivate and accentuate the atmosphere of each location and situation so perfectly that I must make a note of how exceptional they are. This was also a big factor in how emotional the experience was.
Story: If it wasn’t clear from my earlier rant, this is the reason the game is so important to me. To steal the wording of another review I’ve read, NieR is never content to show you something interesting and then rest on its laurels. It gives you one new wonder after another, slowly drawing you into the game’s world and its inhabitant’s lives. A sense of urgency and desire drives you forward, and the unexpected twists and turns will send you reeling, trying to catch your balance as you’re thrown headlong into the thick of it again and again.
Maybe I’m getting more emotional as I get older, but I don’t think I’ve ever legitimately cried because of a game before. Shed a couple tears, sure, but broke down completely… not until NieR.
I give NeiR:Automata a 10 out of 10.
For perspective, in my gaming career I’ve only given 3 games a 10.

UPDATE: I retract a lot of the positive statements that I made about this game being microtransaction-free.. I won't support games that release DLC containing content that players should've been able to unlock by simply playing the game. Also, I haven't played Nier Automata in while because I got all the main endings already.. and because of them I've felt no desire to touch the game again. Most of the endings were not my cup of tea.  This game's replay value has a limit and I reached it after 40plus hours.. Not bad, I'd say, but I think the main endings kinda killed the game for me.
It's still a good game, but I dislike it now, more so than before.
Take note, all you other game developers out there! This game came with multiple endings, weapons, side quests, and none of those things cost us anything extra. Just for that alone, I'd recommend this game for everyone. This game's music is on fleek. The gameplay is solid.. It's not the deepest hack n' slash game ever but it's still fun and because it's pretty simple, I'd say even someone who's new to games like this wouldn't have too hard a time picking it up. There are a lot of little subtle details and things in the game to pick up on and notice that help drive the story.. and speaking of the story; it's awesome too, their are multiple endings, and the storytelling is really nice. The only gripes I have about the game are that the combat was too simple for me; I was really hoping it would be like Bayonetta or DMC, and the full screen bug still has yet to be resolved. - It's not gamebreaking but it does kinda suck if you want to 1080p fullscreen your experience.
And because you want more games to come out  where all the content is included and accessible without any external costs, you should support this game and it's developers.

A potentially interesting premise; shame about the lazy-arsed execution.
No menu options and an incoherently written opening blurb...not the best of starts. We then take a while to load up to mediocre graphics, sub-standard sound effects, and adequately spooky music before settling into a routine of running such ridiculous errands as gathering three large boxes in order to construct a single "lockpick" (which, upon production, looks suspiciously like a bog-standard KEY).
Then there's an electrical puzzle so bafflingly designed that I nearly gave up right there and then, swiftly followed by a number code puzzle which you'd be completely ♥♥♥♥ed for if you didn't write down a four-digit number from a note in the previous load area...which you can, of course, no longer access. (Luckily I've been screwed in other games, and always keep a pen and paper handy at all times. Like a friggin' boy scout, I tell ya.)
And that's about it, really, apart from a crappy "chase" sequence which lasts all of one corridor and about seven seconds. And no, you DON'T get those precious fifteen to twenty minutes of your life back at the end of it all (though I guess you could always request a refund; lucky for the snake oil salesmen of the world, that just ain't my style). There's a couple of mildly creepy moments, maybe, but nothing which remotely justifies the $1.19 which I paid for it (on sale, no less).
Sigh. At least it wasn't made on GameGuru, I guess. Hail Satan for small mercies.

Magicka 2 has a spell system that invokes a large variety of spells (such as significantly less lasers as arcane is now beneath most other spell types) but I honestly think the original Magicka offers better spell choice, as well as a better level of difficulty. While Magicka 2 introduced a lot of limitations and lowered the difficulty to match, the entire game ended up feeling like a bit of a tutorial, albiet still very fun. Magicka 1 has a low skill floor and more powerful spells but a harder game to match, and the difficulty of the situation just gradually rises. Whenever you encounter a wall, it doesn't take long to either get better or just get lucky and move along, the difficulty walls aren't very high, there's just a lot of them. Even once you think you've totally mastered the game and can run it with your eyes closed, the DLCs could give you a run for your money. If not, you can activate challenge mode on most of them and start eating your words there instead.
Also, the spellcasting system is pretty much a mini-game in and of itself, watching the various kinds of spells form, that you play while also avoiding enemies and progressing through the main game. Game Within A Game award nominee.

I load into a basement and walk into a room with a simple desk, drawers, a cardboard box with some boots on it, a cupboard, note and some keys. I hit escape because the resolution is wrong, but there are no options. None at all. Whatever resolution it gave me, I'm stuck with.
Okay, nevermind. I try to interact with the less obvious things. What's in the drawers? Nope can't interact. The cupboard? The desk? This cardboard box? Can I pick up this random pair of boots? No, okay... I can literally just read the note and then the keys are picked up automatically. The game has a lot of props (many of which are repeated, the boots will return later and there's a pizza box in almost every room!) but almost nothing is interactable with - just a couple of objects and doors in the entire game.
"The entire game" isn't saying a lot, since it took me 15 minutes to complete it. It has two "puzzles" I suppose, both of which are inanely easy and simply require you to read something and then follow the instructions. There is an extra layer of challenge in the fact that if you miss the instructions for the first one, you'll have to restart the game since it's past a loading screen and you can't go backwards.
design.
It's supposed to be a horror (or at least a thriller) game, and it does have some spooky effects - but the story doesn't really make any sense and I didn't even feel a slight chill or sense of apprehension for the playthrough. My friends can tell you that I will jump out of my skin at an unexpected sound when in a call with someone and I frequently get trolled by them deliberately trying to spook me. I'm a nervous person and usually find horror games very mentally taxing, but there simply wasn't any sense of atmosphere here at all. I would be okay with my son playing this game, even a child isn't going to find it scary.
I didn't hate my 15 minutes of playtime and the price is cheap, just £1 on release day, but I have to think did I enjoy myself? Not really. I kept waiting for something interesting to happen, and then the game was over. The game feels like a concept demo for something. Perhaps something a new developer might put on their portfolio when applying for a job, released as a free game to get some constructive feedback. There are no steam achievements, but there are steam trading cards. You will have to idle the game for ~4 hours to get them though, as there is zero replayability.

When I was a child, before I knew that computers were the key to the universe, I used to climb up into my dad's chair and play the classic, the only, the original—that's right, Minesweeper. Of course, at such a tender age I had no clue what I was doing. I clicked random squares and there were numbers and I could put flags down if I wanted to, but they didn't seem to actually change anything because sometimes I lost and sometimes I won, but I wasn't quite sure what caused it to go either way. And then I typically got kicked off of the computer anyways.
Hexcells is a game that will take you back to the days when Minesweeper was the only game that the school computers could run. It's an updated version of a classic strategy game with a bit of added style: you play with hexagons instead of squares. The board starts with an oddly shaped field made of orange hexagons. Mines are marked by left-clicking a hexagon, turning it blue. Hexagons are revealed by right-clicking, showing the number underneath if you click correctly and shaking the piece and adding a tally mark to your mistake count if you're too hasty in your decisions.
Unlike the original Minesweeper, Hexcells adds more complex features as the player advances further in its six sets of levels. Soon the board will be marked with various clues. Symbols mark whether or not the mines surrounding a hexagon are grouped together or spread out and how many mines are in a column on a board. These clues are cleverly used in each level to prevent players from reaching the frustrating Minesweeper stalemate: the point in the game where you are forced to rely on chance and click a random piece in order to continue to advance.
The downside to Hexcell's logic-friendly gameplay is its inability to randomly generate levels (at least, in the original Hexcells—more on that in a few seconds). Each level is hand-crafted to prevent players from getting stuck, which means that when you run out of puzzles, well, you run out of puzzles. However, for the cheap price point Hexcells provides a good few hours of entertainment, particularly if you're already fond of Minesweeper or enjoy puzzle games in general. In addition, Hexcells also offers a purchasable expansion called Hexcells Plus, as well as the inexhaustible Hexcells Infinite, which includes a rather effective level generator and the ability to play user-generated content. As such, the Hexcells Complete Pack is a cheap must buy for all puzzle aficionados.

Wow, this is awful. Like, seriously awful.
I should preface this by saying that I bought this game for 10 cents because of a coupon I earned from crafting badges, but it's not even worth 10 cents of your money, so don't bother.
First of all, the game's name is 'Magazime Editor'. Seriously? How little of a damn did the creators give? Baffling.
When you start playing, it doesn't tell you what to do. It doesn't explain which button does what, it doesn't tell you what each icon represents (though it is pretty easy to figure out, it will likely take you a few mistakes to understand which means which, especially since random ones you haven't encountered yet will pop up out of nowhere to ruin your life.) This would be forgivable except for the fact that everything else about this game is terrible.
The gameplay is just straight-up boring. I've played countless free mobile games infinitely more fun and complex than this. The music is fine, I gues. The art style is FINE, I guess. There's nothing visually interesting about it. There is nothing for you to look at other than your journalists leaving their spots, that stack of papers piling up as you accept or reject, and the guy at the desk violently vibrating on occasion....
You hit a button to either accept or reject articles. That's it, seriously. As you progress through the levels, you get more journalists, and you need to accept or reject the articles more quickly. That is the extent of the gameplay here, although I may be wrong since LEVEL 6 IS BROKEN AND YOU *CANNOT* COMPLETE IT.
I slogged through accepting/rejecting over 100 articles respectively on Level 6, annnnd guess what? Nothing! The piles on the floor in front of the desk covered up part of the number counts eventually, so I didn't even have THAT to keep track of. There's not even any point in buying this trash for the achievements, since you literally cannot complete them past Level 6 due to this game-breaking bug. Apparently this has been going on for a long time and has yet to be fixed, so I doubt that it ever will be. Not to mention that once you fail a level, you have to start over from the very beginning.

It's not like I was expecting some sort of hidden gem or masterpiece of a game from this, but I at least wanted to complete it for its achievements. Now I can't even do that, and this is just a stain on my account for the rest of eternity.

Set in a far-future offworld colony, the game sees the protagonist Rose fight mutant alien lifeforms, a robot uprising and other threats together with three other team members. Characters can perform two actions per turn, which are usually a mix of movement orders and ranged or melee attacks.
The turn-based tactical combat is complemented with tile-matching puzzle elements, as Rose and her enemies have to traverse floor tiles of matching colors to move and charge their combat powers. It has a nice story mode progression and maybe slightly different than your used to with RPG strategy games. Some good pros and solid cons
PRO
A: It is not just move and effect. There is a method to it's madness that can be appealing
B: It sets the main action in Ticket to Earth takes place on an isometric grid of coloured squares that resembles a 1970’s disco. Annoying to some, but the kids loved it.
C: In addition, the more tiles you travel over the more damage your next attack will inflict. However, whenever you are hit you not only lose health, but also some of your attack power. Being aware of each power invests your attention.
D: Floor tiles come in four different colours, which relate to four combat powers. An interesting take on tactical puzzling.
E: The numerous plot threads are genuinely interesting and recounted through some superb sci-fi comic strip style artwork
G: Good solid music
F: It is well balanced and intriguing in the power selection process.
CONS
A: Like most Isometric games you seemed boxed in to the redundant battle system that can get dull to serious strategy lovers, but the kids really enjoy it.
B: It's creative strength is also its weakness.  It could be argued that when you pay a premium price you expect to have the full game, BUT at its current price fits its short run. Instead of a full game, you get episodes that may take too long to come out to keep you invested. I would wait till most are released to purchase, but if you cannot wait, Catch the game at the huge sales, like I did in the June sale for a few dollars.
C: The character's can tend to drab on which you could lose important steps. For example, I did not know about the side missions till I was halfway through the game.
D; The game does not go beyond its template so it can be redudant in the same battle theme instead unlocking tactical choices. It has no real party team possibilities either. It is not Xcom or Disgaea, Its one dimensional in its approuch strategically.
E: The game should be much more than it gives you
OVERALL: I love the numerous plot threads are genuinely interesting and recounted through some superb sci-fi comic strip style artwork and there has obviously been a lot of time, effort and love put into Ticket to Earth. However it may not be appealing to everyone. It has to be subjective. Some gamers maybe turned off by it's short total time or comic look.
Ticket to Earth is the start of something. I can see it evolve into a more complex tactical game with massive armies instead of one leader point perspective, it can become Disgaea. However, it is limited by its presentation. I give it thumbs up for effort and it's delivery of an openning salvo. Go to the discussion, see VIDEO of the game prior to purchasing it and get it on sale if you can or wait till more episodes come out before you invest. To me this is not a game to rush to buy despite developers hopes, but a nice start. MY SCORE 2.7 out of 5

Great addictive game.  If you want to sink 100+ hours into a game this is a solid choice.  Paradox has also done a great job at providing new updates to consistently make the game better with UI improvements, combat balance/tweeking, additional music, refined graphics, and a plethora of balance and content improvements.
It feels a lot like playing Star Trek.  You start by exploring the galaxy and inhabiting new worlds.  You meet alien life and choose how you want to interact with them.  The options for leading and creating your space faring empire are numerous and varied.  You can be friendly, forming aliences and creating lasting friendships through trade, free migration, and eventually form the greatest federation the galaxy has seen.  Or you can crush the weaker empires around you enslaving and purging undesirables and putting down rebellions with an iron fist.
The downside is the victory conditions are extremely long and tedious to achieve.  This is only worsened in the late game when all the territory in a galaxy has been occupied and the only way to expand further is through war or forming federations.  The issue with war expansions is that it takes many wars to completely absorb a competing empire's territory and you have to wait a long time between each war before going back to war (it usually takes 1-2 wars to completely absorb or vassalize a smaller empire and can take 3-5+ for larger empires).  The issue with forming a federation is that you lose the ability to go to war when you want to and are subject to the whims of your federation allies.
All that said, it's an excellent game with engaging in game events that always gives you something to work on.  The empire creation system allows for enough customization that you will probably never have a chance to try everything.
If you like sci-fi, strategy, empire building and have the patience to learn a somewhat heavy game (though I hear this is much lighter than Paradox's other titles such as Crusader Kings or Europa Universalis it is definitely more complicated than Civ) I would highly recommend Stellaris.

I fell upon this game and I was rapidly seduced by the concept.
There's one thing I particularly like.
As a big fan of the Civilization franchise, which I play since Civ 2 (you'll see why I speak about another game), I was a bit doubtful about the gameplay changes in Civ V (one unit by hex), even if they are very interesting.
We can't ask Civ to have a welfare like Total War on the other hand, let's be realistic.
But I wanted something more sophisticated, and it's exactly what is implemented in Oriental Empires.
On an hex, there can be an army of maximum 8 units, which can be different, with different formations... So there can be real Total War-like combats inserted in a global Civilization-like 4X gameplay concept. Of course it doesn't match graphically with the huge battle you can see in the TW of the last decade, but there is a real deep strategy, good graphisms, and it's more realistic to prepare your plan during the turn and then to see how everything happens (like in an old game called 'Legion', if you know it, same thing, 8 units an army, and you prepare your formation before the battle), so it's even more realistic than a Total War where you have omniscient powers at every second over every regiment (reminds what Tolstoy writes in War and Peace about the Napoleonian Wars : generals prepare plans before the battle, but the latter happens rarely as planned, orders arrive always too late during it, etc).
So besides that, the game is focused on China, with every faction having its special abilities, well, normal.
There is a manual, everything is explained.
On a darker side, I hope the developpers will see this little complaint, there is little choice about the key bindings, maybe mods will allow a more satisfying game experience. For exemple, I'm used in every strategy game to go east on a map by putting the cursor along the right of the screen, and in the options you can chose whether it happens or not, to match the different habitudes of the different players.
In this game, there is for now no possibility to assign key bindings to open windows, very little options you can chose to put on or off. And for example, to move on the map, you have to click left and to move the mouse, which is a bit unusual to me, and to every Civilization player who would be used to move on the map like I do. It's a little example, but I think the developers should allow more possibilities of key bindings and other practical options to match more to the different ways to play a 4X game.
So to conclud I recommend this game, moreover it's not very expensive, this first week it has 20% sale, so a cost of 23€, barely twice the price of a DLC of Civ VI bringing two civs and one scenario... And even the global price, 30€, is half the price of the biggest licenses of strategy the day of the release of a vanilla, so it does seem a good idea for the fans of these kinds of games to try this 4X turned toward China and with a touch of Total War !
